Anaesthesia and EEG – learning tool

About the app

The brain as the target organ during anaesthesia: components, spectrogram, drugs, perfusion and intensive care.

Created by Heidi Leona Porskrog-Mjelde, nurse anaesthetist (Akershus University Hospital and USN), and Anders Aasheim, nurse anaesthetist and PhD candidate (University of Oslo and Oslo University Hospital).

View:
Spectrogram (schematic)

A learning tool for anaesthesia staff about what general anaesthesia consists of, how the brain responds to it, and what the EEG and spectrogram actually show. Nine in ten cards state their source; where the sources disagree, it says so.

About EEG indices: BIS, PSI and qCON are all EEG indices. That is not in the names, so it is said outright here: the number is not a separate measurement alongside the EEG, it is a summary of the same frontal EEG signal you see as raw EEG and spectrogram. An algorithm weighs several features of the signal into a single number, and much information is lost on the way from waveform to number. The index is a number that an algorithm calculates from frontal EEG. It has many sources of error, including EMG, noise, neuromuscular blockers, ketamine, nitrous oxide, age and seizures, and can be wrong in both directions. Read the raw EEG and spectrogram. Where studies in the app used an index as a tool, the findings are included, and it is worth remembering what the number is built on.

The index is not worthless. It has been shown to reduce the risk of awareness compared with clinical signs alone, but the evidence is uncertain, and against end-tidal anaesthetic gas no difference has been shown. The point is therefore not that the number should be ignored, but that it cannot stand alone.Source: Lewis et al. 2019 (Cochrane). The figures are in the Sources tab.

The content in numbers

About this tool: what, for whom and on what basis

Who made the app. Heidi Leona Porskrog-Mjelde, nurse anaesthetist (Akershus University Hospital and University of South-Eastern Norway), with Anders Aasheim, nurse anaesthetist and PhD candidate (University of Oslo and Oslo University Hospital), as co-author. The content has been compiled and written as an independent learning project.

What it is. An interactive learning tool about general anaesthesia and the brain as the target organ: which components a general anaesthetic consists of, how they can be assessed, and what the EEG and spectrogram look like under different drugs, at different ages and with changes in cerebral perfusion. The tabs cover the components (consciousness, memory, nociception, immobility and autonomic stability), a schematic spectrogram simulator, the effects of drugs on consciousness and memory, perfusion and positioning, sedation in intensive care, burst suppression, a quiz and a combined list of sources.

Who it is for. Nurse anaesthetists and anaesthetists, for teaching and self-study. It assumes basic knowledge of anaesthesia and is designed to give a shared vocabulary and a precise relationship to what the sources actually show. It is not a clinical guideline and gives no dosing advice.

What it is based on. The main sources are twelve chapters of Miller's Anesthesia, 10th edition (2025), each written by its own authors and cited by author name (see Sources), Morgan and Mikhail (2022, chapters 8, 9 and 43) for comparison, and Lobo and Lamperti (2025) on EEG during anaesthesia, supplemented by peer-reviewed original articles and reviews listed in the Sources tab. The claims are tagged with their source. Where the chapters build on original studies, these are listed under “Original references in Miller's”. Miller's Anesthesia is a widely used textbook in anaesthesia. The 10th edition has a new chapter on the brain’s response to anaesthesia and surgery (Sleigh, Gaskell and Hight: “Monitoring the Brain’s Response to Anesthesia and Surgery”). As far as the author knows, no other textbook covers this development as fully. According to the author, the book is also recommended in the Safe Brain Initiative (SBI) and EEG bootcamp community.

Interpretation based on the sources. Some points are marked “interpretation based on the sources”. This means that the conclusion is not stated in any single source, but is drawn by combining findings from several sources or by applying them to a clinical situation the sources have not studied. Such points should be read as reasonable inferences, not as documented knowledge. Reflections and clinical cases from the author are marked separately.

What it is not. The spectrograms in the simulator are schematic models built on the descriptions in the sources, not recordings from patients. Where the sources disagree, or where articles contain internal discrepancies, this has been collected under “Discrepancies and disagreements between sources” in the Sources tab rather than smoothed over. Check the original sources before the content is used in teaching.

Independence. This is not product information. The app is product-neutral and recommends no monitors. Product names appear only where a study or clinical case measured with a specific device, because the index values then belong to that device, and in the conflicts of interest declared by the authors of the sources. No manufacturer or supplier has had any influence on the content. Conflicts of interest declared by the authors of the sources themselves are reproduced where they are relevant. Anders Aasheim is a co-author of the app and at the same time an author of some of the studies discussed; this is stated on the cards concerned.

About the author and independence. The app was made by a nurse anaesthetist in her spare time, with her own funds and her own equipment. It was made without funding from or influence by an employer, educational institution, manufacturers or suppliers. Affiliations are given to show the authors’ background; the institutions have not funded the content. The author has experience in training others to use medical equipment, including EEG monitors. The app is product-neutral and recommends no monitors.

Feedback or requests for missing content: heidimjelde@hotmail.com. Last updated: 3 November 2026.

Components: what general anaesthesia consists of

The goal of general anaesthesia is that the patient should tolerate the trauma that surgery is, and lie still enough for the procedure to be carried out. The components are the way there: loss of consciousness, amnesia, blunting of nociception and immobility, with physiological stability around them. They are affected differently by different drugs, so each must be assessed separately. Start with the concepts below: consciousness and amnesia are not the same thing.

The brain: the regions that are the target organ

General anaesthesia has several components, which is why “depth of anaesthesia” is an imprecise term

General anaesthesia is not one state that becomes deeper or lighter. It is several effects that the drugs produce at the same time, and that can be assessed separately.

ComponentWhat it means
Unconsciousness (hypnosis)The patient experiences nothing.
AmnesiaThe patient does not remember what happens.
Analgesia and reduced nociceptionThe body and brain react less to surgical stimulation.
Akinesia (immobility)The patient does not move in response to painful stimulation.
Physiological stabilityCirculation, breathing, autonomic functions and temperature are kept stable.

Sources: Brown 2010; Sleigh et al. 2025

More components than the four. Sleigh et al. 2025 also count hyperalgesia, neuronal apoptosis, stress responses and immunosuppression among the things anaesthesia should prevent, and the editorial Sleigh 2011 replaces the depth metaphor with a fuse box of seven questions, two of which are postsurgical hyperalgesic responses and immune-inflammatory responses (). In the list above, the stress response belongs under physiological stability and reduced nociception: an unconscious patient can still develop tachycardia, hypertension and hormone release. Hyperalgesia is a consequence rather than a component, and it goes both ways: too little suppression of nociception gives central sensitisation, while the opioids themselves can increase pain sensitivity, particularly remifentanil at high doses and on abrupt cessation. See and .

Why a single measure of “depth” falls short:

  • The components appear at different doses. With volatile agents, memory disappears at approx. 0.25 MAC and consciousness at approx. 0.3–0.5 MAC. 1 MAC prevents movement in half of patients, and burst suppression only appears above approx. 1.3–1.4 MAC. With propofol, half stop responding at 2.3–3.5 µg/ml and burst suppression appears at approx. 5 µg/ml, whereas 15–16 µg/ml is needed to prevent movement at incision.Sources: Perouansky et al. 2025; Vuyk et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025; Pilge 2014
  • The components sit in different parts of the nervous system. Consciousness and memory are brain functions. Immobility under volatile agents arises mainly in the spinal cord. Movement, autonomic responses and brain arousal on stimulation do not closely follow each other.Sources: Perouansky et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025
  • The drugs affect the components differently. Opioids dampen the response to stimulation but change the EEG little and do not produce full unconsciousness. Neuromuscular blocking agents produce immobility without affecting consciousness.Sources: Kim et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025
  • The same patient can be “deep” and “light” at the same time. Under propofol, the brain can be in burst suppression while the patient still moves at incision. Under neuromuscular blockade, the patient can be conscious without moving: in studies using the isolated forearm technique, about one in three responded to command.Sources: Sleigh et al. 2025; Linassi 2018
  • The textbooks themselves warn against the term. A single measure of depth of anaesthesia is considered an inadequate simplification that leads to many errors. An alternative is to ask whether each system has been switched off, instead of whether the depth is right.Sources: Sleigh et al. 2025; Sleigh 2011
  • The Norwegian standard uses the term without further specification. It says that “monitoring of anaesthesia depth (e.g., BIS and EEG) must be individually considered”, but not which component of anaesthesia is meant. At the same time, consciousness and muscle relaxation are named separately: consciousness is to be assessed with clinical signs, and neuromuscular monitoring (for example TOF) is required with non-depolarising muscle relaxants.Source: Leonardsen 2024 (Norwegian standard for anaesthesia)
  • The EEG answers some of the questions, not all. The EEG measures the brain. It says most about consciousness and memory, and can also show that the brain reacts to noxious stimulation (see Analgesia and nociception below). Movement and circulation must be assessed separately.Sources: Sleigh 2011; García 2021; Sleigh et al. 2025

What it means in practice (interpretation based on the sources): Ask instead which component you are assessing. Is the patient unconscious? Is the response to stimulation dampened? Is the patient lying still? Is the circulation stable? Each question has its own answer and its own signs.

Assess each component separately

  • Consciousness, responsiveness and recall are different things. A patient can experience a command without being able to respond, for example under neuromuscular blockade. Amnesia does not mean that consciousness is lost.See and “1. Patient receives low-dose propofol, talks coherently, and remembers nothing afterwards.”
  • Connected consciousness without recall occurs. IFT responses are rarely followed by explicit recall. Frontal alpha–delta does not rule out connected consciousness. The feared complication is awareness with recall (AWR).See and “2. Patient under neuromuscular blockade with frontal alpha–delta squeezes the hand on command (isolated forearm) but remembers nothing.”
  • No drug covers every component equally well. Different concentrations are needed for consciousness, amnesia, pain and immobility. Combinations change the figures considerably, especially opioid with hypnotics. Opioids, for example, do not produce complete loss of consciousness.See
  • Propofol produces burst suppression long before immobility. Half of patients stop responding to speech at 2.3–3.5 µg/ml, and burst suppression appears at about 5 µg/ml. Propofol alone needs 15–16 µg/ml to prevent movement at incision. During TIVA, immobility therefore most often comes from opioid (lowers the propofol requirement at incision by about 80 %) or from neuromuscular blocking agents.See
  • With volatile agents, immobility comes before burst suppression. Consciousness is lost at about 0.3–0.5 MAC, and 1 MAC prevents movement in half of patients. Burst suppression only appears above about 1.3–1.4 MAC. Immobility arises mainly in the spinal cord.See
  • Movement is not a measure of hypnosis. Burst suppression probably rules out responsiveness (few observations), but does not say that the patient lies still under propofol. Increasing propofol until the patient lies still may give unnecessarily deep hypnosis. The EEG says something about the effect on the brain, whereas movement mostly reflects the spinal cord and the nociceptive balance (interpretation based on the sources).See and “6. Deep anaesthesia with burst suppression and no response.”

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

Concepts that are often confused

ConsciousnessSubjective experience. It can be connected (experience of the surroundings, for example surgery) or disconnected (experience that is independent of the surroundings, for example a dream). Mashour and Pryor 2025
ResponsivenessThe ability to respond to stimuli. A patient can experience a command without being able to respond, for example when neuromuscular blocking agents have been given. Mashour and Pryor 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025
Recall and amnesiaRecall is when an experience becomes a lasting, explicit memory. Amnesia is failure of the memory processes. It is not the same as consciousness being absent. Mashour and Pryor 2025

Clinically we often use “awareness” for consciousness and recall together. This is imprecise, because the two can be separated from each other.Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025

Four combinations

No recall afterwardsExplicit recall afterwards
No consciousness during the procedureNormal general anaesthesiaContested, see below
Connected consciousnessHappens. For example IFT response without recallAwareness with recall (AWR)
Can you remember something you were not conscious of? The sources do not fully agree. An explicit memory in principle presupposes that something was experienced consciously. At the same time, it is allowed that AWR can occasionally occur without conscious experience at the time. The question is hard to settle, because a brief conscious period during anaesthesia cannot always be detected at the time, particularly when the patient is paralysed (interpretation based on the sources). Two other distinctions are better documented: consciousness without recall (the patient squeezes a hand on command but does not remember it afterwards), and implicit memory without conscious recall. The latter was found in 36% of cohorts in a meta-analysis.Sources: Mashour and Pryor 2025 and Sleigh et al. 2025 (fig. 36.1); Linassi 2021

Which components do the different drugs affect?

No drug affects all the components equally well, and the concentration needed differs for each component. “Not described” means that the sources here do not mention it, not that the effect is absent.

ConsciousnessAmnesiaPain and nociceptionImmobility
PropofolYes. 50% unresponsive to verbal command at 2.3–3.5 µg/ml (Vuyk et al. 2025)Yes, at a lighter level than loss of response (Glass 1997)Partly. Propofol alone can abolish the response to laryngoscopy, which remifentanil alone does not (Fukuda 2025). The interaction with opioids is markedly synergistic for analgesic effects (Kim et al. 2025), and fentanyl reduces the propofol requirement at incision by about 80% (Smith 1994)Only at high concentrations: 15–16 µg/ml alone (Vuyk et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025). Burst suppression already appears at about 5 µg/ml (Pilge 2014). Muscle tone is reduced, but movement in response to surgical stimulation may occur (Aitkenhead ch. 3). Aitkenhead gives lower figures than Miller's (see Discrepancies)
Inhaled agentsYes. About 0.5 MAC (Perouansky et al. 2025). MAC-awake 0.3–0.4 MAC (Morgan and Mikhail). MAC-awake is the concentration at which half of patients do not respond to verbal command, for example do not open their eyes (Eger 2001)Yes. About 0.25 MAC (Perouansky et al. 2025)Partly. The action in the spinal cord blunts ascending nociceptive impulses and the withdrawal reflex, but inhibition in the dorsal horn matters less than suppression of motor output from the ventral horn (Perouansky et al. 2025). The interaction with opioids is markedly synergistic for analgesic effects (Kim et al. 2025). Aitkenhead writes that halothane produces anaesthesia without analgesiaYes. 1 MAC prevents movement in 50% and about 1.3 MAC in about 95% (Morgan and Mikhail), mainly via the spinal cord (Perouansky et al. 2025, Jinks 2010). All give muscle relaxation sufficient for lower abdominal surgery with spontaneous breathing (Aitkenhead ch. 2). Burst suppression only above about 1.3–1.4 MAC (Pilge 2014)
Nitrous oxideNot potent enough alone. MAC about 105% (Morgan and Mikhail). If nitrous oxide is supplemented only with opioid, awareness occurs in 1–2% (Aitkenhead ch. 2)Amnestic concentrations suppress fear learning in animals (Mashour and Pryor 2025)Yes. “A good analgesic but a weak anaesthetic” (Aitkenhead ch. 2). NMDA antagonist, and 70% nitrous oxide reduced postoperative opioid-induced hyperalgesia (Fukuda 2025)Contributes additively to MAC with other inhaled agents (Morgan and Mikhail)
KetamineDissociative state at 0.6–2 µg/ml. The eyes may be open (Vuyk et al. 2025)Less pronounced than with benzodiazepines (Vuyk et al. 2025). Amnesia often persists for up to 1 hour after consciousness returns (Aitkenhead ch. 3)Yes, somatic. The pain threshold rises at 0.1 µg/ml, well below the level for unconsciousness (Vuyk et al. 2025). It suppresses the response to visceral stimulation poorly, however, so an opioid is recommended when visceral stimulation is expected (Aitkenhead ch. 3)Partly. Muscle tone is often increased and spontaneous movements may occur, but reflex movement in response to surgery is uncommon (Aitkenhead ch. 3). Ketamine was not tested in the study and does not cause burst suppression (Pilge 2014)
ThiopentalYes, a potent hypnotic (Aitkenhead ch. 3)Less pronounced than with benzodiazepines (Vuyk et al. 2025)No. Poor analgesic effect, and at subanaesthetic concentrations the pain threshold is lowered (antanalgesic), which may cause postoperative restlessness (Aitkenhead ch. 3)Poor. Surgical anaesthesia requires large doses, and as the sole agent thiopental gives poor muscle relaxation and frequent movement in response to surgical stimulation (Aitkenhead ch. 3). Barbiturates act to a greater extent above the spinal level (Perouansky et al. 2025)
DexmedetomidineRousable sedation at 0.2–0.3 ng/ml, non-rousable above about 1.9 ng/ml (Ebert 2000)Impaired encoding (Mashour and Pryor 2025). ICU patients remembered more than with propofol (Vuyk et al. 2025)Yes, via α2 receptors in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord (Vuyk et al. 2025)Not described for dexmedetomidine. Clonidine alone does not produce immobility (Hendrickx 2008)
MidazolamHypnosis and amnesia at 100–200 ng/ml (Vuyk et al. 2025)Yes, anterograde. Retrograde memory does not appear to be affected (Vuyk et al. 2025)Not described as an effect in the sourcesNo. Midazolam alone cannot fully abolish movement to noxious stimuli (Hendrickx 2008)
OpioidsNo, not complete. High doses can stop breathing without loss of consciousness (Fukuda 2025)Affect cognition only partly, hence awareness with high-dose opioid (Brown 2010)Yes. Fentanyl C50 about 2 ng/ml for analgesia (Kim et al. 2025)Reduce MAC, but with a ceiling. Do not give full immobility alone (Fukuda 2025, Hendrickx 2008)

The concentrations apply to the drug alone in adults and are population values. Combinations change them a great deal, especially opioid together with hypnotics (see the Drugs tab and Hendrickx 2008).

Propofol and inhaled agents produce immobility in different ways

  • Propofol produces burst suppression long before the patient lies still. Half stop responding to verbal command at 2.3–3.5 µg/ml. Burst suppression already appears at about 5 µg/ml. But given alone, 15–16 µg/ml is needed to prevent movement at incision. Immobility during TIVA therefore most often comes from an opioid, which reduces the propofol requirement at incision by about 80%, or from neuromuscular blocking agents.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025; Pilge 2014; Smith 1994
  • With inhaled agents, the patient lies still before burst suppression. Consciousness is lost at about 0.3–0.5 MAC, and 1 MAC by definition prevents movement in half. Burst suppression only appears above about 1.3–1.4 MAC (sevoflurane 2.93 vol%, isoflurane 1.51 vol%).Source: Pilge 2014
  • Inhaled agents produce immobility mainly in the spinal cord. Not in the cortex. Barbiturates act to a greater extent above the spinal level.Sources: Perouansky et al. 2025; Antognini 1993; Rampil 1993; Jinks 2010
  • Movement says little about how deep the brain is (interpretation based on the sources). Movement under propofol does not necessarily mean the patient is awake. A patient lying still does not mean the brain is at a suitable depth. Increasing propofol until the patient stops moving can give unnecessarily deep hypnosis. The EEG shows the effect on the brain, while movement mostly reflects the spinal cord and the nociceptive balance.
Mashour and Pryor 2025; Kim et al. 2025; Perouansky et al. 2025; Vuyk et al. 2025; Fukuda 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025 Pilge 2014 Hendrickx 2008 Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8

The components

The colour indicates the component.

Test yourself: where does this belong?

Tap a scenario to see the classification.

1. Patient receives low-dose propofol, talks coherently, and remembers nothing afterwards.

Conscious, but no recall. Amnesia without unconsciousness. The drugs have their own amnestic effects.Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025

2. Patient with neuromuscular blockers and frontal alpha-delta squeezes the hand on command (isolated forearm), but remembers nothing.

Connected consciousness without recall. Alpha-delta does not rule out connected consciousness. IFT responses are rarely followed by explicit recall.Sources: Gaskell 2017; Linassi 2018

3. Paralysed patient experiences the surgery and talks about it afterwards.

Awareness with recall (AWR). Consciousness and explicit recall. This is what we know as the feared complication.

4. Patient dreams during the anaesthetic.

Disconnected consciousness. The experience is not connected to the surroundings. Dreaming is also a state in late emergence. Dreams reported “during the anaesthetic” most likely occur just before emergence, with a REM-like EEG in the last 5 minutes before the interview. None of the dreams indicated memory of the operation. See the card on dreaming in the Agents tab.Sources: Mashour and Pryor 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025; Leslie 2009 (300 patients)

5. The patient wakes and follows commands before extubation, but does not remember it later.

Conscious, but no recall. When anaesthetic agents are present, consciousness does not necessarily lead to recall.Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025

6. Deep anaesthesia with burst suppression and no response.

Probably no connected consciousness. Burst suppression probably rules out responsiveness (few observations), but not movement under propofol. Unconsciousness and immobility are two different components.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025

Movement is mostly about spinal cord and analgesia

  • Reflex and voluntary movement are treated differently. A reflex to pain runs through the spinal cord. A voluntary movement requires the patient to be connected, conscious and intending something. With the isolated forearm technique the patient is given a command. Purposeful response: consider more hypnotic. Reflex: consider more analgesia. This applies to the arm shielded from the neuromuscular blocker, not to all movement during anaesthesia.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025, box 36.2. See
  • Immobility under volatile agents arises mainly in the spinal cord, not the cortex. Rats with and without a forebrain needed the same isoflurane concentration to stay still when the tail was clamped. This is how MAC is usually measured in animals. In seven rats the forebrain including the cortex was removed by aspiration, with a cut just in front of the colliculi in the midbrain. The brainstem and spinal cord remained. The rats still moved when the tail was clamped, and MAC was unchanged for up to 11 hours (about 1.3 %). This suggests that what keeps the patient still under volatile agents acts further down, mainly in the spinal cord. The brainstem still influences MAC through descending pathways, and MAC says nothing about consciousness.Sources: Rampil, Mason and Singh. Anesthesiology 1993;78:707–712 (animal study, 14 rats); Jinks et al. 2010. See
  • No movement does not mean unconscious. A considerable proportion of awareness reports come from patients without a neuromuscular blocking agent. The isolated forearm technique may underestimate connected consciousness.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025. See
  • Lighter hypnosis requires attention to analgesia. When EEG guidance gave less volatile agent with the same opioid dose, more patients moved (22.3 % versus 15.4 %). Without neuromuscular blockade it is in practice the analgesia that keeps the patient still. (interpretation based on the sources)Source: Wildes 2019 (ENGAGES). See
  • Different stimuli require different doses. Fentanyl needs about 2 ng/ml for analgesia but about 15 ng/ml to abolish the response to laryngoscopy. MAC and C50 are doses at which half of patients still move. Doses that prevent movement in almost everyone lie just above the 95 % isobole.Source: Kim et al. 2025. See
  • More hypnotic often targets the wrong component. When the EEG shows adequate hypnosis, immobilising agents, analgesia or reflex suppression fit better. Examples are nerve monitoring without neuromuscular blockade, hypertension with a tourniquet and mouth gag insertion in children. The underlying studies are small. (interpretation based on the sources)See

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

Reflex or purposeful movement?

A patient who moves during anaesthesia may do so for different reasons. What the movement means decides what should be done about it.

  • Reflex movement happens in the spinal cord. The patient withdraws from pain without controlling it. Producing immobility during anaesthesia is mainly about suppressing this withdrawal reflex. Rats without a forebrain still move in response to pain.Sources: Rampil, Mason and Singh 1993; Jinks 2010
  • Purposeful movement requires consciousness and volition. Examples are squeezing the hand on command or reaching for the tube. The isolated forearm technique is designed to capture this when the patient has received a neuromuscular blocking agent.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025
  • The isolated forearm can tell them apart. A cuff on the arm keeps the neuromuscular blocker out, and the patient is given a command, for example “Squeeze my hand”. If you see spontaneous movements in that arm, check whether they are purposeful. Purposeful response: consider more hypnotic. Reflex: consider more analgesia. The arm can also unmask reflexes from the brainstem or spinal cord, a possible sign of inadequate antinociception.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025, box 36.2
  • The same EEG can come with different movement. For the same EEG pattern, patients most often move in response to pain under propofol, less often under sevoflurane and least often when an opioid is added. Propofol produces immobility only at very high concentrations.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025
  • No movement does not mean unconscious. A sizable proportion of awareness reports come from patients without a neuromuscular blocking agent. Anaesthesia may impair volition, the link to the self or the brainstem systems needed for purposeful motor activity. The isolated forearm may therefore underestimate connected consciousness.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025
  • Some movements are caused by neither pain nor consciousness. At induction the drugs can cause involuntary movements, especially etomidate (up to 40%), but also propofol and methohexital. Propofol can cause myoclonus during recovery. Ketamine often increases muscle tone and may cause spontaneous movements, but rarely reflex movement in response to surgery.Source: Aitkenhead 2007, ch. 3
  • Why we warn the patient before the needle (reflection from the author of the app): an awake patient is told before the needle goes in, so that the arm is not pulled away. The reflex runs through the spinal cord, but when consciousness is present, the brain can influence it. Under anaesthesia that possibility is gone, so the reflex has to be dampened in other ways. Two small studies in healthy volunteers support this line of thought: withdrawal came later when participants were aware of the stimulus (about 91 versus 74 ms), and unpredictable stimuli gave larger reflexes in some muscles. Even so, a warning does not always make the reflex smaller; in another study a cue increased the reflex response.Sources: Liebermann and Defrin 2009 (n = 8), Jure 2020 (n = 15)
  • More patients move when anaesthesia is lighter. With EEG guidance patients received less volatile agent (median 0.69 versus 0.80 MAC) and similar opioid. Unwanted movement rose from 15.4 % to 22.3 % (p = 0.002). For propofol the gap is large: at least 15 µg/ml is needed to prevent movement at incision, whereas burst suppression occurs at about 5 µg/ml. Fentanyl 3 ng/ml lowers the requirement by 80 %. If the surgeon complains that the patient is “waking up” while the EEG shows burst suppression, an opioid works better than more propofol.Sources: Wildes 2019 (ENGAGES), Sleigh et al. 2025
  • Which component are we treating? (reflection from the author of the app): in teaching, clinicians comment that more patients move and sit up on the table now that they are kept lighter. When the EEG shows adequate hypnosis, the movement is most often a reflex. It is dampened with analgesia, and if needed muscle relaxation, not with more hypnotic. EEG-guided anaesthesia requires us to know which component we are treating.
  • Without muscle relaxant (reflection from the author of the app): many give no muscle relaxant at all. Immobility then has to come from the other drugs, and you need to know how much it takes:
    • Propofol alone: gives very deep hypnosis long before immobility (at least 15 µg/ml versus about 5 µg/ml for burst suppression).Source: Sleigh et al. 2025
    • Propofol with opioid: fentanyl 3 ng/ml lowers the propofol requirement at incision by 80 %.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025 (Smith 1994)
    • Volatile agents: 1 MAC prevents movement in 50 %, about 1.3 MAC in about 95 %. Fentanyl below 2 ng/ml lowers isoflurane MAC by more than 50 %, but above 3 ng/ml the effect levels off, so some volatile agent is probably still needed.Sources: Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8, Kim et al. 2025 (McEwan 1993)
    • 50 % is not enough: MAC and C50 are doses at which half of patients still move. Almost nobody responds at doses just above the 95 % isobole.Source: Kim et al. 2025
    Interpretation based on the sources: without muscle relaxant, analgesia is what in practice keeps the patient still. If hypnosis is kept lighter according to the EEG, the opioid dose must be weighed against the stimulus. Otherwise movement increases, as ENGAGES showed.
  • Anticipate the stimulus, talk to the surgeon, consider relaxant (reflection from the author of the app): perhaps we need to get better at knowing when pain increases during surgery, cooperate better with the surgeon or use muscle relaxant. The sources support that different stimuli require different doses: fentanyl needs about 2 ng/ml for analgesia but about 15 ng/ml for laryngoscopy. The models still do not cover many of the stimuli during surgery. With muscle relaxant, movement is lost as a warning sign. Processed EEG should then be used, and with TIVA plus relaxant it is required (see the Fundamentals tab).Sources: Kim et al. 2025, Klein 2021, NAP5
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): a movement at incision in a patient with a stable alpha–delta pattern is often a reflex, but can also be a purposeful response from an awake patient. If it is a reflex, analgesia is often a better response than more hypnotic. Read the EEG, autonomic signs and the character of the movement together.
Perouansky et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025 Jinks 2010 Aitkenhead 2007, ch. 3 Liebermann and Defrin 2009, Jure 2020 Wildes 2019 (ENGAGES) Kim et al. 2025, Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8 Klein 2021

Three clinical situations where the components must be separated

Three examples from practice, described by the author of the app, where it is easy to treat the wrong component. The suggestions are hers; the sources below show what is documented.

1. Thyroid surgery with nerve monitoring

  • The situation: monitoring of the recurrent laryngeal nerve records EMG from the vocal cords via electrodes on the tracheal tube. The guideline strongly advises against muscle relaxant, but accepts a short-acting dose at intubation (succinylcholine 2–2.5 mg/kg or rocuronium or atracurium 0.5 mg/kg). Avoid lidocaine jelly and other lubricants on the tube. Propofol is standard in most places (the author's experience).Source: Randolph 2011 (international guideline)
  • Movement is a real problem. With rocuronium at intubation and sugammadex before nerve stimulation, 72–83 % of the periods were free of movement, coughing or swallowing. The rest were not.Source: Lu 2022 (116 patients)
  • Suggestion: volatile agent instead of propofol. Volatile agents produce immobility in the spinal cord, whereas propofol alone needs very high concentrations (see above). The guideline accepts both and states that volatile agents, nitrous oxide and opioids do not affect the EMG readings, but the group behind it linked sevoflurane to higher baseline EMG. In a small RCT the first positive EMG signal came later with sevoflurane than with propofol (median 41 versus 37 minutes), and 8 of 20 with sevoflurane had no signal at the first test, versus none with propofol. Amplitudes were similar. All received one dose of cisatracurium at induction. The authors attribute the delay to sevoflurane prolonging the effect of cisatracurium, not to a direct effect of volatile agents on the EMG reading. Everyone in the sevoflurane group had a signal 5–20 minutes later. TOF was not reported.Sources: Randolph 2011; Li 2020 (40 patients)
  • Volatile agents affect different types of nerve monitoring differently. In recurrent laryngeal nerve monitoring the nerve is stimulated directly and the response is recorded in the vocal cord muscle. Spinal cord and cortex are not part of the pathway, and anaesthetic agents have very little effect on peripheral nerves and muscles. In motor evoked potentials (MEP) the signal travels from the motor cortex through the spinal cord, and volatile agents depress it dose-dependently, partly via the synapses in the anterior horn. There, TIVA gives the most reliable recordings, and volatile agents and nitrous oxide should be avoided.Sources: Randolph 2011; Pandin et al. in Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 6
  • Suggestion: multimodal with clonidine and lidocaine. α2 agonists and opioids lower MAC, but clonidine alone does not produce immobility. Whether intravenous lidocaine affects nerve monitoring is not documented in the sources here; results from registered trials have not been available.Sources: Perouansky et al. 2025, Hendrickx 2008
  • Interpretation based on the sources: without muscle relaxant, stillness must come from immobilising components (volatile agent, opioid), not from more propofol. The EEG can show whether hypnosis is already adequate.

2. Orthopaedics with a tourniquet

  • The situation: blood pressure and heart rate rise after some time with the cuff inflated. The surgeon does not want this, and it is often handled by deepening the anaesthetic. The author of the app believes that the problem is seldom hypnosis, but rather the ischaemic response.
  • Tourniquet pain causes sympathetic activation. Blood pressure rises gradually, after a variable time. The pain is carried mainly by unmyelinated C fibres, and plasma noradrenaline rises with blood pressure.Source: Deloughry and Griffiths 2009
  • It also happens when the index indicates adequate hypnosis. With index-guided sevoflurane and remifentanil throughout, 56 % still had a blood pressure rise of at least 30 %. Lidocaine 1.5 mg/kg or ketamine 0.2 mg/kg 10 minutes before inflation reduced this to 16 and 12 %, and less remifentanil was used.Source: Kim 2022 (RCT, 75 patients)
  • Magnesium and ketamine reduced the proportion by about the same amount. In knee surgery with index-guided sevoflurane and no opioid, 63 % had a blood pressure rise of more than 30 % after 70 minutes of tourniquet. In the study, magnesium 30 mg/kg or ketamine 0.25 mg/kg before inflation reduced this to 22 and 19 %. Both are NMDA antagonists. In rats, both reduced spinal c-fos, which suggests less pain transmission. The magnesium dose was chosen without a dose-finding study.Source: Lee 2006 (RCT, 81 patients, and rat experiments)
  • More volatile did not stop the rise. Low-dose ketamine gave a possible reduction. Under enflurane and nitrous oxide, 28 patients received ketamine 0.1 mg/kg or saline before the tourniquet. Enflurane was increased in both groups, yet systolic pressure rose only in the control group. Two patients in that group needed fentanyl despite 3 % enflurane. The proportion with a rise of more than 30 % at 60 minutes was 29 vs 7 %, but the difference was not statistically significant. The study was small and did not measure hypnosis with EEG.Source: Park 2007 (RCT, 28 patients)
  • Deeper anaesthesia helps poorly. Heart rate and blood pressure may rise after 30–60 minutes of tourniquet inflation and persist until deflation. The rise responds poorly to analgesics and deeper anaesthesia. Deflating the tourniquet is the most reliable. The pain is most common under general anaesthesia (53–67 %) and in lower-limb surgery.Source: Kumar 2016 (review)
  • No drug gives full effect. Ketamine, dexmedetomidine, magnesium, clonidine and remifentanil have been tried and may reduce the rise. With spinal anaesthesia, topical local anaesthetic, a wider cuff with lower pressure and adding opioid, clonidine or epinephrine have been tried.Source: Kumar 2016 (review)
  • Other drugs have also been tried. Low-dose ketamine, preoperative clonidine and gabapentin have shown an effect.Source: Deloughry and Griffiths 2009 (review)
  • Clonidine has a downside at deflation. Under spinal anaesthesia, 24 patients received oral clonidine about 5 µg/kg one hour before, or no premedication. Clonidine reduced the proportion with tourniquet pain from 75 to 33 %. But after deflation, mean arterial pressure fell further (to 65 vs 76 mmHg) and reached its lowest point later (after 140 vs 53 seconds). Noradrenaline did not rise as it did in the control group. The study was small, and patients were allocated by day of surgery.Source: Maruyama 2004 (24 patients)
  • Interpretation based on the sources: if the EEG shows adequate hypnosis, more hypnotic probably does not address the mechanism. Drugs against the ischaemic pain and central sensitisation (ketamine, lidocaine, α2 agonist) fit better.
  • Caveats: Li 2020 and Kim 2022 are small single-centre studies. Kim 2022 adjusted remifentanil to blood pressure, which may have influenced the result.

3. Children in ENT surgery

  • The situation: children have active reflexes, move and retch when the mouth gag is inserted. Few give muscle relaxant to these children, and high-dose remifentanil is used for intubation instead (clinical experience of the author of the app).
  • Remifentanil without relaxant is only partly documented. In children aged 2–9 years given propofol 3 mg/kg, remifentanil 3.04 µg/kg gave excellent intubating conditions in half (ED50). The most common adverse event was difficult mask ventilation (4 of 27 children, 15 %). The study was small and did not find the dose that works in almost all.Source: Ono 2018
  • Interpretation based on the sources: intubation and the mouth gag are two different stimuli at different times, and different stimuli require different doses. A dose that covers intubation does not in itself say anything about the need when the gag is inserted. If the EEG shows that the child is asleep, movement and retching at the gag are a question of analgesia and reflex suppression, not of more hypnotic.Source: Kim et al. 2025
Clinical experience of the author of the app Randolph 2011, Lu 2022, Li 2020, Deloughry and Griffiths 2009, Kim 2022, Kumar 2016, Lee 2006, Maruyama 2004, Park 2007, Ono 2018

Rats without a forebrain still move: where in the brainstem is MAC influenced? (Jinks 2010)

Adult male rats received isoflurane. MAC was measured with tail clamp and hindlimb EMG before and at least 90 minutes after a single transection of the brainstem at different levels, or after removal of the cerebellum. In addition, the mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR) in the midbrain was inactivated with lidocaine, and its nerve cells were recorded.Source: Jinks et al. Anesthesiology 2010;112:316–324

  • The cortex is not needed for movement, but the brainstem keeps MAC up. When the forebrain was removed by suction in seven rats, MAC was unchanged (about 1.3%) for up to 11 hours. Chronic spinal transection, however, reduces MAC by about 50%, and when isoflurane reaches only the spinal cord, MAC falls by more than 30%. The brainstem thus counteracts the depression in the spinal cord.Sources: Rampil, Mason and Singh 1993; Jinks 2010
  • Where the cut is made matters a lot for MAC. Intact MAC was 1.3%. Transections in the pons and at the obex clearly lowered MAC (to 60, 55 and 40% of the intact value). Mid-collicular and mid-medullary transections changed little (90 and 91%), but mid-medulla gave only weak single movements. Without the cerebellum MAC was unchanged (not significant).
  • The MLR in the midbrain drives movement. Lidocaine in the MLR on both sides reduced MAC by 32% for 20–60 minutes. Injections just above and below the MLR had no effect.
  • Isoflurane suppresses the MLR neurons. At 1.2 MAC they responded to strong tail clamp with only 13% of the action potentials seen without isoflurane.
  • MAC is the sum of spinal cord and descending pathways. The MLR drives the locomotor circuits in the ventral horn of the spinal cord, where inhaled agents appear to produce immobility. The RVM inhibits nociceptive transmission, while the MdD in the caudal medulla facilitates it (the authors’ model).
  • The study says nothing about consciousness. It is about immobility, and MAC does not measure consciousness (see the Akinesia component).
  • Caveats: rats and isoflurane only. The head was fixed. The RVM was not selectively lesioned. Trauma from the transection could in principle affect MAC, but the authors argue it does not explain the findings. Funded by the NIH.
Jinks et al. Anesthesiology 2010;112:316–324

Stimulation shifts the dose requirement, and the EEG shows it in three patterns

This is the clinical experience most anaesthesia nurses know: when the patient is touched or surgery begins, the dose has to go up, or the anaesthetic becomes too light. García et al. 2021 collect what has been measured on this, and it supports the experience.

The relationship has been measured directly. Röpcke et al. 2001 studied 24 patients in two groups on propofol 2.2 mg/kg with 1 to 1.6 MAC desflurane, measured with frontal EEG and BIS, with surgical stimulation as the stimulus. García et al. report the finding thus: an additional 2% desflurane was required for equivalent sigmoid dose–response relationships in the presence of surgical stimulation. So stimulation moves the whole curve, not just the moment.

Three patterns to recognise, and they look entirely different in the spectrogram:

  • Beta arousal. Beta power rises after a painful stimulus, mainly at lower anaesthetic doses without opioid. It often accompanies somatic movement. This is the arousal that looks like arousal.
  • Paradoxical arousal, also called delta arousal. Delta power, around 0.5 to 4 Hz, rises at higher anaesthetic doses or in balanced anaesthesia. The term comes from Kochs et al. The review notes that this shift towards slower activity is unlike the faster activity seen during emergence, and that it is most prominent with body-cavity surgery.
  • Alpha dropout. A sudden, episodic loss of frontal alpha power, around 8 to 12 Hz. The review calls it a relatively common response to noxious stimulation, and describes it as analogous to a partial beta arousal. It may reflect thalamocortical communication shifting from idling to operational mode. Opioids can prevent or recover an alpha dropout.

And here is the trap you should know. Delta arousal, in the review’s own words, causes EEG indices falsely to suggest that the hypnotic dose is excessive. The patient is stimulated, the EEG answers with more slow activity, the index falls, and whoever is steering by the index may end up reducing the hypnotic at the very moment the patient needs more. That is the opposite of the right action, and it is one of the clearest arguments for reading the raw EEG and spectrogram instead of the number.

What you do when you keep the patient lighter in anticipation of stimulation has a parallel in the review. The authors propose that the pattern must be personalised, and that maximal frontal alpha could be measured after the patient is in a steady state of unconsciousness, before surgical stimulation begins. The quiet window before incision is therefore not merely waiting; it is where you see what this patient’s alpha can actually reach. That matters particularly in older patients and in cognitive impairment, where baseline alpha is lower.

What the authors propose, and what they do not claim. Their proposal is that opioids be titrated to maximise EEG alpha power and avoid alpha dropouts in the face of surgical nociceptive input. But they are explicit that this is a concept and not a validated algorithm: whether it results in improved intraoperative autonomic stability and less postoperative delirium, pain and immune suppression has yet to be evaluated in large clinical trials, and they write that they have insufficient information to determine whether the approach is associated with preferred patient outcomes. They also write that it remains to be determined whether pure EEG nociceptive responses have significant long-term clinical consequences.

Note also an internal discrepancy in the review: the text gives 2% more desflurane, while Table 2 gives beta arousal “up to 8% desflurane” for the same study. The review does not explain the difference. See Discrepancies and disagreements between sources in the Sources tab.

García et al. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:445–57

When alpha disappears and the EEG index falls at the same time: the case that shows why the number is not enough

The case above is worth going through carefully, because all four signals pointed the same way, except the one most people steer by.

  • Alpha dropout is described, and it is common. Hight et al. studied 237 patients during maintenance of general anaesthesia and modelled expected alpha power from the concentrations of volatile agent, propofol and opioid. Unexpected falls below what the model predicted, that is, falls not explicable by dose, occurred in 73 patients, 31%. Median duration was 103 seconds, median peak amplitude −3.5 dB.
  • And it is body-cavity surgery in particular that does it. Dropouts occurred in 55% with body-cavity surgery versus 27% otherwise (p < 0.001), and the association held in the multivariable model (p = 0.003). That fits visceral nociception. The authors propose thalamocortical depolarisation from unsuppressed noxious input, possibly via vagal pathways from the peritoneum.
  • The authors’ conclusion is directly usable: such losses can provide a helpful measure of unsuppressed nociception during surgery.
  • Why the index fell. This is the heart of it. Hight et al. point out that neither BIS nor Entropy explicitly quantifies alpha power, so a loss of alpha is hard to see in the index itself. At the same time slow activity rises, and that is what the index reacts to. García et al. 2021 say it outright about delta arousal: it causes EEG indices falsely to suggest that the hypnotic dose is excessive. The number therefore pointed towards reducing the hypnotic at the very moment the patient lacked analgesia.
  • What the fentanyl did is also in the literature. García et al. 2021 write that opioids can prevent or recover an alpha dropout, and propose that opioids be titrated to maximise alpha power and avoid dropouts under surgical nociceptive input. It remains a concept rather than a validated algorithm, and the authors say they have insufficient information to determine whether the approach produces the preferred patient outcomes.

One important difference between the case and the study, which belongs on the record. In this case arterial pressure and heart rate rose during the dropout. They did not in Hight’s material: mean arterial pressure did not differ significantly from the two minutes before (p = 0.188), and heart rate fell slightly, around 2 beats per minute, which the authors explain by dropouts tending to occur while heart rate was already falling. That every signal moved together here makes the case clearer than the study average, but it also makes it less typical. The point still stands: when alpha disappears, the haemodynamics may be unchanged, and then the EEG is the only thing speaking up.

On skin conductance. The measure rests on sympathetically driven sweat activity in the palm. In this case it moved at the same time as the other signals. The app has no verified peer-reviewed review of how well the measure separates nociceptive stimulation from other sympathetic activation, so it stands here as a simultaneous observation and not as documentation.

Caveats for Hight et al.: observational cross-sectional study, the model assumes a linear dose–response between alpha power and concentration, the 1.5 standard deviation threshold was chosen pragmatically, and patients on total intravenous anaesthesia were excluded. Discrimination was moderate, AUC 0.78. And 48 patients, 19%, had unexpected increases in alpha power, half of them in addition to dropouts. The authors say themselves that this somewhat weakens the nociception interpretation.

Clinical case from the author. Interpretation from the sources: Hight et al.; García et al. 2021.

Hight et al. Br J Anaesth (transient alpha power loss) García et al. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:445–57

Response, experience and recall can be separated

  • Response and recall are different things: Some patients respond to command during anaesthesia, for example 11 % of young adults after intubation, whereas explicit recall is rare.See
  • Neuromuscular blockade hides wakefulness: Neuromuscular blockade is associated with both a higher incidence and more distressing awareness, and the isolated forearm is needed to detect wakefulness when relaxants have been given.See
  • Unresponsive is not the same as unconscious: Dreams and REM sleep show experience without response. Whether an IFT response corresponds to the experience of an awake patient remains unresolved.See
  • Implicit memory is uncertain: About a third of cohorts and studies showed signs of it, but the figures do not express risk for the individual patient. Benzodiazepine premedication was associated with less implicit memory.See
  • Stable haemodynamics and a low index value say little on their own: High-dose opioid gives stable haemodynamics and can increase delta in the EEG, without hypnosis necessarily being adequate.See
  • Frontal alpha–delta does not rule out connected consciousness: Three patients responded to command with dominant alpha–delta, and the index did not distinguish them from the others. The index is better than clinical signs, but not better than an end-tidal gas alarm.See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

High-dose opioid without enough hypnotic: stable circulation, but risk of awareness

The components of anaesthesia can be separated. Analgesia and stable circulation can be achieved without consciousness and memory being sufficiently suppressed. High-dose opioid is a historical example of this.

  • High-dose opioid gave stable circulation, but is used less today. The technique was introduced as “stress-free” anaesthesia for cardiac surgery, first with morphine and later with fentanyl and sufentanil. Bolus fentanyl of 5–75 µg/kg gives plasma concentrations of 10–30 ng/ml. This is often enough for stable haemodynamics through induction and intubation. The technique has not shown better outcomes, is more expensive and fits poorly with early extubation. A meta-analysis found no difference between high and low opioid doses in length of stay, ventilation time, myocardial infarction or stroke in adults.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Opioids do not suppress the cortex enough. They act primarily in the nociceptive pathways and to a lesser extent in the cortex. They reduce arousal and affect cognition only partly. This may explain the high incidence of awareness in cardiac surgery, where high-dose opioids were until recently the primary anaesthetic.Source: Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010
  • Opioids are not complete anaesthetics. They reduce MAC, but with a ceiling. Analgesia is usually not accompanied by loss of consciousness. High doses can stop spontaneous breathing without the patient becoming unconscious, and the patient can then breathe on command.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Cardiac surgery and caesarean section are associated with a higher risk of awareness. The same applies to neuromuscular blocking agents and intravenous anaesthesia. All are among the factors with a higher risk of awareness with recall.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025, box 36.1
  • The EEG can look “deep” under high-dose opioid. High doses of opioid alone (fentanyl above about 8 ng/ml) give more delta and a lower median frequency in the EEG and in the indices. At routine doses together with hypnotics, opioids change the EEG little.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025
  • Nitrous oxide with opioid alone is not enough. Awareness is then reported in 1–2%. The recommendation is therefore to add a low concentration of an inhaled agent.Source: Aitkenhead ch. 2
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): Stable heart rate and blood pressure say little about consciousness and memory. A low index value under high-dose opioid does not necessarily mean that the hypnotic level is sufficient. Each component must be assessed separately.
Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010 Vuyk et al. 2025; Fukuda 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025

Response to command occurs, recall is rare

Some patients respond to command during anaesthesia (the proportion varies widely between studies), but few remember it afterwards. Consciousness and memory are separable processes, and the dose for unconsciousness is higher than the dose for amnesia.Sources: studies using the isolated forearm technique (IFT); Mashour and Avidan 2015

  • Response occurs. In the IFT studies, a median of 37 % responded to command, but with wide variation (0–100 %). After intubation, 11 % of young adults squeezed the hand. The proportion was higher after skin incision than after induction (97 % versus 42 %).Sources: Sanders 2012, Lennertz 2023, Mashour and Avidan 2015, Russell and Wang 2001
  • Recall is rare. IFT response is far more frequent than explicit recall (34.8 % versus 6.2 % in one study). After intubation in young adults, 1 case was judged definite and 5 possible explicit recall (0.3 % and 1.5 %). In the TIVA study, no one had explicit recall. By comparison, a structured Brice interview finds about 1–2 per 1000.Sources: Linassi 2018, Lennertz 2023, Russell and Wang 2001, Mashour and Avidan 2015
  • The response may be about pain. Almost half of those who responded (49 %) indicated that they were in pain. Continuous anaesthesia between induction and laryngoscopy was associated with less response (adjusted OR 0.43). The study is observational and does not show cause.Source: Lennertz 2023
  • Relaxants make wakefulness invisible. Neuromuscular blockade is associated with both a higher incidence and more distressing awareness. IFT is needed to detect wakefulness when relaxants have been given. That view comes from authors who have used the technique in several studies and are not neutral.Sources: Mashour and Avidan 2015, Russell and Wang 2001

The studies in detail:

Russell and Wang 2001 Lennertz 2023 Linassi 2018 Sanders 2012 Mashour and Avidan 2015

What does a response mean, and what does no response mean?

A patient squeezing the hand shows that there is a response. Whether the patient experienced the command, and whether a patient who does not respond is unconscious, is not settled. The sources give partly different answers.

  • Unresponsive is not unconscious. Consciousness, connectedness and responsiveness are three different things. In REM sleep, consciousness is present without connectedness or responsiveness. At least 27 % with propofol and 28 % with desflurane reported dreams, without experiencing the surgery itself. Volunteers under ketamine were unresponsive but reported vivid dreams afterwards.Sources: Sanders 2012, Leslie 2009, Sarasso 2015
  • The response is probably more than a random movement, but the numbers are small. More responded only to command than only to a nonsense sentence (13 versus 4, and 7 to both, p = 0.049), and some followed conditional commands. But three also squeezed to a false condition.Source: Lennertz 2023
  • The field disagrees on what the response means. One view is that an unequivocal IFT response should be regarded as consciousness until shown otherwise. Another is a “third state”, in which the patient follows a simple command without a conscious self, but this is without data. A third is that the response may resemble lucid dreaming, but this needs investigation.Sources: Mashour and Avidan 2015 (consciousness), Pandit (third state), Sanders 2012 (lucid dreaming)
  • Absence of response is also unclear. A missing response may be due to lack of motivation, comprehension or distraction. But no study in the sources has tested commands under an anaesthetic dose of ketamine and also asked about experiences.Source: Lennertz 2023

The studies in detail:

Sanders 2012 Leslie 2009 Sarasso 2015 Lennertz 2023 Mashour and Avidan 2015

Implicit memory: possible, but hard to quantify

Even without explicit recall, something may be stored without the patient knowing it. Signs of such implicit memory appear in about a third of cohorts or studies, but the figures are uncertain.Sources: two meta-analyses, Linassi 2021 and Fu 2021

  • About a third showed signs. This applied to 36.1 % of cohorts in one meta-analysis and 39 % of studies in the other. The figures are proportions of cohorts or studies, not risk for the individual patient. The studies varied greatly in drugs, doses and tests.Sources: Linassi 2021, Fu 2021
  • Explicit recall of sound is rare. Open recall testing was positive in 0.54 % of patients, and free recall showed no explicit memory. Word recognition equalled chance guessing, also among those who responded to command. Among those who responded during TIVA, there was no sign of implicit memory.Sources: Fu 2021, Lennertz 2023, Russell and Wang 2001
  • Benzodiazepine premedication goes with less implicit memory. In one meta-analysis the OR was 0.35. In the other, all studies with signs of implicit memory lacked benzodiazepine premedication, and a study using temazepam found none. This is an association at cohort and study level, not a demonstrated cause (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Linassi 2021, Fu 2021, Russell and Wang 2001
  • Depth and monitoring explained little. There was no difference between “light” and “deep” anaesthesia, but the classification was subjective. Neither BIS monitoring nor BIS-guided anaesthesia gave a significant difference. Deep sedation had fewer cohorts with implicit memory (OR 0.10), but those cohorts had no muscle relaxants and almost no opioids.Source: Linassi 2021
  • The consequences are unclear. There is little evidence that implicit memory causes PTSD. Music during surgery gave less pain and lower opioid requirements afterwards, but this rests on few studies.Sources: Mashour and Avidan 2015, Fu 2021

The studies in detail:

Linassi 2021 Fu 2021 Russell and Wang 2001 Lennertz 2023 Mashour and Avidan 2015

What monitoring can and cannot detect

No single measurement reliably distinguishes conscious from unconscious. Clinical signs, the indices and frontal EEG all have weaknesses, but the index has a place.

  • Clinical signs are not enough. Heart rate, blood pressure, sweating, lacrimation and pupils are not reliable signs of consciousness. The signs were developed when one agent was given at a time, and their lack of reliability was one of the main reasons EEG monitoring was developed. High-dose opioid gives stable haemodynamics, but opioids are not complete anaesthetics and affect cognition only partially.Sources: Sleigh et al. 2025; Aitkenhead 2007 (ch. 18); Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010; Fukuda 2025
  • A low index value is not always enough hypnosis. High doses of opioid alone (fentanyl above about 8 ng/ml) increase delta and lower the median frequency in the EEG and in the indices. A low value under high-dose opioid therefore does not necessarily mean that the hypnotic level is adequate.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025
  • The EEG index is better than clinical signs, but not better than a gas alarm. Five randomised trials give the same picture: BIS is better than clinical signs alone, but not better than an end-tidal gas alarm.Source: Mashour and Avidan 2015
  • Frontal alpha–delta does not rule out response. Three of six who responded after intubation had dominant alpha–delta and BIS values of 44, 37 and 44. None of the measures distinguished them from those who did not respond. Only burst suppression appeared to exclude a response, but this rests on few observations. BIS also could not distinguish the responders in the IFT studies.Sources: Gaskell 2017, Sanders 2012
  • Not nihilism. The findings should be replicated. Response with alpha–delta may be less likely during stable maintenance than just after laryngoscopy (hypothesis). One should not become nihilistic about brain monitoring. Separating measures of connectedness from measures of consciousness may help, but it is unclear what will work.Sources: Mashour and Avidan 2017, Sanders 2012

The studies in detail:

Aitkenhead 2007 Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010 Fukuda 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025 Mashour and Avidan 2015 Gaskell 2017 Mashour and Avidan 2017 Sanders 2012

The brainstem shows the way: signs at induction and emergence

Many clinical signs come from nuclei in the brainstem. The signs say something about which parts of the brainstem are affected, or have recovered.

Emergence in three phases

alpha and beta increase
↓
before response to voice
↓
Tap a phase to read briefly about it.
Source: Brown et al. 2015, box 50-1 (after Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010)
  • At induction several signs disappear together. A patient counting backwards from 100 typically gets no further than 85–90. If the patient follows a finger with the eyes, the eye movements become smaller. Nystagmus and more blinking may appear, and finally the eyes fix in the midline. The oculocephalic and corneal reflexes are lost, but the pupillary light reflex remains intact. The patient becomes apnoeic, atonic and unresponsive at about the same time.Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)
  • The brainstem is reached early. After a bolus the drug reaches the brainstem early through the basilar artery. That may explain why the signs appear together. The corneal reflex can be tested with a drop of sterile water instead of a wisp of cotton, with less risk of corneal abrasion.Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)
  • Emergence comes in phases. Phase 1: breathing returns, first irregular and then regular, and alpha and beta increase in the EEG. Phase 2: heart rate and blood pressure rise, and the patient shows increased salivation and lacrimation, grimaces, swallows, gags and coughs. Muscle tone returns, and the patient may reach for the tube. Phase 3: the patient opens the eyes and follows some commands. Each sign shows that specific brainstem nuclei are working again.Source: Brown et al. 2015, box 50-1 (after Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010)
  • The signs come before the patient responds. Swallowing, coughing and lacrimation often appear before the patient follows commands. According to the chapter, extubation only requires enough airway reflexes and motor function to breathe unaided, not that the patient responds. Guidelines (see below) set stricter requirements. Eye opening is among the last signs, and many follow commands with their eyes closed.Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)
  • The guideline asks for more than the minimum. For routine awake extubation, DAS recommends that neuromuscular block is reversed to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 measured with a nerve stimulator, that the patient breathes regularly with adequate minute ventilation, and that the patient is awake, opens the eyes and obeys commands. Train-of-four ratios of 0.7–0.9 are associated with impaired pharyngeal function and increased risk of aspiration. Deep extubation causes less coughing but more upper airway obstruction, and is reserved for patients with an easy airway and no aspiration risk. The recommendations are partly based on expert opinion.Source: Popat et al. 2012 (DAS)
  • Clinical signs are poor at detecting residual block. Head lift, grip strength, tidal volume and inspiratory force are insensitive. A 5-second head lift detected only 11 % of patients with a train-of-four ratio below 0.9, and healthy volunteers could sustain a head lift at a ratio of 0.45. Fade cannot be reliably seen or felt until the ratio is below 0.4. ASA therefore recommends quantitative monitoring and a ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation, measured at the adductor pollicis, not the eye muscles (strong recommendation, moderate evidence).Source: Thilen et al. 2023 (ASA)
  • The light reflex says little about consciousness. The pupillary light reflex can remain intact even when the patient is profoundly unconscious. After large opioid doses the pupils may stay pinpoint.Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)

What does an IFT response mean? Objections and what remains unresolved

Here the sources are brought together. This is not a new source. The question is whether a hand that squeezes on command must mean that the patient has experienced the command, or whether it could be a reflex or an automatic response, for example while the patient is dreaming.

  • There are five common objections to IFT. The response correlates poorly with clinical signs of light anaesthesia. It can only be used for about 20 minutes. It is difficult to separate conscious movements from reflexes. Response to command does not show that the patient is conscious. And the response does not correlate with recall.Source: Russell and Wang 2001
  • Proponents of IFT consider the objections a misunderstanding. Reflex and conscious movement can be separated by asking the patient to respond in a specific way, for example with conditional commands (“if you have pain, squeeze twice”). Responses have been seen up to 125 minutes into the operation. The lack of correlation with recall is expected, because low doses of propofol and other agents produce consciousness without recall in volunteers. The authors have used the technique in several studies and are not neutral.Source: Russell and Wang 2001
  • Controlled commands were used to test the reflex objection. A response was counted only if it came after the commands started, not in response to the laryngoscopy itself. First came a command and a nonsense sentence with the same number of syllables, in random order. 13 responded only to the command, 4 only to the nonsense and 7 to both (p = 0.049). Five extended two fingers, and four answered correctly to “if fish swim in the sea, squeeze my hand”. But three also squeezed to “if rocks float on water”.Source: Lennertz 2023
  • This argues for more than random movement, but is not proof. More responded to the command than to the nonsense, and some followed conditional commands. But a substantial proportion also responded to the nonsense, three responded to a false condition, and the numbers are small.
  • The IFT state is not necessarily normal wakefulness. It is assumed that a correct response means the patient experienced the command. The authors cannot rule out that the consent process made the response to the name more automatic, or that the responders had cognitive impairment not captured by a simple command.Source: Gaskell 2017
  • Responding correctly requires at least partial connectedness. A dream counts as disconnected consciousness, where the experience comes from within and not from the surroundings. Responding correctly to a command presupposes that the sound has been perceived.Sources: Mashour and Hudetz 2017, Gaskell 2017
  • Positive IFT responses may resemble lucid dreaming. People having a lucid dream can communicate purposefully with pre-agreed eye or hand movements. It is unclear whether a lucid dreamer would respond to a spoken command, and this needs to be investigated.Source: Sanders 2012
  • A negative response is also unclear. An absent response may be due to lack of motivation, lack of comprehension or distraction (for example by pain), in addition to unconsciousness or sensory disconnection. IFT probably underestimates consciousness, because anaesthetics affect motivation, cognition and motor function.Sources: Lennertz 2023, Gaskell 2017
  • Response without recall has been reported during slow-delta. Individual patients responded to verbal commands during anaesthesia-induced slow-delta without remembering it. One possible explanation is that slow-delta is regional, and that behavioural response is possible even with a hyperpolarised prefrontal cortex. This is a hypothesis.Source: Guay 2025 (individual reports)
  • Conclusion (interpretation based on the sources): IFT response to conditional commands is probably the strongest behavioural marker we have for connected consciousness under neuromuscular blockade. The sources do not show that it is the same experience as in an awake patient. This remains unresolved.
Russell and Wang 2001, Lennertz 2023, Gaskell 2017, Mashour and Hudetz 2017 and Guay 2025

Response to command under ketamine: what has been studied?

Has anyone tested whether patients can respond to command during ketamine anaesthesia, for example while they are in a dream-like state? No study in the sources both tests responses to command and records the experiences afterwards.

  • Ketamine can give consciousness without response. Healthy volunteers (18) were behaviourally unresponsive under propofol, xenon and ketamine. After propofol and xenon they reported no experience. After ketamine they reported long, vivid dreams unconnected to the surroundings. TMS-EEG showed high complexity, similar to wakefulness, under ketamine. This shows consciousness without response, that is, unresponsive does not mean unconscious. It does not show response to command while dreaming.Source: Sarasso 2015 (Curr Biol)
  • That ketamine gives no purposeful response is a classification, not a test result. Ketamine is described as a “dissociative” agent with disconnected consciousness, dreams, hallucinations and distorted self-experience. In the model, disconnected consciousness by definition does not produce a “purposeful response to command”. An EEG measure (spectral exponent) resembled wakefulness in unresponsive volunteers with ketamine and mental activity.Sources: Bonhomme 2019 (review article), Colombo 2019 (mentioned there)
  • Ketamine preserves signs of wakefulness, but the content becomes disorganised. Eye opening, movement and high-frequency EEG are preserved, but the patient cannot process the surroundings. This is a hypothesis without its own test of response to command.Source: Mashour and Hudetz 2017
  • A low dose of ketamine at co-induction is not ketamine anaesthesia. All three late responders (D–F, centre 3) had received ketamine 25 mg as co-induction. The responses came after repeated commands (approx. 80–160 seconds after intubation), and the propofol concentration may have fallen in two of them.Source: Gaskell 2017
  • The same unresponsiveness can give different experiences. Unresponsiveness can go together with disconnected consciousness, and different agents produce different subjective states. Response to command under ketamine has not been tested.Source: Hudetz and Mashour 2016
  • What is missing: a study of patients or volunteers given an anaesthetic dose of ketamine and tested with commands and conditional commands (for example with IFT if neuromuscular blockers have been given), who at the same time report their experiences afterwards. That could show whether dream experiences can go together with purposeful responses.
Sarasso 2015, Bonhomme 2019, Mashour and Hudetz 2017, Gaskell 2017
The studies in detail: depth monitoring 2007, IFT and recall, implicit memory, alpha–delta and response, reviews (9 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Depth monitoring as the textbook described it in 2007 (Aitkenhead ch. 18)

  • Clinical signs: “depth” was traditionally judged from heart rate, blood pressure, sweating and pupil size. The chapter writes that such signs are not reliable enough to avoid awareness, particularly with autonomic neuropathy.
  • No shared definition: anaesthesia can be described as lack of perception, lack of responsiveness and inability to recall, but all three are poorly defined. A monitor therefore cannot measure “depth” in the way it measures blood pressure. What is needed is a monitor that predicts awareness before it occurs, and ensures that each patient receives the minimum amount of anaesthetic.
  • Isolated forearm: only shows that the patient is already awake, and its duration is limited by the ischaemia from the cuff.
  • EEG: the raw EEG was considered too complex for use in the operating theatre. Spectral analysis showed lower mean frequency and spectral edge frequency with increasing dose and finally suppression, but was not reliable enough as a measure of depth. BIS was described as apparently reliable, but it was unclear how different agents, hypoxaemia and epileptic activity affect the number.
  • Other methods: auditory evoked potentials, frontalis EMG and lower oesophageal contractility, and respiratory sinus arrhythmia. None was in widespread use.
  • Link to the app: much of this still holds, particularly that clinical depth has several components. The view of the raw EEG has changed: newer sources in the app (Purdon 2015, Hight 2020) recommend reading the raw EEG and spectrogram directly.
Aitkenhead 2007, ch. 18 (Byrne)

Isolated forearm and memory during TIVA (Russell and Wang 2001)

  • Design: 40 women undergoing major gynaecological surgery (double-blind randomisation to two audio tapes) received TIVA with propofol and alfentanil (the Nordström regimen), atracurium as the neuromuscular blocker and an epidural with bupivacaine, after premedication with temazepam 20 mg. The tape was played 1–2 minutes after skin incision and contained first the command “open and close the fingers of your right hand”, then three words the patient was to remember (fruits or vegetables). The isolated forearm technique (IFT) was used to detect response. Memory tests (explicit and implicit) were taken within 2 hours after the operation.
  • Response: 7 of 40 women (2 in the fruit group and 5 in the vegetable group) responded a total of 12 times to commands, at propofol rates of 4–7 mg/kg/h and 34–125 minutes into the operation. Only once did one of them express discomfort, when the surgeon inserted a self-retaining retractor and explored the upper abdomen.
  • Memory: none had explicit recall of anything from the operation or the tapes. Among the 7 who responded there was no sign of implicit memory. Correct answers on the fruit and vegetable test were 24% in the responders versus 17% in the non-responders (not significant, p = 0.48), and for word association 6% versus 6%.
  • Without epidural: of 12 additional women who consented to the memory part but declined an epidural, 5 (42%) woke at propofol rates of 8–4 mg/kg/h. The authors thus estimate the incidence of wakefulness during the procedure at 21% in 52 patients, and none had recall afterwards. For comparison, Nordström 1997 reported recall in 0.2%. The authors argue that the difference shows that wakefulness and recall are two different things, and that IFT is necessary to detect wakefulness when neuromuscular blockers have been given.
  • Why no memory, according to the authors: they consider that the anaesthesia was adequate, that propofol inhibits recall in conscious volunteers, and that the epidural meant that surgical stimulation did not increase wakefulness. They also write that memory may only be “stored” if the anaesthesia becomes lighter or the stimulation stronger while the patient is responding. These are interpretations, not tested.
  • The authors' view of IFT: a patient who responds to command cannot be called unconscious, regardless of clinical signs. They consider the 20-minute limit a misunderstanding and that clinical signs do not predict who is awake. This is a position taken by authors who have used the technique in several studies. Linassi 2018 (in the app) found that IFT response was far more frequent than explicit recall (34.8% versus 6.2%), which is consistent with response and recall being different things.
  • Caveats: small study, no EEG or processed EEG measured, and testing only within 2 hours. Temazepam premedication, epidural and many tests without adjustment for multiple comparisons may affect the result. The study cannot prove that implicit memory never occurs, only that it was not found here.
Russell and Wang. Br J Anaesth 2001;86:196–202

Implicit memory during anaesthesia: meta-analysis (Linassi 2021)
