  • Design: systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA, registered in PROSPERO) of studies from 1980 to March 2021 in adults after deep sedation (OAA/S 0–1 with spontaneous breathing) or general anaesthesia, with standardised tests of implicit memory (for example word association, word-stem completion and process dissociation). 61 studies (44 randomised), 3906 patients and 119 cohorts were included.
  • Main finding: implicit memory was reported in 43 of 119 cohorts (36.1%). This is the proportion of cohorts with at least one such event and not the proportion of patients, so the figure cannot be read as a risk for the individual patient. Heterogeneity was moderate to high, with different agents, doses and tests.
  • Significant differences (cohort level): ASA III–IV versus I–II gave OR 3.48 (95% CI 1.18–10.25). Deep sedation versus general anaesthesia gave OR 0.10 (0.01–0.76), with implicit memory in 1 of 16 cohorts (6.3%) versus 42 of 103 (40.8%). Benzodiazepine as premedication before general anaesthesia gave OR 0.35 (0.13–0.93, p = 0.05), most pronounced with volatile anaesthesia (OR 0.26, not significant).
  • Not significant: age over 50 years (OR 2.06), duration over 60 minutes (OR 2.56), opioids (OR 2.68, p = 0.08), neuromuscular blockers (OR 3.02, p = 0.09), auditory task during surgical stimulation (OR 2.53, p = 0.13), BIS monitoring (OR 1.07) and BIS-guided anaesthesia (OR 0.62). The authors also found no difference between “light” and “deep” anaesthesia, but the classification was subjective and made by the authors based on agent and dose.
  • Caveat for deep sedation: these cohorts (7 studies) had no neuromuscular blockers, almost no opioids and rarely an auditory task during surgical stimulation (25% versus 88% with general anaesthesia). The difference may therefore be due to something other than depth itself.
  • The authors' interpretation: ASA III–IV may go together with lighter anaesthesia because of haemodynamics, and a stress response with noradrenaline may produce amygdala activation that promotes implicit learning. That brain monitoring does not help is explained by the monitors not capturing structures such as the amygdala and hippocampus. These are hypotheses, not tested.
  • Limitations: the analysis is at cohort level, too few sedation cohorts for subgroup analyses, different tests and time points, and large variation in anaesthetic regimens. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Linassi et al. Life 2021;11:850

Hearing and implicit memory during general anaesthesia: randomised studies (Fu 2021)

  • Design: systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA, PROSPERO) of randomised, blinded studies in adult surgical patients under general anaesthesia with auditory exposure during the procedure (music, positive suggestions, word lists or stories). Search up to 15 October 2020. 53 studies and 4200 patients were included.
  • Explicit memory: open recall testing (43 studies, 3320 patients) was positive in 3 studies (0.54% of patients). Two of these reported 6 and 3 patients, and none remembered having heard the sounds. In one study of total knee replacement, 9 of 15 reported being aware of music. Recognition tests (10 studies, 798 patients) showed above-chance recognition in four studies, but the patients were mostly uncertain and guessing. Free recall (5 studies, 277 patients) showed no explicit memory.
  • Implicit memory: 23 studies (1864 patients). Of 17 studies on perceptual learning or “priming”, 7 (41%) showed signs of implicit memory, and of 6 studies on behavioural change after suggestion, 2 (33%) did. In total 9 of 23 (39%). It was not possible to pool the results in a meta-analysis, because of the reporting and because several studies lacked good controls.
  • Pattern by test: association to the story (“story-related free association”) was positive in all four studies (balanced anaesthesia, without premedication). Word-pair association, word-stem completion and “presented facts” gave mixed results (for example Jelicic 1992 positive and 1993 negative). Category exemplar and preference showed no effect. The studies without signs of implicit memory that used equivalent tests and regimens often had benzodiazepine premedication (Russell and Wang 2001, Westmoreland 1993).
  • The authors' conclusion: sound can be perceived and processed during clinically adequate general anaesthesia and produce implicit memory without explicit recall. That is a strong conclusion, based on 7 of 17 studies that are very different, and several are from the 1990s. The authors themselves write that the incidence, consequences and possible therapeutic use are not clear, and that no factors could be identified. They mention that benzodiazepine premedication may matter, since all the studies with signs of implicit memory (and the music studies) lacked it.
  • Music and postoperative pain: music during the procedure gave lower pain (SMD −0.51 in the first three hours, five studies and 320 patients, and −0.84 after 24 hours, three studies and 226 patients) and less opioid requirement (SMD −0.29, 95% CI −0.57 to −0.02, five studies and 336 patients). Positive suggestions had no effect. The figures rest on few studies.
  • Limitations: randomisation and allocation were not described in 51% of the studies, the studies used different tests and time points, and many used nitrous oxide. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Fu et al. Can J Anesth 2021;68:1231–1253

Connected consciousness after intubation in young adults (Lennertz 2023)

  • Design: prospective cohort study at 10 hospitals in several countries. Patients aged 18–40 years under general anaesthesia with tracheal intubation (not rapid sequence) were tested with the isolated forearm technique (IFT) from 10 seconds after intubation. 338 completed (mean age 30 years, 69% women). Recruitment was stopped early (500 planned) because of funding. Almost all received propofol at induction.
  • Response: 37 of 338 (11%, 95% CI 8–15) squeezed the hand in response. Among women 13% (31/232) and among men 6% (6/106). The adjusted odds ratio for women was 2.7 (CI 1.1–7.6, p = 0.022). Age was not a risk factor, but the study included only young people.
  • Continuous anaesthesia before laryngoscopy (volatile, propofol infusion or repeated propofol bolus doses between induction and laryngoscopy): adjusted odds ratio 0.43 (CI 0.20–0.96). 35% of those who responded and 55% of those who did not respond had received continuous anaesthesia. The induction dose (propofol approx. 2.1–2.2 mg/kg), the time from induction to laryngoscopy (approx. 4 minutes) and the number of attempts did not differ between the groups. The authors suggest that continuous anaesthesia is a simple way to reduce the incidence, but the study is observational and does not show causation.
  • Is the response voluntary? The first two statements were a command and a nonsense sentence, in random order. 13 responded only to the command (3.8%) versus 4 only to the nonsense (1.2%), and 7 responded to both (p = 0.049). Five extended two fingers on command, four answered correctly to “if fish swim in the sea, squeeze my hand”, and three answered incorrectly to “if rocks float on water”.
  • Pain: 18 of 37 (49%) indicated that they had pain when asked “if you have pain, squeeze twice”. Movement in response to laryngoscopy was more common in those who responded (76% versus 42%).
  • Memory: word recognition (16 pairs, 60 minutes after arrival in recovery) was the same for responders and non-responders (8 of 16 in both, equivalent to chance guessing, p = 0.52). There is no sign of implicit memory here. With the modified Brice questionnaire, 5 cases were judged as possible and 1 as definite explicit recall (1.5% and 0.3%). Only one of the two who described the IFT testing had responded during the test.
  • Delirium (Nu-DESC): 14% of the responders versus 7% of the others at 15 minutes (OR 2.0, CI 0.5–5.9) and 3% versus 4% at 30 minutes. No significant difference.
  • The authors' interpretation: connected consciousness without recall is more than one order of magnitude more frequent than explicit recall (0.1–0.2% in other studies). They consider that responding to command and reporting pain is “a higher level of consciousness” than patients and anaesthetists expect. They also write that women may need new research on sensitivity to anaesthetics, and that the doses did not explain the difference.
  • Limitations: tested only after intubation (consciousness may occur later), the IFT assessor was not blinded to the drugs, EEG was not measured, the interpretation of a negative response is unclear (lack of motivation, comprehension or distraction may give an absent response), and the study covers only young adults who received propofol. One author (Raz) declares consulting agreements with Medtronic and Neuroindex.
Lennertz et al. Br J Anaesth 2023;130:e217–e224, published online 2022

Frontal alpha-delta and volitional response (Gaskell 2017)

  • Design: sub-study of EEG recordings from three centres (Waikato, Wisconsin, Liège) in a larger international IFT study. Adults (16 years and older) at laryngoscopy and intubation. EEG from 86 of 90 patients was analysed (four excluded because the timing of the commands was uncertain). None had explicit recall. The anaesthetic was chosen by an independent anaesthetist.
  • Pre-defined test: the authors proposed in advance that a single responder with frontal alpha-delta would refute the claim that the pattern means unconsciousness (“falsification”). The study is not powered to compare means and was not planned for that.
  • Result: 6 of 90 (6.7%) had a clear volitional response. Three (A–C, centres 1 and 2, BIS) responded right after the first command, within one minute after intubation, while the EEG had dominant alpha-delta (delta above 20 dB, alpha above 10 dB) both before laryngoscopy and during the response. Their spectra did not differ from the patients who did not respond. The other three (D–F, centre 3, NeuroSENSE) had received ketamine 25 mg and sufentanil, responded later (approx. 80–160 seconds after intubation, after repeated commands) and had lower delta power and more fast activity.
  • Indices: BIS was 44, 37 and 44 in the alpha-delta responders (all below 45), versus a median of 37 (30–44) in those who did not respond. Permutation entropy, slow wave activity saturation (SWAS) and alpha-delta phase-amplitude coupling (PmaxI) could not separate the responders from the others. PmaxI was below 1 in all six responders, but also in 30 of those who did not respond.
  • Burst suppression: no responder had burst suppression (15 of 60 at centres 1 and 2 and 1 of 20 at centre 3 among those who did not respond). The authors write that burst suppression is the only frontal pattern that appeared to exclude response. That rests on few observations.
  • The authors' conclusion: alpha-delta is not sufficient for unconsciousness. Nor is the pattern necessary, since many patients at centre 3 were unresponsive without alpha-delta. In the discussion they go further and write that the pattern is “not causally linked” to unconsciousness and can be seen as a sign of GABAergic hyperpolarisation rather than unconsciousness itself. That is a stronger claim than the data alone support, and the editorial (Mashour and Avidan) asks for the findings to be replicated.
  • Alternative explanations: the response occurred after the strong stimulation of laryngoscopy and intubation. IFT may underestimate consciousness (anaesthetics affect motivation, cognition and motor function), and the authors write that many who did not respond may have been conscious. They also cannot rule out that the consent process made the response more automatic, and that the responders were not “normally awake”.
  • Limitations: only six responders, different anaesthetic regimens and two different EEG monitors (ketamine attenuates alpha-delta), short 20-second windows and frontal EEG only. The authors propose measuring from more areas than the frontal region.
Gaskell et al. Br J Anaesth 2017;119:664–673

Black swans: commentary on Gaskell 2017 (Mashour and Avidan 2017)

This is an editorial in BJA, that is, the authors’ assessment and not a data study. It comments on Gaskell et al. 2017, which is covered in the app.

  • Background: the article recounts that frontal alpha and slow activity have been studied for several decades as a marker of anaesthesia-induced unconsciousness, including in hundreds of surgical patients and healthy volunteers. They point out that not all unconscious states produce anteriorised alpha. This applies to ketamine and slowly titrated sevoflurane (Blain-Moraes), and alpha is affected by age (Cornelissen 2015, Purdon 2015).
  • The Gaskell finding as described: a secondary analysis of an international IFT study (about 5% of 260 patients responded meaningfully after laryngoscopy). Of 90 patients with EEG, six responded, and three of them had frontal alpha-delta. The other three had received ketamine, which according to Akeju 2016 attenuates frontal alpha and slow power in volunteers on ether, so they could have had alpha-delta without ketamine. The latter is an assumption.
  • The time aspect: the responses came after laryngoscopy, a dynamic phase. The authors suggest that the frontal cortex may be disconnected from the surroundings before other areas, and that response together with alpha-delta is less likely during a stable maintenance phase. This is a hypothesis, not demonstrated.
  • What needs to be clarified according to them: (1) that the findings are replicated, (2) whether response with frontal alpha-delta also occurs in stable periods, and (3) whether EEG over other areas shows classic signs of unconsciousness at the time of response. They consider that the finding could in that case weaken a mechanistic view of frontal oscillations, but not necessarily the clinical utility.
  • The authors’ conclusion: processed indices such as BIS are “not perfect” for detecting consciousness and unconsciousness, but they believe they can probably still reduce the incidence of awareness with recall, and that one should not become nihilistic about brain monitoring. This is their assessment. The results in BAG-RECALL (covered in the app) did not show that BIS was better than end-tidal gas.
  • Beyond EEG: the editorial also refers to arguments that the frontal cortex is not necessarily required for consciousness (disconnection of frontal areas is due to disturbances in posterior network hubs, and children without a cortex show signs of simple subjective experience, Merker 2007). These are theoretical points without their own data.
Mashour and Avidan. Br J Anaesth 2017;119:563–565

Unresponsiveness is not unconsciousness (Sanders 2012)

Review article and hypothesis (Anesthesiology 2012;116:946–959). It builds up the concepts the app uses about consciousness, connectedness and response, and reviews the IFT literature.

  • Three concepts: consciousness (subjective experience), connectedness to the surroundings, and responsiveness (spontaneous or goal-directed, for example following a command). In the awake state all three are present. In deep NREM sleep none are present. In REM sleep consciousness is present, but not connectedness and responsiveness. The authors argue that this shows unresponsiveness is not the same as unconsciousness.
  • Dreaming during anaesthesia: dreams were reported in at least 27% with propofol and 28% with desflurane (Leslie 2009, 300 patients). None of those who reported dreaming described experiencing the surgery itself. The authors interpret this as disconnected consciousness, but the figures are probably too low since the report requires the dream to be remembered. Scopolamine prevented dreaming during propofol and nitrous oxide (Toscano 2007), and physostigmine restored consciousness in sedated volunteers (Meuret 2000). This suggests that dreaming is driven by cholinergic activity.
  • IFT overview: of 18 studies, 5 were excluded (irrelevant stimuli), and in the remainder a median of 37% responded (range 0–100%). The studies were too heterogeneous to be pooled in a meta-analysis. BIS could not distinguish responders from non-responders (Schneider 2002: BIS rose from about 52 to about 70 in both groups after laryngoscopy, and 40% became responsive).
  • Lucid dreaming and IFT: people having a lucid dream can communicate with pre-agreed eye or hand movements, that is, goal-directed behaviour without spontaneous movement. The authors argue that positive IFT responses may resemble this, and refer to a patient who was not paralysed and who moved the hand on command without spontaneous movements (Andrade 2008). They write in a footnote that it is unclear whether a lucid dreamer would respond directly to a verbal command, and that this must be investigated. They also write that the studies of lucid dreaming and IFT all used predefined commands, and that this may be important.
  • Hypothesis on connectedness: the authors propose that noradrenaline signalling maintains connectedness (ventral attention network, locus coeruleus), since GABAergic agents weaken histamine and orexin, but not noradrenaline. Alpha2 agonists could therefore help disconnect the patient. This is a hypothesis that must be tested, and partial support comes from a single patient in an fMRI study (the authors themselves write that it is prone to false positive findings). They do not advocate an alpha2 agonist as the sole agent.
  • Unresponsiveness is subcortical: unresponsiveness to verbal command occurs at lower propofol doses than those that weaken cortico-thalamic coupling (Mhuircheartaigh 2010, Boveroux 2010). The authors propose that the amygdala and putamen (motivation and action selection) play a role in the patient not moving spontaneously, yet still being able to follow a command.
  • The goal of anaesthesia: they argue that the goal is to prevent the experience of surgery and not merely to prevent it being remembered, and calculate that the number needed to treat to prevent recall is about 1.002 (0.2% awareness), whereas it is about 1.587 to prevent connected consciousness (median 37%). This is their argument, and there is an opposing view (amnesia and immobility as the minimum) which they themselves mention.
  • Monitoring: current monitors rest on the assumption that responsiveness and connected consciousness go together, and the authors argue that this gives both false positive and false negative answers that more advanced signal processing cannot correct. They propose that measures of connectedness and of consciousness should be separated, and mention TMS-EEG, long-latency evoked potentials and activity in the ventral attention network as possible avenues, but write that it is unclear which features will work.
  • Caveats: one of the authors reports lecture fees from Hospira, without influence on the article. Much of the theory consists of hypotheses, and the underlying studies (IFT) are heterogeneous.
Sanders et al. Anesthesiology 2012;116:946–959

Awareness: controversies and non-controversies (Mashour and Avidan 2015)

Narrative review (Br J Anaesth 2015;115 suppl 1:i20–i26) that sorts the field into what the authors regard as settled and unsettled. This is the same Mashour who co-authored Mashour and Pryor 2025.

  • Settled, detection: a structured Brice interview consistently gives about 1–2 per 1000 (or higher), whereas spontaneous reports, quality data and non-specific questionnaires give an order of magnitude lower (table 1 in the article). In one population of about 19,000 patients the Brice interview found 19 definite cases, only 3 of which were reported spontaneously, and no spontaneous cases were missed by the interview.
  • Settled, awareness without recall is more common than with: consciousness and memory are separable processes, and the dose for unconsciousness is higher than the dose for amnesia. IFT studies: 42% responded 2–5 minutes after induction (Tunstall and Sheikh, 113 patients) and 97% after skin incision (King 1993), none with explicit recall.
  • Settled, BIS: five randomised trials give the same picture: BIS is better than clinical signs alone (B-Aware, and with TIVA), but not better than an alarm on end-tidal gas (B-Unaware, BAG-RECALL, Michigan Awareness Control Study). In B-Aware, 2 patients (0.17 %) had awareness with BIS versus 11 (0.91 %) with clinical monitoring. In the only large trial of propofol TIVA (Zhang 2011), the rate fell from 0.65 % to 0.14 % with BIS.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025 (table 36.4)
  • Settled, neuromuscular blocking agents: both incidence and distressing awareness are higher with neuromuscular blockade (Sandin: 0.18% versus 0.1%; NAP5). The authors consider that avoiding or limiting neuromuscular blockers may be the most effective available measure against traumatic awareness.
  • Unsettled, true versus false reports: the Brice questions are not psychometrically validated and may “elicit false reports or memories”. Many report awareness only at later interviews. Distinguishing true from false reports is difficult, and experts often disagree about “possible” awareness. Most dream reports are probably unrelated to awareness and likely occur during emergence (Leslie 2007 and 2009), but Samuelsson 2008 found awareness 19 times more common among patients who reported dreaming, so the relationship is unsettled.
  • Unsettled, IFT as a distinct state: the authors consider that an unequivocal IFT response should be regarded as consciousness until the opposite is shown. Pandit proposes a “third state” (“dysanaesthesia”) in which the patient follows a simple command without a conscious self, but without data.
  • Otherwise unsettled: a genetic component, the psychological consequences of awareness without recall (little evidence that implicit memory causes PTSD), and whether unwanted awareness during sedation is a clinical problem.
  • Relevance for Mashour and Pryor 2025 versus figure 36.1: that the Brice interview can produce false reports or false memories, and that an AWR report cannot be verified against an objective measurement, is the closest support in the sources for the sentence “Occasionally AWR may present absent of conscious experience at the time”. Read this way, the sentence is about reports, not about genuine episodic memory being formed without experience, and then it does not conflict with Mashour and Pryor 2025. This is an interpretation; neither chapter says so explicitly.
  • Caveats: narrative review without a systematic search. Avidan was on the BJA editorial board. Several of the cited studies are the authors’ own.
Mashour and Avidan. Br J Anaesth 2015;115(suppl 1):i20–i26

Consciousness is lost in networks, differently per drug

  • Each drug gives its own EEG picture. Propofol gives more slow activity and frontal alpha at loss of response. Ketamine gives more theta and gamma, and alpha does not move forward.See
  • Loss of response is a gradual transition. Under propofol, the response to clicks disappeared before the response to words and names. The transition to loss of response took a median of 23.9 minutes.See
  • Network disconnection may be a common end point. Connectivity from frontal to parietal regions is weakened with propofol, sevoflurane and ketamine. But dexmedetomidine does not fully fit, and subanaesthetic ketamine also weakens connectivity in awake subjects.See
  • Consciousness has several dimensions. Level, content and connectedness are affected differently by the drugs. Under ketamine, cortical complexity was as in wakefulness, and all six reported vivid dreams.See
  • Frontal EEG alone does not reliably separate conscious from unconscious. Patients with frontal alpha–delta can respond to command, and patients without the pattern can be unresponsive. New measures are promising but not clinically established.See

The theme cards below explain the connections. Each study is summarised under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Each drug has its own EEG picture

Unconsciousness does not look the same in the EEG for all drugs. Propofol and ketamine give almost opposite pictures, and xenon differs from both.

  • Propofol gives slow activity, and alpha moves from the back of the head to the forehead. At loss of response, slow power (0.1–1 Hz) rose more than tenfold. Occipital alpha, that is alpha over the back of the head, disappeared, and coherent frontal alpha emerged instead. This shift from the back of the head to the front is called anteriorisation. Everything reversed when the response returned. The response to clicks disappeared before the response to words and names, and the transition took a median of 23.9 minutes (ten healthy volunteers).Source: Purdon 2013
  • Ketamine gives theta and gamma, and alpha does not move forward. Frontal theta rises (from 0.64 to 4.25 dB), posterior alpha declines without moving forward, and gamma and delta increase. Measured with depth electrodes in ten epilepsy patients, subanaesthetic ketamine gave more gamma frontally and in the cingulate, lower alpha almost everywhere and a 3–4 Hz rhythm in the posteromedial cortex.Sources: Vlisides 2017, Tian 2023
  • Propofol on top of ketamine reverses much of the ketamine picture. The frontal gamma increase and the alpha decrease reversed in most regions. Occipital alpha, however, fell further, and 3–4 Hz increased further. The study reported no p-values.Source: Tian 2023
  • Xenon is a third variant. All three drugs increased slow activity, but to different degrees: 24.3 slow waves per minute with xenon, 12.8 with propofol and 2.8 with ketamine. Gamma fell with xenon and rose with ketamine. Only six participants per drug.Source: Sarasso 2015
  • More frontal theta may mean the ketamine dose is high enough for anaesthesia. Theta rose clearly at the anaesthetic dose, but not at the low dose. The authors therefore think monitors with frontal electrodes only can probably detect it. This is a suggestion and has not been tested clinically. The studies are small and were done in healthy volunteers and epilepsy patients.Sources: Vlisides 2017, Tian 2023

The studies in detail:

Purdon 2013 Vlisides 2017 Tian 2023 Sarasso 2015

Network disconnection: a possible common end point

If the drugs act so differently, what do they have in common? Probably a breakdown in communication between cortical regions, especially between frontal and parietal regions. These are hypotheses built on correlative findings.

  • Weakened frontal-to-parietal connectivity may be common to the drugs. Reduced frontal-to-parietal connectivity has been shown with propofol, sevoflurane and ketamine. Higher-order networks break down, sensorimotor networks are relatively preserved, and complexity falls. This is a hypothesis.Sources: Hudetz and Mashour 2016, Lee 2013, Montupil 2023
  • Some findings do not fit. Dexmedetomidine disrupted thalamocortical but not frontoparietal connectivity. Granger causality has given opposite results. Subanaesthetic ketamine also weakens connectivity in awake subjects. The degree of loss may therefore be what distinguishes.Sources: Akeju 2014, Hudetz and Mashour 2016, Muthukumaraswamy 2015, Vlisides 2017
  • The information arrives but does not pass on. In monkeys given ketamine, touch could still be decoded in the primary somatosensory cortex. In the motor cortex, decoding fell to chance level, and the transfer of information between the regions fell. Only three monkeys, and it is unclear whether the disconnection causes the unconsciousness or merely accompanies it.Source: Schroeder 2016
  • Alpha moving forward is probably a consequence, not the cause. Ketamine weakened frontal-to-parietal connectivity without producing anteriorised alpha. Anteriorisation is therefore probably caused by disrupted feedback.Source: Hudetz and Mashour 2016
  • Disconnection is also seen in simple organisms. Under isoflurane, the fruit fly loses feedback from higher to lower brain centres. It has been proposed to describe general anaesthesia as disconnection from the environment. Network measures from many channels may become better clinical tools, but this has not been shown in clinical use.Sources: Kelz and Mashour 2019, Liu 2023

The studies in detail:

Hudetz and Mashour 2016 Lee 2013 Akeju 2014 Muthukumaraswamy 2015 Vlisides 2017 Schroeder 2016 Montupil 2023 Kelz and Mashour 2019 Liu 2023

Consciousness has several dimensions

Consciousness is not an on-off switch. It can be divided into level (arousal), content and connectedness to the environment, and the drugs affect these dimensions differently. The models are theories, not proven.

  • The drugs act on different dimensions. Dexmedetomidine probably acts mainly on level, and ketamine disrupts content. Propofol and halogenated ethers are thought to affect both. This is a hypothesis, and the distinction is not sharp.Source: Mashour and Hudetz 2017
  • No response does not mean no consciousness. Internal awareness (one’s own thoughts) is distinguished from external awareness, also called connectedness. In dreams and under ketamine, internal but not external awareness is present. Volitional response indicates connected consciousness.Source: Montupil 2023
  • Ketamine can give consciousness without response. The complexity of the cortical response to magnetic stimulation (PCI) was low under propofol (0.24) and xenon (0.17). Under ketamine (0.44) it did not differ from wakefulness. All six given ketamine reported vivid dreams. None of the 12 given propofol or xenon reported experiences.Source: Sarasso 2015
  • Disconnection, not the absence of all experience, is the common end point. Hudetz and Mashour argue that what the drugs have in common is that contact with the environment is broken, seen clinically as unresponsiveness. This is called the disconnection hypothesis. What must be prevented is connected consciousness, that is the patient perceiving and reacting to what is happening around them. Disconnected consciousness, such as a dream, may persist without the patient taking in the surgery, and different drugs produce different subjective states even at the same level of unresponsiveness. The authors stress that the hypothesis concerns connected consciousness that can be tracked by behaviour, not consciousness in general, and that the underlying mechanism is unknown.Source: Hudetz and Mashour 2016
  • Anaesthesia may fragment the sense of self. One perspective is that anaesthesia gradually produces an “anaesthetic depersonalisation”, in which the patient is passive and usually pain-free. This fits poorly with the proportion of IFT responders in pain ranging from 0 to 100 % across studies, and being 49 % in another study.Sources: Sleigh, Warnaby and Tracey 2018 (perspective article); Sanders 2012; Lennertz 2023

The studies in detail:

Mashour and Hudetz 2017 Montupil 2023 Sarasso 2015 Hudetz and Mashour 2016 Sleigh, Warnaby and Tracey 2018

What EEG can and cannot say about consciousness

The EEG says a great deal about the state of the brain, but frontal EEG alone does not reliably distinguish conscious from unconscious. Several new measures are being tested.

  • Alpha–delta is the expected pattern, not proof of unconsciousness. Montupil 2023 writes that frontal alpha–delta is seen almost always during surgical anaesthesia, meaning anaesthesia with propofol and the inhalational agents. It does not apply to ketamine, and the pattern is weak or absent in the oldest patients and in infants. The point is that the pattern neither proves nor excludes consciousness: patients who have it can respond to command, and patients without it can be unresponsive. Slow-wave saturation probably cannot distinguish unconsciousness from disconnected consciousness either. The network involved is distributed over frontal and parietal cortex.Sources: Montupil 2023, Hudetz and Mashour 2016
  • Read the raw EEG and spectrogram, not just the index. There are arguments against “black box” indices. Phase–amplitude coupling here means where on the slow wave the alpha oscillation is largest. With “peak-max” the alpha is largest at the peak of the slow wave, and this is seen during deep unconsciousness. With “trough-max” the alpha is largest in the trough, and this is seen around the transitions in and out. When the coupling shifted from peak-max to trough-max, it signalled that consciousness could return, and both can be seen in the raw EEG. Frontal indices from one or two channels vary with the drug and rise, for example, with nitrous oxide and ketamine.Sources: Purdon 2013, Liu 2023
  • Patients respond differently to the same dose. In some volunteers, light propofol sedation gave a transient increase in EEG complexity, whereas others went straight towards suppression. The complexity of the resting EEG before the drug was related to the change. The samples are small, and Newman is retrospective and not tested clinically.Source: Newman 2026
  • New measures are promising but not clinically established. The perturbational complexity index (PCI) measures how complex the response becomes when the brain is perturbed with a magnetic pulse through the skull (TMS): a rich, long-lasting response gives a high PCI, a brief stereotyped one a low PCI. An EEG-based consciousness indicator (ECI) tries to give the same without magnetic stimulation. The P3 is a response in the EEG about 300 ms after a sound that breaks the pattern in a series of identical sounds, an oddball. An EEG-based attention index (CEI) was higher in sedated patients who later remembered the procedure. One proposal is that PCI measures the capacity for experience, whereas frontoparietal connectivity and the P3b rather reflect connectedness.Sources: Montupil 2023, Sarasso 2015
  • The goal may be to prevent patient distress, not to prove unconsciousness. Distress here means that the patient experiences something painful or frightening, not the physiological stress response to surgery. The authors describe patients with connected consciousness during anaesthesia, shown with the isolated forearm technique, as usually passive and apparently pain-free: they have lost sentience and agency, but not necessarily the higher functions. They call the state anaesthetic depersonalisation. They write that anterior slow-wave saturation, the alpha–delta pattern and parieto-frontal dys-synchrony may be sufficiently good biomarkers of the loss of sentience and agency to preclude patient distress, but that more work is needed. They put it conditionally: if prevention of patient distress is an acceptable therapeutic target for general anaesthesia, this may be a sufficient goal. The evidence rests on few formally assessed patients, and this is a perspective article, not a new study.Source: Sleigh, Warnaby and Tracey 2018

The studies in detail:

Montupil 2023 Hudetz and Mashour 2016 Purdon 2013 Liu 2023 Newman 2026 Sarasso 2015 Sleigh, Warnaby and Tracey 2018

An aside: anaesthesia acts on very different organisms

From Kelz and Mashour (Curr Biol 2019;29:R1199–R1210), a review of what general anaesthesia does to organisms from single-celled animals to primates. Not part of the curriculum, but good stories for a lecture.

  • The word: Oliver Wendell Holmes proposed “anaesthesia” in November 1846, one month after the first public ether demonstration. It is Greek for insensibility: a state in which the organism is no longer receptive to stimuli from the outside world.
  • Claude Bernard in the 1800s: experiments with plants led him to propose that the capacity to be anaesthetised is a definition of life: “that which lives must sense and can be anaesthetised, the rest is dead”.
  • Roughly the same dose for everyone: from bacteria and yeast to worms, flies, plants and humans, it takes roughly the same amount of volatile anaesthetic before function fails. The whole span is only about tenfold, and between the most and least sensitive mouse strains the difference is less than 40%. Interpretation based on the source: a span that small between organisms that different points to a site of action conserved through evolution.
  • Plants: ether and lidocaine stop leaf closure in Mimosa pudica, the trap in the Venus flytrap and the tentacles in sundew, and block the action potentials in the Venus flytrap. Plants can moreover emit anaesthetic gases when stressed, perhaps as a self-regulating loop.Source: Kelz and Mashour 2019
  • The firefly enzyme: Meyer and Overton’s correlation between lipid solubility and potency holds over six orders of magnitude. But so does the inhibition of firefly luciferase by anaesthetics in a cell-free system, and mirror-image isomers with equal lipid solubility have different potency. This helped bring down the pure lipid theory.
  • Mitochondria: in the roundworm C. elegans the gas-1 mutation in complex I gives a 25–80% lower effective dose of several ethers. The same applies to mice, and humans with complex I disease are highly sensitive to volatile anaesthetics, whereas those with defects in complexes II–IV are not.
  • Without a brain, without neurons: C. elegans has no brain and the paramecium has not a single neuron, yet the paramecium loses both chemoresponsiveness and motility in a dose-dependent manner. Under isoflurane the fruit fly selectively loses feedback from higher to lower brain centres, as mammals do, and C. elegans develops desynchronised neurons and less information exchange.
  • The authors’ proposed definition: since unconsciousness is only meaningful for a few species, they propose that general anaesthesia is best described as disconnection from the surroundings, both the receiving side (sensing) and the executing side (movement), with a common network principle: lower efficiency and more modularity, so that information is no longer exchanged.
Kelz and Mashour. Curr Biol 2019;29:R1199–R1210
The studies in detail: networks and disconnection, propofol and ketamine in the EEG, complexity, theories of consciousness, paradoxical excitation (11 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Common endpoint: disconnection of frontoparietal networks (Hudetz and Mashour 2016)

Review article and hypothesis (Anesth Analg 2016;123:1228–1240), not a data study. The authors argue that different anaesthetics share a functional endpoint, and that this endpoint is unresponsiveness, not a common subjective state.

  • The hypothesis: depression or disconnection of the lateral frontoparietal network, particularly frontal-to-parietal feedback, is a common correlate of disrupted connected consciousness, seen clinically as unresponsiveness. The authors stress that this is not a classic “unitary hypothesis”, and that the underlying mechanism (cortico-cortical or thalamocortical) is not known.
  • Support: John 2001 (176 surgical patients, EEG coherence) found that reduced 40 Hz gamma coherence from frontal to parietal best tracked loss and return of response. Studies with propofol, sevoflurane and ketamine (including Lee 2013 in surgical patients, Boly 2012 and Jordan 2013 in volunteers) showed reduced frontal-to-parietal connectivity during unconsciousness. During surgical anaesthesia both directions were reduced. The authors mention that such findings have also been made in animals (including Imas 2005 and Raz 2014).
  • Ketamine: frontal-to-parietal coupling was also reduced by ketamine (Lee 2013, surgical patients, and MEG at subanaesthetic doses, Muthukumaraswamy 2015), even though ketamine does not produce anteriorised alpha and lowers alpha power (Blain-Moraes 2014). The authors therefore consider that anteriorisation is probably a consequence of disrupted feedback and not the cause (modelling study, Zhou 2015).
  • Conflicting findings: dexmedetomidine disrupted thalamocortical, but not frontoparietal, functional connectivity (Akeju 2014), even though the areas were metabolically suppressed. Granger causality gave opposite results (increased connectivity in Barrett 2012 and Nicolaou 2012), and some fMRI studies found increased connectivity in the default mode network during propofol. The authors write that there is no absolute relationship between a particular direction of information transfer and consciousness.
  • Possible mechanisms: reorganisation of network hubs (particularly in the posterior parietal cortex, Lee 2013 and modelling by Moon 2015), and fragmentation in time (alternating active and silent states with propofol, Lewis 2012, in three epilepsy patients) and fewer available network states. The mesocircuit hypothesis (Schiff) is mentioned as a possible subcortical explanation.
  • Dreaming and unresponsiveness: the authors write that unresponsiveness can still coexist with disconnected consciousness, for example a dream, and that different agents produce different subjective states even at the same level of unresponsiveness (Noreika 2011). They state that their hypothesis concerns connected consciousness that can be tracked behaviourally, not consciousness in general.
  • Alternative views: the authors mention subcortical arousal systems and the thalamus as necessary for consciousness (lesions in midline nuclei of the pons and intralaminar thalamic nuclei cause coma), and that the final effect on consciousness probably depends on cortical function.
  • Limitations they themselves mention: most of the studies are correlative, often with a factorial design that may mix in changes occurring before the actual transition, and there is a need for a reliable, generally accepted way of measuring information transfer and a measure of experience that is independent of behaviour.
  • Connection within the app: the hypothesis explains why frontal EEG may have limited value as the sole marker (cf. Gaskell and the editorial on black swans), since the network being studied is distributed over frontal and parietal cortex.
Hudetz and Mashour. Anesth Analg 2016;123:1228–1240

Brain networks and anaesthesia: methods and findings (Liu 2023)

Narrative review (Engineering 2023;20:77–95) from an engineering group in China. It is not systematic and does not assess study quality. The authors searched Web of Science in July 2021 and selected 27 EEG-based and 16 fMRI-based network studies as representative.

  • Micro level: the review mentions GABAA, NMDA (most inhaled agents inhibit NMDA, to varying degrees) and two-pore potassium channels (mice lacking these channels are less sensitive to inhaled agents).
  • Macro level: three explanatory models are disrupted connections between thalamus and cortex, effects on the sleep–wake systems, and cortical fragmentation. Propofol and sevoflurane act earlier in the cortex than subcortically (Velly 2007).
  • Three types of connectivity: structural (physical pathways), functional (statistical co-variation, for example coherence, PLI, wPLI and PLV) and effective (directed influence, for example Granger causality and transfer entropy).
  • Graph theory: the brain is described as a small-world network balancing local specialisation and global integration. Measures such as clustering coefficient, path length, efficiency, modularity and hubs (rich club) are used to describe how the network changes. Dynamic connectivity is analysed with sliding time windows.
  • Findings: frontoparietal disconnection under propofol has been shown in several studies.
  • Clinical: BIS and entropy are frontal measures from one or two channels and vary with the drug. BIS rises with nitrous oxide and ketamine, and is affected by opioids, muscle relaxants and EMG. The authors believe network measures from 25–64 channels could become better clinical tools, but this has not been shown in clinical use, and dynamic analyses require long signals.
  • Unresponsiveness: the review stresses that unresponsiveness is not the same as unconsciousness (Sanders 2012).
  • Caveats: several citations do not match the claims (see Discrepancies). No conflicts of interest declared, public Chinese funding.
Liu et al. Engineering 2023;20:77–95

Propofol with 64-channel EEG: what happens as consciousness is lost and returns (Purdon 2013)

The study on which most of the propofol signatures in the app are based (PNAS 2013;110:E1142–E1151). Ten healthy volunteers received propofol with effect-site targets of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 µg/ml for 14 minutes per step, followed by stepwise reduction. Every 4 seconds a sound was played (click or word/own name) to be answered with a button press, so that response could be tracked almost continuously. 64-channel EEG, eyes closed, Laplacian reference. Three anaesthetists present, arterial blood pressure and phenylephrine as needed.

  • The response disappears gradually and depends on how salient the stimulus is: in 10 of 10, response to clicks was lost before response to words and name during induction, and during emergence response to words returned before clicks. The transition from first effect to loss of consciousness took a median of 23.9 minutes (6.7–32.8), and from first recovered response to full response a median of 25.5 minutes. No “switch”, but a sliding zone in which the answer depends on the stimulus.
  • Three things happen simultaneously at loss of response: power in the slow band (0.1–1 Hz) increases more than tenfold and is spread over the whole head; the spatially coherent occipital alpha (awake, eyes closed) disappears; and a spatially coherent frontal alpha (about 10 Hz) emerges. All of this reverses when the response returns. This is what “anteriorisation of alpha” means.
  • “Traveling peak”: in the 30 minutes before loss of response, broad gamma/beta power increased frontally (paradoxical excitation), and the median frequency in the 2–40 Hz range fell from 23.1 to 12.0 Hz with narrower bandwidth (17.4 to 9.1 Hz) towards loss of response. During emergence it rose from 11.8 to 21.9 Hz. The authors consider that gamma, beta and alpha are not separate phenomena, but the same thalamocortical oscillation changing frequency with dose.
  • Two types of phase-amplitude coupling: “trough-max” (alpha largest in the trough of the slow wave) around the transitions, from about 20 minutes before to 10 minutes after loss of response, and again about 15 minutes before emergence; “peak-max” (alpha largest at the peak) during deep unconsciousness 10–40 minutes after. The transition from peak-max to trough-max signalled that consciousness could return. Both can be seen in the raw EEG. This is also what Sepúlveda 2026 uses (Kmod) to show that the brain is not the same after burst suppression.
  • Mechanism (the authors’ interpretation): frontal alpha emerges when cortex and thalamus mutually lock into synchronised oscillations (the Ching 2010 model); the slow oscillation resembles the slow wave of sleep and reflects alternating “up” and “down” states in the cortex. Hyperpolarisation of thalamic relay neurons may explain why occipital alpha disappears at the same time as frontal alpha emerges.
  • What it means for monitoring: the authors argue against “black box” indices and for reading the spectrogram and raw EEG directly, as the app does. The study is the basis for the signatures in Purdon 2015 Part I and the simulator in the Spectrogram tab.
  • Caveats: ten healthy, young volunteers with slow, stepwise dosing and without surgery, opioid or neuromuscular blocking agents; consciousness measured as response to sound (cf. “unresponsiveness is not unconsciousness”, Sanders 2012). Purdon and Brown report a patent application on anaesthesia monitoring.
Purdon et al. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 2013;110:E1142–E1151

Ketamine alone with high-density EEG: theta and loss of anterior-to-posterior alpha connectivity (Vlisides 2017)

The counterpart to Purdon 2013 (the card above), from Mashour’s group (Anesthesiology 2017;127:58–69). Ten healthy volunteers (20–40 years, ASA 1) received ketamine as the only drug, with 128-channel EEG through four states: awake rest, subanaesthetic infusion (0.5 mg/kg over 40 min), anaesthetic bolus (1.5 mg/kg) and emergence. Loss of consciousness was defined as failure to respond to two consecutive commands (hand squeeze).

  • Clinical course: all ten lost the response to command after the bolus, on average 1.2 minutes after injection, and were without response for an average of 10.7 minutes (SD 3.5). 6 of 10 had nausea and vomiting, one needed a jaw thrust.
  • Theta is the main signature: frontal theta power (4–8 Hz) rose from 0.64 dB (awake) to 4.25 dB during ketamine anaesthesia (subanaesthetic 0.60, emergence 0.68; p < 0.001), and was elevated both frontally and posteriorly. The authors refer to Domino’s first ketamine study from 1965, which described “thetalike waves” at coma doses.
  • Alpha falls, no anteriorisation: posterior alpha declined gradually from the subanaesthetic dose, and alpha did not shift frontally as it does during propofol. Gamma and delta increased during anaesthesia.
  • Connectivity: phase locking (wPLI) shifted from alpha to theta during anaesthesia, with the highest theta connectivity within anterior areas (0.23) and between anterior and posterior (0.22). Directed alpha connectivity from anterior to posterior areas (dPLI) was lowest during anaesthesia (0.028) and was unchanged at the subanaesthetic dose, so the loss appeared to be dose-dependent. Everything returned towards baseline on emergence.
  • The authors’ interpretation: increased theta power and theta connectivity together with loss of anterior-to-posterior alpha connectivity may reflect a network imbalance, explicitly called speculative. Clinically they suggest that more frontal theta may mean the ketamine dose is high enough for anaesthesia, and that frontal electrodes alone are probably enough to see it.
  • Relation to propofol: loss of frontal-to-parietal connectivity has been described for propofol, sevoflurane and ketamine (Lee 2013, Mashour 2013), but subanaesthetic ketamine also disrupts frontoparietal connectivity in awake subjects (Muthukumaraswamy 2015), so the loss of connectivity is not necessarily the same as loss of consciousness. The authors suggest that the degree of loss, not its presence, may be what distinguishes.
  • Caveats: ten participants, the subanaesthetic infusion immediately before the bolus may have affected the anaesthetic phase, 86–91 of 128 channels were retained, ondansetron and scopolamine were given, gamma was not analysed for connectivity because of possible EMG, and the spectral and connectivity analyses were based on different artefact cleaning. No conflicts of interest declared, funded by the NIH.
Vlisides et al. Anesthesiology 2017;127:58–69

Ketamine measured inside the brain: frontal gamma, 3 Hz and interaction with propofol (Tian 2023)

Nature Communications 2023;14:1748. Ten epilepsy patients (22–59 years) with depth electrodes received subanaesthetic ketamine (0.5 mg/kg over 14 minutes) before electrode removal, followed by a propofol bolus for induction. 824 bipolar channels from ten patients under ketamine, and 606 channels from seven patients after propofol. Dissociation was measured with an abbreviated CADSS scale with yes/no answers.

  • Ketamine: gamma (25–55 Hz) rose most in the anterior and posterior cingulate and frontal areas, and also in the hippocampus/amygdala and striatum among others, but fell occipitally. Alpha (8–15 Hz) fell in almost all areas, most in the postcentral and occipital cortex. Slow and delta fell in most areas. Beta fell in many places but rose in the hippocampus/amygdala.
  • 3 Hz rhythm: increased 3–4 Hz power in the posterior and isthmus cingulate (posteromedial cortex) and pars opercularis, peaking between 3 and 6 Hz. This rhythm has previously been proposed as a mechanism for dissociation, based on experiments in mice.
  • When propofol was added: the frontal gamma increase (40–55 Hz) was reversed, and the alpha decrease was reversed in most areas, but occipital alpha fell further. Beta, theta, slow and delta rose almost everywhere, and 3–4 Hz rose further.
  • The authors’ interpretation: effects counteracted by propofol are interpreted as NMDA-mediated disinhibition. Effects that are enhanced are interpreted as shared HCN1 inhibition. Frontal and hippocampal gamma are linked to the antidepressant effect of ketamine, but the study measured neither depression nor antidepressant effect.
  • Caveats: epilepsy patients with electrodes placed for clinical reasons, and dissociation was assessed only with yes/no. The authors report effect sizes and bootstrap confidence intervals, but no p values and no correction for multiple comparisons. The propofol phase is missing for three patients, and doses of the anaesthetic drugs are given for only five. Some dB values are implausibly high (see Discrepancies). Purdon, Brown and Akeju report patents licensed to Masimo, and Purdon and Brown are co-founders of PASCALL Systems.
Tian et al. Nat Commun 2023;14:1748

Ketamine in monkeys: sensory information reaches the cortex but does not pass on (Schroeder 2016)

NeuroImage 2016;134:459–465, from the groups of Mashour and Chestek. Three rhesus monkeys with microelectrodes in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and motor cortex (M1). The fingers were stroked twice per second before and after ketamine 10 mg/kg intramuscularly.

  • Starting point: ketamine fits poorly with the usual explanations of anaesthesia. The authors write that ketamine does not bind with high affinity to GABAA, does not depress thalamic metabolism, does not activate the sleep-promoting preoptic nucleus and does not depress high-frequency EEG.
  • Decoding touch: which finger was touched could be decoded from neural activity in S1 (89.3% correct) and M1 (68.7%) in awake animals. 10–30 minutes after ketamine, M1 fell to chance level (27.4%, chance 33.3%), while S1 was preserved. After four hours, M1 was back at 54.4%. Overall firing rates did not change.
  • Coupling between neurons: transfer entropy, a measure of directed information transfer, fell between S1 and M1, and also within S1.
  • Oscillations in S1: beta fell, while gamma and delta rose, as described in scalp EEG in humans under ketamine anaesthesia.
  • Interpretation: transfer from the thalamus to S1 appears preserved, while transfer between cortical areas fails. The authors see this as a possible common endpoint for drugs with different molecular targets. They note themselves that subanaesthetic ketamine doses also change coupling in humans, so it is unclear whether the disconnection causes unconsciousness or merely accompanies it.
  • Caveats: three monkeys, one of which completed only an abbreviated experiment, and the transfer entropy and spectral analyses are based on two of them. Blood concentrations were not measured, and consciousness was judged from reflexes. The study was funded by the NIH.
Schroeder et al. NeuroImage 2016;134:459–465

Cortical complexity under propofol, xenon and ketamine (Sarasso 2015)

Curr Biol 2015;25:3099–3105. 18 healthy volunteers were assigned to three experiments, six per drug. The cortex was stimulated with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over premotor (BA 6) or parietal (BA 7) cortex, and the response was recorded with 60-channel EEG, first awake and then at deep unresponsiveness (Ramsay 6). After emergence, participants were asked about experiences.

  • PCI: the perturbational complexity index measures how complex the response to stimulation is. It is high when the signal spreads to many areas that respond differently (integration and differentiation). Awake PCI was about 0.47–0.50. Under propofol PCI was 0.24 (0.20–0.30), under xenon 0.17 (0.08–0.24) and under ketamine 0.44 (0.35–0.55), which did not differ from wakefulness.
  • Propofol: a local, low-amplitude response that did not spread, i.e. loss of integration. The authors link this to GABA enhancement triggering local «down states» in the cortex.
  • Xenon: a large, stereotyped slow wave spreading over the whole cortex, similar to the response in NREM sleep, i.e. loss of differentiation. The authors link this to xenon enhancing two-pore potassium channels in addition to blocking NMDA.
  • Ketamine: a fast, complex response as in wakefulness. Ketamine enhances neither GABA nor potassium currents and increases cortical acetylcholine. The response resembles that described in REM sleep, but here with high-amplitude slow waves in the spontaneous EEG and with participants unrousable.
  • Spontaneous EEG: all three drugs increased slow activity (0.5–4.5 Hz), most with propofol and xenon, and theta rose equally with all three. Sigma (12–16 Hz) rose only with propofol. Gamma (30–40 Hz) fell with xenon and rose with ketamine. Slow waves per minute were 12.8 with propofol, 24.3 with xenon and 2.8 with ketamine.
  • Reports: none of the 12 who received propofol or xenon reported experiences. One xenon participant had a feeling of having experienced something just before awakening, without explicit recall. All six who received ketamine reported long, vivid dreams unrelated to the surroundings, and four of six had hallucinations at emergence.
  • Interpretation: consciousness and responsiveness can dissociate. The authors believe PCI measures the brain’s capacity for experience, while frontoparietal connectivity and the P3b response reflect connectedness to the environment, since they fall with both propofol and ketamine.
  • Caveats: six participants per drug and different people in each experiment. Reports may be forgotten or confabulated, which the authors discuss. TMS-EEG is a research method. Tononi reports a research collaboration with Philips Respironics unrelated to this study, and Rex reports research funding from Air Liquide.
Sarasso et al. Curr Biol 2015;25:3099–3105

Anaesthesia as fragmentation of the sense of self (Sleigh, Warnaby and Tracey 2018)

Perspective article (Br J Anaesth 2018;121:233–240), that is, a theory and interpretation based on earlier EEG and imaging studies, not a new study.

  • Main idea: the authors propose describing anaesthesia as gradual fragmentation of the “sense of self” rather than as loss of consciousness. The sense of self is divided into a core (the experience of existing), bodily feeling (sentience), agency and will, higher cognitive functions (including metacognition) and a narrative sense of self (memory and biography). The model is hierarchical, with the core remaining until last.
  • Four clinical states: awake and distressed, awake without distress (“anaesthetic depersonalisation”), dreaming and oblivion (no experience). The authors assume that the brain is in a labile state right at the border of wakefulness at loss of response to verbal command, and that this resembles the state at positive IFT.
  • Depersonalisation: patients with positive IFT are described as passive and usually without pain, without spontaneous movements, with loss of bodily feeling and agency, but with much of the higher functions intact. The authors consider that this is probably common and specific to general anaesthesia, and that it differs from natural sleep, where loss of agency and feeling accompanies or follows loss of self-awareness. Table 1 also lists lucid dreaming as a possible state, but the article says nothing about response to verbal command in it.
  • Neural correlates: at about 0.5–0.7 MAC (or the propofol equivalent) anterior brain areas are affected first, and the connection from anterior to posterior cortex and thalamus is weakened. The connection between anterior and posterior medial parietal areas (under Pz) is lost roughly when response to command disappears. Connections within posterior areas are maintained even at high concentrations (propofol about 4 µg/ml), and activity in the posterior cingulate is proposed as a possible marker of the core, a “pilot light” that is only extinguished at burst suppression. This is a hypothesis.
  • The salience network and insula: propofol suppresses activity in the dorsal anterior insula (Warnaby 2016), at about 2 µg/ml and before slow waves dominate the EEG, in step with loss of volitional response. The authors propose that this is an important difference from natural sleep, and that “interoceptive suppression” may explain the depersonalisation. Why the insula should be especially sensitive is unclear, and they speculate about receptor types and network architecture. Dexmedetomidine and sleep preserve thalamic connectivity to arousal and salience networks better than propofol does (Guldenmund 2017).
  • Implications for monitoring: if the goal is complete unconsciousness, one must demonstrate weakened connectivity in the posterior cingulate or find a reliable anterior EEG marker for it. If the goal is only to prevent distress, interoceptive suppression may be sufficient. The authors write that anterior slow-delta saturation and the alpha-delta pattern (and dyssynchrony between parietal and frontal) may be good enough markers of loss of feeling and agency to prevent distress, but that the evidence rests on few formally assessed patients and more work is needed.
  • Caveats: much is hypothesis and speculation. The claim that depersonalised patients are usually pain-free is in tension with the fact that the proportion of IFT responders with pain varied from 0 to 100% between the studies in Sanders 2012 (table 2) and was 49% in Lennertz 2023. The authors Warnaby and Tracey are listed as inventors on pending patents concerning loss of perception during anaesthesia and saturation of slow-wave activity.
Sleigh et al. Br J Anaesth 2018;121:233–240

Level and content: two dimensions of consciousness (Mashour and Hudetz 2017)

This is a hypothesis and theory article, not a data study. The authors propose that different mechanisms of anaesthetic agents can be linked to two dimensions of consciousness. The result is an explanatory model and is not proven.

  • Level (wakefulness, arousal): governed by bottom-up mechanisms in the brainstem, hypothalamus and thalamus (sleep-wake networks). Anaesthetics can suppress wake-promoting nuclei and activate sleep-promoting ones (isoflurane activates the VLPO, Moore 2012, and dexmedetomidine acts via α2 receptors in the hypothalamus, Zhang 2015).
  • Content (what one experiences): governed by top-down mechanisms in cortical and thalamocortical networks. Frontal-parietal disconnection is a consistent finding in studies of propofol, sevoflurane and ketamine.
  • Dexmedetomidine: acts mainly via bottom-up mechanisms with relatively preserved frontal-parietal connectivity (even though the areas are metabolically suppressed). The authors propose that preserved “machinery” for content may explain the rapid reversibility.
  • Ketamine: activates wake-promoting nuclei, increases high-frequency EEG and preserves signs of wakefulness such as eye opening and movement, but disrupts content so that the patient loses connected consciousness.
  • Propofol and halogenated ethers: assumed to affect both level and content, and thereby produce a deeper effect. That dexmedetomidine and ketamine have more one-dimensional effects is proposed as a possible explanation for why they are limited as sole agents for maintenance.
  • Nuances: the authors stress that level and content cannot be fully separated, and that the distinction between bottom-up and top-down is unlikely to be sharp. They also mention that two dimensions may be too few, and refer to a model with three axes (consciousness, wakefulness and motility).
  • This helps in understanding the distinction between connected and disconnected consciousness in the scenarios above, but the article is not a direct source for EEG patterns.
Mashour and Hudetz. Front Neural Circuits 2017;11:44

The nature of consciousness in anaesthesia: states and theories (Montupil 2023)

Narrative review from Liège (BJA Open 2023;8:100224; Montupil, Cardone, Staquet et al. and Bonhomme). The starting point is that consciousness does not simply disappear during anaesthesia: the brain passes through different states with varying content and varying contact with the environment.

  • Three clinical dimensions: wakefulness (arousal), awareness and responsiveness. Awareness is divided into internal awareness (one's own thoughts, inner speech) and external awareness, also called connectedness, meaning perception of the environment. In disconnected consciousness there is internal but no external awareness, as in dreams during anaesthesia or sleep and under ketamine. In connected consciousness both are present.
  • Responsiveness is not consciousness: volitional responsiveness suggests connected consciousness, but its absence does not mean absence of internal or external awareness. A reflex, such as withdrawing the arm from a painful stimulus, is not a volitional response either. Using the isolated forearm technique, connected consciousness after laryngoscopy has been estimated at close to 5 %, 11 % in young patients and 13 % in women, and it is rarely followed by explicit recall.
  • The arousal system: propofol, sevoflurane and xenon reduce activity in the thalamus and the ascending arousal network. Dexmedetomidine inhibits the locus coeruleus, so that the preoptic area inhibits the arousal centres, as in NREM sleep. Ketamine inhibits inhibitory interneurones and produces a hyperglutamatergic state. Whether the drugs act first in the cortex or below it is unresolved; the authors think the truth probably lies in between and depends on drug and dose. Stimulation of the central thalamus reversed anaesthesia in monkeys, but this may be a non-specific arousal effect.
  • Five theories: the global neuronal workspace (information becomes conscious when it «ignites» and is broadcast frontoparietally), integrated information (a posterior «hot zone» in the temporal, parietal and occipital lobes, measured as complexity), recurrent processing, predictive processing and higher-order theory. All are challenged, and adversarial collaborations have both confirmed and challenged the first two.
  • Common to the anaesthetics: breakdown of higher-order networks, especially frontoparietal connectivity, relatively preserved sensorimotor networks, reduced complexity and breakdown of the posterior «hot zone». Authors disagree on whether it is feedback or feedforward connectivity that breaks down.
  • What EEG can and cannot do: frontal alpha–delta is seen almost always during surgical anaesthesia and was first taken as a sign of unconsciousness, but patients with the pattern may still respond to command, and patients without it can be unresponsive. Slow-wave activity saturation is probably not specific enough to distinguish unconsciousness from disconnected consciousness. Promising but not clinically established measures include the perturbational complexity index (PCI, with TMS), an EEG-based consciousness indicator (ECI), the P3 response to oddball tones and an EEG-based attention index (CEI), which was higher in sedated patients who later recalled the procedure.
  • Caveats: narrative review. Most studies compare wakefulness with unresponsiveness, which is not necessarily unconsciousness. Bonhomme reports financial relationships with Orion Pharma, Medtronic, Edwards and Elsevier.
Montupil et al. BJA Open 2023;8:100224

Paradoxical excitation under propofol: complexity and entropy (Newman 2026)

Retrospective analysis of existing EEG from two small datasets of healthy adults (McGill/Montreal, Boston, Michigan; Br J Anaesth 2026;137:525–534). The question: why do some people get a transient increase in EEG complexity at light propofol sedation (“paradoxical excitation”) while others go straight towards suppression, and can the resting EEG before the drug say anything about it?

  • Datasets: Chennu (n = 20, mean 30.8 years): rest, mild (0.6 µg/ml) and moderate (1.2 µg/ml) propofol sedation, then rest; effect-site concentration estimated from blood samples; 13 “responsive” and 7 “drowsy” by a hit-rate threshold of 60% in an auditory task at moderate sedation. ReCCognition (n = 8, mean 24.7 years): propofol infusion 100, 200 and 300 µg/kg/min, 5 minutes each, up to deep sedation where everyone lost responsiveness.
  • The measures: Lempel–Ziv complexity (LZC, type I) rises with randomness. Statistical complexity (SC, type II) follows an inverted U against entropy and is highest when order and randomness are balanced (SC = permutation entropy multiplied by the Jensen–Shannon distance to a reference distribution). They are plotted together on a “complexity–entropy causal plane” (CECP). Median values over 10-second epochs and channels, EEG filtered 0.5–45 Hz.
  • Group differences at moderate sedation: in the responsive group LZC rose and SC fell (both significant, p about 0.02–0.05; text and table differ somewhat, see “Discrepancies”). In the drowsy group there was no significant change. In ReCCognition LZC rose at light and moderate sedation and fell clearly at deep sedation, when everyone lost responsiveness; SC did the opposite. The authors interpret this as the paradoxical increase existing only at moderate sedation and vanishing when responsiveness vanishes.
  • Resting EEG and individual response: in Chennu, baseline SC was negatively correlated with the change in SC at moderate sedation (r = −0.70, p < 0.001; strongest in the responsive, r = −0.89, and absent in the drowsy, r = −0.19). This was repeated in ReCCognition (r = −0.81, p = 0.028, n = 7). In the drowsy, those with higher baseline SC had a lower hit rate (r = −0.88, p = 0.009, n = 7), but not in the responsive (r = −0.36, p = 0.22). Baseline SC was not significantly correlated with time to loss of consciousness (r = −0.46, p = 0.30, n = 7) or with estimated effect-site concentration (r = 0.65 in drowsy and r = −0.30 in responsive, both not significant). Concentration and hit rate correlated across the whole sample (r = −0.59, p = 0.006).
  • Inflection point: where the regression line for change in SC against baseline SC crosses zero lies a “threshold” of about 0.13–0.14 (figure 4 gives ~0.1378). From the sign of the regression and table 1 (baseline medians 0.143 for responsive and 0.128 for drowsy), SC falls in those with baseline above the threshold (paradoxical excitation) and rises in those below (suppression). The text and figure legend describe the direction the other way round, see “Discrepancies”.
  • The path in the plane: the ReCCognition group average follows a non-linear path: from intermediate complexity and entropy at rest, via lower complexity and higher entropy (“more disorder”) at light and moderate sedation, to higher complexity and lower entropy at deep sedation. All participants passed through a shared intermediate zone of high entropy and low complexity. The paths lay close to simulated coloured noise, but with higher SC, which the authors read as preserved temporal dependencies.
  • The authors’ interpretation: the brain’s state before the drug, not pharmacokinetics, decides the response, since baseline SC did not correlate significantly with concentration. This is indirect: non-significant correlations in groups of 7 and 13 do not show that concentration is irrelevant.
  • Caveats: small samples of healthy people (20 and 8, several analyses with n = 7), retrospective, propofol only, no demographic covariates (individual data were missing in Chennu), and the threshold is taken from one dataset and compared with another, not tested prospectively. The authors suggest that baseline SC and position in the plane could guide individual titration and reduce the risk of awareness or excessive suppression, but this has not been tried. The study says nothing about clinical indices. No conflicts of interest declared; funding from the Fondation pour la recherche médicale, NSERC and a Canada Research Chair.
Newman, Maschke, Mashour and Blain-Moraes. Br J Anaesth 2026;137:525–534
The content is written in the author's own words and uses Miller's as a map to the original sources. See the Sources tab for which originals should be checked.
Spectrogram: the pattern over time

The spectrogram shows how EEG power is distributed across frequencies and time, and the pattern depends on drug, dose and age.

More about this tab

The “Simulators” sub-tab lets you try it yourself. The tab also explains how the spectrogram is built, how it looks different in older patients and children, why the effect lags behind the concentration, and which artefacts can produce misleading numbers. The main message is to read the raw EEG and spectrogram together with the index, not the index alone.

From raw EEG to spectrogram (DSA): step by step

This is how the monitor builds the spectrogram. The figure calculates the spectrogram from a synthetic EEG signal while you watch, one window at a time. Choose a step to see it highlighted.

How the spectrogram is computed (4 steps)
  1. The raw EEG is divided into short windows, 2 seconds in the figure.
  2. The Fourier transform breaks each window down into sine waves of different frequency and amplitude (delta, theta, alpha, beta).
  3. Power per frequency is drawn as a spectrum, and power is translated into colour.
  4. The colour strips are placed side by side along the time axis, one per window, and become a spectrogram (density spectral array): time across, frequency upwards and power in colour.

Window length and calculation method vary between monitors and studies. Power can be shown in decibels (logarithmic scale), because it can differ by orders of magnitude across frequencies. The figure can show both multitaper (2 s windows, three tapers, time-bandwidth product 2, as in Guay 2025) and a single Hann window. The figure moves the window one second at a time, while Guay 2025 let the windows overlap by 0.2 seconds. The signal is synthetic and time is compressed: the changes leading up to loss of responsiveness took about 30 minutes in the study, here one minute.Sources: Guay 2025 Part 2, Purdon 2013

Purpose-made figure, synthetic signal Guay 2025 Part 2, Purdon 2013, Purdon 2015 Part I
