From raw EEG to spectrogram: two figures (Sleigh et al. 2025)

How a spectrogram is made, and what it shows, based on Miller's chapter 36. The figures are original drawings with simulated data for teaching, not patient recordings.

  • 1 Raw EEG is shown in microvolts over time. It changes constantly and gives only a brief glimpse of the brain state.
  • 2 Power spectrum: a few seconds of EEG are broken down into frequencies with the Fourier transform. Power is amplitude squared and is shown for each frequency. Power falls with increasing frequency (the background, 1/f), and oscillations such as delta and alpha appear as peaks above it.
  • 3 Spectrogram: the spectra are stacked one after another over time. Time runs to the right, frequency upwards, and colour shows power: red is a lot, blue is little. The whole course can be read at a glance.
  • What you see: the transitions are gradual. Burst suppression gives vertical stripes, blue (suppression) alternating with red (bursts). Alpha–delta gives red bands around 10 Hz and at the bottom. During emergence the background becomes less steep, and alpha gradually shifts towards higher frequency.
  • There is high power in slow-delta and alpha, above a background where power falls with increasing frequency.
  • How steeply the background falls is affected by the dose. It is hard to see in the raw EEG, but easy to see in the spectrum.
Frequency bandNameProposed origin
0.1–2 HzSlow waveIntracortical
0.5–4 HzDeltaThalamocortical and cortical
4–8 HzThetaThalamocortical as alpha slows into this range, otherwise unknown
8–12 HzAlphaThalamocortical
12–30 HzBetaIntracortical

Table: the classic frequency bands as the chapter gives them. Slow wave and delta overlap. Other sources in the app use slightly different limits, for example alpha 8–13 Hz.

  • As the concentration rises, fast activity above 20 Hz disappears (the colour turns dark blue), and narrow bands appear in delta, theta and alpha. This may suggest thalamocortical hyperpolarisation.
  • Above about 1.7 % alpha becomes slower (from about 10 Hz down towards 7–8 Hz) and weaker, so that almost all activity lies in a broader delta band (B). The chapter compares this to the shift from light to deep slow-wave sleep. At even higher concentrations burst suppression can occur.
  • As the concentration falls, the pattern roughly reverses (C).

Source: Sleigh et al. 2025 (Miller's ch. 36, figs. 36.3, 36.4, 36.5 and 36.7 and table 36.1). The figures are redrawn with simulated data, not copied.

Sleigh et al. 2025

Raw EEG: seven patterns side by side

Here you see schematic raw EEG traces (5 or 10 seconds, same scale for all) from the same patient in different states under propofol. Awake with EMG has been added to show what muscle activity looks like. The traces are synthetic, not patient data, and the amplitudes are only approximate ratios between the patterns.Source: Purdon 2015 Part I, fig. 2

Purdon 2015 Part I, fig. 2 Schematic, not patient data

What happens to alpha as the dose rises

Alpha behaves differently as the dose rises, and the three pictures you see on the screen are not three separate phenomena. They are three points on one axis: how deeply thalamus and cortex are hyperpolarised.

  • Alpha sliding down towards theta: mostly the inhaled agents. As the sevoflurane concentration rises above about 1.7%, the peak alpha frequency falls from around 10 Hz to below the band limit, about 7 to 8 Hz, and alpha power fades, so that almost all the activity lies in a broadened delta band. The shift from alpha to delta dominance is described as pathognomonic of a more deeply hyperpolarised thalamocortical system, analogous to the shift from light to deep slow-wave sleep.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025
  • Theta under anaesthesia is often alpha that has slowed. In the band table, theta is listed as thalamocortical as alpha slows into this range, otherwise unknown. That is why theta here is not a separate phenomenon with a mechanism of its own.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025
  • Alpha that simply disappears: mostly propofol. Propofol gives the same basic pattern as the gases, but with three differences: alpha and delta are narrower and stronger, a theta peak is less common, and the peak alpha frequency does not generally slow below 10 Hz. Propofol alpha therefore does not slide into theta in the same way. It goes away, and delta takes over.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025
  • Alpha within the bursts: the burst mirrors the EEG just before the suppression. Under propofol that is often alpha and slow-delta, so you see alpha inside the bursts. If the EEG had already become mostly slow-delta, that is what the bursts contain. Deeper anaesthesia mainly gives longer suppression periods and rarer bursts, not a different content within the burst.Sources: Ching 2012 (the model’s prediction); Sleigh et al. 2025
  • The mechanism, as the model explains it. Frontal alpha arises in the loop between thalamus and cortex, and it requires a fairly narrow window of hyperpolarisation: enough for the loop to oscillate around 10 Hz, but not so much that it stops oscillating. As hyperpolarisation increases, the oscillation first slows, then the loop can no longer sustain it, and slow-delta takes over. Further still, the cortex cannot keep activity going continuously, and the alternation between burst and suppression appears. This is a model, not a measurement.Sources: Ching 2010; Ching 2012
  • Two caveats. In older patients alpha fades at lower doses, and the bursts are weaker and the suppression shallower, so the pattern is harder to recognise. And loss of alpha does not always mean dose: the same picture appears when the circulation fails.Sources: Sleigh et al. 2025; Guay 2025
  • Does alpha within the bursts carry a meaning of its own? This is poorly supported. The closest is one study in which the content of the bursts distinguished successful from failed weaning, while the pause length did not. It had 19 patients.Source: Johnson 2016, reported in the Burst suppression tab

Further:

Sleigh et al. 2025 Ching 2010 Ching 2012

Key points

  • The spectrogram is raw EEG broken down into frequencies: Raw EEG is divided into short windows, the Fourier transform breaks each window down into frequencies, and power is shown as colour along the time axis. Window length and computation method vary between monitors and studies.See
  • Raw EEG has recognisable patterns: The patterns range from awake with and without EMG, through fast beta, alpha–delta and slow-delta, to burst suppression and isoelectric EEG. Recognising them makes the spectrogram easier to interpret. (interpretation based on the sources)See
  • Alpha during emergence appears to matter: Absence of clear frontal alpha during emergence appears to be associated with an increased risk of delirium, and burst suppression during maintenance was also associated with delirium. Older patients more often move into and remain in delta-dominant and suppressed patterns.See
  • Suppressed EEG lowers cerebral oxygen consumption, but only up to a point: At burst suppression CMRO2 is reduced by about 60 %, and more anaesthetic than is needed for full suppression gives no further reduction. Ketamine and nitrous oxide are exceptions.See
  • A spectrogram without alpha may reflect age, deep anaesthesia or both: The index can look “normal” even when the alpha–delta pattern is absent. Older patients have visibly less alpha, and at high sevoflurane concentrations alpha power can fade.See “Clinical example: spectrogram without a clear alpha band (“spectral fade”)”

The simulators are in the “Simulators” sub-tab. The cards below explain the background.

Slow-wave anaesthesia: ddSWA, sdSWA and NSWA (Gruenbaum and García, Lobo and Lamperti ch. 5)

Four spectral patterns describe the EEG at the end of maintenance and during emergence. The terms are used in teaching on EEG during anaesthesia.Sources: Peri-operative Brain Monitoring (Gruenbaum and García, Springer 2025), ch. 5; Chander 2014 (PLoS ONE)

  • ddSWA (delta-dominant slow-wave anaesthesia): more power in the delta band than in the spindle band. The raw EEG is dominated by slow waves.
  • sdSWA (spindle-dominant slow-wave anaesthesia): more power in the spindle band than in delta. The spectrogram shows a clear band in the alpha range above delta.
  • NSWA (non-slow-wave anaesthesia): low power in both the spindle and the delta band. The raw EEG has very low amplitude.
  • Burst suppression: shown for comparison, with a spectrogram in which burst suppression turns into ddSWA.
  • The “spindle band” is the alpha band you see in the spectrogram. The name is borrowed from sleep research. Sleep spindles are generated in the thalamus and wax and wane in strength. Chander and colleagues use the same name for the frontal alpha oscillations during both sleep and anaesthesia, and called the 8–14 Hz band “alpha/spindle”. Delta was 0.5–4 Hz. The authors stress that sleep and anaesthesia are not the same, although circuits, neurotransmitters and EEG patterns overlap. Anaesthetics can shift the thalamocortical oscillations outside the classic alpha band (8–12 Hz), so some use an extended alpha band of 7–17 Hz.Sources: Chander 2014; Gruenbaum and García, Lobo and Lamperti ch. 5; García 2021
  • The EEG during emergence is linked to pain afterwards. Patients who spent a long time in a pattern with little delta and little alpha (NSWA) before waking more often woke with little pain. The 31 % who woke directly from the slow-wave pattern more often had severe pain. The authors compare NSWA with REM sleep. The study observed 100 patients in orthopaedic surgery under volatile anaesthesia and recorded only frontal EEG, so it shows an association, not a cause. Strong frontal alpha, followed by a fall in total frontal power, is linked to a lower risk of pain in the PACU.Sources: Chander 2014; Gruenbaum and García, Lobo and Lamperti ch. 5
  • Missing alpha during emergence is associated with an increased risk of delirium. This applies particularly when the patient has received ketamine or nitrous oxide. Burst suppression during maintenance was also associated with delirium in the PACU.Sources: Gruenbaum and García, Lobo and Lamperti ch. 5; Hesse 2019
  • The course of emergence is linked to delirium in the PACU. Of 626 patients, 125 had delirium in the PACU (CAM-ICU). The most favourable course was ddSWA → sdSWA → NSWA → awake. Compared with this course, the odds were about 4 times higher when the patient went abruptly from ddSWA straight to awake, and about 8 times higher when emergence started in NSWA. When the spindle phase (sdSWA) was missing and the patient had received ketamine or nitrous oxide, the odds were 6.5 times higher. Burst suppression during maintenance had OR 1.86. Patients with delirium were more often readmitted (OR 2.17) and twice as often stayed more than 6 days in hospital. The study is observational.Source: Hesse 2019 (626 patients)
  • The EEG indices capture the course only partly. EEG from 59 patients on sevoflurane was replayed to four monitors. With the favourable course the index rose almost linearly. With the abrupt course it stayed low for a long time and then rose suddenly. With a start in NSWA it was high early. The monitors separated the courses differently, and agreement between them was only moderate. The authors’ advice: know the monitor you use.Source: Obert et al. 2026 (Anesth Analg)
  • Caveats. The sample was small and retrospective, only sevoflurane was used, and the favourable group was much younger (median 37 versus 61 years). Cognitive outcome was not measured in this analysis. Four authors hold patents on EEG features, and two have received support from several monitor manufacturers for EEG teaching.Source: Obert et al. 2026
  • Older patients more easily end up in slow and suppressed patterns. Younger patients more often reach and keep an alpha-dominant pattern. Older patients have less alpha to begin with, so alpha loss as a sign of nociception is harder to interpret in them.Source: Gruenbaum and García, Lobo and Lamperti ch. 5, fig. 5.1
  • Link to the raw EEG card and the simulator (interpretation based on the sources): ddSWA corresponds roughly to “Slow-delta” and sdSWA roughly to “Alpha–delta” in the raw EEG card above. NSWA has low amplitude in all bands. The transition from sdSWA via NSWA to awake is what the simulator shows as emergence.
  • Caveats: the chapter is an overview, not a systematic review. Chander 2014 is presented via the chapter, not from the original article. García is a co-author of both the chapter and Chander 2014.

Why do EEG and the brain's energy use track each other?

Around 60% of the brain's energy use goes to electrophysiological function, which is what the EEG shows. When the EEG is suppressed with barbiturates, isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane, propofol or etomidate, the brain's oxygen consumption (CMRO₂) falls. At burst suppression it is reduced by about 60%. More anaesthetic than is needed for complete suppression gives no further reduction, because the “housekeeping” portion is not affected. Ketamine and nitrous oxide are exceptions, and ketamine can increase CMR. The figures vary slightly between chapters: about a 60% reduction at burst suppression, and about 50% of baseline at isoelectric EEG with thiopental.Sources: Patel et al. 2025; Vuyk et al. 2025

Patel et al. 2025

Clinical example: spectrogram without a distinct alpha band (“spectral fade”)

Schematic drawing based on a clinical screenshot. The screenshot is not reproduced.

  • What the screenshot showed: BIS 50, SEF 19 Hz, SR 0 and low EMG over about 50 minutes. In the DSA image the power lies in the delta range (red/yellow band below about 4 Hz), whereas theta, alpha and beta have uniformly low power (green-blue) without a distinct, stronger alpha band around 8–12 Hz. The amplitude curve at the bottom is low and stable.
  • Interpretation: “spectral fade” is a clinical term for the higher frequencies, particularly alpha, fading in the spectrogram, so that only the slow activity remains. The index can look “normal” even though the characteristic alpha-delta pattern is missing. The pattern is described in older patients, but age, drug and dose for this example are not given here.Sources: Purdon 2015, BJA; Lobo and Lamperti ch. 3
  • Alpha can be missing because of age, deep anaesthesia or both. In older patients (70–90 years) alpha power and alpha coherence are visibly absent from the group spectrogram, under both propofol and sevoflurane. The young (18–38 years) have distinct alpha. With deep sevoflurane (above about 1.7%) the alpha peak shows slowing to 7–8 Hz and the alpha power fades, so that almost all activity lies in an extended delta band. The Purdon article does not use the word “fade”. Miller's uses “the alpha power fades” about deep sevoflurane.Sources: Purdon, Pavone and colleagues, Br J Anaesth 2015;115:i46–i57, figs. 3 and 4; Sleigh et al. 2025, fig. 36.7
Clinical example, drawn schematically Purdon 2015, BJA

Older patients: low-amplitude EEG, lower doses

  • The EEG becomes low-amplitude with age: In 70–90-year-olds the oscillations were about 2–3 times smaller than in 18–38-year-olds. Under propofol, alpha was about 2.7 times and slow-delta about 1.8 times smaller. The pattern was the same, so you often need to adjust the scale to see it. Whether alpha falls more than the rest is unresolved: one study found it, another found distinct alpha with slow induction.See
  • EEG age does not always follow calendar age. Variation between patients was large, and middle-aged patients lay somewhere between young and older patients. The authors suggest that the raw EEG and spectrogram may show the individual’s “brain age” better than their year of birth.Source: Purdon 2015 BJA
  • An index value can mislead in older patients: Indices not adjusted for age may give raised values in older patients. Dosing towards a target index value may then cause burst suppression. This is an untested hypothesis.See
  • Older patients stopped responding at a higher index. In 30 patients (18 under and 12 over 65 years) given a slow propofol infusion, BIS averaged 77 in older and 59 in younger patients when they stopped responding, about 18 points higher. The calculated effect-site concentration (Schnider model) was similar in the groups (4.3 and 4.8 µg/ml). Older patients also had lower alpha power, lower total power and higher SEF95 (17 vs 12 Hz). Lempel–Ziv complexity was higher in older patients, whereas permutation entropy was similar in both groups. The authors suggest permutation entropy may become an age-independent measure, but the study is small.Source: Biggs 2022
  • Burst suppression may be about the dose: In three studies with slow induction, no one developed burst suppression, and an EEG “frailty” score mostly measured age. Whether burst suppression reflects vulnerability, overdosing or both is unresolved.See
  • Low alpha and burst suppression are linked to delirium: Patients who developed delirium had lower alpha power and alpha peak frequency, also after adjustment for age. Burst suppression had an OR of 2.51. Theta has not been shown to be a marker.See
  • Older patients need less on average: MAC and MAC-awake fall by about 6 % per decade after age 30. The textbook suggests lower doses to avoid burst suppression, even though large RCTs have not consistently shown less delirium with EEG-guided anaesthesia.See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Lower amplitude with age, but alpha is there

With age, the EEG during anaesthesia becomes low-amplitude. The question is whether this is just a weaker signal, or whether the pattern changes too.

  • Older patients have smaller oscillations in all bands. In 70–90-year-olds the oscillations were about 2–3 times smaller than in 18–38-year-olds, under both propofol and sevoflurane. Patients aged 65 years or older also had lower absolute power in all bands.Sources: Purdon 2015, Obert 2024
  • Whether alpha falls most is unresolved. In one study, alpha power and alpha coherence fell more than the other bands, most clearly under propofol. With slow induction, even the oldest showed distinct alpha and the classic pattern with delta and alpha, only at lower amplitude (when power was normalised to total power). One possible explanation is method of induction and timing: ordinary bolus induction and maintenance during surgery in the first study, slow titration and the first minutes after loss of response in the second. Both studies are small (only 8 older patients in the propofol group in the first).Sources: Purdon 2015, Obert 2024, Mehler 2024
  • Alpha also becomes slower, not just weaker. In older patients both alpha coherence and the alpha peak frequency were significantly lower than in younger ones, on top of the fall in power across all bands. A child or a young adult therefore has a faster alpha peak than an old patient. Within childhood it is alpha power and coherence that develop: alpha emerges at about 3–4 months and becomes coherent at about 10 months, and the sources give no alpha peak frequency for the youngest.Sources: Purdon 2015 (155 patients aged 18–90); Cornelissen 2015, 2018
  • Two explanations. Cortical atrophy and a thicker CSF layer may attenuate amplitude equally at all frequencies. An additional fall in alpha may indicate altered function in frontal thalamocortical circuits. This is an argument, not tested. Normal ageing brings less white matter and reduced connectivity, but not substantial neuronal loss. This fits with lower amplitude and preserved spectral structure.Sources: Purdon 2015, Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025
  • Index values may be too high in older patients. Indices not adjusted for age may give raised values in older patients because power is lower. Dosing towards a target index value may then cause burst suppression. The authors propose adjusting the scale of raw EEG and spectrogram for age. This is a hypothesis not tested in the study.Source: Purdon 2015

The studies in detail:

Purdon 2015 Obert 2024 Mehler 2024 Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025

Burst suppression in older patients: vulnerable brain or too much drug?

Older patients more often develop burst suppression. The studies disagree about why, and the answer affects what one should do.

  • Burst suppression occurred often in ordinary practice in the studies. The probability of an episode increased with age, approaching 1 in the oldest under propofol and about 0.6 under sevoflurane. The episodes were short. The literature reports up to 70 % burst suppression with bolus induction in older patients.Sources: Purdon 2015, Mehler 2024 (citing the literature)
  • With slow induction, no one developed burst suppression. This held in three studies, with 51, 23 (over 69 years) and 75 patients. Burst suppression at induction is interpreted as “overshoot” after a bolus, to which older, frail brains respond. The last study is based on patients from the Chilean slow-induction studies, so the three findings are not fully independent of each other (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Obert 2024, Mehler 2024, Ostertag 2025
  • An EEG “frailty” score mostly measures age. The score was proposed to detect a “frail brain” and linked to burst suppression at induction. But the score and all its components correlated with age, and it “probably only detects an older brain”. Burst suppression with rapid bolus induction may say more about overdosing than about vulnerability.Sources: Touchard 2019, Ostertag 2025
  • The cause is unresolved. Burst suppression may reflect a vulnerable brain, anaesthesia-induced metabolic failure or both. Age and low physical activity are associated with burst suppression. Whether burst suppression is cause or marker is not discussed in the textbook.Sources: Xu 2025, Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025

The studies in detail:

Purdon 2015 Obert 2024 Mehler 2024 Ostertag 2025 Touchard 2019 Xu 2025

Anaesthesia as a stress test for the ageing brain

  • Anaesthesia may reveal a vulnerable brain. The authors regard anaesthesia and surgery as a “stress test” for the ageing brain. The EEG during anaesthesia may say something about brain health, not only about depth. This is a hypothesis, not established practice.Source: Berger 2023 (review)
  • Little frontal alpha during anaesthesia is linked to poorer cognition before surgery. Patients with cognitive impairment before surgery had lower alpha power during anaesthesia. Low alpha was also linked to more delirium afterwards.Source: Berger 2023 (review)
  • Burst suppression at a low dose may be a warning. When burst suppression appears at a lower concentration than usual, it may suggest a more sensitive brain. It was linked to a higher risk of delirium.Source: Berger 2023 (review)
  • Emergence without frontal alpha is linked to delirium in recovery. The pattern was not accurate enough for diagnosis, but predicted delirium better than age alone.Source: Berger 2023 (review)
  • It can be useful to attach the electrodes before induction. This gives you a picture of the patient’s awake EEG for comparison. Slowing in the EEG before surgery has been linked to delirium afterwards.Source: Berger 2023 (review)
  • It has not been shown that dosing by alpha prevents delirium. One randomised trial found a shorter hospital stay as a secondary finding. The index value (BIS) usually did not distinguish between patients with and without delirium.Source: Berger 2023 (review)

What the EEG during anaesthesia says about delirium

A meta-analysis of 42 studies with 13,115 patients brings together which EEG measures during anaesthesia are associated with postoperative delirium. Indices were not included as measures.Source: Xu 2025

  • Low alpha is linked to delirium. Patients who developed delirium had lower alpha power (−1.43 dB) and lower alpha peak frequency (−0.73 Hz). In three studies that adjusted for age, the OR was 0.86 per dB of alpha power. So alpha seems to say something beyond age. Broadband power loss is more easily explained by age-related changes. Disproportionately low alpha may point to disturbance in thalamocortical circuits.Sources: Xu 2025, Purdon 2015
  • Burst suppression is linked to delirium. Occurrence had OR 2.51 (95% CI 1.65–3.81), robust in all subanalyses. Suppression ratio (BSR) was not associated. Severe EEG suppression has consistently been associated with delirium.Sources: Xu 2025, Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025 (Fritz 2016, 2018)
  • Theta has not been shown to be a marker. Most studies found no difference in theta or delta power, and “EEG slowing” was not associated with delirium overall.Source: Xu 2025
  • Low alpha is not always a warning sign. Under dexmedetomidine, older patients had low alpha without a fall in MoCA one hour after emergence. It is an open question whether low alpha is only a risk marker under purely GABAergic regimens. This is a pilot with 23 patients, and delirium after the recovery unit was not measured.Source: Mehler 2024
  • Association, not cause. Index guidance weakened, but did not remove, the association. Guidance aiming for higher alpha rather than an index value could conceivably reduce delirium. This is a hypothesis now being investigated.Source: Xu 2025

The studies in detail:

Xu 2025 Purdon 2015 Mehler 2024 Fritz 2016 Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025

Dosing in older patients: lower requirements, and avoid burst suppression

Older patients need less anaesthetic on average. The textbook and the induction studies point in the same direction, but rest on different kinds of evidence.

  • Older patients need lower doses on average. MAC and MAC-awake fall by about 6 % per decade after age 30, and older patients are more sensitive to midazolam and opioids. Propofol above 1.5 mg/kg at induction is associated with severe hypotension, which affects 22 % of older patients. With slow induction, older patients needed 1.06 versus 1.35 mg/kg propofol, and the effect-site concentration at loss of response was 2.6 versus 3.15 µg/ml.Sources: Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025, Obert 2024
  • The models are uncertain in older patients. The Schnider model is based on only nine healthy volunteers over 65 years. The Eleveld model gives lower calculated effect-site concentrations than Schnider. In an observational study, older women more often had excessive depth and burst suppression with Eleveld than with Schnider.Sources: Obert 2024, Linassi 2023
  • The spectrogram may possibly be used to find the patient’s own dose. Propofol was given as a slow infusion until loss of response, and maintenance was adjusted according to a visible alpha band and SEF. The authors argue that this allows one to find the patient’s own dose. Whether this improves cognitive outcome has not been tested, and cognition was measured only one hour after emergence.Sources: Obert 2024, Mehler 2024 (the Chilean studies)
  • The textbook suggests avoiding burst suppression. Large RCTs (ENGAGES, Evered 2021) have not consistently shown less delirium with EEG-guided anaesthesia, partly because the doses did not differ enough between the groups. Even so, it suggests monitoring depth of anaesthesia with single-channel or processed EEG and avoiding burst suppression with lower induction and maintenance doses. This is given as the authors’ suggestion, and whether burst suppression is cause or marker is not discussed.Sources: Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025, Evered 2021

The studies in detail:

Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025 Schonberger 2022 Obert 2024 Mehler 2024 Evered 2021

The cards on burst suppression are collected in the tab.

The studies in detail: age and EEG, slow induction, delirium meta-analysis, frailty score, textbook chapter (6 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Age and EEG under propofol and sevoflurane: 18–90 years (Purdon 2015, BJA)

  • Design: retrospective observational study at MGH of 155 adults (propofol 60, sevoflurane 95), analysed in a 2-minute window about 10 minutes after the start of surgery with four-channel frontal EEG. Windows with burst suppression, artefacts and transition to emergence were excluded. The young (18–38 years) and older (70–90 years) groups had 18 and 8 patients for propofol and 34 and 12 for sevoflurane. Anaesthesia was not protocol-driven.
  • Power fell with age in all bands: in older patients slow power was 4.9 dB lower (propofol, about 1.8 times smaller amplitude) and 5.5 dB lower (sevoflurane, about 1.9 times). Alpha power was 8.7 dB lower (propofol, about 2.7 times) and 8.6 dB lower (sevoflurane, about 2.7 times). Overall the oscillations were about 2–3 times smaller in older patients.
  • Alpha fell the most: the ratio between alpha and slow power was 2.8 dB lower in older patients under propofol (95% CI −3.0 to −2.6) and 2.1 dB lower under sevoflurane. Alpha coherence was lower, and the peak frequency of alpha coherence was 0.97 Hz lower (propofol, CI −1.48 to −0.66) and 0.49 Hz lower (sevoflurane). The figure legend states that alpha coherence declines from about 65 years. The effect on alpha was more pronounced under propofol than under sevoflurane.
  • Regression: alpha power fell about 0.18 dB per year under propofol and about 0.15 dB under sevoflurane (r² 0.43 and 0.46), and alpha coherence fell about 0.002 and 0.003 per year (r² 0.21 and 0.32). Middle-aged patients lay between young and older.
  • Burst suppression: the probability of an episode increased with age. It approached 1 for the oldest under propofol and about 0.6 under sevoflurane. The episodes were short, at most a few minutes, and were defined as at least three suppression events within one minute.
  • Dose: end-tidal sevoflurane was about 1 age-adjusted MAC in the whole group, with no trend with age. The propofol rate decreased slightly with age. The authors therefore consider that the differences are more likely due to neurophysiology than to a higher effective dose in older patients, but they cannot rule out hidden differences. Opioid was also given during maintenance: remifentanil in 48 of 60 in the propofol group.
  • What it means for indices: the authors propose that commercial indices (not age-adjusted) may give elevated values at concentrations that produce unconsciousness in older patients, because power in the slow, delta and alpha bands is lower. Adjusting the dose to reach a target index may then cause burst suppression. They refer to a clinical study (Besch 2011) that found more burst suppression in older patients within the recommended index range. They propose that unprocessed EEG and the spectrogram can take age into account by adjusting the scale. This is a hypothesis not tested in this study.
  • Explanation: cortical atrophy and a thicker CSF layer may attenuate EEG amplitude in general (equally at all frequencies), but the authors consider that the additional decline in alpha indicates altered function in frontal thalamocortical circuits. This is an argument, not something they have tested.
  • Opioid: the patients received fentanyl at induction (about 160 µg on average) and often more during maintenance, and remifentanil in 48 of 60 in the propofol group. The opioid effect is not analysed. Balanza 2022 found increased frontal theta with increasing fentanyl concentration in awake patients before induction, so opioid is an uncontrolled factor, particularly for theta.
  • Caveats: few older patients in each group (propofol n = 8), short windows without burst suppression, no behavioural measures and no controlled dosing. Patents are licensed to Masimo, and Purdon, Akeju and Brown report royalties or consulting agreements.
Purdon et al. Br J Anaesth 2015;115(Suppl 1):i46–i57

Slow induction: older patients develop alpha and no burst suppression (Obert 2024)

  • Design: retrospective analysis of EEG from two randomised trials at one hospital in Chile (J Clin Anesth 2024;99:111672): 26 patients under 65 years (median 50) and 25 aged 65 years or older (median 75), ASA 1–3, without neurological disease or centrally acting drugs. Propofol was given as a slow infusion (8 mg/kg/h in older patients, 10 in younger) until loss of response (LOR), tested every 30 seconds. At LOR the pump was switched to TCI (Schnider) with the effect-site concentration at LOR as the target, then remifentanil 4.5 ng/ml and rocuronium. Frontal four-channel EEG (SedLine), spectrogram and band power 0.7–30 Hz; the analysis period was from start to LOR (normalised to 100%) and five minutes after LOR, without surgical stimulus.
  • Time and dose: time to LOR about 8 minutes in both groups (480 versus 473 seconds). Older patients needed 1.06 mg/kg propofol versus 1.35 in younger, and effect-site concentration at LOR 2.6 versus 3.15 µg/ml (p < 0.001). PSI at LOR 75 versus 64 (not significant), SEF 20 versus 18 Hz.
  • No burst suppression: none of the 51 patients, in either age group, had burst suppression from the start of induction to five minutes after LOR.
  • Absolute power falls with age, the composition does not: absolute power in all bands was lower in older patients (delta, theta, alpha and beta, all p < 0.05, strongest after LOR). When power was normalised to total power, the spectra were similar in the two groups; the only difference was that older patients developed alpha slightly earlier in induction (55–80% of the time to LOR) and had slightly higher relative theta after LOR (p = 0.043). Older patients thus showed distinct alpha, only with lower amplitude.
  • The authors’ interpretation: burst suppression at induction is probably due to “overshoot” after a bolus, and older, frail brains respond to the excess with burst suppression. Slow, spectrogram-guided induction allows one to find the patient's own dose, use alpha at LOR as a reference going forward, and avoid the excess. They also point out that the Schnider model is based on only nine healthy volunteers over 65 years, and that the Eleveld model gives lower calculated effect-site concentrations than Schnider.
  • Versus Purdon 2015 (BJA): there the probability of burst suppression approached 1 in the oldest under propofol, and alpha fell more than the other bands. Obert finds no burst suppression and preserved relative alpha. The difference is the method of induction (bolus in clinical practice versus slow titration) and the timing (induction and the first minutes versus maintenance during surgery). The authors themselves write that the finding “appears to contradict” the literature on age-related changes in EEG architecture.
  • Caveats: small retrospective study without a power calculation, arbitrary age cut-off (65), propofol only (not examined for sevoflurane induction), only five minutes after LOR without neuromuscular blockers and surgery, one hospital and one population, and no test of whether slow induction actually improves cognitive outcome. The conflict of interest statement in the article reads only “The other authors declare no competing interests”, without any author being named before it.
Obert et al. J Clin Anesth 2024;99:111672

Which EEG measures are associated with postoperative delirium? Meta-analysis (Xu 2025)

Systematic review and meta-analysis from Melbourne (BJA 2025;135:1684–1703, PROSPERO CRD42024564983) of non-proprietary EEG measures during anaesthesia and delirium after discharge from the recovery unit. 42 studies, 13,115 patients, mean delirium incidence 18.8%, 49 different EEG measures. Indices were excluded as measures, and studies in which anaesthesia was guided by an index were analysed separately, because index guidance changes the dose and thereby the EEG (“drug-titration paradox”).

  • Alpha: lower mean alpha power (−1.43 dB; −1.67 dB in studies without index guidance) and lower alpha peak frequency (−0.73 Hz; −1.03 Hz without index guidance, I² = 0%) in those who developed delirium. In three studies that adjusted for age, the OR was 0.86 per dB of alpha power, so alpha seems to say something beyond age. The authors argue that disproportionately low alpha points to disturbance in alpha-generating thalamocortical circuits, whereas broadband power loss is more easily explained by biophysical age-related changes (thinner cortex, more cerebrospinal fluid).
  • Theta and delta: most studies found no difference in theta or delta power. Lower delta was associated with delirium in the main analysis, but not in studies without index guidance or in non-cardiac surgery, and the authors warn against building mechanistic hypotheses on EEG features that appear only under index-guided anaesthesia. “EEG slowing” (≥ 50% more delta/theta or less alpha/beta, five studies from the same group) was not associated with delirium overall.
  • Burst suppression: occurrence (yes/no) had OR 2.51 (95% CI 1.65–3.81, I² = 15%), robust in all subanalyses. Duration was 12 minutes longer in those with delirium, but not significant with the conservative method; adjusted for age and duration of surgery OR 1.02 per minute. Suppression ratio (BSR) was not associated, probably because many studies calculated it over the whole procedure and got very low figures. SEF was marginally lower (−0.94 Hz, three studies).
  • What index guidance does: it weakened, but did not remove, the association between alpha, burst suppression and delirium. The authors see this as an opportunity: guidance aiming for higher alpha power and frequency, rather than an index value, could conceivably reduce delirium. This is now being investigated in an ongoing study, and is thus a hypothesis.
  • Mechanism and vulnerability: burst suppression may reflect a vulnerable brain, anaesthesia-induced metabolic failure (cf. Ching 2012) or both; age and low physical activity are associated with burst suppression. Studies should adjust for both age and effect-site concentration, and a “dose-adjusted” alpha (alpha divided by remaining MAC distance) was associated with delirium in one study.
  • Limitations: great heterogeneity in montage, analysis and delirium tools; low threshold (three studies) for meta-analysis; the subanalyses are exploratory; publication bias could not be assessed formally; functional connectivity and “other” measures could not be pooled. No conflicts of interest.
  • Connection in the app: supports Gutiérrez 2019 and Kim 2024 (alpha), Fritz 2016 (suppression) and Manquat 2022 (lower alpha peak frequency as a marker of something wrong), and nuances Hogan 2020 and Jegarl 2026 (vulnerability versus dose). For the sevoflurane theta hypothesis in the card above, the conclusion is that theta has not been shown to be a marker.
Xu, Arnaout, Scott, McGuigan. Br J Anaesth 2025;135:1684–1703

Slow induction in patients over 69 years, with and without dexmedetomidine (Mehler 2024)

  • Design: randomised unblinded pilot study from Osorno (J Clin Monit Comput 2024;38:803–815, NCT05425069): 23 patients over 69 years (median 74.5 and 82 years in the groups), ASA 1–3, non-neurological surgery over 60 minutes. Group 1 (n = 10): propofol 8 mg/kg/h until loss of response, then Schnider TCI with Ce set 15% below the level at loss of response, remifentanil 4.5 ng/ml, propofol adjusted according to visible alpha band and SEF95 of at least 10 Hz. Group 2 (n = 13): dexmedetomidine 0.8 µg/kg/h without bolus for 10 minutes, then propofol TCI 2.0 µg/ml until loss of response, thereafter 0.5 µg/ml adjusted according to SEF above 8 Hz. SedLine, four frontal channels; only relative power analysed because of amplitude problems in the export. MoCA before and one hour after emergence.
  • No burst suppression: in none of the 23, neither at induction, maintenance nor emergence, in a group where the literature reports up to 70% burst suppression with bolus induction.
  • Dose: time from propofol start to loss of response 9 versus 2 minutes; Ce at loss of response 2.65 versus 2.0 µg/ml; maintenance Ce 1.9 versus 0.5 µg/ml. Time from propofol stop to response 13 versus 17 minutes (not significant).
  • EEG: the propofol group showed the classic “railroad track pattern” with delta and alpha, also in the oldest, with a beta activation around 40% of the way through induction. The dexmedetomidine group had more relative delta and less alpha and beta throughout the course; SEF at loss of response 10 versus 20.5 Hz, PSI 83 versus 74 (not significant). The differences persisted until just before emergence.
  • Cognition: no difference in MoCA before and after in either group, no individual patient with a significant fall, all calm and cooperative (SAS 4) at 10, 30 and 60 minutes. The authors therefore ask whether low alpha power is only a risk marker under purely GABAergic regimens, since the dexmedetomidine group had low alpha without worse outcome.
  • Reservations: pilot with 23 patients, not blinded, no power calculation, only immediate postoperative cognition (not delirium after the recovery unit), low educational level and low baseline MoCA values, no haemodynamic data. Kreuzer, Obert and Schneider have patent applications on EEG monitoring; the others declare no conflicts of interest. No funding.
Mehler et al. J Clin Monit Comput 2024;38:803–815

“Frailty” scores from EEG mostly measure age (Ostertag 2025)

  • Background: Touchard 2019 proposed a composite score (BPTIVA: total power, alpha power and propofol Ce at SEF 8–13 Hz) as a marker of a “frail brain”, linked to burst suppression at induction. Ostertag and colleagues (TU Munich and Osorno, Clin Neurophysiol Pract 2025;10:209–217) attempted to reproduce the score in 75 patients aged 18–91 years from the Chilean slow-induction studies (SedLine 63, BIS 12).
  • Findings: the score correlated moderately negatively with age (ρ = −0.44), and so did all its components: propofol Ce at loss of response (−0.45), alpha power (−0.32) and total power (−0.36). Alpha and total power were strongly correlated with each other (0.82), that is, multicollinearity. “Low scorers” were older (median 73.5 versus 59 years), had higher ASA, lower Ce at loss of response (2.35 versus 2.9 µg/ml) and lower SEF.
  • No burst suppression: none of the 75 developed burst suppression during the slow induction, so the endpoint the score was meant to predict did not exist. The authors conclude that the score “probably only detects an older brain”, and that burst suppression with rapid bolus induction may say more about overdosing than about vulnerability.
  • Early signal: the differences in band power between high and low scorers were visible already 5 minutes before loss of response, so the assessment can be made during induction, not after.
  • Reservations: retrospective, the score had to be modified (SEF window 8–20 Hz) to be calculable in 70 of 75, no outcome data. Kreuzer and Schneider have patent applications on EEG features and age, and Kreuzer declares funding from Masimo, Narcotrend, Medtronic and Fresenius Kabi for EEG training and lecture fees.
Ostertag et al. Clin Neurophysiol Pract 2025;10:209–217

The older patient: brain, dose and depth of anaesthesia (Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025)

The chapter “Geriatric Anesthesia” (Mahanna Gabrielli, Schenning and Deiner) is a broad chapter on physiology, preoperative assessment and delirium. What concerns EEG and dosing is collected here.

  • The ageing brain: less white matter in the prefrontal cortex and anterior corpus callosum, reduced synaptic function and connectivity (hippocampus, prefrontal and temporal cortex). Contrary to older textbooks, normal ageing is not associated with substantial neuronal loss in the neocortex or hippocampus (Morrison and Baxter 2012). This fits with EEG amplitude falling with age while the spectral structure may be preserved (Purdon 2015, Obert 2024).
  • Hidden cognitive impairment: mild cognitive impairment in 10–20% over 65 years, and over 20% of patients over 65 presenting for preoperative assessment have undetected cognitive impairment (Culley 2016). Preoperative cognitive impairment is the most consistent risk factor for perioperative neurocognitive disorders, and up to 40% of delirium is thought to be preventable.
  • Dose: MAC and MAC-awake fall by about 6% per decade after age 30 (Mapleson 1996, Nickalls and Mapleson 2003). Propofol above 1.5 mg/kg at induction is associated with severe hypotension (MAP below 55 mmHg), which affects 22% of older patients (Schonberger 2022). Older patients are more sensitive to midazolam and opioids, and take longer to regain consciousness after TIVA with propofol (Linassi 2020).
  • Depth of anaesthesia and delirium, in the chapter's wording: early studies showed less delirium with pEEG-guided anaesthesia, but large multicentre RCTs (ENGAGES, Evered 2021) have not shown this consistently, partly because the doses did not differ enough between the groups. “Despite this equipoise”, severe EEG suppression, including burst suppression, has consistently been associated with delirium (Fritz 2016, 2018). The authors “suggest monitoring depth of anaesthesia with single-channel or processed EEG and avoiding burst suppression with lower induction and maintenance doses”.
  • Drugs and delirium: the AGS advises against benzodiazepines; chronic use and benzodiazepine sedation in intensive care increase the risk, while a single preoperative dose is unresolved (Wang 2021). Dexmedetomidine has conflicting studies, but a meta-analysis found less delirium (Duan 2018). A review from MGH calls dexmedetomidine the only sedative shown to reduce delirium (Akeju and Brown 2017). Ketamine as multimodal analgesia does not reduce delirium (Avidan 2017, PODCAST). Gabapentinoids are strongly discouraged. Drugs on the Beers list should be avoided when possible, because they increase the risk of delirium. The list includes first-generation antihistamines (diphenhydramine), scopolamine, phenothiazine-type antiemetics, meperidine (pethidine), corticosteroids, antipsychotics and benzodiazepines. Spinal versus general anaesthesia gave no difference in delirium (REGAIN, RAGA).
  • Blood pressure: the chapter reproduces the POQI consensus (McEvoy 2019): MAP below 60–70 mmHg is associated with myocardial injury, kidney injury and death, and injury is a function of depth and duration. The consensus is not specific to older patients, and it does not mention the brain. See the Perfusion tab for what EEG can show at low pressure.
  • Reservations: the recommendation on pEEG and avoiding burst suppression is given as the authors' suggestion (“we suggest”) despite the RCTs being inconclusive, and the chapter does not discuss whether burst suppression is cause or marker (see Hogan 2020 and Jegarl 2026 in the Burst suppression tab). The chapter does not describe raw EEG or spectrogram in older patients.
Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025 (Miller's Anesthesia, 10th ed.)

The effect lags behind the concentration

  • The effect lags behind the concentration: The effect-site model describes the delay, and for propofol the time to equilibrium for the EEG effect is about 2.5 minutes. At emergence from sevoflurane, the end-tidal model predicted emergence too early. (see “The effect lags behind: effect site and end-tidal gas”)
  • Whether hysteresis exists in humans is debated: Hysteresis means the patient loses response at a higher concentration than the one at which it returns. The textbook calls this neural inertia, that is, the brain itself lagging in the state it is already in. The problem is how one would show it: the effect-site concentration cannot be measured, it is calculated by a model with a time constant that is itself an estimate, and that estimate is often chosen precisely so as to make the hysteresis as small as possible. Choose one time constant and the hysteresis is there. Choose another and it disappears. So we do not know whether the lag lies in the brain or in the model. (see “Hysteresis: does it exist in humans?”)
  • Hysteresis can be seen in the EEG without being seen in behaviour: In 16 volunteers there was no consistent difference in concentration for loss and return of response, but clear hysteresis for saturation of slow-wave activity. (see “Hysteresis: does it exist in humans?”)
  • Requirements vary widely, and emergence can be abrupt: The concentration at saturation of slow-wave activity varied widely between patients. Abrupt emergence was more common in older patients and was associated with more confusion, but the finding is preliminary. (see “Neural inertia in practice: variation and abrupt emergence”)
  • Low alpha is associated with delirium, theta has not been shown to be a marker: Low frontal alpha power during anaesthesia is associated with delirium, whereas theta has not been shown to be a risk marker. Dosing sevoflurane “to alpha without theta” is a hypothesis not tested in adults. (see “Sevoflurane theta as a dosing target: a hypothesis, and what the evidence actually says”)

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

The effect lags behind: effect site and end-tidal gas

When the concentration changes, for example at induction and emergence, the effect in the brain lags behind the concentration in the blood and in exhaled gas. The effect-site model describes this delay.Source: Kim et al. 2025

  • Propofol needs about 2.5 minutes before the EEG effect is in equilibrium. That is the equilibration time between blood and effect site for the EEG effect (time to peak about 90–100 seconds). For the haemodynamic depression it takes about 7 minutes.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • End-tidal sevoflurane predicts emergence too early. In 20 adults, patients woke on average 0.9 minutes after the time predicted by the effect-site model, but 4.1 minutes after the time predicted by the end-tidal model. At emergence, mean end-tidal sevoflurane was 0.13 vol %, whereas the calculated effect-site concentration was 0.44 vol %.Source: Johnson 2010
  • This applies when the concentration changes rapidly. End-tidal sevoflurane does not mirror the brain concentration during rapid changes, such as at emergence or when the vaporiser setting is changed. The study says nothing about concentrations at loss of response.Sources: Johnson 2010, Kim et al. 2025
  • The finding is uncertain. The study was small (20 patients), and the authors write that much larger studies are needed. The model assumed constant cardiac output and cerebral blood flow. Four authors had financial interests linked to an equipment manufacturer with an interest in the result.Source: Johnson 2010

The studies in detail:

Kim et al. 2025 Vuyk et al. 2025 Johnson 2010

Hysteresis: does it exist in humans?

Hysteresis means that responsiveness is lost at a higher concentration than the one at which it returns. The sources disagree on how much is due to pharmacokinetics and how much is neural inertia.

  • According to the textbook, patients need a higher concentration to lose response than the one at which they wake. The difference cannot be fully explained by pharmacokinetics and is called neural inertia. Older age and dexmedetomidine appear to increase the hysteresis.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025
  • For propofol the concentrations are equal when equilibration is allowed. The waking concentration (about 2.2 µg/ml) equals the concentration for loss of response when blood and effect site have time to equilibrate.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025, Kazama 1998
  • Hysteresis can be seen in the EEG without being seen in behaviour. In 16 volunteers there was no consistent difference in propofol concentration for loss and return of response (1.5 versus 1.4 µg/ml). The concentration for saturation of slow-wave activity, by contrast, showed clear hysteresis.Source: Warnaby 2017
  • The answer depends on the model. The effect-site concentration cannot be measured. The time constant is often estimated precisely so that hysteresis is minimised. In simulations, the hysteresis could appear or disappear depending on which time constant was assumed.Source: Proekt and Kelz 2021
  • The inertia may lie in the network itself. In models with two stable neural states, the system tends to stay in the state it is in. Hysteresis then arises even at a fixed concentration. This is a modelling study: it shows that the finding depends on the model, not that hysteresis exists in humans. In fruit flies and mice, induction occurs at a higher concentration than emergence.Sources: Proekt and Kelz 2021, Friedman 2010

The studies in detail:

Sleigh et al. 2025 Vuyk et al. 2025 Kazama 1998 Warnaby 2017 Proekt and Kelz 2021

Neural inertia in practice: variation and abrupt emergence

Saturation of slow-wave activity (0.5–1.5 Hz) was used as an EEG measure in 393 recordings. The findings show how differently patients respond. They do, however, rest on model-calculated concentrations in a secondary analysis.Source: Warnaby 2017

  • Patients need very different doses. In those who reached saturation, the sevoflurane concentration ranged from 0.24 to 0.9 MAC. For propofol it was roughly halved when opioids and neuromuscular blockers were used. The authors believe about half of patients receive twice as much anaesthetic as they need. This is an extrapolation that rests on the assumption that saturation means loss of perception.Source: Warnaby 2017
  • About a third woke abruptly. In these patients (among those with a successful fit) slow activity persisted until just before the response returned. The authors call this neural inertia. Abrupt emergence was more common with higher age (OR 1.5 per decade), with lower power at saturation and with desflurane than with sevoflurane.Source: Warnaby 2017
  • Abrupt emergence went with more confusion. 15 minutes after emergence, 18 % were confused after abrupt emergence, compared with under 2 % after gradual emergence. The finding is preliminary and comes from one study. No adjustment for age is reported, and age is linked to both abrupt emergence and confusion.Source: Warnaby 2017
  • There may be a link to delirium. One speculation is that delirium and cognitive impairment after anaesthesia result from the brain getting “stuck” in intermediate states on the way back. Neural dynamics must, however, first be demonstrated in humans. That this fits with the findings on abrupt emergence and confusion is an interpretation based on the sources.Sources: Proekt and Kelz 2021, Warnaby 2017

The studies in detail:

Warnaby 2017 Proekt and Kelz 2021

Sevoflurane theta as a dosing target: a hypothesis, and what the evidence actually says

Under sevoflurane, theta “fills in” between delta and alpha, and more theta comes with higher concentration. An obvious clinical hypothesis is that sevoflurane should be dosed to alpha without theta, and that this may give less delirium. Here it is important to separate hypothesis from evidence.Sources: Akeju 2014, Purdon 2015 Part I

  • Shown: low alpha during anaesthesia is associated with delirium. In older patients who developed delirium, the usual alpha increase under anaesthesia failed to appear, even though the dose was the same. Relative alpha was 0.09 versus 0.21. Delta rose equally in both groups, and theta did not separate the groups. The authors interpret low alpha as failure of the thalamocortical loop that the anaesthesia “unmasks”. In sevoflurane patients with delirium, power was also lower in 7.5–31.5 Hz and alpha coherence was reduced, but not in desflurane patients. Higher end-tidal concentration gave more suppression, and suppression was also associated with delirium.Sources: Gutiérrez 2019, Kim 2024, Fritz 2016
  • Not shown in adults: that theta is a risk marker, or that dosing “to alpha without theta” reduces delirium. None of the studies above tested theta as a target. EEG-guided anaesthesia that avoided suppression did not give, in ENGAGES, less delirium either.Source: ENGAGES (Wildes 2019)
  • The closest evidence is in children. In an RCT of 177 children (aged 1–6 years), sevoflurane was titrated to the lowest concentration that maintained alpha + slow-delta. They ended at about 0.36 MAC versus 1.0 MAC, and had less emergence delirium (21 versus 35%, marginally significant) and faster emergence. They did not steer by theta, but the picture is the same: alpha without fill above and below. In adults the hypothesis remains untested.Source: Miyasaka 2025 (the card in the Spectrogram tab)
  • “More receptors” and “neural inertia” are two different claims. That sevoflurane acts on more target molecules than GABAA is pharmacology and a possible explanation for theta. That “more disconnection requires more to reconnect” is neural inertia (hysteresis). This has been shown for propofol in humans and in animal experiments (see the card in the Fundamentals tab), but not linked to theta specifically. Propofol + sevoflurane is additive, so “more receptors” does not in itself produce synergy.Sources: Purdon 2015 Part I, Huang 2021, Sepúlveda 2026, Hendrickx 2008
  • Practical, with reservations: a distinct alpha band without broad theta fill may be a sign that sevoflurane is not higher than necessary in an adult. It is consistent with low dose and preserved alpha both being favourable markers. But it is an interpretation, not a documented dosing rule, and in children theta is a normal part of the picture.
  • The meta-analysis gives the closest answer: low alpha is the best-supported marker, whereas nothing has been shown for theta. Across 42 studies, lower alpha power and lower alpha peak frequency were robustly associated with delirium, also adjusted for age. Theta power did not discriminate in most studies.Source: Xu 2025 (the card below)
  • Reservation: the adult studies are small. Gutiérrez 2019 and Kim 2024 are small observational studies. In Gutiérrez 2019 only 6.7% developed full delirium, and interrater reliability was not assessed.
Gutiérrez 2019, Kim 2024, Fritz 2016, Akeju 2014, Purdon 2015 Part I

Hysteresis and neural inertia

When the concentration changes, for example at induction and emergence, the effect lags behind the plasma concentration. The effect-site model describes the delay.Source: Kim et al. 2025

  • Propofol needs time to equilibrate. Between blood and effect site it takes about 2.5 minutes for the EEG effect (time to peak about 90–100 seconds) and about 7 minutes for the haemodynamic depression.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • According to the textbook, patients need a higher concentration to lose response than the one at which they wake. This is called neural inertia. The difference cannot be fully explained by pharmacokinetics. Older age and dexmedetomidine appear to increase the hysteresis.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025
  • There is debate about how much is due to pharmacokinetics. For propofol, the waking concentration (about 2.2 µg/ml) equals the concentration for loss of response when equilibration between blood and effect site is allowed. In 16 volunteers there was no difference in mean propofol concentration for loss and return of response, but hysteresis for saturation of slow-wave activity.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025, Kazama 1998, Warnaby 2017 (see “The studies in detail” below)
  • The previous state determines the current state. In the zone where hysteresis applies, the same concentration can produce either an awake or an unconscious patient, depending on the state the patient came from. This may explain two things that pharmacokinetic models have difficulty explaining: a patient on a low concentration at the end of surgery can be roused abruptly by voice or a light touch, and the EEG can fluctuate between lighter and deeper patterns at a fixed concentration without stimulation. In mice on isoflurane and zebrafish larvae on propofol, at a dose where half respond, each animal switched between responding and not responding. Those that did not respond on the previous trial more often stayed unresponsive. In humans the findings are mixed, because the effect-site concentration cannot be measured.Source: McKinstry-Wu, Proekt and Kelz 2020
  • Neural inertia is seen in individual mice and decreases over time. In 6 mice at the same isoflurane concentration (0.6%, the dose at which half the mice lose the righting reflex), the EEG spectrum differed depending on whether the mouse came from wakefulness or deep anaesthesia. This applied to each individual mouse, measured when the brain concentration was stable. The difference decreased over time, and the degree of inertia varied between mice. The authors suggest that people with much or little inertia may be at higher risk of awareness, delayed emergence or confusion, but this has not been tested in humans.Source: Wasilczuk, Meng and McKinstry-Wu 2022 (animal study)
  • Emergence has its own mechanisms. In animals, inhibiting the orexin system delayed emergence without affecting induction. Stimulating many different areas can reverse anaesthesia in animals, including the thalamus, the ventral tegmental area, locus coeruleus, the parabrachial nucleus, the basal forebrain and the prefrontal cortex. No single structure appears to control emergence on its own.Source: Mashour 2024 (review in Neuron)
  • Hypothesis: neural inertia as post-anaesthetic “sleep inertia”. The authors propose that the inertia resembles the groggy confusion after ordinary awakening, and that the orexin and noradrenaline systems stabilise the transition. This could explain why older people and patients with narcolepsy show more inertia. This is a hypothesis, not tested findings.Source: Luppi et al. 2021 (hypothesis article)
  • With slow induction, induction and emergence can look alike. When propofol is given slowly and without other drugs, the raw EEG passes through the same patterns in reverse order at emergence: small fast waves, then alpha spindles, then theta and delta, and finally burst suppression. In volunteers, the effect-site concentration at loss and return of responsiveness was almost the same. In clinical practice, emergence is complicated by pain, opioids and nerve blocks. Opioids lower the propofol concentration at which the patient stops responding to voice, but the index is then higher, and the author suggests the patient may be more awake than it appears.Source: Hagihira 2017 (opinion article)
  • Clinical relevance (interpretation based on the sources): be cautious about going below the level that produced unconsciousness. The concentration at which the patient wakes may be lower than the one at which responsiveness was lost (MAC-awake lower than MAC at loss of responsiveness), but for propofol in volunteers the concentrations were almost the same (see above). If the volatile agent is reduced below the level that produced unconsciousness because the EEG still looks “anaesthetised”, the patient may wake without warning. Delta power may stay unchanged right up until the patient wakes. Once the patient is awake, a large increase in hypnotic may be needed to restore unconsciousness. Hysteresis appears to be more marked when arousal systems are impaired, for example in old age, narcolepsy and after droperidol, clonidine or antimuscarinic drugs.Source: Hight 2020
  • End-tidal sevoflurane is inaccurate when the vaporiser setting is changed. It does not account for the delay to the effect site.Sources: Kim et al. 2025, Johnson 2010 (see “The studies in detail” below)

The simulator above does not model hysteresis. Induction and emergence are symmetrical.

Kim et al. 2025; Vuyk et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025; McKinstry-Wu 2020; Wasilczuk 2022; Mashour 2024; Luppi 2021
The studies in detail: effect-site models and hysteresis, saturation of slow-wave activity, end-tidal versus effect site (3 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Can effect-site models explain hysteresis? (Proekt and Kelz 2021)

  • What it is: a modelling study (simulations), not a patient study (Br J Anaesth 2021;126:265–278). The authors want to show that an effect-site model can almost always be chosen so that hysteresis disappears, without that meaning the hysteresis is due only to drug distribution.
  • Background: in fruit flies and mice, induction occurs at a higher concentration than emergence, and the difference is not fully explained by pharmacokinetics (Friedman 2010). In humans, Warnaby 2017 found hysteresis in the saturation of slow-wave activity, but not in behaviour.
  • Main point: the effect site is a theoretical space where the concentration cannot be measured. The time constant is moreover often estimated precisely so that hysteresis is minimised. Two models with identical plasma concentration and effect, but different (unmeasurable) effect-site concentrations, cannot be distinguished experimentally. In simulations of a target-controlled infusion study, the hysteresis could either be present or disappear depending on which effect-site time constant was assumed.
  • Alternative mechanism: in models where neural activity has two stable states (a simple “double-well” model and a network of two neurons), hysteresis arises at constant concentration, because the system tends to remain in the state it is in, particularly with little noise. Here the hysteresis did not disappear when the true effect-site concentration was used.
  • Proposed test in humans: examine fluctuations in response at constant drug concentration (as in studies in mice and zebrafish where the chance of failing on the next stimulus increases if the previous stimulus was not answered), and possibly measurement of xenon concentration in the brain with imaging. The authors think the xenon measurements probably will not settle the debate on their own.
  • Speculation: the authors suggest that delirium and cognitive impairment after anaesthesia may be due to the brain becoming “locked” in intermediate states on the way back, but stress that neural dynamics must first be demonstrated in humans.
  • What it means: the article shows that finding or not finding hysteresis in humans depends on the assumed effect-site model. It does not show that hysteresis exists in humans. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Proekt and Kelz. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:265–278

Saturation of slow-wave activity and neural inertia (Warnaby 2017)

  • Design: advanced secondary analysis of 393 EEG recordings from four studies: 16 healthy volunteers with slow propofol induction and 32-channel EEG, 21 patients given sevoflurane before surgery, 102 patients given desflurane and fentanyl, and 254 patients in routine clinical practice (age 17–90 years). Effect-site concentrations were calculated with population models. For each recording, the dose-response for slow-wave activity (0.5–1.5 Hz, called SWA) was fitted to a sigmoid curve, and “SWAS” (saturation) was defined as the plateau where power no longer increases with increasing dose.
  • Saturation at induction: found in 92% overall (propofol 100% in volunteers, sevoflurane 86%, clinical 91–95%). Failures were due to movement and muscle artefacts or the dose not being high enough. The concentration for saturation was on average 2.7 µg/ml propofol in volunteers with slow infusion, about 0.6–0.7 MAC sevoflurane, and roughly halved (0.9–1.4 µg/ml propofol) when opioid and neuromuscular blocking agents were used. Neuromuscular blockers made no difference. The amount of power at saturation was independent of agent, but fell with age (r about −0.6).
  • Variation: the concentration for saturation varied widely between patients (0.24–0.9 MAC sevoflurane in those who reached it, and 0.03–1.6 MAC at emergence). The authors interpret this as roughly half receiving twice as much anaesthesia as they need, and about 20% not reaching full unconsciousness at 0.7 MAC. This rests on the assumption that saturation means loss of perception (earlier study in 16 volunteers) and is an extrapolation.
  • Hysteresis: in the 16 volunteers there was no consistent difference in the mean concentration for loss and return of response (1.5 versus 1.4 µg/ml), but clear hysteresis in the concentration for saturation. In roughly half, saturation at emergence came at a lower concentration and close to the return of response.
  • Abrupt or gradual emergence: of patients with successful fitting at emergence, about a third had an abrupt transition in which slow activity persisted until just before the response came (26% of all in the largest study and 20% in the other). The authors interpret this as “neural inertia”, defined as a tendency for the central nervous system to resist transitions between conscious and unconscious states. Abrupt emergence was more common with higher age (OR 1.5 per decade), lower power at saturation (OR 0.75 per dB) and desflurane (sevoflurane OR 0.20), with 78% accuracy.
  • Confusion: 15 minutes after emergence, 12 of 65 (18%) were confused after abrupt emergence versus 2 of 110 (under 2%) after gradual emergence (p < 0.001), and CAM-ICU was positive in 17 of 65 versus 14 of 110 (p = 0.02). Pain and wakefulness did not differ. The authors call this preliminary, and the figures rest on one study, and the article does not report adjustment for age, which is linked to both abrupt emergence and confusion.
  • Limitations: secondary analysis, model-derived concentrations, 30% failed fittings at emergence (often because the volatile agent was tapered or because of muscle artefacts), and the volunteer study used different electrodes from the clinical ones. Warnaby, Jbabdi and Tracey are listed as inventors on patent applications on detection of loss of perception.
  • Against Sleigh et al. 2025: the chapter says that patients need a higher concentration to lose response than the one at which they wake. Warnaby did not find that for behaviour (1.5 versus 1.4 µg/ml) in volunteers, but did for EEG saturation. The study itself writes that this differs from the animal experiment it builds on (Friedman 2010).
Warnaby et al. Anesthesiology 2017;127:645–657

End-tidal versus effect-site sevoflurane at emergence (Johnson 2010)

  • Design: 20 adults for elective surgery (mean 45 years) received midazolam 12.5 µg/kg before surgery, induction with remifentanil and propofol and maintenance with sevoflurane and remifentanil. During emergence, response was assessed with OAA/S every 20 seconds after sevoflurane and remifentanil were switched off. Emergence was defined as two consecutive OAA/S values above 1. The authors tested two models for the probability of unresponsiveness (built on an earlier volunteer study), one with measured end-tidal sevoflurane and one with calculated sevoflurane at the effect site (Lerou model).
  • Result: during anaesthesia the model's probability of unresponsiveness was 99% or more, and no patients responded. At emergence the probability varied from 1 to 97%. Patients woke on average 5.3 minutes after the anaesthesia was ended, 0.9 ± 4.3 minutes after the effect-site model predicted 50% probability of unresponsiveness and 4.1 ± 4.9 minutes after the end-tidal model (p = 0.02). The end-tidal model thus predicted emergence too early. Mean end-tidal sevoflurane at emergence was 0.13 ± 0.13 vol%, calculated effect-site concentration 0.44 ± 0.17 vol%.
  • Pain in recovery: 13 of 20 needed fentanyl in recovery. The end-tidal and effect-site models predicted alike (61% and 59%, p = 0.893), because sevoflurane was by then practically gone and both models become a pure remifentanil model.
  • Reservations: only 20 patients, and the authors write that the model's ability to distinguish awake from asleep in the clinically interesting time window cannot be assessed without much larger studies. The effect-site model assumed constant cardiac output and cerebral blood flow (without changes in PaCO₂ or bleeding), and the volunteer study behind the response model had no endotracheal tube or pain. Midazolam and propofol may have prolonged emergence slightly. Four authors hold shares in and receive salary or fees from Medvis (an equipment manufacturer with an interest in the result), and the study was partly funded by GE Healthcare and NIH (SBIR).
  • Connection with Kim et al. 2025: the study supports that end-tidal sevoflurane does not reflect the brain concentration when the concentration changes rapidly, as at emergence. It says nothing about concentrations at loss of response.
Johnson et al. Anesth Analg 2010;111:387–394

Read the raw EEG before trusting the number

  • Wrong scaling can hide a good alpha–delta pattern. With too large a µV scale, alpha–delta can look like awake EEG or an isoelectric line. With too small a scale it looks like noise. Set the spectrogram colour scale higher in young patients and lower in older patients.See
  • Artefacts have recognisable features in raw EEG and spectrogram. Blinks give thin vertical lines. Electrocautery gives a block of high power across all frequencies. ECG gives horizontal stripes, and EMG a broad increase in power. EMG is not just noise: it may indicate that the patient needs more anaesthesia or analgesia.See
  • Awake subjects under neuromuscular blockade can have an index like that under anaesthesia. When EMG disappears, the index can fall to the same level as under anaesthesia in awake volunteers. But alpha–delta is absent from the raw EEG and spectrogram. A syringe swap that gives a neuromuscular blocking agent to an awake patient is an example of a false negative.See
  • EMG activation at emergence does not mean the patient is waking. The activation is often hidden, without visible movement. It occurs over a wide range of concentrations and can raise the index. Median emergence concentration was 0.09 MAC, far lower than the roughly 0.3 often quoted.See
  • Epileptiform activity can look “deep enough”. Sevoflurane can cause epileptiform patterns in children without motor signs. The index can either rise or fall during seizures. When suspected: read the raw EEG, and do not guide the dose by the index.See on the index and spectrogram”

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

Artefacts and sources of error in EEG

EEG is highly sensitive to noise. Below are the most common patterns and how they appear in raw EEG and spectrogram.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025

  • Wrong scaling can make a good pattern look wrong. If μV per division is too large (for example 200 μV), an alpha-delta wave of about 40 μV looks small. It can then be mistaken for awake EEG or an isoelectric line. If the scale is too small, the same wave looks like noise. Set the spectrogram colour scale higher in the young (larger amplitude) and lower in older patients.
  • Impedance should be low and even. Usually under 5–8 kΩ (check the limit for your monitor), and roughly equal for all electrodes. Clean the skin with an alcohol wipe or adjust the electrodes.
  • Eye blinks and movement can mimic delta. They give large deflections frontally. In the spectrogram, blinks appear as thin, vertical red lines. Persistent blinking or head and eye movement can be mistaken for strong delta activity.
  • Electrocautery fills the whole spectrogram. It gives high-amplitude, high-frequency deflections in raw EEG and a block of high power across all frequencies in the spectrogram.
  • ECG gives deflections that follow the pulse. Sharp peaks in time with the heart rate in the raw EEG, particularly in patients with a short, thick neck and during burst suppression, where the EEG itself is low in amplitude. The raw EEG is where you recognise it, because the deflections are regular and in time with the pulse on the monitor. How much shows in the spectrogram varies with the monitor’s filters and the colour scale, so the absence of bands does not rule out ECG artefact.
  • EMG is a signal, not just noise. It increases power broadly across many frequencies, and raw EEG looks “fuzzy”. EMG may mean the patient is grimacing and probably needs more anaesthesia or analgesia. It is often present at induction and emergence.

When neuromuscular blockers are given and EMG disappears, BIS can fall to the same level as under anaesthesia in awake volunteers. Alpha-delta was nevertheless absent in raw EEG and spectrogram, so the state could be recognised. An example of a false negative is a syringe swap that gives a neuromuscular blocker to an awake patient.Sources: Sleigh et al. 2025; Schuller 2015

Scenario (table 36.3)Type
Neuromuscular blocker given to an awake patient, EMG disappears and the index falls to the same level as under anaesthesiaFalse negative
Connected consciousness (IFT response) with apparently adequate anaesthesia and alpha-delta, without recallFalse negative
Wrong scaling: good alpha-delta interpreted as awake or noiseFalse negative
Burst suppression with noisy baseline interpreted as “awake”, and a deeply anaesthetised patient receives moreFalse positive
Low amplitude in older patients gives a high index and excess anaesthesiaFalse positive
Sleigh et al. 2025 (Schuller 2015, Hight 2017)

BIS in awake subjects with neuromuscular blockade (Schuller 2015)

  • Awake anaesthetists received neuromuscular blockers and were tested throughout. 11 healthy anaesthetists received suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg in one trial and rocuronium 0.7 mg/kg in another. Rocuronium was reversed with sugammadex. An isolated forearm allowed them to respond with hand signals. Two BIS monitors (Vista and A2000) were used simultaneously, with standard 22-channel EEG. Cognition was tested with mental arithmetic and a short story to be remembered.
  • BIS fell in every trial, although nobody was asleep. The fall came in two stages: first to about 75–85, then after about 4 minutes to lower values (median 66 after suxamethonium and 73 after rocuronium). The lowest value was 44. BIS was below 60 for several minutes in some trials. BIS did not return to baseline until muscle activity had returned.
  • The participants were fully awake. All answered questions, the arithmetic was 96% correct and the story was retold with 94% accuracy. Raw EEG looked awake, with low amplitude and high frequency, just without EMG and eye movements. “BetaRatio” (a sub-parameter in the algorithm) fell in all.
  • Signal quality looked best when BIS was most misleading. SQI rose to 90–100 when the block set in. After sugammadex, first movement came after 27 seconds on average, and BIS was above 90 just over a minute later.
  • The same applies to Entropy and qCON. Both fell below 60 in awake subjects in most trials and did not return until movement returned. The indices therefore need muscle activity to generate correct values in awake subjects. Studies conducted without neuromuscular block can give misleading guidance for paralysed patients.Sources: Schuller 2023, Schuller 2025
  • Reservations: a small study, and it does not show how often this happens in patients. Only ten subjects per drug. The monitors had electrodes on opposite sides of the forehead and could differ by up to 15 units. The findings apply to BIS and two versions of the algorithm. The authors argue that BIS values with and without neuromuscular blockers are not comparable, and that 60–75 towards the end of the procedure may be compatible with full consciousness when neuromuscular blockers have been given. No conflicts of interest are declared, and the study was funded by the Cairns Anaesthetists' Association.
Schuller et al. Br J Anaesth 2015;115 suppl 1:i95–i103

EMG activation at emergence (Hight 2017)

  • The study measured forehead EMG during emergence in 273 adults. Observational study from one hospital in New Zealand.
