Frontal EEG and EMG (70–110 Hz, as BIS calculates it) were recorded during emergence after volatile anaesthesia, with an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask. The concentration in the brain (CeMAC, without age correction) was calculated from end-tidal gas with a model. Pain was assessed immediately after emergence.
  • EMG activation is often hidden and often follows an external stimulus. It most often came abruptly, as an increase of 10–20 dB, and some had several activations. In some it came already at a surgical level of anaesthesia, in others only when they responded to command. More than half came after an external stimulus, such as transfer to another bed. 43% had increased muscle tone without visible movement.
  • There are two types of activation. “High-MAC” activation occurred independently of emergence, while EEG still showed delta and alpha. It was not linked to severe pain afterwards and was more common with endotracheal tube. “Low-MAC” activation occurred near zero MAC, at the same time as the patient woke, and nearly all of these had a laryngeal mask. The two were divided at 0.07 MAC.
  • Patients woke at a lower concentration than often assumed. Median CeMAC at emergence was 0.09, far lower than the roughly 0.3 often quoted. Around 20% woke only near zero, which the authors interpret as neural inertia. The cause is unclear, and the explanations are hypotheses.
  • Pain did not lead to earlier emergence. The difference in CeMAC between EMG activation and emergence was the same with high and low pain.
  • EMG activation does not mean the patient is waking. It is often hidden, occurs across a wide span of concentrations and can raise the BIS value. The authors refer to Schuller 2015 on how muscle activity affects BIS.
  • Reservations: observational study. There may be hidden confounders. Choice of agent and airway device is linked to type of surgery and age. Opioid concentrations are calculated from models, and TIVA was not included. No conflicts of interest are declared, and the study is funded by the James S. McDonnell Foundation.
Hight et al. J Clin Monit Comput 2017;31:813–823

Epileptiform activity during anaesthesia: can look “deep” on the EEG index and spectrogram

  • Sevoflurane can cause epileptiform patterns in children, without motor signs. During mask induction, such patterns were seen in 20–76% of children, depending on the study and protocol. More children had the patterns at higher concentration. The sources recommend a lower concentration, a shorter time at high concentration and EEG to catch those who react, since it cannot be predicted.Sources: Schultz 2012, Kreuzer 2014
  • The EEG index does not help to detect seizures. The index most often rose during seizures, but fell in some studies. In the randomised trial BIS ranged from 11 to 97 during epileptiform discharges, with no difference compared with patients without them. Raw EEG from the BIS monitor can also miss periodic discharges. Processed EEG should therefore not be used alone to rule out non-convulsive status. An unexpected index (high or low) relative to the clinical picture should prompt conventional EEG.Source: Gimson 2021 (scoping review, almost all BIS)
  • A pattern that is easily overlooked looks “deep enough”. The spectrogram can show two things. (1) “Flames”: broadband vertical power peaks that build up and subside over minutes (image 14). (2) A low-frequency, apparently deep pattern with low SEF and low index. Here only the raw EEG shows that the waves are periodic and have a sharp component (image 19). The same type of activity can give an index around 45 (image 20) or around 25 (image 19). The second pattern is the easiest to miss, because everything on the screen looks “deep enough”.Sources: Taccone 2026; Ntahe 2018; Gimson 2021
  • When you suspect it: read the raw EEG, not the index. Look at all four channels (periodicity, sharpness, symmetry). Check the sevoflurane concentration and EtCO2: hyperventilation and high concentration are described triggers in the literature Kreuzer cites. Possible measures (interpretation based on the sources): lowering the concentration or switching to propofol, and request a full EEG. Do not steer the dose by the index. Frontal four-channel EEG cannot confirm the diagnosis.
  • The evidence base is thin. Both paediatric studies are from the same centre (Hannover), with the same monitor (Narcotrend) and one visual rater. Adult data are mainly case reports. The clinical significance of subclinical epileptiform patterns during sevoflurane has not been clarified.
Schultz et al. PLoS ONE 2012;7:e40903 · Kreuzer et al. PLoS ONE 2014;9:e89191 · Gimson and Smith, Seizure 2021;91:198–206

Children: age determines what the EEG shows

  • The infant EEG matures over the first months. Under 3 months slow-delta dominates. Theta and alpha appear around 4 months, and frontal alpha becomes coherent from about 10–14 months. Indices developed in adults may give inaccurate estimates, especially in the first three months.See
  • Above 1 year the structure is as in adults, but with more power. Slow-delta and coherent frontal alpha are seen in the studies at all ages above 1 year. Total power peaks in childhood, and beta and gamma are higher than in adults.See
  • The EEG index may read too high in children. Children with clear alpha and slow-delta had a mean index of 66. Raw EEG and spectrogram tell you more than a fixed index threshold.See
  • Spectrogram-guided sevoflurane may allow lower doses and less delirium. Titrating to the lowest concentration that maintained alpha and slow-delta gave about 0.36 MAC versus 1.0 MAC. Emergence delirium was less common (21 versus 35 %), but the effect is marginal, and the trial is from a single centre.See
  • In autism the EEG may resemble an older brain. Young people with autism had lower alpha, and burst suppression occurred in 23.0 % versus 12.2 %, even with lower propofol doses. It may be better to judge the dose by the EEG than by age alone (interpretation based on the sources).See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Infants: the EEG matures over the first months

The sevoflurane EEG changes clearly over the first year of life. The authors link the changes to maturation of thalamocortical connections.Sources: Cornelissen 2015 and 2018 (two observational studies from the same group)

  • The EEG matures step by step in the first year. Under 3 months slow-delta dominates, with very little power above 4 Hz. Theta and alpha appear around 4 months, alpha becomes frontal around 7–9 months, and frontal alpha becomes coherent from about 10–14 months. Under 1 year, alpha coherence is absent.Sources: Cornelissen 2018; Lee 2017; Akeju 2015 (only 4 children under 1 year)
  • Emergence looks different from adults. At 4–6 months, theta and alpha fell when end-tidal sevoflurane dropped below 1.2 %, around when the child began to move. At 0–3 months, EEG power did not clearly follow concentration. The older infants also showed no spatial shift of alpha of the kind adults have.Source: Cornelissen 2015
  • The youngest received less sevoflurane. During maintenance, 0–3 months received less (median 2.0 %) than 4–6 months (2.6 %). The EEG difference was also present at equal concentration, so it is probably not explained by dose alone.Source: Cornelissen 2015
  • Adult indices fit infants poorly. Indices developed in adults may give inaccurate estimates, especially in the first three months. Raw EEG and spectrogram tell you more than a fixed index threshold. Caveats: few children in each age group (7–9 months, n = 8), sevoflurane only, and movement on video as a crude marker of emergence.Sources: Cornelissen 2015 and 2018

The studies in detail:

Cornelissen 2015 Cornelissen 2018 Lee 2017 Akeju 2015

Above 1 year: adult structure, more power, and the EEG index may read too high

From about 1 year, the EEG during anaesthesia resembles the adult picture. But children have more power, and that affects the index.

  • Above 1 year the EEG has the same structure as in adults. Under both propofol and sevoflurane, slow-delta and coherent frontal alpha are seen in all age groups above 1 year. The adult patterns, including burst suppression with overdosing, are seen in children above about 1 year, but with higher power.Sources: Lee 2017 (propofol); Akeju 2015 (sevoflurane); Brandt 2020
  • Children have more EEG power than adults. Total power under sevoflurane increases from infancy to a peak in childhood and then declines. The sources place the peak differently (about 6 years, 5–8 years or 6–8 years). Beta and gamma are higher than in adults. The authors consider that dose does not explain the difference in amplitude. Caveats: neuromuscular blockers were used differently in the groups, and the study is retrospective.Source: Akeju 2015
  • The EEG index may read too high in children. Children with clear alpha and slow-delta had a mean PSI of 66, versus 42 in the control group. Two explanations have been proposed: the indices are calibrated against practice in which 1.0 MAC is considered adequate (Miyasaka), and raised beta and gamma give falsely high values in adequately anaesthetised children (an assumption by Brandt). The two explanations do not exclude each other (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Miyasaka 2025; Brandt 2020
  • Take age into account, and look at the raw EEG and spectrogram. They tell you more than indices developed in adults. Caveat: apart from Miyasaka 2025, the studies are observational studies and case reports.Sources: Akeju 2015; Brandt 2020

The studies in detail:

Lee 2017 Akeju 2015 Brandt 2020 Miyasaka 2025

Spectrogram-guided sevoflurane: lower dose and less delirium?

If the index reads too high in children, dosing to the index may give more sevoflurane than needed. One randomised trial has tested guiding by the spectrogram instead.Source: Miyasaka 2025

  • Spectrogram guidance gave a lower dose and faster emergence. In 177 children aged 1 to under 6 years, sevoflurane was titrated to the lowest concentration that maintained a continuous alpha and slow-delta pattern. This gave about 0.36 MAC versus 1.0 MAC, emergence 21 minutes earlier and a shorter stay in recovery. Burst suppression was equally common in both groups (22 versus 23 %). All received remifentanil and a block.Source: Miyasaka 2025
  • Less delirium, but uncertain. Emergence delirium occurred in 21 versus 35 %. The authors call the effect marginal: with a different PAED threshold the difference was not significant. Caveats: one anaesthetist with EEG training gave all the anaesthetics at a single centre, and awareness was not assessed with a structured interview.Source: Miyasaka 2025
  • How the child wakes up may matter. All children passed through a delta-dominated state before emergence. Children who developed delirium had a broader delta band and slightly more beta in the minute before eye opening. Delirium may therefore relate more to the course of emergence than to total exposure.Source: Miyasaka 2025
  • The EEG may warn before the child moves. In a 9-month-old child, the EEG changed about 4–5 minutes before the child moved. A subsequent overcorrection caused about 6 minutes of burst suppression and a fall in blood pressure. Caveats: the EEG was not used to guide the anaesthetic, and it is a single case report.Source: Brandt 2020

The studies in detail:

Miyasaka 2025 Brandt 2020

When the child does not follow the age pattern: autism

Age is not always a good guide. In children and young people with autism, the EEG under propofol may resemble what is seen in older adults.

  • Young people with autism had less alpha and more burst suppression. The structure was the same, but alpha was lower, and the difference grew with age. The adjusted difference in alpha was, however, not significant. Burst suppression occurred in 23.0 % versus 12.2 %, despite lower propofol doses.Source: Walsh 2018
  • One possible explanation is accelerated ageing. The pattern resembles that of older adults, and may reflect abnormal inhibitory circuits. The authors call it “a form of accelerated neuronal aging”, but it is a hypothesis.Sources: Walsh 2018; Purdon 2015 (older adults)
  • A case report: prolonged burst suppression after propofol. A 19-year-old with severe autism developed burst suppression with apnoea three minutes after the start of propofol, followed by 12 minutes of isoelectric EEG, and did not wake for over 2 hours. The patient had received ketamine and midazolam as premedication, and the authors note that valproate lowers anaesthetic requirements.Source: Brandt 2020
  • Judge the dose by the EEG, not by age alone (interpretation based on the sources). An EEG that looks like an “older brain” in a young patient with autism is not necessarily wrong. Caveats: observational study without controlled dosing, and the groups differed in age, sex, midazolam and epilepsy.Source: Walsh 2018

The studies in detail:

Walsh 2018 Purdon 2015 Brandt 2020
This is a schematic model built on EEG signatures described in the literature, not real patient data. It shows qualitative patterns and is not suitable for clinical interpretation. Ketamine and dexmedetomidine are only described in younger adults in the sources, and for midazolam the sources do not describe age differences. Older patients, children and infants are therefore only available for propofol and sevoflurane.

What the textbook says about children, anaesthesia and the EEG (Vutskits et al. 2025)

  • MAC changes a great deal in the first year of life. MAC is lowest in preterm neonates, increases by about 30% from birth and peaks at 1–6 months. Infants have a higher MAC than older children and adults. For sevoflurane, MAC is 3.3% in neonates, 3.2% at 1–6 months and 2.5% above 6 months. Why MAC varies with age in this way is not known.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • The gas reaches the brain faster in children. Equilibrium between inspired gas and the brain is reached faster than in adults, most for more soluble agents such as isoflurane and less for sevoflurane and desflurane. In neonates this increases the risk of overdose, particularly when induction uses a high inspired concentration.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • The EEG and MAC are less closely related in children. Children have a higher BIS at the same fraction of MAC. In infants, the relationship between MAC and the EEG is substantially different from adults, and the cause is unknown. Both the raw and the processed EEG are unreliable measures of anaesthetic effect in infants.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • The younger the child, the higher the propofol induction dose. The ED50 for loss of the eyelash reflex is about 3 mg/kg at 1–6 months and 1.3–1.6 mg/kg at 1–12 years. In neonates, propofol is associated with profound hypotension.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • Sevoflurane can cause epileptiform EEG changes and emergence delirium. Epileptiform EEG changes have been described in children at high concentrations, and sevoflurane causes more emergence delirium than halothane. The cause is unknown. See also the card on epileptiform activity under anaesthesia in Artefacts and pitfalls.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • Preschool children easily develop agitation or delirium on emergence. The agitation can have many causes, including pain, fear and hunger.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • Clonidine and dexmedetomidine may be better premedication than midazolam. Clonidine gave better sedation and less agitation and pain after surgery than midazolam. Several studies found intranasal dexmedetomidine superior to midazolam as premedication.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • Dexmedetomidine produces sleep-like sedation. Children may be roused more easily from dexmedetomidine than from other sedatives.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • Remifentanil stands out. The half-life is 3–6 minutes regardless of age, and neonates eliminate it faster than older children, unlike most other drugs.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): MAC values and index values from adults cannot be transferred directly to the youngest. The raw EEG and spectrogram must be read with knowledge of what is normal for the age (see the infant cards above).Sources: Vutskits et al. 2025; Cornelissen 2018
Vutskits et al. 2025

The developing brain: can anaesthesia harm it? (Vutskits et al. 2025)

Short answer: animal studies have shown harm, but studies in children give no clear support that anaesthesia itself harms the brain. This card explains why the question is asked and what we know.

From immature brain to possible harm

↓
↓
↓
↓
uncertain meaning in children
Tap a step to read a short note about it.
Sources: Vutskits et al. 2025; Ben-Ari 2002
  • The FDA issued a warning in 2016. The risk may be greater with long and repeated anaesthetics in children under 3 years. The warning is controversial because it is based on animal data and few human studies.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • Animal data cannot be transferred directly. Developmental stages are hard to compare between species, and surgery and deranged homeostasis play a part. The human brain develops and compensates over a longer period, and genes and environment matter greatly.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • Cell death is small and does not necessarily explain the deficits. Fewer than 2 % of cells showed apoptosis, and the number of neurons did not fall. Both short and long exposures caused apoptosis, but only long exposures caused learning deficits. In neonatal rats isoflurane caused apoptosis in both sexes, but behavioural changes only in males.Source: Vutskits and Xie 2016 (review)
  • Synapses are affected differently by age. Early in the brain growth spurt, young rats lost dendritic spines and synapses within hours, and the changes could last into adulthood. Later in the period the number increased instead, even after 30 minutes of sevoflurane. After the first postnatal month in rats, which corresponds to the first years of life in humans, no such effect was found.Source: Vutskits and Xie 2016 (review)
  • Not all drugs cause apoptosis. Xenon, opioids and dexmedetomidine may have a non-apoptotic profile at therapeutic concentrations.Source: Vutskits and Xie 2016 (review)
  • Sevoflurane reduced glucose metabolism in young mice. Mice aged 14 days given 3 % sevoflurane for 2 hours on three consecutive days had less of the glucose transporter GLUT3, lower glucose metabolism in the hippocampus and temporal lobe, more apoptosis and impaired learning and memory. A review suggests that dose and duration of sevoflurane should be considered in long procedures in children.Sources: Zhu 2020 (animal study); Apai 2021 (review)
  • Children who have anaesthesia are not like other children. The illness or procedure may itself affect development. This is called confounding, and may also explain why several anaesthetics look worse than one.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • Population studies find small differences. Most large studies found a small difference in school grades or school readiness, smaller than the difference by sex or month of birth. Studies of diagnoses more often found learning or behavioural disorders, especially after several anaesthetics.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • The randomised trial found no difference. About one hour of general anaesthesia in infancy gave no difference in IQ at 5 years compared with regional anaesthesia.Sources: Vutskits et al. 2025; GAS, McCann 2019
  • Cleft lip and palate: the type of cleft mattered more than the anaesthetics. A Danish register study compared ninth-grade exam results in 558 adolescents with clefts, 509 of whom had surgery under anaesthesia, with 14,677 controls. Only children with isolated cleft palate did worse and more often lacked an exam result. Number and timing of operations were not associated with the outcome. A neurotoxic effect cannot be completely excluded.Source: Clausen 2017
  • Do not delay necessary surgery. Most paediatric anaesthesia societies do not recommend delaying surgery or changing the anaesthetic technique. Delay has its own risk, and no one knows a “safe” age. Be ready to answer parents who ask.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • Neonates having major surgery are a separate group. They have a higher risk of neurological injury. This may be due to illness, altered cerebral perfusion, hypotension, inflammation, hypoxia, hypercarbia, stress and pain, and not necessarily the anaesthetic.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • The EEG under anaesthesia differs in children born prematurely. In children around 5 years old under 2.5 % sevoflurane, those born prematurely had lower alpha and beta power than term-born children. The response to cannulation (more delta) was the same. Differences in background EEG may matter when the EEG is used to titrate dose.Source: Poorun 2016
Vutskits et al. 2025 Ben-Ari 2002 Davidson 2016 Sun 2016 Vutskits and Xie 2016 Clausen 2017 Zhu 2020 Apai 2021 Poorun 2016
The studies in detail: infants, autism, children 1–17 years, EEG-guided sevoflurane, case reports (5 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Infants and small children under sevoflurane: EEG develops with age

Two observational studies from the same group (Boston Children's Hospital) show that sevoflurane EEG changes markedly through the first years. The children were ASA I–II, without known neurological or cardiovascular disease, and received anaesthesia at the anaesthetist's discretion. 5 minutes from a period of stable end-tidal sevoflurane were analysed.

AgeFindings during maintenance (Cornelissen 2018, 91 children)
0–3 months (n = 17)Slow-delta (0.1–4 Hz). Very little power above 4 Hz. Frontal slow-delta is coherent.
4–6 months (n = 23)Theta and alpha emerge around 4 months, broadly distributed and without coherence.
7–9 months (n = 8)Alpha increases and becomes frontal. Slow-delta is no longer coherent from about 8–9 months.
10–14 months (n = 17)Alpha power levels off (about 6 dB frontally). Frontal alpha becomes coherent, at a very low level and with variation between children.
15 months and older (n = 26)Coherent frontal alpha persists and becomes stronger (until about 20 months). Beta and gamma are negligible at all ages.
  • Older eLife study (Cornelissen 2015, 36 children aged 0–6 months, 30 analysed): at 0–3 months alpha was negligible (peak −6.5 dB at 8 Hz), and at 4–6 months the peak was 6.7 dB at 9 Hz. Frontal alpha dominance over occipital was small and only present at 4–6 months. Frontal coherence (F7–F8) was high (about 0.6) in slow-delta and low otherwise, with no difference between the age groups. Global coherence was weak (under 0.2) in all bands.
  • What changed at emergence (2015): at 4–6 months, theta and alpha power fell when end-tidal sevoflurane dropped below 1.2%, roughly when movement began. No children moved at 1.2% or higher. Median end-tidal sevoflurane at first movement was 0.6% (0–3 months) and 0.4% (4–6 months). At 0–3 months there was no clear relationship between EEG power and concentration. Slow-delta was stable.
  • Dosing: the sevoflurane requirement during maintenance was lower at 0–3 months (median 2.0%) than at 4–6 months (2.6%). The authors also compared at the same end-tidal concentration (1.8%) and found the same age difference, so it is probably not explained by dose alone.
  • Interpretation: the authors link the changes to maturation of thalamocortical and cortico-cortical connections (synaptogenesis, myelination). They conclude that EEG indices developed in adults may give inaccurate estimates in infants, especially in the first three months, and that methods that take age into account are needed. Raw EEG and spectrogram are therefore more informative than a fixed index threshold.
  • Use in the app: the simulator shows only the youngest (under 1 year), and the sevoflurane text has been updated with these findings.
  • Reservations: observational studies without controlled dose titration, only sevoflurane, few children in each age group (especially 7–9 months, n = 8), and no formal assessment of consciousness (movement on video is used as a rough marker in 2015). The authors Purdon and Brown declare patent applications and a licence agreement with Masimo.
  • Awake versus maintenance (2015): in the 4–6 month group (n = 12 with awake recordings) theta and alpha power rose from the awake state to maintenance; in the 0–3 month group (n = 7) there was no change. Slow-delta was unchanged. “Awake” was defined as open eyes, movement or crying.
  • No alpha shift at emergence (2015): in the older infants there was no spatial shift of alpha at any sevoflurane concentration, unlike adults, in whom frontal alpha disappears and posterior alpha returns when consciousness is regained. The study could not assess anteriorisation (frontal shift of alpha), because the dose was not raised and lowered gradually during continuous recording. Two infants in the 0–3 group (107 and 116 days, almost 4 months) had low alpha that fell at emergence, in line with the circuits starting to mature around 4 months.
  • Anaesthetic conditions (2015): all had sevoflurane induction, with nitrous oxide in 29 of 36. Propofol for intubation was used in 19 of 36 according to the methods (table 1 gives 11 of the 30 analysed, see “Discrepancies”). No one received midazolam or other premedication. The analysed period was a median of 77 minutes (IQR 32–93) after propofol or nitrous oxide. End-tidal sevoflurane was adjusted by the anaesthetist’s judgement, not to a fixed concentration.
  • More caveats (2015): movement on video is a crude marker of emergence, and the infants may still have been sedated even though movement had returned. Slow-delta may carry a lot of movement noise. Funding: NIH, Boston Children’s Hospital, Massachusetts General Hospital and a foundation; the funders had no role in the study.
Cornelissen et al. eLife 2015;4:e06513 and Br J Anaesth 2018;120:1274–1286

Autism: the propofol EEG changes differently with age, and burst suppression is about twice as common (Walsh 2018)

  • Design: prospective observation at MGH, four-channel frontal EEG (SedLine) during routine endoscopy, 2014–2016. Primary cohort 42 patients with ASD (DSM-5) and 110 neurotypical, 2–23 years, 120 seconds of stable propofol infusion with no other drugs in the preceding 5 minutes. Secondary cohort 56 vs 123 (2–30 years) for burst suppression. Dosing at clinical discretion; Bayesian regression adjusted for sex, propofol dose, midazolam, fentanyl and epilepsy.
  • Findings: the structure (slow-delta + frontal coherent alpha) was the same, but the evolution with age differed. Slow power (0.1–1 Hz) was higher in ASD at 2.3 years (17.05 vs 14.20 dB) and lower at 10.8 years (16.93 vs 18.99 dB, 80.8% certainty) and 22.5 years; adjusted difference −1.93 dB (80% CI −3.38 to −0.54). Alpha was lower in ASD already at 5.4 years (17.65 vs 18.86 dB) and the decline accelerated to 22.5 years (6.37 vs 11.89 dB, 80.2% certainty); adjusted mean difference −0.47 dB, not significant. Burst suppression occurred in 23.0% vs 12.2% (probability 0.973 of higher incidence), despite lower propofol doses in the ASD group.
  • Interpretation (the authors'): the pattern resembles that of older adults (less alpha, more burst suppression, Purdon 2015) and may reflect abnormal GABAergic inhibitory circuits (fewer PV+ interneurons, accelerated cortical thinning in adolescence) and a higher NKCC1:KCC2 ratio with more intracellular potassium, which in the Ching 2012 model gives a greater propensity for burst suppression. They call it “a form of accelerated neuronal aging”, as a hypothesis.
  • Clinical: an index or spectrogram that looks like an “older brain” in a young patient with autism is not necessarily wrong, and the authors suggest titrating the dose to the EEG, not to age. Caveats: observational study without controlled dosing; the ASD group was younger, more male, received more midazolam (mean 0.01 mg/kg, clinically negligible) and had 9.5% epilepsy; in the burst-suppression analysis the ASD patients were older and 21.4% had epilepsy. The abstract gives p < 0.01 for burst suppression, the results section p < 0.05.
Walsh et al. Front Syst Neurosci 2018;12:23

Children 1–17 years: more power, but the same structure as in adults

  • Structure: in patients over 1 year, propofol-induced EEG is qualitatively similar regardless of age, with slow-delta and coherent frontal alpha. Under 1 year, alpha is not coherent (Lee 2017, 97 patients aged 0–21 years, but only 4 under 1 year). The same applies to sevoflurane: alpha coherence is absent under 1 year (Akeju 2015, 54 patients 0–28 years; only 4 were under 1 year).
  • Power: total EEG power during sevoflurane increased from infancy to about 6 years and then declined to a level that remained stable from about 21 years (Akeju 2015). The results section in Akeju 2015 gives the peak as 5–8 years, while the abstract gives about 6 years. Reviews and later articles citing Lee 2017 and Akeju 2015 give about 6–8 years. The timing varies somewhat between sources.
  • Higher frequencies: according to Akeju 2015, power in the higher frequency bands (beta and gamma) is higher in children over 1 year than in adults at a surgical level of anaesthesia. The alpha peak and the structure were similar across ages over 1 year.
  • Caveats (Akeju 2015): retrospective study of routine recordings with SedLine (Fp1, Fp2, F7 and F8) in 54 patients, with sevoflurane as the only hypnotic. The groups were divided by visual assessment and had different treatment: end-tidal sevoflurane fell from 3.0 vol% in those under 1 year to 1.9 vol% in 22–28-year-olds (1.3 to 1.0 MAC), and neuromuscular blocking agents were used in none under 1 year and in 9–10 adults. The authors argue that the dose cannot explain an approximately threefold difference in amplitude (about 9–10 dB) in children over 1 year, and that the differing use of neuromuscular blockers may explain some of the difference at high frequency (beta and gamma) but not the power below 24 Hz. They also discuss that skull conductivity changes with age, but conclude that the findings reflect brain development. Three authors (Akeju, Brown and Purdon) have filed a provisional patent application on the use of the EEG measures.
  • Alpha frequency: the sources do not state that the alpha peak is faster in children over 1 year than in adults. In infants, an alpha/beta oscillation is described that appears around 9 months and decreases in peak frequency towards about 1 year, but that applies to infants. In older patients the alpha peak shows slowing: in a series of 155 patients aged 18 to 90, both alpha coherence and the alpha peak frequency were significantly lower in the oldest (Purdon 2015, Sleigh et al. 2025). Comparing a child with an old patient, the child therefore has faster alpha, but that is ageing at the other end rather than a separate paediatric frequency. The simulator for children therefore changes power and sevoflurane beta, but not alpha frequency.
  • Why 1 year keeps appearing as the lower limit: frontal alpha becomes coherent at about 10 months (Cornelissen 2015, 2018), and from 1 year the structure is qualitatively like that of adults (Lee 2017). It is the same limit used when paediatric versions of EEG indices are stated to apply from 1 year. Below 1 year the pattern the indices are built on is missing, and then the raw EEG and the spectrogram are what you have.
  • Practical: the authors suggest that age must be taken into account when interpreting EEG, and that raw EEG and spectrogram are more informative than indices developed in adults. The studies are observational studies of patients who received anaesthesia at the anaesthetist's discretion.
Akeju 2015, Lee 2017

EEG-guided sevoflurane in children 1–6 years: less emergence delirium (Miyasaka 2025, RCT)

Randomised single-centre study from Tokyo (JAMA Pediatr 2025;179:704–712), 177 children aged 1 to under 6 years undergoing procedures with good regional/opioid analgesia. Control: mask induction with 5% sevoflurane and maintenance at 1.0 MAC (2.5%). Intervention: sevoflurane titrated to the lowest concentration that maintained a continuous alpha and slow-delta pattern on the spectrogram, adjusted in 0.1% steps, typically from 2% downwards. All received remifentanil 0.5 µg/kg/min plus a block.

  • Main finding: emergence delirium (PAED ≥ 10) in 21% versus 35% (difference 14%, p = 0.04). Sevoflurane during maintenance 0.9% (about 0.36 MAC) versus 2.5%; exposure 0.8 versus 2.1 MAC-hours. Emergence 21 minutes earlier and 16.5 minutes shorter in the recovery unit.
  • The most important point for EEG interpretation: PSI during surgery averaged 66 in the EEG group versus 42 in the control group, and SEF 24 versus 17 Hz. The index thus said “too light” (above 50) in children who, in the authors' assessment, were deeply unconscious with clear alpha and slow-delta. The authors explain this by the indices being calibrated against conventional practice where 1.0 MAC is regarded as adequate, so that index-guided dosing favours 1.0 MAC. Burst suppression occurred equally often in both groups (22 versus 23%, mostly seconds).
  • What they steered by: not theta, but alpha + slow-delta. At lower concentration the alpha frequency rose and alpha began to dissolve into higher frequencies while delta persisted; this was regarded as the start of a lighter state, and sevoflurane was increased again. In practice this is the same picture as “alpha without theta fill”.
  • The emergence course: all the children passed through a delta-dominated state before emergence. Children who developed delirium had a broader delta band and slightly more beta in the minute before eye opening. The authors suggest that PAED may be more related to the emergence course than to total exposure (cf. Hesse 2019 in adults).
  • The authors' own caveats: the effect on delirium was “marginal” relative to the large dose reduction; with a PAED threshold of 12 instead of 10 the difference was not significant, and an interim analysis means that p = 0.04 does not fully control the error rate (adjusted p = 0.03 with Lan-DeMets, 0.05 with O'Brien-Fleming). One anaesthetist with EEG training delivered all the anaesthetics, at Japan's largest children's hospital, so the result is not readily transferable. Awareness was not investigated with a structured interview; the maintenance concentration was about 1.4 × MAC-awake for the age group.
  • Conflicts of interest: Masimo provided Root, SedLine and paediatric sensors; Miyasaka and Nagasaka report non-financial support from Masimo, Nagasaka is a consultant for Masimo, and Brown receives royalties from Masimo. Masimo saw the manuscript without editorial rights.
  • Context in the app: supports that the indices cannot be used uncritically in children (images 1, 7 and 18 in the image quiz), and is the closest evidence for the hypothesis of dosing sevoflurane to the alpha pattern and no higher (the card on sevoflurane theta). Earlier RCTs with index-guided dosing (Frederick 2016, Long 2022, Han 2022) gave much smaller dose reductions.
Miyasaka et al. JAMA Pediatr 2025;179:704–712

Three case reports with EEG in children (Brandt 2020)

Narrative review with case reports from Purdon's group (Anesth Analg 2020;131:1043–1056). EEG was recorded observationally and not used to guide the anaesthetic.

  • 2 years, propofol for endoscopy and colonoscopy: at 100 µg/kg/min the spectrogram showed beta/gamma oscillations, as in sedated adults, and the child moved at the start of colonoscopy. After a bolus and 250 µg/kg/min the power shifted down to alpha and slow-delta, the same pattern as in unconscious adults, and the child lay still.
  • 9 months, isoflurane and nitrous oxide for ureteroureterostomy: from an unconscious state with slow-delta and a widened alpha/beta band (7–23 Hz), the 7–15 Hz power weakened and beta shifted upwards from minute 204; the child moved at minute 208, while the heart rate only changed at the movement. The EEG thus warned of emergence about 4–5 minutes before clinical signs. Propofol 40 mg and higher isoflurane then gave about 6 minutes of burst suppression with isoelectric periods and a MAP fall of 20 mmHg to 35 mmHg. The authors call this overcorrection.
  • 19 years with severe autism, propofol for sigmoidoscopy: after ketamine and midazolam as premedication, the EEG showed broad beta. Three minutes after starting propofol 350 µg/kg/min, burst suppression occurred with apnoea and SpO₂ 82%, followed by 12 minutes of isoelectric EEG despite reduction to 200 µg/kg/min, with stable haemodynamics and SpO₂ above 99%. The patient did not wake for over 2 hours. In Walsh 2018, young people with autism had about twice the incidence of burst suppression despite lower doses, and valproate lowers anaesthetic requirements.
  • The authors' point: the patterns from adults (beta/gamma during sedation, alpha and slow-delta during unconsciousness, “unzipping” at emergence, burst suppression with overdosing) are also seen in children over about 1 year, with higher power. Indices are assumed to give too high values in adequately anaesthetised children, because beta and gamma are elevated, and raw EEG with spectrogram is proposed as an alternative.
  • Caveats: case reports, no control, and Purdon reports patents licensed to Masimo, speaker fees from Masimo and co-founding of PASCALL Systems.
Brandt et al. Anesth Analg 2020;131:1043–1056

Burst suppression is common in children under 3 years (Gao 2021)

Retrospective pilot study from a children’s hospital in Beijing: 54 children aged 1–36 months received sevoflurane or propofol with remifentanil. The EEG was recorded but not used to guide anaesthesia.

  • More than half had burst suppression. 30 of 54 (56%) had burst suppression at some point, most often during induction. During surgery itself, 18 of 54 (33%) had it, and they were younger (median 5 vs 14.5 months).
  • More with sevoflurane, boluses and low blood pressure. Burst suppression occurred in 72% with sevoflurane and 41% with propofol, and in 8 of 9 who received a propofol bolus. Of the children with burst suppression, 77% had mild or moderate hypotension, vs 25% of those without. End-tidal sevoflurane and propofol dose did not differ during maintenance.
  • Caveat: a small retrospective study without adjustment for other factors. The authors themselves write that the associations may reflect chance and confounding, for example a bolus causing both deeper anaesthesia and lower blood pressure. The study says nothing about outcomes. The definition is given as voltage ≤ 5.0 mV, which probably should be µV (see Discrepancies).
Source: Gao 2021 Gao et al. Pediatr Investig 2021;5:271–276

Key points

  • In the first three months the anaesthesia EEG looks different: Under sevoflurane slow-delta dominates, and theta and alpha only appear around 4 months. Indices developed in adults may therefore give misleading numbers in the youngest.See Spectrogram → Children, “Infants: the EEG matures over the first months”
  • Preterm-born children are a group of their own: Children born prematurely had less alpha and beta under sevoflurane several years later than term-born children. In the Nordic countries, anaesthesia for preterm infants varies greatly, with up to 20-fold differences in dose, and EEG is not mentioned among the monitoring.See
  • A nearly flat EEG is common in the youngest under anaesthesia: Among 648 children under 3 years, 32 % had at least one episode of an almost flat EEG, and 59 % of those under 3 months. The episodes were associated with a propofol bolus, lower blood pressure and a slightly higher sevoflurane concentration. What they mean for the brain in the long term is not known.See

More on the maturation of the EEG in . EEG monitoring of newborns in intensive care with aEEG is described in .

Preterm-born children: a different EEG and wide variation in practice

  • Children born preterm have a different anaesthesia EEG even years later. In children aged 1–12 years who received sevoflurane alone (stable 2.5 % end-tidal), the 15 born prematurely (mean 29 weeks) had lower background alpha and beta power than the 30 born at term. The difference was significant (p = 0.048). Cannulation produced an equal increase in delta in both groups. The authors suggest that a different background EEG may matter when EEG is used to dose anaesthesia.Source: Poorun 2016
  • Anaesthesia for preterm infants varies widely in the Nordic countries. The paediatric anaesthesiologists reported 15 combinations for induction (most often fentanyl and thiopental) and 13 for maintenance (most often fentanyl and sevoflurane). Doses varied up to 20-fold between the lowest and the highest.Source: van der Heijden and Frykholm 2026 (survey of 57 paediatric anaesthesiologists at 14 hospitals in the five Nordic countries, 2024)
  • EEG is not part of the monitoring. EEG is not mentioned among the monitoring methods in the survey. 86 % used gestational age in weeks as the lowest acceptable mean arterial pressure in mmHg. NIRS was used by 40 %, most without a fixed threshold for intervention.Source: van der Heijden and Frykholm 2026
  • Research and evidence-based protocols are needed for this vulnerable group. That is the authors' conclusion from the wide variation. Caveat: the response rate was about 30 %, and the answers reflect what the doctors report, not measured practice.
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): in the youngest and most immature, anaesthesia is currently dosed without looking at the target organ, and the EEG looks different both with age and after preterm birth. An age pattern in the spectrogram therefore cannot be transferred directly from adults or older children.
Poorun 2016 van der Heijden and Frykholm 2026

Nearly flat EEG in infants and toddlers under anaesthesia (Yuan 2020 and 2022)

This card is about how often the EEG becomes almost flat during anaesthesia in children under 3 years. The findings concern anaesthesia for surgery, not sedation in intensive care.Sources: Yuan 2020 (Anesth Analg) and Yuan 2022 (Anesthesiology), same research group

  • An almost flat EEG is common in the youngest, especially under 3 months. Among 648 children under 3 years at 15 hospitals, 32 % had at least one episode: 59 % at 0–3 months and 24–28 % in the older groups. The proportion varied from 9 to 88 % between hospitals. In a smaller pilot study 63 % had at least one episode, but the episodes made up only 0.1 % of anaesthetic time.Sources: Yuan 2022 (Australia, China, Europe and the USA; sevoflurane or propofol); Yuan 2020 (51 children)
  • The episodes occur mostly early in the anaesthetic. They were most common before incision (19 %) and during maintenance (18 %). In the pilot study most occurred between induction and incision.Sources: Yuan 2022; Yuan 2020
  • The studies defined “flat” slightly differently. The pilot study used below 20 µV for at least 2 seconds. The large study recorded frontally with four channels (SedLine) and required below ±10 µV for at least 2 seconds in all four channels simultaneously.Sources: Yuan 2020; Yuan 2022
  • Young age, a propofol bolus and low blood pressure were associated with the episodes. The strongest were young age (0–3 months, OR 4.4 versus 19–36 months) and a propofol bolus after sevoflurane induction (OR 2.9). Moderate and severe hypotension had 3.5–7 times higher odds, although the difference in mean arterial pressure was only 4–5 mmHg. A tracheal tube rather than a laryngeal mask and slightly higher sevoflurane (about 0.2 percentage points) were also associated with episodes, while neuromuscular blockade for intubation was associated with fewer.Source: Yuan 2022
  • The significance for outcome is unclear. The episodes were not associated with emergence behaviour. Quality of life at 30 days was measured, but the analysis was exploratory and cannot be interpreted with confidence.Source: Yuan 2022
  • Caveats: observational studies, so they show associations, not causes. Frontal EEG does not see the whole brain. The manufacturer supplied the monitors and sensors, and two of the authors have received fees from the manufacturer.
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): in the youngest, anaesthesia may become deeper than necessary when the dose is guided by age, weight and circulation alone. The raw EEG and spectrogram can show this as it happens, and the findings fit with the EEG in infants under 3 months looking different (see the Children sub-tab). Whether avoiding the episodes improves outcome has not been studied.
Yuan 2020 Yuan 2022

A rapidly developing brain: what the textbook says (Vutskits et al. 2025)

  • The brain grows fastest from the third trimester to the first years of life. In this period, very many synapses are formed, and neural activity guides how the networks develop. Drugs that interfere with normal activity in this period may affect brain development.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • Neonates respond to pain, but differently. Preterm and term neonates respond more diffusely and less specifically to noxious stimulation than older children. When pain begins to be experienced is unresolved. Early painful experiences may nevertheless alter later function of the central nervous system, even if they are not conscious, and adequate pain relief can improve outcome.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • Neurotoxicity has been shown in the laboratory but is uncertain in humans. Both inhaled and intravenous anaesthetics cause neurotoxicity and behavioural changes in laboratory studies. Some human studies find an association between anaesthesia early in life and later developmental problems, but this may be explained by other factors.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): In the youngest, both too deep anaesthesia and inadequate pain relief are possible concerns. What the episodes of isoelectric EEG mean in the long term is not known (see the Yuan card above).Sources: Vutskits et al. 2025; Yuan 2022
Vutskits et al. 2025
Drugs: consciousness and amnesia

Each drug is described separately here: where it acts, what it does to consciousness, memory, pain and movement, and how it looks in the EEG. The figures are population averages from the literature with large individual variation, and they are not dosing advice. Why the dose is only a prediction is explained in the “Dose and prediction” sub-tab.

Where the agents act: receptors and regions

The agents at a glance

Each agent has its own EEG signature, because they act on different receptors and circuits. Tap an agent to read more.

AgentActs viaEEG signatureNote
GABAASlow-delta and coherent frontal alpha. Occipital alpha disappears.Half lose response at 2.3–3.5 µg/ml, and burst suppression appears at about 5 µg/ml. Given alone, 15–16 µg/ml is needed to prevent movement at incision. Burst suppression therefore comes long before the patient lies still, so movement does not by itself mean the hypnosis is too light.
GABAABeta at sedative doses, which can resemble ketamine. At higher doses more slow-delta is described.Hypnosis and amnesia usually at 100–200 ng/ml. The patient may seem awake and still not remember.
NMDA blockadeActive EEG: generalised theta, alternating slow-delta and gamma. Alpha does not move forward.Dissociative anaesthesia. Increases CMRO₂ and usually gives no burst suppression.
α2 agonistSlow-delta and spindles around 9–15 Hz. Resembles NREM 2.The patient can be woken. Rousable sedation at about 0.2–0.3 ng/ml.
α2 agonist, less selectiveNo spectral study of clonidine combined with propofol or a volatile agent.Enhances other hypnotics, but does not produce hypnosis alone. MAC-awake down 17–21 %, with a ceiling.
GABAAFrom fast activity through slow activity to burst suppression and isoelectric EEG at large doses.CMRO₂ falls to about 50 % when the EEG becomes isoelectric, and no further.
GABAA and othersThe same basic pattern as propofol: slow-delta with frontal alpha. Sevoflurane also fills in theta at 1 MAC and above.1 MAC is the alveolar concentration at which half of patients do not move at incision: about 2.0 vol % for sevoflurane, 1.2 % for isoflurane and 6.0 % for desflurane at 30–55 years.
NMDA blockadeBeta and gamma, so the index can rise even though the patient is unconscious. On switching from an ether agent to over 70 % nitrous oxide, a strong, transient slow-delta can appear before beta and gamma come. The sources disagree about how much the index is affected.Too weak alone, MAC 105 %. Used as an adjunct.
μ receptorUsual doses change the EEG little. Very high doses give slow delta waves, with a ceiling. Fentanyl gives frontal theta.Not complete anaesthetics. They lower MAC, but with a ceiling.

Sources: Purdon 2015 Part I; Vuyk et al. 2025; Perouansky et al. 2025; Kim et al. 2025; Akeju 2014; Vlisides 2017; Brandt 2020; Sutter and Kaplan 2012; Kim 2024; Pilge 2014. The figures and caveats are on each agent's card.

Key points

  • The agents act on different receptors and circuits. Propofol, barbiturates, etomidate and benzodiazepines act via the GABAA receptor. Ketamine blocks the NMDA receptor. Dexmedetomidine and clonidine act on α2 receptors. The EEG signatures are thought to arise because the drugs act on specific receptors in specific circuits.See “Basic concepts: receptors, ion channels and circuits”
  • Amnesia, unconsciousness and immobility need different doses. With propofol, memory is lost at a lighter hypnotic level than response. Preventing movement at incision needs a much higher concentration (about 15–16 µg/ml with no other drugs). Midazolam causes anterograde amnesia but did not reliably produce retrograde amnesia in the studies.See
  • Slow waves do not mean the same for every drug. Under dexmedetomidine the EEG resembles NREM 2 sleep, connectivity within the cortex is preserved, and the patient can be roused. Increased delta after clonidine should not be read as just as much deeper hypnosis as the same change after more propofol. Ketamine gives an active EEG with theta and gamma.See
  • When benzodiazepines fail, the NMDA side may explain why. In alcohol withdrawal and prolonged seizures, GABAA inhibition weakens while the NMDA system becomes overactive. Propofol or ketamine has been used when benzodiazepines do not work. The studies are small and retrospective. (interpretation based on the sources)See “Propofol and midazolam: alone, together and in withdrawal”
  • Involuntary movements with propofol can mislead the index. Seizure-like phenomena are rare and occur mostly at induction and emergence. The muscle noise can raise the index. So look at the raw EEG and the patient. Consider full EEG for prolonged or repeated episodes or known epilepsy. (interpretation based on the sources)See “Propofol and involuntary movements: dyskinesia and seizure-like phenomena”
  • Age and opioids lower requirements, but the sources give different figures. MAC falls by 4–6 % per decade, depending on the source. Opioids lower MAC, but with a ceiling. High doses can stop spontaneous breathing without the patient losing consciousness.See
  • The dose is a prediction, not a measurement. The numbers on the pump and in the tables apply to an average patient. With fast induction the pump showed almost double the concentration of slow induction, for the same endpoint. After brief burst suppression the same calculated concentration gave a deeper effect than the model predicted. The brain's response must therefore be observed.See

Each drug has its own sub-tab. The basic concepts of receptors and circuits are below this overview.

Basic concepts: receptors, ion channels and circuits
Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025 Purdon 2015 Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010

Each drug below has its own section on the micro level: which receptors the drug binds to, what happens in the nerve cell, and which circuits are affected. Much of this knowledge comes from animal experiments, cell studies and modelling. The mechanisms are probable, not fully mapped.

  • The GABAA receptor comes in many variants. It is a chloride channel made of five subunits. It can be built from 18 or more different subunits, and the α subunit exists in six variants (α1–α6). Different parts of the brain have different combinations. The drugs bind at the interfaces between subunits, and the combination determines how well, for example, propofol, etomidate or pentobarbital binds.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • When the channel opens, the nerve cell is inhibited. Chloride flows in, the cell membrane is hyperpolarised, and it takes more for the nerve cell to fire. This is why the GABA system is called inhibitory.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • The drugs enhance GABA, and at high doses activate the channel themselves. At clinical concentrations propofol, barbiturates and etomidate enhance the action of GABA, so less GABA is needed. At higher concentrations they can open the channel directly, without GABA. Benzodiazepines only enhance the GABA response.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • The hippocampus has its own sustained inhibition. It has many GABAA receptors with the α5 subunit, which is almost absent elsewhere in the cortex. They give sustained (tonic) inhibition of CA1 pyramidal cells and regulate long-term potentiation (LTP) with stimulation in the theta range. This is linked to amnesia, see etomidate and inhaled agents.Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Ketamine blocks the NMDA receptor only when the channel is open. The NMDA receptor is a glutamate-gated ion channel, and ketamine is a channel blocker.Source: Purdon 2015
  • α2 adrenoceptors act via G proteins. They inhibit adenylate cyclase and affect calcium and potassium channels.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Wakefulness is maintained by several arousal centres. These are nuclei in the brainstem, hypothalamus and basal forebrain: locus coeruleus (noradrenaline), raphe (serotonin), tuberomammillary nucleus (histamine), ventral tegmental area (dopamine), basal forebrain and the laterodorsal and pedunculopontine tegmental nuclei (acetylcholine), and lateral hypothalamus (orexin). The preoptic area of the hypothalamus sends inhibitory GABA and galanin pathways to these centres. Activation of these pathways is thought to be a key part of how NREM sleep begins.Sources: Brown 2010, Purdon 2015
  • The EEG signatures reflect receptors and circuits. The signatures are thought to arise because the drugs act on specific receptors in specific circuits. With propofol, thalamus and cortex do not switch off when inhibited. They are tightly connected and instead oscillate in rhythms such as alpha and beta.Source: Purdon 2015
  • Interactions give clues about the site of action. Additivity suggests a shared site, synergy different sites. See the card «Synergy between agents and isoelectric EEG».Source: Hendrickx 2008

Slow waves do not mean the same for every drug

An EEG dominated by slow waves is easily read as deep hypnosis. But its meaning depends on which drug produces the waves, and on what happens in the circuits behind them.

  • Dexmedetomidine resembles sleep. During deep dexmedetomidine sedation the EEG resembled NREM sleep stage 2. The spindles were like those in normal sleep, but lasted longer (1.11 vs 0.88 seconds). In an earlier study by the same group, participants could be roused with verbal commands, even at 5.1 ng/ml. Spindles and slow waves are smaller than under propofol, which may possibly explain why the patient can be roused. The study is small, with one channel.Sources: Huupponen 2008 (and an earlier study by the same group), Purdon 2015
  • The cortex stays in contact. During dexmedetomidine-induced loss of response to command, coupling between the thalamus and the default mode network was disrupted, but coupling between cortical areas was preserved in an fMRI study. The authors propose a hierarchy: lighter states (NREM 2 sleep, dexmedetomidine) disrupt thalamocortical coupling. Deeper states (propofol anaesthesia) also disrupt cortical coupling. Caveat: connectivity in fMRI is co-variation, not directly measured communication between nerve cells.Source: Akeju, Loggia et al. 2014
  • The starting point is thought to be the locus coeruleus. Dexmedetomidine hyperpolarises nerve cells in the locus coeruleus. Less noradrenaline is then released, and the preoptic area inhibits the arousal centres. In rats, antisense against α2A in the locus coeruleus delayed and shortened loss of righting reflex, while antisense against α2C had no effect (4–5 rats per group). Mice that cannot make noradrenaline are nevertheless hypersensitive to dexmedetomidine. This suggests that other mechanisms also exist.Sources: Purdon 2015, Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025, Mizobe 1996
  • Clonidine enhances other hypnotics, but does not produce hypnosis alone. Propofol and clonidine were additive for hypnosis, and clonidine lowered sevoflurane MAC-awake by 17–21 %, with a ceiling. Fentanyl and clonidine produced hypnosis together in animals even though neither did alone. No spectral study of clonidine combined with propofol or a volatile agent was found. When dexmedetomidine was given under propofol, delta–theta rose from 4.5 to 7.7 dB and PSI fell from 30 to 23, but consciousness was not tested. Interpretation based on the sources: increased delta after clonidine should not be read as just as much deeper hypnosis as the same change after more propofol. Nor should the volatile agent be lowered below what is needed for unconsciousness.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, Zhang 2021, Hight 2020
  • Ketamine pulls the EEG the other way. Ketamine gives an active EEG with generalised theta, plus alternating slow-delta and gamma, even though the patient is unconscious in a dissociative state. Ketamine also increases cerebral metabolism.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025, Akeju

The studies in detail:

Huupponen 2008 Akeju, Loggia et al. 2014 Mizobe 1996 Purdon 2015 Hendrickx 2008 Zhang 2021 Hight 2020 Mashour and Pryor 2025; Vuyk et al. 2025
The studies in detail: Morgan and Mikhail (1 card)

What another textbook says: Morgan and Mikhail 2022 (ch. 8, 9 and 43)

Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 7th edition (Butterworth, Mackey, Wasnick, McGraw Hill 2022). The chapters on volatile agents, intravenous agents and geriatric anaesthesia contain little on EEG, but three things are worth keeping alongside Miller's.

  • MAC-awake (Mashour and Pryor 2025): 0.3–0.4 MAC (the figure is not in the chapter by Mashour and Pryor, but in Morgan and Mikhail) is associated with awakening when the volatile agent is the only thing maintaining the anaesthetic, versus 1.3 MAC to prevent movement in about 95%. The distance between “no movement” and “awake” may allow the EEG pattern to look adequate close to emergence (interpretation based on the sources; see neural inertia in Hight 2020, Fundamentals tab).
  • MAC and age: Mashour and Pryor 2025 gives a 6% fall in MAC per decade “regardless of agent”, ch. 43 gives 4% per decade over 40 years (see discrepancies). Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025 gives 6% per decade after 30 years (Mapleson 1996).
  • Barbiturates and EEG (Vuyk et al. 2025): the EEG goes from low-voltage fast activity at small doses to high-voltage slow activity, burst suppression and electrical silence at large doses, in parallel with the fall in cerebral metabolism (about 50% at isoelectric EEG). Thiopental accumulates with repeated or prolonged dosing and then delays emergence. delayed extubation and a need for inotropes. Ketamine “dissociates” sensory impulses from the limbic cortex, and the patient can look awake (eye opening, swallowing) without necessarily being so.
  • Older patients (ch. 43): the chapter says that “some have suggested” that BIS monitoring may reduce cognitive impairment, and that the mechanism of perioperative neurocognitive disorder is unclear. This is more weakly worded than Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025, which proposes pEEG to avoid burst suppression.
Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 7th ed. 2022, ch. 8, 9 and 43
Propofol
EEG signature (Purdon 2015) Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Half lose response at 2.3–3.5 µg/ml. This applies when no other agents are given. In volunteers, half were unresponsive at BIS 63 and 95% at BIS 51.
  • Memory goes before response. 95% had no recall at BIS 77. Amnesia thus sets in at a lighter level of hypnosis than loss of response. Unstimulated volunteers needed an infusion of at least 2 mg/kg/h for amnesia.Sources: Glass 1997; Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Much more propofol is needed to prevent movement. Half did not move at incision at 16 µg/ml without other agents (Sleigh et al. 2025: at least 15). With opioid, markedly less is needed. Muscle tone is reduced, but movement in response to surgical stimulation may occur. Aitkenhead gives lower figures (see Discrepancies).Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025; Aitkenhead ch. 3
  • Awareness can occur shortly after induction. Propofol is rapidly redistributed and metabolised. The risk may increase during intubation after a non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking agent, or at the start of surgery, unless an inhaled agent or more propofol is given.Source: Aitkenhead ch. 3
  • The EEG shows alpha-delta during maintenance. See the Spectrogram tab.
  • Blood pressure falls later than the EEG changes. The half-time for equilibration between blood and effect is about 2.5 minutes for the EEG and about 7 minutes for haemodynamic depression. Hypotension may increase some minutes after loss of consciousness.
  • Older patients need much less, but the numbers differ. The sources disagree on how much less patients aged 80 years or more need than 20-year-olds: about half the dose (Vuyk et al. 2025) or a 65% lower dose (Kim et al. 2025, Schnider 1999).Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Kim et al. 2025; Schnider 1999

The BIS values above are from healthy volunteers. Individual patients can become conscious at BIS values from 40 to 90.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Propofol acts mainly via the β subunit of the GABAA receptor. Sites on β1, β2 and β3 in the part of the receptor that crosses the cell membrane are important. The α and γ2 subunits also seem to contribute.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Propofol enhances GABA, and at high concentrations it opens the channel itself. The enhancement shifts the concentration–response curve to the left. At higher concentrations propofol activates the channel directly.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Propofol also acts at many other sites. It inhibits NMDA receptors widely (through modulation of sodium channel gating) and acts on GABAA and glycine receptors in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. It increases dopamine in the nucleus accumbens (well-being), reduces serotonin in the area postrema (antiemetic) and inhibits release of acetylcholine in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. The α2 system seems to play an indirect role in sedation.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • More inhibition in cortex and thalamus is thought to give beta, then alpha and slow-delta, as the dose rises. In the cortex, propofol enhances the inhibition of pyramidal cells by inhibitory interneurons. In the thalamus, propofol enhances GABA inhibition in the reticular nucleus, which controls what the thalamus passes on to the cortex. Because thalamus and cortex are tightly connected, this may produce oscillations first in beta at sedative doses, and then in alpha once the dose is large enough for loss of consciousness. It is alpha together with slow-delta that is the pattern under general anaesthesia, not beta. Propofol also enhances the inhibitory GABA pathways from the preoptic area to the arousal centres, and release of histamine from the tuberomammillary nucleus is inhibited. Less excitatory input from thalamus and brainstem hyperpolarises the cortex and gives slow-delta.Sources: Purdon 2015, Brown 2010
  • After a bolus, propofol probably acts rapidly in the brainstem. Slow-delta appears within seconds, together with loss of response, loss of the oculocephalic reflex, apnoea and atonia. This is interpreted as action on cranial nerve nuclei III, IV and VI (eye movements), the respiratory centres in the medulla and pons (apnoea) and reticular nuclei in the pons and medulla (atonia).Source: Purdon 2015
  • Alpha and slow waves disrupt communication in different ways. Frontal alpha is highly coherent and may arise in circuits between thalamus and frontal cortex. The slow waves are not coherent. Recordings with electrodes in the cortex show that they bracket brief periods of firing. The proposal is that alpha prevents normal communication between thalamus and cortex, and that the slow waves prevent communication within the cortex.Source: Purdon 2015
  • Paradoxical excitation has two proposed explanations. One is GABAA-mediated inhibition of the inhibitory pathways from the globus pallidus to the thalamus, so that the thalamus drives the cortex more. The other (from simulation studies) is transient blockade of slow potassium currents in cortical nerve cells.Source: Purdon 2015
  • Propofol appears to prevent new learning in the hippocampus, but does not weaken what is already learned. When we learn something new, the connections between nerve cells in the hippocampus become stronger and stay strong. This is called long-term potentiation (LTP) and is regarded as a cellular mechanism of learning. Propofol appears to prevent such strengthening from getting started, but does not weaken strengthening that has already taken place. Connections becoming weaker (long-term depression, LTD) is not reliably affected. The effect acts via the GABAA receptor, because it disappears when the receptor is blocked with picrotoxin. In one study, LTP was inhibited only at doses that produce anaesthesia, not at lower doses that only cause memory loss. In addition, the cortex and hippocampus stop oscillating together in the theta rhythm (4–8 Hz), via the β3 subunit of the GABAA receptor. This fits with words learned before propofol being remembered normally in Veselis 2004, while words learned while propofol was acting were lost faster (interpretation based on the sources, see the card on Veselis 2004).Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Physostigmine has reversed propofol-induced unconsciousness. Brown 2010 writes that clinical studies have shown this, but refers to a study in volunteers (Meuret 2000). Physostigmine increases cholinergic activity throughout the cortex.Source: Brown 2010
  • Propofol can both suppress seizures and produce epileptiform changes. It suppresses seizures through GABA, NMDA inhibition and slow calcium channels. GABA agonism and glycine antagonism can also produce epileptiform changes, especially at induction and emergence.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
Propofol and involuntary movements: dyskinesia and seizure-like phenomena
Walder 2002 San-juan 2010 Lee 2020 Bilotta 2006 Reddy 1993
  • Serious events are rare, but movements at induction are more common. In adults, 5.5% had movements with propofol, versus 86.6% with etomidate. In children, 3 mg/kg gave spontaneous movements in 90%, versus 20% at 4 mg/kg.Sources: Reddy 1993, Borgeat 1997
  • Repeated boluses for sedation give more movement than infusion. During ERCP, 21% had involuntary movements with boluses, versus 3.5% with continuous infusion. The authors link this to the peaks and troughs in concentration that boluses produce.Source: Lee 2020
  • There are several possible explanations. Glycine antagonism in structures below the cortex, enhanced GABA inhibition giving uncoordinated oscillations, or an imbalance between acetylcholine and dopamine in the basal ganglia triggered by a rapid change in propofol concentration. In the laboratory, propofol is mainly anticonvulsant but also has a weaker pro-convulsant effect.Sources: San-juan 2010, Jeon 2007, Voss 2015
  • Patients with Parkinson's disease can develop dyskinesias. Patients operated on off levodopa developed dyskinesias resembling their levodopa dyskinesias. One patient had severe dyskinesia about 20 minutes after a small propofol dose.Sources: Krauss 1996, Nakajima 2022
  • Lidocaine, fentanyl and infusion can reduce movements. Lidocaine 2 mg/kg before propofol in 358 children gave movements in 2.5% versus 29% with saline, but more coughing (62.5 versus 17.5%). Fentanyl 1.5 µg/kg gave fewer excitatory events (1 of 32 versus 13 of 32). For sedation, continuous infusion can be used instead of boluses.Sources: Bilotta 2006, Middle East J Anesthesiol 1996, Lee 2020
  • It usually resolves on its own. In the case reports it lasts from a few hours to 21 days. Benzodiazepines have had variable effect.Source: Tam 2009
  • The EEG is usually normal, but that does not exclude seizures. One study found no seizure activity with propofol. But a normal scalp EEG does not exclude epileptic activity deeper in the brain, and in one patient polyspike-and-wave complexes coincided with the jerks.Sources: Reddy 1993; Voss 2015; Jeon 2007
  • The movements can make the patient look light on the monitor (interpretation based on the sources). Muscle artefact raises the index. Look at the raw EEG and the patient. For prolonged, recurrent or delayed episodes, or known epilepsy, a full EEG should be considered.
Midazolam (benzodiazepines)
Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Hypnosis and amnesia during surgery usually need 100–200 ng/ml in plasma. Patients usually wake below 50 ng/ml.
  • Midazolam does not reliably remove memories from before the dose. The amnesia is anterograde, and retrograde memory does not appear to be reliably affected. After an anaesthetic dose the amnesia lasts about 1–2 hours.
  • The patient can seem awake and still not remember. During benzodiazepine sedation patients can be awake and coherent and still not remember the procedure. This is scenario 1 in the Components tab.
  • Flumazenil reverses sleep and respiratory depression more than amnesia. This is usually the case. It is a pharmacological example of how amnesia and sedation can be separated.
  • Different subunits may underlie amnesia for different agents. For benzodiazepines, sedation and anterograde amnesia are linked to GABA-A receptors with the α1 subunit. For etomidate in mice, amnesia is linked to α5 subunits. These are not necessarily contradictions.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Older patients need less.Source: Jacobs 1995
  • Poisoning can cause “beta coma”, which usually resolves. In poisoning with and withdrawal from benzodiazepines and barbiturates, beta (12–16 Hz) is seen, mostly frontal, mixed with spindle-like activity, alpha or delta. It is largely reversible with a good prognosis. Alpha coma and spindle coma can also be seen in poisoning. See the simulator in the Spectrogram tab and the alpha coma case in the Intensive care tab.Source: Sutter and Kaplan 2012
  • Midazolam at sedative doses is associated with beta, which can resemble ketamine. A child who received ketamine and midazolam as premedication had beta and gamma at the start. The authors think this probably reflects both drugs together. What the EEG looks like at higher doses of midazolam is not described in the sources here.Source: Brandt 2020

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Benzodiazepines enhance GABA at the GABAA receptor. They facilitate opening of the chloride channel, and the cell is hyperpolarised. The benzodiazepine site is different from the site where propofol, barbiturates and etomidate act.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025, Hendrickx 2008
  • Each subunit accounts for different effects. α1 is linked to sedation, anterograde amnesia and anticonvulsant effect, α2 to anxiolysis and muscle relaxation. α2 and α3 are linked to the rewarding effects and thus addiction.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Where the receptors are: highest density in the olfactory bulb, cerebral cortex, cerebellum, hippocampus, substantia nigra and inferior colliculus, lower in the striatum, lower brainstem and spinal cord.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Lorazepam is the most potent, diazepam the least. Affinity is lorazepam > midazolam > diazepam. Midazolam is about 3–6 and lorazepam 5–10 times as potent as diazepam.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Midazolam alone cannot abolish movement, propofol alone can. Midazolam alone cannot fully abolish movement to noxious stimuli, whereas propofol alone can. This is one argument that the drugs act differently, even though both act through GABAA, and may support that the combination is synergistic.Source: Hendrickx 2008
  • The effect of flumazenil depends on how much agonist occupies the receptors. Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist with high affinity and almost no intrinsic effect. After a very high agonist dose, a small dose of flumazenil attenuates the deep CNS depression (unconsciousness, respiratory depression) without reducing the effects that need only low receptor occupancy (drowsiness, amnesia). Large doses of flumazenil with little agonist reverse everything. Flumazenil is cleared rapidly, so sedation can return.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Remimazolam is broken down quickly and does not accumulate. It resembles midazolam and binds selectively to the benzodiazepine site. Tissue esterases rapidly break down a carboxylic ester side chain to an inactive metabolite (CNS7054), not via CYP. Clearance is about 70 l/h, and long infusions do not cause accumulation. Pharmacokinetics were unchanged in end-stage renal failure, but caution is advised in hepatic failure, and lower doses should be considered in the frail elderly. Flumazenil reverses it in about 1 minute (10.5 minutes with placebo) without resedation. For endoscopy, sedation success was comparable to propofol and better than midazolam.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Remimazolam and propofol gave broadly similar EEGs at induction in older patients. In a randomised substudy of 52 patients over 65, patients received remimazolam 6 mg/kg/h or propofol TCI 3.5 µg/ml, both with remifentanil. Remimazolam produced alpha and delta, and there were no significant differences in spectral power or BIS. Both produced alpha anteriorisation and reduced frontal-to-parietal feedback connectivity. Only induction was measured, and no patient had burst suppression. The study was partly funded by Hana Pharmaceutical, which according to the article had no role in the analysis. Interpretation based on the sources: that remimazolam produced alpha and delta, whereas midazolam is linked to beta, may reflect dose (anaesthesia vs sedation) and is not necessarily a difference between the drugs.Sources: Kim 2024, Brandt 2020
Propofol and midazolam: alone, together and in withdrawal
Vuyk et al. 2025; Kim et al. 2025 Hendrickx 2008 Olsen and Liang 2017 Lorentzen 2014 Shah 2018 Zhou 2014
  • Midazolam needs GABA to work, and its effect has a ceiling. It binds the benzodiazepine site on the GABAA receptor and enhances the response to GABA by facilitating chloride channel opening. Alone, it cannot fully abolish movement to noxious stimuli.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025, Hendrickx 2008
  • Propofol can open the channel without GABA. It binds the β subunit, a different site. At clinical concentrations propofol enhances GABA. At higher concentrations it can open the channel directly. Propofol also inhibits NMDA receptors.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • The sources disagree on whether the combination is synergistic or additive. Because the drugs bind different sites, several studies found synergy for hypnosis, and midazolam often acts synergistically with other hypnotics (Vuyk et al. 2025). Kim et al. 2025 instead calls the interaction «primarily additive», see Discrepancies.Sources: Hendrickx 2008 (Short and Chui 1991, McClune 1992, Short 1992); Vuyk et al. 2025; Kim et al. 2025
  • The drugs also raise each other's blood concentrations. A sedative midazolam concentration (200 ng/ml) raises propofol concentration by about 25 %, probably via altered circulation and hepatic perfusion. Propofol raises midazolam concentration by 27 %. Propofol also inhibits CYP3A4, which metabolises midazolam (about 37 % lower activity at 3 µg/ml). Interpretation based on the sources: both synergy and higher concentrations point towards lower dose requirements when the drugs are given together.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • In the ICU, switching from midazolam to propofol before waking gave faster extubation and less agitation. Benzodiazepines give amnesia and haemodynamic stability, but accumulate (active metabolite, especially in renal failure) and cause more delirium than dexmedetomidine. Propofol gives fast awakening but more hypotension. In a randomised, open-label, single-centre study (n=124 ventilated patients), time to extubation was 45 hours with midazolam alone, 3 hours with propofol alone and 2 hours after switching. Hypotension: 23 %, 52 % and 21 %. Agitation after stopping: 49 % with midazolam alone vs 19 % after switching. The authors suggest propofol may mask midazolam withdrawal. Note: this was switching, not simultaneous use, and patients with alcoholism were excluded.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025, Zhou 2014

Micro level: why benzodiazepines can fail in alcohol withdrawal

  • Alcohol enhances GABAA and inhibits NMDA. With chronic use GABAA function weakens. When alcohol is withdrawn, the NMDA system is left unopposed.Sources: Lorentzen 2014, Shah 2018
  • Repeated alcohol remodels the receptors (rat). A «subunit switch» occurs: extrasynaptic δ-containing receptors (tonic inhibition) and α1 are down-regulated, while α4, γ2 and α2 are up-regulated. The rats became tolerant to the sedative effect of alcohol, benzodiazepines and neurosteroids, while anticonvulsant and anxiolytic effects showed little tolerance. After repeated cycles the changes lasted at least 120 days. In humans this is a hypothesis.Source: Olsen and Liang 2017
  • Clinicians explain the resistance by «saturated» receptors and an overactive NMDA system. GABAA receptors become «saturated», and benzodiazepines have no effect on the overactive NMDA system.Sources: Lorentzen 2014, Shah 2018
  • Propofol acts on both systems. Propofol has a «dual effect»: GABAA via a different site and NMDA inhibition. Interpretation based on the sources: since propofol at higher concentrations can open the channel without GABA, it is biologically plausible that it works where benzodiazepines have reached their ceiling. This is not tested in the sources.Source: Lorentzen 2014
  • Propofol successfully treated 12 of 15 with benzodiazepine-refractory delirium tremens. The study was retrospective. The patients had not responded to up to 2000 mg benzodiazepines. They received propofol a mean 4.22 mg/kg/h over 48 hours (max 5.65), RASS −4 to −5, ventilated. 7 of 15 developed pneumonia, none developed propofol infusion syndrome, and mean ICU stay was 4.67 days.Source: Lorentzen 2014
  • According to Aitkenhead (2007) this is an alternative, but most patients were intubated. Retrospective study, n=30 with benzodiazepine-resistant withdrawal (more than 40 mg diazepam per hour). Ketamine blocks NMDA directly. Lorazepam requirement fell by 4 mg/h at 24 hours, but 73 % were intubated.Source: Shah 2018
  • Caveats: the studies are small, retrospective and uncontrolled. Deep sedation with propofol requires a secured airway. The sources here concern alcohol withdrawal.
