Other poisonings (mixed overdose, stimulants, GHB) are not covered. EEG in benzodiazepine poisoning and withdrawal (beta coma) is described in the midazolam card.
Ketamine
EEG “gamma burst” (Akeju, 12 patients) Vuyk et al. 2025; Patel et al. 2025
  • Ketamine gives dissociative anaesthesia, not sleep. The patient may have open eyes and some reflexes left. Do not assume that the reflexes are protective.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Pain is dampened at far lower levels than those causing unconsciousness. The pain threshold is raised from 0.1 µg/ml. General anaesthesia requires at least 0.6–2 µg/ml.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • The patient does not recall surgery, but the amnesia is weaker than with benzodiazepines.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Ketamine increases brain metabolism. Both CMRO₂ and blood flow increase.Sources: Patel et al. 2025; Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Theta is the shared finding in the EEG under ketamine. Miller's describes generalised theta and seizure-like (petit mal) activity in the hippocampus, but not gamma or slow-delta. Akeju also describes alternating slow-delta and gamma. The sources thus differ in scope rather than conflict.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Akeju

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Ketamine blocks the NMDA receptor. Ketamine is a channel blocker. The channel therefore has to be open for ketamine to act.Source: Purdon 2015
  • At low to moderate doses the inhibitory interneurons are hit first. Their NMDA channels are generally more active than those of pyramidal cells. The pyramidal cells then become less inhibited. This may explain increased metabolism, and that cortex, hippocampus and amygdala keep communicating but without coordination in time and space. The result is thought to be hallucinations, dissociation, euphoria and dysphoria. At higher doses the NMDA receptors on the excitatory nerve cells are also blocked, and this is thought to cause loss of consciousness.Sources: Purdon 2015; Brown 2010
  • The hallucinations are probably enhanced by disrupted dopamine transmission in the prefrontal cortex. This is partly due to increased glutamate activity at glutamate receptors other than NMDA.Source: Purdon 2015
  • Ketamine also acts on several other receptors. These include opioid receptors and monoaminergic receptors. At high concentrations sigma receptors are also affected, muscarinic receptors are blocked and GABA transmission is facilitated. S(+)-ketamine has some μ-opioid activity. Experiments in μ-knockout mice suggest that the μ system contributes to respiratory depression and supraspinal antinociception. Increased activity in the locus coeruleus appears to contribute to the anaesthetic effect.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Ketamine dampens pain already in the spinal cord. The spinal analgesia is linked to inhibition of wide dynamic range neurons in the dorsal horn. Ketamine also inhibits central sensitisation and opioid-induced hyperalgesia. Purdon 2015 places the analgesia at «the dorsal root ganglia, the first synapse of the pain pathway in the spinal cord».Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Purdon 2015
  • Ketamine causes functional disorganisation, not uniform depression. Parts of the cortex (especially association areas) and the thalamus are depressed, while limbic areas, including the hippocampus, are stimulated. Many anaesthetics reduce metabolism in the thalamus, but ketamine is the exception.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • The active EEG fits with the disinhibition. At a low dose of ketamine alone, beta–gamma at about 25–32 Hz is seen. No specific antagonist reverses all the effects of ketamine.Sources: Purdon; Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Ketamine also inhibits the HCN1 channel. HCN1 is activated by hyperpolarisation and is important for rhythmic activity. Mice lacking HCN1 do not lose the righting reflex with ketamine. Propofol also inhibits HCN1. The proposal is that frontal gamma results from NMDA-mediated disinhibition (counteracted by the GABA effect of propofol), while the shared HCN1 inhibition may explain why occipital alpha falls further when propofol is added. See the card in the Components tab.Source: Tian 2023
  • Under ketamine, sensory information stops before the motor cortex. In monkeys the signals reached the primary somatosensory cortex but did not pass on to the motor cortex. The directed coupling between neurons in the two areas fell.Source: Schroeder 2016
Ketamine in refractory status epilepticus: when GABAergic drugs lose their grip
Espinosa 2023 Gaspard 2013
  • In continuous seizures, GABAA receptors disappear from the cell surface. After a few minutes they move into the cell («internalisation»), while more glutamate and NMDA receptors move out to the surface («externalisation»). Inhibition weakens and excitation increases. This has been shown in animal models.Source: Espinosa 2023
  • Benzodiazepines work less well the longer the seizure lasts. It is not GABA that is missing, but the receptors the drugs act on. Sensitivity to GABA agonists declines with prolonged seizures, whereas sensitivity to NMDA antagonists does not.Source: Gaspard 2013
  • Ketamine targets the part of the system that is up-regulated. Ketamine blocks the NMDA receptor and causes little respiratory or cardiovascular depression.Source: Gaspard 2013
  • Ketamine may help control seizures, but probably only at a high enough dose and if not started too late. In a retrospective study from ten centres (58 patients), 57 % achieved permanent seizure control. Ketamine was always given with other drugs, and the response was judged likely in only 12 % and possible in 20 %. Likely responses required at least 0.9 mg/kg/h and were not seen when ketamine was started 8 days or more after onset, or after 7 or more failed drugs. Mortality was 43 %: 16 % when seizures were controlled within 24 hours of ketamine vs 56 % otherwise. ICP did not rise in monitored patients, except two with anoxic cerebral oedema.Source: Gaspard 2013
  • The evidence does not support ketamine as first choice or monotherapy. A scoping review found about 20 publications, mostly case reports and small series, with widely varying doses (loading 0.5–5 mg/kg, infusion 0.05–10.5 mg/kg/h). Of 19 case reports, 63 % achieved complete seizure control, usually within 12 hours, but seizures recurred in 10–60 % after withdrawal. Adverse effects were arrhythmias, cardiovascular collapse and metabolic acidosis, with unclear causality in patients on many drugs.Source: Espinosa 2023
  • The pattern resembles alcohol withdrawal. Interpretation based on the sources: there too GABAA function is weakened and the NMDA system overactive, and ketamine and propofol are used when benzodiazepines fail (the propofol and midazolam card above).
  • Ketamine does not usually cause classic burst suppression. Continuous EEG is used to guide treatment and to detect non-convulsive seizures (Intensive care tab). Ketamine produces a more activated EEG with beta and gamma, and not classic burst suppression at clinical doses (see the ketamine card). Interpretation based on the sources: the treatment target should therefore be judged on the raw EEG.
  • Caveats: no randomised trials. Gaspard 2013 is retrospective and may be biased, because the most severe cases more often received ketamine. Several authors disclose ties to the pharmaceutical industry (including UCB, GSK and Pfizer). Espinosa 2023 reports no conflicts of interest.

“Dexmedetomidine causes less delirium”: compared with what?

The claim is often heard from the lectern, and it is right in one particular comparison and wrong in another. What matters is what the agent is compared with.

  • Against midazolam: yes, and the difference is large. SEDCOM randomised 366 ventilated ICU patients at 68 centres in five countries, double-blind, targeting light sedation. Delirium occurred in 54% (132 of 244) with dexmedetomidine versus 76.6% (93 of 122) with midazolam, a difference of 22.6 percentage points (95% CI 14–33, p < 0.001). Time to extubation was 1.9 days shorter (3.7 versus 5.6 days, p = 0.01).
  • But three caveats belong with that finding. The trial’s primary outcome was negative: time within the sedation target did not differ (77.3% versus 75.1%, p = 0.18). Open-label midazolam rescue was used more often in the dexmedetomidine group than in the midazolam group (63% versus 49%). And the trial was funded by Hospira, which makes the drug, with Hospira employees involved in design, interpretation and manuscript review.
  • And the most important objection is logical, not methodological. The finding may mean that midazolam causes delirium just as readily as that dexmedetomidine prevents it. Benzodiazepines are independently associated with delirium in ICU patients, which makes “less than midazolam” a low bar to clear.
  • Against propofol: no. MENDS2 is the methodologically strongest trial on the question: double-blind, 422 ventilated adults with sepsis at 13 centres, targeting light sedation (RASS 0 to −2). Days alive without delirium or coma were 10.7 versus 10.8, adjusted OR 0.96 (95% CI 0.74–1.26, p = 0.79). Ventilator-free days 23.7 versus 24.0. Death at 90 days 38% versus 39%. Cognition at 6 months no different. The authors’ own conclusion is that outcomes did not differ, and that this supports guidelines recommending either agent.
  • A recent meta-analysis points the other way, but weakly. Zhang et al. 2026 pooled 8 randomised trials with 1156 patients and found OR 0.52 (95% CI 0.33–0.80, p = 0.010) favouring dexmedetomidine over propofol. But delirium was a secondary outcome, most trials were open-label, and the authors note themselves that the finding does not reach their own adjusted significance threshold of about 0.007. They call it a signal requiring dedicated confirmation. Against one double-blind trial with a predefined primary outcome, it weighs little.
  • Postoperatively the picture is better. A network meta-analysis of 41 randomised trials and 6679 patients ranked dexmedetomidine first of four sedatives for preventing postoperative delirium: OR 0.42 versus saline (95% CI 0.33–0.54) and OR 0.47 versus propofol (95% CI 0.25–0.90). But the review carries no GRADE rating, two studies were at high and five at medium risk of bias, and the authors point out that delirium is multifactorial and the rating scales subjective.
  • As sedation for regional anaesthesia: yes, in two randomised trials. Shin et al. 2023 randomised 748 patients aged 65 and over, double-blind, to dexmedetomidine or propofol sedation during spinal anaesthesia for lower limb orthopaedic surgery. Delirium measured with CAM over the first three days occurred in 3.0% versus 6.6% (OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.86, p = 0.036). Mean arterial pressure was higher during sedation with dexmedetomidine but lower in recovery, and heart rate was lower in both places.Source: Shin et al. 2023
  • And depth matters most for propofol. Zhu et al. 2023 randomised 219 patients aged 65 and over for hip fracture surgery under spinal anaesthesia to four groups: light or deep sedation with each of the two agents. Dexmedetomidine overall gave 11.9% versus 23.6% (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.93, p = 0.024). The most interesting finding lies inside the propofol group: deep sedation gave 32.7% versus 14.5% with light sedation (RR 2.25, 95% CI 1.07 to 4.74, p = 0.025), while depth made no difference in the dexmedetomidine group. The trial is single-centre, without EEG monitoring, and followed patients only to the third day.Source: Zhu et al. 2023
  • The meta-analysis on the same question is weaker than the numbers look. Wang et al. 2024 pooled 17 randomised trials with 2763 patients over 60 under regional anaesthesia and found RR 0.48 (95% CI 0.37 to 0.63) for delirium, with no heterogeneity. But all the trials are from Asian countries, 12 of 17 were rated as having "some concerns" for bias, none of them reported adverse effects, and the review is not consistent with itself about the number of trials or about the figures for cognitive dysfunction.Source: Wang et al. 2024
  • The price is bradycardia. In SEDCOM, bradycardia occurred in 42.2% versus 18.9% (p < 0.001). Bradycardia requiring intervention was 4.9% versus 0.8% (p = 0.07). The network meta-analysis also found more bradycardia than with saline.

The precise answer: against benzodiazepines yes, postoperatively probably yes with moderate certainty, as sedation for regional anaesthesia in older patients yes in two randomised trials, and against propofol in the ICU no. When someone says “dexmedetomidine causes less delirium” without saying compared with what, the claim is not wrong, but it is incomplete in a way that changes what it means clinically.

Interpretation from the sources: the assembly of the four studies, and the inference that the comparator decides, appears in none of them.

Riker et al. JAMA 2009;301:489–499 Hughes et al. N Engl J Med 2021 (MENDS2) Huang et al. BMC Cardiovasc Disord 2024;24:147 Zhang et al. Front Neurol 2026;17:1875240
Dexmedetomidine
EEG (Akeju 2016, 8 volunteers) Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • The patient can be roused. Patients can be roused and follow commands, and fall asleep when not stimulated. The pattern resembles natural NREM sleep.
  • Low concentrations give rousable sedation, high concentrations deep sedation. Rousable sedation at about 0.2–0.3 ng/ml. Above about 1.9 ng/ml the patient cannot be roused.Source: Ebert 2000
  • The patient may remember more than with propofol. In intensive care, patients on dexmedetomidine remembered more of their stay than patients on propofol. In an experimental low-dose study, memory encoding failed. The findings are not directly comparable.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Hysteresis: dexmedetomidine appears to increase neural inertia.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Receptor: α2 agonist. Dexmedetomidine acts at G-protein-coupled α2 adrenoceptors. Inside the cell, adenylate cyclase and L- and P-type calcium channels are inhibited, and calcium-activated potassium channels conduct more easily.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Subtypes: α2A, α2B and α2C. α2A is mainly peripheral, α2B and α2C are in the brain and spinal cord. Analgesia in the dorsal horn is linked to α2C and α2A. In rats, antisense against α2A in the locus coeruleus delayed and shortened loss of righting reflex after dexmedetomidine (see Discrepancies in the Sources tab).Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Circuit: less noradrenaline from the locus coeruleus. Dexmedetomidine binds presynaptically on nerve cells from the locus coeruleus and hyperpolarises them, so that less noradrenaline is released. This removes the inhibition of the preoptic area. The preoptic area then inhibits the arousal centres with GABA and galanin, including histamine release from the tuberomammillary nucleus. In addition, the basal forebrain, the intralaminar thalamic nuclei and the cortex lose their noradrenaline supply.Sources: Purdon 2015, Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Animal studies point to the locus coeruleus, but not only there. Microinjection of dexmedetomidine into the locus coeruleus lowers the level of consciousness, and the α2 antagonist atipamezole prevents this. Mice that cannot make noradrenaline are hypersensitive to dexmedetomidine. This suggests that other mechanisms also exist.Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • To the EEG: spindles and slow-delta, but weaker than with propofol. The spindles (9–15 Hz) probably arise, like propofol frontal alpha and sleep spindles, in loops between thalamus and cortex, but they are brief and episodic. Slow-delta arises because the cortex receives less excitatory input. Both spindles and slow waves are smaller than under propofol. Purdon interprets this as less disruption of nerve cell activity, and as a possible explanation for why the patient can be roused.Source: Purdon 2015
  • Cognition may be better preserved. Data suggest that reduced expression of α5-GABAA receptors after anaesthesia may contribute to better preserved cognition with dexmedetomidine.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Reversal: atipamezole, but not in humans. The α2 antagonist atipamezole reverses the effect, but is not approved for humans.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • α2A in the locus coeruleus matters for loss of righting reflex in rats. Antisense against α2A in the locus coeruleus delayed and shortened loss of righting reflex after dexmedetomidine. Antisense against α2C had no effect. See the card below and Discrepancies.Source: Mizobe 1996
  • The thalamus disconnects, while the cortex stays connected. During dexmedetomidine-induced loss of consciousness, coupling between cortical areas was preserved. Coupling between the thalamus and the default mode network was disrupted. See the card below.Source: Akeju, Loggia et al. 2014
  • The spindles resemble NREM 2 sleep, but last longer. During deep sedation, spindles had the same density, amplitude and frequency as spindles in normal NREM 2 sleep. See the card below.Source: Huupponen 2008
Clonidine
Vuyk et al. 2025; Patel et al. 2025; Fukuda 2025 Hendrickx 2008 Hight 2020 Giovannitti 2015 Zhang 2021
  • Clonidine is an α2 agonist that is less selective and less potent than dexmedetomidine. The ratio of α2 to α1 binding is about 220:1, versus 1600:1 for dexmedetomidine.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Patel et al. 2025
  • Clonidine paved the way for dexmedetomidine. Experience with patients taking clonidine showed that α2 agonists could be used in anaesthesia. One study found lower halothane MAC in such patients.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Clonidine lowers MAC, but the effect has a ceiling. In humans, MAC fell by about 30% for isoflurane and 17–34% for sevoflurane. MAC-awake fell by 30% (isoflurane) and 17–21% (sevoflurane). In children, doubling the dose did not further reduce sevoflurane MAC-awake. Clonidine alone does not produce immobility at clinically used doses.Source: Hendrickx 2008
  • Clonidine appears to enhance other hypnotics. With propofol the effect was additive in humans. With midazolam it was synergistic in rats. Fentanyl and clonidine produced hypnosis together in animals even though neither did alone. The infusion dose should be reduced when clonidine is combined with propofol.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Clonidine does not appear to enhance opioid respiratory depression. This applies to fentanyl and other opioids. Intravenous clonidine abolished the sympathetic activation from μ blockade in opioid-dependent patients, and α2 agonists can suppress fentanyl cough.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • The EEG resembles sleep, and hysteresis may be more marked. Hight 2020 writes that α2 agonists produce a slow-wave-dominant EEG with intermittent spindles, sharing features with sleep stages 2 and 3. The pattern is documented for dexmedetomidine; for clonidine alone we found no spectral study, so how well it fits is unknown. Take care when lowering the inhaled agent concentration below that needed for unconsciousness.Source: Hight 2020
  • EEG when clonidine is added to propofol or a volatile agent: more hypnosis or just a different EEG? A question from the author of the app. The sources give a split answer.
    • Part of the effect is hypnosis, not just a different EEG: propofol and clonidine were additive for hypnosis in humans, and clonidine lowered MAC-awake for sevoflurane by 17–21 %. The infusion dose should be lower when clonidine is combined with propofol.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, Vuyk et al. 2025
    • The EEG change in combination has only been studied for dexmedetomidine: there is no study of clonidine plus propofol or volatile agent with spectral analysis. When dexmedetomidine was given under propofol, the alpha peak fell (but the confidence interval crossed zero), delta–theta rose, and PSI fell from 30 to 23. The authors interpret this as deeper anaesthesia, but consciousness was not tested, because the patients were already unconscious.Source: Zhang 2021 (21 patients)
    • Slow waves from α2 agonists do not mean the same as from propofol: under dexmedetomidine alone the patient can be roused even though the EEG is dominated by slow waves and spindles (see dexmedetomidine).Source: Purdon 2015 Part I
    • Clinical observation from the author of the app: with clonidine the alpha peak appears to become lower, without much else changing clearly. That points the same way as what Zhang 2021 measured for dexmedetomidine under propofol, but it is one person's impression from practice, not systematically recorded or measured.
    • Ceiling: doubling the clonidine dose gave no further fall in MAC-awake for sevoflurane in children.Source: Hendrickx 2008
    • Interpretation based on the sources: the answer is probably both. Part of the alpha loss and delta increase reflects a real, additive hypnotic effect, and the propofol or volatile dose can then be reduced somewhat. But increased delta after clonidine should not be read as just as much deeper hypnosis as the same change after more propofol. The hypnotic should not be reduced just because the index falls, and the volatile agent should not be lowered below what is needed for unconsciousness when clonidine has been given. Remember also that alpha loss can have other causes, such as nociception.Sources: Hight 2020, García 2021
  • Clonidine is long-acting: the half-life is 12–16 hours. Clonidine is the original α2 agonist. It is used mostly for hypertension, but also for anxiety, ADHD, chronic pain, withdrawal and postoperative shivering. About 50% is metabolised in the liver, and 40–60% is excreted unchanged in the urine.Source: Giovannitti 2015
  • Abrupt withdrawal can cause rebound hypertension. After long-term use, blood pressure can rise up to 20 hours after the last dose. An early case report described a hypertensive crisis when one dose was withheld before anaesthesia. At initiation, blood pressure may rise transiently because peripheral postjunctional α1 receptors are stimulated.Source: Giovannitti 2015
  • As premedication in children, clonidine gives better mask acceptance than midazolam, but acts later. Clonidine improves mask acceptance at induction and reduces anaesthetic requirements by 40–60% (see Discrepancies). In a study of 45 children (2–8 years), oral clonidine gave better sedation, separation and mask acceptance and less shivering than midazolam. Onset was after 60 minutes, versus 30 for midazolam.Source: Giovannitti 2015

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Receptor: α2 adrenoceptors, like dexmedetomidine. The receptors are G-protein-coupled and inhibit adenylate cyclase (see dexmedetomidine). The circuit mechanism (locus coeruleus and preoptic area) is described for dexmedetomidine, not specifically for clonidine.
  • Imidazoline receptors may contribute to bradycardia. Clonidine and dexmedetomidine both belong to the imidazole subclass. The clinically available α2 agonists have an imidazole ring that also activates imidazoline binding sites, and they do not discriminate between α2 subtypes. Bradycardia may partly be due to imidazoline receptors in the brainstem.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025, Mizobe 1996
  • Neuroprotection in animals. Clonidine lowered plasma catecholamines and improved outcome after incomplete ischaemia in rats.Source: Patel et al. 2025
  • Signalling pathway: less noradrenaline gives sedation and lower heart rate and blood pressure. All three α2 subtypes inhibit adenylate cyclase. In the locus coeruleus, lower cAMP leads to potassium efflux through calcium-activated channels, calcium cannot enter the nerve terminal, and firing is suppressed. Less noradrenaline and less activity in the ascending noradrenergic pathways give hypnosis and sedation. The same negative feedback lowers heart rate and blood pressure and dampens the stress response.Source: Giovannitti 2015
  • Subtypes: α2A and α2C act centrally, α2B in the vessel wall. α2A and α2C are found mainly in the central nervous system and probably account for sedation, analgesia and sympatholysis. α2B is found mostly on vascular smooth muscle and causes vasoconstriction.Source: Giovannitti 2015
  • Most of the analgesia happens in the spinal cord. α2 receptors in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord inhibit nociceptive neurons and reduce substance P release. There is also evidence for supraspinal and peripheral sites.Source: Giovannitti 2015
Dexmedetomidine and clonidine compared
Mashour and Pryor 2025; Patel et al. 2025; Vuyk et al. 2025 Giovannitti 2015 Hendrickx 2008 Walsh 2025 (A2B)

Both are α2 agonists (they stimulate the receptor); atipamezole is an example of an α2 antagonist. Even so, they are quite different.

  • Dexmedetomidine is much more selective for α2. Dexmedetomidine binds α2 over α1 in a ratio of about 1600:1, clonidine about 220:1. Clonidine is also less potent. Clonidine's α1 effect can cause a transient rise in blood pressure at the start.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Patel et al. 2025, Giovannitti 2015
  • Both act in the locus coeruleus. Dexmedetomidine being “more specific” refers to the receptor type (α2 over α1), not the brain region. The animal studies linking loss of consciousness to α2A receptors in the locus coeruleus were done with dexmedetomidine. The sources do not describe a separate circuit mechanism for clonidine.Sources: Mashour and Pryor 2025, Mizobe 1996
  • Both have an imidazole ring. They can therefore also activate imidazoline binding sites, which may contribute to bradycardia.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025, Mizobe 1996
  • Clonidine lasts much longer and is harder to titrate. The half-life is 12–16 hours for clonidine (the A2B protocol gives about 13 hours), versus about 2 hours for dexmedetomidine. Clonidine therefore takes longer to wear off.Sources: Giovannitti 2015, A2B protocol
  • Clonidine has a ceiling, dexmedetomidine can give deep sedation. Clonidine lowers MAC-awake for sevoflurane by 17–21 %, but no further. Dexmedetomidine gives rousable sedation at 0.2–0.3 ng/ml and non-rousable sedation above about 1.9 ng/ml.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, Ebert 2000
  • Both give a sleep-like EEG. The pattern has slow waves and spindles. Spectral studies exist for dexmedetomidine, but not for clonidine in the sources here.Sources: Hight 2020; Akeju, Purdon, Huupponen
  • In intensive care, neither gave faster extubation than propofol. Both caused more agitation (RR 1.54 and 1.55) and more severe bradycardia (RR 1.62 and 1.58). Clonidine is not licensed for ICU sedation in the UK, but is much cheaper.Source: Walsh 2025 (A2B)
Dexmedetomidine in children: maturation, circulation and pallor
Chrysostomou 2014 Morse 2020 Janse van Rensburg 2025 Potts 2010 Yuen 2008, 2010
  • Newborns break down dexmedetomidine more slowly. The younger the child, the lower the clearance and the longer the half-life. The half-life is 7.6 hours in preterm infants and 3.2 hours in term infants. Term newborns have about 42% of adult clearance, and by 3 years it is about 80%. The half-life is about 2.3 hours under 2 years and 1.6 hours at 2–11 years.Sources: Chrysostomou 2014, Morse 2020, Janse van Rensburg 2025
  • The liver enzymes are not fully developed at birth. Dexmedetomidine is broken down in the liver, partly via CYP2A6 and partly by direct glucuronidation (UGT1A4 and UGT2B10). On cardiopulmonary bypass, clearance falls by about 95%.Sources: Precedex prescribing information, Janse van Rensburg 2025
  • Intranasally, it works after 20–30 minutes. The dose is 2–3 µg/kg, and the effect lasts about 85 minutes. 0.5 and 1 µg/kg gave more sedation at separation from the parents than midazolam.Sources: Janse van Rensburg 2025, Yuen 2010, Yuen 2008
  • Blood pressure and heart rate fall slightly. In a meta-analysis of 13 RCTs, intranasal dexmedetomidine lowered systolic blood pressure by 6.7 mmHg and heart rate by 6.8 beats/min compared with control. A review reports hypotension and bradycardia in 10–20%, and transient hypertension via peripheral α2B receptors.Sources: Can J Anesth 2017, JPPT 2010
  • Low concentrations lower blood pressure, high concentrations raise it. In children, low concentrations lowered blood pressure (half effect at 0.10 µg/L, maximum −12.3 mmHg). Higher concentrations raised it (half effect at 1.1 µg/L, maximum +50.3 mmHg). Above about 1 µg/L, mean arterial pressure rose about 20%. The rise comes from peripheral vasoconstriction.Source: Potts 2010
  • Pallor is not documented as a side effect. No peer-reviewed source describes pallor as a side effect of intranasal dexmedetomidine in children. The closest is a case report of local vasoconstriction in a newborn after a block with dexmedetomidine. A possible explanation is that α2B receptors in skin vessels constrict, while a lower heart rate gives a lower cardiac output. This is an interpretation based on the sources, not a documented explanation. In practice: check heart rate, blood pressure and capillary refill. If the circulation is otherwise good, the pallor is probably harmless, but that is not documented either.Source: Guensch 2023 (only the title was read)
  • Whether maturation of the noradrenaline system affects sensitivity has not been studied. No studies link the maturation of the locus coeruleus or the noradrenaline system in children to how sensitive they are to dexmedetomidine. The experiment with mice lacking noradrenaline concerns genetically modified animals and cannot be transferred directly. In 7-day-old rats, dexmedetomidine was not neurotoxic and reduced cell death from isoflurane, but long-term outcome data in children are lacking.Source: Sanders 2009
  • The EEG in children is sleep-like, but infants may lack spindles. Of 107 children given intramuscular dexmedetomidine, 55 reached N3 and 51 N2. Spindles are not synchronous in infants: at 3 months it is normal to lack spindles, and they become synchronous around 2 years of age. Missing spindles under dexmedetomidine in an infant are therefore not a sign that the drug acts differently (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Mason 2012, Yune 2026
The studies in detail: dexmedetomidine and sleep spindles, dexmedetomidine and the thalamus, the α2 receptor (3 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Dexmedetomidine and sleep spindles: like NREM 2 sleep (Huupponen 2008)

Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2008;52:289–294. Eleven healthy young men (20–28 years) received dexmedetomidine as a target-controlled infusion, first 0.5 ng/ml for 25 minutes and then 3.2 ng/ml for 30 minutes. Measured plasma concentration during deep sedation was 5.1 ng/ml (SD 1.0). EEG was recorded from a single frontal channel with the Entropy Module. The control group was ten other healthy people (seven men, 21–43 years) during normal night sleep, with the first sleep cycle analysed.

  • Visual: the EEG during deep dexmedetomidine sedation resembled NREM sleep stage 2, with slight to moderate slow activity and abundant spindles. The low dose (0.5 ng/ml) did not induce sleep in everyone and was excluded from analysis.
  • Quantitative: spindle density (1.17 vs 1.26 per minute), amplitude and frequency (11.5 vs 12.0 Hz) did not differ between groups. Spindles lasted longer under dexmedetomidine (1.11 vs 0.88 seconds, p = 0.0014). The authors mention that longer spindles might mean stronger sleep protection, but call this only one possible explanation.
  • Frequency and origin: frontal spindles are slower than central ones (11–12 Hz frontally vs 13–14 Hz centrally in normal sleep). The authors believe the frontal spindles are probably generated in the mediodorsal thalamic nucleus, and that the same pathway is active under dexmedetomidine.
  • Arousal: in an earlier study by the same group, participants could be roused with verbal commands and possibly light shaking, even at 5.1 ng/ml (see Discrepancies).
  • Caveats: different people in the two groups, morning versus night recording, a single channel and small groups. The number of spindles per person ranged from 1 to 174. Three of the authors are from GE Healthcare, which makes the Entropy Module, and one author does contract research and consulting for Orion Pharma, which manufactures dexmedetomidine.
Huupponen et al. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2008;52:289–294

Dexmedetomidine and the thalamus: cortical coupling preserved, thalamocortical disrupted (Akeju, Loggia et al. 2014)

eLife 2014;3:e04499. Healthy volunteers (18–36 years, ASA I) received dexmedetomidine 1 µg/kg over 10 minutes followed by 0.7 µg/kg/h. Loss of consciousness was defined as sustained eye closure and no response to a request to open the eyes. Glucose metabolism was measured with FDG-PET (ten participants, two visits each), and blood flow (ASL) and functional connectivity (BOLD) were measured simultaneously with MRI (17 participants, complete BOLD data in 15). Not the same study as «Akeju 2014» on sevoflurane elsewhere in the app.

  • Metabolism and blood flow: glucose metabolism and blood flow fell most in the thalamus, the default mode network (DMN) and both frontoparietal networks. Blood flow and metabolism fell together, so the coupling between them was preserved.
  • Connectivity: coupling between cortical areas within the DMN and frontoparietal networks was preserved. Coupling between the thalamus and the DMN was disrupted, especially towards the posterior cingulate, precuneus and inferior parietal lobule. The thalamic region corresponded to intralaminar, midline, mediodorsal and ventral anterior nuclei, but the method could not resolve the nuclei precisely.
  • Recovery: coupling between the thalamus and the DMN, especially the posterior cingulate, returned when participants again responded to commands, while blood flow did not rise. The authors interpret this as coupling being restored before metabolism normalises, and recovery happening gradually.
  • A hierarchy of unconsciousness: the authors propose that lighter states (NREM 2 sleep, dexmedetomidine) involve disrupted thalamocortical coupling with preserved cortical coupling, while deeper states (propofol anaesthesia, some disorders of consciousness) also disrupt cortical coupling. Preserved cortical coupling may explain why the patient is easily roused.
  • Caveats: loss of response was defined by failure to open the eyes on request. Functional connectivity in fMRI is co-variation in slow BOLD fluctuations, not directly measured communication between nerve cells. No conflicts of interest declared. Funded by the NIH and FAER.
Akeju, Loggia et al. eLife 2014;3:e04499

Which α2 receptor carries the sedative effect? α2A in the locus coeruleus (Mizobe 1996)

J Clin Invest 1996;98:1076–1080, from the Maze group. Rats received antisense oligonucleotides (short DNA strands that prevent a specific receptor from being made) against α2A or α2C directly into the locus coeruleus, followed by dexmedetomidine 7 µg into the same area.

  • Cell studies: antisense against α2A reduced α2A receptors by about 30%, and antisense against α2C reduced α2C by nearly 40%, without affecting the other subtype.
  • Rats: after α2A antisense, loss of righting reflex came later and lasted shorter, and the effect was gone eight days after the last dose. α2C antisense, scrambled control sequences and saline had no effect.
  • The authors’ conclusion: α2A is the subtype mediating the hypnotic effect in the locus coeruleus. The authors write that α2A and α2C predominate in the central nervous system, while α2B is sparsely represented.
  • Side effects: the authors write that the rise in blood pressure after a rapid bolus is probably due to α2B (knockout mouse experiments), and that the bradycardia may partly be due to imidazoline receptors in the brainstem.
  • Caveats: 4–5 rats per group, and receptor reduction was measured only in cell cultures, not in the locus coeruleus itself. Funded by Veterans Affairs, the NIH and the Uehara Foundation.
Mizobe et al. J Clin Invest 1996;98:1076–1080
Thiopental and etomidate
Vuyk et al. 2025; Patel et al. 2025
  • Thiopental gives weaker amnesia than benzodiazepines. When the EEG becomes isoelectric, brain metabolism is about 50% of baseline.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Etomidate lowers cerebral blood flow and metabolism without changing blood pressure. At 0.2–0.3 mg/kg, CBF falls by 34% and CMRO₂ by 45%, without change in mean arterial pressure.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Patel et al. 2025

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Barbiturates act through the GABAA receptor. It is the only proven site of barbiturate anaesthesia. At low concentrations GABA dissociates from the receptor more slowly, and the channel stays open longer. This probably gives sedation and hypnosis. At higher concentrations barbiturates open the channel without GABA, which may explain the anaesthesia itself. They also inhibit excitatory transmission (glutamate, acetylcholine). In rats, thiopental reduced glutamate levels and NMDA currents in the prefrontal cortex.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Barbiturates can only halve the brain's energy use. CMRO₂ falls to about 50% when the EEG becomes isoelectric, and no further. Barbiturates reduce the energy used for signalling, not the energy used to keep cells alive. According to the source, only hypothermia can reduce that.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Etomidate acts almost exclusively through GABAA. At clinical concentrations it enhances the GABA effect (positive modulation). At higher concentrations it activates the receptor directly. Two independent binding sites on the α1β2γ2 receptor contribute equally.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Amnesia and hypnosis can run through different receptor variants. In mice, etomidate blocks LTP in CA1, but not in mice lacking the α5 subunit. These mice are resistant to the amnesia but not to the anaesthesia. The effect is reversed by an α5-selective drug with the opposite action (inverse agonist, L-655,708). The β3 subunit does not appear to be involved in the amnesia from etomidate.Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Etomidate increases EEG activity in epileptogenic foci. It has therefore been used for mapping before epilepsy surgery.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
Inhaled agents (sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane)
Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8 Purdon 2015 Mashour and Pryor 2025; Fukuda 2025 Hendrickx 2008
  • MAC is the concentration at which half of patients do not move at incision. It is the alveolar concentration, and only one point on the concentration–response curve (equivalent to the EC50). About 1.3 MAC prevents movement in about 95%.Source: Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8
  • MAC differs between agents. For 30–55-year-olds, MAC is about 2.0% for sevoflurane, 1.2% for isoflurane and 6.0% for desflurane.Source: Morgan and Mikhail
  • Patients wake at around 0.3–0.4 MAC. Hight 2017, by contrast, found a median of 0.09 (calculated effect-site MAC) for response to command in 273 surgical patients, and about 20 % woke only near zero. This is called MAC-awake and applies when the inhaled agent is the only anaesthetic.Source: Morgan and Mikhail
  • Two inhaled agents roughly add up. 0.5 MAC nitrous oxide and 0.5 MAC isoflurane give the same effect as 1.0 MAC isoflurane. There is no synergy between two inhaled agents, but usually synergy with intravenous agents. Opioids reduce MAC, but with a ceiling.Sources: Morgan and Mikhail; Hendrickx 2008; Fukuda 2025
  • MAC falls with age. The fall is about 6% per decade, regardless of agent. Another chapter of the same book gives a different figure (see Discrepancies).Sources: Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8 and 43
  • Desflurane gives very rapid induction and emergence. The effect comes when the brain concentration reaches a therapeutic level, and it follows the alveolar concentration. Desflurane has low solubility in blood and tissues, which makes it fast.Source: Morgan and Mikhail
  • Sevoflurane resembles propofol in the EEG, but adds theta at higher doses. Below 1 MAC, sevoflurane gives strong alpha and slow-delta. At 1 MAC and above, theta appears and fills in between slow-delta and alpha. When the concentration is lowered, theta disappears first. At emergence, alpha gives way to lower-amplitude beta and gamma, like a zipper opening. Isoflurane and desflurane give the same pattern, and high doses give burst suppression. See the Spectrogram tab.Source: Purdon 2015

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Inhaled agents act on many targets, and no obligatory site of action has been found. They enhance GABAA inhibition, block two-pore potassium channels and HCN channels, and inhibit glutamate release via NMDA receptors. They also enhance the glycine receptor α1 subunit, and nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are another target.Sources: Purdon 2015; Morgan and Mikhail
  • Potency follows lipid solubility, but only approximately (Meyer–Overton). This correlation once supported a shared mechanism for all inhaled agents.Source: Morgan and Mikhail
  • Immobility arises mainly in the spinal cord. Morgan and Mikhail write that MAC is unchanged after spinal cord transection in rats, but according to Jinks 2010 chronic transection lowered MAC by about 50 % (see Discrepancies and the Jinks 2010 card in the Components tab). The muscle-relaxing effect is thought to result from action on receptors and channels in the spinal cord. Two inhaled agents show no synergy for MAC, which is interpreted as a shared site for immobility despite different receptor effects.Sources: Morgan and Mikhail; Purdon 2015; Hendrickx 2008
  • Specific circuits modulate isoflurane anaesthesia. Noradrenergic nerve cells in the locus coeruleus modulate both the anaesthesia and emergence from it. In the pontine reticular formation, lower GABA levels are linked to unconsciousness. So GABA does not always inhibit wakefulness.Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Memory loss involves several receptors in the hippocampus. Isoflurane and sevoflurane inhibit LTP in the hippocampus, and the effect is abolished by GABAA antagonists. Low, amnestic concentrations enhance tonic inhibition through α5 receptors. Mouse studies point to α4 and β3 for isoflurane and HCN1 for sevoflurane, while α1 and α2 do not appear to be involved. For isoflurane, the α4β2 nicotinic receptor is also implicated. In rodents, impaired memory 24–48 hours after isoflurane appears to be mediated by α5.Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • The dose can change which effects matter most. Sevoflurane acts on all its targets all the time, but sensitivity differs. Low concentrations (about 0.5 MAC) enhance both GABA- and glycine-mediated inhibition. At higher concentrations (1.5 MAC) the GABA effect weakens or is blocked, and inhibition runs mainly via glycine receptors. NMDA inhibition increases with dose but is below 30 % at MAC, far less than the potentiation of GABA and glycine. There is no fixed order in which each target comes into play. Caveat: these are cell and animal studies, and none links theta in the human EEG to a specific target.Sources: Eckle 2013; Hapfelmeier 2001; Brosnan and Thiesen 2012 (rats); Hemmings 2019
  • GABA probably explains alpha and slow-delta, while theta may have another mechanism. Below 1 MAC, sevoflurane resembles propofol, which is interpreted as GABA enhancement being the main mechanism. Theta at 1 MAC and above may reflect one of the other mechanisms. The effect of sevoflurane on hippocampal theta may involve TASK-3 channels. Akeju 2014 (30 patients on sevoflurane vs 30 on propofol) found highly coherent frontal theta around 5 Hz only with sevoflurane, and suggests it may reflect effects on T-type calcium channels in the thalamus and indicate profound thalamic deafferentation. All of these are hypotheses.Sources: Purdon 2015; Mashour and Pryor 2025; Akeju 2014
  • Sevoflurane dampens the network but makes single cells easier to fire. In brain slices from young rats (cerebellum), sevoflurane strongly increased GABA inhibition and almost completely blocked the NMDA current, while AMPA was unaffected. At the same time it lowered the firing threshold of the cells. The net result was fewer and more regular action potentials: communication became poorer but was not switched off. The NMDA effect recovered more slowly than the GABA effect. The authors speculate that this may contribute to slower recovery, emergence delirium and seizure tendency in predisposed patients. These are cell studies, not measured in patients.Source: Mapelli 2021 (animal study, brain slices)
Nitrous oxide
Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8 Purdon 2015 Mashour and Pryor 2025; Fukuda 2025 Hendrickx 2008
  • Nitrous oxide is too weak to give anaesthesia on its own. It is therefore used as an adjunct. MAC is 105%, i.e. above one atmosphere. Trying to give enough nitrous oxide alone for unconsciousness may cause nausea and vomiting.Sources: Purdon 2015; Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8
  • Textbooks recommend 100% oxygen after nitrous oxide to prevent diffusion hypoxia. Nitrous oxide is eliminated so rapidly that alveolar oxygen and CO₂ are diluted. Morgan and Mikhail describe 100% oxygen for 5–10 minutes after nitrous oxide is turned off.Source: Morgan and Mikhail
  • Prolonged exposure can harm bone marrow and nerves. The side effects are bone marrow depression (megaloblastic anaemia) and peripheral neuropathies.Source: Morgan and Mikhail
  • Nitrous oxide gives beta and gamma in the EEG, and BIS can rise even though the patient is unconscious. When switching from an ether agent to more than 70% nitrous oxide, a transient strong slow-delta can appear.Sources: Liu 2023; Purdon 2015

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • The site of action is not fully clear. The EEG patterns of nitrous oxide are linked to NMDA receptors. At the same time, nitrous oxide is counted among the inhaled agents with a less clear site of action.Sources: Purdon 2015; Hendrickx 2008
  • The mechanism behind the EEG patterns is unknown. Nitrous oxide typically gives beta–gamma. When switching from an ether agent to above 70% nitrous oxide, strong transient slow-delta can appear with loss of power above about 10 Hz. One hypothesis is blockade of NMDA-mediated excitatory signals from the parabrachial nucleus and the medial pontine reticular formation to the basal forebrain and thalamus. The beta–gamma may share its mechanism with ketamine.Source: Purdon 2015
  • The more the theta peak frequency is slowed, the more memory is impaired in animals. Amnestic concentrations of nitrous oxide, isoflurane and halothane suppress hippocampus-dependent fear learning in animals, in proportion to how much the theta peak frequency is slowed.Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Nitrous oxide and isoflurane are possibly infra-additive.Source: Hendrickx 2008
  • In mice, nitrous oxide relieves pain via the κ receptor, not μ. The analgesia runs via the κ receptor and descending inhibitory pathways in the spinal cord. The hypnotic effect does not depend on κ. 70% nitrous oxide is an effective NMDA antagonist that reduced opioid-induced hyperalgesia.Source: Fukuda 2025

The numbers in the textbooks: MAC, age and discrepancies

The figures in this sub-tab come mostly from Miller's. Morgan and Mikhail 2022 contains little on EEG, but gives useful figures alongside. The books do not always agree, and sometimes neither do chapters of the same book.

  • MAC is only one point on the curve. MAC corresponds to the EC50 for movement at incision. About 1.3 MAC prevents movement in about 95 %, while 0.3–0.4 MAC is associated with awakening when the inhaled agent is the only anaesthetic. The distance between ‘no movement’ and ‘awake’ may allow the EEG pattern to look adequate close to emergence (interpretation based on the sources). Opioids lower MAC, but with a ceiling, and high doses can stop spontaneous breathing without the patient losing consciousness.Sources: Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8; Fukuda 2025
  • Age: MAC falls 4 or 6 % per decade, depending on the source. Two chapters of Morgan and Mikhail give different figures: 6 % per decade “regardless of agent” and 4 % per decade over 40 years. Miller's gives 6 % per decade after 30 years. For propofol the figures also differ: 80-year-olds need about half the dose of 20-year-olds, or the dose should be reduced by 65 %, depending on the chapter.Sources: Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8 and 43; Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025 (Mapleson 1996); Vuyk et al. 2025; Kim et al. 2025 (Schnider 1999)
  • Synergistic or additive? The sources disagree on propofol and midazolam. Studies have found synergy for hypnosis between propofol and midazolam, and midazolam often acts synergistically with other hypnotics. Another chapter of Miller's, however, describes the interaction as “primarily additive”.Sources: Hendrickx 2008; Vuyk et al. 2025; Kim et al. 2025
  • Barbiturates depress the EEG more as the dose rises, and ketamine can mislead. Small doses of barbiturates give low-amplitude fast activity. Large doses give high-amplitude slow activity, burst suppression and electrical silence, in parallel with the fall in cerebral metabolism (up to 50 %). Thiopental doses that maintain burst suppression or a flat line give prolonged emergence, delayed extubation and a need for inotropes. With ketamine the patient can look awake without necessarily being so.Source: Morgan and Mikhail ch. 9
  • Morgan and Mikhail are more cautious than Miller's about EEG monitoring in older patients. Morgan and Mikhail only say that “some have suggested” that BIS monitoring may reduce cognitive impairment. Miller's proposes processed EEG to avoid burst suppression.Sources: Morgan and Mikhail ch. 43; Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025

The studies in detail:

Morgan and Mikhail 2022 Kim et al. 2025; Vuyk et al. 2025; Fukuda 2025; Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025 Hendrickx 2008 Schnider 1999 Mapleson 1996
Opioids
Fukuda 2025 Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010 Hendrickx 2008 Balanza 2022

This card describes opioid action from receptor to clinic. Much of the mechanistic knowledge comes from cell studies and animal experiments.Source: Fukuda 2025 (Fukuda)

  • Opioids are not complete anaesthetics. They reduce MAC, but with a ceiling, and must be combined with other drugs. Analgesia is not usually accompanied by loss of consciousness. High doses can abolish spontaneous breathing without unconsciousness, and the patient may breathe on command. Fentanyl alone does not give full hypnosis. This may be part of the explanation for awareness in cardiac surgery with high-dose opioids.Sources: Fukuda 2025; Brown 2010; Hendrickx 2008
  • High doses give slow delta waves, but with a ceiling. Fentanyl, alfentanil, sufentanil and remifentanil give the same pattern. Small doses of fentanyl (2–5 µg/kg) change the EEG minimally, while high doses (30–70 µg/kg) give high-amplitude slow delta waves. After large doses, isolated transient sharp waves (usually frontotemporal) can be seen. In children and adolescents, morphine reduced alpha and beta, while delta and theta were unchanged. The spectral edge frequency follows remifentanil concentration with almost no delay, but lags for fentanyl and sufentanil. Frontal theta has also been found with fentanyl (see the card below and Discrepancies).Sources: Fukuda 2025; Montandon 2016; Balanza 2022
  • Respiratory depression is mainly caused by μ receptors in the brainstem. Opioids act directly on the respiratory centres. The preBötzinger complex mediates only part of the effect (timing, not the fall in rate). G-protein-gated potassium channels contribute. Mice lacking the μ receptor do not get respiratory depression from morphine. Analgesia and respiratory depression appear to use different signalling pathways: the A118G gene variant alters analgesia but not respiratory depression from morphine-6-glucuronide. In monkeys, tolerance developed to analgesia but not to respiratory depression.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Opioids can increase pain sensitivity (hyperalgesia). In animal experiments this is linked to sensitisation to glutamate and substance P, NMDA plasticity and AMPA receptors in the dorsal horn. Ketamine, nitrous oxide, magnesium and buprenorphine reduced it in studies. With long-term use the cAMP system in the locus coeruleus is upregulated.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Muscle rigidity does not appear to be caused by action on the muscle. Proposed mechanisms are the nucleus raphe pontis, caudate nucleus and fentanyl action in the locus coeruleus on spinal motor neurons. Naloxone has been used to reverse the rigidity, but the sources disagree (see below).Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Fentanyl can also act outside the opioid receptors. Fentanyl, but not morphine, bound to human α1A and α1B receptors, dopamine D1 and D4 receptors and VMAT2 (Ki about 0.9–1.7 µM). Noradrenergic effects may therefore contribute to chest wall rigidity, but this is an untested hypothesis. In rats, repeated high fentanyl doses gave a 291 % increase in EMG and respiratory depression without clear tolerance, while time to righting became shorter (50 to 16 minutes). The sources disagree on naloxone: in his lecture at Høstmøtet 2026, Ken Solt said that rigidity with synthetic opioids is resistant to naloxone and probably does not act via the μ receptor. He showed case reports involving haloperidol and Parkinson's disease (see Discrepancies).Sources: Torralva 2020; Obert 2025; Ken Solt, Høstmøtet 2026

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • All opioid receptors are G-protein-coupled receptors. μ, δ, κ and the nociceptin receptor share about 50% amino acid sequence. They have seven segments crossing the cell membrane, and the ligand binds deep within a large pocket. Endogenous ligands are β-endorphin and endomorphins (μ), enkephalins (δ), dynorphins (κ) and nociceptin. The sigma receptor is no longer regarded as an opioid receptor. Morphine, fentanyl, sufentanil, alfentanil and remifentanil are μ agonists.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Opioids make the nerve cell less excitable. The receptor activates Gi/o proteins. Adenylate cyclase is inhibited (less cAMP), voltage-gated calcium channels are inhibited and inwardly rectifying potassium channels are activated.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • In the spinal cord, opioids dampen the pain signal both before and after the synapse. Opioid receptors are abundant in the substantia gelatinosa. Presynaptically, inhibited calcium channels reduce release of glutamate and substance P from primary sensory neurons. Postsynaptically, open potassium channels hyperpolarise the dorsal horn projection neuron, so glutamate excites it less easily.Sources: Fukuda 2025; Brown 2010
  • In the brainstem, opioids inhibit the inhibition. In the periaqueductal grey (PAG), they inhibit GABA release from tonically active interneurons. This releases descending pathways via the medulla, which release noradrenaline and serotonin that dampen pain signals in the dorsal horn.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Opioids also act higher up in the brain. PET with remifentanil showed activation in the anterior cingulate, insula, orbitofrontal cortex and brainstem. In rats, action in the amygdala contributes to analgesia.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Opioids reduce acetylcholine release. In rats, morphine reduced acetylcholine in the prefrontal cortex, given both intravenously and directly into the basal forebrain. This is a possible neurochemical basis for altered consciousness. Fentanyl reduces acetylcholine in the medial pontine reticular formation.Sources: Fukuda 2025; Brown 2010
  • It is unresolved whether G-protein-biased opioids have fewer side effects. The theory of biased agonism is that Gi/o signalling gives analgesia, while β-arrestin gives side effects such as respiratory depression, constipation and euphoria. Mice lacking β-arrestin-2 had less respiratory depression from morphine in one study, but not in a newer one.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • μ and δ agonists are rewarding, κ agonists aversive. Opioids inhibit GABA neurons in the ventral tegmental area and nucleus accumbens, so that more dopamine is released in the nucleus accumbens. Activity in the locus coeruleus is inhibited.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Several opioids also have other targets. Buprenorphine blocks sodium channels, d-methadone is an NMDA antagonist, pethidine acts at the α2B adrenoceptor (a possible explanation for its anti-shivering effect), and morphine and hydromorphone inhibit the 5-HT3A receptor. In mice lacking the μ receptor, ketamine-induced respiratory depression and antinociception were reduced, and the MAC of sevoflurane was higher.Source: Fukuda 2025

Key points

  • Each effect has its own concentration. Different effects of the same drug have different C50 values. Kim et al. 2025 suggest aiming for a 95–99 % probability of effect, not 50 %. Drug displays rely on population models that do not fit everyone.Source: Kim et al. 2025. See
  • A slow EEG is not the same as hypnosis. Fentanyl and α2 agonists give slow activity without unconsciousness. Lidocaine and magnesium appear to act by dampening arousal. Nociception pulls the other way, and no EEG measure has been shown to reflect memory. Look for the hypnotic's own signature, and watch how the picture changes with stimulation.Sources: see “When the EEG slows without hypnosis: direct effect or dampened arousal”
  • Opioids change the EEG little but depress breathing early. With fentanyl, theta and slow-delta increase with concentration. This is clear in the spectrogram but hardly visible in the raw EEG. Breathing falls at far lower concentrations than those that prolong reaction time. The study is small and was done before induction, not during anaesthesia.Source: Balanza 2022. See
  • Drugs from different classes mostly enhance each other. Opioid + hypnotic is synergistic, and propofol + midazolam is synergistic for hypnosis. Two inhalational agents, and propofol + sevoflurane, are only additive. Ketamine showed no synergy with GABAergic drugs in any study.Source: Hendrickx 2008. See
  • A sudden flat EEG after several simultaneous boluses is the extreme end of burst suppression. Older patients are most at risk. Titrate one drug at a time (interpretation based on the sources), and look at the raw EEG and suppression ratio after each bolus, not just the index. A clean flat line with normal impedance, appearing right after the doses, distinguishes it from a technical fault.Sources: see “Synergy between agents and isoelectric EEG”
  • Lidocaine and magnesium spare dose, but are not hypnotics. Neither has a known EEG signature of its own at clinical doses. They lower the hypnotic requirement mainly through antinociception, and should be counted as opioid-sparing when weighing synergy. With lidocaine during volatile anaesthesia, MAC was lower but BIS higher. If you guide only by MAC and blood pressure, hypnosis may be lighter than you think. The study measured only the index, not the EEG signature, and the evidence base is small.Sources: Bazin 2018 and others. See

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

Several effects, different concentrations

Each drug has a dynamic range: the concentration at which the effect changes. Below the range little happens. Above it, more drug does not give more effect. Different effects of the same agent have different C50 values.Source: Kim et al. 2025

Hypnotics and opioids enhance each other. The analgesic effect is enhanced markedly, the hypnotic effect moderately. Two GABAergic hypnotics together are largely just additive. Kim et al. 2025 suggest aiming for a 95–99% probability of effect, not 50% as MAC does. Drug displays show predicted effect, but are based on population models that do not fit everyone.Sources: Kim et al. 2025 (Hendrickx 2008, Bouillon 2004, Egan 2001)

Kim et al. 2025 (Hendrickx 2008, Bouillon 2004, Egan 2001)

Fentanyl and EEG: frontal theta (Balanza 2022)

  • A small study, done before induction. 25 patients received fentanyl 2 µg/kg (ideal body weight) every 2 minutes, two or three doses, before general anaesthesia. They performed an auditory task and were monitored with frontal EEG, respiratory belts and pulse oximetry. The effect-site concentration is model-derived, not measured. Recruitment stopped early because of covid-19.Source: Balanza 2022
  • Theta rises with fentanyl, but differently from patient to patient. More fentanyl gave more theta (4–8 Hz) and slow-delta (below 4 Hz). Theta is hard to see in the raw EEG, but clear in the spectrogram. Concentration alone explained little (marginal R² 0.15), because patients differed a great deal.Source: Balanza 2022
  • Breathing falls already after the first dose. Minute ventilation fell 30% after the first dose, 55% after the second and 60% after the third. SpO₂ stayed at 95–100%, but patients were preoxygenated. More theta was linked to lower ventilation.Source: Balanza 2022
  • Breathing falls long before reactions slow. Reaction time increased on average 277 seconds after ventilation began to fall. The concentration that gave a 10% fall in ventilation was about 1750 times lower than the one that prolonged reaction time. 16 of 25 stopped responding. All could be roused, and four needed a jaw thrust. Slow-delta tracked loss of response better than theta.Source: Balanza 2022
  • The EEG might warn of respiratory depression, but this has not been tested. It is the authors' hypothesis. The study is small and did not measure during anaesthesia.Source: Balanza 2022
  • The numbers cannot be compared directly with the textbook. Miller's gives fentanyl C50 of about 2 ng/ml for analgesia, 4 for ventilatory depression and 20 for EEG changes. Balanza saw theta rise across the whole range 0–15 ng/ml, but found no threshold. The endpoints and methods differ.Sources: Kim et al. 2025 (Egan 2001), Balanza 2022
  • Caveat – conflict of interest: Purdon reports patents, a licence to Masimo and co-founding of a company developing closed-loop systems.
Balanza et al. PNAS Nexus 2022;1:pgac158

When the EEG slows without hypnosis: direct effect or dampened arousal

Which agents reinforce each other, and which do not

This is the practical consequence of synergy: two agents at doses that each look modest can together produce far deeper anaesthesia than the doses would suggest. But it does not apply to every combination, and it is worth knowing which.

CombinationWhat happensWhat it means
Opioid + hypnotic (intravenous or inhaled)SynergyOpioids alone give neither full hypnosis nor immobility, so any reduction above 10% counts as synergy.
Propofol + midazolamSynergyProbably because they bind different sites on the GABAA receptor. Midazolam 0.13 mg/kg halved the propofol dose, from 1.93 to 0.93 mg/kg. The fall in blood pressure was reinforced just as much.
Volatile agent + intravenous agentSynergyAcross the classes they reinforce each other.
Propofol + sevofluraneAdditiveThe doses simply add up.
Volatile + volatileAdditiveWithin the same class there is no reinforcement.
Propofol + thiopentalAdditiveAs above.
Propofol + ketamineAdditive, and infra-additive for immobility on reanalysisKetamine showed no synergy with GABAergic agents in any study, even though it acts on a different receptor.
Midazolam + ketamineInfra-additive for hypnosisThat is, weaker than the sum.
Clonidine + propofolAdditive for hypnosisBut clonidine lowers MAC awake for sevoflurane by 17 to 21% and MAC by 17 to 34%, with a ceiling effect, and that counts as synergy.

The thresholds used: a sum of normalised doses below 0.9 is synergy, 0.9 to 1.1 is additive, and above 1.1 is infra-additive.Sources: Hendrickx et al. 2008; Short and Chui 1991; Higuchi et al. 2002

This applies as much during maintenance as at induction. Synergy is not a bolus phenomenon. During an operation there is usually a volatile agent or propofol underneath with an opioid infusion on top, and two synergistic agents are then already running. If a third is added, clonidine say, or an opioid bolus before incision, the whole combination moves down the isobologram without any single dose looking large. This is what makes the EEG go into burst suppression at doses that each look cautious, and it reaches older patients first.

The mechanism, the numbers from the studies and how isobolograms and response-surface models measure this are in .

Hendrickx et al. 2008 Short and Chui 1991 Higuchi et al. 2002

Many drugs change the EEG without producing unconsciousness or amnesia themselves. This happens in two different ways, and they mean different things for how much hypnotic the patient needs. At the same time nociception pulls in the opposite direction. You therefore need to know what has been given, and what is happening in the surgical field.

  • Some drugs slow the EEG without producing unconsciousness. Fentanyl gives more theta and slow delta, and breathing falls long before reaction time increases. High opioid doses alone (fentanyl above about 8 ng/ml) give more delta and a lower median frequency. Usual doses together with hypnotics change the EEG little. α2 agonists give slow waves and spindles, but the patient can be roused. Dexmedetomidine under propofol gave more delta–theta and a lower PSI.Sources: Balanza 2022, Sleigh et al. 2025, Hight 2020, Purdon 2015, Zhang 2021
  • Lidocaine and magnesium appear to act by dampening arousal. Lidocaine changed neither BIS nor propofol requirements without surgical stimulation, only during stimulation. During volatile anaesthesia, lidocaine gave lower MAC but higher BIS. Magnesium gave no BIS difference in one study (where sufentanil was adjusted to keep BIS in the same range) and lower BIS in another. There, less muscle activity may be part of the explanation, but that is a hypothesis. Spinal lidocaine sedated healthy volunteers, probably because less sensory input reached the brain. None of these has a known EEG signature of its own at clinical doses.Sources: Hans 2010, Bazin 2018, Memiş 2003, Walia 2018, Pollock 2000
  • Pain can both lighten and apparently “deepen” the EEG. A noxious stimulus can give beta arousal, delta arousal or alpha dropout. The last two can make the index show deeper anaesthesia, even though the patient is reacting.Source: García 2021
  • The hypnotic requirement appears to follow the stimulation. Opioids and hypnotics enhance each other, and lidocaine spared propofol only while surgery was ongoing. When stimulation falls, or adjuvants dampen it, less hypnotic is needed. When stimulation rises, or the adjuvant wears off, more is needed.Sources: Kim et al. 2025, Hendrickx 2008, Hans 2010
  • It has not been shown that any EEG measure shows memory. With propofol, memory is lost at a lighter level than response, but this cannot be transferred to other drugs. Frontal alpha–delta did not exclude response to command.Sources: Glass 1997, Gaskell 2017
  • Look for the hypnotic's own signature, not just a slow EEG (interpretation based on the sources). With propofol and sevoflurane, this is frontal alpha above slow activity. Consider which drugs have been given and when, and watch how the picture changes with stimulation. Do not reduce the hypnotic just because the index falls after an opioid, α2 agonist or adjuvant. When clonidine has been given, the volatile should not be lowered below what is needed for unconsciousness.Source: Hight 2020
  • Reflection from the author of the app: when several drugs affect the EEG without producing hypnosis or amnesia, and nociception at the same time pulls the other way, interpretation becomes harder. The EEG must then be read together with what has been given, when it was given and what is happening surgically.
  • Caveat: the studies are small and use different measures. For lidocaine and magnesium there are almost only index data, no spectrogram studies.

More on this: . The cards on fentanyl, lidocaine and magnesium are in this section, and clonidine and dexmedetomidine under “The drugs”.

Balanza 2022 Kim et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025 Hight 2020 Zhang 2021 Hans 2010 Bazin 2018 Memiş 2003 Walia 2018 Pollock 2000 García 2021 Gaskell 2017

Synergy between agents and isoelectric EEG

A clinical picture many will recognise: several agents are given at the same time in large doses, for example at induction, or because the patient moves during the procedure (more volatile agent, opioid, clonidine and esketamine all at once). The EEG abruptly becomes completely flat, without bursts, and only returns when the bolus effect has worn off. Older patients are most at risk. This does not appear to be a separate phenomenon, but the extreme end of burst suppression.

  • A flat EEG is the end of burst suppression, and must be told apart from a technical fault. Suppression is amplitude below 10 µV. Isoelectric EEG is 2 µV or lower. Burst suppression is a continuum: the suppression ratio increases with dose until the EEG is completely flat. The monitor shows this as SR near 100. A loose electrode or a cable break gives noise, an impedance alarm or a lot of artefact. Isoelectric EEG is a clean flat line in all channels, with normal impedance, and appears in relation to the doses.Sources: Guay 2025, Ching 2012
  • Drugs from different classes mostly enhance each other. Opioids are synergistic with both intravenous and inhaled hypnotics. Opioids alone cannot produce full hypnosis or immobility, so any reduction of more than 10% counts as synergy. Propofol + midazolam is synergistic for hypnosis, probably because they bind to different sites on the GABAA receptor. Volatile agents are synergistic with intravenous agents, but only additive with each other. Propofol + sevoflurane is additive. The cut-offs: a sum of normalised doses below 0.9 is synergy, 0.9–1.1 additive and above 1.1 infra-additive.Sources: Hendrickx 2008 (systematic review, Anesth Analg 2008;107:494–506), Short and Chui 1991, McClune 1992, Short 1992
  • Ketamine does not appear to enhance GABAergic drugs. Ketamine showed no synergy with GABAergic agents in any study. Propofol + ketamine was additive, and on reanalysis infra-additive for immobility. Midazolam + ketamine was infra-additive for hypnosis. The same is seen in dogs: ketamine before propofol did not change the propofol requirement for intubation, but gave more apnoea at the highest dose.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, Hui 1995, Mair 2009
  • In the example above, the synergy comes from sevoflurane + fentanyl (+ clonidine), not from esketamine. Clonidine + propofol was additive for hypnosis. But clonidine lowers MACawake for sevoflurane by 17–21% and MAC by 17–34%, with a ceiling effect, which counts as synergy. Synergy for side effects such as respiratory depression and hypotension is little studied.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, Higuchi 2002
  • Midazolam halved the propofol dose in one study, and the fall in blood pressure is enhanced just as much. In 200 young women, the combination gave hypnosis in 85% on a dose that gave hypnosis in only 50% with each agent alone. Midazolam 0.13 mg/kg halved the propofol dose for anaesthesia (no response to a tetanic stimulus), from 1.93 to 0.93 mg/kg. Midazolam alone never produced anaesthesia. Blood pressure fell as much with the combination as with each agent at equipotent dose, that is, synergy for the hypotension too.Source: Short and Chui 1991 (BJA 67:539–545)
  • Whether a combination is called synergy depends on the model. Interactions are measured with isobolograms (straight line = additive, curved towards the origin = synergy) or response surface models, where the effect is shown as a surface over two doses. A single parameter cannot capture synergy in one dose range and antagonism in another.Sources: Minto 2000, Lee 2010 (Korean J Anaesthesiol)
  • Older age and low blood pressure make suppression more likely. Older patients are more sensitive to propofol, and MAC falls with age. Hypotension after a bolus can in itself produce suppression. Suppression is linked to reduced cerebral metabolism. Ketamine increases CMRO₂ and does not produce classic burst suppression at clinical doses.Sources: Schnider 1999, Purdon 2015 (BJA), Georgii 2022, Ching 2012 (Burst suppression tab)
  • The EEG does not necessarily go straight back to baseline. When the effect wears off, activity returns, often as high-amplitude slow activity before the alpha band is back. At the same calculated concentration, the picture is not the same as before.Source: Sepúlveda 2026 (Burst suppression tab)
  • It has not been shown that a brief flat period gives a worse outcome. Suppression is associated with delirium, but ENGAGES reduced suppression time without reducing delirium. “Cortical collapse” is an image, not a technical term. “Reboot”, on the other hand, is used for the abrupt jump in connectivity between deep brain regions and the cortex at emergence; see the card on hysteresis and neural inertia in the Fundamentals tab.Sources: Fritz 2016 (Burst suppression tab), Wildes 2019, Huang 2021 (Neuroimage)
  • Antiseizure drugs can both enhance and counteract. Chronic use can enhance hypnotics, but raise the requirement for opioids and neuromuscular blockers. See the card “Antiseizure drugs and anaesthetic drugs: do they enhance or counteract?” under Metabolism and tolerance.
  • Movement does not necessarily mean that hypnosis is too light. Movement is often a spinal response to nociception (see the Fundamentals tab: nociception). Titrate one agent at a time, slowly in older patients (interpretation based on the sources), and look at the raw EEG and SR after each bolus, not only at the index. See image 16 in the image quiz.Sources: Obert 2024, Sepúlveda 2020
Hendrickx 2008, Short & Chui 1991, Minto 2000, Lee 2010, Ching 2012, Guay 2025

Multimodal anaesthesia: lidocaine and magnesium in the EEG

Lidocaine and magnesium are used to spare opioid and hypnotic. The question is whether they have an EEG signature of their own, whether they take part in the synergy between agents, and whether they affect the coupling between brain regions. There is little research, and almost all of it deals with dose sparing measured with BIS.

  • Lidocaine dampens the response to surgery, but does not produce hypnosis. Lidocaine lowered the propofol requirement (guided by BIS) only during surgical stimulation. Without stimulation, neither BIS nor haemodynamics changed. The effect appears to be antinociceptive, not hypnotic.Source: Hans 2010 (BJA, 40 patients)
  • With lidocaine and a volatile agent, MAC was lower but BIS higher. In a small, randomised, blinded study in open colorectal surgery, the volatile and fentanyl were titrated to blood pressure and heart rate, and the anaesthesiologists could not see BIS. With lidocaine, age-adjusted MAC was lower (1.0 versus 1.1), while BIS was higher (45 versus 39), especially late in the operation. Either hypnosis was lighter with lidocaine, or BIS does not capture its effect below the cortex. The authors advise caution with low MAC when lidocaine is given and depth is guided by haemodynamics. Only the index number was measured, not the raw EEG or spectrogram. Caveats: 25 patients, volatile agents only, and fentanyl was titrated rather than standardised. No conflicts of interest.Source: Bazin 2018
  • Look at the spectrogram, not just MAC and blood pressure, when lidocaine is given (interpretation based on the sources). Lidocaine can lower the requirement for volatile agent without lowering the index. If depth is guided by blood pressure and heart rate, the patient may end up in lighter hypnosis than the MAC value suggests. What the spectrogram looks like with lidocaine has hardly been studied (only two cases).Sources: Bazin 2018, Firdaus 2026
  • The type of interaction lidocaine has is unclear in humans. In animals, lidocaine lowers MAC for volatile agents, with a ceiling of about 50% MAC reduction, which counts as synergy. One animal study found synergy with propofol for hypnosis, and in rats lidocaine + thiopental was infra-additive. Lidocaine potentiates midazolam in humans, but the type is unknown. No human isobolograms exist, and the studies stopped below 10 µg/mL because of the risk of seizures.Source: Hendrickx 2008
  • Only two cases describe lidocaine on the spectrogram. Two craniotomy patients with TIVA and lidocaine: one kept an alpha–delta pattern, the other developed delta dominance with weaker alpha and episodes of burst suppression. The authors themselves say that no dose–response or causal relationship can be drawn. High plasma levels of lidocaine are proconvulsant, so the EEG effect does not rise steadily with dose.Source: Firdaus 2026
  • Magnesium spares propofol and opioid, but does not always change BIS. MgSO4 30 mg/kg before induction lowered the propofol requirement with index-guided dosing and gave lower BIS for the first 40 minutes, but less than dexmedetomidine. Mg also spared vecuronium. The patients were ASA I–II with isoflurane and nitrous oxide for maintenance, and the Ramsay score was slightly higher than with placebo (1.9 versus 1.4), that is light sedation (Walia 2018). In 30 intensive care patients, Mg lowered sufentanil requirements, and BIS was kept in the same range (61–88) by adjusting sufentanil (Memiş 2003). Mg does not produce sedation at serum levels below 8 mmol/L when ventilation is adequate.Sources: Walia 2018, Memiş 2003
  • “Propofol sparing” is not the same as an EEG effect. Magnesium crosses the blood–brain barrier poorly. A reasonable reading (an interpretation, not from a source) is that the saving in BIS studies is a mixture of reduced nociceptive response, haemodynamics and less muscle activity. Mg potentiates neuromuscular blockade and thus the EMG contribution to the index. This is a hypothesis.
  • No one knows whether lidocaine or magnesium changes the coupling between brain regions. No human studies on this during anaesthesia were found. What exists on connectivity concerns propofol and sevoflurane (Fundamentals tab), ketamine (Components tab) and dexmedetomidine.Source: Vlisides 2017 (ketamine)
  • Opioid-free anaesthesia with dexmedetomidine gave severe bradycardia and more complications (POFA). 314 patients received propofol, desflurane, lidocaine and ketamine, and either remifentanil or dexmedetomidine, guided by an index. The trial was stopped early after severe bradycardia in five patients on dexmedetomidine, three of them with asystole. Four of the cases occurred during CO₂ insufflation for laparoscopy. Hypoxaemia, ileus or cognitive dysfunction within 48 hours occurred in 78% with dexmedetomidine versus 67% with remifentanil, mostly due to hypoxaemia. Dexmedetomidine gave less morphine use and nausea afterwards, similar analgesia, but later extubation and a longer stay in the recovery unit. Dexmedetomidine was dosed by heart rate, because validated monitors of nociception and depth are lacking, and the mean dose of 1.2 µg/kg/h may have been too high. Caveat: several authors report fees from Orion Pharma, which manufactures dexmedetomidine.Source: Beloeil 2021
  • BIS 40–60 may mean something different with dexmedetomidine than with remifentanil (interpretation based on the sources). Dexmedetomidine can shift the index independently of hypnotic depth (see Fundamentals → Monitoring and artefacts). When no monitor is validated for dosing, the raw EEG and the spectrogram at least give a picture of what the drugs do to the brain, rather than titrating by heart rate and numbers alone.
  • In summary: lidocaine and magnesium are opioid-sparing, not extra hypnotics. Neither has a known EEG signature of its own at clinical doses, as propofol, sevoflurane, ketamine and dexmedetomidine have. They lower the need for hypnotic, mostly via antinociception. The EEG change you see is therefore most often indirect: less arousal response to surgery, or the hypnotic being dosed lower. The evidence base is small, and spectrogram studies of adequate size are lacking.
