Deep EEG activity in a patient who is not meant to be deeply sedated is a signal to look for a cause first (oxygen, temperature, glucose) and then review the dose. Whether PSI-guided sedation improves outcome needs further study.Sources: Guay 2025, Favre 2023

The studies in detail:

Rasulo 2023 Watson 2008 Favre 2023 Devlin 2018 Guay 2025 Part 2

The cards on burst suppression are collected in the tab.

The studies in detail: Guay 2025, Rasulo 2023, Favre 2023, Taccone 2026 and PADIS 2018 (5 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Expect a pattern: EEG-guided management of the critically ill (Guay 2025 Part 2)

Part 2 of the review from the Brown group (Anesthesiology 2025;143:1595–1618) gives a framework for frontal EEG in intensive care, built on the comparison with the ECG: periodic discharges resemble extrasystoles, seizures resemble ventricular tachycardia, and signs of too little oxygen to the brain resemble ST changes.

  • Step 1, expect a pattern: based on age, vital signs, disease, sedatives and neurological examination. A healthy 40-year-old on propofol 50 µg/kg/min who opens her eyes to voice is expected to show alpha–delta with bursts of beta and gamma when spoken to. A 78-year-old in septic shock on propofol 20 µg/kg/min who does not respond is expected to show slow-delta, burst suppression or suppression.
  • RASS and EEG: RASS −5 without neurological disease is expected to give alpha–delta, slow-delta or burst suppression. RASS −4 to −1 typically gives abrupt beta and gamma on top of slow-delta when the patient is stimulated. RASS 0 to +1 gives sustained beta and gamma, and RASS +2 to +4 gives a lot of movement and EMG artefact. Natural sleep may also be seen.
  • Step 2, signal quality: low impedance, good gel contact, no leads touching other electrical equipment, and electrodes replaced every 24 hours or as recommended by the manufacturer. The amplitude scale is set as low (sensitive) as possible without clipping the peaks, and the power scale is adapted to what you are looking for. Which scales are available varies between monitors. Clinical experience suggests that a very sensitive scale, for example 1 µV/mm, magnifies the trace so much that ordinary activity can look sharp and epileptiform and the peaks are clipped. Choose the most sensitive scale at which the waves are still shown in full, and change the scale before interpreting anything as epileptiform activity. The raw EEG shows the current state, the spectrogram shows the trend.
  • Step 3, when the pattern does not fit: suspected seizures prompt a full EEG, a neurologist and consideration of antiseizure drugs and more sedation. Unexpected beta and gamma during deep sedation or paralysis prompt more sedation and/or antinociception. Unexpected low activity (shift to lower frequencies, broadband power loss, burst suppression) should first be assessed as an imbalance between oxygen delivery and consumption: hypoxaemia, anaemia and low blood flow, as well as hypothermia, hypoglycaemia and severe hypercapnia. Only then is sedation reduced. If the pattern persists without sedation, primary neurological disease should be investigated.
  • How often: there is no guideline. As with blood pressure and SpO₂, the EEG can be assessed every time you enter the patient's room, more often the more unstable the patient.
  • Case 1: a 39-year-old with respiratory failure in burst suppression on propofol 50 µg/kg/min without signs of oxygen deficit. Reduction to 40 and then 20 µg/kg/min gave alpha–delta. Two days later, burst suppression appeared every time MAP was below 70 mmHg, with right heart failure and rising CVP, and disappeared with adrenaline.
  • Case 2: an elderly patient after mitral valve surgery with falling amplitude (from 30–40 to 10–20 µV) before burst suppression, at a cardiac index of 1.3. After mechanical circulatory support (cardiac index 2.7) the activity returned. The next day, during a sedation hold, she was still unresponsive after 4 hours, and the frontal EEG showed triphasic periodic discharges (10–15 per 10 seconds). A full EEG confirmed nonconvulsive seizures, which were treated, and she woke without deficits.
  • Caveats: a review with cases from a single institution, not an outcome study. Frontal EEG has limited sensitivity for seizures and ischaemia outside the frontal lobe. Brown reports patents, royalties from Masimo and co-founding a company developing control of physiological states during anaesthesia. Brown and Guay hold a joint patent, and Guay has received travel support from Masimo.
Guay et al. Anesthesiology 2025;143:1595–1618

Consensus on processed EEG during sedation of the critically ill (Rasulo 2023)

International expert panel (Neurocrit Care 2023;38:296–311), 21 clinicians in neurointensive care and neuroanaesthesia, Delphi method without a systematic literature review. 59 statements: 47 rated appropriate with strong consensus, 2 inappropriate, 3 with weak consensus, 2 uncertain and 5 without consensus. The document is to be revised after 5 years.

  • Technique: pEEG is suitable for monitoring sedation level; four to five channels are sufficient, a frontal montage is sufficient, and the monitor should display raw EEG with adjustable speed and amplitude scale as well as a continuous colour spectrogram with adjustable power scale (all strong consensus). Whether two channels are enough reached no consensus.
  • The EEG index number: the panel could not recommend dimensionless indices as sufficient for monitoring sedation depth in the critically ill (uncertain, but with strong consensus about the uncertainty). If they are used, the number should always be checked against the raw EEG rhythm.
  • Burst suppression: should be avoided in all situations except to control raised intracranial pressure (strong consensus). Suppression ratio (SR) is a good measure of whether burst suppression is present, and “if burst suppression is used”, SR should be kept below 5% (strong consensus). The statements sit under the question of whether burst suppression should be avoided, so 5% is read here as the limit during ordinary sedation, in practice without burst suppression. The article does not justify the figure. The background notes that age and comorbidity lower the amplitude and weaken alpha, which increases the propensity for burst suppression.
  • Who: all sedated patients where clinical assessment is not possible, all who need deep sedation (RASS ≤ −3), patients on ECMO, patients receiving brief deep sedation for procedures, and separate criteria for older patients (all strong consensus). After cardiac arrest, continuous EEG is recommended during cooling and rewarming or in the event of seizures. During neuromuscular blockade, pEEG should be the main method for sedation assessment (strong consensus).
  • Who not: patients with only light sedation (RASS 0 to −2) do not benefit from it. RASS and SAS remain the most valid tools, and pEEG should supplement, not replace, the scales. In non-comatose, non-paralysed patients the panel could not recommend indices as the main method. Start as early as possible and measure continuously.
  • Interpretation: pEEG values vary between patients at the same clinical sedation level, and are affected by blood flow, hypothermia, age and brain injury. During light sedation, EMG can artificially raise the values.
  • Training: structured training with certification, in the frequency, time and power domains, rapid recognition of typical patterns, and access to a neurointensivist or neurophysiologist when needed (strong consensus).
  • Barriers and caveats: the panel itself mentions lack of knowledge, lack of validation in prolonged sedation, lack of standardisation between monitors with different algorithms, and cost. No systematic literature review, and the panel selection may have introduced bias: nine of the authors report speaker fees or positions with Masimo, Medtronic, Edwards or Nihon Kohden, and one is a medical director at Masimo.
Rasulo et al. Neurocrit Care 2023;38:296–311

Deep sedation, low PSI and delirium (Favre 2023)

Favre, Bernini, Miroz, Abed-Maillard, Ramelet and Oddo (Nurs Crit Care 2023, doi 10.1111/nicc.13009). A retrospective single-centre study in a general intensive care unit in Lausanne (2018–2020): 97 non-neurological patients who received deep sedation under a standardised guideline and were monitored with frontal processed EEG (PSI) for a median of 43 hours.

  • A lot of time with low PSI: PSI below 25 for a median of 49 % of the monitoring time (IQR 10–84).
  • Delirium in 42 %: 41 of 97, CAM-ICU positive on at least two days.
  • More low PSI with delirium: a median of 67 % of the time with PSI below 25 versus 47 % without delirium. Adjusted for sedatives and analgesics, the OR was 1.014 per percentage point (95 % CI 1.001–1.027).
  • Caveats: an association, not a cause. The study measures PSI below 25, not burst suppression directly. It is retrospective and from a single centre, so it cannot show whether deep sedation causes delirium or whether vulnerable patients get both low PSI and delirium (interpretation based on the sources). The authors say PSI-guided sedation needs further study.
Favre et al. Nurs Crit Care 2023

EEG as a bedside monitor in intensive care: the intensivist's perspective (Taccone 2026)

Perspective article in Critical Care 2026;30:195 (Taccone, Ozkaya, Baggiani, Rasulo). No original data; an argument for how EEG can become a genuine bedside monitoring tool in intensive care.

  • The problem: EEG is non-invasive, cheap and meaningful, but does not meet the requirements of a bedside monitor (immediately available, continuously interpretable, directly actionable). Electrode placement requires technicians, continuous EEG cannot be offered to everyone, visual interpretation of raw EEG by experts remains the reference standard, and even experts have only moderate agreement on patterns on the ictal-interictal continuum (Jing 2023). For many intensive care teams the EEG machine is “a foreign body” at the bedside.
  • Four things the intensivist needs: background activity (continuous, discontinuous or suppressed), asymmetry, burst suppression (spontaneous or drug-induced) and ictal or highly epileptiform activity (ACNS 2021 terminology). Brief, structured training improves classification by intensivists and nurses (Citerio, Taran). The parallel is echocardiography and lung ultrasound, which intensivists use without being cardiologists.
  • Montage according to the question: continuous EEG is superior for seizure detection and DCI after SAH, whereas brief intermittent recordings may suffice for prognosis after cardiac arrest. A full 10–20 is needed for localisation, whereas simplified montages may be adequate to detect burst suppression from oversedation or highly malignant patterns after hypoxia. Continuous and intermittent EEG are not interchangeable even though outcome studies have not shown a difference.
  • Four levels of interpretation: (1) a binary “red” alarm signal on the patient monitor for nurses without EEG training, for example a brain icon indicating the side; (2) type of abnormality for doctors without formal EEG training; (3) quantitative trends (spectrogram, SEF, amplitude trend, alpha/delta ratio, burst suppression ratio, seizure probability) for EEG-trained intensive care clinicians; (4) raw EEG with montages and filters for the neurophysiologist. Taccone holds that no treatment decision should be made by untrained staff on the basis of the alarm alone.
  • Spectrogram and SEF: the spectrogram is suited to seeing progressive background slowing (oversedation or raised ICP) and burst suppression (black bars). Low SEF means deeper suppression, whereas apparently increased high-frequency power may be EMG. Seizures appear as focal “hot spots” that build up and fade gradually, in contrast to artefacts, which are abrupt and do not evolve.
  • Drug signatures: the article reproduces Purdon 2015: propofol gives increasing delta and alpha and burst suppression at high doses, dexmedetomidine a sleep-like delta pattern, ketamine an activated picture with high beta and low gamma, and volatile agents propofol-like alpha at low concentrations, “but higher doses add theta activity and a broader spectral distribution”. This agrees with the theta fill-in in the simulator in the Spectrogram tab.
  • EEG reactivity: has shown diagnostic and prognostic value, but reproducibility varies and there is no standardised stimulation protocol, so for now it belongs at the expert level.
  • Caveats: a perspective without data, with proposals (alarm levels, AI detection) that have not been validated in multicentre studies; alarm fatigue and costs are unresolved. Taccone is a scientific adviser for Neuroptics and Nihon Kohden, and Rasulo reports speaker fees from Masimo. No funding.
Taccone et al. Crit Care 2026;30:195

PADIS 2018: what the guideline says about sedation depth and EEG monitoring (Devlin 2018)

The Society of Critical Care Medicine guideline for pain, agitation/sedation, delirium, immobility and sleep in adult intensive care patients (Crit Care Med 2018;46:e825–e873). GRADE methodology, with patient representatives on the panel.

  • Light sedation: recommends light rather than deep sedation in ventilated patients (conditional recommendation, low quality). Light sedation was defined as RASS −2 to +1 in the studies. Eight RCTs: shorter time to extubation (−0.77 days) and fewer tracheostomies (RR 0.57), but no difference in 90-day mortality (RR 1.01), delirium (RR 0.96), PTSD or self-extubation. The panel considers the old definition (RASS ≥ −2 with eye opening for 10 minutes) probably deeper than necessary.
  • Daily sedation interruption or nurse-driven protocol: both can achieve and maintain light sedation (ungraded). A brief sedation interruption should not be used as an excuse for deep sedation for the rest of the day.
  • Choice of agent: propofol or dexmedetomidine rather than benzodiazepines (conditional, low quality). Dexmedetomidine should not be used when deep sedation (with or without neuromuscular blockade) is required. Dexmedetomidine is suggested in delirium where agitation prevents weaning.
  • Objective sedation monitoring (ungraded): BIS “appears best suited for titration during deep sedation or neuromuscular blockade”, and can improve titration when a sedation scale cannot be used. 32 intensive care studies of BIS against scales were reviewed. Three studies of BIS-guided sedation showed lower sedative use and faster awakening, fewer procedure-related events, and lower midazolam and fentanyl doses, less agitation, fewer tracheostomies and shorter length of stay.
  • Why scale and EEG do not track each other: the scales bottom out at RASS −5, while the EEG can continue down to an isoelectric line; during agitation BIS tops out at 100 while the scales continue upwards. The scales also require stimulation, which in itself raises the index, so the timing of the EEG reading relative to the stimulation determines the agreement. Studies that did not account for this had the poorest agreement.
  • Sleep: advises against routine physiological sleep monitoring (actigraphy, BIS, EEG, polysomnography) clinically (conditional, very low quality).
  • Caveats: most of the recommendations are conditional with low quality of evidence. Several panel members report conflicts of interest, including an EEG-based delirium monitor under development.
Devlin et al. Crit Care Med 2018;46:e825–e873

Key points

  • Seizures without convulsions are common. Of 550 children on continuous EEG in intensive care, 30 % had electrographic seizures, and in 36 % of them all seizures lacked clinical signs. In adults in a medical ICU, 10 % had seizures and 22 % seizures or periodic discharges.See
  • Sepsis raises the risk, and status epilepticus is linked to higher mortality. Sepsis was the only independent risk factor in adults (32 % versus 9 %), and among children sepsis had the highest proportion of seizures. In children, electrographic status was associated with higher mortality (OR 2.42).See
  • Many ICU conditions lower the seizure threshold. Electrolyte disturbances, low blood glucose, cefepime, carbapenems and withdrawal can trigger seizures in patients without brain disease. GABA-enhancing sedatives can mask convulsions without stopping electrical seizures (interpretation based on the sources).See
  • The EEG index can look like deep sedation during seizures. In a published case, the index and suppression ratio barely changed while the raw EEG showed spikes and spike-and-wave. It is the raw EEG that reveals the pattern.See
  • Spectrogram patterns must be read against the raw EEG. Solid flames corresponded to seizures or seizure-like patterns in about 69 %, irregular flames in about 39 %. A pattern is a suspicion.Source: Zafar 2020. See
  • Frontal raw EEG catches a lot, but not everything. In 32 comatose patients after cardiac arrest, status epilepticus was detected with 86 % sensitivity, but periodic epileptiform discharges in only 25 % of cases. A frontal trace does not replace a full EEG and a neurologist.See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Seizures without convulsions are common, especially in sepsis

The terms: seizure, convulsion and status. What they actually mean

The words are used interchangeably in the clinic, and that creates confusion exactly where precision matters. Here is what the field means by them.

A seizure is defined by the ILAE as a transient occurrence of signs or symptoms due to abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain. Note that the definition says nothing about movement.

"Convulsion" is not the same as seizure. Convulsions are the motor expression, that is, what you see. Many seizures have no motor expression at all, and those are precisely the common ones in intensive care. The ILAE removed the word "convulsion" from the classification in 2017, remarking that it will undoubtedly persist in popular usage. Use "seizure" for the phenomenon and "convulsion" only for the motor part.

How seizures are classified under ILAE 2017. One begins with a single question: where does it start?

  • Focal seizure. Originating within networks limited to one hemisphere. These can additionally be labelled by awareness: focal aware or focal with impaired awareness. Awareness is defined operationally as knowledge of self and environment during the seizure, not as knowledge that a seizure occurred. If awareness is impaired during any part of the seizure, the whole seizure counts as focal with impaired awareness.
  • Generalized seizure. Originating at some point within, and rapidly engaging, bilaterally distributed networks. Divided into motor types, including tonic–clonic, myoclonic–atonic and myoclonic–tonic–clonic, and non-motor types, which are absences.
  • Unknown onset. The ILAE calls this "a placeholder—not a characteristic of the seizure, but of ignorance." A label on our ignorance, not on the seizure. It is an honest category, and a useful one in intensive care where the onset is rarely witnessed.
  • Focal seizures are divided further into motor and non-motor onset. The non-motor focal types are automatisms, autonomic, behaviour arrest, cognitive, emotional, hyperkinetic and sensory. Note behaviour arrest: the patient simply stops. That is a seizure, and it is easy to miss in a sedated patient.

Terms that have been abandoned, and that you will still hear. "Partial" is now "focal". "Simple partial" corresponds to focal aware, and "complex partial" to focal with impaired awareness. Both were eliminated, along with "dyscognitive" and "psychic". "Secondarily generalized" is now "focal to bilateral tonic–clonic", because "bilateral" is used for propagation patterns while "generalized" is reserved for seizures involving bilateral networks from onset.

Fisher et al. Epilepsia 2017;58:522–530

When does a seizure become status epilepticus? t1 and t2

The ILAE definition from 2015 rests on two time points, and the point of having two is that they answer different questions.

  • t1 is when the seizure is abnormally prolonged. It is the point at which the seizure can no longer be expected to stop on its own, and therefore when treatment should begin.
  • t2 is when it starts to cost. It is the point at which continuing seizure activity carries a risk of long-term consequences: neuronal death, neuronal injury and altered neuronal networks.

The times differ by seizure type, and this is where many go wrong:

Type of status epilepticust1, start treatmentt2, risk of injury
Tonic–clonic5 minutes30 minutes
Focal with impaired consciousness10 minutesmore than 60 minutes
Absence10 to 15 minutesunknown

What this means in practice. Five minutes of tonic–clonic convulsions is status epilepticus, not "a long seizure". And conversely: for focal seizures with impaired consciousness, the form you most often meet in intensive care without seeing it, t1 is ten minutes and t2 is over an hour. That allows more time, but it also means a longer window in which nothing is visible from the outside.

The ILAE report also proposes a classification along four axes: semiology, aetiology, EEG correlate and age. Note that t2 for absence status is given as unknown. That is not an oversight, it is an admission.

Trinka et al. Epilepsia 2015;56:1515–1523

What the EEG report means: the ACNS definitions from 2021

When the neurophysiologist writes "electrographic seizure" or "ictal–interictal continuum" in the report, these are defined terms with numbers behind them. Here they are, as the ACNS defines them.

  • Electrographic seizure (ESz). Either epileptiform discharges averaging more than 2.5 Hz for at least 10 seconds, that is, more than 25 discharges in 10 seconds, or any pattern with definite evolution lasting at least 10 seconds. Sharply contoured discharges longer than 200 ms may count, even though they are not technically epileptiform.
  • Electroclinical seizure (ECSz). Either a definite clinical correlate time-locked to the EEG pattern, or improvement in both EEG and clinical state after a parenteral antiseizure medication. There is no minimum duration here. The clinical correlate may be very subtle, such as face twitching, eye deviation or nystagmus. An electroclinical seizure need not meet the criteria for an electrographic seizure, and may be shorter than 10 seconds.
  • Electrographic status epilepticus (ESE). An electrographic seizure for at least 10 continuous minutes, or for a total of at least 20% of any 60-minute period of recording.
  • Electroclinical status epilepticus (ECSE). The same thresholds, 10 continuous minutes or 20% of any 60-minute period. But ongoing bilateral tonic–clonic motor activity needs only 5 continuous minutes, in line with the ILAE t1.
  • BIRDs, brief potentially ictal rhythmic discharges. Focal or generalized rhythmic activity faster than 4 Hz, at least six waves at a regular rate, lasting at least 0.5 seconds but less than 10 seconds, without a definite clinical correlate, not consistent with a known normal pattern or benign variant, and not part of burst suppression or burst attenuation.
  • Ictal–interictal continuum (IIC). Synonymous with "possible electrographic seizure". This is a purely electrographic term, not a diagnosis, and the pattern specifically does not qualify as a seizure or as status. It includes, among others, periodic discharges or spike-and-wave averaging more than 1.0 and up to 2.5 Hz over 10 seconds, and lateralized rhythmic delta activity over 1 Hz for at least 10 seconds with a plus modifier or fluctuation.

And what "definite evolution" means, since that is what separates a seizure from a periodic pattern: at least two unequivocal, sequential changes in frequency, morphology or location, within the same category. For frequency, at least two consecutive changes in the same direction of at least 0.5 Hz each. For morphology, at least two consecutive changes to a novel morphology. For location, spread into or out of at least two different standard 10–20 electrode positions. Each stage must last at least three cycles, and the feature being evolved must not remain unchanged for five or more continuous minutes. A change in voltage alone does not qualify.

Why this is worth knowing for an anaesthesia or intensive care nurse: it explains why the answer is so often "ictal–interictal continuum" rather than yes or no. That is not vagueness from the neurophysiologist, it is a defined category meaning the pattern lies in between. The treatment decision is then made clinically, not by the terminology.

Hirsch et al. J Clin Neurophysiol 2021;38:1–29

Many intensive care patients have electrical seizures that cannot be seen without EEG. This holds across different patient groups.

  • In children, many seizures have no clinical signs at all. Of 550 children on continuous EEG in the paediatric ICU, 30 % had electrographic seizures, and 38 % of these had electrographic status epilepticus. In 36 %, all seizures were without clinical signs.Source: Abend 2013
  • Sepsis raises the risk of seizures. Among children, sepsis had the highest proportion of seizures (58 %), but the group was only 19 children.Sources: Abend 2013, Lobo and Lamperti ch. 1
  • Status epilepticus matters for outcome. In children, electrographic status epilepticus was associated with higher mortality (OR 2.42, 95 % CI 1.08–5.40), whereas seizures without status were not. The study is retrospective, and EEGs were read locally.Source: Abend 2013
  • Many ICU conditions lower the seizure threshold. Electrolyte disturbances, low blood glucose, cefepime (especially with impaired renal function), carbapenems and withdrawal can trigger seizures in patients without brain disease. GABA-enhancing sedatives can mask clinical convulsions without stopping electrical seizures, so the threshold for EEG should be low (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Nardone 2016, Cryer 2007, Payne 2017, Radkowski 2025

The studies in detail:

Abend 2013 Lobo and Lamperti ch. 1 Nardone 2016 Payne 2017

The EEG index can resemble deep sedation during seizures

Nonconvulsive seizures can look like deep sedation on a frontal monitor. In the published examples, it was the raw EEG and the spectrogram, not the index, that revealed the seizures.

  • The EEG index stood still while the raw EEG showed seizures. A 75-year-old woman was comatose after cardiac arrest. BIS lay between 25 and 35 and SR between 20 and 35. When hypnotics were weaned, the raw EEG showed spikes, spike-and-wave and polyspikes, but BIS and SR did not change significantly.Source: Ntahe 2018
  • The EEG index measures frequency, not seizures (interpretation based on the sources). The index tells you where the power lies in frequency, not whether the activity is epileptiform. Low-frequency periodic discharges can therefore give a low index and low SEF that resemble deep sedation. Broadband discharges can give higher numbers.Source: Gimson 2021
  • The spectrogram can raise suspicion. In an infant with status epilepticus, the colours in the low frequencies shifted to dark red without clinical convulsions. The pattern disappeared after thiopental. Solid flames corresponded to seizures or seizure-like patterns in about 69 %, irregular flames in about 39 %.Sources: Hernández-Hernández 2016, Zafar 2020
  • The evidence is thin. The examples are case reports and a small single-centre study, all with BIS. None of them tells how often the index misses.

The studies in detail:

Ntahe 2018 Gimson 2021 Hernández-Hernández 2016 Zafar 2020

Frontal EEG raises suspicion, full EEG gives the answer

A frontal monitor can catch a lot, but it does not replace a full EEG and a neurologist.

  • Frontal raw EEG is good for status, but weak for periodic discharges. In 32 comatose patients after cardiac arrest, frontal raw EEG detected status epilepticus with 86 % sensitivity and 100 % specificity when two neurophysiologists agreed. Inexperienced investigators had a sensitivity of 70–90 %. Periodic epileptiform discharges were picked up in only 25 % of cases, probably because only frontotemporal leads were recorded.Source: Haesen 2018
  • A pattern is a suspicion. The spectrogram should always be read against the raw EEG, and the BIS monitor cannot replace conventional EEG.Sources: Zafar 2020, Ntahe 2018
  • A neurophysiologist or intensivist interprets seizures (interpretation based on the sources). Someone using a frontal monitor should recognise the pattern and ask for a full EEG.
  • Practise the patterns in the simulator. It shows schematic, synthetic traces of epileptiform patterns and a pitfall with ECG artefact. They are not patient data, and a frontal trace does not replace a full EEG and a neurologist.

The studies in detail:

Haesen 2018 Ntahe 2018 Zafar 2020

Simulator: epileptiform patterns in the raw EEG

Schematic, synthetic traces with four frontal channels (L1, R1, L2, R2) on a sedated alpha–delta background. The shapes are drawn from descriptions in a textbook and journal articles. They are not patient data, and a frontal trace does not replace a full EEG and a neurologist. Amplitudes and scale are approximate: the sources give duration and frequency, not amplitude, and 1 mm on screen is not necessarily 1 mm on the monitor.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti ch. 4, Guay 2025, Sutter and Kaplan 2012

Time window
Scale

ACNS 2021 (Hirsch et al.) Lobo and Lamperti ch. 4 Guay 2025 Part 2 Sutter and Kaplan 2012 Schematic, not patient data

The balance between excitation and inhibition: why ICU patients without brain disease can have seizures

The brain is kept stable by a balance between excitation (mostly glutamate) and inhibition (mostly GABA). If the balance shifts towards excitation, the seizure threshold falls: less is needed to trigger a seizure. (A higher seizure threshold means the opposite, that more is needed.) The model is simplified: GABA can be excitatory in some situations, and the balance depends among other things on the chloride transporters NKCC1 and KCC2 and on sustained (tonic) inhibition outside the synapses.Source: Fritschy 2008

  • Sepsis affects the brain. Inflammatory mediators (including TNF-α) and bacterial toxins damage the blood–brain barrier and cause septic encephalopathy with a slow EEG. Exactly how this shifts the balance towards excitation is not described in the source.Source: Kuperberg and Wadgaonkar 2017
  • Sodium, calcium and magnesium disorders can cause seizures, potassium disorders usually do not. Hyponatraemia most often causes seizures when sodium falls rapidly below 115 mmol/L. Hypocalcaemia causes seizures in 20–25% of acute cases. Hypomagnesaemia causes seizures mostly below about 1 mEq/L. Magnesium normally blocks the NMDA receptor, one of the glutamate receptors.Source: Nardone 2016
  • Very low blood glucose can cause seizures. Symptoms from the brain appear at about 3.0 mmol/L, cognitive dysfunction at about 2.8 mmol/L, and then seizures and coma at about 2.3–2.7 mmol/L.Source: Cryer 2007
  • Some antibiotics can cause seizures, especially with renal impairment. Of 135 cases of cefepime neurotoxicity, 80% had renal impairment, and 25% of those who had an EEG had non-convulsive status epilepticus. 26% developed neurotoxicity despite correct dosing. Beta-lactams, especially imipenem, are thought to inhibit the GABAA receptor. Carbapenems lower valproate levels by 50–88%.Sources: Payne 2017, Radkowski 2025
  • Withdrawal seizures come in a typical time window. With alcohol they usually occur 6–48 hours after the last drink and involve NMDA and GABA receptors. GHB withdrawal starts 1–6 hours after the last dose. Seizure-like phenomena with propofol occur mostly at induction and emergence, rarely during maintenance.Sources: Hillbom 2003, Karila 2024, Kumar 2021
  • Why withdrawal causes seizures (interpretation based on the sources): with long-term use of substances that enhance GABA (alcohol, benzodiazepines, GHB, propofol), the brain adapts with less inhibition or more excitation. When the substance disappears suddenly, the adapted excitation is left without a counterweight.
  • Keep a low threshold for EEG in patients at risk (interpretation based on the sources). GABA-enhancing sedatives raise the seizure threshold and can hide clinical convulsions without stopping electrical seizures. This applies especially in sepsis, renal failure, electrolyte disorders, cefepime or a carbapenem, or possible withdrawal.
Fritschy 2008 Nardone 2016 Cryer 2007 Payne 2017 Radkowski 2025 Hillbom 2003
The studies in detail: flames in the spectrogram, seizures in children and published examples (3 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Spectrogram patterns and seizures: “flames” (Zafar 2020)

Zafar et al. (Clin Neurophysiol 2020;131:2298–2306), “A standardized nomenclature for spectrogram EEG patterns: inter-rater agreement and correspondence with common intensive care unit EEG patterns”. The study names patterns in the spectrogram and examines how they correspond to common EEG patterns in intensive care.

  • Solid flames: corresponded to seizures or seizure-like patterns in about 69 %.
  • Irregular flames: corresponded to them in about 39 %.
  • A pattern is a suspicion, not a diagnosis: the spectrogram must always be read against the raw EEG.
  • Interpretation based on the sources: interpreting seizures belongs with a neurophysiologist or intensivist. The point for someone using a frontal monitor is to recognise the pattern and ask for a full EEG.
Zafar et al. Clin Neurophysiol 2020;131:2298–2306

Electrographic seizures in children in intensive care (Abend 2013)

Retrospective cohort from 11 centres in the USA and Canada (Neurology 2013;81:383–391): 550 children aged 1 month to 21 years with continuous EEG in the paediatric ICU, ordered on clinical indication and at least 6 hours long.

  • How common: 162 of 550 (30 %) had electrographic seizures, and 61 of these (38 %) had electrographic status epilepticus. In 59 of 162 (36 %) all seizures were without clinical signs.
  • By diagnosis: sepsis had the highest proportion (58 % of 19), followed by epilepsy (48 % of 159), brain malformation (38 %), CNS inflammation or autoimmune disease (33 %), stroke and traumatic brain injury (30 %), metabolic causes and CNS infection (29 %) and hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy (18 % of 73). Children only pharmacologically sedated with no known neurological problem: 13 % of 15. After neuromuscular blockade: 8 % of 26. A child could have several diagnoses.
  • The seizures: 38 % lasted 10–59 seconds, 40 % 1–5 minutes, 16 % 6–30 minutes and 6 % more than 30 minutes. Onset was focal in 53 %, multifocal in 19 % and generalised in 24 %.
  • Risk and outcome: younger age, clinical seizures before EEG, abnormal background and interictal epileptiform discharges increased risk. Electrographic status epilepticus was associated with higher mortality (OR 2.42, 95 % CI 1.08–5.40), whereas seizures without status were not.
  • Caveats: retrospective, EEGs read locally without central review, and practice varied between centres. Small groups per diagnosis (sepsis: 19 children). Several authors report fees and research funding; there was no targeted funding for the study.
Abend et al. Neurology 2013;81:383–391

When the EEG index does not see the seizure: published examples

Nonconvulsive seizures can look like deep sedation on a frontal monitor. Three published papers show how, and what revealed the seizures.

  • Ntahe 2018 (case report): a 75-year-old woman, comatose after cardiac arrest, with nonconvulsive status epilepticus diagnosed with conventional EEG. During treatment BIS lay between 25 and 35 and SR between 20 and 35. When hypnotics were weaned on day 3, the raw EEG from the BIS monitor showed high-amplitude, irregular waves with spikes, spike-and-wave and polyspikes, alternating with a flat signal, while BIS and SR did not change significantly. Conventional EEG confirmed recurrence with continuous, generalised rhythmic spikes and spike-and-wave at 1–1.5 Hz. The conclusion is that the BIS monitor cannot replace conventional EEG, and that the raw EEG must be read together with the numbers.
  • Haesen 2018 (validation study): 32 comatose patients after cardiac arrest in whom the raw EEG from the BIS monitor was compared with full EEG. For status epilepticus, sensitivity was 86 % and specificity 100 % by consensus between two neurophysiologists. Two inexperienced investigators identified status epilepticus with sensitivity 70–90 % and specificity 92–96 %. Periodic epileptiform discharges were picked up in only 25 % of cases, probably because only frontotemporal leads were recorded.
  • Hernández-Hernández 2016 (two children): bilateral BIS spectrogram during status epilepticus in a 5-month-old infant and a 7-year-old child. In the infant the seizure activity appeared as the colours in the low frequencies shifting from orange, yellow and green to dark red, without clinical convulsions. The pattern disappeared after thiopental.
  • Sepsis: sepsis can cause electrographic seizures and periodic discharges (Lobo and Lamperti ch. 1), and among children in intensive care, sepsis had the highest proportion of seizures (Abend 2013, above).
  • Interpretation based on the sources: the index tells you where the power lies in frequency, not whether the activity is epileptiform. Low-frequency periodic discharges can therefore give a low index and low SEF that resemble deep sedation, while broadband discharges can give higher numbers (Gimson 2021). It is the raw EEG that reveals the pattern. See the simulator above and images 19 and 20 in the image quiz.
  • Caveats: case reports and a small retrospective single-centre study, all with BIS. None of them tells how often the index misses. In Ntahe 2018 the sensor was changed from four to two channels on day 3. Ntahe 2018 and Haesen 2018 report no conflicts of interest.
Ntahe 2018, Haesen 2018, Hernández-Hernández 2016, Gimson 2021

Key points

  • The same pattern can carry a completely different prognosis. Almost every coma pattern occurs both in intoxication or sedation, usually reversible, and in hypoxic-ischaemic injury, usually not. Whether the EEG reacts to a noxious stimulus tells you more than the pattern itself.See
  • Prognosis needs time and several predictors. After cardiac arrest, prognosis is assessed no earlier than 72 hours, and residual sedation should always be considered. A poor outcome is regarded as likely only when two or more of six predictors are present.See
  • EEG responds when blood flow falls. According to Ko and Engelhard, EEG slowing appears at a cerebral blood flow of about 20 and an isoelectric EEG at about 15 ml/100 g/min. Other sources give different thresholds (see the Perfusion tab). In unconscious neurocritical care patients, EEG should be used continuously to detect non-convulsive seizures.See
  • ICP and CPP thresholds are uncertain. Both the indication and the threshold for ICP (22 mmHg) are more expert- than evidence-based. PRx is used to find the patient’s own optimal CPP instead of a single common target.See
  • Muscle activity and myoclonus can drown out the frontal EEG. Stronger EMG is associated with a higher index, so look at the raw EEG, the EMG indicator and the patient. Myoclonus after cardiac arrest does not automatically mean a poor prognosis: about 9 % had a good outcome.See
  • EEG may warn of herniation before the clinical signs, but this has only been described in four patients. With full EEG over the whole head, the EEG changed 20 minutes to 1 hour before the clinical signs appeared. Both patients in one of the reports still died, so early warning has not been shown to improve outcome. Nobody has shown that a frontal monitor on the forehead picks up the same changes.Sources: two case reports. See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Same pattern, different prognosis: cause, reactivity and time decide

A coma pattern on the EEG says little on its own. The cause, whether the EEG responds to stimulation, and when the assessment is made matter more than the pattern itself.

  • The same pattern can lead to two very different outcomes. Almost every coma pattern occurs both in intoxication or sedation, usually reversible, and in hypoxic-ischaemic injury, usually not. Alpha coma from intoxication showed recovery in up to 90 %, whereas diffuse alpha coma in hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy had a mortality of over 90 %.Source: Sutter and Kaplan 2012
  • Reactivity appears to discriminate better than the pattern. An EEG that reacts to a noxious stimulus distinguishes the conditions better, and preserved reactivity favours a good outcome after anoxia. The underlying studies are small: in one, 10 of 11 with preserved reactivity regained consciousness. Reactivity was not standardised.Sources: Sutter and Kaplan 2012, Ko and Engelhard 2025, Thenayan 2010
  • Burst suppression is not always a bad sign. The sources disagree. Ko and Engelhard 2025 calls burst suppression, alpha coma and low-amplitude delta malignant patterns after anoxia, but without a reference and without distinguishing spontaneous from drug-induced burst suppression. In the table of Sutter and Kaplan, interrupted burst suppression from sedatives, anaesthetic agents or hypothermia usually has a favourable outcome. The most reliable predictor of not waking after anoxic coma is bilateral absence of N20.Sources: Ko and Engelhard 2025, Sutter and Kaplan 2012, Zandbergen 2006, Sandroni 2020
  • Wait, and exclude sedation. Prognosis after cardiac arrest is assessed no earlier than 72 hours after return of circulation, and residual sedation should always be considered. A poor outcome is regarded as likely only when two or more of six predictors are present. Electrocerebral inactivity requires a core temperature above 34 °C, because hypothermia can cause reversible inactivity.Sources: ERC-ESICM 2025, Sutter and Kaplan 2012
  • Caveats. The main source is a narrative review with many case reports from the 1980s. The table gives the most common outcome, not predictive values.Source: Sutter and Kaplan 2012

The studies in detail:

Sutter and Kaplan 2012 Ko and Engelhard 2025 ERC-ESICM 2025 Zandbergen 2006 Sandroni 2020

Blood flow, pressure and oxygen: EEG as one of several monitors

In the brain-injured patient, EEG is used together with ICP, CPP, PbtO2 and microdialysis to tailor treatment to the individual. Many of the thresholds are uncertain.Sources: Ko and Engelhard 2025, Lobo and Lamperti ch. 12

  • The EEG changes when blood flow falls. Normal cerebral blood flow is 50 ml/100 g/min. EEG slowing appears at 20 and an isoelectric EEG at 15. This is why EEG can be used as an ischaemia monitor. The figures have no separate reference in the textbook. Other sources give different thresholds (Foreman and Claassen, van Putten and Hofmeijer; see the Perfusion tab).Source: Ko and Engelhard 2025
  • The ICP threshold is more expert- than evidence-based. It has changed across four editions of the Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines and is now 22 mmHg. The optimal threshold varies between patients. The only randomised trial found no effect of ICP measurement on long-term outcome.Sources: Ko and Engelhard 2025, Lobo and Lamperti ch. 12, Chesnut 2012
  • Each patient has their own optimal CPP. PRx is the correlation between ICP and arterial pressure over time, and reflects autoregulation. It is used to find the patient's optimal CPP instead of a single common target of 60–70 mmHg.Sources: Ko and Engelhard 2025, Lobo and Lamperti ch. 12
  • Tissue oxygen sees what pressure does not. PbtO2 below 20 mmHg is seen in over 70 % of TBI patients in the first days, even with normal ICP and CPP. The measurement is focal, so the placement determines what is measured.Source: Lobo and Lamperti ch. 12
  • Unconscious patients should have continuous EEG to catch seizures. Non-convulsive seizures are frequent and cause ICP rises and metabolic crisis. Automatic seizure detection cannot replace an EEG-trained neurologist.Source: Ko and Engelhard 2025

The studies in detail:

Ko and Engelhard 2025 Lobo and Lamperti ch. 12 Chesnut 2012

What a frontal monitor can and cannot do in neurocritical care

A frontal monitor sees only a small part of the cortex and sits right on the forehead muscles. It has both possibilities and clear limits.

  • The EEG trend can change before the clinical signs, but this has only been shown in case reports with four patients in total. The QEEG changed from 20 minutes to about 1 hour before clinical signs of herniation. Both patients in one of the reports died, so the EEG did not change the outcome. Both reports used cEEG with regional and lateralised information, not a frontal monitor.Sources: Mullaguri 2020 and a similar report from 2021
  • Muscle can drown out the EEG. The frontalis muscle peaks around 30–40 Hz, and in sedated ICU patients without neuromuscular blockade, stronger EMG is associated with a higher BIS. Quantitative trends cannot be interpreted without the raw EEG, and changes should be confirmed by an EEG expert.Sources: Xin 2023, Herman 2015
  • Myoclonus after cardiac arrest does not automatically mean a poor prognosis. 18 % of 2,532 patients had myoclonus, and about 9 % of them had a good outcome. The EEG type distinguished between the groups, and the EEG should be recorded while the jerks are present. Treatment choices are the doctor's.Sources: Seder 2015, Elmer 2016, ERC-ESICM 2025
  • Few electrodes give a limited answer. Hairline montages found 54–72 % of the seizures that full EEG found. The author of the app suggests a frontal monitor as a trend monitor for change in the same patient, not for diagnosis. Suspicion should lead to clinical assessment, imaging and a full EEG (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Herman 2015

The studies in detail:

Mullaguri 2020 Xin 2023 Herman 2015 Seder 2015 Elmer 2016 ERC-ESICM 2025

EEG patterns in coma: same pattern, different prognosis (Sutter and Kaplan 2012)

Review article from Johns Hopkins (Epileptologie 2012;29:201–209), built on Husain's classification. The main point is that almost every coma pattern occurs both in intoxication or sedation (usually reversible) and in hypoxic-ischaemic injury (usually not), and that reactivity to a noxious stimulus discriminates better than the pattern itself.

PatternTypical causesReactivity*Most common outcome
Beta coma (12–16 Hz, frontal)Intoxication or withdrawal (barbiturates, benzodiazepines), severe hyperthyroidism+ / −Favourable
Brainstem lesion−Unfavourable
Alpha coma (8–13 Hz), diffuseIntoxication (barbiturates, benzodiazepines, anaesthetic agents)+Favourable (recovery in up to 90%)
Monomorphic, posteriorBrainstem lesion, locked-in+ / −Unfavourable
DiffuseHypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy(+) / −Unfavourable (mortality over 90%)
Theta coma (4–7 Hz)Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, mild to moderate metabolic encephalopathy, severe systemic infection(+) / −Unfavourable
High-voltage delta coma (1–3 Hz), anterior or focalMetabolic encephalopathy, focal white matter lesion+Favourable
DiffuseSevere metabolic encephalopathy, encephalitis, vasculitis, large white matter lesions, markedly raised ICP(+) / −Unfavourable
Spindle coma (theta/delta with symmetrical spindles up to 14 Hz)TBI, intracerebral haemorrhage, postictal, intoxication+Favourable
Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, severe TBI, large haemorrhage(+) / −Unfavourable
Burst suppression, interruptedIntoxication (sedatives), anaesthetic agents, hypothermia+ / (−)Favourable
UninterruptedHypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, severe intoxication(+) / − (disputed)Unfavourable
Low-voltage delta coma (below 20 µV) with alpha/beta componentsTBI, healthy individuals+Favourable
Without faster componentsHypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, severe TBI(+) / −Unfavourable
Electrocerebral inactivity (below 2 µV)Marked hypothermia, severe intoxication with CNS depressants−Favourable
Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy−Unfavourable

* Reactivity to a noxious stimulus: + preserved, − absent, (+) partial. Translated and abridged from table 2 in the article.

  • Burst suppression: in deeper coma the proportion of bursts decreases, and the suppression can become continuous. Hypoxic-ischaemic injury, sedatives, anaesthetic agents and hypothermia are the main causes “that determine the outcome”. It is unresolved whether a burst suppression pattern that is interrupted by stimulation means a better outcome.
  • Reactivity after cardiac arrest: absent reactivity during hypothermia gave 0–7% false positives for poor outcome, and 10 of 11 with preserved reactivity regained consciousness. The studies are small and prospective.Sources: Rossetti 2010 and 2012, Thenayan 2010 (table 1 in the article)
  • Electrocerebral inactivity: requires below 2 µV with double electrode spacing, core temperature above 34 °C and at least 30 minutes, without response to intense stimulation. Hypothermia must be excluded because it can cause reversible inactivity.
  • Historical: progressive EEG slowing with increasing depth of anaesthesia (figure 1) is the same continuum as in the Spectrogram tab.Source: Sutter and Kaplan 2012, figure 1
  • Caveats: narrative review without a systematic search, many of the sources are case reports from the 1980s, and the table gives “most common outcome”, not predictive values. Reactivity was not standardised (see Taccone 2026). The article is from 2012, before the ACNS 2021 terminology and before Forgacs 2020 on burst suppression with theta in the bursts. No relevant conflicts of interest declared.
Sutter and Kaplan. Epileptologie 2012;29:201–209

Myoclonus and EMG drowning out the frontal EEG, especially after cardiac arrest

In intensive care, muscle activity is often stronger than the EEG signal on the forehead, and the index and spectrogram then mostly show muscle. After cardiac arrest, myoclonus comes on top of this. Below is why, what it means and what can be done. Treatment choices are the doctor's.

  • A frontal EEG sits right on the muscles. Muscle activity has a bandwidth of 20–300 Hz. The frontalis muscle peaks around 30–40 Hz and the temporal muscle around 40–80 Hz, and the contamination is greatest at the edges of the electrode montage. In volunteers who were paralysed, power at 40 Hz was about 5 times and at 80 Hz about 10 times higher without paralysis.Source: Muthukumaraswamy 2013
  • The EEG index cannot be read alone when EMG is high. BIS uses, among other things, 30–47 Hz in its calculation, and the EMG indicator 70–110 Hz. In sedated ICU patients without a neuromuscular blocker, stronger EMG is associated with a higher BIS. The reverse also holds: in awake volunteers given a neuromuscular blocker, BIS fell to 44–47.Sources: Xin 2023, Schuller 2015
  • Myoclonus after cardiac arrest is not in itself a sign of futility. In an international registry, 18% of 2,532 patients had myoclonus, and about 9% of them had a good outcome at discharge.Source: Seder 2015
  • The EEG type separates myoclonus with a very poor and a better prognosis. Of 69 patients with early myoclonus, 74% had burst suppression with myoclonus time-locked to the bursts, and none of them had a good outcome. A smaller group (12%) had a different EEG type, and half of them woke up with a good outcome after 1–2 weeks of coma. In early Lance-Adams syndrome (1.5%) the EEG is reactive, and the patients woke after 3–23 days. This is why the EEG should be recorded while the jerks are present.Sources: Elmer 2016, Aicua Rapun 2017, ERC-ESICM 2025

What can be done

  • 1. Check the signal: impedance under 10 kΩ and good skin preparation. Look at the raw EEG and the EMG indicator, and look at the patient: if the peaks coincide with the jerks, it is muscle or myoclonus.Sources: ACNS, Herman 2015
  • 2. Do not trust the trend alone: quantitative EEG trends cannot be interpreted without the raw EEG, and changes should be confirmed by an EEG expert before treatment is changed.Source: Herman 2015
  • 3. Use filters with care: filters can remove muscle artefact, but fast activity is lost too. In one patient an asymmetric burst suppression was missed because of filtering.Source: Newey 2017
  • 4. Treat the myoclonus (the doctor's decision): first line is levetiracetam or sodium valproate in addition to sedation. A higher dose of propofol or a benzodiazepine can be considered to suppress myoclonus and electrographic seizures. In Lance-Adams, aggressive treatment can confound the clinical examination and lead to an overly pessimistic prognosis.Source: ERC-ESICM 2025
  • 5. Neuromuscular blockade only as a deliberate test: in 12 patients with myoclonus after cardiac arrest, cisatracurium improved the EEG in 9. It revealed underlying patterns such as burst suppression and periodic discharges, and seizures in 3. But the guideline advises against routine neuromuscular blockade in comatose post-arrest patients, and it interferes with the clinical examination. It should therefore be a time-limited test decided by the doctor, with sedation and ventilation (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Newey 2017, ERC-ESICM 2025
  • 6. Shivering during temperature control: shivering is a common seizure mimic. It can be managed with opioids and sedation, and neuromuscular blockade may be considered for severe shivering. Shivering can be assessed with a simple four-point scale (BSAS).Sources: ERC-ESICM 2021, Badjatia 2012, Olson 2013
  • 7. Ask for a full EEG: with few electrodes, interpretation is limited. Hairline montages found 54–72% of the seizures that full EEG found. When in doubt, full EEG is the answer.Source: Herman 2015

Prognosis

  • Wait and exclude sedation: prognosis is assessed no earlier than 72 hours after return of circulation, in patients who have not woken up, and residual sedation should always be considered. No single predictor is 100% accurate, and a poor outcome is considered likely only when two or more of six predictors are present. Status myoclonus (continuous generalised myoclonus for 30 minutes or more) is one of them.Source: ERC-ESICM 2025
  • Myoclonus alone does not decide: in patients with rhythmic or periodic patterns, myoclonus could not predict a poor outcome without false positives.Source: Nutma 2023
ERC-ESICM 2021 and 2025 Muthukumaraswamy 2013 Xin 2023 Schuller 2015 Seder 2015 Elmer 2016 Newey 2017 Herman 2015 (ACNS) Nutma 2023
The studies in detail: invasive neuromonitoring, neurocritical care (Ko and Engelhard 2025) and herniation (3 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Invasive neuromonitoring in intensive care: ICP, PRx, PbtO2 and microdialysis (Lobo and Lamperti, ch. 12)

The chapter (Pusateri and Robba) deals with the brain-injured patient and supplements the EEG material in the Perfusion tab.

  • ICP: normally 5–15 mmHg when supine. The Brain Trauma Foundation has changed the treatment threshold across four editions (20, 20–25, 20 and most recently 22 mmHg), and the chapter stresses that the optimal threshold is uncertain: below 20 may be harmful for some, above the threshold may be tolerated by others. Indication for invasive measurement in severe TBI (GCS 3–8) with abnormal CT, or normal CT with two of: age over 40, motor posturing, systolic BP below 90.
  • PRx: the correlation coefficient between ICP and MAP over time, as a measure of pressure autoregulation. Negative PRx means good cerebrovascular reserve, around 0 a compensated phase, positive PRx poor reserve. Used to find the patient's optimal CPP (CPPopt) instead of a single common target (BTF recommends 60–70 mmHg).
  • PbtO2: tissue oxygen measured with a probe in white matter; normally 20–35 mmHg, below 20 compromised, below 15 brain hypoxia. Below 20 mmHg is seen in over 70% of TBI patients in the first days even with normal ICP and CPP. Focal measurement, so the placement determines what is measured.
  • Microdialysis: glucose, lactate, pyruvate, glycerol and glutamate from the interstitium. The lactate/pyruvate ratio (normally 15–20) rises with anaerobic metabolism; low glucose, high LPR, high glutamate and glycerol suggest ischaemia or secondary injury.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 12

Neurointensive care: CBF thresholds, CPP, ICP and EEG as prognosis (Ko and Engelhard 2025)

The chapter “Neurocritical Care” (Ko and Engelhard) deals with the brain-injured intensive care patient. What concerns EEG, sedation and perfusion is collected here; the rest (SAH, stroke, neuromuscular disease, brain death) is omitted.

  • Functional CBF thresholds (table 80.5): normal CBF 50 ml/100 g/min, EEG slowing at 20, isoelectric EEG at 15, ischaemic penumbra 6–15, neuronal death below 6. The table has no separate reference in the chapter. This is the background for using EEG as an ischaemia monitor (see van Putten and Hofmeijer and Foreman and Claassen in the Perfusion tab).
  • CPP: MAP minus ICP, with the zero point for MAP at the external auditory meatus (the same reference Kalmar 2010 used). Recommended 60–70 mmHg after TBI; both higher and lower worsen outcome, and CPP above 90 mmHg with fluids and pressors increases the risk of respiratory failure. The chapter points out that measures that lower ICP, such as head elevation and barbiturate coma, also lower MAP and can thereby lower CPP. Individual CPPopt (Aries 2012, Petkus 2020) is mentioned as an alternative to a single common target.
  • ICP: threshold 22 mmHg (BTF 2017, Carney), but the chapter states outright that both indication and threshold are more expert- than evidence-based. The only randomised trial (Chesnut 2012, BEST-TRIP) found no effect of ICP measurement on long-term outcome, while an observational study from 146 ICUs suggested lower 6-month mortality. Time above threshold counts: ICP 20 mmHg for over 37 minutes worsened outcome, shorter episodes did not (Güiza 2015), and impaired autoregulation or CPP below 50 makes the patient less tolerant of high ICP.
  • Autoregulation: PRx (correlation of ICP against arterial pressure, −1 to +1) is the established continuous measure, but TCD velocity, PbtO2 or NIRS can be used instead of ICP to calculate an autoregulation index. Absent autoregulation is more often associated with poor outcome.
  • Oxygenation: SjvO2 normally 55–75%, both below 50 and above 75 are associated with poor outcome, but the method is on its way out. PbtO2 normally 20–45 mmHg, below 15–20 is regarded as ischaemia, below 10 severe ischaemia; treatment guided by ICP, CPP and PbtO2 above 20 was better than ICP and CPP alone (Lin 2015, Spiotta 2010, Nangunoori 2012). NIRS normally 60–75%, but low sensitivity for isolated cerebral hypoperfusion in TBI and SAH, good as a trend monitor during systemic changes (cardiac surgery).
  • Continuous EEG in neurointensive care: in unconscious patients EEG should be used continuously to detect non-convulsive seizures, which are frequent and cause ICP rises and metabolic crisis (Vespa 2007; ESICM consensus, Claassen 2013). Automatic seizure detection has many false positives and negatives and cannot replace an EEG-trained neurologist (Schramm 2017). The chapter mentions that pEEG monitors for depth of anaesthesia use the same frequencies.
  • EEG as prognosis after anoxia: burst suppression, alpha coma and low-voltage delta are called malignant patterns associated with poor outcome, while preserved EEG reactivity favours good outcome. The sentence stands without a reference in the chapter. Bilateral absence of N20 (SSEP after median nerve stimulation) is the most reliable predictor of not waking after anoxic coma (Zandbergen 2006, Sandroni 2020). Note that Forgacs 2020 and Jegarl 2026 (Burst suppression tab) describe burst suppression after cardiac arrest as a pattern that can progress to good consciousness; the chapter uses the term without distinguishing between spontaneous and drug-induced burst suppression.
  • Sedation in TBI: agents with a short context-sensitive half-time (propofol) to allow daily neurological examination, with a warning about propofol infusion syndrome at high doses over several days (Cremer 2001). Barbiturates and benzodiazepines have long half-lives and are less suitable; barbiturate treatment for refractory ICP “under EEG monitoring” appears as item 8 in the checklist (box 80.2), after sedation, CSF drainage and osmotherapy. High-dose propofol, prophylactic hyperventilation (PaCO2 below 30), steroids and therapeutic hypothermia are on the list of measures that are not recommended. Ketamine is no longer regarded as contraindicated in intubated and ventilated TBI patients (Kolenda 1997). Targets: PaO2 80–120 and PaCO2 35–38 mmHg.
  • Status epilepticus: third line is midazolam or propofol infusion, possibly thiopental or pentobarbital; in super-refractory status, volatile anaesthetics and ketamine are mentioned. Continuous EEG is recommended to guide treatment and to detect non-convulsive seizures in comatose patients, and prolonged neuromuscular blockade should be avoided because it masks seizures. See the card on ketamine in refractory status epilepticus in the Agents tab.
  • Multimodal monitoring: ICP, autoregulation, PbtO2, continuous EEG and microdialysis together to individualise treatment; the chapter stresses that clinical neurophysiology only describes current function and cannot predict complications.
Ko and Engelhard 2025 (Miller's Anesthesia, 10th ed.)

Can an EEG trend warn of herniation? Two case reports (Mullaguri 2020)

Mullaguri, Beary and Newey (BMC Neurol 2020;20:406, doi 10.1186/s12883-020-01988-7). A case report of two non-traumatic intensive care patients with continuous EEG (cEEG) and quantitative EEG (QEEG).

  • Patient 1: multiorgan failure and an intracerebral haemorrhage that expanded (coagulopathy). cEEG showed increasing regional or lateralised slowing. QEEG showed lower frequencies, increasing asymmetry, falling amplitude and a rising burst suppression ratio, up to 2 hours before burst suppression. The abstract states that the cEEG changes came up to 1 hour before the clinical changes.
  • Patient 2: a 76-year-old with intraventricular haemorrhage and worsening obstructive hydrocephalus. QEEG showed loss of rhythmicity, increasing asymmetry, falling amplitude and a rising burst suppression ratio 20 minutes before the clinical change (fixed, dilated pupils and loss of brainstem reflexes).
  • Outcome: both died, and the EEG monitoring did not change the outcome.
  • What the article refers to (cited, not assessed here): a relationship between EEG frequency and cerebral perfusion pressure, a negative correlation between delta power and ICP in 62 patients (Chen), and generalised rhythmic delta with attenuation of fast activity up to 24 hours before clinical changes (Sheikh 2020).
  • A similar report from 2021: “Early detection of cerebral herniation by continuous electroencephalography and quantitative analysis” describes two patients: unilateral cerebral oedema with uncal herniation (asymmetric changes) and diffuse oedema with transtentorial herniation (symmetric changes). The changes were detected about 1 hour before clinical changes. The authors suggest QEEG can be used as surveillance by ICU staff without EEG training.
  • Caveats: case reports only. Retrospective, very small, and only non-traumatic patients. No effect on outcome has been shown, and the authors call for larger studies. Both reports used cEEG with regional and lateralised information, not a frontal monitor.
  • Suggestion from the author of the app: a frontal monitor on neurological patients can be used as a trend monitor for change in the same patient, not for diagnosis, and to document whether the patient gets physiological sleep. The sources do not show that a frontal monitor detects herniation. Four frontal channels do not see focal or lateralised changes elsewhere, so suspicion should lead to clinical assessment, imaging and a full EEG. Herniation is otherwise followed with clinical examination, pupils, ICP and imaging (interpretation based on the sources).
Mullaguri et al. BMC Neurol 2020;20:406 Early detection of cerebral herniation by continuous electroencephalography and quantitative analysis (2021)

Key points

  • Sedation is not sleep. According to Akeju and Brown, neither anaesthetic drugs nor sleep medications produce physiological sleep. A sedation EEG with alpha–delta or burst suppression is not sleep, even when the patient lies still with closed eyes.See
  • Sleep in intensive care is severely disrupted. During sedation and mechanical ventilation, deep NREM, REM and circadian rhythm are greatly reduced or abolished. About half of sleep occurs during the day.See
  • Outcomes were worse without REM sleep, but the direction is unclear. REM was absent in half, and they more often had a poor outcome (24 % versus 9 %). That is an association, not a cause. The idea that the brain clears waste during sleep comes from mice.Source: Marchasson 2024. See
  • Light sedation is supported, no sedation has not been shown to be better. Mortality did not differ without sedation, and no sedation required more staff. α2 agonists did not give faster extubation.Sources: NONSEDA, Strøm 2010, A2B. See
  • Movement does not necessarily mean too little hypnotic. Hypnotics must be given at very high doses to prevent movement, pain should be treated first, and deep sedation can increase asynchrony. If the EEG shows the patient is already deeply sedated, something else needs treating (interpretation based on the sources).See
  • General EEG slowing does not identify delirium. It was burst suppression, rhythmic or periodic patterns and seizures that distinguished the delirious, not dominant frequency or amplitude.See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Sedation is not sleep

The sleep stages, and what they resemble under anaesthesia

The app states in several places that sedation and anaesthesia are not sleep. These are the stages being compared, and what they actually resemble in the EEG. Sleep goes from N1 to N2 to N3 and on to REM, and the cycle repeats roughly every 90 to 120 minutes.Source: Akeju and Brown 2017

StageEEG featuresWhat it resembles under anaesthesia
N1Alpha over the back of the head, which belongs to relaxed wakefulness, disappears, and beta power (13–25 Hz) falls. What remains is low-amplitude, mixed-frequency activity, predominantly 4–7 Hz, that is theta. Slow eye movements and vertex sharp waves also belong to the stage.The same happens early in induction: occipital alpha disappears. Under anaesthesia, coherent alpha also appears over the forehead, that is anteriorisation.
N2Slow-delta, K-complexes and sleep spindles. The K-complex is a well-delineated negative sharp wave immediately followed by a positive component standing out from the background, reflecting reduced cortical activity. The spindles arise from rebound bursting in thalamocortical neurons. The AASM gives spindles as 11–16 Hz, most commonly 12–14 Hz, lasting at least 0.5 seconds; Akeju and Brown write 12–16 Hz.Dexmedetomidine produces slow-delta and spindles that, according to the source, very closely approximate N2. It is the closest resemblance between a sedative and physiological sleep.
N3Slow-delta dominates, with larger amplitude than the slow oscillations of N2. They result from profound hyperpolarisation of the cortex and thalamus. The stage is scored when at least 20 % of the epoch consists of 0.5–2 Hz activity with amplitude above 75 µV over the frontal regions.Propofol and the inhalational agents also produce slow-delta, but the waves behave differently: in sleep they are synchronous with brief pauses in neuronal activity, under propofol asynchronous with prolonged pauses.
REMAn activated EEG of mixed frequencies, without K-complexes and without spindles, and without the awake-state alpha. Saw-tooth waves are trains of sharply contoured or triangular, often serrated, 2–6 Hz waves maximal over the central regions. Low chin muscle tone and rapid eye movements belong to the stage.None of the agents in the sources produces a REM-like pattern. Opioids suppress REM sleep.
  • Why it is not the same. Anaesthesia is a deeper state than sleep. The drugs act not only on the arousal nuclei of the brainstem but also on the thalamus and the cortex, which is why sensory, memory and cognitive circuits are affected as well.Source: Akeju and Brown 2017
  • The dose continues where sleep stops. The amplitude of slow-delta under anaesthesia increases with dose until it plateaus. Increase the dose further and burst suppression follows, and finally an isoelectric EEG. There is no equivalent in physiological sleep.Source: Akeju and Brown 2017
  • The authors' conclusion. “We conclude that the principal anesthetic drugs and sleep medications do not produce physiological sleep.” They allow a possible exception for dexmedetomidine.Source: Akeju and Brown 2017
Akeju and Brown 2017 AASM 2012

Sedation is not sleep, and sleep in intensive care is disrupted

Brown, Lydic and Schiff write that general anaesthesia is “in fact a reversible drug-induced coma”, and that the word “sleep” is used to avoid worrying patients. The difference is also visible on the EEG, and intensive care patients get little true sleep.Source: Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010

  • The EEG separates sedation from sleep. According to Akeju and Brown, burst suppression and isoelectric EEG do not occur in normal sleep. GABAergic alpha lies in the same frequency range as sleep spindles but lacks the spindles’ shape. Dexmedetomidine produces spindles and slow waves resembling N2, but K-complexes have not been described. The patterns look alike, but they differ.Sources: Akeju and Brown 2017, Eikermann et al. 2025
  • The drugs alter sleep architecture. Propofol suppresses slow-wave sleep. Benzodiazepines reduce both slow-wave sleep and REM. Opioids suppress both, more so at higher doses. In long-term ventilated patients, propofol sedation abolishes REM.Sources: Telias and Wilcox 2019, Kondili 2012
  • Propofol at night has not been shown to improve sleep. A Cochrane review found only four small randomised trials with a total of 149 ICU patients, using different comparisons and measurement tools. The evidence was of very low quality and insufficient to say whether propofol improves sleep quality or quantity.Source: Lewis 2018 (Cochrane)
  • ICU sleep is fragmented. During sedation and mechanical ventilation, deep NREM, REM and circadian rhythm are severely reduced or abolished, and about half of sleep occurs during the day. In up to 70 % of sedated or ventilated patients the EEG does not fit standard sleep criteria, but the figure comes from a single study. Even in non-sedated intensive care patients, REM was completely absent in half.Sources: Eikermann et al. 2025, Marchasson 2024
  • Under continuous sedation, the organisation of sleep disappears. In 21 ventilated medical ICU patients on continuous intravenous sedation, polysomnography was recorded for a total of about 820 hours. Only 2 of 21 had REM sleep. Slow-wave activity lacked its normal diurnal rhythm and cycling through the night, and the EEG was equally slow by day and night. The melatonin rhythm was preserved in 13 of 16, but only 4 had normal timing. The authors describe an abnormal state bearing little resemblance to either sleep or wakefulness.Source: Gehlbach 2012
  • Natural sleep is also regulated by the brain’s support cells. In mice, calcium signals in astrocytes fell sharply during sleep and rose just before waking from deep sleep, often before the ECoG and EMG showed that the mouse was waking. When an important astrocytic calcium pathway was switched off, deep sleep became fragmented, with more microarousals, lower delta power and more sleep spindles. The authors stress that anaesthesia resembles sleep in behaviour but is fundamentally different from natural sleep, lacking among other things awakenings and the natural cycling between sleep stages.Source: Bojarskaite et al. 2020 (animal study)
  • The EEG can show whether it is sedation or sleep. A sedation EEG with alpha–delta or burst suppression is not sleep, even if the patient lies still with eyes closed. The spectrogram can show whether the patient is in a drug-induced state or in sleep with spindles and cyclic alternation. Only polysomnography determines sleep stage precisely.Source: Eikermann et al. 2025

The studies in detail:

Brown 2010 Akeju and Brown 2017 Telias and Wilcox 2019 Eikermann et al. 2025 Kondili 2012 Bojarskaite 2020

Lost sleep, REM and delirium: associations, not proof

Lost sleep is linked to poorer brain function and a worse course. Almost all the findings, however, come from mice, healthy volunteers or observational studies.

  • Sleep appears to be important for the brain. In mice the interstitial space increased by about 60 % in both natural sleep and anaesthesia, and β-amyloid was cleared faster. In healthy adults, β-amyloid increased by about 5 % after a night without sleep. At 6 hours in bed or less, cognitive impairment built up gradually, without participants noticing how impaired they were.Sources: Xie 2013, Shokri-Kojori 2018, Van Dongen 2003
  • Little REM is linked to a worse course and delirium. Non-sedated intensive care patients without REM (66 of 131) more often had a poor outcome (24 % versus 9 %). GABA agonists are linked to deeper sedation, less REM and more neurocognitive disorders, but this comes from a retrospective cohort.Sources: Marchasson 2024, Azimaraghi 2022
  • The direction is unclear. Sleep loss is regarded as a potentially modifiable risk factor for delirium. But delirium also disturbs sleep, and they may share pathophysiology. Sleep-promoting agents can themselves increase the risk of delirium.Sources: Telias and Wilcox 2019, Eikermann et al. 2025
  • Caveats. The finding on waste clearance in the brain comes from mice, and it has not been shown that sedation has the same effect in intensive care patients. The REM study is small, single-centre and of non-sedated patients, and shows an association, not a cause.Sources: Xie 2013, Marchasson 2024

The studies in detail:

Xie 2013 Shokri-Kojori 2018 Van Dongen 2003 Marchasson 2024 Azimaraghi 2022

How light should sedation be?

The goal of sedation in intensive care is safe ventilator treatment with as little drug as possible. Light sedation is supported, but no sedation has not been shown to be better.Sources: PADIS 2018, Rasulo 2023

  • Light sedation is suggested over deep. The guideline suggests light rather than deep sedation (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). Prolonged deep sedation (RASS ≤ −3) is linked to longer ICU and hospital stays, and to delirium.Sources: PADIS (Devlin 2018), Eikermann et al. 2025
  • No sedation has both benefits and drawbacks. In a small single-unit study (140 patients), no sedation gave more ventilator-free days, but more delirium (20 % versus 7 %) and more often a need for extra staffing (20 % versus 5 %). In a larger study (700 patients), there was no significant difference in 90-day mortality. There, 27 % of the no-sedation group still received sedation within 24 hours, most often because of agitation.Sources: Strøm 2010, NONSEDA (Olsen 2020)
  • α2 agonists are no shortcut. Neither dexmedetomidine nor clonidine gave faster extubation than propofol. Agitation and severe bradycardia were more frequent.Source: A2B (Walsh 2025)
  • Staffing matters. The no-sedation study was done in a unit with 1:1 nursing, and NONSEDA did not measure nurses’ workload. Reflection from the author of the app: the patient was sometimes sedated because he could not be managed awake. Interpretation based on the sources: the goal is as light as is safe and manageable with the staffing the unit has, and the EEG can show whether the patient is sedated deeper than necessary.Sources: Strøm 2010, NONSEDA

The studies in detail:

Devlin 2018 Strøm 2010 NONSEDA (Olsen 2020) Walsh 2025 Eikermann et al. 2025

Agitation, delirium and asynchrony: what the EEG can and cannot tell

When the patient is agitated or delirious, it is tempting to increase the hypnotic. The EEG can show whether the patient is already deeply sedated, but cannot make the diagnosis.

  • General slowing does not identify delirium. In ventilated patients with new-onset altered consciousness, it was burst suppression, rhythmic or periodic patterns and seizures that distinguished the delirious from the others. Dominant frequency and amplitude did not. The study was small (91 patients), and the EEG was mostly recorded while delirium was already present.Source: Eskioglou 2021
  • Hypnotics alone often do not prevent movement at usual doses. Midazolam alone cannot abolish movement in response to painful stimuli. Propofol alone must reach 15–16 µg/ml to prevent movement at incision (Vuyk et al. 2025 gives 16), whereas burst suppression occurs at about 5 µg/ml (Sleigh et al. 2025). Vuyk et al. 2025 gives over 8 µg/ml with rapid infusion. According to PADIS, pain should be treated before a sedative is considered.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, PADIS (Devlin 2018)
  • Deep sedation can increase asynchrony. Ineffective triggering rose from 7.6 % under light to 21.8 % under deep propofol sedation, in a small study (14 patients). In reverse triggering, increasing sedation is not suggested.Sources: Vaschetto 2014, Saavedra 2022
  • Interpretation based on the sources. If the EEG shows that the patient is already deeply sedated, movement and fighting the ventilator are a sign that something other than hypnosis needs treating: pain, discomfort, ventilation or surroundings.

The studies in detail:

Eskioglou 2021 Hendrickx 2008 Devlin 2018 Vaschetto 2014 Saavedra 2022

How light should sedation be? NONSEDA, Strøm and workload

The goal of sedation in intensive care is safe ventilator treatment with as little drug as possible. Light rather than deep sedation is suggested (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). Two randomised trials have examined how far down one can go.Sources: PADIS 2018, Rasulo 2023

  • No sedation gave more ventilator-free days, but more delirium and more need for staff. The trial randomised 140 patients in one unit in Denmark. No sedation gave more ventilator-free days (13.8 versus 9.6; difference 4.2 days, 95 % CI 0.3–8.1) and a shorter intensive care stay. Delirium was more frequent without sedation (20 % versus 7 %), and 20 % versus 5 % needed extra staffing. Caveats: the unit had 1:1 nursing and an intensivist present at all times, only about a third of those assessed were randomised, the study was not blinded, and 18 % in the no-sedation group still received continuous sedation.Source: Strøm 2010 (Lancet 375:475–480)
  • No sedation gave no significant difference in mortality. The trial had 700 patients in 8 units in Denmark, Norway and Sweden. 90-day mortality was 42.4 % without sedation and 37.0 % with light sedation (difference 5.4 percentage points, 95 % CI −2.2 to 12.2; p = 0.65). 27 % of the no-sedation group received sedation within 24 hours, most often because of agitation. Reintubation after accidental extubation was more frequent without sedation (8.9 % versus 4 %).
