Days free of coma or delirium and days in intensive care were similar.Source: NONSEDA (Olsen et al., N Engl J Med 2020)
  • NONSEDA has important caveats. The groups differed by only about one RASS point, and the study was not blinded. It did not measure nurses' workload or psychological after-effects. The result may not apply to units without 1:1 nursing.
  • α2 agonists did not give faster extubation. Dexmedetomidine and clonidine gave neither faster extubation than propofol nor less restlessness. Agitation was more frequent (see “Movement and fighting the ventilator”).Source: A2B (Walsh 2025)
  • Reflection from the author of the app (experience from cardiac postoperative care): the doctors wanted the patients as light as possible, preferably awake. For the nurses it was sometimes difficult and unpredictable, and the patient was sedated because he could not be managed awake. This fits with agitation being the most common reason for sedation in NONSEDA, and with no sedation requiring more staff in Strøm.
  • Interpretation based on the sources: light sedation is supported, but no sedation has not been shown to be better. The goal is as light as is safe for the patient and possible to manage with the staffing the unit has. The EEG can show whether the patient is sedated deeper than necessary (alpha–delta, burst suppression), but is not in itself an argument for no sedation.
Strøm et al. Lancet 2010;375:475–480 Olsen et al. N Engl J Med 2020 (NONSEDA) Devlin 2018 (PADIS) Walsh 2025 (A2B)

Movement and fighting the ventilator: less stress before more hypnotic

Suggestion from the author of the app: when an intensive care patient moves or fights the ventilator, one should look for the cause and reduce stress before increasing the hypnotic dose. These are the individual measures:

  • Hypnotics often do not prevent movement well. Midazolam alone cannot abolish movement in response to painful stimuli. Propofol alone must reach 15–16 µg/ml before movement at incision is prevented (Vuyk et al. 2025 gives 16), whereas burst suppression occurs at about 5 µg/ml (Sleigh et al. 2025). Vuyk et al. 2025 gives over 8 µg/ml with rapid infusion. Immobility appears to arise mainly in the spinal cord (see the Components tab). Increasing the hypnotic until the patient lies still can therefore give very deep hypnosis.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, Vuyk et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025
  • Treat pain first. According to PADIS, pain should be treated before a sedative is considered (good practice statement). Pain and sedation should be managed step by step, guided by assessment and a protocol (conditional recommendation, moderate evidence).Source: PADIS 2018
  • Less light and noise. Strategies that reduce noise and light are suggested to improve sleep (conditional, low evidence).Source: PADIS 2018
  • Ventilator settings. Assist-control ventilation at night is suggested rather than pressure support to improve sleep (conditional, low evidence). The guideline makes no recommendation on adaptive modes. Whether fighting the ventilator is best solved with other settings is not covered in the sources here.Source: PADIS 2018
  • Check for a full bladder. Acute urinary retention has been described as a cause of delirium in older people (“cystocerebral syndrome”). The proposed mechanism is increased adrenergic activity when the bladder cannot be emptied. The evidence is weak, but it is a simple thing to check.Source: Ble 2001 (case report and literature review)
  • α2 agonists are not the answer to agitation in themselves. In 1404 ventilated patients in 41 UK intensive care units, neither dexmedetomidine nor clonidine gave faster extubation than propofol. Agitation was more frequent with dexmedetomidine (RR 1.54) and clonidine (RR 1.55), as was severe bradycardia (RR 1.62 and 1.58).Source: A2B (Walsh 2025)
  • Interpretation based on the sources: if the EEG shows that the patient is already deeply sedated, movement and fighting the ventilator are a sign that something other than hypnosis needs treating: pain, discomfort, ventilation or surroundings.
Suggestion from the author of the app Devlin 2018 (PADIS), Hendrickx 2008, Vuyk et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025, Ble 2001, Walsh 2025 (A2B)

What can be done to help the patient cooperate with the ventilator?

When patient and ventilator are out of step, it is called asynchrony: a mismatch between what the patient demands and what the ventilator delivers. Asynchrony is associated with worse outcomes. The first step is to identify the type, because the measures differ.Source: Saavedra 2022

  • The patient tries but the ventilator does not respond (ineffective triggering): possible causes are an insensitive trigger setting, long inspiratory time, weak drive, inadequate PEEP and auto-PEEP. Measures are adjusting the trigger, shortening inspiratory time, reducing pressure support and titrating PEEP.
  • Air hunger (insufficient flow): often with low flow or low tidal volume, or high drive from agitation, pain or fever. Measures are more flow or tidal volume, shorter rise time, or switching to pressure support.
  • Double triggering (two breaths stacked): with low tidal volume, insufficient flow, high drive or short inspiratory time. Measures are larger tidal volume, more flow or longer inspiratory time, and optimal analgesia and sedation. Neuromuscular blockade can be considered when strict lung-protective ventilation is needed.
  • Premature or late cycling: the ventilator's inspiratory time does not match the patient's own. The measure is to match the mechanical inspiratory time to the patient's.
  • Reverse triggering: the patient's diaphragm contracts in response to a ventilator breath. Increasing sedation is not suggested as treatment. A lower respiratory rate or a somewhat higher tidal volume has helped, and neuromuscular blockade gave only temporary improvement.
  • Deep sedation can increase asynchrony. In a small study (14 patients) the proportion of ineffective triggering during pressure support rose from 7.6 % with light propofol sedation to 21.8 % with deep sedation (about 2.5 µg/ml). With NAVA, where the ventilator is driven by the electrical activity of the diaphragm, it was 0 % regardless of depth.Source: Vaschetto 2014
  • Spontaneous modes can help. Patients who do not need deep sedation may benefit from a spontaneous mode.Source: Saavedra 2022
  • Interpretation based on the sources, step by step: (1) look at the pressure and flow curves and identify the type of asynchrony; (2) adjust the ventilator for that type; (3) treat what increases the drive: pain, fever, agitation, discomfort and surroundings (see the card above); (4) review the depth of sedation, and use the EEG to see whether the patient is already deeply sedated. More hypnotic can make asynchrony worse.
Saavedra 2022, Vaschetto 2014

What happens in the brain in delirium

There is no single mechanism. The review in Nature Reviews Disease Primers describes several pathways that can lead to the same clinical picture, and frames it this way: delirium is a failure of the vulnerable brain to show resilience in response to an acute stressor. The more cognitive impairment there is beforehand, the less it takes. That is why the same operation causes delirium in one patient and not another.

  1. Inflammation outside, striking inwards. Peripheral inflammation is a well-established trigger. Signalling molecules such as IL-1β and TNF act on brain cells, and in animal models microglia already primed by neurodegeneration are exaggeratedly quick to produce IL-1 in response to acute systemic inflammation. But the decisive point is this: inflammatory markers rise in everyone with sepsis, trauma or surgery, not only in those who become delirious. It is the prior vulnerability, not the inflammation alone, that appears to decide who is affected.Source: Wilson et al. 2020
  2. Norwegian research has found the traces in the cerebrospinal fluid. Watne et al. examined the kynurenine pathway in 586 participants at four hospitals in the Oslo region: 450 hip fracture patients, 24 with medical delirium and 112 cognitively unimpaired adults for elective surgery. Quinolinic acid, a breakdown product of tryptophan that acts on the NMDA receptor, was the single factor most strongly associated with delirium: median 41 nmol/l in hip fracture patients without delirium, against 69 with delirium and 84 in medical delirium (OR 2.26, 95% CI 1.78 to 2.87). The level was also associated with neurofilament light chain, that is with actual neuronal injury, and most strongly in those with prior cognitive impairment. And it predicted death: of the 450, 99 died within the first year, and quinolinic acid above 100 nmol/l gave a hazard ratio of 4.35 (2.93 to 6.45) unadjusted, 1.76 (1.32 to 2.33) per standard deviation after adjustment. Their interpretation is that systemic inflammation activates the enzyme IDO, which shifts tryptophan metabolism towards the neurotoxic branch. The study is observational, the fluid was sampled only once, and the neurotoxicity threshold comes from animal studies.Source: Watne et al. 2023
  3. And the immune activation is measurable. Hall et al. measured neopterin, a marker of cell-mediated immune activation and oxidative stress, in 139 older patients with hip fracture in Oslo and Edinburgh. 64 of them developed delirium. Neopterin in cerebrospinal fluid was 29.6 against 24.7 nmol/ml (p = 0.003), and after adjustment for risk factors a high level remained associated with delirium (OR 3.31, 95% CI 1.24 to 8.86). High values were also linked to death or new nursing home admission within a year.Source: Hall et al. 2016
  4. In surgery it is the tissue injury that starts it. Damaged tissue releases DAMP molecules, among them HMGB1, which activate innate immunity. In mouse models monocyte-derived macrophages migrate into the brain parenchyma after surgery, the blood-brain barrier opens, and fibrinogen is deposited in the hippocampus. In humans the findings are weaker and more indirect: raised MCP-1 in the cerebrospinal fluid of some patients with delirium after orthopaedic surgery, microglial activation on PET in some with cognitive deficits three months after abdominal surgery, and blood-brain barrier opening on gadolinium MRI after cardiac surgery. What role anaesthesia itself plays is still unclear.Source: Subramaniyan and Terrando 2019
  5. The blood-brain barrier is the most assumed and least proven part. The review states outright that no direct evidence exists that barrier failure causes delirium in humans, and that permeability across the blood-cerebrospinal fluid barrier was not increased in most patients with delirium.Source: Wilson et al. 2020
  6. The transmitters: one of them can be enough, but none of them is the whole answer. Cholinergic blockade produces EEG slowing and can trigger frank delirium, so robust disruption of cholinergic function is sufficient. Even so, cholinesterase inhibitors have not reduced delirium in trials. The hyperdopaminergic hypothesis is significantly undermined by the failure of antipsychotics, although they are still used for agitation. On the GABA side, benzodiazepines increase the risk of transition to delirium in the ICU.Source: Wilson et al. 2020
  7. Noradrenaline and stress hormones, in both directions. Both too much and too little noradrenergic activity impairs frontal function, and the authors speculate that this may underlie the difference between hyperactive and hypoactive delirium. Raised blood noradrenaline was significantly associated with postoperative delirium in older patients. Increased cortisol has been linked to delirium in several settings. Considerable research is still needed here, they write themselves.Source: Wilson et al. 2020
  8. Energy: the brain does not get what it is using. The cerebral metabolic insufficiency hypothesis holds that delirium arises when energy demand is not met, through hypoxia, hypoperfusion, hypoglycaemia or insulin resistance. FDG-PET shows reduced glucose metabolism during delirium. The authors call it a plausible explanation, but a direct causal role has not been confirmed.Source: Wilson et al. 2020
  9. The networks fall apart, and that may be the final common path. Imaging shows that the normal relationship between the executive network and the default mode network is reversed, that subcortical connectivity is reduced, and that networks globally become less integrated. The authors propose that impaired network connectivity may be the final driver of the delirium syndrome, but whether it is cause or consequence is not established.Source: Wilson et al. 2020
  10. And on the EEG. Clinical EEG in delirium shows occipital slowing, reduced alpha and increased delta and theta. Perhaps the single strongest finding in the whole mechanistic literature comes from experimental hypoxia in volunteers: EEG slowing appears before attention fails. The authors call this the clearest evidence that hypoxia alone can cause delirium. Hypoglycaemia produces the same slowing. At the same time they write that the role of EEG in screening and diagnosis of delirium remains undefined.Source: Wilson et al. 2020

Where you see it, and why it looks so different. The clinical situations that produce delirium come in through different doors but end in the same picture.

  • Older patients with a urinary tract infection. The association is real but weaker and less certain than the use made of it. A meta-analysis of 29 studies with 16,618 participants over 65 found OR 2.67 (95% CI 2.12 to 3.36) for delirium with urinary tract infection, but with high heterogeneity and publication bias. For asymptomatic bacteriuria there was only one study, and it found no significant association (OR 1.62, 95% CI 0.57 to 4.65). The authors stress that the design cannot say which came first, and that whether treating the infection improves the delirium is unresolved. A positive dipstick in a confused older patient is therefore not an explanation one can settle for. An important distinction: a symptomatic infection with fever and systemic illness is a real acute illness, and it should be treated. What is contested is the confused patient with a positive dipstick and no urinary symptoms. A systematic review of four studies with 652 participants found that none of them showed that antibiotics improved delirium in afebrile patients over 60 with asymptomatic pyuria or bacteriuria. Three of the four studies were at high risk of bias, so the evidence is thin in both directions, and a randomised trial is now under way (NCT06004739).Sources: Krinitski et al. 2021; Stall et al. 2024
  • Hypoxia, in divers and at altitude. Here the documentation is unusually clean, because it has been done experimentally: hypoxia alone produces delirium in healthy volunteers, and EEG slowing appears before attention fails. The same holds for hypoglycaemia. These two, together with cholinergic blockade, are the only conditions in which delirium from a single cause has been shown in humans.Source: Wilson et al. 2020
  • Children given less sevoflurane. In a randomised trial of 177 children aged 1 to 6, sevoflurane titrated by the spectrogram, to the lowest concentration that maintained alpha and slow delta, gave emergence delirium in 21% against 35% with a fixed 1.0 MAC. Exposure was 0.8 against 2.1 MAC-hours. Here the dose itself is the door in, in brains without any of the vulnerabilities the reviews describe. The whole trial is in .

What is actually established: that delirium has several triggers, that inflammation and hypoxia can trigger it experimentally, and that anticholinergics and benzodiazepines raise the risk. What is not established: whether there is one common pathway, whether the blood-brain barrier is involved, whether dopamine has a role, whether metabolic failure is causal, what the stress hormones do, and whether delirium causes lasting brain injury or merely reveals it.

The measures actually deployed against postoperative delirium, of which EEG is only one, are in .

Wilson et al. 2020 Subramaniyan and Terrando 2019

Glymphatic failure as a hypothesis for delirium

A recent review proposes that impaired clearance of waste from the brain is a common mechanism behind delirium. It is a hypothesis, not established knowledge: the authors state themselves that direct human evidence of a causal relationship is lacking. It is included here because it ties together sleep, noradrenaline, sedative drugs and mechanical ventilation, all of which the app already covers.Sources: Boesen 2026; Liu and Du 2025 (preprint)

  • Clearance is greatest during sleep. Boesen 2026 writes that glymphatic function is most active during sleep, and that human studies using contrast-enhanced MRI confirm that sleep enhances clearance. The fluid enters along the arteries in the perivascular spaces, and pulsations from respiration and slow vasomotion are both major drivers of the flow.Source: Boesen 2026
  • Noradrenaline is the switch. The sleep-associated increase in glymphatic activity is enabled by reduced noradrenaline levels. Infra-slow noradrenaline oscillations from the locus coeruleus drive a slow vasomotion that facilitates the influx of cerebrospinal fluid, whereas the high noradrenaline level during wakefulness suppresses both vasomotion and glymphatic function.Source: Boesen 2026
  • The agents pull in opposite directions, but the data are from rodents. Ketamine–xylazine and α2-agonists are said to preserve clearance at levels comparable to NREM sleep, and dexmedetomidine to enhance glymphatic flow in mice. Propofol and pentobarbital are said to inhibit it potently, but the propofol entry in the article's table is marked as unpublished data from one of the authors and therefore has no published source. Isoflurane and sevoflurane inhibit it, given as a 30–80 % reduction in rodents. Morphine reduces flow in mice, while opioids are otherwise listed as “not studied”; in humans, opioids suppress slow-wave and REM sleep.Source: Boesen 2026
  • Positive-pressure ventilation is the proposed link to intensive care. The negative pressure of natural breathing facilitates the efflux of cerebrospinal fluid, whereas positive-pressure ventilation increases intrathoracic pressure, reduces venous return and elevates intracranial pressure. The authors write that further work is needed to confirm whether a clinical association stems from positive-pressure ventilation itself.Source: Boesen 2026
  • The mouse study, which is not yet peer reviewed. Healthy mice received two hours of isoflurane 2.5 % with fentanyl, either by nose cone with spontaneous breathing or on a ventilator. Only the ventilated group had reduced glymphatic influx and reduced clearance. Maximum intracranial pressure was higher during ventilation (10.55 ± 0.72 versus 7.56 ± 0.63 mmHg, p = 0.014). At six hours, TNF-α, IL-5, KC and MCP-1 were increased in the brain, with only sparse changes in serum. At 24 hours the mice travelled shorter distances more slowly, were immobile for longer and stayed more in the periphery and corners. The nose-cone group did not differ from controls.Source: Liu and Du 2025 (preprint)
  • The study measures ICP, not CPP. Cerebral perfusion pressure is not reported, and blood pressure and blood gases are not given. That perfusion pressure falls follows only if blood pressure is unchanged, and that was not examined here.Source: Liu and Du 2025 (preprint)
  • Caveats. The review is a Perspective, that is a hypothesis with a review of the literature, not a systematic review. The mouse study is a preprint without peer review: the imaging was done in anaesthetised animals, the sample size was not determined by power analysis, and the fentanyl dose in the methods is given in a way that looks like a typographical error. Neither source shows that this applies to humans.Sources: Boesen 2026; Liu and Du 2025
  • After head injury clearance almost stops, and adrenergic blockade reversed it in mice. After traumatic brain injury, cerebrospinal fluid production fell by at least 90 %, and noradrenaline in the brain interstitial fluid rose to five to eight times baseline. A combination of prazosin, propranolol and atipamezole almost entirely eliminated the cerebral oedema, normalised influx and restored lymph flow in the neck. These are mice, and it has not been tried clinically.Source: Hussain 2023. See “Head injury, noradrenaline and glymphatic drainage (Hussain 2023)”
  • Interpretation based on the sources: this does not change what is done with the EEG today. What the EEG can contribute is the same as before: showing whether the patient actually gets physiological sleep, and showing when sedation is deeper than necessary. The relationship between an EEG pattern and glymphatic function has not been measured in humans.
Boesen 2026 Liu and Du 2025 (preprint)
The studies in detail: glymphatic failure and delirium (3 cards)

Summaries of each article, with numbers and caveats. The theme card above builds on these.

Glymphatic dysfunction as a unifying hypothesis for delirium (Boesen 2026)

Perspective article in Nature Reviews Neurology 2026;22:309–323 (Boesen, Du, Goldman and Nedergaard). The hypothesis is that impaired glymphatic flow is a central mechanism in the development of delirium.

  • The basis: glymphatic function is most active during sleep. In humans this has been shown with contrast-enhanced MRI. The driving forces are pulsations from respiration and slow vasomotion in the arteries, and sleep expands the extracellular space, as in rodent studies.
  • Noradrenaline: the sleep-associated increase in glymphatic activity is enabled by reduced noradrenaline levels. Infra-slow noradrenaline oscillations from the locus coeruleus drive the vasomotion that facilitates the influx of cerebrospinal fluid. High noradrenaline during wakefulness suppresses both vasomotion and glymphatic function.
  • The agents: ketamine–xylazine is used as a comparator, and α2-agonists together with ketamine are said to preserve clearance at levels comparable to NREM sleep (mouse and rat studies). Dexmedetomidine appears in the table as enhancing glymphatic flow in mice, and clinically as associated with less delirium than other sedatives, though not superior to the alternatives as the primary sedative during mechanical ventilation in some trials. Propofol and pentobarbital are said to inhibit potently, but the propofol entry in the table is marked as unpublished data from one of the authors. Isoflurane and sevoflurane inhibit, given as a 30–80 % reduction in rodents. Morphine reduces flow in mice; opioids are otherwise listed as “not studied”, while human data show that opioids suppress slow-wave and REM sleep.
  • Ventilation: the negative pressure of natural breathing facilitates the efflux of cerebrospinal fluid, whereas positive-pressure ventilation increases intrathoracic pressure, reduces venous return and elevates intracranial pressure. For humans the authors write that further work is needed to confirm whether an association stems from positive-pressure ventilation itself.
  • What is human data: MRI showing that sleep enhances clearance, MRI studies of reduced flow in several diseases, delirium epidemiology, and clinical trials of sedatives and melatonin. Experimental sleep deprivation in humans induces a delirium-like state, but glymphatic flow was not the measured outcome in that study.
  • The authors' own caveats: they acknowledge the lack of direct human evidence for a causal relationship between impaired glymphatic flow and delirium, and that no human studies have examined glymphatic function in inflammation.
Boesen et al. Nat Rev Neurol 2026;22:309–323

Mechanical ventilation and glymphatic function in mice (Liu and Du 2025, preprint)

Preprint on bioRxiv, that is not peer reviewed. “Mechanical Ventilation Suppresses Glymphatic Function in Parallel with Delirium-Like Symptoms in Mice”.

  • The set-up: healthy mice received two hours of isoflurane 2.5 % with intraperitoneal fentanyl, either by nose cone with spontaneous breathing or on a ventilator. Both groups were compared with untreated controls.
  • Glymphatic function: influx of tracer from the cisterna magna, imaged through the skull for 30 minutes, was markedly reduced during ventilation. The nose-cone group did not differ from controls. Clearance from brain to blood, measured by fibre photometry over the superior sagittal sinus, was also significantly reduced in the ventilated group (p below 0.0001).
  • Pressure: maximum intracranial pressure over the two hours was higher during ventilation than with the nose cone, 10.55 ± 0.72 versus 7.56 ± 0.63 mmHg (p = 0.014). The area under the pressure curve rose by about 52 %. Cerebral perfusion pressure, blood pressure, blood volume and blood gases are not reported; oxygenation was followed only by hindlimb pulse oximetry.
  • Inflammation: at six hours, TNF-α, IL-5, KC and MCP-1 were increased in the brain. In serum the changes were sparse, with only IL-1α increased.
  • Behaviour at 24 hours: in the open field the mice travelled shorter distances more slowly and were immobile for longer, crossed fewer zones and stayed more in the periphery and corners. In the Barnes maze, ventilation did not change the latency to reach the target hole, but the mice made more non-target entries. The nose-cone group did not differ from controls in either test.
  • Caveats: a preprint without peer review, an animal study, the tracer imaging was done in anaesthetised mice, and the sample size was not determined by power analysis. The fentanyl dose in the methods is given in a way that looks like a unit error and should be checked against a final published version.
Liu, Du et al. bioRxiv 2025 (preprint)

Head injury, noradrenaline and glymphatic drainage (Hussain 2023)

Animal study in Nature 2023;623:992–1000 (Hussain, Nedergaard et al.). Male and female mice aged 8–12 weeks, closed-skull traumatic brain injury of moderate severity.

  • What happens acutely: the injury reduced ventricular cerebrospinal fluid production by at least 90 %, and tracer transport into the brain fell acutely. Increased water content in the injured hemisphere was measurable as early as 30 minutes after the injury.
  • Noradrenaline: the plasma concentration rose sharply immediately after the injury, and in the brain interstitial fluid it rose to five to eight times both baseline and the level in uninjured controls.
  • The cervical lymphatic vessels: lymph flow was significantly reduced after the injury. Noradrenaline reduced both the frequency and the amplitude of contractions in the lymphatic vessels, dose-dependently.
  • The treatment: prazosin 10 µg/g, propranolol 10 µg/g and atipamezole 1 µg/g given intraperitoneally after the injury, with two further doses at 24-hour intervals. Prazosin blocks α1, propranolol β and atipamezole α2.
  • The effect: the treatment almost entirely eliminated the oedema, increased and largely normalised cerebrospinal fluid inflow and production, increased uptake on the injured side and gave enhanced efflux. Lymph flow in the neck was restored.
  • Over time: at 12 weeks locomotor function had recovered either way, but anxiety-like behaviour persisted in the injured mice unless they had been treated. At 6 months glymphatic function was still persistently reduced compared with age-matched controls. The treatment also suppressed the accumulation of hyperphosphorylated tau.
  • Caveats: these are mice, not humans, and it has not been tried clinically. The authors note that noradrenaline receptors are broadly expressed, so a direct effect of the combination on other cell types cannot be excluded, and that the injury model gives variable outcomes. Applied to intensive care patients this is so far only a hypothesis: none of the drugs has been studied for this purpose in humans, and each has its own circulatory effects.
Hussain et al. Nature 2023;623:992–1000
The studies in detail: sedation and sleep, sleep medicine (Eikermann et al. 2025), sleep and the brain, REM sleep, NONSEDA and Strøm, EEG in delirium (6 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Safe Brain Initiative: the whole bundle, in which EEG is one of 18 measures

The Safe Brain Initiative is not an EEG project. It is a care bundle against postoperative delirium in which EEG monitoring is item 13 of 18. The whole list is worth knowing, both because most of the items cost nothing and because it explains why the results from the bundle cannot be attributed to EEG alone.

The items are given here as they are listed in table 1 of Meco et al. 2024, in their order. The paper does not group them into before, during and after.

  1. Regular screening for delirium.
  2. Regular patient-reported screening for postoperative pain, with subsequent adjustment of treatment.
  3. Reducing nausea and vomiting by considering the patient's risk level and using antiemetics, with regular screening and adjustment.
  4. Reducing preoperative fluid fasting time to two hours through patient education and staff training, giving a drink during recovery and screening for thirst.
  5. Ensuring the patient is oriented in space and time, with hearing aids, dentures, glasses, clocks and verbal orientation.
  6. Communication: using assistive devices and aids and fostering open dialogue.
  7. Keeping noise levels down in the perioperative environment.
  8. Considering the circadian rhythm, and offering earplugs and eyeshades, with less noise and light during recovery.
  9. Addressing and treating pain before surgery.
  10. Patient-centred practice: increasing patient engagement and integrating preferences, needs and values into care decisions.
  11. Using nociception monitoring and continuous analgesia techniques, such as remifentanil.
  12. Reducing anticholinergic load by promoting alternatives, minimising doses and raising awareness of the risks.
  13. Monitoring brain activity with EEG to detect and prevent adverse neurological events during medium to deep sedation.
  14. Using capnography in sedated patients.
  15. Reducing stress through staff training in relaxation measures, with regular screening for stress.
  16. Measuring and addressing patient satisfaction with treatment.
  17. Reducing anxiety through training in communication and distraction techniques, screening for anxiety, patient education and the offer of counselling.
  18. Monitoring and controlling temperature to prevent hypothermia and hyperthermia.

What the bundle has shown, and what it cannot show. Across four hospitals in Denmark and Turkey, 18,697 patients, delirium in recovery fell the longer the bundle had been in use (adjusted OR 0.96 per month). At one hospital in Switzerland it fell from 22.45% to 18.11% from the first to the last six months. But neither study has a control group or randomisation, EEG use is not reported, and delirium was screened only in recovery. Seventeen other measures changed at the same time, so none of the effect can be attributed to the EEG part alone. Both studies have financial ties to a monitor manufacturer, and the Swiss one was funded by it.

Why this is an argument in the discussion of cause versus marker is in .

Meco et al. 2024 Saunders et al. 2026

Propofol and midazolam do not produce physiological sleep: sleep deprivation as part of ICU delirium

  • The claim: Brown, Lydic and Schiff (NEJM 2010) write that general anaesthesia “is, in fact, a reversible drug-induced coma”, and that anaesthesiologists call it “sleep” to avoid disquieting patients, but unfortunately also in technical descriptions. At surgical depth anaesthesia can functionally approximate brain-stem death (unconscious, depressed brain-stem reflexes, no response to nociception, no respiratory drive), and emergence follows the same steps as recovery from coma (table 1 in the article). Sleep is actively generated by nuclei in the hypothalamus, brain stem and basal forebrain, cycles between NREM and REM every 90–120 minutes, and serves cardiovascular, immune and cognitive function. Brown has said the same publicly: patients are told they will “go to sleep”, but that is not the state they are in, and he has used the Michael Jackson case as an example (NPR interview 2011).
  • How the EEG separates sleep from anaesthesia (Akeju and Brown 2017): (1) Slow waves occur in both, but in sleep they are synchronous with brief pauses in cortical firing, under propofol asynchronous with prolonged pauses, and with more cortical sources. (2) Alpha is not a feature of NREM sleep; GABAergic alpha is frontal, high-amplitude and coherent, lies in the same frequency range as sleep spindles (12–16 Hz), but lacks the spindles' transient envelope and refractory period of several seconds, and occurs only together with slow waves. (3) Burst suppression and isoelectric EEG never occur in normal sleep; they belong to anoxic brain injury, hypothermia and Ohtahara syndrome. (4) Gamma in REM is not the same as ketamine's narrow-band 30–45 Hz “gamma burst”. (5) Sedation with GABAergic agents produces beta activity, whereas NREM sleep reduces beta; the common sleep medications (zolpidem, benzodiazepines) produce the same beta and similar cognitive side effects. (6) Dexmedetomidine produces spindles and slow waves resembling N2, but K-complexes have not been described. Their conclusion: neither anaesthetics nor sleep medications produce physiological sleep, they are unlikely to compensate for sleep need, and the oscillations they produce probably contribute to drug-induced brain dysfunction. The authors declare no competing interests.
  • ICU delirium and paradoxical excitation: Brown 2010 proposes that delirium with benzodiazepine sedation in the ICU may share a circuit mechanism with the paradoxical excitation seen at low doses of nearly every anaesthetic (GABA-mediated disinhibition in striatothalamic pathways), in line with zolpidem “waking” some patients in a minimally conscious state. This is a hypothesis in the article, not a finding.
  • What sedatives do to sleep architecture (Telias and Wilcox 2019, review): propofol is a potent suppressor of slow-wave sleep (SWS) and produces burst suppression at high doses; benzodiazepines shorten sleep latency but reduce both SWS and REM; opioids suppress SWS and REM dose-dependently. Sedation frequently produces “atypical” EEG patterns not seen in normal sleep.
  • Sleep loss and delirium: sleep deprivation is regarded as a potentially modifiable risk factor for delirium, but the direction is unclear: delirium also disturbs sleep, and they may share pathophysiology. Dexmedetomidine resembles natural sleep more than the GABA agonists do (spindles and slow waves, see the Agents tab); small pilot studies showed better sleep efficiency, and low-dose nocturnal dexmedetomidine reduced delirium without improving self-reported sleep quality.
  • What EEG can contribute: a sedation EEG with alpha-delta or burst suppression is not sleep, even if the patient lies still with eyes closed. It is an argument for measuring rather than assuming: the spectrogram shows whether the patient is in a drug-induced state or in sleep with spindles and cyclic alternation. Drouot scoring of “pathological wakefulness” and “atypical sleep” is validated only in non-sedated patients.
  • The Michael Jackson case, what is documented: Jackson received propofol at home for insomnia and died in 2009; his physician Conrad Murray was convicted of involuntary manslaughter in 2011. Expert witnesses at the trial included the anaesthesiologists Steven Shafer (for the prosecution) and Paul White (for the defence) and the sleep specialist Nader Kamangar, who testified that propofol has no medical benefit for insomnia. Emery Brown was not a witness in the case but has used it in public communication. Whether chronic propofol “sleep” made Jackson sleep-deprived is a hypothesis raised publicly, not a forensic finding.
  • Terminology: the sources in this app use “unconsciousness”, “hypnosis” and “sedation”, not “sleep”. Telling patients and relatives that they will “sleep” is established practice, but it is worth knowing that it is misleading, and that “sedation for days” does not meet the need for sleep.
Brown, Lydic and Schiff. N Engl J Med 2010;363:2638–2650 · Akeju and Brown. Curr Opin Neurobiol 2017;44:178–185 · Telias and Wilcox. Crit Care 2019;23:82 · NPR Fresh Air 2011 · Medscape and CNN, trial 2011

What the textbook chapter on sleep medicine adds (Eikermann et al. 2025, Eikermann, Fassbender and Azimaraghi)

  • Sleep onset is sharp, induction is gradual: physiological sleep begins as a sharp alpha–theta transition in the EEG, without intermediate stages, and the same applies to the NREM→REM switch (pontine “flip-flop” switches). Anaesthetic induction, by contrast, is a continuous decline from awake through reduced responsiveness to unresponsive. Sleep has spontaneous onset and termination, is readily reversed by noxious stimuli and is homeostatically regulated; anaesthesia lacks the stage structure, and arousal from drug-induced unconsciousness requires some drug elimination. The chapter states that EEG patterns during sleep and anaesthesia differ despite similarities between slow-wave sleep and anaesthesia, citing Brown 2010.
  • The stages as the chapter defines them: N1 is the alpha→theta transition, N2 has spindles and K-complexes, N3 is slow-wave sleep (delta), REM is low-amplitude mixed activity with atonia and eye movements. Benzodiazepines, opioids and antidepressants suppress REM; the elderly have less slow-wave sleep. Polysomnography (EEG, EOG, chin EMG) is the only method that determines sleep stage precisely; actigraphy and questionnaires do not.
  • The “shared circuit” hypothesis, and why it does not hold for anaesthesia: many sedatives (dexmedetomidine, ethanol, isoflurane) activate sleep-promoting VLPO neurons, and loss of VLPO neurons attenuates the sedative response to dexmedetomidine, suggesting a causal role for sedation. But animals with complete VLPO lesions can still be anaesthetised (transient resistance to volatile agents, later increased sensitivity owing to increased homeostatic sleep drive), and direct inhibition of the TMN produces sedation, not anaesthesia. The chapter's conclusion (fig. 9.12): anaesthetics activate VLPO/MnPO and induce arousable unconsciousness (sedation) at low doses, but general anaesthesia cannot be achieved via arousal-inhibiting circuits alone; at anaesthetic doses, circuits downstream (including the neocortex) are modulated simultaneously so that the brain's information processing is disrupted across spatial and temporal scales. Thalamocortical networks remain active during sleep, unlike during anaesthesia.
  • Postoperative sleep: REM falls substantially on the first night after surgery and anaesthesia, with REM rebound (more and more intense REM) on nights 2–4; disturbances can last up to 6 months depending on the extent of surgery. Surgery alone (without general anaesthesia) reduces REM; pain, inflammation, immobility and anxiety contribute. In long-term ventilated patients propofol sedation abolishes REM and diminishes sleep quality (Kondili 2012), whereas low-dose propofol permits REM. Ketamine is little studied, probably with mild REM effects. Circadian effects of anaesthetics are unresolved; 3 hours of anaesthesia did not alter the body-temperature rhythm in humans.
  • Sleep in the ICU: sleep fragmentation occurs consistently during sedation and mechanical ventilation; deep NREM, REM and circadian rhythms are severely reduced or abolished, and about half of sleep occurs during the daytime. In up to 70% of sedated or ventilated patients the EEG is “atypical” and does not fit standard criteria for sleep and wakefulness; alternative ICU scoring systems (Watson 2013) have been proposed but not validated. Frontal portable EEG monitors with electrode placements approximating the AASM recommendation can be used. In 11 stable, non-sedated ventilated patients being weaned, the median sound level was 72 dBC, and above 77 dBC arousals (OR 3.9) and sleep-to-wake transitions (OR 7.6) increased. Monitor and ventilator alarms were the most disruptive (Elbaz 2017); dim light around the clock hinders photoentrainment. Earplugs and eye masks consistently improve sleep quality.
  • Sedation depth, REM and delirium: prolonged deep sedation (RASS ≤ −3) is associated with longer ICU and hospital stays and delirium; GABA agonists (propofol, benzodiazepines) may increase sedation depth, reduce REM and thereby increase neurocognitive disorders (Azimaraghi 2022, retrospective cohort from the same author group). Opioids reduce REM and worsen sleep apnoea; unrecognised pain leads to excessive sedative use. Melatonin has produced conflicting results; the orexin antagonist suvorexant is promising but not studied in the critically ill. Sleep deprivation impairs immune function, glucose tolerance, produces a catabolic stress response, respiratory muscle fatigue, impaired attention and working memory and increased vulnerability to delirium, but sleep-promoting agents can themselves increase delirium risk.
  • Narcolepsy: these patients have increased sensitivity to anaesthetics with delayed emergence, postoperative hypersomnia and apnoeic episodes; the chapter recommends monitoring of anaesthetic depth in this group, without specifying the method.
  • Caveats: the chapter is a textbook review; many of the mechanistic findings are animal studies (VLPO lesions in rats and mice), and the 70% atypical-EEG figure comes from a single study. Conflicts of interest are not stated in the chapter text available to us.
Eikermann et al. 2025 (Miller's Anesthesia, 10th ed.) · the chapter's references: Brown 2010, Akeju and Brown 2017, Moore 2012, Kondili 2012, Watson 2013, Elbaz 2017, Azimaraghi 2022

Why sleep matters for the brain: waste clearance, amyloid and cognition

Three studies and the textbook chapter on sleep medicine show why lost sleep is more than tiredness. The findings are from mice and from small experiments in healthy people, not from sedated intensive care patients.

  • Waste clearance (Xie 2013, Science 342:373–377): in mice the interstitial space increased by about 60 % in both natural sleep and anaesthesia. This gave faster exchange between cerebrospinal fluid and interstitial fluid and faster clearance of β-amyloid.
  • Amyloid in humans (Shokri-Kojori 2018, PNAS): 20 healthy adults (22–72 years) had PET after a night of sleep and after a night without sleep (about 31 hours awake). β-amyloid increased by about 5 %, including in the thalamus and hippocampus, and a larger increase was associated with worse mood.
  • Cognition (Van Dongen 2003, Sleep 26:117–126): 48 healthy people (21–38 years) spent 4, 6 or 8 hours in bed for 14 days. At 6 hours or less, cognitive impairment accumulated in a dose-dependent way, equivalent to up to 2 nights without any sleep. Self-reported sleepiness rose at first and then levelled off, so participants were largely unaware of how impaired they were.
  • Health and mortality (Eikermann et al. 2025): sleep restriction is an independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease, metabolic disease and all-cause mortality, and adults are advised to get at least 7 hours. Sleep deprivation delays the antibody response to influenza vaccine, impairs glucose tolerance and causes insulin resistance in healthy young people, and produces a catabolic state with increased oxygen consumption, CO2 production and catecholamines.
  • Caveats: Xie is an animal study, and anaesthesia also increased the interstitial space in the mice. That sedation in intensive care patients has the same effect has not been shown. Shokri-Kojori and Van Dongen are small studies in healthy people. The relationship between sleep loss and delirium may run in both directions.
Xie 2013 Shokri-Kojori 2018 Van Dongen 2003 Eikermann et al. 2025

Sleep in intensive care: outcomes were worse without REM sleep (Marchasson 2024)

Marchasson et al. (Crit Care 2024;28:331, doi 10.1186/s13054-024-05118-4), “Impact of sleep disturbances on outcomes in intensive care units”. A post-hoc analysis of three observational studies of 131 conscious patients without continuous sedation who had full polysomnography at different times during the intensive care stay: 34 with acute respiratory failure, 45 on mechanical ventilation with weaning difficulties and 52 immediately after extubation.

  • Deep sleep: preserved in acute respiratory failure, but markedly reduced under mechanical ventilation and after extubation (p < 0.01).
  • Atypical sleep: more frequent under mechanical ventilation than in patients breathing spontaneously (p < 0.01).
  • REM sleep: uncommon at all time points and completely absent in 66 of 131 (50 %), and in 63 % after extubation.
  • Outcome: a poor outcome (intubation, prolonged weaning or reintubation) occurred in 22 of 131 (17 %). Patients without REM sleep more often had a poor outcome than those with preserved REM: 24 % versus 9 % (p = 0.03). ICU mortality did not differ significantly (12 % versus 3 %, p = 0.11).
  • Caveats: an association, not a cause. A small single-centre study with single recordings. The patients were not sedated, so the findings cannot be transferred directly to a sedated intensive care patient. The study does not show what makes REM sleep disappear.
Marchasson et al. Crit Care 2024;28:331

EEG in ventilated patients with new-onset altered consciousness and delirium (Eskioglou 2021)

Pre-planned analysis from the CERTA study (Acta Neurol Scand 2021;144:296–302): 91 non-neurological intensive care patients in Lausanne (median 66 years, sepsis most common) who had an EEG because of new-onset altered consciousness, median 5 days after admission. 64% were sedated during the EEG (propofol and/or midazolam). The EEG was interpreted according to the 2012 ACNS nomenclature, blinded to delirium. 42 (46%) developed delirium, half diagnosed with CAM-ICU and the rest from the chart and antipsychotic use.

  • Burst suppression only in the delirious: 10% versus 0% (p = 0.02). Of the four, two were unsedated and two received propofol 2.2–2.5 mg/kg/h; all had sepsis, two died.
  • Rhythmic or periodic patterns (the ictal-interictal continuum) in 43% versus 22% (p = 0.03), and seizures or status epilepticus in 7% versus 0% (p = 0.05).
  • At least one of the three findings in 32 of 91 (35%) gave a higher delirium rate (42 versus 15%, p = 0.006).
  • What did not discriminate: dominant frequency (theta in about 70% in both groups), amplitude, reactivity, triphasic waves (33 versus 27%), NREM sleep elements and sedative doses during the first 5 days. General EEG slowing, which is often linked to delirium, therefore did not discriminate here, because it is common in intensive care patients regardless of cause.
  • ACNS definitions used: continuous (suppression below 10%), discontinuous (10–49%), burst suppression (≥ 50%) and suppressed (below 10 µV).
  • Caveats: small sample, selected population without acute brain injury, EEG mostly recorded while delirium was already present (81 of 91), CAM-ICU missing in half, borderline significance for seizures, no correction for multiple comparisons. Funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation.
Eskioglou et al. Acta Neurol Scand 2021;144:296–302

Melatonin and circadian rhythm in delirium: what the studies actually show

Circadian disruption has been proposed as a mechanism behind delirium, and melatonin is the most studied intervention. The evidence is uneven, and the strongest part concerns prevention after surgery, not the intensive care patient.

  • The pooled analysis is positive, but with caveats. Barnes et al. 2023 pooled 11 randomised trials with a total of 1244 patients, melatonin or ramelteon against control. The combined odds ratio for postoperative delirium was 0.41 (95% CI 0.21–0.80, p = 0.01), and the NNT 8.4. Heterogeneity was high (I² = 72%), and the authors rated the certainty as moderate under GRADE, downgraded precisely for inconsistency. Eight different tools were used to diagnose delirium across the included trials. Egger's test gave no evidence of publication bias (p = 0.128).Source: Barnes et al. 2023 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 11 RCTs, 1244 patients)
  • Intensive care is not the same as postoperative. Barnes et al. 2023 report that the largest intensive care trial, Pro-MEDIC, found no effect of melatonin on delirium in intensive care patients. That is one reason heterogeneity is high, and a reason the finding cannot simply be carried over to the intensive care unit.Source: Barnes et al. 2023, reporting Pro-MEDIC
  • Cardiac surgery: striking numbers, but no randomisation. Artemiou et al. 2015 gave melatonin 5 mg from the evening before surgery to the third postoperative day to 250 cardiac surgery patients, and compared them with 250 patients without. Delirium occurred in 8.4% versus 20.8% (p = 0.001), assessed with CAM-ICU every twelve hours. The study is observational, the groups ran consecutively in time, no cognitive screening was done before surgery, and only hyperactive delirium was recorded. The authors state these limitations themselves.Source: Artemiou et al. 2015 (prospective observational study, 2 × 250 patients)
  • The anaesthetic method affects the rhythm. Song et al. 2021 followed 138 patients over 65 with hip fracture, 69 with subarachnoid anaesthesia and 69 with general anaesthesia. The general anaesthesia group had a lower melatonin peak, lower mesor and lower amplitude on the first postoperative day, more awakenings and poorer sleep on the day of surgery. Delirium occurred in 17.4% versus 34.8% (p = 0.020), adjusted OR 0.287 (95% CI 0.115–0.718, p = 0.008). Patients were not randomised: the method was chosen from the patient's wishes and the clinician's judgement, and MMSE differed between the groups before surgery (p = 0.020).Source: Song et al. 2021 (prospective cohort, 138 patients)
  • The rhythm can be influenced without drugs. Song et al. 2021 kept light below 10 lux at the patient's eye level at night, used a penlight instead of the ceiling light for blood sampling and nursing care, and shielded patients from noise, and from food and drink that affect melatonin. These are measures a unit can take whether or not melatonin is given.Source: Song et al. 2021, the methods section
  • Arousal itself resets the clock. Rutter, Reick and McKnight 2002 summarise that sleep deprivation can rapidly reset behavioural rhythms, and that the range of stimuli that do so, including simple arousal, suggests that merely being awake and processing sensory information is enough to impinge on the oscillator controlling rhythmic behaviour. Translated to the ICU: it is not only the light and the missing night that shifts the rhythm, it is being woken and stimulated at all. The review is from 2002 and rests on mice, hamsters, fruit flies and cell culture, not on patients, and it concerns the molecular biology of the clock, not melatonin as a treatment.Source: Rutter, Reick and McKnight 2002 (review, animals and cell culture)
  • What to take away. The best documentation concerns prevention of postoperative delirium, not treatment of established delirium, and not the intensive care patient. The two studies with the most striking numbers are not randomised. The certainty is moderate, not high, and it is downgraded because the studies disagree.Interpretation from the sources: Barnes et al. 2023; Artemiou et al. 2015; Song et al. 2021
Barnes et al. BMJ Open 2023;13:e069950 Song et al. EBioMedicine 2021;70:103490

When the patient fights the ventilator: what to do before deepening sedation

Patient–ventilator dyssynchrony takes several forms, and they are corrected by different measures. Sottile et al. 2020 divide them into triggering (double-triggering, reverse-triggering, auto-triggering and ineffective triggering), flow and cycling (premature and delayed).

  • Double-triggering. A 1 mL/kg increase in tidal volume per predicted body weight lowered the odds of double-triggering by around 60% in 20 ARDS patients. A longer inspiratory time was associated, in an observational study, with double-triggering almost disappearing. Switching to pressure support also nearly eliminated it, but raised tidal volume by a median of 4 mL/kg, which is a volutrauma risk.
  • Flow-limited breaths. Increasing ventilator flow reduced the number in 16 patients.
  • Ineffective triggering. PEEP reduces these when significant auto-PEEP from obstructive lung disease is present. Pressure support produced more ineffective triggering than other modes.
  • Cycling. Lowering flow lengthens inspiratory time and may improve cycling dyssynchrony, but can increase flow dyssynchrony at the same time. It is a trade-off, not a clean improvement.
  • Auto-triggering and reverse-triggering. The review gives no setting-based correction for these two.

What sedation actually does to dyssynchrony, and what it costs. The picture is not uniform. More sedation was associated in one study with 14 percentage points fewer double-triggered breaths, but in another with more ineffective triggering. In a third, deep sedation reduced double-triggered, flow-limited and ineffective breaths, and neuromuscular blockade eliminated every type. The price is diaphragmatic weakness, deconditioning and longer ventilation with deep sedation.

The review concludes that optimising ventilator settings appears to be the safest way to reduce dyssynchrony, and that the decision to use deep sedation or neuromuscular blockade must be balanced against its harms. The authors also say the optimal use of these agents to reduce dyssynchrony and improve outcomes is unknown.

Note what this is not: a narrative review, not a guideline, and the numbers above come from small studies, several of which had patients already deeply sedated. The order "look at the waveforms and the settings first" is well supported. The individual numbers should be used with care.

Sottile et al. Ann Thorac Med 2020;15:190–198

EMG in the frontal EEG as a sign of stress and pain

EMG in the frontal signal is usually treated as nothing but noise. Stewart et al. 2022 asked whether it is also information. They followed 30 postoperative, ventilated ICU patients on propofol or midazolam and measured BIS, frontal EMG power, an EMG-based responsiveness index and blood pressure variability, against RASS and around painful procedures such as bronchoscopy and chest tube insertion.

  • EMG was about as good as the index at indicating sedation level. Prediction probability against RASS was 0.776 for BIS, 0.761 for EMG and 0.763 for the responsiveness index. The authors themselves point out that BIS did not do substantially better than the EMG the monitor already displays.
  • On painful stimulation, EMG responded most consistently. BIS, EMG and blood pressure variability all gave significant pre- and post-stimulus changes. Responses were most consistent at RASS −4 and −3, with an increase in around 75% of events. The BIS reactivity at those levels was attributed to that same EMG activation.
  • At RASS −5, frontal EMG was the last response left. That is the clinically most interesting finding: in the most deeply sedated patient, who can say nothing, muscle activity in the forehead was the only thing still reacting.
  • Blood pressure variability said nothing about sedation level. Heart rate had to be excluded because around 19% of the ECG data was not sinus rhythm.

The authors conclude that EMG may form part of ICU monitoring where neuromuscular blockers are not routinely used, and that EMG power may help detect responses to painful stimulation in patients who cannot communicate.

The limitations are substantial and the authors state them: explorative design, 30 patients, results described as hypothesis-generating, a stimulus protocol that was not strictly standardised, and sedation and analgesia that were not standardised in dose or type. Data were collected 2007–2009 and the analysis came late. Conflict of interest: two research nurses and one co-author were employed by GE Healthcare, and GE covered the nurses’ salaries for this work. That does not make the finding wrong, but it belongs on the record.

So what do you do with it? EMG rising without any change in dose is a question, not an answer. It may be pain, it may be the patient waking, and it may be shivering, coughing or chewing. It points to something stimulating the patient. It does not say what.Interpretation from the sources: Stewart et al. 2022

Stewart et al. BMC Anesthesiol 2022;22:353

Light, sound and stimulation: what is documented and what is not

Dorsch et al. 2019 review the measures for sleep in the ICU. It is worth drawing a sharp line here between what has been measured and what is assumed, because the crack runs straight through this topic.

  • Sound levels are too high, and that has been measured. The WHO recommends background sound at or below 30 dB and nocturnal peaks below 40 dB. Alarms from ventilators, suction and syringe pumps all exceed this. Excess sound is linked to 17–20% of awakenings in ICU patients.
  • The light is wrong in both directions, and lux alone is a misleading measure. Nocturnal light averages below 20 lux, but severe illness is associated with more exposure to high lux values, which can fragment sleep. And the daytime light in the studies cited, 42–158 lux, is often too little to entrain the circadian rhythm at all. So the problem is not only the ceiling light at night, but also that the day is too dark.
  • And it is not only about intensity, but about direction and source. A patient lying supine looks straight into the ceiling fitting. That is a different burden from the same quantity of light arriving from the side or reflected off a wall, because it meets the eye directly and cannot be avoided by someone who cannot turn away. The closest published example of changing the source rather than merely dimming it is the method of Song et al. 2021: a penlight instead of the ceiling light for blood sampling and nursing care at night, and below 10 lux at the patient’s eyes. But let us be straight about this: the app’s author has not found peer-reviewed studies that tested angle or light source as an intervention in its own right, against dimmed overhead light as the comparator. That direct light in the eye is more irritating than indirect light is well grounded, but it is not documented as an ICU intervention.Interpretation from the sources, with the method of Song et al. 2021 as the only published example
  • This is where the documentation stops. The review reports no direct physiological outcome data for sound or light. The links to lung, metabolism, immune function and circulation are largely extrapolated from studies outside the ICU. That bright light and sound are stimulating and stressful is therefore well grounded as a mechanism, but not measured as an outcome in these patients.
  • Earplugs and eye masks: mixed. Kamdar 2013, with 300 patients, found no difference in sleep quality but lower perceived sound and less delirium. Patel 2014, with 59 patients and a bundled intervention, found better sleep quality, lower sound and light and less delirium. Boyko 2017, with 17 patients, found no difference. Patients often declined the earplugs or found them uncomfortable.
  • On sedative requirement there is almost nothing. The review does not report sedative requirement as an outcome for the bundles. The only sedative-use finding comes from a music trial, where sedative use fell in the music group. That less stimulation lowers dose requirement is therefore a reasonable hypothesis, not a documented finding.
  • Ventilator mode at night. Controlled modes gave better sleep than pressure support in several studies, including during weaning in tracheostomised patients. Findings across the mode studies are inconsistent.

What the guideline says. The 2018 PADIS guideline gives a conditional recommendation for sleep-promoting bundles involving sound and light reduction and clustering of care, and a conditional recommendation for assist-control ventilation at night. It does not recommend propofol for sleep, and it makes no recommendation on dexmedetomidine or melatonin for sleep. This account is as Dorsch et al. 2019 summarise the guideline, not the guideline’s own wording.

Practical reading: the measures are cheap, low risk, mechanistically plausible and carry a conditional recommendation. That is enough reason to do them. It is not enough to claim they lower dose requirement, because that has not been measured.

Dorsch et al. Semin Respir Crit Care Med 2019;40:614–628

The night dose: the norm is to increase it, and the authors themselves conclude it should be minimised

Here the observation from practice is worth turning around. The question is not whether the dose should be reduced at night, but what happens when it is increased, and that has been studied closely.

Mehta et al. 2016 is a secondary analysis of the SLEAP trial, a randomised study in 16 medical-surgical ICUs in North America with 423 ventilated adults. Nurses applied SAS or RASS hourly and titrated infusions towards light sedation, targeting SAS 3–4 or RASS −3 to 0. Night was defined as 19:00 to 07:00 and day as 07:00 to 19:00, so the evening shift falls inside the night figures. Patients after cardiac arrest or traumatic brain injury, and patients on neuromuscular blockade, were excluded.

  • Doses were higher at night, not lower. Benzodiazepines by a mean of 23.3 mg midazolam equivalents (95% CI 12.9–33.8, p < 0.0001) and opioids by 356 µg fentanyl equivalents (95% CI 130–582, p = 0.002). Opioid boluses, by contrast, were more frequent during the day. This held in both arms of the trial, with and without daily sedation interruption.
  • And it was not because patients were more agitated at night. The opposite. SAS scores were similar and on target (3.2 versus 3.3, p = 0.35), and nurses’ self-reported workload was similar (3.9 versus 4.0, p = 0.38). But patients pulled out equipment themselves more often during the day: at least one unintentional removal in 15.9% by day versus 9.1% at night, including self-extubation in 4.0% versus 1.7%. Patients were therefore more awake during the day, and still received less.
  • The associations found were found on the night–day difference. A larger difference between night and day midazolam dose was associated with lower odds of meeting spontaneous breathing trial criteria (OR 0.994 per mg, 95% CI 0.989–0.998, p = 0.0004), and with higher odds of not being extubated despite passing the trial (OR 1.0145 per mg, 95% CI 1.0039–1.0253, p = 0.007). A larger night–day difference in fentanyl was associated with lower odds of passing the trial (OR 0.973 per 100 µg, 95% CI 0.952–0.994, p = 0.01).
  • The authors do not know why. They suggest patients are kept awake during the day for physiotherapy, procedures, investigations, visits and weaning, and that staff then give something extra so they can rest at night. They also point to the expectation of conventional sleep and signs of poor sleep prompting more sedation, to perceived discomfort from nocturnal changes in ventilator settings, and to daytime doses being weaned more aggressively because over-sedation is more visible when someone is watching.
  • That last explanation has support in an older study. Weinert and Calvin studied 274 ventilated adults and found that daytime nursing staff were more likely to judge a patient over-sedated than their nighttime counterparts, despite only small differences in both dosing and patient behaviour. So it is the assessment that shifts with the shift, not only the patient.
  • The evening shift may be the real peak. Pisani et al. studied 309 patients aged 60 and over and found lorazepam and haloperidol doses were higher on evening shifts, 16:00 to midnight, than on day or night shifts.
  • The earlier study: nocturnal increases are common. Seymour et al. 2012 followed 140 ventilated patients from the ABC trial. Nocturnal increases occurred for benzodiazepines on 40% and for propofol on 41% of patient-days, and the increase was associated with failed breathing trials, coma and delirium.

The authors’ own conclusion is the one you are looking for: the findings underscore the importance of minimising sedation at night as well as during the day, and of frequently reassessing the patient’s sedative and analgesic needs, including through the night.

And the rationale does not hold, however well meant. The authors’ most likely explanation is that the patient should get some rest. But propofol and midazolam do not give physiological sleep: they suppress deep NREM and REM rather than providing them, as the cards above in this tab set out. The patient is therefore not rested by the night dose, only more deeply sedated, and the sleep that should have restored the brain is still owed. What then also remains an open question is whether the glymphatic fluid exchange that increases during natural sleep is missed too. Here we should be careful: in the animal experiment where the effect was shown, anaesthesia with ketamine and xylazine actually reproduced the increase in interstitial volume, 22.7% versus 13.6% in awake animals. That weakens the simple inference that sedation necessarily stops it.Interpretation from the sources; see the cards on propofol and midazolam and on the glymphatic system in this tab

Limitations the authors state: the secondary analysis is observational, and association is not causation. Generalisability to shorter-acting agents such as dexmedetomidine and propofol may be limited, since the study concerned benzodiazepines and opioids. No formal pain scale was used. And the similar SAS scores may themselves reflect inaccurate night-time scoring if nurses were reluctant to wake the patient, or a mean SAS insensitive to small but clinically important differences. The authors declare no competing interests. The study was supported in part by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and Mount Sinai Hospital.

On physical restraints: in the study, 76.3% of patients were restrained during the day and 73.7% at night. That is part of the evidence that patients were more awake during the day, but mechanical restraint is not ordinary practice in Norway and is strictly regulated. There the same problem is met with staffing. The figure should not be used as a description of Norwegian intensive care practice.

The figures from Seymour et al. 2012 are reported as Mehta et al. 2016 cite them. The reference itself is confirmed from Mehta’s reference list: Seymour CW, Pandharipande PP, Koestner T, Hudson LD, Thompson JL, Shintani AK, Ely EW, Girard TD. Crit Care Med 2012;40(10):2788–96.

Mehta et al. Crit Care 2016;20:233 Seymour et al. Crit Care Med 2012;40:2788–96 Weinert and Calvin, Crit Care Med 2007;35:393–401 Pisani et al. Am J Crit Care 2013;22:e62–9

Burst suppression at night with no increase in dose: what we know, and where the hypothesis breaks

This is a good clinical observation, and it deserves an honest answer in three parts: the phenomenon is documented, one alternative explanation can be ruled out, and the most obvious mechanism is not supported by the only study that tested it directly.

  • First: the phenomenon is documented, and it is commoner than one would think. Watson et al. 2008 monitored 125 ventilated ICU patients. Burst suppression occurred in 49 of them, 39%, and in 46 of 93 comatose patients, 49%. In none of the records was there any documented intent to induce burst suppression. The authors themselves describe the rate as unexpectedly high. So what you are seeing is not an outlier.
  • And it was not clearly explained by dose. The daily lorazepam dose was higher before burst suppression (27.75 mg versus 7.51 mg, p = 0.004), but the difference was not significant after adjusting for weight. For propofol, morphine and fentanyl there were no significant differences. The authors tested no dose threshold, so the study does not show whether it happened at ordinary doses. But it does show that dose alone did not explain it.
  • The finding is not harmless. Six-month mortality was 59% versus 33%, adjusted hazard ratio 2.04 (95% CI 1.12–3.70, p = 0.02). ICU and hospital mortality pointed the same way but were not significant. The study is post hoc and hypothesis-generating, so it cannot show causation, and burst suppression may mark a sicker brain rather than be the injury itself. The authors also note that intermittent monitoring may have underestimated how often it occurred.
  • One alternative explanation can be crossed off: it is not propofol pharmacology changing across the day. Bienert et al. 2010 measured hourly arterial propofol concentrations and BIS on days 2 and 3 of continuous infusion in ICU patients, looking specifically for circadian rhythm. They found none in either pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics, and none in BIS. Heart rate and body temperature had statistically significant rhythms, but with very small amplitudes, around 4.8% and 0.32% of the mean, and the authors describe the rhythms as severely disturbed compared with healthy people. The study is small, 11 patients with one excluded, and only clinically stable patients without head injury were included. But as far as it goes: the same infusion does not produce a higher effect-site concentration at night.
  • The mechanism you propose has indirect support. García et al. 2021 summarise that surgical stimulation shifts the concentration–response curve: around 2% more desflurane was needed in the presence of stimulation. Turned around, that means the same dose appears relatively deeper when the stimulation is removed. The review does not say this itself, so it is an inference, not a quotation. They also show that epidural blockade completely prevented both the delta and the alpha response to incision, that is, that nociceptive input is indeed what drives those EEG changes.
  • But this is where the simple version breaks. The only randomised study that has manipulated nociceptive input and measured burst suppression directly found the opposite direction. Jung et al. 2019 gave 65 women propofol to an effect-site concentration of 5 µg/mL, and half also received remifentanil to an effect site of 5 ng/mL. The remifentanil group had less burst suppression, not more: at 10 minutes, 8 of 32 controls had burst suppression versus 2 of 33 on remifentanil. BIS did not distinguish the groups at all. The authors’ suggested explanation is that remifentanil in deep anaesthesia increases alpha and reduces delta. So: blocking nociception pharmacologically made the EEG lighter, not deeper.
  • How this may still hang together. Removing external stimuli, noise, light, handling and touch, is not the same as blocking nociception with an opioid. The opioid does something to the EEG through its own chemistry, whether or not there is stimulation to block. So the two findings are not necessarily in conflict, but they are not the same question, and one cannot be used to support the other.
  • And at least two other explanations remain unanswered. Accumulation: Watson et al. link burst suppression in this setting to high cumulative dose over time, and night always comes after a day. And physiological sleep: deep NREM in itself produces slow, high-amplitude activity, and in an EEG under sedation that grey zone can be hard to separate from early suppression. None of the sources above has studied this in ICU patients at night.

What you can say safely: that burst suppression arises with no change in dose is documented and common, that it is associated with increased mortality, and that it is not caused by circadian variation in propofol pharmacology. That reduced stimulation is the cause is a reasonable hypothesis built on an inverted dose–response relationship, and it has not been tested in ICU patients. The most important practical point needs none of the explanations: if the EEG can deepen by itself once the night turns quiet, that is an argument for titrating downward at night rather than upward.

Interpretation from the sources: Watson et al. 2008; Bienert et al. 2010; García et al. 2021; Jung et al. 2019. The synthesis appears in none of them.

Watson et al. Crit Care Med 2008;36:3171–7 Bienert et al. J Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn 2010;37:289–304 García et al. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:445–57 Jung et al. J Clin Med 2019;8:1186

Together: what can lie behind the patient fighting the ventilator

This is a summary across the cards above, not a guideline. The points are in no ranked order. In practice sedation is often the first thing adjusted, and the effect of that varies across the sources.

  • Look at the waveforms. Which dyssynchrony is it? Double-triggering, ineffective triggering, flow or cycling point to different measures.
  • Change the setting that belongs to it. Tidal volume, inspiratory time, flow, PEEP for auto-PEEP. The review calls this the safest route.
  • Rule out pain and whatever is stimulating. Creased sheets, positioning, a full bladder, the tube and suctioning, temperature, catheters. Rising EMG with no dose change warns that something is stimulating the patient, even though it does not say what.
  • Calm the environment. Turn off the ceiling light, use a penlight for night-time care, cluster the care, lower alarm volumes where that is safe. Low risk, low cost, conditionally recommended.
  • Provide light during the day. That is as much of the point as darkness at night, since daytime light levels in the ICU are often too low to entrain the rhythm.
  • Reconsider the dose, downward too. If the dose has crept up across the night, it is worth asking what that increase actually solved.

Interpretation from the sources: Sottile et al. 2020; Stewart et al. 2022; Dorsch et al. 2019; Mehta et al. 2016. The assembly appears in none of them.

Artemiou et al. Kardiochir Torakochirurgia Pol 2015;12:126–133

Children in intensive care: delirium is common, the brain is rarely monitored

Children develop both delirium and seizures without convulsions. Delirium has a validated scale that is strongly recommended, whereas depth of sedation is followed with behavioural scales and not with EEG. Continuous EEG is recorded on indication, and the paediatric intensive care guideline itself calls the usefulness of brain activity monitors an unanswered research question.Sources: PANDEM 2022, Herman 2015, Shi 2026, Zhu 2022, Abend 2013

  • Delirium is common in critically ill children. A meta-analysis of 40 observational studies and 18,875 children found a pooled prevalence of 38.1 % (95 % CI 32.5–43.8). The authors warn against using the figure as a fixed estimate: the prediction interval was 3.6–72.4 %, and individual studies report from 7.7 to 83.8 %. Low figures may also reflect that mild delirium is missed without systematic screening.Source: Shi 2026
  • Benzodiazepines are the risk factor you can change yourself. In a meta-analysis of 10 studies and 4,343 children, benzodiazepine use was associated with delirium (OR 5.05, CI 3.65–6.97), anticholinergic drugs 5.04 (3.62–7.00), mechanical ventilation 4.11 (3.13–5.40) and developmental delay 3.34 (2.46–4.53). Each extra day in paediatric intensive care gave OR 1.10 (1.05–1.15), and children under 2 years had a higher risk than older children. These are observational data, so the associations are not necessarily causal.Source: Zhu 2022
  • The guideline recommends screening, not EEG. PANDEM 2022 strongly recommends, with high quality of evidence, screening for delirium with the psCAM-ICU, pCAM-ICU or CAPD, from admission to discharge, and strongly recommends, with moderate quality, minimising benzodiazepine-based sedation. Level of sedation is assessed with the COMFORT-B Scale or the State Behavioral Scale (strong recommendation, moderate quality), and the patient should be assigned a target depth of sedation at least once daily.Source: PANDEM 2022
  • EEG-based depth monitoring is mentioned only as a possible adjunct. PANDEM 2022 writes that EEG-based monitoring “may be a useful adjunct” for assessing depth of sedation in children receiving neuromuscular blocking agents. It stands as a good practice statement, without graded evidence. According to the guideline, BIS is better suited to trending than to targeting a specific value, and the SNAP II monitor is inadequately studied in paediatric intensive care. No pain or sedation tool has been validated for children receiving neuromuscular blockers.Source: PANDEM 2022
  • The guideline itself treats this as unsettled. Its research questions include the role and usefulness of brain activity-based monitors for assessing depth of sedation, whether such monitors correlate with delirium, and finding objective measures of sleep in paediatric intensive care. So it is not only practice that is missing, but the evidence.Source: PANDEM 2022, table 3
  • Continuous EEG is tied to indications. The ACNS consensus statement, which covers adults and children, lists the indications: diagnosing seizures without convulsions, nonconvulsive status epilepticus and other paroxysmal events; assessing the response to treatment of seizures and status epilepticus; identifying ischaemia in patients at high risk; assessing level of consciousness during intravenous sedation or pharmacologically induced coma; and assessing the severity and prognosis of encephalopathy. For most indications a minimum of 24 hours of recording is recommended. For sedation the wording is weaker, and no study has addressed the optimal timing or duration. Neonates are excluded; they have separate recommendations.Source: Herman 2015
  • Seizures without convulsions are common in children. The ACNS statement reports that they occur in 6–47 % of children with altered mental status, that children may be at higher risk than adults, and infants at higher risk than older children. Of 550 children with continuous EEG in paediatric intensive care, 30 % had electrographic seizures, 38 % of those electrographic status epilepticus, and in 36 % all seizures were without clinical signs.Sources: Herman 2015, Abend 2013. See “Electrographic seizures in children in intensive care (Abend 2013)”
  • Interpretation based on the sources: both delirium and seizures without convulsions are frequent in children, and both are invisible unless someone looks for them. For delirium there is a scale that needs no equipment, and it is strongly recommended. For the brain during sedation there is no equivalent recommendation, and index values from adults fit the youngest children poorly. What remains is to recognise the pattern on the raw EEG and the spectrogram once a monitor is on, and to ask for a full EEG when seizures are suspected.
PANDEM 2022 Herman 2015 Shi 2026 Zhu 2022 Abend 2013
The studies in detail: children in intensive care (4 cards)

Summaries of each article, with numbers and caveats. The theme card above builds on these.

PANDEM 2022: the paediatric intensive care guideline (Smith et al. 2022)

Guideline from the Society of Critical Care Medicine on pain, agitation, neuromuscular blockade and delirium in critically ill children, with the ICU environment and early mobility (Pediatr Crit Care Med 2022;23(2):e74–e110). It applies to the medical, surgical and cardiac paediatric ICU, not routinely to neonatal intensive care.

  • Level of sedation: the COMFORT-B Scale or the State Behavioral Scale is strongly recommended (moderate quality) in mechanically ventilated children. RASS is suggested (conditional, low quality).
