Patients should be assigned a target depth of sedation with a validated tool at least once daily (conditional, low quality).
  • EEG: “Electroencephalogram-based monitoring may be a useful adjunct for assessment of sedation depth in critically ill pediatric patients receiving NMBAs.” This stands as a good practice statement, that is, without a graded quality of evidence. The rationale notes that BIS is better suited to trending sedation depth than to targeting a specific score, that BIS is sensitive to ketamine, and that the SNAP II monitor is inadequately studied in the PICU. No pain or sedation tool has been validated for children receiving neuromuscular blockers.
  • Delirium: strong recommendation (high quality) to use the psCAM-ICU, pCAM-ICU or CAPD, and strong recommendation (high quality) for routine screening from admission through discharge or transfer. The pCAM-ICU was originally validated in children over 5 years, the psCAM-ICU in children under 5 years and later in infants under 6 months. For the CAPD the text gives no age range for the initial validation, but a later reliability study found lower agreement between scorers, particularly in children under 2 years.
  • Benzodiazepines: strong recommendation (moderate quality) to minimise benzodiazepine-based sedation when feasible, to decrease the incidence, duration or severity of delirium. The rationale cites adult randomised trials in which dexmedetomidine gave less delirium than benzodiazepines, and states that comparable PICU studies do not exist.
  • What the authors themselves call unsettled (table 3): the role and utility of brain activity-based monitors for assessing depth of sedation, whether such monitors correlate with delirium, how to detect unintended awareness during neuromuscular blockade, and objective measures of sleep in the PICU.
  • Caveat: a guideline is not a study. The recommendations rest on the literature available in 2022, and several of them are conditional with low quality of evidence.
Smith HAB et al. Pediatr Crit Care Med 2022;23:e74–e110

How common is delirium in critically ill children? (Shi 2026)

Meta-analysis of 40 observational studies with a total of 18,875 critically ill children (Front Pediatr 2026;14:1888789).

  • Main figure: pooled prevalence 38.1 % (95 % CI 32.5–43.8).
  • How uncertain it is: the prediction interval was 3.6–72.4 %. The authors state that the estimate is too heterogeneous to be used as a fixed figure. Earlier studies have reported from 7.7 to 83.8 %.
  • What may explain the spread: higher figures in high-income settings may reflect more systematic screening, and lower figures in middle-income settings may reflect mild delirium going undetected. Several possible moderators, including how often screening was done, could not be analysed because studies did not report them consistently.
  • Caveats: observational studies only, substantial heterogeneity, and different tools and thresholds between studies.
Shi et al. Front Pediatr 2026;14:1888789

Risk factors for delirium in paediatric intensive care (Zhu 2022)

Meta-analysis of 10 studies with 4,343 children (PLoS ONE 2022;17(7):e0270639). The study does not report a pooled prevalence, only risk factors.

  • Drugs: benzodiazepines OR 5.05 (3.65–6.97, 2 studies, 1,635 children) and anticholinergic drugs OR 5.04 (3.62–7.00, 2 studies, 1,703 children).
  • Condition and treatment: mechanical ventilation OR 4.11 (3.13–5.40), developmental delay OR 3.34 (2.46–4.53) and PICU length of stay OR 1.10 per day (1.05–1.15).
  • Age: children aged 2–5 years had OR 0.48 (0.25–0.92) and children aged 5–13 years OR 0.39 (0.26–0.59) compared with children under 2 years. Values below 1 therefore mean a lower risk than in the youngest group. The group over 13 years was not significant (p = 0.060).
  • Caveats: few studies behind each association, observational data only, and the article's own wording about age is misleading: the conclusion lists age as a risk factor, while the figures show that the youngest children are the ones at highest risk. The study does not address physical restraints.
Zhu et al. PLoS ONE 2022;17:e0270639

ACNS consensus: when should continuous EEG be used? (Herman 2015)

Consensus statement from the American Clinical Neurophysiology Society on continuous EEG in critically ill adults and children, part I on indications (J Clin Neurophysiol 2015;32(2):87–95).

  • The indications: diagnosing seizures without convulsions, nonconvulsive status epilepticus and other paroxysmal events; assessing the response to therapy for seizures and status epilepticus; identifying ischaemia in patients at high risk; assessing level of consciousness during intravenous sedation or pharmacologically induced coma; and assessing the severity and prognosis of encephalopathy.
  • Duration: for most indications a minimum of 24 hours of recording is recommended. Longer or shorter recording may be appropriate depending on the patient and the indication.
  • Children: seizures without convulsions occur in 6–47 % of children with altered mental status. Children who had convulsive seizures or generalised convulsive status epilepticus before monitoring are at higher risk. Children may be at higher risk than adults, and infants at higher risk than older children.
  • Sedation: here the wording is weaker than for the other indications, and the statement notes that no studies have addressed the optimal timing or duration for this purpose. Continuous EEG is therefore not recommended for all sedated patients.
  • Scope: the statement applies to critically ill adults and children, not to neonates, who are covered by separate ACNS recommendations.
Herman et al. J Clin Neurophysiol 2015;32:87–95

Key points

  • EEG during poisoning says most about the drug and little about prognosis. In poisoning, burst suppression is not in itself a sign of brain injury. Four patients with alpha or beta coma after poisoning without hypoxia all recovered. Assessment of prognosis and brain death must wait until the drugs have cleared (interpretation based on the sources).See “EEG in toxic coma: patterns that can mislead”
  • Poisoning can mimic brain death. In baclofen poisoning, pupillary reflexes were absent in all nine described cases, and the EEG showed burst suppression. Yet the patient recovered fully. A review found 56 such cases involving 19 different substances.See “EEG in toxic coma: patterns that can mislead”
  • Tolerance and synergy make habitual dosing unreliable. With chronic alcohol use, tolerance is probably mostly a matter of adaptation in the brain, but how much it changes the propofol requirement is not quantified in the sources. Opioids combined with benzodiazepines cause more respiratory depression. The spectrogram can show where the patient actually is (interpretation based on the sources).See “Alcohol: tolerance, induction and withdrawal”, “Opioids, benzodiazepines and gabapentinoids: tolerance and synergy”
  • GHB can cause abrupt coma and abrupt awakening. The half-life is about 20–40 minutes, and patients often wake suddenly. There are no EEG data from GHB poisoning in humans. When used for sedation, GHB produced slow activity, and about one in three had burst suppression.See “GHB: sudden coma, sudden awakening and dangerous withdrawal”
  • Withdrawal can be severe and should be anticipated. GHB withdrawal starts 1–6 hours after the last dose, often fulminant, and lasts 3–21 days. Abrupt discontinuation of benzodiazepines after prolonged sedation can cause withdrawal with seizures. Patients on methadone or buprenorphine should, according to Smith 2022, be allowed to continue it in intensive care.See “GHB: sudden coma, sudden awakening and dangerous withdrawal”, “Opioids, benzodiazepines and gabapentinoids: tolerance and synergy”

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

Poisoning and recreational drugs in intensive care: synergy, tolerance and EEG

Poisoned patients often have several substances in the body at once. Many of them act on the same receptors as the sedatives. This can give a stronger effect (synergy), a weaker effect (tolerance) or withdrawal when the substance wears off. The cards below are based on peer-reviewed literature. Where data are lacking, it says so.

GHB: sudden coma, sudden awakening and dangerous withdrawal
Andresen 2008 Liakoni 2016 Aronsen 2020 Entholzner 1995 Karila 2024
  • How GHB works is unclear. GHB activates GABAB receptors at high concentrations and a separate GHB receptor at low ones.Source: Andresen 2008
  • The patient can arrive in deep coma and wake suddenly (in a Swiss series, awakening was abrupt in 32 %). The picture ranges from alcohol-like intoxication to coma, bradycardia and respiratory depression. The pupils are typically not small, unlike with opioids. The half-life is about 20–40 minutes.Source: Andresen 2008
  • In Oslo most had reduced consciousness, but only one was intubated. Of 329 cases at the Oslo emergency clinic 2013–15, 69% had GCS below 15 and 14% GCS 7 or lower. 29% had also taken alcohol. 9% were given naloxone, and 48% were sent on to hospital.Source: Aronsen 2020
  • Many also take alcohol, but it made no clear difference to coma. In a Swiss series (78 cases), 65% had also taken alcohol or other drugs. With alcohol, coma was somewhat more frequent and lasted somewhat longer, but the differences were not significant. Median time to awakening was 90 minutes, and in 32% it came suddenly.Source: Liakoni 2016
  • There are no human EEG data from GHB poisoning. Used for sedation, GHB (50 mg/kg) gave slow activity (delta–theta or pure delta) and less alpha and beta within 10 minutes. About one patient in three had burst suppression. No seizure activity was seen. Deep GHB coma can therefore probably give a very slow EEG and burst suppression that disappears when the drug is gone (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Entholzner 1995
  • GHB withdrawal comes quickly and can be severe. It starts 1–6 hours after the last dose, often with a fulminant course, and lasts 3–21 days, about 9 on average. High-dose benzodiazepines are first choice. If there is no response after 24 hours, phenobarbital in the ICU is proposed. Propofol and pentobarbital are also mentioned. There are no RCTs.Source: Karila 2024
  • Dexmedetomidine in GHB withdrawal is described in only one case report. It was given as an adjunct in benzodiazepine-resistant delirium, and the patient did not need ventilation. Bradycardia and hypotension limited the dose.Source: Tay 2016

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • The brain makes GHB itself. It is formed from GABA via succinic semialdehyde. In the rare inherited disease SSADH deficiency, the enzyme that converts succinic semialdehyde further is missing, and GHB accumulates.Source: Lee 2022
  • The effects go via GABAB. GABAB is a G-protein-coupled receptor, not an ion channel like GABAA, and the inhibition is slower. In mice lacking GABAB1, GHB no longer reduced activity or body temperature or induced delta waves on the EEG. The GHB binding sites were still present, so they are something other than GABAB.Source: Kaupmann 2003
  • GHB and baclofen both act on GABAB, but on different neurons. In the VTA (ventral tegmental area), GABAB opens potassium channels (GIRK) much more easily in the inhibitory GABA neurons than in the dopamine neurons. Baclofen inhibited both cell types, GHB only the GABA neurons. The dopamine neurons are then released from inhibition. This is a likely explanation for why GHB can be rewarding and addictive, unlike baclofen.Source: Cruz 2004
  • The high-affinity binding site is probably the enzyme CaMKIIα. It appears to be the hub domain of the enzyme. What the binding does is not clear, and it has not been shown to contribute to sedation. Certain GABAA variants have also been proposed as binding sites.Sources: Leurs 2021, Bay 2014
  • The delta waves from GHB require GABAB. They disappeared in mice without GABAB. In narcolepsy, sodium oxybate gave more deep sleep and more delta power. It could not be decided whether this was true sleep or a drug effect resembling anaesthesia.Sources: Kaupmann 2003, Black 2010
  • Benzodiazepines may fall short in GHB withdrawal (interpretation based on the sources). Benzodiazepines enhance GABAA, while the main effects of GHB go via GABAB. How the receptors change with tolerance has only been proposed, not shown in primary studies.Sources: Kaupmann 2003, Bay 2014, Brunt 2014
Alcohol: tolerance, induction and withdrawal
Ultane prescribing information Rayner 2012 Umar 2023
  • The tolerance probably lies mostly in the brain, not in breakdown. Chronic alcohol use can induce CYP2E1, which breaks down sevoflurane. For most anaesthetics, however, the tolerance is probably more related to adaptation in the brain than to faster breakdown (interpretation, not examined in the sources).Source: Ultane prescribing information
  • How much acute intoxication lowers the anaesthetic requirement has not been quantified. No studies on this were found.
  • Dexmedetomidine can spare benzodiazepines in alcohol withdrawal, but should not be used alone. In 20 patients with benzodiazepine-resistant withdrawal, benzodiazepine use fell by 61.5% in the first 24 hours. Heart rate fell by about 23 beats/min, and one patient had two 9-second pauses without a heartbeat. Dexmedetomidine may not prevent withdrawal seizures.Source: Rayner 2012
  • Phenobarbital was associated with a shorter hospital stay. A meta-analysis found a 2.6-day shorter hospital stay, but no clear difference in ICU stay or intubation.Source: Umar 2023
Opioids, benzodiazepines and gabapentinoids: tolerance and synergy
Smith 2022 Midazolam SmPC FDA 2016 Sun 2017 Gomes 2017
  • Patients on methadone or buprenorphine should, according to Smith 2022, be allowed to continue it in intensive care. It is given in addition to analgesia, and the patient should be assessed for withdrawal.Source: Smith 2022
  • Long-term benzodiazepine sedation can cause tolerance and withdrawal. Tolerance may mean the dose has to be increased. Abrupt discontinuation after ICU sedation can cause withdrawal with convulsions. The risk of dependence is higher with a history of alcohol or drug abuse.Source: Midazolam SmPC
  • Opioids and benzodiazepines together give more respiratory depression. In 2016 the FDA added its strongest warning to both. In patients with an opioid prescription, overdose was 2.42% per year with a concurrent benzodiazepine, versus 1.16% without (adjusted OR 2.14).Sources: FDA 2016, Sun 2017
  • Gabapentin together with opioids is associated with more opioid-related deaths. The adjusted OR was 1.49. The interaction between hypnotics and opioids is described in the cards on Hendrickx 2008.Source: Gomes 2017
  • The spectrogram can show where the patient actually is (interpretation based on the sources). Tolerance means that the same dose gives less effect in the brain, and synergy that it gives more. Both make dosing by habit uncertain.
EEG in toxic coma: patterns that can mislead
Rayi (StatPearls) 2025 Carroll and Mastaglia 1979 Sutter and Kaplan 2012 Shanker 2021 Farhat 2020 Murphy 2021
  • Benzodiazepines and barbiturates can give lots of beta. The EEG may then show abundant fast beta activity.Source: Rayi 2025
  • Alpha and beta coma after poisoning can have a good prognosis. Four patients with poisoning without hypoxia had alpha or beta coma, and all recovered. Beta and triphasic patterns may suggest a good prognosis, but this depends on the cause. See also the shared case of alpha coma in a child with benzodiazepine poisoning above.Sources: Carroll and Mastaglia 1979, Sutter and Kaplan 2012
  • Triphasic waves can be caused by drugs. They are also seen in drug-induced encephalopathy, not only in hepatic or renal failure.Source: Rayi 2025
  • In poisoning, burst suppression is not in itself a sign of brain injury. High doses of sevoflurane, barbiturates, propofol and etomidate give burst suppression.Source: Shanker 2021
  • Poisoning can mimic brain death. In baclofen poisoning the pupillary reflexes were absent in all nine reported cases, and the EEG showed burst suppression. The patient nevertheless recovered fully. A review found 56 such cases involving 19 different substances, most often snake envenomation, baclofen, tricyclic antidepressants and bupropion.Sources: Farhat 2020, Murphy 2021
  • In practice, the EEG says most about the drug and little about prognosis (interpretation based on the sources). This applies especially without hypoxia. Assessment of prognosis and brain death must wait until the substances have left the body.

Key points

  • aEEG is a heavily simplified EEG for newborns. The signal from two or four electrodes is filtered, rectified and compressed in time. Many hours then fit on the screen as a band. The upper and lower margins show the highest and lowest voltage. (see “What aEEG is, and how the trace is made”)
  • Read the pattern, not just the voltage. The background is classified as continuous normal, discontinuous normal, burst suppression, low voltage and flat trace. Voltage limits alone can mislead, for example when the ECG or baseline drift lifts the lower margin. (see “The background: pattern and voltage”)
  • aEEG is good for trends and prognosis, but weak for seizures. aEEG identified neonates with seizures with a sensitivity of 71 % and specificity of 84 %, with low certainty. Short seizures and seizures far from the electrodes are missed, and artefacts can look like seizures. Full EEG is the reference. (see “Seizures: aEEG raises suspicion, full EEG gives the answer”)
  • Cooling changes the time frame for prognosis. With cooling, an abnormal aEEG in the first 6 hours means less. Infants with a good outcome had a normal background within 24 hours without cooling and within 48 hours with cooling. (see “Prognosis after oxygen deprivation at birth, with and without cooling (Thoresen 2010)”)
  • Drugs and artefacts can change the trace. Phenobarbital, morphine and midazolam depress the aEEG. The ECG, movement and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation can lift the lower margin or mimic seizures. The raw EEG alongside the band is the most important safeguard. (see “Drugs and artefacts”)
  • Sleep–wake cycling is a good sign. Infants who never developed cycling most often had a poor outcome. (see “Prognosis after oxygen deprivation at birth, with and without cooling (Thoresen 2010)”)

The theme cards below explain the context, with the sources under each point.

What aEEG is, and how the trace is made

aEEG (amplitude-integrated EEG) is widely used in neonatal intensive care because the staff can apply the electrodes and read the trace at the bedside. It shows how the brain's electrical activity changes over hours and days, but says little about the details.

  • aEEG turns the raw EEG into a band. The raw EEG from two or four electrodes is filtered, rectified and compressed in time. The upper and lower margins of the band correspond to the highest and lowest voltage in the raw EEG. The vertical axis is linear from 0 to 10 µV and logarithmic from 10 to 100 µV. This enhances low signals and attenuates high ones. The trace is usually written at 6 cm per hour.Sources: Cochrane 2025, Tao and Mathur 2010
  • The electrodes sit close to the watershed areas. Either one pair over both parietal lobes (P3–P4) or two channels, one on each side (C3–P3 and C4–P4). The watershed areas are often affected by oxygen deprivation at birth, and these positions are less prone to artefacts. Two channels were better than one, especially with injury on one side.Sources: Cochrane 2025, Tao and Mathur 2010
  • The raw EEG alongside the band helps. Newer devices show the raw EEG together with the band. This makes it easier to tell seizures from artefacts.Sources: Cochrane 2025, Tao and Mathur 2010
  • Simplification has a price. With few electrodes and compressed time, short seizures, especially those under 30 seconds, and seizures far from the electrodes are easily missed. Seizure duration is often underestimated.Source: Cochrane 2025
Cochrane 2025 Tao and Mathur 2010 Thoresen 2010

The background: pattern and voltage

The background can be assessed in two ways: by its pattern or by the voltage of the upper and lower margins. The two can be used together.Source: Thoresen 2010

  • The pattern separates normal from abnormal. Continuous normal voltage (CNV) and discontinuous normal voltage (DNV) are regarded as normal. CNV has no periods of low amplitude, whereas DNV has short quiet periods. Burst suppression (BS), low voltage (LV) and flat trace (FT) are regarded as abnormal. Burst suppression means virtually absent activity (below 2 µV) between bursts above 25 µV.Source: Thoresen 2010
  • Voltage can mislead. The ECG and other continuous artefacts can lift the lower margin. Baseline drift can lift the lower margin above 5 µV. Burst suppression may then be read as normal voltage, and an infant who should have been cooled may be missed. Conversely, DNV may end up as moderately abnormal because the quiet periods pull the lower margin down.
  • Always look for the pattern, even when using the voltage limits. The voltage method is easiest for the inexperienced. The pattern method together with the raw EEG performed best. In one study without raw EEG, readers agreed more with the voltage method, but agreement with full EEG was only fair for both methods.Sources: Thoresen 2010, Tao and Mathur 2010
  • Sleep–wake cycling shows as a band that changes width. The variations are regular. A narrow band means wakefulness or active sleep, a wide band means quiet sleep.Source: Tao and Mathur 2010
  • During cooling, drugs act for longer. Anticonvulsant and sedative drugs have a longer half-life during cooling. They may depress the aEEG and delay a normal background and sleep–wake cycling.Source: Thoresen 2010 (discussion)
Thoresen 2010 Tao and Mathur 2010

Prognosis after oxygen deprivation at birth, with and without cooling (Thoresen 2010)

74 term infants with asphyxia, 31 without and 43 with cooling, were followed with aEEG for up to 72 hours and had a developmental test at 18 months.Source: Thoresen, Hellström-Westas, Liu and de Vries, Pediatrics 2010;126:e131–e139

  • An abnormal aEEG in the first 6 hours means less when the infant is cooled. An abnormal pattern (BS, LV or FT) at 3–6 hours predicted a poor outcome with a positive predictive value of 84 % without cooling, but only 59 % with cooling. A normal pattern predicted a good outcome in all 15 cooled infants. Moderately abnormal voltage did not predict outcome.
  • Time to a normal background was the best predictor. All infants with a good outcome had a normal background within 24 hours without cooling and within 48 hours with cooling. All who never regained a normal background had a poor outcome, and 72 % of them died.
  • Without sleep–wake cycling, the outcome was most often poor. 29 of 33 infants who never developed cycling had a poor outcome. In infants with a good outcome, cycling appeared after a median of 24 hours without and 36 hours with cooling.
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): in an infant who is being cooled, a poor aEEG in the first hours should not be read as a verdict. It is the course over the first 48 hours that counts.
  • Caveat: the sample is small. 74 infants from the neonatal units in Bristol between 1998 and 2008, recorded with a single channel (P3–P4). The infants took part in randomised cooling trials. The study was funded in part by the manufacturer of the aEEG device used.
Thoresen et al. Pediatrics 2010 Tao and Mathur 2010

Preterm infants

In preterm infants aEEG is still a field of research, but the patterns change predictably with maturation.Source for the whole card: Tao and Mathur 2010

  • The more immature the infant, the more discontinuous the trace. The background has more bursts and longer periods of low voltage. The proportion of continuous activity increases with gestational age and with age after birth.
  • Cycling can be seen early. Cyclical variations have been seen as early as a mean gestational age of 28 weeks. A cycle was defined as regular variations lasting at least 20 minutes.
  • Brain haemorrhage worsens the trace. Preterm infants under 30 weeks with intraventricular haemorrhage had a more discontinuous trace, more seizures and less cycling, more so the larger the bleed. With progressive ventricular dilatation, the changes appeared before clinical signs of raised pressure. In most, they improved after drainage.
  • Many bursts and early cycling are good signs. More bursts per hour and earlier cycling are associated with better outcomes. Fewer than 130 bursts per hour are associated with poorer outcomes.
Tao and Mathur 2010

Drugs and artefacts

  • Drugs depress the trace, usually transiently. This applies to anticonvulsants and opioids. Phenobarbital gives lower voltage and longer pauses between bursts. Morphine and midazolam act similarly, and the changes were reversed with naloxone. Surfactant also gave less activity and fewer bursts. Three or more anticonvulsants delayed sleep–wake cycling. During cooling the drugs last longer.Sources: Tao and Mathur 2010, Thoresen 2010
  • Artefacts are common. In published studies, artefacts made up 12–60 % of recordings, even with the raw EEG available. The ECG, movement, high-frequency oscillatory ventilation and electrode placement affect the trace.
  • ECG artefact can make a depressed trace look better. When the background is severely depressed, ECG artefact can lift the lower margin. A lower margin above 5 µV may then look more reassuring than it is.
  • Some things look like seizures without being seizures. High-frequency oscillatory ventilation and muscle activity on both sides can produce waves that resemble seizures. Comparison with the raw EEG is important.
  • Interpretation based on the sources: these are the same sources of error as with frontal EEG in adults, and the same answer applies: read the raw EEG, not just the trend.
  • Frontal anaesthesia monitors are not an alternative to aEEG. The knowledge about aEEG, with its voltage limits, timings and accuracy, applies to aEEG with electrodes over central and parietal areas near the watershed zones. No peer-reviewed studies have been found in which frontal monitors of anaesthetic depth were tested for background, seizures or prognosis in neonatal intensive care. Frontal EEG cannot rule out seizures. For anaesthesia in small children, by contrast, frontal EEG has been studied (see Spectrogram → Newborns and preterm).Source: Gimson and Smith 2021
Tao and Mathur 2010 Thoresen 2010

Seizures: aEEG raises suspicion, full EEG gives the answer

Full EEG is the reference for seizures in newborns. A Cochrane review compared aEEG with full EEG in 16 studies with 562 neonates.Source: Rakshasbhuvankar and colleagues, Cochrane 2025

  • Most neonatal seizures cannot be seen. 65–80 % of seizures have no visible signs, and many events that look like seizures are not. Clinical observation alone therefore gives both too few and too many diagnoses.
  • aEEG misses some infants with seizures, and the certainty is low. Sensitivity was 71 % and specificity 84 %. The figures were lower in the three studies with the lowest risk of bias. When aEEG was interpreted at the bedside in real time, sensitivity was 0 and 57 % in the two studies that did so.
  • A seizure shows as a brief rise of the lower margin. Often the upper margin rises too. The raw EEG then shows repetitive discharges that evolve and last at least 10 seconds.
  • Raw EEG and experience decide how many seizures are found. Short seizures, seizures far from the electrodes, low voltage and an inexperienced reader cause seizures to be missed. For individual seizures, sensitivity was 76 % with raw EEG versus 39 % without. Without the raw EEG, neonatologists detected only 12–38 % of individual seizures. With two channels and the raw EEG, sensitivity and specificity approached 80 %. A seizure algorithm detected 73 % of seizures over 30 seconds and 87 % of seizures over 60 seconds.Sources: Cochrane 2025 (earlier review), Tao and Mathur 2010
  • False seizures are most common with bedside reading and among the inexperienced. The causes are muscle movement, patting, hiccups and poor electrode contact.
  • The conclusion: aEEG should not be the main method for treating neonatal seizures. It risks both too little and too much anticonvulsant treatment. Full EEG is recommended for 24 hours in high-risk neonates, but is not available everywhere. aEEG probably adds to clinical observation alone.

The same principle as in adults: a simplified monitor raises suspicion, full EEG and a neurologist give the answer. See also and .

Cochrane 2025 Tao and Mathur 2010

Key points

  • The spectrogram can mirror systemic perfusion. In septic shock, the EEG showed slow theta, delta and suppression that persisted after propofol was stopped. Alpha and beta returned with haemodynamic improvement. Septic encephalopathy also slows the EEG, however, so the cause cannot be separated in a single case.See
  • One-sided suppression does not fit sedation alone. Sedation acts on both hemispheres, so marked one-sided suppression argues against sedation alone being the explanation. New asymmetry should first be checked for technical causes. It should then lead to clinical assessment and imaging, not just an adjustment of sedation (interpretation based on the sources).See “Clinical example: one-sided suppression in an ECMO patient revealed a blood clot (shared case)”
  • Reactivity can be seen in everyday care. In a comatose patient with only delta, power increased from theta into beta when relatives were present. Test reactivity deliberately, note the time and repeat over days. Increased beta can also be EMG, so check the raw EEG and the EMG indicator (interpretation based on the sources).See “Clinical example: comatose patient with only delta responds when relatives visit (shared case)”
  • Alpha coma can be poisoning. In an unconscious child, the EEG showed a strong band around 10–12 Hz, and the cause was a benzodiazepine overdose. Such a picture may raise suspicion of a GABAergic drug, but the diagnosis is made clinically and with tests, not from the EEG alone (interpretation based on the sources).See
  • The examples illustrate, they do not prove. The shared cases are unpublished, not peer reviewed and described from screenshots. A frontal monitor covers only a small part of the cortex.See “Clinical example: one-sided suppression in an ECMO patient revealed a blood clot (shared case)”, “Clinical example: alpha coma in an unconscious child turned out to be benzodiazepine poisoning (shared case)”

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

Clinical example: the spectrogram as a mirror of systemic perfusion in septic shock (Fischer 2026)

Case report from Clínica Universidad de los Andes, Chile. A 70-year-old man without comorbidity, septic shock with multi-organ failure after bowel perforation, APACHE II 29, SOFA 11, three vasoactive agents, high-volume haemofiltration. The unit uses frontal 4-channel pEEG with spectrogram routinely in all patients with continuous sedation or GCS below 8.

  • Early phase (skin hypoperfusion, high lactate): slow theta background (3.5–7 Hz), continuous diffuse delta and periods of suppression. Propofol was stopped because the theta background persisted. Deep sedation, theta and suppression episodes nevertheless continued without sedation.
  • After haemodynamic improvement (adrenaline discontinued, milrinone started, lower vasopressor doses, better skin perfusion and organ function): alpha (8–13 Hz) and beta emerged, the suppression periods disappeared, and consciousness improved to SAS 3/RASS −2. Discharged home, Rankin 2 after six months.
  • The authors link the pattern to reduced cerebral perfusion. Low systemic perfusion coincided with burst suppression and slow waves, even without known vascular disease. On improvement the fast waves returned. This fits the cerebral blood flow thresholds: alpha and beta fall at 25–35 ml/100 g/min, and delta and theta increase below 17–18. Seizures (standard EEG), structural injury (CT), hypothermia and metabolic causes were excluded.
  • Caveats: one patient and no direct measurement of cerebral blood flow. Sepsis encephalopathy in itself gives a slow EEG independent of perfusion, so the cause cannot be separated. The same phenomenon is described in the Perfusion tab.Source: Guay 2025
Fischer et al. Rev Chil Anest 2026;55:234–238

Clinical example: unilateral suppression in an ECMO patient revealed a blood clot (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed. It is described from one screenshot of the spectrogram over about 17 minutes and information from the person who shared it. The screenshot is not reproduced in the app.

  • The patient: an ICU patient with COVID-19 on ECMO, sedated.
  • What the spectrogram showed: a clear difference between the hemispheres. In the upper panel activity was almost absent, interrupted only by short, scattered bursts, a picture resembling burst suppression. In the lower panel there was continuous activity with power in delta and even, low power up towards 30 Hz.
  • The course: according to the person who shared the case, there was a blood clot in the brain. It showed up nowhere other than in the EEG, and the patient was sent for intervention and recovered.
  • Unilateral suppression does not fit with sedation alone. In a sedated patient the neurological examination is severely limited, and a stroke can be missed. Sedation acts on both hemispheres, so marked unilateral suppression argues against sedation alone being the explanation. Ischaemia can cause loss of activity and asymmetry. A similar asymmetry has been seen with carotid stenosis and low blood pressure.Sources: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016, Sheorajpanday 2009, Nycz 2022
  • What to do (interpretation based on the sources): new or increasing asymmetry should first be checked for technical causes such as electrode contact and impedance. If the signal is good, it should prompt clinical assessment and imaging, not just adjustment of sedation.
  • Caveats: one case, described from one screenshot. It is not known which side and which vessel were affected, or which drugs and doses the patient received. A frontal monitor covers only a small part of the cortex and can miss infarcts elsewhere.
Shared clinical example van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016, Sheorajpanday 2009, Nycz 2022

Clinical example: comatose patient with only delta reacts when relatives visit (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed. It is described from two screenshots of the spectrogram and information from the person who shared it. The screenshots are not reproduced in the app.

  • The patient: a comatose ICU patient without sedation, with an EEG that for long periods showed only delta.
  • Without visitors: in one picture (about 20 minutes) the power in both hemispheres lay below about 4 Hz, with very little activity above. The picture was stable without changes.
  • With relatives present: in the other picture, power from theta up into beta, about 15–30 Hz, increased in both hemispheres in periods, while delta persisted.
  • Preserved reactivity favours a good outcome, and it may return late. EEG reactivity means that frequency or amplitude changes when the patient is stimulated. Reactivity distinguishes between coma states better than the pattern itself. Preserved reactivity favours a good outcome after anoxic brain injury. In three patients who eventually became independent after prolonged coma following cardiac arrest, reactivity returned after 3, 8 and 73 days. This case shows that relatives' voices and touch can produce a reaction visible on a frontal monitor.Sources: Sutter and Kaplan 2012, Ko and Engelhard 2025, Forgacs 2020
  • What can be done (interpretation based on the sources): test reactivity deliberately, with speech, touch and possibly a noxious stimulus. Note the time so the change can be found in the spectrogram. Repeat the test over days, since reactivity may return late.
  • Caveats: increased beta can also come from muscle activity (EMG), movement or other artefacts, so the raw EEG and the EMG indicator should be checked. Formal assessment of reactivity is done with standardised stimuli and a full EEG. One case, and the patient's outcome is not known.
Shared clinical example Sutter and Kaplan 2012, Ko and Engelhard 2025, Forgacs 2020

Clinical example: alpha coma in an unconscious child turned out to be benzodiazepine poisoning (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed. It is described from one screenshot and information from the person who shared it. The screenshot is not reproduced in the app.

  • The patient: an unconscious 3-year-old child. At first it was unclear what had happened.
  • What the EEG showed: a strong, continuous band around 10–12 Hz in both hemispheres, together with delta, and little activity above about 20 Hz. The pattern was symmetrical and stable over about 20 minutes. The raw EEG showed regular, high-amplitude waves in the alpha range. The index was 34.
  • The explanation: it turned out to be a benzodiazepine overdose.
  • The same alpha pattern can mean very different things depending on the cause. Alpha coma is alpha activity (8–13 Hz) in a patient who cannot be roused. Alpha is mostly seen frontally. In poisoning, for example with barbiturates, benzodiazepines and anaesthetics, alpha is more diffuse, reactivity is usually preserved and up to 90% recover. With brainstem lesions, alpha is posterior and often varies with external stimuli, but the prognosis is poor. After cardiac arrest (hypoxic-ischaemic injury), alpha is also more diffuse, but reactivity is usually absent and the outcome is mostly poor. So it is the cause and the reactivity, not the location, that distinguish poisoning from cardiac arrest.Source: Sutter and Kaplan 2012
  • Why it is instructive (interpretation based on the sources): the pattern resembles alpha–delta under anaesthesia with propofol or sevoflurane. Benzodiazepines also act on the GABAA receptor (see the Drugs tab), and children generally have stronger alpha under GABAergic anaesthesia than adults. In an unconscious patient of unknown cause, such a picture may therefore raise suspicion of a GABAergic drug. The diagnosis is nevertheless made clinically and with tests, not from the EEG alone.Sources: Lee 2017, Akeju 2015
  • Caveats: one case, described from one screenshot. The source on alpha coma mainly discusses adults. It is not known which benzodiazepine or dose, whether reactivity was tested, or how the child fared.
Shared clinical example Sutter and Kaplan 2012, Lee 2017, Akeju 2015
Fundamentals: what EEG is and how it is measured

Basics: what EEG is, how it is measured and what it cannot tell you. This tab is for readers new to EEG, and the other tabs build on it. The main message is that EEG is the only routine measure of the brain's electrical activity, that a TCI pump shows a prediction rather than a measurement, and that the index number must always be read together with the raw EEG and spectrogram.

Raw EEG, frequency bands and spectrogram

Key points

  • EEG measures the target organ itself. The signal arises from summed postsynaptic potentials in cortical pyramidal cells and shows cortical function in real time, not structure. During anaesthesia it is the only routine measure of the brain's electrical activity.See
  • A frequency band is a description, not a mechanism. Frontal alpha under propofol has a different origin from posterior alpha in an awake person with closed eyes, even though both are 8–13 Hz. A frontal monitor does not see the posterior alpha.See
  • What looks like gamma is often muscle. Gamma is attenuated by skull and skin and overlaps with muscle activity. In a patient without neuromuscular blockade, “gamma” on a frontal monitor is therefore often EMG from the forehead and eye muscles.See
  • Frontal monitors have a limited view. They use only the front part of the 10–20 system. That is enough for frontal alpha and slow activity, but not for localising seizures or seeing posterior alpha. Only sensors with electrodes over both sides can show asymmetry.See
  • The pattern tells you more than the number. Sustained alpha spindles around 10 Hz coupled to slow delta suggest adequate hypnosis under propofol and volatile agents. This does not apply to ketamine or nitrous oxide, and older patients produce weaker alpha. Burst suppression and sustained suppression are the clearest, though non-specific, signs of too much.See “An ‘imperfect but useful mirror’: an introduction to EEG monitoring (Hight 2020)”

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

What EEG is

  • EEG is the sum of many small potentials in the cortex. It consists of voltage differences in microvolts between electrodes on the scalp. They are created by summed postsynaptic potentials in large populations of cortical pyramidal cells lying in parallel. Action potentials contribute little. The signal from deep structures weakens with the square of the distance, and skull and skin attenuate the fast frequencies in particular.
  • The first human EEG was recorded in 1924 and published in 1929. Caton recorded spontaneous potentials from the animal brain in 1875. Hans Berger in Jena later made single-channel recordings in humans, first in patients with skull defects, and published the first human EEG in 1929. He described alpha and beta waves, alpha blocking on visual stimulation, and the difference between adults and infants. Adrian and Matthews confirmed the findings in 1934 and gave Berger the credit.
  • EEG shows how the cortex is working, not what the patient is thinking. EEG describes cortical function in real time, not structure. During anaesthesia it is the only routine measure of the brain's electrical activity; all other monitors measure circulation, respiration or drug concentration.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 4

A weak signal: electrodes, impedance and noise

  • EEG is much weaker than the ECG. EEG on the scalp is about 1–100 µV, while the ECG on the skin is about 1–2 mV. EEG is therefore ten to several thousand times weaker.Source: Brown and Gupta 2008
  • This is why noise easily becomes larger than the brain signal. Muscles, eye movements, the mains supply (50 Hz), diathermy and poor electrode contact produce signals that can drown out the EEG.Source: Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • Impedance is the resistance between skin and electrode. High impedance, and especially unequal impedance between the electrodes, makes the EEG more susceptible to noise from the mains. The skin is prepared to obtain low and equal impedance.Sources: Ferree 2001; Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • An impedance alarm means poor contact, not a change in the brain. A loose electrode or a broken cable gives noise, an impedance alarm or many artefacts. A truly flat EEG has normal impedance in all channels.Sources: Guay 2025; Ching 2012
  • Check the scale, as you would on an ECG. The gain (µV/mm) and the colour scale determine how strong the EEG looks. Check the settings at the start of every anaesthetic.Source: Hight 2020

The frequency bands

  • A band is a description, not a mechanism. The same frequency can have different origins. Frontal alpha under propofol (it arises in loops between the thalamus and the cortex, see the Spectrogram tab) is not the same as posterior alpha in an awake person with eyes closed, even though both are 8–13 Hz.
  • Posterior alpha weakens when the eyes open, and also shows how activated the brain is. In an awake person resting with closed eyes, alpha is strongest at the back of the head. This is called the posterior dominant rhythm. When the eyes open, alpha becomes weaker. This was described in the very first EEG recordings of humans and is still used to test whether the EEG reacts. The reason is not only visual input: alpha falls evenly across the whole head, not only at the back, and at the same time skin conductance rises, which is a measure of how activated the body is. The other frequency bands change more in specific areas, which is interpreted as processing of what is seen. In short: at rest much alpha, with increased activation less alpha.Source: Barry 2007 (28 students)
  • Alpha may be active inhibition. A widely used explanation is that alpha marks areas that are inhibited because they are not needed at the moment, so that information is routed to the areas in use (“gating by inhibition”). With eyes closed the visual cortex has little to do and shows much alpha; when it is engaged, alpha falls. This is a well-supported hypothesis, not definitively proven.Source: Jensen and Mazaheri 2010
  • What it means for anaesthesia and intensive care (interpretation based on the sources): a frontal monitor does not see posterior alpha, but often sees alpha coma. At loss of consciousness under propofol the posterior alpha disappears and a frontal alpha with a different origin appears (see the Components tab). So a frontal monitor does not see the normal alpha of an awake person with closed eyes. Alpha coma is something else: the alpha is mostly seen frontally, unlike the posterior distribution of healthy subjects. The distribution nevertheless depends on the cause: more diffuse alpha in poisoning and hypoxic-ischaemic injury, posterior alpha with brainstem lesions, and incomplete forms may also have a more posterior alpha. A frontal monitor can therefore often see alpha coma, but not every form. In intensive care, reactivity is the key: alpha that changes with stimulation suggests preserved function, while alpha that does not react may be alpha coma (see the Intensive care tab). Reactivity is formally assessed with standardised stimuli and full EEG. On a frontal monitor a change with stimulation can be seen in the spectrogram, but increased fast activity may also be EMG, so the raw EEG and the EMG indicator must be checked (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Purdon 2013; Sutter and Kaplan 2012; Degano 2025; Amoranto and Fernandez 2024
  • The EEG signal is so small that noise easily outgrows it. EEG is measured in microvolts (µV), millionths of a volt. Interference from muscles, eye movements, the mains (50 Hz), diathermy or poor electrode contact easily becomes larger than the brain signal itself. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) decides what can be interpreted. Low and equal impedance and good skin preparation therefore matter a great deal (see the card “Electrodes” below). Amplitude also falls with age.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti ch. 4; Purdon 2015; Obert 2024
  • An image: the rowing wave in the stands. Think of the rowing wave Norwegian supporters made during the 2026 football World Cup, which received international attention: thousands sit down on the benches and row in the same calm rhythm while shouting “Ro!” (“Row!”), and the whole stand moves as one large, slow wave. That is what slow waves in the EEG are like: large networks of neurons work in synchrony, and the deflection becomes large. Fast waves resemble the rest of the stadium: some clap, some shout, some take flash photos, but not in time. The result is many small movements that do not add up, and the deflection is small. Fast activity with large amplitude does not fit the picture, and usually comes from muscle, not from the brain (see the points below).
  • Slow waves have high amplitude, fast waves low (1/f). EEG power falls steadily with frequency (see “Aperiodic EEG activity”). Amplitude depends on how many neurons are active in synchrony, and the larger the network involved, the lower the frequency. The reason lies in the brain’s physical architecture: most connections between neurons are local, and signals take time to travel through axons and synapses. Fast rhythms therefore stay within a small area, whereas slow rhythms can recruit very large, synchronous networks. Sustained fast activity with high amplitude therefore does not come from the cortex, but from muscle (EMG) or other artefacts (interpretation based on the sources). This makes strong EMG easy to see in the raw EEG.Sources: Avella Gonzalez 2014; Lea-Carnall 2016; Buzsáki and Draguhn 2004
  • What looks like beta and gamma on a frontal monitor is often muscle. Gamma from the brain has very low amplitude and is largely filtered out by skull and skin. Muscle activity lies in the same frequency range (about 20–300 Hz), but can reach about 100 µV in EEG, whereas high-frequency brain activity may be below 1 µV, several orders of magnitude smaller. Strong EMG is therefore easy to see in the raw EEG as fast activity with high amplitude. The difficulty is weak, sustained muscle tension, which can pass visual screening. In volunteers who were paralysed, even “clean” resting EEG turned out to be heavily contaminated by muscle activity above about 20 Hz: without paralysis, power was about 5 times higher at 40 Hz and about 10 times higher at 80 Hz. In a patient without neuromuscular blockers, beta and gamma in the spectrogram are therefore often EMG from the forehead and temples, even when the raw EEG looks calm. Frontal EMG, blinking and eye movements, together with low amplitude and fast activity, are precisely what characterise an awake EEG.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti ch. 4 (30–80 Hz is “typically filtered out by the skull and not visible on conventional surface EEG”); Muthukumaraswamy 2013
  • Without EMG, the index can read “asleep” in an awake patient. Awake volunteers given neuromuscular blockers were fully awake and calculated correctly. Even so, BIS fell to 44–47, and Entropy and qCON fell below 60 in most trials. These indices thus need muscle activity (EMG) to generate correct values in an awake person, and may therefore be unreliable for detecting awareness when the patient has received neuromuscular blockers. The raw EEG still looked awake, with low amplitude and fast activity, just without EMG and eye movements. So it is the index that becomes misleading, not the EEG (see Schuller 2015 and Hight 2017 in the Spectrogram tab).Sources: Schuller 2015 (BIS); Schuller 2023 (Entropy, 17 of 19 trials); Schuller 2025 (qCON, 15 of 19 trials)
  • Ketamine can produce real low gamma, but on the monitor it may still be EMG. Low gamma (25–40 Hz) under ketamine has been demonstrated with surface EEG in research studies. On a clinical monitor without neuromuscular blockers, part of what is shown as gamma may still be weak EMG, because weak muscle activity is not always visible in the raw EEG (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Purdon 2015; Vlisides 2017
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 4 and 5

Electrodes, the 10–20 system and frontal monitors

  • The 10–20 system gives the electrodes fixed positions. Electrodes are placed at 10% and 20% of the distances nasion–inion and between the preauricular points. The letters denote region (Fp frontopolar, F frontal, C central, T temporal, P parietal, O occipital), odd numbers left, even numbers right, z the midline. The standard set-up has 21 positions; the IFCN now recommends 25 with an inferior temporal row. Note that F7 and F8 actually lie over the anterior temporal lobe.
  • Impedance should be low and balanced. Modern equipment accepts up to 10 kΩ as long as the electrodes are balanced; below 100 Ω suggests a salt bridge or a fault. The skin is prepared to lower the impedance.
  • Too high a high-pass filter can hide the slow activity that anaesthesia produces. The differential amplifier measures the difference between two inputs (active and reference) against ground. Before digitisation an anti-aliasing filter is used (Nyquist: the sampling frequency must be at least twice the highest frequency, recommended at least 256 Hz). For display, a low-pass filter (commonly 70 Hz), a high-pass filter (0.5–1 Hz) and a notch filter (50 Hz in Europe) are used.
  • Bipolar and referential montages complement each other. A bipolar montage shows the difference between two neighbouring electrodes. A referential montage shows each electrode against a common reference (ear, Cz or average). Both should be used, because they give complementary information; neither of them is “old-fashioned”. The Laplacian montage uses a weighted average of the neighbouring electrodes as a local reference.
  • Frontal anaesthesia monitors see only the front of the head. All use only the anterior part of the 10–20 system. The sensors vary: some have four channels over both sides (F7, Fp1, Fp2, F8), others have electrodes over one side of the forehead or one to two channels. Only sensors with electrodes over both sides can show asymmetry. Common to all: they are sufficient for frontal alpha and slow activity under GABAergic agents, but not for lateralisation further back, seizure localisation or posterior alpha, and a unilateral sensor cannot tell the sides apart (see Nycz 2022 in the Perfusion tab). That is why the ICU literature distinguishes between questions that can be answered with a simplified montage and questions that require full 10–20.Sources: Mehler 2024 (four-channel montage); Rasulo 2023; Taccone 2026
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 4; Mehler 2024 (four-channel montage)

Aperiodic EEG activity (“1/f”): the background is signal, not noise

New research, not yet clinical practice. The card is included because it helps explain why the same change on the monitor can have different causes. As far as the sources show, no monitor displays this today.

What it is: the spectrogram splits the EEG into frequencies. You then see two things at once:

  • The rhythms: clear bands at particular frequencies, for example alpha around 10 Hz under propofol. This is called the periodic part.
  • The background: an even “foundation” that is always there, even when there is no rhythm. It is strongest at the slow frequencies and becomes weaker the faster the frequency. This is called the aperiodic part (without a fixed rhythm), or “1/f”, because power falls roughly as 1 divided by the frequency.
  • The slope: how quickly the background falls from slow to fast frequencies. A steep slope means much slow and little fast activity. A flat slope means relatively more fast activity.

Why it is useful to know: when the power in a frequency band changes, it may be because the rhythm changes, because the background changes, or both. The monitor does not distinguish between them. One example is weak alpha in older patients: some of it is a weaker alpha rhythm, and some is a lower background. The figure shows the principle.Sources: Tröndle 2023; Leroy 2023

What research has shown so far:

  • The slope separates wakefulness from both anaesthesia and sleep, including REM sleep. In one of the early human studies (2020), the background between 30 and 45 Hz became steeper under propofol, both in scalp EEG and with electrodes inside the brain (470 of 485 depth electrodes, 96.9%). It also separated wakefulness from deep sleep and from REM sleep, which otherwise resembles wakefulness in the EEG. The slope correctly classified awake versus propofol anaesthesia in approx. 77% of cases, compared with approx. 52% for slow waves. Caveats: small groups (9 and 12 patients under anaesthesia), and all received midazolam premedication, which the authors suggest may have increased slow waves already before induction. The anaesthesia data are from Oslo University Hospital. The study did not test use in clinical monitoring. Frontal EEG at 30–45 Hz can also contain muscle activity (EMG), so the slope can hardly be read directly from an anaesthesia monitor (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Lendner 2020
  • Anaesthesia makes the background steeper. In one study the slope separated awake from anaesthetised patients very well.Source: Widmann 2025
  • Age makes it flatter. At rest, older people have a lower and flatter background than young people. Under propofol, much of the difference between young and old lay in the background, not in the rhythms.Sources: Tröndle 2023; Leroy 2023
  • Alpha frequency falls with age, but whether alpha also becomes weaker is unresolved. That alpha frequency falls with age is well documented in large studies. Lower alpha frequency predicted greater cognitive decline over ten years, particularly when alpha frequency and background did not match. A large atlas shows that alpha frequency rises in childhood, stays high through young and middle adulthood and falls later, but it is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed. All these studies find that the background becomes flatter with age. Whether the alpha rhythm itself becomes weaker is disputed: three studies found weaker alpha even after subtracting the background (in one of them mostly posteriorly, while beta was stronger over sensorimotor areas in older adults), whereas one large study found no age difference in alpha power when controlling for the background. The studies concern resting EEG in awake people, not alpha under anaesthesia.Sources: Cesnaite 2023 (1703 people, mean age 70); Finley 2024 (235 people); Bonyadian 2026 (2172 people, aged 5 to 89, preprint); Donoghue 2020; Tröndle 2023; Park 2025 (54 people)
  • Caveats: few and small studies, the numbers depend on the analysis method, and values from different studies cannot be compared directly.

How is it calculated? From Fourier to FOOOF

  1. Fourier gives the spectrum. The raw EEG is divided into short windows, and the Fourier transform breaks each window down into sine waves of different frequency. The result is a power spectrum: how much power there is at each frequency. This is the same as what lies behind the spectrogram. Fourier does not distinguish rhythm from background: all power at 10 Hz is counted as “alpha”, whether it comes from an alpha rhythm or from the background.
  2. FOOOF separates rhythm from background. FOOOF stands for “fitting oscillations and one over f”. The method takes the spectrum from step 1 and does four things:
    • first draws a line through the background, ignoring the peaks;
    • subtracts the line, so that only the peaks remain;
    • finds the peaks one by one as bell-shaped curves, as long as they rise above the noise level;
    • redraws the background line without the peaks, so that it becomes more precise.
    Source: Donoghue 2020
  3. What you get. For the background: the level (offset), the slope (the exponent) and possibly a “knee” where the line bends. For each rhythm: the frequency of the peak, how high it rises above the background, and how wide it is.
  4. Without FOOOF the age difference in alpha may be exaggerated. The same fall in “alpha power” may be due to the rhythm becoming weaker, the peak shifting (for example from 10 to 8 Hz), or the background changing. A frequency band can also show power without a real rhythm being there. FOOOF separates these. An example from resting EEG: older adults (60–70 years, n = 14) had a lower alpha frequency than young adults (20–30 years, n = 16) (9.6 versus 10.7 Hz), weaker alpha above the background and a flatter background (exponent 0.75 versus 1.43). The age difference in alpha is exaggerated when rhythm and background are not separated, partly because more of the older adults’ alpha lies below 8 Hz, outside the usual alpha band. The result still depends on the settings, for example whether a knee is included or not.Source: Donoghue 2020

More on Fourier and the spectrogram:

The studies in detail (numbers and method)
  • The exponent followed hypnosis in one study. Frontal EEG in 62 awake subjects and 125 during maintenance with propofol, sevoflurane or desflurane was decomposed with the FOOOF algorithm. α was 1.61 awake versus 2.60 under anaesthesia (AUC 0.98). When the usual spectral parameters (beta ratio, SEF95, spectral entropy, alpha/delta ratio) were computed on the aperiodic model alone instead of the whole spectrum, the ability to separate awake from anaesthetised rose from AUC 0.71–0.95 to 0.98 for all four, on a par with permutation and approximate entropy. The interpretation is that the aperiodic part reflects the hypnotic component, while the periodic oscillations, especially alpha, disturb the indices and rather say something about the quality of the anaesthesia (nociception, frailty) than about the level of consciousness. Simulations link α to the balance between synaptic excitation and inhibition.Sources: Widmann 2025 (BJA); Gao 2017 (simulations)
  • Much of the age difference at loss of consciousness appears to lie in the background (small pilot). 9 young (18–30 years) and 14 older (over 70 years) subjects were followed during manual propofol induction with 21 electrodes. Loss of consciousness produced an increased exponent and offset in both groups, the alpha peak shifted from about 10 to 11 Hz, and the adjusted alpha power above the background increased. The older subjects received half the propofol dose (1.8 versus 3.4 mg/kg), but 4 of 14 developed burst suppression versus 2 of 9 young. The young showed a “travelling” burst of power from gamma via beta to alpha around loss of consciousness (as in Purdon 2013), and in 8 of 9 young the exponent fell just before loss of consciousness, consistent with paradoxical excitation. When the background was subtracted, older and young looked far more alike. Exploratory pilot without correction for multiple testing.Source: Leroy 2023
  • Separating out the background changes the interpretation. According to Connor 2026, today's indices compute on the whole spectrum and treat all agents alike. Furthermore, when the aperiodic part is subtracted, alpha and beta rise before loss of consciousness, while delta rises abruptly at loss of consciousness.Sources: Connor 2026 (editorial); Brake 2024
  • This fits with other findings on age and alpha. Lower power in older patients has been described before; much of that may be the background, not the rhythms. Alpha as a “quality marker” fits with findings on nociception, delirium and low alpha with a propensity for burst suppression. As far as the sources show, no commercial monitor displays the exponent today; this is research, not a clinical tool.Sources: Kratzer 2020 and Purdon 2015 (BJA, lower power); Leroy 2023 (background); García 2021 (nociception); Gutiérrez 2019 (delirium); Shao 2020 (burst suppression)
  • Conventional analysis may overestimate the age difference in alpha. Eyes-closed resting EEG in healthy young and older adults, 533 people pooled across three samples. Total alpha power was lower in older adults, but the offset and slope of the background were also lower (a flatter line). Because the whole spectrum shifts, conventional analysis of total alpha power may overestimate the age difference. When the background was removed, adjusted alpha power was still lower in older adults. This is resting EEG without anaesthesia.Source: Tröndle 2023 (registered report, Cortex)
  • The direction is not the same (interpretation based on the sources): at rest the background becomes flatter with age, whereas anaesthesia makes it steeper. Lower total alpha in an older patient may therefore reflect both less rhythmic alpha and a lower background, and the numbers on the monitor do not separate them.Sources: Tröndle 2023; Widmann 2025
  • Caveats: Widmann is a signal-analytic study without control for doses or age. The FOOOF settings (with or without a “knee” around 20 Hz) affect the numbers, so exponent values from different studies cannot be compared directly. Conflicts of interest: Kreuzer, García, Kratzer and Schneider hold patents on intraoperative EEG analysis, García is co-founder of Lantern Laboratories, Kreuzer has received funds from Masimo, Narcotrend, Medtronic and Fresenius for EEG teaching; Koch (Leroy 2023) holds patents sold to Medtronic. Connor reports none of relevance.

Typical tendencies, not diagnostic criteria

Younger, more robust brainOlder or more vulnerable brain
Total EEG power under anaesthesiaHigherLower (Purdon 2015, Kratzer 2020)
Frontal alpha under propofol and volatile agentsClearWeaker or absent; low alpha is linked to a greater tendency to burst suppression (Shao 2020)
Aperiodic backgroundReferenceAt rest lower and flatter (Tröndle 2023); under propofol much of the age difference lies in the background (Leroy 2023)
Burst suppressionLess frequentMore frequent, even at lower doses: 4 of 14 older patients on half the dose versus 2 of 9 young (Leroy 2023)

Age, drug, dose, haemodynamics, artefacts and suppression all affect the EEG. Low alpha or a changed slope alone shows neither excessively deep anaesthesia nor a vulnerable brain. EEG-based “frailty scores” mostly measured age.Source: Ostertag 2025 (see the Spectrogram tab)

Widmann 2025, Leroy 2023, Connor 2026, Tröndle 2023

An “imperfect but useful mirror”: an introduction to EEG monitoring (Hight 2020)

Course and review article (Continuing Professional Development) in Can J Anesth 2020 by Hight, Kaiser, Sleigh and Avidan. It deals with raw EEG and the spectrogram, explicitly not with the proprietary indices. Much of the content is covered in more detail in the Spectrogram tab; here is what it adds.

  • EEG can be displayed in three ways: raw EEG, power spectrum and spectrogram. Raw EEG (amplitude over time), power spectrum (power per frequency) and spectrogram/DSA (power per frequency over time). The frequency bands are arbitrarily defined and do not reflect the biology of the brain, and Fourier analysis in bands can lose information (for example phase-amplitude coupling between delta and alpha).
  • Sustained alpha spindles suggest adequate hypnosis. The pattern is alpha spindles around 10 Hz, phase-amplitude coupled with slow delta around 1 Hz, under propofol and volatile agents. Exceptions: ketamine and nitrous oxide do not produce the pattern, and older patients and patients with neurodegenerative disease produce weaker alpha.
  • Faster and intermittent spindles suggest too little. As the dose falls, the spindle frequency increases before the spindles become intermittent and disappear. There is a risk of underdosing during “Mind the Gap” (transport without end-tidal measurement) and with propofol plus neuromuscular blockers.
  • Burst suppression and sustained suppression suggest too much. They are the clearest, but non-specific, signs. MAC is defined by movement (spinal cord), not cortex, so an EEG-based MAC could say more about the effect on the brain. An association between suppression time and delirium has been shown, but “it is not yet clear whether prolonged EEG suppression is harmful”.
  • With delta arousal, consider analgesia rather than reducing the anaesthetic agent. Nociceptive responses are beta arousal, delta arousal (first reported in the early 1990s, “rarely heeded since”) and alpha dropout. Delta arousal may be a sign of endogenous antinociception.
  • A lower concentration is needed to wake up than to lose consciousness (neural inertia). This has been described in fruit flies, mice and humans (in humans the findings are debated, see Induction and emergence), and is more pronounced when the arousal systems are weakened (age, narcolepsy, droperidol, clonidine, antimuscarinic agents). So be cautious about lowering the concentration below the one that produced unconsciousness in reliance on an “anaesthesia pattern”: once consciousness returns, a large dose increase may be required. MACawake is probably lower than the MAC for loss of consciousness.
  • A frontal “deep” pattern does not exclude connected consciousness. The isolated forearm shows this (no reports during burst suppression), and the reason is unresolved. Perhaps the forehead is the wrong place (posterior “hot zone”), or consciousness depends on connectivity between regions (frontoparietal, also for ketamine). Avidan is a co-author here and lead author of the “black swans” commentary in the Components tab.
  • EEG was proposed for anaesthesia as early as 1937. Gibbs, Gibbs and Lennox then recommended that anaesthetists should use EEG routinely. The idea is thus almost 90 years old, not a new trend. Even so, EEG has not become a fixed standard the way pulse oximetry and capnography did (see ).
  • Conflicts of interest: none declared. The article was funded by the Bangerter-Rhyner Foundation and Inselspital.
Hight, Kaiser, Sleigh, Avidan. Can J Anesth 2020

Key points

  • The number is used, the curves rarely. Almost everyone uses the index value. Only a small minority use the raw EEG, spectrogram and suppression ratio. Only 27 % said they could recognise burst suppression, and 86 % wanted more knowledge.Source: Aasheim 2024 (see “How the monitors are used in Norwegian practice”)
  • The sickest are monitored least and lie deepest. At OUS only 21 % of patients receiving muscle relaxants had BIS. At least 5 minutes below BIS 30 occurred in about 26 % in ASA 1 and 50 % in ASA 4. The study is observational and does not show cause.Source: Aasheim 2026 (see “How the monitors are used in Norwegian practice”)
  • The same number means different things on different monitors. The monitors calculate differently and use different scales, and two monitors on the same patient often disagreed. Indices are algorithms with many sources of error. Interpret the raw EEG and spectrogram, not the number.Source: Schneider 2004 (see “Same number, different scale: the indices cannot be compared directly”)
  • If the index is unexpected or changes abruptly, work through the sources of error. Ketamine can raise the index. Dexmedetomidine, neuromuscular blockers, ephedrine and magnesium can shift it regardless of hypnotic depth. Rule out dosing errors first, and look at the raw EEG and spectrogram before changing the dose.Sources: Pinheiro 2026, Takizawa 2006, Altıparmak 2018 (see “When the EEG index surprises: the sources of error”)
  • The standard only requires measurement of muscle relaxation. The Norwegian standard 2024 requires neuromuscular monitoring. Consciousness is to be assessed with clinical signs, but these have been shown to be unreliable under neuromuscular block. Monitoring of anaesthesia depth “must be individually considered”. The British guideline states that processed EEG should be used with TIVA and neuromuscular blockade, and that the index value alone should not be relied upon.Sources: Leonardsen 2024, Klein 2021 (see “What the standards require”)
  • The same evidence standard for every monitor. A common argument against EEG is that large studies have not shown better outcomes. Neither has pulse oximetry: it detected more episodes of low SpO₂, but did not reduce complications or mortality. Pulse oximetry and capnography nevertheless became standard because they show something we would otherwise not see, and give early warning of deterioration. That does not mean EEG is proven useful, but that EEG should be judged by the same standard as the other monitors (the author's assessment based on the sources).Sources: Pedersen 2014, Aitkenhead ch. 18 (see “The demand for proof: pulse oximetry and capnography became standard without outcome studies”)

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Same number, different scale: the indices cannot be compared directly

A number such as “index 25” or “index 40” means nothing until you know which monitor it comes from. The monitors calculate differently and use different scales. Indices are algorithms with many sources of error, and it is the raw EEG and spectrogram that should be interpreted.

  • Each monitor has its own scale. The same number can therefore mean different things on different monitors. The sources do not show that any of the scales has been validated as a reliable target for the individual patient.Sources: Schneider 2004, Lewis 2019 (Cochrane), Pantalacci 2023
  • The monitors agree poorly. BIS and PSI measured simultaneously in 57 patients correlated only moderately (r = 0.67). The monitors often disagreed about whether the patient was “deep enough”. The indices are intended by their manufacturers to measure the same thing, but do not give the same answer.Source: Schneider 2004
  • For practice (interpretation based on the sources): always state which monitor the number comes from. This applies in the record, in teaching and when studies are compared. If a unit changes monitor, familiar numbers cannot be transferred. Read the raw EEG and spectrogram.
  • Nor do the raw EEG and spectrogram look the same on every monitor. The number and placement of electrodes, filter settings, the way the spectrogram is calculated (for example ordinary Fourier analysis or multitaper, which gives less noise) and the scales for amplitude and colour vary. The same EEG can therefore look different on two monitors. The patterns, such as alpha–delta or burst suppression, can still be recognised when you know how the display is set up (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Lobo and Lamperti ch. 4, Prerau 2017. See
Schneider 2004 Lewis 2019 (Cochrane) Pantalacci 2023

How the monitors are used in Norwegian practice

Two Norwegian studies show how EEG monitors are actually used: a survey of anaesthesia staff at Norwegian hospitals, and BIS data from the electronic chart in 97,733 patients at Oslo University Hospital. The monitors are widely used, but not always in the way or where one might expect.Sources: Aasheim 2024 (the survey), Aasheim 2026 (the OUS data)

  • The number is used, the curves rarely. The index value is used by almost everyone (99 % of the anaesthetists, 98 % of the nurses). Raw EEG, spectrogram and suppression ratio are used by between 7 and 18 %. Only 27 % said they could recognise burst suppression (67 % of the anaesthetists, 18 % of the nurses). Even so, over 60 % felt they had sufficient knowledge, and 86 % wanted more.Source: Aasheim 2024
  • More fear of awareness than of anaesthesia becoming too deep. 90 % increased the dose at a high index, but only 55 % reduced it at a low one. The authors interpret this as a stronger fear of awareness than of anaesthesia becoming too deep.Source: Aasheim 2024
  • The monitor is used least in the sickest. At OUS, 27 % had continuous BIS: 33 % with TIVA, 7 % with volatile anaesthesia and only 21 % of those who received muscle relaxants. The proportion fell with ASA class. The typical BIS patient was ASA 1–2 on TIVA without relaxants. In the survey, by contrast, 68 % reported using the monitor mainly with neuromuscular blockade. Self-reported use and recorded data thus point in different directions, but the samples differ (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Aasheim 2026, Aasheim 2024
  • The old and sick were deepest. BIS fell with age and ASA class, and women were 2.4 units lower than men. The differences in means are small. What is clinically interesting is the tails: at least 5 minutes below BIS 30 occurred in about 26 % of ASA 1 and 50 % of ASA 4. The authors ask whether Schnider TCI is sufficiently individualised for vulnerable patients.Source: Aasheim 2026
  • Caveats. The survey is voluntary and self-reported, without a reliable response rate. The cohort study is observational, had only the index (not raw EEG or suppression ratio) and lacked dosing data. The findings should not be interpreted as cause and effect.Sources: Aasheim 2024, Aasheim 2026

The studies in detail:

Aasheim 2024 Aasheim 2026

When the EEG index surprises: the sources of error

The index alone cannot be trusted. If it is unexpectedly high or low without an obvious reason, the sources of error should be gone through systematically with the ANESTHESIA mnemonic. The first step is to rule out dosing errors.Source: Pinheiro 2026 (narrative review)

  • Drugs can shift the number regardless of depth. Ketamine gives more beta/gamma and raises the index even as anaesthesia deepens. Dexmedetomidine and clonidine lower it, also at moderate sedation. Neuromuscular blockers lower the index because EMG disappears, also in awake patients. Sugammadex and neostigmine raise it. When the block is reversed, muscle activity in the forehead returns (EMG), but in one study beta also increased and delta fell without EMG explaining it. Whether the rise is artefact, genuinely lighter anaesthesia or signals from the muscles to the brain is unresolved. The rise was small (BIS about 44 to 50), and no one woke up. On nitrous oxide the sources disagree: Pinheiro holds that usual adjunct doses change the index little, whereas Purdon lists nitrous oxide with ketamine as the agents that most often make clinicians doubt the index.Sources: Pinheiro 2026, Purdon 2015; Kim 2023; Rubio-Baines 2023
  • An abrupt change is not necessarily a change in depth. Ephedrine raised BIS under propofol (8 of 20 above 60) without a change in propofol concentration, whereas phenylephrine did not. Magnesium gave a lower BIS throughout caesarean section in an RCT. Spinal lidocaine sedated healthy volunteers, but BIS did not differ between groups in the blinded part. So look at the raw EEG and spectrogram before changing the hypnotic dose.Sources: Takizawa 2006, Altıparmak 2018, Pollock 2000
  • The EEG index lags behind. The BIS value appears 20–30 seconds after the EEG it is calculated from. During rapid changes, such as at induction, the raw EEG and spectrogram therefore show the change before the number (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)
  • Equipment and patient can also cause errors. Diathermy, facial nerve stimulators (even in standby), forced-air warming near the head and arterial pulsation can produce artefacts, and SQI may remain high. Genetically low-amplitude EEG in 5–10 %, hypothermia, ischaemia, seizures and neurological disease can also give unexpected values. So note the baseline index and DSA before induction.Source: Pinheiro 2026
  • The monitor itself plays a part. Different monitors, also from the same manufacturer, give different values at the same depth. This fits with BIS and PSI measured simultaneously correlating only moderately.Sources: Pinheiro 2026, Schneider 2004
  • Caveats. The review has no systematic search or quality assessment, and many claims rest on case reports. Not every unexpected value is an artefact.Source: Pinheiro 2026

The studies in detail:

Pinheiro 2026 Purdon 2015 Takizawa 2006 Altıparmak 2018 Pollock 2000 Schneider 2004

The EEG index rises after sugammadex: was the patient too light?

  • The EEG index often rises a little when the block is reversed. BIS rose from about 44 to 50 and PSI from 32 to 36 under stable sevoflurane. Some patients moved or coughed, but all were unresponsive and no one remembered anything.Source: Kim 2023 (46 patients)
  • The EEG itself also changes. Beta and spectral edge frequency rose and delta fell, and this was not explained by muscle activity. The pattern resembled lighter anaesthesia, but no one woke up.Source: Rubio-Baines 2023 (25 patients)
  • One possible explanation is signals from the muscles to the brain. When the block is reversed, the muscles are stretched and working again, and their sense organs send signals upwards. This may give the brain a small arousal signal. It has been proposed but not tested. EMG artefact and redistribution of drugs are other suggestions.Sources: Kim 2023; Rubio-Baines 2023
