  • How much happens depends on how deep the patient was. In a randomised trial under propofol and remifentanil, 12 of 33 patients in the light group (EEG index 45–55) showed clinical signs of waking after sugammadex, against none of 33 in the deep group (EEG index 25–35). The EEG index rose in both groups.Source: Kim 2023 (randomised, 66 patients)
  • A rise after sugammadex is not in itself a sign that the patient was too light. Look at what had been given, how the raw EEG and spectrogram looked before reversal, and whether the rise came together with EMG and movement. (interpretation based on the sources)See also “Movement is mostly about spinal cord and analgesia”
  • But a paralysed patient can be conscious without being able to show it. With the isolated forearm technique, about one in three responded to command during anaesthesia, but few remembered it. Follow up patients you are unsure about with questions about recall.Sources: Sleigh et al. 2025; Linassi 2018

What the standards require

The standards say different things about EEG monitoring, but share one feature: responsibility for interpretation lies with the person at the patient’s side.

  • Norway: the components are treated differently. General anaesthesia consists of several components: unconsciousness, amnesia, suppression of nociception and immobility. They must be assessed separately. The Norwegian standard 2024 treats them differently (points below).Source: Leonardsen 2024. See
  • Muscle relaxation must be measured. Neuromuscular monitoring is a minimum requirement with non-depolarising blockers.
  • Consciousness is to be assessed clinically. “Clinical assessment of level of consciousness, respiration and circulation” is a minimum requirement in sedation. The requirements for regional and general anaesthesia come in addition, so this applies there too.
  • Anaesthesia depth is considered individually. “Monitoring of anaesthesia depth (e.g., BIS and EEG) must be individually considered”. The standard does not define anaesthesia depth, and separates it from consciousness without explaining the difference.
  • Analgesia (nociception) has no requirement of its own. The standard has no separate monitoring requirement for nociception.
  • The paradox (interpretation based on the sources): the only component that must be measured objectively is muscle relaxation. That is precisely the one that removes the patient’s ability to show that they are awake. Consciousness is to be assessed with clinical signs, but these signs have been shown to be unreliable, particularly when the patient is paralysed (see the points below).
  • Reflection from the author of the app: EEG ought to be listed under the assessment of consciousness, not under an undefined concept such as “anaesthesia depth”. EEG measures the brain, the organ where consciousness resides. At the same time, EEG cannot rule out consciousness either: connected consciousness has been demonstrated in patients with frontal alpha–delta and BIS 37–44. EEG improves the assessment, but does not make it certain.Source: Gaskell 2017 (see the Components tab)
  • Which clinical signs show consciousness? In sedation, one looks at whether the patient responds to speech or touch, and whether protective reflexes such as coughing are preserved. Under general anaesthesia, movement and autonomic signs have traditionally been used. The points below show how unreliable these signs are.Source: Leonardsen 2024
  • Movement disappears with neuromuscular block. It is then no longer a warning.
  • Heart rate and blood pressure are unreliable. Surgery and other drugs also affect them. In published awareness cases only 20% had tachycardia and 18% hypertension. In US closed claims the figures were 7% and 15%.Sources: NAP5 ch. 19, Ghoneim 2009, Domino 1999
  • Lacrimation is just as unreliable. Lacrimation is named explicitly, together with heart rate and blood pressure, as an unreliable sign of consciousness, for the same reason.Source: NAP5 ch. 19
  • Sweating is not reliable enough either. Sweating is counted, together with heart rate, blood pressure and pupils, among signs that are not reliable enough to prevent awareness, particularly with autonomic neuropathy. The sources here do not quantify sweating on its own.Source: Aitkenhead ch. 18
  • The pupils say more about nociception and opioids than about consciousness. Opioids cause small pupils (miosis). Pupillary dilation in response to a noxious stimulus is a brainstem reflex that measures nociception, and is unaffected by neuromuscular blockers. It is blunted by opioids but not by volatile agents. Under propofol TIVA, patients could have a brisk pupillary reflex without moving.Source: Packiasabapathy 2021
  • Overall: under general anaesthesia with neuromuscular block the clinical signs of consciousness are few and uncertain. This is where EEG can provide information that is otherwise missing (interpretation based on the sources).
  • United Kingdom: processed EEG should be used with TIVA and neuromuscular blockade. This applies from before induction until full recovery from the block. It should be considered with inhalational anaesthesia and in high-risk patients. The rationale is NAP5: most awareness cases occurred with a neuromuscular blocker, and almost two-thirds before the start or after the end of surgery. The index value alone should not be relied upon, and a basic understanding of the raw EEG and spectrogram is needed. The guideline is thus more binding than the Norwegian standard.Source: Klein 2021
  • Practice lags behind the British recommendation. Only 49 % in the Norwegian survey had guidelines for use, and at OUS 21 % of patients receiving muscle relaxants had BIS. Measured against the British recommendation, there is a gap (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Aasheim 2024, Aasheim 2026
  • The aims of anaesthesia also concern the brain. In a Delphi consensus, 23 experts defined what anaesthesia should achieve. The definition reads: “The aim of anaesthesia, following a shared and supported decision-making process, is to provide state-of-the-art, safe, effective, individualised, patient-centred, empathetic care. Its focus is on maintaining or enhancing patient outcomes while ensuring optimal conditions for surgery and other procedures, executed in a sustainable and efficient manner” (82.6 % agreement). The aims include, among others, an adequate level of anaesthesia without oversedation, protecting cognitive function, avoiding postoperative delirium and preserving organ function, including the brain. The document does not mention EEG. But these aims concern the brain, and EEG is the only routine monitor that measures the brain's electrical activity directly (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Berger-Estilita 2026
  • Few experts see awareness as a barrier to TIVA. Only 20.6–21.5% agreed that the risk of awareness is a barrier to using TIVA. Lack of TCI pumps and processed EEG was mentioned as a practical barrier, but that statement did not reach consensus.Source: Uitenbosch 2022 (international Delphi consensus on TIVA)
  • Not built on outcome studies. The requirement for processed EEG rests on the same logic as for other monitors: early warning of errors and deterioration, not randomised outcome studies.Source: Klein 2021

The studies in detail:

Leonardsen 2024 Klein 2021 Berger-Estilita 2026 Uitenbosch 2022 Aasheim 2024 Aasheim 2026

Artefacts and interpretation: where to find it

Eye movements, EMG, electrode movement, 50 Hz and ECG are described in the card “Artefacts and sources of error in EEG” in the Spectrogram tab. Reactivity and coma patterns are described in the Intensive care tab. Normal sleep phenomena (vertex waves, spindles, K-complexes) can resemble anaesthesia patterns. Sleep spindles at 12–14 Hz during N2 have the same thalamocortical origin as frontal alpha under propofol, but not the same frequency or duration.Source for reactivity and coma patterns: Sutter and Kaplan 2012

The demand for proof: pulse oximetry and capnography became standard without outcome studies

A common argument against EEG monitoring is that large randomised trials have not shown better outcomes. But the established monitors have no such proof either.

  • No one has compared anaesthesia with and without monitoring. Now that standards are mandatory, «it will be impossible to prove that monitors make a difference». The rationale is instead that monitoring detects errors and deterioration early. In one study, modern monitoring standards halved the number of cardiac arrests, mainly because fewer had respiratory causes. In the Australian Incident Monitoring Study, 52 % of incidents were first detected by a monitor, and in more than half of these it was the pulse oximeter or capnograph.Source: Aitkenhead ch. 18
  • Pulse oximetry found more problems, but did not improve outcomes. Continuous pulse oximetry gave fewer episodes of SpO₂ below 90 % (235 participants) and more changes in treatment. There was nevertheless no reduction in cardiac, respiratory, neurological or infectious complications, and no difference in in-hospital mortality (20,802 and 22,021 participants). Pulse oximetry is nevertheless a minimum standard.Sources: Pedersen 2014 (Cochrane), Norwegian standard 2024, Klein 2021
  • The standards justify monitoring by early warning. Monitoring reduces the risk of incidents by detecting the consequences of errors and giving early warning of deterioration. The requirement for processed EEG during TIVA with neuromuscular blockade rests on the same logic and on NAP5, not on randomised outcome studies (see “What the standards require”).Source: Klein 2021
  • The EEG trials give mixed answers. ENGAGES and ENGAGES-Canada reduced burst suppression without reducing delirium, whereas Balanced found less delirium. Several authors point out that the trials measured indices, not the raw EEG.Sources: Burst suppression tab, Gruenbaum 2026
  • Reflection from the author of the app: we have demanded this much of few other monitors before adopting them. Pulse oximetry and capnography became standard because they show something we cannot otherwise see, not because they were proven to save lives. The EEG is the only routine monitor that measures the brain's electrical activity.
  • From surviving anaesthesia to preserving organ function. When the EEG is read as a picture of cortical integrity rather than a number for anaesthetic depth, anaesthesia becomes a matter of organ protection and not only of immobility. This is just as perfusion is titrated to protect the heart. EEG in the critically ill may usher in «a new era for brain health». Mortality has fallen sharply, even though patients have become sicker. Anaesthesia-related mortality fell from 357 per million before the 1970s to 34 per million in the 1990s and 2000s, and total perioperative mortality from about 10,600 to about 1,200 per million (meta-analysis of more than 21 million anaesthetics). No comparable pooled figures exist for the period before 1950. Reflection from the author of the app: the goal is no longer just to survive the anaesthetic. It is to preserve all organ functions throughout the whole course of care, including the brain's.Sources: Gruenbaum 2026, Guay 2025, Bainbridge 2012
Aitkenhead ch. 18 (2007) Pedersen et al. Cochrane 2014 Klein et al. 2021
The studies in detail: Norwegian use (Aasheim 2024 and 2026), sources of error (Pinheiro 2026), standards and consensus (4 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

How EEG monitors are used in Norway (Aasheim 2024)

Cross-sectional survey with a web form sent to anaesthesia staff at all 54 Norwegian hospitals from autumn 2020 to June 2021 (Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2024;68:781–787), based on an Australian questionnaire (Ben-Menachem). 391 responded: 324 nurse anaesthetists and 67 anaesthetists, out of an estimated 1,800 and 1,500 in the country. More than half had over ten years of experience.

  • Access and use: 76% reported that a monitor was present in over 80% of operating rooms. 62% used it on more than half of their patients, 4% never. 49% had guidelines for use, 31% did not, 19% did not know. Used most often with neuromuscular blockade (68%), TIVA (43%) and obesity (29%); 22% “always when available”. 49% never used a monitor in children.
  • What is used: the index value in 99% of the anaesthetists and 98% of the nurses (BIS is the most widely used monitor, entropy exists at some hospitals). Raw EEG in 15% and 10%, spectrogram in 18% and 7%, suppression ratio in 18% and 9%, SEF95 in 1% and 3%. Heart rate (100%) and blood pressure (96%) were the dominant clinical signs, and 58% considered clinical signs more reliable than BIS.
  • Burst suppression: 27% reported that they could recognise the pattern (67% of the anaesthetists, 18% of the nurses, p < 0.0001), and 39% knew that it means too deep anaesthesia. At the same time, over 60% in both groups felt they had sufficient knowledge, and 86% wanted more.
  • Asymmetric dosing: 90% increased the dose at high index values, 55% reduced it at low values. Respondents were neutral to the statement that an index below 40 is associated with complications, and rated the monitor as more useful against awareness (76% agreed) than for reducing dose and emergence time. The authors interpret this as a stronger fear of awareness than of anaesthesia becoming too deep.
  • Conclusion: widespread use, but the information beyond the index number (raw EEG, spectrogram, suppression) is little used, and the ability to recognise burst suppression is low. The authors call for training and more standardised guidelines. That is the background for this app.
  • Caveats: voluntary, anonymous web survey without a response rate that can be calculated reliably (about 18% of the nurses and 4% of the anaesthetists in the country), possible bias towards those who use the monitor a lot or are strongly opposed, no demographics (urban versus rural), self-reported knowledge. No conflicts of interest, no external funding. The discussion refers to BIS-guided anaesthesia reducing POCD at three months in older patients (ref. 19); see the Intensive care and Spectrogram tabs for the more divergent RCT evidence (ENGAGES, Evered 2021).
Aasheim, Rosseland, Leonardsen, Romundstad. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2024;68:781–787

Conflict of interest: the first author, Anders Aasheim, is a co-author of this app.

Who gets the lowest BIS in Norwegian practice: age, sex and ASA (Aasheim 2026)

Observational cohort study from the four hospitals of Oslo University Hospital, 2017–2020 (Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2026;70:e70281). BIS values were extracted automatically from the electronic chart (MetaVision) and analysed with a linear mixed model with time, age, ASA and sex as covariates and patient as a random effect. Standard TIVA at the hospitals was Schnider TCI for propofol and Minto for remifentanil; 82% of BIS patients received TIVA.

  • Who was monitored: 97,733 patients received general anaesthesia, 26,650 (27%) had continuous BIS. BIS was used in 33% of TIVA patients versus 7% with volatile anaesthesia, and in only 21% of the 55,965 who received muscle relaxants. The proportion monitored fell with ASA class (ASA 1 TIVA 34%, ASA 4 TIVA 22%, ASA 4 volatile 4%). The typical BIS patient was ASA 1–2 on TIVA without relaxants, that is, not the patients at greatest risk of awareness and delirium. The authors call this unexpected and a patient-safety concern.
  • Who was deepest: in the adjusted model (table 3) men had BIS values 2.4 units higher than women (95% CI 2.3–2.8), each year of age lowered BIS by 0.05 (−0.055 to −0.045), and ASA 2, 3 and 4 were 0.2, 0.56 and 0.86 lower than ASA 1 respectively. Mean BIS rose with time into surgery (about 39 at the start), most clearly in ASA 1 (to nearly 48 after 300 min), whereas ASA 4 fell to around 30–35 (fig. 4). The differences are statistically significant because of the sample size but small in absolute terms; what is clinically interesting is the tails.
  • Burst-suppression level (BIS below 30): the proportion with a mean BIS below 30 for the whole procedure rose with ASA class, roughly 10% in ASA 1–2, 15% in ASA 3 and 22% in ASA 4 (fig. 5, read from the figure). At least 5 minutes below 30 occurred in about 26% of ASA 1 and 50% of ASA 4 (fig. 6). Mean BIS above 65 was rare (1–2%) and evenly distributed across sex and ASA. The authors cite Bruhn 2000: BIS below 30 corresponds to increasing suppression.
  • The authors' interpretation: lower BIS in the old and sick with standard Schnider TCI may mean that the model, or the way it is applied, is not sufficiently individualised for vulnerable patients; they cite Obert 2024 on slow induction (Spectrogram tab). Lower BIS in women may reflect clinicians perceiving female sex as a risk factor for awareness and dosing higher, or the Schnider model's fixed central volume (V1) not accounting for body composition, unlike Eleveld. They stress themselves that the associations should not be interpreted causally.
  • What is missing: only the BIS index was available, not raw EEG, suppression ratio or SEF, so artefacts and actual suppression could not be confirmed. No dosing data, no delirium data, BIS used selectively (not randomly), no pre-registration, and mean BIS hides within-procedure variation. The authors call for studies combining BIS with raw EEG, spectrogram and suppression measures, and measuring delirium in the frail.
  • The editorial comment in the journal points to what remains unresolved: whether deeper anaesthesia in the old and sick should be met with lower doses, or with better brain perfusion (see the Perfusion tab on autoregulation and alpha dropout).
  • Conflicts of interest: the authors declare no conflicts of interest and no funding. The study was approved by the data protection officer at OUS; the regional ethics committee judged that ethical approval was not required.
Aasheim, Rosseland, Ponzi, Kristiansen, Romundstad. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2026;70:e70281

Conflict of interest: the first author, Anders Aasheim, is a co-author of this app.

Artefacts and pitfalls in processed EEG: the ANESTHESIA mnemonic (Pinheiro 2026)

Narrative review (Cureus 2026, PubMed to August 2025, selection at the authors' discretion). The point: the index alone cannot be trusted, and when it is unexpectedly high or low without an obvious reason, the sources of error should be gone through systematically. The authors group them in four.

  • Pharmacological: ketamine gives more beta/gamma and less delta and raises the index despite deeper anaesthesia. Dexmedetomidine and clonidine give spindles and slow waves and lower the index, also at moderate sedation. Nitrous oxide (an NMDA antagonist, like ketamine) changes the index little according to Pinheiro when given in usual adjunct doses on top of GABAergic anaesthesia, but Purdon 2015 (Part I) lists nitrous oxide with ketamine as the two agents that most often make clinicians doubt the index: both produce beta/gamma that tends to raise the index at clinically accepted doses, and on switching to above 70% nitrous oxide a transient, profound slow-delta pattern appears after 2–4 minutes before beta/gamma takes over. Abrupt withdrawal can lower the index paradoxically (“withdrawal-suppression”); rapid washout of isoflurane/sevoflurane can give a paradoxically low-amplitude EEG with a falsely low index and burst suppression. Neuromuscular blockers lower the index by removing EMG, also in awake patients; sugammadex and neostigmine raise it, mostly via EMG, and sugammadex can produce an arousal effect under propofol. Opioids in analgesic doses change the index little, high doses can lower it. Neuraxial block, vasopressors, methylene blue and magnesium can also shift the index (next point).
  • Blocks, vasopressors, methylene blue and magnesium, explained: the common denominator is that the index measures how active the cortex is, and anything that increases or dampens activation shifts the number.
    • Neuraxial block: the block shuts off much of the sensory input from the body, so the arousal system in the brainstem receives fewer signals. In a randomised, blinded study, healthy volunteers were measurably sedated by spinal lidocaine, and the authors attribute the early sedation to reduced afferent input. BIS nevertheless did not differ between groups in the blinded part, so the sedation itself is better documented than the effect on the index (Pollock 2000).
    • Vasopressors: under propofol anaesthesia, ephedrine raised BIS (8 of 20 went above 60), while phenylephrine did not. Propofol concentration and cardiac output were unchanged, so the rise was not due to less propofol but probably to an effect on the brain (Takizawa 2006). That phenylephrine differs may relate to it acting almost only on alpha-1 receptors in the vessels, while ephedrine, adrenaline and isoprenaline also act on beta receptors and ephedrine is a central stimulant (interpretation based on the sources). For isoprenaline there is one case report.
    • Magnesium: in a double-blind RCT of 100 women having caesarean section under general anaesthesia (sevoflurane), magnesium 30 mg/kg followed by 10 mg/kg/h gave a lower BIS throughout surgery, with no difference in fentanyl use or haemodynamics, and less pain afterwards. The authors call the mechanism unclear and point to NMDA and calcium channels (Altıparmak 2018). Magnesium crosses the blood–brain barrier poorly, so the effect may equally be due to less nociceptive activation (interpretation based on the sources).
    • In practice: when the index changes abruptly after a vasopressor, magnesium or a block, it does not automatically mean that hypnotic depth has changed. Look at the raw EEG and the spectrogram before changing the hypnotic dose.
  • Electromagnetic and mechanical: high impedance (temperature, humidity, poor skin preparation), pacemakers and other implants, diathermy, EMG tubes, facial nerve stimulators (even in standby, because of impedance testing), navigation equipment near the head, forced-air warming blankets near the head, endoscopic shavers, Doppler, pulsatile cardiopulmonary bypass and arterial pulsation (images 15 and 2 in the image quiz). SQI may remain high during such artefacts. ECG can dominate a low-voltage EEG.
  • Pathophysiological: age (the indices were built on adults; infants under 1 year and older patients deviate, see the Spectrogram tab), nociception (beta arousal, delta arousal, alpha dropout after García 2021), genetically low-voltage EEG in 5–10% of the population (check the baseline before induction), ischaemia, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, seizures and the post-ictal phase (a slow pattern that may persist after consciousness has returned), haemodynamics and positioning (forehead oedema in prolonged Trendelenburg), space-occupying lesions (side-to-side difference, a pseudomeningocele can mimic ictal activity), neurological disease (Alzheimer, vascular dementia, cerebral palsy give a lower index).
  • Model-dependent: different monitors, also from the same manufacturer, give different values at the same depth because of different algorithms and artefact filters; each new model has its learning curve.
  • ANESTHESIA (the mnemonic): Anaesthetic agents and other drugs (end-tidal/age-adjusted MAC, pump, TCI target, extravasation, backflow, occlusion); Neuromuscular blockade and reversal, neurological disease; Equipment (SQI, electrodes, sweat); Stimulus (nociception, nociception monitor, EEG patterns); Temperature, metabolism, tumour; Haemodynamics and positioning; Electromagnetic and mechanical interference; Seizure (pro- and anticonvulsants); Ischaemia and injury (NIRS if available); Age (infants, older patients). First: exclude dosing errors before other sources. Before induction: note the baseline index and DSA. If the artefact cannot be removed, it should at least be taken into account when the dose is adjusted.
  • Caveats: narrative review without systematic search or quality assessment; many claims rest on case reports. The authors stress that not every unexpected value is an artefact. One author reports speaker fees from MSD, unrelated to the work.
Pinheiro et al. Cureus 2026;18:e103656

What standards and consensus documents say about EEG monitoring

  • Norwegian standard for the safe practice of anaesthesia, 2024 revision (Leonardsen 2024): minimum monitoring in general anaesthesia is pulse oximetry, clinical assessment of level of consciousness, respiration and circulation, ECG, blood pressure, oxygen alarm, capnography, disconnection alarm, multigas analysis with volatile agents and neuromuscular monitoring with non-depolarising blockers. “Monitoring of anaesthesia depth (e.g., BIS and EEG) must be individually considered.” The anaesthetic record must document monitoring equipment, with BIS given as an example. Adopted by the Norwegian Association of Anaesthesiologists and the Norwegian Association of Nurse Anaesthetists, in force from 1 March 2024; the authors declare no conflicts of interest.
  • Association of Anaesthetists 2021 (Klein 2021): processed EEG “should be used” when TIVA is given with a neuromuscular blocker, from before induction until full recovery from the block is confirmed, and “should be considered” with inhalational anaesthesia and in high-risk patients. The rationale is NAP5: most definite or probable awareness cases occurred with a neuromuscular blocker, and almost two-thirds before the start or after the end of surgery, where end-tidal gas monitoring does not help. With volatile anaesthesia an alarm at end-tidal below 0.7 age-adjusted MAC is recommended. The guideline also states that anaesthetists should not rely solely on the index value, but develop a basic understanding of the raw EEG, power spectrum, spectrogram and relative band powers. With manual charts pEEG should be recorded at least every 5 minutes. The first author reports educational grants/honoraria from, among others, Masimo (spelled “Massimo” in the article).
  • Definition and aims of anaesthesia, Delphi consensus (Berger-Estilita 2026): 23 experts, three rounds, 80% agreement as threshold, 49 aims in seven domains. Relevant aims: “a sufficient level of sedation/anaesthesia and avoid oversedation” (INT7), “protect cognitive functions and avoid postoperative delirium” (PRE5, DIS4, DIS5), “avoid long-term cognition disturbances” (LTO6), and “preserving or enhancing organ function, inclusive of brain and cognitive function” in the definition itself. The document does not mention EEG, but the aims are those EEG monitoring targets. Patient experiences (PREMs) were not included as aims. Several authors report honoraria or travel support from Medtronic and other suppliers.
  • Multinational Delphi consensus on TIVA (Uitenbosch 2022): 29 panellists, 79% European, 12 statements, strong consensus at ≥ 75%. Only four reached consensus: TIVA is useful in paediatric anaesthesia, reduces PONV, is better for the environment, and physiological effects (airway, haemodynamics) guide the choice. “The risk of awareness is an obstacle to TIVA” received only 20.6–21.5% agreement. Access to TCI pumps and pEEG was mentioned as a practical barrier, but the statement on practical obstacles did not reach consensus (34.4 → 64.3%). Evidence for less emergence agitation in children reached 74.1%, just below the threshold.
  • Norwegian practice: Aasheim 2024 (Fundamentals tab) shows what Norwegian departments actually do. Taken together: the British guideline is more binding than the Norwegian standard, and both place the responsibility for interpretation with the person at the patient's side.
Leonardsen et al. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2024;68:567–574 · Klein et al. Anaesthesia 2021;76:1212–1223 · Berger-Estilita et al. Anaesth Crit Care Pain Med 2026;45:101614 · Uitenbosch et al. J Clin Med 2022;11:3486

Key points

  • TCI is a prediction, not a measurement. The pump calculates an expected concentration from age, weight, height, sex and what it has delivered. Nothing is measured. Schnider and Eleveld give different numbers for the same patient and dose.See
  • The number on the pump says as much about speed and model as about the patient. The patients lost response after about the same amount of propofol, whether it was given fast or slowly. Even so, the pump showed almost twice the concentration with fast induction (4.6 versus 2.6 µg/ml). Only Eleveld showed the same number with fast and slow induction, yet the brain behaved differently in the two groups (16 patients). In older patients, Eleveld more often gave excessive depth than Schnider in one study.See
  • The effect-site number is built on simplifications. It is calculated from an assumption about how quickly the drug reaches the brain. That assumption comes from rapid bolus doses, is not adjusted for age in the propofol models used clinically, and assumes that the patient loses and regains response at the same concentration. None of these holds fully.See
  • Do not use the induction number for the rest of the operation. The effect keeps increasing after the number is reached. In one study the index kept falling for 11 minutes to a deeper level than intended. This argues for adjusting the dose according to the raw EEG and spectrogram (interpretation based on the sources).See
  • Fast and slow induction are two different routes. With fast induction, the pupillary and corneal reflexes were already gone as the patient stopped responding, and the three oldest developed burst suppression. With slow induction, the reflexes were preserved and alpha appeared in the EEG before the patient stopped responding. Slow induction may be gentler, particularly for older patients, but it has not been shown to improve outcome (small studies found no burst suppression with slow induction, see the Spectrogram tab).See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

TCI is a prediction, not a measurement

  • TCI means you set a target concentration, not a rate. The pump works out what it takes to reach and hold the target, from a population model, what you entered about the patient, and what it has already given. It measures nothing in the patient.
  • The number you see is a calculated concentration. The pump shows two: Cp, the calculated concentration in the blood, and Ce, the calculated concentration at the effect site. You choose which one the pump targets. Target Cp and the pump holds the blood concentration steady, with Ce lagging a few minutes behind. Target Ce and the pump deliberately gives too much at first, so the blood concentration overshoots for a while to get the brain there sooner. Both numbers come from the model, neither is measured in the patient, and the deviation from a measured concentration is typically of the order of 20–30% even for models regarded as good. And because it is ke0 that sets how fast Ce rises, the same Ce target gives a different dose in different models: a model with a high ke0 assumes the brain follows quickly and therefore gives a smaller bolus, while a model with a low ke0 gives more to reach the same number. Marsh has 0.26 per minute originally and 1.21 in the modified version, Schnider exists in one variant with a fixed ke0 and one with a fixed time to peak effect, and Schnider assumes a higher ke0 than Eleveld. That is why "Ce 4" does not mean the same thing from pump to pump.Sources: Šafránková and Bruthans 2025; Chatzistavridis et al. 2026
  • The compartments are arithmetic, not organs. The model divides the body into three rooms: a central one (V1, blood and well-perfused tissue), a fast peripheral one and a slow one. The drug distributes between them and is eliminated from the central one. In addition comes the effect site, an imagined room without volume, linked to the blood by the rate constant ke0, which only expresses the delay from blood to brain.Source: Šafránková and Bruthans 2025
  • What actually separates the models. Marsh uses weight only: V1 is set at 0.228 litres per kilogram, so everything scales directly with the weight you enter. Schnider has a fixed V1, the same central volume whatever the patient weighs, and instead uses age, height, sex and calculated lean body mass (the James equation) in the other terms. Eleveld is built on the largest dataset, has the most patient covariates and scales allometrically, that is not directly proportionally with weight. The ke0 varies too: the original Marsh used 0.26 per minute, while 'modified Marsh' uses 1.21.Sources: Šafránková and Bruthans 2025; Schnider 1999; Eleveld 2014
  • In obesity it can go wrong in both directions. Marsh with total body weight gives large bolus doses and more hypotension. In Schnider the James equation turns around at about BMI 42 in men and 37 in women: calculated lean body mass starts to fall as the patient gets heavier, which can give too high a calculated clearance. Many therefore dose by lean weight to be on the safe side, and then the patient may be underdosed: among 60 patients with BMI above 40, 60% of those dosed by lean weight needed more propofol, against 3% of those titrated to an EEG index. The pumps also have their own limits, often 150 kg for Marsh and a BMI limit for Schnider.Sources: Chatzistavridis et al. 2026 (Subramani 2017, Wu 2018)
  • A little history. The first pumps were locked to one drug and one model. Later came open pumps with several models and several drugs, and with the effect site as a target alongside plasma. An error was also found in the fat-free mass formula in open systems, which manufacturers later corrected.Source: Šafránková and Bruthans 2025
  • Different models give different numbers for the same patient. The Schnider model is built on healthy volunteers, only nine of them over 65. The Eleveld model is built on a broader population and gives a lower calculated effect-site concentration than Schnider for the same patient and dose. The patient is the same; the prediction is not.Sources: Schnider 1999, Eleveld 2014, Obert 2024
  • EEG shows how this particular brain responds. The models are uncertain during induction because the phase is dynamic. With age and disease, the patient also deviates from the population. Slow, spectrogram-guided induction is one attempt to let the response, not the model, determine the dose.Sources: Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025 and Obert 2024 (see the Spectrogram tab)
  • The effect-site concentration is also a model quantity. It is based on ke0 and is not measured.Source: Proekt and Kelz 2021 on hysteresis (see the Spectrogram tab)
Schnider 1999, Eleveld 2014, Obert 2024

Same patient, different numbers: model and speed

The number the pump shows as the patient stops responding (calculated effect-site concentration, Ce) depends both on how fast propofol is given and on which model does the calculation.Sources: three studies from the Sepúlveda group and one from Ghent (Sepúlveda 2010, Sepúlveda 2020, Sepúlveda 2021, Coppens 2010)

  • Slow induction gives lower numbers on the pump. The patients stopped responding at a calculated 2.6 µg/ml with slow induction, versus 4.6 µg/ml with fast induction. The dose was about the same (1.67 versus 1.91 mg/kg). The same pattern has been seen in healthy volunteers and is described clinically: around 5 µg/ml with fast and around 2.5 with stepwise slow induction.Sources: Sepúlveda 2020, Sepúlveda 2010, Sepúlveda and Demaría 2019
  • The models disagree. For the same patients, Schnider gave twice the number with fast as with slow induction (6.6 versus 3.2 µg/ml). Eleveld gave almost the same (3.1 versus 3.2) and was the only one of four models not affected by speed. Original Marsh went in the opposite direction. At the same endpoint, Ce ranged from 1.96 (Marsh) to 5.54 µg/ml (Schnider).Sources: Sepúlveda 2021, Sepúlveda 2010, Coppens 2010
  • The same number does not mean the same brain. All the patients stopped responding, and Eleveld showed roughly the same concentration in both groups. Yet the brainstem reflexes were gone and alpha appeared later with fast induction. With slow induction, the reflexes were preserved and alpha appeared early. The same calculated concentration can therefore correspond to different brain states depending on how the patient got there, and only the EEG shows the difference (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Sepúlveda 2021, Sepúlveda 2020, Obert 2020
  • Eleveld may give excessive depth in older patients. In women aged 65 and over, guided by BIS, Eleveld more often gave excessive depth than Schnider (63.2% versus 27.3%) and more often burst suppression (31.6% versus 4.5%). The authors recommend particular attention when the model is used in older patients. Caveat: observational study of 78 women undergoing breast surgery, not randomised, and the concentrations are calculated, not measured.Source: Linassi 2023
  • Fast administration gives a brief, high peak in the blood. 50 patients (30–76 years) received the same dose, 1.2 mg/kg, given at five different rates from 10 to 160 mg/kg/h. At the fastest rate, measured arterial concentration reached about 20–37 µg/ml within the first minute, versus only 3–5 µg/ml at the slowest. After about two minutes it fell again to around 2–5 µg/ml (read from Figure 2 of the article). Slow administration thus gives a low, steady rise. Three findings are useful:
    • TCI models assume that propofol mixes in the blood instantly. That is not true, so they miss the concentration in the first minutes. This is also when variability between patients is greatest.
    • The rate changed how the blood concentration developed, and in older patients it took longer before propofol reached the artery.
    • The rate did not change how fast propofol moved from the blood to the brain (ke0), measured with BIS. The authors warn against extrapolating this to fast manual bolus doses.
    This does not contradict Sepúlveda. Masui measured only BIS, whereas Sepúlveda and Obert measured reflexes and EEG patterns and found that the brain reached unconsciousness in different ways (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Masui 2009
  • The EEG index did not follow the number on the pump. CSI was the same at loss of responsiveness after bolus and infusion (70 versus 71). PSI was higher with fast than with slow induction (87 versus 67), that is, a higher index in the group that had received the most.Sources: Sepúlveda 2010, Sepúlveda 2021
  • The model rests on assumptions that do not hold during induction. ke0 in Schnider and modified Marsh is derived from time to peak effect after a rapid bolus, and the models describe the early distribution after a bolus poorly. ke0 also assumes a linear relationship between concentration and effect, and is not age-adjusted in the propofol models in clinical use. In addition, patients lose and regain response at different concentrations. That does not fit a single concentration–effect curve.Sources: Sepúlveda 2021, Sepúlveda 2010, Sepúlveda and Demaría 2019
  • Caveats. The studies are small (16 patients or volunteers) and have no plasma measurements. The 2019 review is narrative and rests partly on unpublished data.

The studies in detail:

Sepúlveda 2020 Sepúlveda 2021 Sepúlveda 2010 Coppens 2010 Sepúlveda and Demaría 2019

The number at loss of responsiveness is not a maintenance target

It is tempting to let the pump hold the number it showed as the patient lost response for the rest of the anaesthetic. This does not work.Sources: Coppens 2010, Sepúlveda 2010, Sepúlveda 2020

  • The effect continues after the number is reached. 60 patients received propofol until they stopped responding to their name. The pump then held the Ce from that moment for 20 minutes. With both Schnider variants, BIS kept falling for 11 minutes, to a deeper level than intended. With Marsh, all patients woke up, because the pump stood still for 233 seconds.Source: Coppens 2010
  • The number after a bolus leads to overdosing. Ce at loss of responsiveness after an induction dose should not be used as a reference for maintenance, because it would lead to overdosing.Sources: Sepúlveda 2010, Sepúlveda 2020
  • The model is good at keeping the state stable, not at predicting the effect. The strength of effect-site TCI is not to predict the effect in the individual, but to keep the state stable once a clinical endpoint has been reached. Surrogate measures such as BIS are needed to see when steady state is reached.Source: Coppens 2010
  • EEG or an index is needed to find the patient’s own level. The number depends on model and speed, and the same number gives a different effect over time. One example: after slow induction with Schnider, Ce is reduced by 15% below the level at loss of response.Source: Mehler 2024

The studies in detail:

Coppens 2010 Sepúlveda 2010 Sepúlveda 2020 Mehler 2024

Two routes to loss of responsiveness: fast and slow induction

With fast and slow induction the patients reach the same endpoint, but the brain gets there in different ways. This was shown by one randomised study in ASA 1 patients, published in two parts. It compared fast induction (equivalent to a bolus) with slow infusion until loss of response.Sources: Sepúlveda 2020, Obert 2020 (Santiago)

  • Fast induction appears to work bottom-up, slow induction top-down. As the response disappeared, pupillary and corneal reflexes were absent in all 8 in the fast group and preserved in all 8 in the slow group. The authors interpret fast induction as “bottom-up” (brainstem inhibition) and slow as “top-down” (loss of cortical integration).Source: Sepúlveda 2020
  • With slow induction, alpha appears before the patient stops responding. With fast induction, frontal alpha only appeared several minutes afterwards. With slow induction, the pattern regarded as “adequate anaesthesia” was already present before loss of response to verbal command. The authors write that “anyone can become a black swan with slow induction”.Source: Obert 2020
  • The EEG indices follow different courses. The beta ratio fell steeply before loss of response to pain with fast induction, but was low long before with slow induction. Relative alpha and the alpha/delta ratio tracked loss of response to verbal command best.Source: Obert 2020
  • Burst suppression occurred only with fast induction. Three of nine in the fast group developed it (Sepúlveda 2020 gives eight per group, see discrepancies), the oldest (57, 57 and 61 years). None in the slow group did. Larger materials show the same. The authors propose slow induction as safer, especially in older patients, but say themselves that this must be tested in a clinical trial.Sources: Sepúlveda 2020, Obert 2024, Ostertag 2025
  • Caveats. 16 patients (Obert 2020 reports 18 included), only healthy subjects under 65, only frontal EEG, and consciousness measured as response, not as experience.

The studies in detail:

Sepúlveda 2020 Obert 2020 Obert 2024 Ostertag 2025

The cards on burst suppression are collected in the tab.

The studies in detail: fast versus slow induction, Ce as a maintenance target, the effect-site model (3 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Fast versus slow induction: two routes to loss of response (Sepúlveda 2020, Obert 2020)

One randomised study from Clínica Alemana in Santiago (NCT03140982), published in two parts: the clinical and neurological part in Anaesthesia 2020;75:196–201 and the EEG analysis in Sci Rep 2020;10:19444. ASA 1 patients aged 18–65 for hip arthroscopy received either propofol TCI to an effect site of 5.4 µg/ml (Marsh, ke0 1.21, “fast”, equivalent to a bolus) or 10 mg/kg/h until loss of response (“slow”). A neurologist blinded to group tested the FOUR score every 30 seconds. Frontal four-channel EEG (SedLine).

  • Time and concentration: loss of responsiveness after a median of 10.5 minutes (slow) versus 1.4 (fast). Calculated effect-site concentration at loss of response 2.6 versus 4.6 µg/ml, cumulative dose 1.67 versus 1.91 mg/kg. Same endpoint, almost double the model concentration.
  • Brainstem reflexes: preserved (pupillary and corneal reflexes) in all 8 in the slow group, absent in all 8 in the fast group at the moment the response disappeared (p = 0.010). The authors interpret fast induction as “bottom-up” (brainstem inhibition) and slow as “top-down” (loss of cortical integration), with reference to Mashour and Hudetz 2017 (see the Components tab).
  • Alpha before or after: with slow induction, frontal alpha power rose before loss of response; with fast induction, alpha only appeared several minutes afterwards. Obert 2020 shows that with slow induction, loss of response to verbal command (LOvR) could be distinguished from loss of response to pain (LOpR, 0–210 seconds later), and that the alpha and delta pattern regarded as “adequate anaesthesia” was already present before LOvR. The authors write that “anyone can become a black swan with slow induction” (cf. Gaskell 2017 and Mashour and Avidan 2017 in the Components tab).
  • Beta ratio and indices: the beta ratio (BIS surrogate) fell steeply before LOpR with fast induction, but was already low long before with slow induction, so the index follows different courses depending on speed. Relative beta remained high for minutes after LOpR with slow induction, that is, a prolonged “paradoxical excitation”. Relative alpha and the alpha/delta ratio tracked the transition to LOvR best, the beta/alpha ratio tracked LOpR best.
  • Burst suppression only with fast induction: three of nine in the fast group (57, 57 and 61 years, the oldest) developed burst suppression during induction and were excluded from the EEG analysis. None in the slow group. Obert 2024 and Ostertag 2025 found the same in larger materials from the same research group.
  • Clinical message from the authors: the effect-site concentration at loss of response after a bolus (Marsh, ke0 1.21) cannot be used as a maintenance target, because it would lead to overdosing. Slow induction is proposed as safer, especially in older patients, but the authors themselves say this must be tested in a clinical trial.
  • Same patients, four models (Sepúlveda 2021, Rev Esp Anestesiol Reanim): an additional analysis of the same 16 patients calculated the effect-site concentration at loss of responsiveness with four models. Slow versus fast induction: original Marsh (ke0 0.2) 2.15 versus 1.8 µg/ml; modified Marsh 2.7 versus 4.6; Schnider 3.2 versus 6.6; Eleveld 3.2 versus 3.1. Only Eleveld gave the same number regardless of speed. PSI at loss of responsiveness was 67 (slow) versus 87 (fast), that is, a higher index in the group that had received the most. The authors call the numbers “contradictory” and point out that ke0 in Schnider and modified Marsh is derived from time to peak effect after a rapid bolus, while Schnider's own Emax model gives an EC50 of 2.35 µg/ml for loss of consciousness with slow infusion.
  • Caveats: 16 patients (8 + 8) in Sepúlveda 2020 and 2021, while Obert 2020 reports 18 included (see discrepancies). Only healthy subjects under 65, only frontal EEG, Marsh model (not Schnider or Eleveld), and consciousness measured as response (FOUR score), not as experience. No conflicts of interest in Sepúlveda 2020; none in Obert 2020.
Sepúlveda et al. Anaesthesia 2020;75:196–201; Obert et al. Sci Rep 2020;10:19444; Sepúlveda et al. Rev Esp Anestesiol Reanim 2021;68:245–251

Why Ce at loss of responsiveness after a bolus cannot be used as a maintenance target (Sepúlveda 2010, Coppens 2010)

Two studies from 2010 that form the basis for most of the criticism above.

  • Sepúlveda 2010 (Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2010;54:447–452): 16 healthy volunteers aged 21–45 received, in randomised order, both a bolus of 1.8 mg/kg (1,200 ml/h) and an infusion of 12 mg/kg/h, with the Cerebral State Index as monitor. Loss of responsiveness after 0.97 minutes (bolus) versus 6.8 minutes (infusion). Calculated Ce at loss of responsiveness, bolus versus infusion: Schnider (ke0 0.45) 4.40 versus 2.81 µg/ml; modified Marsh (ke0 1.21) 3.55 versus 2.50; original Marsh (ke0 0.26) 1.28 versus 1.72. CSI at loss of responsiveness was the same (70 versus 71). Conclusion: “Ce predicted at loss of consciousness after a TCI induction dose should not be used as a reference value for titrating hypnosis during maintenance.” The authors believe the error lies in the “front-end” kinetics: the models describe the early distribution after a bolus poorly. No plasma measurements. No conflicts of interest, departmentally funded.
  • Coppens 2010 (Br J Anaesth 2010;104:452–458, Ghent, with Schnider as co-author): 60 patients received propofol at 300 ml/h until they stopped responding to their name, and the calculated Ce at that moment was set as the effect-site target for 20 minutes with one of three models. Ce at loss of response was 1.96 (Marsh, ke0 0.26), 5.54 (Schnider, fixed ke0 0.456) and 5.08 µg/ml (Schnider, ke0 adjusted to time to peak effect 1.6 min). With Marsh, all patients woke up (after an average of 401 seconds, because the pump stood still for 233 seconds); with the two Schnider variants, BIS kept falling for 11 minutes to a deeper level than intended, and one patient woke up. Conclusion: targeting Ce at loss of consciousness does not give an immediately constant effect with any of the models, and surrogate measures such as BIS are needed to see when steady state is reached. The authors write that the strength of effect-site TCI is not to predict the effect in the individual, but to keep the state stable once a clinical endpoint has been reached.
  • What the two show together: the number the pump displays at loss of responsiveness depends on model and speed, and the same number gives a different effect over time. That is why EEG (or an index) is necessary to find the patient's own level, and why the Sepúlveda group proposes slow induction, in which Ce and effect have time to follow each other. Mehler 2024 (Spectrogram tab) draws the consequence and reduces Ce by 15% below the level at loss of response when Schnider is used after slow induction.
Sepúlveda et al. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2010;54:447–452; Coppens et al. Br J Anaesth 2010;104:452–458

A critical look at the effect-site model for propofol (Sepúlveda and Demaría 2019)

Review article in Rev Esp Anestesiol Reanim 2019;66:425–433.

  • The questions the article raises: do the EEG indices represent the effect? Are the indices used to build the models comparable, and what is the real response time of the monitors? Is ke0 affected by infusion rate and by age? Are induction and emergence mirror images, as the Emax models assume?
  • ke0: a first-order transfer constant in a linear, proportional model, tied to one specific PK model. The models are useful as a titration reference, but incomplete for induction, changes of plan and emergence, because they assume a linear relationship between plasma concentration and effect.
  • Clinical observation: fast induction towards an arbitrary EC95 requires a Ce of around 5 µg/ml (equivalent to about a 2 mg/kg bolus), while stepwise slow induction gives loss of consciousness at around 2.5 µg/ml.
  • Age and ke0: for remifentanil, equilibration is about three times slower in older patients (Minto), and similar is seen for fentanyl, cisatracurium and sevoflurane, but ke0 is not age-adjusted in the propofol models in clinical use.
  • Neural inertia: different concentrations for losing and regaining response (Friedman 2010, fruit flies and mice) do not fit a single concentration–effect curve. See Proekt and Kelz 2021 and Warnaby 2017 in the Spectrogram tab.
  • Caveats: narrative review; some of the arguments rest on unpublished data (EuroSIVA 2009). No conflicts of interest declared.
Sepúlveda and Demaría. Rev Esp Anestesiol Reanim 2019;66:425–433

Key points

  • Emergence is not induction in reverse: Consciousness is lost at a higher concentration than the one at which it returns (hysteresis), induction is gradual while emergence is abrupt, and several circuits govern only one of the two transitions. Hysteresis in humans remains debated, however. (see “Emergence is not induction in reverse”)
  • Emergence is an active process: Dopamine from the VTA, noradrenaline, orexin and acetylcholine can hasten emergence in animal studies, often without altering induction. No nucleus appears to act alone; the network appears to decide. (see “The brain has its own arousal pathways”)
  • Deep structures wake before the functions: The brainstem and thalamus are active as consciousness returns, whereas cognitive functions return stepwise over the following hours. The findings measure different phases and do not contradict each other. (see “What wakes first”)
  • Awake is not the same as conscious: Dopaminergic arousal reversed most agents, but not ketamine, and a drug that changed the EEG did not wake the animals. This fits with the arousal pathways acting on level, whereas ketamine disrupts content. (see “Awake is not the same as conscious”)
  • Clinically today: Emergence is still driven mainly by elimination of the agent. A low dose or “alpha without theta” does not guarantee rapid emergence, and no dopaminergic method is established in humans. (see “What it means clinically today”)

The theme cards below tell the story, with the sources under each point. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Emergence is not induction in reverse

For a long time, emergence was seen as a passive process: the agent disappears, the concentration falls below a critical value, and the brain goes back the same way. Three findings fit poorly with that picture.Source: Kelz 2019

  • Consciousness is lost at a higher concentration than the one at which it returns. This is called anaesthetic hysteresis. It is explained by neural inertia: the brain resists changing state, in both directions. In healthy volunteers given propofol TCI, pharmacokinetics alone did not explain this loop. One review considers hysteresis a general property of the nervous system.Sources: Friedman 2010, Huang 2021, Kelz 2019
  • Induction is gradual, emergence is abrupt. During induction the whole brain changed gradually. Emergence came as an abrupt jump in connectivity between thalamus, brainstem and cortex. The authors call it a “reboot” of consciousness.Source: Huang 2021
  • Some circuits govern only one of the transitions. Inhibiting orexin delayed emergence without altering induction. Several nuclei govern only emergence, while others (PnO) govern only induction. Other circuits take part in both: inhibiting the PPT in the brainstem gave both faster induction and slower emergence in mice.Sources: Zhang and Wei 2025, Li 2024
  • Hysteresis in humans is not settled. Some studies found hysteresis, whereas Warnaby 2017 did not find it in behaviour for propofol. The concentrations are model-calculated, not measured.Sources: found hysteresis: Sepúlveda 2019, Huang 2021. Did not find hysteresis in behaviour: Warnaby 2017

The studies in detail:

Friedman 2010 Huang 2021 Kelz 2019 Zhang and Wei 2025 Li 2024

What happens in the brain with a slow and a fast induction

The two ways of inducing anaesthesia reach the brain in opposite order. The same amount of drug reaches the brain; the speed decides what is knocked out first.

  • Slow induction: from the top down. First frontal alpha rises while the patient is still answering you. Then she stops responding, because the cortex can no longer bind information together. The brainstem is still working: pupillary and corneal reflexes were preserved in all 8 in the slow group at the moment responsiveness was lost. The brainstem is therefore reached last, and only if you go deeper than you need.Source: Sepúlveda 2020
  • Fast induction: from the bottom up. The concentration overshoots the level needed, and the brainstem is inhibited at once. In all 8 in the fast group, pupillary and corneal reflexes were already gone when responsiveness was lost (p = 0.010), and frontal alpha appeared only several minutes later. Burst suppression occurred only in this group, in the three oldest.Source: Sepúlveda 2020
  • Why it matters in practice. With a slow induction you see the brain's response as it happens, and you can stop when you see alpha and loss of response. With a fast induction you see the response afterwards, and by then you are already past it. This is also where the fall in blood pressure and the burst suppression in the oldest come from.
  • The terms. 'Bottom-up' means the drug knocks out the arousal nuclei in the brainstem and hypothalamus, and the cortex follows. 'Top-down' means the cortex's own integration fails first, while the arousal nuclei below are still working. The two are described as different ways in which agents can abolish consciousness.Source: Mashour and Hudetz 2017 (hypothesis and theory)
  • Caveats. The material is small, 8 patients per group, and the reflexes were examined at one particular moment. Larger series from the same group point the same way.Sources: Sepúlveda 2020, Obert 2020

The study in detail:

Sepúlveda 2020 Obert 2020 Mashour and Hudetz 2017

The brain has its own arousal pathways, and they act as a network

If emergence were merely the absence of agent, it could not be hastened without removing the agent. In animal studies it can: animals can be woken while the gas is still running. Emergence appears to be actively driven by arousal systems in the brainstem and hypothalamus.Source: Solt 2011

  • Dopamine from the VTA can wake animals during ongoing anaesthesia. Methylphenidate, dextroamphetamine and electrical stimulation of the VTA woke rats while the agent was still being given. Stimulation of the substantia nigra, which also contains dopamine neurons, did not work, and D1 blockade abolished the effect of dextroamphetamine. The effect applied to sevoflurane, isoflurane, propofol, dexmedetomidine and fentanyl, but not ketamine. Which receptors carried it varied with the agent.Sources: Solt 2011, Solt 2014, Kenny 2015, Kato 2021, Vincent 2024
  • Noradrenaline primes the brain for emergence but does not keep it awake on its own. Mice without noradrenaline woke much later, and noradrenaline in the central thalamus hastened emergence from propofol. But atomoxetine, which raises noradrenaline, woke none of the rats.Sources: Kelz 2019, Kenny 2015
  • Orexin, acetylcholine and adenosine also affect emergence. Orexin affects emergence, not induction, and plasma orexin-A rises during emergence in patients. Cholinergic stimulation in the central thalamus and prefrontal cortex woke animals under gas, but physostigmine has not had a consistent effect in humans. Caffeine hastened emergence in rats and in healthy volunteers.Sources: Zhang and Wei 2025, Kelz 2019
  • No nucleus appears to act alone; the network appears to decide. The PPT in the brainstem could wake mice under sevoflurane, but its activity only returned as the mice woke. The PPT is therefore “one node among many”. In animal experiments, stimulation of the thalamus, parabrachial nucleus, VTA, locus coeruleus, basal forebrain or prefrontal cortex has also reversed anaesthesia.Sources: Li 2024, McKinstry-Wu and Kelz 2024 (editorial), Mashour 2022

The studies in detail:

Solt 2011 Solt 2014 Kenny 2015 Kato 2021 Vincent 2024 Kelz 2019 Zhang and Wei 2025 Li 2024 McKinstry-Wu and Kelz 2024 Mashour 2022

Orexin: stabilises wakefulness and helps emergence

Orexin (also called hypocretin) is made by neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. It keeps us awake, and seems to be important for emerging from anaesthesia, but not for going under.

  • Volatile agents dampen the orexin neurons. In mice, isoflurane and sevoflurane suppressed activity in the orexin neurons, but not in the neighbouring neurons that make MCH.Source: Kelz 2008 (animal study)
  • Without orexin, emergence is slower. Mice without orexin neurons, and mice given an orexin-1 receptor blocker, took longer to emerge but went under just as fast. The authors conclude that induction and emergence use different pathways, and that emergence requires wake-promoting centres to be recruited and stabilised.Source: Kelz 2008 (animal study)
  • Orexin drives the locus coeruleus. Orexin increases firing of the noradrenaline neurons in the locus coeruleus. The locus coeruleus also receives input from several other arousal systems, and inhibitory input from the preoptic area.Sources: Hasegawa 2014; Lyu 2022
  • Narcolepsy type 1 is loss of orexin. Narcolepsy type 1 is caused by loss of the orexin neurons, probably through an autoimmune attack. In dogs with narcolepsy the locus coeruleus neurons stop firing during cataplexy, and drugs that increase noradrenaline strongly suppress cataplexy.Sources: Mahoney 2019; Hasegawa 2014
  • Orexin antagonists are used as sleeping pills. Suvorexant blocks orexin and has been proposed against sleep disturbance in intensive care, but has not been studied in the critically ill.Source: Eikermann et al. 2025
Kelz 2008 Hasegawa 2014 Mahoney 2019 Lyu 2022

What wakes first: deep structures, then the functions

The studies asking what returns first seem to point in different directions, but they measure different phases of emergence.

  • Deep structures start as consciousness returns. The brainstem, thalamus, hypothalamus and anterior cingulate were active (PET) at return of consciousness in 20 healthy volunteers, after both dexmedetomidine and propofol. These are the deepest and oldest parts of the brain: the brainstem keeps wakefulness going, the thalamus passes sensory signals on to the cortex, the hypothalamus governs sleep and wakefulness, and the anterior cingulate helps direct attention. Connectivity between thalamus, brainstem and cortex jumped at the same moment. Emergence therefore appears to proceed from below upwards, from caudal to rostral structures, rather than starting in the cortex.Sources: Långsjö 2012, Huang 2021, Mashour 2022
  • Cognitive functions return stepwise in the hours afterwards. In 60 healthy adults, abstract problem solving (prefrontal function) returned first, reaction time and attention later. After about 3 hours they were on a par with awake controls.Source: Mashour 2021
  • The findings do not contradict each other (interpretation based on the sources). One study measures the moment consciousness returns, and there deep structures start first. The other measures how cognitive functions return after the person is already awake. “Prefrontal first” thus refers to the order among cognitive functions, not to which part of the brain wakes first.Sources: Långsjö 2012, Mashour 2021
  • Frontal EEG may not see the start. Frontal EEG measures the cortex. The authors speculate that monitors measuring the cortex may miss that consciousness starts in deeper structures.Source: Långsjö 2012

The studies in detail:

Långsjö 2012 Huang 2021 Mashour 2022 Mashour 2021

Awake is not the same as conscious: level and content

Wakefulness (arousal) and consciousness (awareness) are different things: response is not the same as consciousness, and lack of response is not the same as unconsciousness. This distinction helps in understanding what the arousal experiments actually show.Sources: Mashour 2022, Sanders 2012

  • Level and content may be governed by different networks (hypothesis). On this view, the level of consciousness is governed bottom-up from the brainstem, hypothalamus and thalamus, whereas content is governed top-down in cortical and thalamocortical networks. Dexmedetomidine acts mainly on level. Ketamine activates arousal-promoting nuclei but disrupts content.Source: Mashour and Hudetz 2017
  • The rat experiments measure level, not content. The endpoint is whether the animal regains the righting reflex, that is, whether it is awake enough to turn over. That is a measure of level (arousal), and it says little about the content of experience (interpretation based on the sources).Source: the rat experiments of Solt and colleagues
  • Ketamine could not be reversed. VTA stimulation and d-amphetamine woke rats from dexmedetomidine, sevoflurane and fentanyl, but not from ketamine. Interpretation based on the sources: this fits with ketamine acting not by lowering level but by disrupting content, so turning up the arousal system does not help. This has not been tested directly.Sources: Kato 2021, Vincent 2024
  • An EEG that looks more awake is not an awake animal. Atomoxetine shifted the EEG towards theta without waking the animals.Source: Kenny 2015

The studies in detail:

Mashour 2022 Sanders 2012 Mashour and Hudetz 2017 Kato 2021 Vincent 2024 Kenny 2015

What it means clinically today

The research changes how emergence is understood, but little of it is clinical practice yet.

  • Elimination is still the main route. Emergence is still driven mainly by elimination of the agent. Possible interventions fall into three groups: altering pharmacokinetics, acting directly at the binding site, or using the brain’s own arousal pathways. No dopaminergic method is established in humans, methylphenidate is not approved for this, and amphetamines cause a rise in blood pressure and tachycardia.Source: Vincent 2025
  • A low dose is no guarantee. Because the inertia lies in the network and not only in the concentration, neither a low dose nor “alpha without theta” guarantees rapid emergence.
  • Hysteresis can be seen in the EEG. After burst suppression, the EEG does not return to its baseline pattern at the same calculated concentration. Emergence from sevoflurane often passes through a delta-dominated stage. The course, not only the dose, may matter for delirium.Sources: Sepúlveda 2026, Hesse 2019, Miyasaka 2025
  • Physostigmine does not reliably reverse anaesthesia. It has been called standard treatment for emergence delirium, but as a means of reversing anaesthesia its effect has not been consistent. Centrally anticholinergic drugs are advised against in older patients perioperatively.Sources: Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010, Kelz 2019, Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025
  • Sleep, disease and sex may affect emergence. Sleep deprivation lowered the dose needed for unconsciousness in rats, and some patients with narcolepsy wake later. Female rats woke later than male rats after dexmedetomidine. Transfer to humans is unknown.Sources: Kelz 2019, Kato 2021

The studies in detail:

Vincent 2025 Sepúlveda 2026 Hesse 2019 Miyasaka 2025 Brown 2010 Kelz 2019 Kato 2021
The studies in detail: hysteresis, the neurotransmitters, dopamine and the VTA, the PPT (four cards)

Summaries of each article, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Emergence is not induction in reverse: hysteresis, neural inertia and “reboot”

Traditionally, emergence has been seen as induction in reverse: the agent disappears, and the brain returns along the same path. Several lines of evidence say that this is not correct. The phenomenon is called anaesthetic hysteresis (the patient stops responding at a higher concentration than the one at which responsiveness returns) and is explained by neural inertia: the brain resists changing state in both directions.Source: Friedman 2010

  • In humans, consciousness returns with an abrupt jump, a “reboot”. 26 healthy volunteers (18 analysed) received propofol TCI (Marsh), stepped up by 0.4 µg/ml every 5 minutes to loss of response, then free emergence. Loss of response occurred at a higher calculated effect-site concentration than return of response (p < 0.0001), a hysteresis loop. Induction was gradual: the time scale of neural processing (autocorrelation) increased across the whole brain and connectivity fell. Emergence was abrupt: the cortical time scale normalised suddenly, and connectivity between thalamus, pallidum, brainstem and cortex jumped. The authors themselves use the word reboot: “a rapid increase in the speed of cortical processing and subcortico-cortical interactions may be a mechanism that reboots consciousness”. Pharmacokinetics alone did not explain the asymmetry. Limitation: the concentration is model-calculated, not measured, and only propofol.Source: Huang 2021, Neuroimage (fMRI)
  • Many nuclei govern only emergence, not induction. This applies to orexin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus: removal of orexin delayed emergence without altering the EC50 for loss of righting. The same applies to serotonergic neurons in the dorsal raphe, dopaminergic neurons in the VTA, orexinergic terminals in the basal forebrain and locus coeruleus, PVT, lateral habenula and prefrontal cortex. Other nuclei (PnO) control only induction. In patients, plasma orexin-A rises during emergence, not during induction. Caveats: almost exclusively male mice and rats, mostly isoflurane, and only 3 of the studies report EC50; the patterns vary between agents.Sources: Zhang and Wei 2025 (review of animal studies), Kelz 2008
  • Emergence can be actively induced. In rats, methylphenidate (dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor) halved the time to emergence (median 280 to 91 s) and restored righting in 11 of 12 animals during ongoing isoflurane. The EEG shifted from delta to theta within 30 seconds, and ventilation increased. Droperidol (D2/α1 antagonist) blocked everything. Emergence is thus an active arousal process from the brainstem and hypothalamus, not merely the absence of agent. Methylphenidate is not approved for this in humans.Source: Solt 2011, Anesthesiology
  • Wakefulness and consciousness are different things. Response is not the same as consciousness, and lack of response is not the same as unconsciousness (“unresponsiveness ≠ unconsciousness”). In animal experiments, stimulation of the thalamus, parabrachial nucleus, VTA, locus coeruleus, basal forebrain or prefrontal cortex reverses anaesthesia, and recovery probably proceeds from caudal to rostral structures. Conflict of interest: Mashour is a consultant for TRYP Therapeutics.Sources: Mashour 2022, Anesth Analg; Sanders 2012
  • Clinically, hysteresis can be seen in the EEG, and a low dose does not guarantee rapid emergence. That the EEG does not return to the baseline pattern at the same calculated concentration after burst suppression is hysteresis seen in the EEG. Emergence from sevoflurane often passes through a delta-dominated stage, and the course, not just the dose, may matter for delirium. “Alpha without theta” or a low dose does not guarantee rapid emergence, because the inertia resides in the network, not only in the concentration. Hysteresis in humans is nevertheless debated: some studies did not find it for propofol, others did.Sources: Sepúlveda 2026 (Burst suppression tab), Hesse 2019, Miyasaka 2025, Warnaby 2017, Sepúlveda 2019, Huang 2021
Huang 2021, Zhang and Wei 2025, Solt 2011, Mashour 2022

How the brain wakes up: the neurotransmitters behind emergence (Kelz 2019)

Narrative review. Emergence was long seen as a passive process occurring when concentration falls below a critical value. Here it is described as an active, controllable process that can be driven by mechanisms distinct from induction. Much rests on animal studies, but only signalling systems for which there are also human data are included.Source: Kelz, García, Mashour and Solt, Anesth Analg 2019;128:726–736

  • Emergence is not induction in reverse, for two reasons. Some neuronal groups for sleep and wakefulness take part differently in the two transitions. And there is hysteresis: the concentration at which consciousness is lost is higher than that at which it returns. This has traditionally been explained by pharmacokinetics, but the authors argue newer data suggest hysteresis is a general property of the nervous system.
  • Acetylcholine can wake, but physostigmine does not work consistently in humans. Propofol and volatile agents lower cortical acetylcholine, ketamine and nitrous oxide raise it. A nicotinic agonist in the central thalamus reversed sevoflurane and desflurane during ongoing administration, whereas a nicotinic antagonist did not change induction. A cholinergic agonist (carbachol) in prefrontal cortex produced full arousal in rats at about 1 MAC sevoflurane, but not in parietal cortex. Physostigmine has reversed sevoflurane and propofol in humans, but not consistently. Low-dose ketamine during isoflurane produced burst suppression but faster emergence (about 45 %), called «paradoxical emergence».
  • Physostigmine is used for agitation on emergence. It has been called «a standard treatment for emergence delirium». Physostigmine crosses the blood–brain barrier and increases cholinergic activity in the cortex. Atropine, scopolamine, first-generation antihistamines and phenothiazine antiemetics are advised against in older patients perioperatively because of central anticholinergic effects. Reflection from the author of the app: on a cardiac intensive care unit many years ago, physostigmine was given when patients woke agitated after cardiac surgery. The indication was agitation; whether central anticholinergic syndrome was suspected, for example after atropine, is not known.Sources: Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010; Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025
  • Norepinephrine primes the brain for emergence but does not keep it awake on its own. Mice without norepinephrine were 10–20 % more sensitive at induction, but the largest difference was that they woke much later. Norepinephrine in the central thalamus hastened emergence from propofol without changing induction.
  • Orexin was the first sign that emergence is not a mirror image of induction. Blocking orexin did not change induction but delayed emergence from isoflurane and sevoflurane in rodents. Some patients with narcolepsy wake later after anaesthesia. High CO₂ hastens emergence, perhaps because orexin neurones are activated by CO₂.
  • Dopamine wakes, and the D1 receptor appears most important. Methylphenidate (Ritalin) and dextroamphetamine restored wake-like behaviour in animals during ongoing isoflurane, sevoflurane and propofol. The effect is mainly via dopamine, because the pure norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor atomoxetine did not rouse the rats. The source is the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
  • Sleep deprivation lowers the dose needed, and caffeine hastens emergence. Sleep deprivation lowered the dose needed for unconsciousness with propofol, sevoflurane and isoflurane in rats. Caffeine hastened emergence from isoflurane and propofol in rats, and from isoflurane in healthy volunteers in a double-blind crossover study.
  • Flumazenil may give faster or clearer emergence, even without benzodiazepines. In patients who had not received benzodiazepines, flumazenil produced EEG signs of arousal and faster emergence in one study with propofol and remifentanil. In another study it did not speed emergence but improved cognition in recovery.
  • None of the methods is clinically established. Narrative review, mostly animal studies. Effects in humans are small or uncertain. No conflicts of interest, NIH-funded.
Kelz, García, Mashour and Solt. Anesth Analg 2019;128:726–736

Dopamine and the VTA: emergence has its own circuits (Solt, Norwegian Autumn Meeting 2026)

At the Norwegian Autumn Meeting (Høstmøtet) 2026, Ken Solt (Massachusetts General Hospital) presented research from his group supporting the view that emergence is an active process in its own circuits, and that dopamine from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) in the midbrain is an important part of it. Almost everything is from rat experiments, where return of the righting reflex is used as a measure of consciousness.Source: Solt, lecture Høstmøtet 2026

  • Each anaesthetic acts on many targets. Each agent affects a range of receptors and ion channels, not a single target. This is one reason to look for shared circuits of consciousness rather than a shared site of action.Source: Alkire, Hudetz and Tononi 2008 (review in Science)
  • The old core network appears to wake first. 20 healthy volunteers were woken from dexmedetomidine or propofol in a PET scanner. At return of consciousness, the brainstem, thalamus, hypothalamus and anterior cingulate were active with both drugs, that is deep, evolutionarily old structures rather than the neocortex. The authors argue that a “primitive” level of consciousness must return before higher functions, and speculate that monitors measuring the cortex may miss this distinction.Source: Långsjö 2012
  • It was the VTA, not the substantia nigra, that woke the rats. Electrical stimulation of the VTA restored the righting reflex in 5 of 5 rats during ongoing isoflurane and 5 of 5 during propofol. Stimulation of the substantia nigra, which also contains dopamine neurons, woke none (0 of 5). The EEG shifted from delta towards theta. Small groups, and dopamine release was not measured.Source: Solt 2014
  • Dopamine wakes rats, noradrenaline alone does not. Dextroamphetamine 1 mg/kg woke 6 of 6 rats during ongoing sevoflurane (mean 160 seconds) and shortened emergence after propofol from 641 to 404 seconds. Atomoxetine, which raises noradrenaline, woke none, even though the EEG shifted towards theta. A D1 antagonist blocked the effect of dextroamphetamine. An EEG that looks more awake is therefore not the same as an awake animal.Source: Kenny 2015
  • Dopamine reverses dexmedetomidine, but not ketamine. After dexmedetomidine the rats woke after about 113 minutes with saline, but after 1.8 minutes with d-amphetamine 3 mg/kg. After ketamine the time was the same (19.7 versus 20.3 minutes). D1/D5 blockade abolished the effect after dexmedetomidine. Female rats woke 51 minutes later than males after dexmedetomidine with saline, but not with d-amphetamine.Source: Kato 2021
  • VTA stimulation works across agents, but not with ketamine. In 16 rats, VTA stimulation restored consciousness after sevoflurane, dexmedetomidine and fentanyl, but not after ketamine. D1 blockade weakened the effect after sevoflurane and fentanyl, but not after dexmedetomidine. Which receptors carry emergence thus depends on the agent.Source: Vincent 2024
  • Cognition returns in steps. 60 healthy adults, half under 3 hours of general anaesthesia and half awake controls. Abstract problem solving (prefrontal function) returned first, reaction time and attention later, and within about 3 hours the anaesthetised were at the level of the controls. Unpublished rat data also showed that activating dopamine neurons in the VTA gave faster cognitive recovery after high-dose dexmedetomidine.Sources: Mashour 2021; unpublished data shown by Solt in the lecture
  • Emergence is still mainly driven by elimination of the agent. Possible measures fall into three groups: altering pharmacokinetics, acting directly at the binding site, and using the brain's own arousal pathways. The first agents for speeding emergence are on their way, but no dopaminergic method is established in humans.Source: Vincent 2025 (review from the same group)
  • No region appears to act alone. Neuronal populations are not independent, and the network determines their activity.Source: McKinstry-Wu and Kelz, BJA editorial 2024 (shown in the lecture)
  • The EEG and consciousness can be separated (interpretation based on the sources). Atomoxetine changed the EEG without waking the animal, and ketamine could not be reversed with dopamine. This fits with the EEG and consciousness being separable, and with ketamine acting on other circuits and giving a different EEG from the GABA agents and dexmedetomidine.
