It also supports emergence not being induction in reverse (see the card on hysteresis above).
  • Patients taking Ritalin may need more during sedation and light anaesthesia. Methylphenidate woke rats under both isoflurane and propofol, but not during deep isoflurane with burst suppression. In humans there are only case reports: a child who was not sedated by usual doses of midazolam and ketamine, and two adults who needed more thiopental at induction but also took other psychotropic drugs. In 34 children there was no difference in BIS at 1 MAC sevoflurane.Sources: Solt 2011; Chemali 2012; Kenny 2016; Ririe 1997; Kasuga 2008; Chambers 2012
  • What does it mean in practice? At a high enough dose it probably matters little. If the patient has taken the drug the same day, the EEG gives a better picture of whether hypnosis is adequate than the dose and clinical signs. Whether the drug should be withheld before surgery has not been studied. (interpretation based on the sources)
  • None of this is clinical practice today. Rat experiments with small groups and the righting reflex as the measure of consciousness. Amphetamines raise blood pressure and heart rate.
Solt, lecture Høstmøtet 2026 Alkire 2008 Långsjö 2012 Solt 2014 Kenny 2015 Kato 2021 Vincent 2024 Mashour 2021 Vincent 2025

A brainstem switch for induction and emergence: the PPT and sevoflurane (Li 2024)

Animal study in mice of glutamatergic neurones in the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPT) of the brainstem. The PPT projects to, among others, the thalamus, hypothalamus, basal forebrain and the ventral tegmental area (VTA), which is important for wakefulness and reward.Source: Li 2024, Br J Anaesth 2024;132:320–333

  • Activity in the PPT follows consciousness. Neuronal activity fell before the mice lost the righting reflex under sevoflurane, stayed low while they were unconscious, and rose again as they woke.
  • Inhibition gives faster induction and slower emergence. When the neurones were inhibited chemogenetically, the mice lost consciousness faster (76 versus 121 seconds) and woke later (278 versus 145 seconds), and became more sensitive to sevoflurane. The EEG showed more delta.
  • Stimulation wakes during ongoing volatile anaesthesia. Light stimulation of the neurones, or of the pathway from the PPT to the VTA, produced awake-like behaviour during steady sevoflurane anaesthesia and activated the cortex. During sevoflurane-induced burst suppression, the suppression ratio fell from about 55 % to about 6 % during stimulation.
  • There may be shared circuits for both transitions. Because both induction and emergence were affected, the authors interpret this as shared circuits for loss and recovery of consciousness. This nuances the finding that orexin delayed emergence without changing induction.Source for the orexin finding: Kelz 2019 (see the card above and Discrepancies)
  • The brainstem helps regulate consciousness (interpretation based on the sources). The finding supports that consciousness under anaesthesia is regulated by brainstem networks and not only by the cortex, and that emergence can be actively influenced. It is not clinically transferable today.
  • Caveats: few mice and sevoflurane only. Few animals per group (8–14). The authors do not know whether sevoflurane acts directly on the neurones or via their inputs. High-frequency light stimulation may also activate other pathways. No conflicts of interest, funded by Chinese research councils.
  • The PPT is one node among many. The finding supports the hypothesis that sleep and anaesthesia share circuits. But the PPT is only one of many neuronal populations in the forebrain, midbrain and brainstem that can promote or oppose anaesthesia, including the parabrachial nucleus, VTA, nucleus accumbens, thalamus, basal forebrain and preoptic area. If induction and emergence were mirror images, and the PPT were a master regulator, activity in the PPT should have recovered before emergence. It did not: it rose only as the mice woke. The next step is to understand how the network works together. Calling a neuronal population causal requires three things: its activity is altered by the anaesthetic, altering its activity changes the anaesthetic state, and it is connected to the rest of the network. Anaesthesia is, according to the editorial, no longer understood as a “wet blanket” that dampens the whole brain equally. No conflicts of interest; Kelz is also first author of the 2019 review above.Source: McKinstry-Wu and Kelz 2024, editorial “One node among many”
Li, Hu, Tan, Li, Huang and Wang. Br J Anaesth 2024;132:320–333 McKinstry-Wu and Kelz. Br J Anaesth 2024;132:220–223

Key points

  • Nociception is not pain. Nociception is the neural process that encodes noxious stimuli. Pain is a conscious experience. Anaesthesia can remove the experience without removing the process. That is why an unconscious patient can still develop tachycardia, hypertension and a stress response.See and “Pain and nociception: the definitions and the pathway”
  • Nociception can produce one of three EEG patterns. Beta arousal typically occurs in light anaesthesia with little opioid. Delta arousal occurs in deeper or balanced anaesthesia with too little opioid, especially with visceral stimulation. In alpha dropout, frontal alpha disappears transiently. The patterns do not always occur, and not all at once. Delta arousal and alpha dropout can make the index read the EEG as deeper anaesthesia, even though the patient is responding to stimulation.Source: García 2021. See
  • With delta arousal or alpha dropout, consider analgesia rather than less hypnotic. This applies when other signs of inadequate anaesthesia are absent. Concurrent autonomic signs such as heart rate, blood pressure and skin conductance point towards nociception. Weakened alpha alone has several possible causes.Source: García 2021. See and “Clinical example: alpha disappears with visceral pain (shared case)”
  • The signal continues under general anaesthesia. Volatile agents prevent movement at the spinal cord. The adrenergic response to incision is blocked only at doses well above those needed for unconsciousness. The nervous system thus processes the signal even though the patient does not experience it.See
  • The right dose, not the most. There is good reason to treat nociception to keep the circulation stable and dampen the stress response. Prevention of chronic pain in adults has not been shown. High intraoperative opioid doses, especially remifentanil, can cause somewhat more pain afterwards.See and “Neuroplasticity: when pain signals change the nervous system”
  • Remifentanil can cause hyperalgesia, especially at high doses and with abrupt withdrawal. The mechanism is probably central sensitisation via the NMDA receptor. Gradual tapering may prevent it, but this needs confirmation in larger trials. Ketamine spares opioid, but that it must be given before incision has not been shown.See
  • Caesarean section under general anaesthesia is a particularly vulnerable period. From induction until the baby is delivered, nociception is strong and the risk of awareness high (about 1 in 670). This argues for an adequate hypnotic dose. A short-acting opioid at induction may be considered according to local procedures and in consultation with the anaesthetist (interpretation based on the sources).Source: NAP5 (Pandit 2014). See

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

Hypnosis or analgesia? The pain pathway to heart and vessels

Hypnosis and analgesia are two different components and need different measures. If heart rate and blood pressure rise with surgical stimulation while the EEG is unchanged, and other causes are ruled out, analgesia is probably inadequate. Hypnosis may well be enough.Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)

Anaesthesia inhibits the transfer here
↑
heart rate and BP rise
↑
reflex movement
↑
↑
Tap a step to read briefly about it.
Sources: Yam 2018; D'Mello and Dickenson 2008; Sleigh et al. 2025; Brown et al. 2015
  • The pathway runs through the brainstem. The signal travels from the dorsal horn to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) in the medulla. From there sympathetic output increases via the ventrolateral medulla and the sympathetic ganglia to the heart and vessels, and vagal output to the sinoatrial node is reduced via the nucleus ambiguus. The pathway is called the nociceptive-medullary-autonomic circuit.Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)
  • If hypnosis is adequate, the EEG will probably not change. The response runs through spinal cord and brainstem. Heart rate and blood pressure can therefore rise while the EEG and index are unchanged.Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)
  • Rule out other causes, then give analgesia. Consider bleeding, hypoxaemia, disconnection of the breathing circuit and inadequate neuromuscular block. Check relaxation, oxygen saturation and EEG. If it is still unexplained, the chapter suggests more analgesia.Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)
  • More hypnotic is an ineffective route. Blocking the adrenergic response to incision in half the patients required 1.45–1.60 MAC (halothane and enflurane with nitrous oxide, that is, older agents), well above what is needed for unconsciousness. For movement under propofol, an opioid works better than more propofol.Sources: Roizen 1981; Sleigh et al. 2025
  • Other signs of inadequate analgesia. Sweating, lacrimation, dilated pupils and return of muscle tone and movement. The last two are not seen when the patient has received a neuromuscular blocker.Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)
  • When does the EEG change? If the stimulus is strong and hypnosis too light to keep the patient unconscious, the EEG and index may change and warn that consciousness is returning. Nociception can also produce its own EEG patterns (see the cards below).Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)

Nociception is not pain, and EEG shows only part of it

Sources: Yam 2018; D'Mello and Dickenson 2008; Sleigh et al. 2025; Brown et al. 2015
Show detailed figure
  • Anaesthesia can remove pain without removing nociception. Nociception is the neurophysiological process (receptor, peripheral nerve, dorsal horn, thalamus). Pain is a conscious experience that requires cortical processing. That is why an unconscious patient can still develop tachycardia, hypertension, a stress response and postoperative hyperalgesia.
  • EEG shows hypnotic level, but noxious stimulation leaves traces. An EEG that becomes “deeper” (more delta, less alpha) during surgery may therefore be a nociceptive phenomenon, not overdosing. The three patterns are described in the card below. See also the card on fentanyl and frontal theta in the Agents tab.Sources: García 2021, Balanza 2022
  • No monitor measures the experience of pain directly. EEG shows hypnosis. Nociception monitors (pupillometry, skin conductance, heart rate variability and the like) show the autonomic response. Haemodynamics show the circulation. The evidence that nociception-guided opioid dosing improves patient outcomes is still limited. The figure therefore describes a rationale, not a documented effect.
García 2021, Hight 2020, Balanza 2022

Three EEG reactions to a noxious stimulus: beta arousal, delta arousal and alpha dropout (García 2021)

This is a narrative review, not a systematic search. The authors started from key articles and their references. They grouped the literature into index studies, raw-EEG studies and animal studies.Source: García, Kreuzer, Hight, Sleigh. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:445–457

  • The nociceptive response has four dimensions, and EEG shows only one of them. The four are somatic (spinal reflexes, movement), autonomic (brainstem and hypothalamus: heart rate, respiration, vasoconstriction, pupil), cognitive arousal and memory (subcortical and midbrain, via forebrain and cortex), and endocrine, coagulation and immune responses. The EEG responses are more transient and do not always occur at the same time as the autonomic ones. They still show that the anaesthesia has not completely blocked the brain's response to tissue injury.
  • 1 Beta arousal: more activity at 12–25 Hz, and the index rises. It typically occurs at low dose (0.5–1.0 MAC without opioid), often together with movement. The mechanism is well known: aminergic and cholinergic activation from the brainstem depolarises the thalamus and inhibits the slow thalamocortical oscillations. The indices are designed to capture precisely this.Source: García 2021
  • 2 Delta arousal (“paradoxical arousal”): more delta, which the index misreads as deeper anaesthesia. Power at 0.5–4 Hz increases. It occurs at higher doses or in balanced anaesthesia with too little opioid, especially with visceral stimulation. The mechanism is unclear, but the midbrain reticular formation appears to be involved. The response need not mean that the patient is heading towards consciousness. The problem is that the indices then “wrongly suggest that the hypnotic dose is too high”.Source: García 2021
  • 3 Alpha dropout: frontal alpha disappears suddenly, and opioid can bring it back. Alpha is lost in episodes, while delta often persists or increases. The interpretation is that the thalamus switches from hyperpolarised “burst” mode (idling) to continuous firing. Thalamocortical communication thus resumes, while the cortex is still GABAergically depressed. That delta can increase while alpha falls suggests that slow oscillations can be cortical and independent of the thalamus.Source: García 2021
  • With delta arousal or alpha dropout, do not reduce the hypnotic, but consider more analgesia. The exception is when there are other signs of inadequate anaesthesia. Analgesia can be opioid or a regional block. The authors propose titrating opioid to maximal frontal alpha power, with an individual reference (age, cognition, possibly a preoperative baseline or alpha at steady state before surgery). This is an unsolved problem for closed-loop dosing systems. Autonomic responses are linked to cardiovascular complications, but whether pure EEG responses matter for outcome is unknown.Source: García 2021
  • No monitor captures all three patterns. Most commercial “pain monitors” do not use EEG. They use heart rate variability, modelled opioid concentrations, the spinal flexor reflex, the plethysmographic pulse wave and heart interval, or a multivariable model. The multivariable model improved opioid titration and cardiovascular stability in two studies. A few monitors are EEG-based. The article does not mention skin conductance. It measures the number and amplitude of sympathetically triggered sweat fluctuations in the palm, and is thus an autonomic marker on a par with the others.Source: García 2021
  • Skin conductance reacts to airway stimulation, but is no better than heart rate at incision. In a prospective observational study of 49 patients (monitors blinded to staff), NOL and the skin conductance index SCA reacted to jaw thrust, laryngoscopy and intubation more often than heart rate did. They flagged two to three times as many patients as a 10% rise in heart rate. At skin incision neither was better than heart rate, and NOL flagged more patients than SCA. In a Norwegian pilot of 10 patients (HIPEC), SCA rose in 9 of 10 when core temperature rose from 36.2 to 38.4 °C, without other signs of pain. The method is therefore unreliable during rapid temperature changes. Neither study has outcome measures. The manufacturer's own claims about documentation are not reproduced here.Sources (outside the García article): Widarsson Norbeck 2025, BMC Anesthesiol 2025;25:51; Scand J Pain 2024
  • The evidence base is thin, and the benefit has not been tested. The review is narrative, not systematic. The studies are few and small, many from the 1990s, with different agents and stimuli. No randomised trials have tested whether EEG-guided analgesia improves outcome, which the authors themselves emphasise. No conflicts of interest; funded by the James S. McDonnell Foundation.
García, Kreuzer, Hight, Sleigh. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:445–457

Clinical example: alpha disappears during visceral pain (shared case)

Shared case from Norwegian clinical practice. It is not published and not peer reviewed. The description is based on one screenshot of a frontal EEG monitor with a skin conductance monitor alongside, and on information from the person who shared it. The screenshot is not reproduced here.

  • Alpha suddenly weakened, while delta remained. First there was a clear alpha band and strong slow-delta in both hemispheres. Around 14:00 the alpha band suddenly became much weaker in both hemispheres, while the power below about 4 Hz remained. Towards the end of the picture alpha partly returned. The spectral edge frequency (SEF) was about 10 Hz, and artefacts 0%.
  • At the same time, skin conductance, heart rate and blood pressure rose. This was reported by the person who shared the case. The stimulation was visceral.
  • The picture fits alpha dropout. Alpha falls suddenly while delta persists. Delta arousal (“paradoxical arousal”) is also seen particularly with visceral stimulation. Both patterns can make the indices read the EEG as deeper anaesthesia, even though the patient is responding to pain. García 2021 then recommends considering more analgesia rather than reducing the hypnotic.Source: García 2021
  • It is the simultaneous autonomic signs that point towards nociception. Weakening of alpha alone has several possible causes, for example lower cardiac output (see the card on alpha and cardiac output in the Perfusion tab) or a changed dose.
  • Caveat: one case, one screenshot. It is not known which drugs and doses the patient received, whether anything was changed, or what was done afterwards.
Shared clinical example; García 2021

Pain and nociception: the definitions and the pathway

IASP (International Association for the Study of Pain) clearly distinguishes the two terms.

Anaesthesia inhibits the transfer here
↑
heart rate and BP rise
↑
reflex movement
↑
↑
Tap a step to read briefly about it.
Sources: Yam 2018; D'Mello and Dickenson 2008; Sleigh et al. 2025; Brown et al. 2015
  • Pain is an experience. IASP defines pain as “An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage”.Sources: IASP, revised 2020; Raja 2020
  • Nociception is a neural process. IASP defines nociception as “The neural process of encoding noxious stimuli.” The consequences may be autonomic (e.g. elevated blood pressure) or behavioural (a withdrawal reflex). Pain sensation is not necessarily implied.Source: IASP
  • Pain cannot be inferred solely from activity in sensory neurons. Pain and nociception are different phenomena. Inability to communicate does not negate the possibility that pain is experienced.Source: notes to the IASP definition
  • The signal first travels from the tissue to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Nociceptors convert noxious stimuli into nerve signals (transduction). Aδ fibres are myelinated and fast and give pricking pain. C fibres are unmyelinated and slow. Both are thought to end in the dorsal horn, which is the first relay site.Sources: Yam 2018; D'Mello and Dickenson 2008
  • From the dorsal horn the signal goes to the brainstem and thalamus. Nociceptive-specific cells lie mainly in laminae I–II, wide-dynamic-range cells deeper, in lamina V. Lamina I projects to the parabrachial nucleus and the PAG (periaqueductal grey) in the brainstem. Lamina V projects mainly to the thalamus via the spinothalamic tract.Source: D'Mello and Dickenson 2008
  • The brain itself regulates how much of the signal gets through. From the PAG, signals run via the RVM (rostral ventromedial medulla) down to the dorsal horn with serotonin and noradrenaline. This control can both inhibit and facilitate the signals.Sources: Yam 2018; D'Mello and Dickenson 2008

The brain’s own pain control

↓
↓
inhibits or facilitates
Tap a step to read briefly about it.
Sources: Yam 2018; D'Mello and Dickenson 2008
IASP terminology Raja 2020 D'Mello and Dickenson 2008 Yam 2018

Under general anaesthesia the signal still travels, even though the patient does not experience it

  • Volatile agents prevent movement via the spinal cord, below the cortex. When only the brain of goats received isoflurane, the dose that prevented movement had to be increased from 1.2 to 2.9%. Below 1 MAC, noxious stimuli still activated the midbrain reticular formation, the thalamus and the frontal EEG. At 1.1 MAC or more the activation was blunted.Sources: Antognini and Schwartz 1993; Antognini and Carstens 1999
  • The stress response needs more than unconsciousness. The dose that blocked the adrenergic response to incision in half of patients (MAC-BAR) was 1.45 MAC for halothane and 1.60 MAC for enflurane, with 60% nitrous oxide. That is well above what is needed for unconsciousness and immobility. Spinal anaesthesia blocked the response completely.Source: Roizen 1981
  • Nociception leaves traces in the EEG. It can give beta arousal, paradoxical delta arousal or alpha dropout (see the card above). It could perhaps measure nociception, but it is not validated.Source: García 2021
  • The patient does not experience pain, but the nervous system processes the signal. This happens in the spinal cord, brainstem and partly the thalamus and cortex. It shows up in circulation, hormones and the EEG.
  • Laryngoscopy under general anaesthesia is nociception and reflex, not pain. The blade and the tube stimulate nerves in the pharynx and larynx, and the signal travels to the brainstem. From there comes a reflex with increased sympathetic activity, higher blood pressure and heart rate, and protective reflexes such as gagging, coughing and laryngospasm. Pain is an experience, and that is absent under general anaesthesia. Intubation adds more than the blade: laryngoscopy with intubation gave higher blood pressure and heart rate than laryngoscopy alone of the same duration (randomised study, 80 patients).Sources: Khan and Ullah 2013; Smith 2008
  • In awake patients with good airway anaesthesia, laryngoscopy is mostly discomfort, but some feel pain. Awake laryngoscopy is performed with topical airway anaesthesia and sedation. With the right remifentanil dose, blood pressure and heart rate were stable and none recalled discomfort or pain. With nebulised lidocaine alone, 70% of healthy volunteers showed no reaction at all (two of the authors hold a patent on the nebuliser). Without adequate airway anaesthesia it is uncomfortable and triggers gagging and coughing. Pain is rarely the main outcome in the studies. Interpretation based on the sources: pain occurs particularly when the anaesthesia is incomplete. Direct laryngoscopy without anaesthesia has not been studied in awake people.Sources: Chin Med J 2009; Markerink 2024; Whited 2021
  • The drugs act at different points in the reflex. Topical anaesthesia stops the incoming signal, opioids dampen central processing, and beta-blockers only dampen the effect on heart and vessels. Beta-blockers, opioids, lidocaine and calcium channel blockers all reduced arrhythmias at intubation. Only lidocaine clearly reduced myocardial ischaemia, and then in one study. Interpretation based on the sources: when a beta-blocker dampens the rise in blood pressure, the signal to the brain is not gone. A calm blood pressure does not mean the nociception has been treated.Source: Khan and Ullah 2013 (Cochrane review)

Laryngoscopy under anaesthesia: a reflex, not pain
