The surgical stress response: what it does, how long it lasts and what blunts it

  • The stress response is started by nerve signals and inflammation. The nerve signals come from the injured area and are both somatic and autonomic. The inflammatory mediators come from the tissue.Source: Burton 2004
  • The hormones stay elevated for hours to days. Cortisol rises within 4–6 hours. ACTH and cortisol stay elevated for a period that depends on the size of the operation. ADH causes water retention that may last 3–5 days. Blood glucose above 12 mmol/L impairs wound healing and increases infection risk.Source: Burton 2004
  • Inflammation peaks within the first day. IL-6 peaks 12–24 hours after surgery.Source: Burton 2004
  • High-dose opioids and regional anaesthesia can blunt the hormonal response, but with limitations. High-dose opioids can abolish it in pelvic and abdominal surgery, but delay recovery and more often require postoperative ventilation. Regional anaesthesia abolishes it only when both the somatic and the autonomic nerve supply are blocked, and the inflammatory response is unchanged. Etomidate inhibits cortisol synthesis for up to 8 hours.Source: Burton 2004
  • That blunting improves outcome has not been shown consistently. This concerns the benefit of regional techniques.Source: Burton 2004
  • In newborns, fentanyl gave a smaller stress response and fewer complications. The study included 8 + 8 preterm infants undergoing surgery. Fentanyl also gave less protein breakdown in the first days. The study was very small, but it helped change the practice of operating on newborns without analgesia.Source: Anand 1987
  • The stress response fades over days. It is proportional to the size of the operation. Part of it is driven by inflammation, so even good analgesia cannot remove it completely.
Burton, Nicholson and Hall 2004 Anand 1987

Neuroplasticity: when pain signals change the nervous system

  • Pain signals can make the nervous system more sensitive. In peripheral sensitisation, nociceptors in the tissue respond more easily and have a lower threshold. In central sensitisation, nociceptive neurons in the central nervous system respond more strongly to normal or weak input.Source: IASP
  • The NMDA receptor is an essential step in central sensitisation. Its activation is needed both to start and to maintain the sensitisation. The phenomenon is prominent after surgical injury.Source: Latremoliere and Woolf 2009
  • Central sensitisation lasts minutes to hours, and the early phase passes. Wind-up, where repeated C-fibre input gives an ever stronger response, disappears within seconds. The authors advise against calling it LTP in the spinal cord.Source: Latremoliere and Woolf 2009
  • Opioids can also cause hyperalgesia, so more is not automatically better. High intraoperative opioid doses gave somewhat more pain afterwards and higher morphine consumption at 24 hours, mainly linked to remifentanil. The effect was small.Source: Fletcher and Martinez 2014 (meta-analysis of 27 RCTs)
  • Ketamine spares opioid and gives slightly less pain. Opioid consumption was 19% lower and pain at rest 5 of 100 points lower at 24 hours. The effect on the area of hyperalgesia was uncertain.Source: Brinck 2018 (Cochrane review, 130 studies)
  • The immature brain may be affected, but the cause is unclear. Extremely preterm-born individuals had altered sensory function at 18–20 years, most after neonatal surgery. The study is observational and cannot separate pain signals from illness and other factors. About one hour of general anaesthesia in infancy gave no difference in IQ at 5 years compared with regional anaesthesia.Sources: Walker 2018; GAS, McCann 2019
Latremoliere and Woolf 2009 Fletcher and Martinez 2014 Brinck 2018 Walker 2018 McCann 2019

Why nociception should be treated properly, and how strong the evidence is

Reflection from the author of the app: the signal is sent even though the patient does not process it, and it gives a stress reaction. It should therefore be dampened. The points below show what the sources support in this.
  • Treatment keeps the circulation stable (strong evidence). Without enough antinociception, surgical stimulation raises blood pressure and heart rate. Nociception-guided remifentanil (NOL) gave fewer episodes of hypotension (5 versus 28%) and 30% less remifentanil.Sources: Roizen 1981; Meijer 2019
  • Treatment blunts the stress response (strong as a biological effect, weak for patient outcomes). Opioids and regional blocks blunt the hormonal response, but better outcomes in adults have not been shown consistently.Sources: Burton 2004; Anand 1987
  • Sensitisation is a known mechanism (strong in animal studies and as a mechanism, weak in clinical trials). Preventive analgesia before incision had an effect for epidural (effect size 0.38), wound infiltration and NSAIDs. For NMDA antagonists and opioids it was equivocal.Source: Ong 2005
  • Much pain after surgery is associated with chronic pain (moderate for association, weak for cause). Persistent pain occurs in 10–50% after common operations, severe in 2–10%. Nerve injury during surgery is probably the main cause. Each 10% more time in severe pain on day 1 gave a 30% higher incidence of chronic pain at one year. This concerns pain after surgery, not nociception during it.Sources: Kehlet 2006; Fletcher 2015
  • Nociception monitors reduce intraoperative opioid, but not pain afterwards. A meta-analysis of 21 RCTs found no difference in postoperative pain or opioid requirement. One small study found lower pain in recovery with NOL.Sources: Ma 2022; Meijer 2020
  • Conclusion (interpretation based on the sources): treat nociception, but with the right dose. There is good reason to treat nociception under general anaesthesia to keep the circulation stable and blunt the stress response, and because sensitisation is a known mechanism. That this in itself prevents chronic pain in adults has not been shown. The stress response fades over days. The aim is the right dose, not as much as possible, because high doses of remifentanil can cause hyperalgesia.
Roizen 1981 Meijer 2019, 2020 Ong 2005 Kehlet 2006 Fletcher 2015 Ma 2022

Hyperalgesia after remifentanil: why it happens, and what may prevent it

Opioid-induced hyperalgesia means that the patient becomes more sensitive to pain because of the opioid itself: the same stimulus gives stronger pain. Remifentanil is the opioid most clearly associated with the phenomenon. In short, the nervous system counter-regulates the strong opioid effect. When remifentanil disappears abruptly, the counter-regulation remains.Source: Santonocito 2018

  • High doses give slightly more pain afterwards, mostly with remifentanil. High intraoperative opioid doses gave somewhat more pain and higher morphine consumption after one day. The effect was small. There is no fixed dose threshold. Studies typically compare 0.05 with 0.3 µg/kg/min. The effect was greatest at high doses and in younger patients in cardiac surgery.Sources: Fletcher and Martinez 2014 (meta-analysis of 27 RCTs); Santonocito 2018
  • The main mechanism is central sensitisation via the NMDA receptor. Remifentanil increases phosphorylation of NMDA receptor subunits in the dorsal horn. More calcium flows in, and signalling pathways (PKC, CaMKII) amplify pain transmission. NMDA receptor activation is also a necessary step in central sensitisation after surgical injury (see the card on neuroplasticity).Sources: Zhu 2025; Latremoliere and Woolf 2009
  • Several other mechanisms have been proposed, mostly from animal studies. Descending pathways from the brainstem shift from inhibiting to facilitating pain signals. Remifentanil downregulates μ receptors in the PAG. Glial cells and inflammatory mediators in the spinal cord are activated. How much each mechanism contributes is unclear. Doses and durations in animal studies are often higher than in clinical practice.Sources: Santonocito 2018; Zhu 2025
  • Gradual tapering is simple and inexpensive, but its benefit needs confirmation. It may prevent hyperalgesia, but this must be confirmed in larger clinical trials. The most reasonable approach is to limit the intraoperative remifentanil dose (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Santonocito 2018
  • Ketamine spares opioid, whenever it is given. Overall, ketamine gave 19 % lower opioid consumption and 5 of 100 points lower pain at rest after one day. The results were similar whether ketamine was given before, during or after surgery.Source: Brinck 2018 (Cochrane review, 130 studies, 8341 adults)
  • What seems to matter most is ketamine being present through the painful period, not giving it before incision. The idea of giving ketamine before incision is to prevent sensitisation before it starts (“pre-emptive” analgesia). Analgesia before incision worked for epidural, wound infiltration and NSAIDs, but the effect was uncertain for NMDA antagonists and opioids. When asking instead whether the effect outlasted the drug itself (“preventive” analgesia), 58 % of ketamine studies found this, and none of four magnesium studies did.Sources: Ong 2005; McCartney 2004
  • Other drugs have some support, but from few studies. Dexmedetomidine reduced remifentanil hyperalgesia in animal studies and in one human study. Magnesium had an effect only at high remifentanil doses. Nitrous oxide reduced hyperalgesia in one human study.Source: Santonocito 2018
  • For practice (interpretation based on the sources): as little remifentanil as needed, and taper. Use as little remifentanil as needed to keep nociception under control. Consider tapering rather than stopping abruptly. Plan longer-acting analgesia before remifentanil is stopped. Ketamine has a documented opioid-sparing effect, but that it must be given before incision has not been shown.
  • Caveat: the mechanisms are shown almost only in rats and mice. The clinical effects are small and inconsistent. Zhu 2025 is a narrative review.
Santonocito 2018 Zhu 2025 Fletcher and Martinez 2014 Brinck 2018 Ong 2005 McCartney 2004 Latremoliere and Woolf 2009

Emergency caesarean section under general anaesthesia: before the baby is delivered

In general anaesthesia for caesarean section, opioid has traditionally been withheld until the baby is delivered, to avoid affecting the baby. The mother then has intubation and incision with only a hypnotic and a neuromuscular blocker.

  • Opioid at induction blunts the circulatory response. Remifentanil, alfentanil and fentanyl lowered peak systolic pressure, mean arterial pressure and heart rate compared with placebo. None of them changed the 1-minute Apgar. Fentanyl gave a lower 5-minute Apgar; remifentanil and alfentanil did not. The authors call for an adequately powered trial.Source: White 2019 (meta-analysis of 17 RCTs, 987 women)
  • The risk of awareness is high in caesarean section. It is about 1 in 670 for caesarean section, versus about 1 in 19,600 overall. The OAA and DAS guideline therefore stresses an adequate dose of induction agent.Sources: NAP5 (Pandit 2014); Mushambi 2015
  • The guidelines say little about opioid at induction. OAA/DAS 2015 gives no recommendation on it. A more recent review describes short-acting or low-dose opioids as safe. A separate “OAA/AAGBI 2018” guideline for general anaesthesia was not found.Sources: Mushambi 2015; Bone and Hoskins 2022
  • That untreated nociception before delivery gives lasting pain has not been shown. The study that exists concerns spinal anaesthesia, not general anaesthesia. 443 women having caesarean section under spinal were randomly allocated to different doses of bupivacaine and opioid, with or without an NSAID, and 402 were followed up at 3 months. 11.4% had chronic pain. Those with more pain in the first days after surgery more often developed chronic pain. A low bupivacaine dose (8 mg) and no NSAID gave the most chronic pain (about 20%), versus 2.2% with 15 mg. The study says nothing about general anaesthesia or the time before delivery.Source: Cançado 2012 (randomised, 443 women)
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): enough hypnotic, and consider a short-acting opioid. The period from induction until delivery combines strong nociception with a high risk of awareness. That argues for enough hypnotic, and for considering a short-acting opioid at induction. The paediatrician should then be told. The choice must follow local procedures and be made with the anaesthetist.
White 2019 Pandit 2014 (NAP5) Mushambi 2015 Cançado 2012
The brain: perfusion, pressure and positioning

The point of this tab: during anaesthesia we must think perfusion, not just dose. The brain spends much of its energy on the electrical activity the EEG measures, so when blood supply fails it can show in the EEG, and it can look like anaesthesia that is too deep. Start with “Key message”. The other sub-tabs go into detail.

Autoregulation and EEG with falling perfusion

Why think perfusion during anaesthesia?

  1. The EEG can show whether the brain gets enough energy. About 60% of the brain's energy goes to signalling between nerve cells, which is the activity the EEG reflects (Patel et al. 2025). When blood supply fails, it is this signalling that fails first. It can show in the EEG before the cells are damaged. Read more: .Sources: Patel et al. 2025; van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016
  2. Alpha and faster activity disappear first. In moderate ischaemia, alpha and beta fall. Then more delta appears, and finally suppression. In carotid surgery, a fall of more than 50% in 8–15 Hz is regarded as a sign of too little blood flow. A frontal alpha band that weakens without a change in dose may therefore be a perfusion signal.Sources: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016; Guay 2025
  3. Low perfusion can look like anaesthesia that is too deep. Too little oxygen to the brain can give the same picture as more hypnotic: lower frequencies, less power and burst suppression. Other causes of the same picture include hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, hypercapnia, anaemia and hypoxaemia.Source: Guay 2025
  4. Autoregulation is not guaranteed, so MAP 65 is not a safe target for everyone. The lower blood pressure limit of autoregulation varies from 40 to 90 mmHg in adults. According to Patel et al., in most it probably does not lie below 70 mmHg. Chronic hypertension shifts the limit, and hypercapnia and sevoflurane can impair autoregulation. Read more: . Read more: .Sources: Guay 2025; Patel et al. 2025
  5. Blood flow to the brain is about cardiac output, not just MAP. In Trendelenburg, cardiac output was the best predictor of blood flow to the brain. MAP mattered little within the autoregulatory range. Treating low blood pressure with a vasopressor alone can reduce cardiac output.Sources: Nordum 2024 (Ahus); Patel et al. 2025
  6. Positioning affects brain perfusion. Trendelenburg, sitting position, PEEP and head rotation change perfusion pressure and venous drainage from the brain. Read more: .Source: Patel et al. 2025; Breyer and Roth 2025
  7. Check perfusion before adjusting the hypnotic (interpretation based on the sources). When the EEG changes without a change in dose, first check blood pressure, cardiac output, CO₂, haemoglobin, temperature and position. Sometimes it is perfusion, not the anaesthetic dose, that needs optimising.

The physiology behind it, with normal values, energy use and CBF thresholds, is in .

Patel et al. 2025; Breyer and Roth 2025 van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 Guay 2025 Nordum 2024

Anaesthetic agents affect autoregulation differently

Autoregulation is not something the patient either has or does not have. It is affected by the agent and by the dose. That means the same blood pressure does not give the same safety margin under every anaesthetic regimen.

  1. Propofol preserves autoregulation. In a randomised study of 42 healthy adults, both the fast response (dynamic autoregulation, measured as the rate of recovery after an abrupt fall in blood pressure) and the slow one (static autoregulation, measured during a slow pressure rise with phenylephrine) were measured with transcranial Doppler. Propofol 100 and 200 µg/kg/min changed neither of them.Source: Strebel et al. 1995
  2. Isoflurane and desflurane impair it, and the impairment grows with dose. At 0.5 MAC the dynamic response became slower while the static one was largely preserved. At 1.5 MAC autoregulation was abolished on both measures. The dynamic process therefore fails before the static one: the ability to respond quickly is lost before the ability to respond at all.Source: Strebel et al. 1995
  3. Sevoflurane dilates the cerebral vessels less than isoflurane. In 20 patients with an isoelectric EEG from propofol, so that the agents' own vascular effect could be measured without brain activity changing, middle cerebral artery flow velocity rose 4% at 0.5 MAC and 17% at 1.5 MAC with sevoflurane, against 19% and 72% with isoflurane. The effect is dose-dependent for both, but weaker for sevoflurane.Source: Matta et al. 1999
  4. Compared directly in the clinic, propofol came out best. 30 patients for robot-assisted prostatectomy, with pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg, were randomised to sevoflurane or propofol. Autoregulation was tested by raising mean arterial pressure from about 80 to 100 mmHg with phenylephrine. At the last test before the end of surgery, autoregulation was significantly impaired in 6 of 15 with sevoflurane and in none of 15 with propofol. Some in the propofol group were impaired at earlier tests.Source: Robertson et al. 2022
  5. What it means at the bedside (interpretation from the sources). The higher the MAC of a volatile agent, the more cerebral blood flow passively follows arterial pressure. A fall in pressure then reaches the perfusion faster, and the margin before the EEG changes becomes smaller. That is one reason a lower pressure limit cannot be set independently of which agent is used and how deep the patient is.
  6. Caveats. All three studies are small, in adults without known brain disease. All measure middle cerebral artery flow velocity with transcranial Doppler, not blood flow, and assume the vessel diameter is unchanged. In the Strebel study all measurements were made on a background of fentanyl and 70% nitrous oxide, and desflurane was dosed by inspired concentration. The Robertson study is in men in steep Trendelenburg, a situation that loads autoregulation in itself.

Where the lower limit lies in the individual patient, and why MAP 65 is not a safe target for everyone, is in .

Strebel et al. 1995 Matta et al. 1999 Robertson et al. 2022

Read the EEG and haemodynamics together

  • Low perfusion can mimic excessive anaesthetic depth. Too little oxygen to the brain can produce lower frequencies, broadband power loss and burst suppression on the frontal EEG, just like deeper anaesthesia. Find the cause before the dose is changed.More in “Low perfusion can mimic excessive anaesthetic depth”
  • Cardiac output matters, not just MAP. Alpha can weaken when cardiac index falls at an unchanged dose, and the EEG can return to normal when it rises. In an 89-year-old the EEG normalised when the cardiac index rose from 1.3 to 2.7.More in “Low perfusion can mimic excessive anaesthetic depth”
  • One MAP threshold does not fit everyone. The lower MAP limit of autoregulation ranges from 40 to 90 mmHg in adults. In one patient the EEG was asymmetric until MAP was above 95 mmHg, and lost autoregulation may give alpha slowing (9.4 vs 10.5 Hz).More in “Autoregulation is individual”
  • The evidence on the blood pressure threshold is divergent. MAP below 55 mmHg or a 40% fall is linked to harm, but several studies find no association. In older patients a MAP target above baseline gave less delirium on day 1 (4% vs 16–22%).More in “How low can blood pressure go? The evidence is divergent”
  • No monitor proves hypoperfusion on its own. rSO₂ has a wide normal range and did not identify lost autoregulation in a pilot study. The frontal EEG has blind spots. So read the EEG and haemodynamics together before changing the dose.More in “What NIRS and frontal EEG can and cannot show”

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Low perfusion can mimic excessive anaesthetic depth

The frontal EEG cannot on its own distinguish too much hypnotic from too little oxygen to the brain. Both can produce the same picture. The cause must therefore be clarified before the anaesthetic is adjusted.Source: Guay 2025

  • Same pattern, different causes. Too little oxygen to the brain produces a shift towards lower frequencies, broadband power loss, burst suppression and sustained suppression, as with deeper anaesthesia. With normal oxygen delivery the picture may be due to anaesthetic, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, hypercapnia, postictal suppression or noxious stimulation. With reduced delivery it may be due to shock, intracranial hypertension, venous congestion, hypoxaemia, hypocapnia, anaemia or stroke.Source: Guay 2025
  • The EEG followed the circulation in individual patients. In three case reports the EEG changed with pressure and cardiac output. Loss of alpha and burst suppression appeared when the circulation failed (MAP below 70 mmHg with right heart failure), and the EEG returned to normal when the circulation improved, after adrenaline or when the cardiac index rose from 1.3 to 2.7. In one case the arterial pressure showed MAP 80–90 while directly measured aortic pressure was 35 mmHg. A shared case shows the same: alpha weakened when MAP and cardiac index fell at an unchanged dose, and returned when the circulation improved.Sources: Guay 2025; shared case
  • It is unclear whether perfusion or concentration is at work. In a randomised trial, burst suppression disappeared in more than 50% when MAP was raised to the baseline value. The authors say it is unclear whether this is due to physiology, pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics. Shock and low cardiac output can also increase the propofol concentration and make the brain more sensitive.Sources: Georgii 2022, Guay 2025
  • The EEG does not prove hypoperfusion. Loss of alpha can also be caused by noxious stimulation. The case reports illustrate but do not validate. There is no threshold for which MAP or cardiac index produces EEG change in the individual patient. The schematic example is simulated and therefore shows no cause.Sources: García 2021; Guay 2025

The studies in detail:

Guay 2025 Georgii 2022 García 2021

Autoregulation is individual

The lower MAP limit of autoregulation ranges from 40 to 90 mmHg in adults, and autoregulation is impaired in many critically ill patients. The aim is therefore to find the patient’s own limit instead of using one number for everyone.Source: Guay 2025

  • EEG asymmetry can be a warning. In one patient with an occluded left and severely stenosed right internal carotid artery, the EEG became asymmetric at low pressure (SEF 10 Hz on the right and 25 Hz on the left). It became almost symmetric only at MAP above 95 mmHg, and the asymmetry returned when pressure fell to 75 mmHg. The authors argue that MAP alone cannot always be trusted when autoregulation is impaired. Caveat: a single case report without blood flow measurement, and ketamine and sevoflurane affect the EEG.Source: Nycz 2022
  • Lost autoregulation may give alpha slowing. In a pilot study with 36 analysed patients, the alpha peak frequency was lower with lost autoregulation (9.4 vs 10.5 Hz). Alpha power did not differ, and the groups were similar in MAP, PSI and SEF. Alpha frequency also falls with age and deeper propofol effect. The finding is therefore a hypothesis worth noticing, not something to act on alone.Source: Manquat 2022
  • Autoregulation can be measured. A Johns Hopkins protocol uses the correlation between MAP and flow velocity (Mx) to keep MAP above the patient’s own lower limit on cardiopulmonary bypass. The endpoint is postoperative delirium. Only the protocol is available, not results. Invasively, PRx and optimal CPP are used. With NIRS, TOx and COx can serve as surrogates, but with lower precision.Sources: Brown and Hogue (protocol); Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • Not validated for the individual (interpretation based on the sources). The EEG may be able to show when the patient’s limit is reached. But the suggestion about EEG asymmetry has not been tested, and the cut-off for lost autoregulation in the pilot study is not validated under anaesthesia.Sources: Nycz 2022; Manquat 2022

The studies in detail:

Guay 2025 Nycz 2022 Manquat 2022 Brown and Hogue (protocol) Lobo and Lamperti 2025

How low can blood pressure go? The evidence is divergent

The sources do not agree on a single blood pressure threshold, and the studies do not even define the baseline in the same way.

  • Low pressure is linked to harm. Expert consensus recommends MAP above 60–70 mmHg. Long cumulative time with low pressure, a fall of 40% from baseline and MAP below 55 mmHg are linked to cardiac and brain injury, including delirium, and to cognitive impairment and dementia within one year.Source: Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • But not everyone finds the association. A meta-analysis found no association between permitted MAP below 60 and mortality. Several studies also found no association between hypotension and postoperative neurocognitive impairment.Source: Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • A higher MAP target gave less early delirium. In a randomised trial of 150 older patients (65–80) undergoing hip arthroplasty, fewer had delirium on day 1 the higher the MAP target: 22%, 16% and 4% with targets 10–20% below, 0–10% below and 0–10% above baseline. On days 2 and 3 there was no difference. The group with the highest target had higher rSO₂, while BIS was similar. Caveat: a small, single-centre study that shows an association without testing the mechanism.Source: Xu 2020
  • “Triple low” means that blood pressure, the EEG index and the volatile concentration are low at the same time. In the largest study the thresholds were MAP below 75 mmHg, BIS below 45 and below 0.8 MAC. Such episodes are associated with higher mortality, but they may be a sign that the patient was vulnerable beforehand, not what causes the harm. In a randomised trial of 7,569 patients, anaesthesia staff were alerted to triple-low events without any reduction in 90-day mortality (8.3% with alerts vs 7.3% without). About half the patients received an appropriate intervention in both groups (51% and 47%), so treatment differed little, and the trial does not settle the question. The same pattern is seen with burst suppression: deliberately induced burst suppression has been associated with lower mortality after traumatic brain injury, whereas unintended burst suppression in intensive care is associated with higher mortality. The authors interpret this as the underlying disease, not burst suppression itself, driving the risk.Sources: Sessler 2019; Lobo and Lamperti 2025; Guay 2025
  • The blood pressure studies measure from different starting points. Georgii 2022 uses the lowest measured MAP before anaesthesia as baseline, whereas Xu 2020 uses the average of measurements before surgery. “Baseline” therefore does not mean the same blood pressure in the two studies, and the results cannot be compared directly.Sources: Georgii 2022; Xu 2020

The studies in detail:

Lobo and Lamperti 2025 Xu 2020 Georgii 2022 Guay 2025

What NIRS and frontal EEG can and cannot show

The EEG does not stand alone. Cerebral oximetry can add something, but both NIRS and the frontal EEG have weaknesses.

  • rSO₂ has a wide normal range. Normal is 55–80%. A fall of 15–20% from baseline, or values below 50%, is regarded as significant. In carotid surgery, a 20% fall after clamping has a high negative but low positive predictive value. Many therefore use rSO₂ more to guide haemodynamics than to decide on shunting.Source: Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • NIRS can miss. In a pilot study, rSO₂ did not distinguish lost from preserved autoregulation (minimum 50 vs 57%, p = 0.08). Possible reasons are extracranial contamination and vasoconstrictor.Source: Manquat 2022
  • The frontal EEG has blind spots. A frontal montage can miss focal temporal seizures and occipital strokes, and acute strokes rarely produce burst suppression frontally. Reduced blood flow can go unnoticed with high haemoglobin and high saturation, whereas anaemic and hypoxaemic patients tolerate less.Source: Guay 2025
  • Several monitors together gave less delirium. In a randomised trial of 255 patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy, guidance with EEG spectrogram, NIRS, transcranial Doppler and haemodynamics gave less delirium. In the shared case, it was the haemodynamic trend alongside that prevented the loss of alpha from being interpreted as nociception.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti 2025 (discusses the trial); shared case

The studies in detail:

Lobo and Lamperti 2025 Manquat 2022 Guay 2025

Schematic example: fall in cardiac output and loss of alpha

The image was made for teaching and is simulated. It is not patient data and not a printout from any equipment. It shows haemodynamics (arterial pressure, MAP and CI) above an EEG spectrogram for the left and right hemispheres. The fall in CI and the loss of alpha start at the same time.

  • What is simulated: CI goes from about 3.1 to about 1.7 l/min/m², stroke volume falls, and MAP and pulse pressure fall. Alpha (about 8–12 Hz) disappears in both hemispheres while delta (below 4 Hz) persists. The numbers were chosen to illustrate the pattern.
  • That the changes start together is a choice: Quantitative EEG captures changes in blood flow and metabolism within 28–104 seconds. The delay between a fall in cardiac output and EEG change will vary, and the image does not show it.Source: Foreman and Claassen 2012
  • Loss of alpha has several possible causes: Both an increase and a reduction in alpha have been reported with noxious stimulation. Sedatives and sleep can also confound the picture. Both noxious stimulation and low cardiac output are possible causes of such changes on frontal EEG. The image therefore shows no cause, and it cannot be used to distinguish perfusion from other causes.Sources: Sleigh et al. 2025; Foreman and Claassen 2012; Guay 2025
Foreman and Claassen 2012, Sleigh et al. 2025

Clinical example: alpha weakens when cardiac output falls (shared case)

One shared case from Norwegian clinical practice, from the author of the app. It is not published and not peer reviewed. It is included because it illustrates the same thing the sources describe.Sources: Guay 2025; Manquat 2022

  • What was seen: an adult during maintenance with an unchanged hypnotic dose, PSI 30, SR 0, EMG 0, SEF 10–11 Hz. On the same screen, a pulse contour monitor showed MAP and cardiac index falling for a few minutes (CI down towards about 1 l/min/m²). Over the same period the alpha band became weaker and drifted downwards in both hemispheres, and the spectrogram became “thinner” without suppression. When MAP was 83 mmHg and CI 3.5 again, the alpha band was back as before.
  • Why it is instructive: without the haemodynamic trend alongside, the picture would easily have been interpreted as nociceptive loss of alpha or as a dose that “drifts”. The timing with cardiac output, the unchanged dose and the complete return of alpha point to transient cerebral hypoperfusion. The same has been described in an 89-year-old in whom the EEG normalised when CI rose from 1.3 to 2.7.Sources: García 2021; Guay 2025
  • Caveat: one case, no measurement of CBF, NIRS or Doppler, and alpha weakening has several possible causes. The point is not that EEG “proves” hypoperfusion, but that EEG and haemodynamics should be read together. See image 17 in the image quiz.
Own clinical example; Guay 2025, Manquat 2022, Nycz 2022

The cards on burst suppression are collected in the tab.

The studies in detail: Guay, Manquat, Nycz, Xu, the Johns Hopkins protocol and two textbook chapters (7 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Frontal EEG as a perfusion marker in clinical practice (Guay 2025)

Review article from MGH and MIT (Anesthesiology 2025;143:1595–1618) on physiological EEG signatures in the critically ill, with three case reports.

  • Main point: signs of reduced cerebral oxygen delivery (CDO₂) during sedation or general anaesthesia resemble deeper anaesthesia on frontal EEG: a shift of power towards lower frequencies, broadband power loss, burst suppression and sustained suppression. The same applies to hypothermia and increased GABAergic effect. They must therefore be distinguished from one another before the anaesthetic is adjusted. CDO₂ is proportional to CBF, haemoglobin and SpO₂, and the authors emphasise the balance between CDO₂ and oxygen consumption (CMRO₂) more than the exact numbers.
  • Differential diagnosis for reduced neuronal activity: with normal CDO₂: anaesthetic effect, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, hypercapnia, postictal suppression and noxious stimulation. With reduced CDO₂: shock, intracranial hypertension, venous congestion, hypoxaemia, hypocapnia, anaemia and stroke. Primary brain injury can produce both.
  • Carotid surgery: the criteria for shunting (more than 50% power reduction in 8–15 Hz, more than 50% increase in slow-delta, more than 50% broadband reduction, or suppression) typically arise when global CBF falls to below 35–40% of normal (about 18–20 versus 50–55 ml/100 g/min).
  • CPP and autoregulation: CPP is MAP minus the greater of ICP and CVP. The lower MAP limit for autoregulation varies from 40 to 90 mmHg in adults, and autoregulation is impaired in many critically ill patients. Reduced CBF can go unnoticed with high haemoglobin and high saturation, whereas anaemic and hypoxaemic patients tolerate less.
  • Burst suppression: suppression is amplitude below 10 µV (typically below 5 µV), and electrocerebral inactivity is 2 µV or lower. In dogs with haemorrhagic shock (fentanyl and nitrous oxide), burst suppression appeared at MAP 31 ± 7 mmHg together with loss of diastolic transcranial Doppler flow (Werner 1995). A randomised trial (Georgii 2022) abolished burst suppression in more than 50% by raising MAP to the baseline value. The authors say it is unclear whether this is due to physiology, pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics. Shock can increase the propofol concentration and make the brain more sensitive.
  • Unintended burst suppression and “triple low”: sedation-induced burst suppression has been linked to lower mortality after traumatic brain injury, whereas unintended burst suppression is linked to higher mortality in intensive care. The authors interpret this as the patient's underlying disease, not burst suppression in itself, driving the risk.
  • Age and alpha: frontal alpha is weaker in old age, poor cognitive function, frailty and severe illness. In older patients without visible alpha, a broadband fall in power may be the first warning.
  • Loss of alpha can also occur with noxious stimulation under inadequate analgesia (García 2021), and unexpected beta and gamma during neuromuscular blockade should lead to more anaesthesia and analgesia.
  • Case reports (one patient each): (1) 39-year-old on propofol: burst suppression disappeared with lower propofol. Two days later, loss of alpha and burst suppression appeared when MAP fell below 70 mmHg with right heart failure and rising CVP, and the EEG normalised after adrenaline. The authors also mention that reduced cardiac output may have increased the propofol concentration. (2) 89-year-old after mitral valve surgery: broadband fall in power (slow-delta from 30–40 to 10–20 µV) and then burst suppression at a cardiac index of 1.3. The EEG normalised when CI increased to 2.7 after PVAD. (3) 65-year-old in LVAD surgery: burst suppression during weaning from cardiopulmonary bypass, while the arterial pressure showed MAP 80–90. Directly measured aortic pressure was 35 mmHg, probably due to vasoplegia and a fault in the arterial pressure measurement.
  • Limitations: a frontal montage can miss focal temporal seizures and occipital strokes, and acute strokes rarely produce burst suppression frontally. The case reports illustrate, but do not validate, and the article shows no EEG data from patients with raised ICP. They give no thresholds for which MAP or CI produces EEG change in an individual patient.
  • Caveat: Brown reports royalties from Masimo, and Guay reports travel support from Masimo.
Guay et al. Anesthesiology 2025;143:1595–1618

Alpha peak frequency as a marker of lost autoregulation under propofol (Manquat 2022)

Prospective pilot study from Lariboisière (Paris), BJA Open 2022;1:100004. The hypothesis was that frontal EEG can show whether cerebral autoregulation is preserved during propofol anaesthesia.

  • Patients and set-up: 56 included, 36 analysed (median age 57.5 years), elective interventional neuroradiology. Propofol TCI (Schnider, starting at 5 µg/ml) and remifentanil; noradrenaline for MAP above 65 mmHg. SedLine with four frontal channels (Fp1, Fp2, F7, F8; spectrum from Fp2), NIRS, transcranial Doppler in the middle cerebral artery during induction and 30 minutes after, and continuous MAP from a finger cuff (Clearsight).
  • Autoregulation: Mxa = correlation between 10-second averages of MAP and Doppler velocity over 30 epochs. Mxa ≥ 0.3 was regarded as lost autoregulation (CA−); the cut-off is taken from traumatic brain injury. The EEG was analysed only in stable windows (PSI 25–35, no burst suppression, SEF 8–15 Hz, MAP above 65, stable for at least 5 minutes).
  • Main finding: 18 CA+ and 18 CA−. The groups were similar in age (53 versus 57 years), MAP (71 mmHg), Doppler velocity, PSI and SEF. Alpha peak frequency was lower with lost autoregulation: 9.4 [9.0–9.9] versus 10.5 [10.1–10.9] Hz (p < 0.001), with a correlation of r = −0.556 against Mxa. Alpha, delta and total power did not differ. Univariate AUC 0.88; in a multivariate model OR 0.038 [0.004–0.409] per Hz (p = 0.007). Lower alpha peak frequency is also associated with postoperative delirium in the meta-analysis by Xu 2025 (Spectrogram tab) and in Gutiérrez 2019. Adding alpha peak frequency to age, ASA and noradrenaline dose increased the AUC from 0.76 to 0.93.
  • What did not discriminate: NIRS (rSO₂ minimum 50 versus 57%, p = 0.08). The CA− group had a higher ASA class and more noradrenaline (0.06 versus 0.03 µg/kg/min). The authors consider NIRS to be insensitive here (extracranial contamination, vasoconstrictor), and that the indices hide the frequency information.
  • Interpretation: alpha frequency, not alpha power, appeared to track loss of autoregulation, and does so independently of age. Power loss and slow waves (Guay 2025, the carotid criteria) probably only appear with more severe ischaemia. A slower alpha may thus be an earlier and more subtle sign than the patterns described in the cards above. This is a hypothesis from a single pilot study.
  • Limitations: small, single centre, short Mxa window, static analysis (one time point), no clinical outcome measure, and the Mxa cut-off is not validated under anaesthesia. Alpha frequency also falls with age (Purdon 2015 BJA) and with deeper propofol effect, so a low value in an individual patient cannot simply be interpreted as loss of autoregulation. The authors call for a dynamic study. No conflicts of interest declared; funded by the AP-HP foundation.
  • Practical (interpretation based on the sources): The alpha peak frequency can be read approximately from the spectrogram, also where the monitor does not display it as a number. An alpha band sitting around 9 Hz in a middle-aged patient with stable PSI and MAP is worth noticing, not acting on alone.
Manquat et al. BJA Open 2022;1:100004

Hemispheric asymmetry on frontal EEG and blood pressure (Nycz 2022, case report)

  • Patient: one 65-year-old man with dialysis-dependent renal failure, complete left-sided ICA occlusion and severe (70–99%) right-sided ICA stenosis, for first rib resection and balloon dilatation of the subclavian vein. Preoperative MAP was 81 mmHg. Induction with fentanyl, lidocaine, propofol, suxamethonium, rocuronium and ketamine, then sevoflurane at 0.7 age-adjusted MAC guided by EEG. The EEG monitor was applied after induction, and the text mentions no EEG baseline before induction.
  • The event: after induction, hypotension occurred (MAP 50–60 mmHg, non-invasive 50–80), treated with noradrenaline boluses and later an infusion. The EEG showed asymmetry: spectral edge frequency (SEF) 10 Hz on the right and 25 Hz on the left, with a hot band at 20–30 Hz probably due to ketamine. When MAP was above 95 mmHg the spectrogram became almost symmetrical.
  • Reduced support: the authors set the lower MAP limit to above 70 mmHg (85% of baseline) and reduced the noradrenaline infusion. Within minutes, fast activity above 12 Hz disappeared in both hemispheres, most on the right (nadir 65 mmHg according to the figure legend). Symmetry returned at MAP above 95 mmHg. The pattern returned after a new fall to 75 mmHg (at 10:32) and did not recur after MAP was kept above 95. The patient was extubated on low-dose noradrenaline, had no new neurological deficits, and at 6 months the stenoses were unchanged.
  • The authors' interpretation: the pattern is “concerning for focal ischaemia”. They also mention possible intracerebral “steal” with exhausted vascular reactivity and increased venous pressure during manipulation of the superior vena cava, and that ketamine disturbs the EEG. They write this is the first reported case of cerebral hypoperfusion captured by frontal EEG in a non-carotid procedure.
  • The authors' suggestion: MAP alone cannot always be relied on in patients with impaired autoregulation, and the lower MAP limit can be set from EEG symmetry on beat-to-beat arterial pressure. This is a suggestion from one case and has not been tested.
  • Limitations: case report. No CBF, NIRS, Doppler or imaging was measured to confirm ischaemia, the patient had no new deficits, and ketamine and sevoflurane affect the EEG. The edge frequency and asymmetry may have other explanations, and the authors point out that EEG interpretation is not a core skill in anaesthesia training.
  • Connection within the app: the pattern agrees with ischaemia first producing loss of fast activity (Foreman and Claassen) and with asymmetry as a sign of hemispheric involvement (BSI, Sheorajpanday). Guay 2025 describes other case reports in which pressure and cardiac output affect frontal EEG. All are single cases or reviews, not proof.
Nycz et al. Neurol Int 2022;14:1018–1023

Blood pressure targets and delirium (Xu 2020)

  • Design: randomised trial at a single hospital. 150 patients aged 65–80 years underwent hip arthroplasty and were divided into three groups by MAP target: 10–20% below baseline (D), 0–10% below (M) and 0–10% above (H). The anaesthetist could not be blinded.
  • Delirium day 1: 22% (D), 16% (M) and 4% (H), p = 0.031. On days 2 and 3 there was no difference.
  • Group H had higher rSO₂ from five minutes after incision, less emergence agitation (24%, 22% and 6%), a shorter stay in the recovery room (63 versus 92 minutes) and a shorter hospital stay (12 versus 15 days). BIS was similar between the groups.
  • The authors consider that higher rSO₂ may explain the effect. The study shows an association and does not test the mechanism.
  • Caveats: small sample, only one method for delirium, no blood markers, and discrepancies between text and tables (see Sources).
Xu et al. J Clin Anesth 2020;62:109730

Individual blood pressure targets from autoregulation monitoring: Johns Hopkins protocol (Brown and Hogue)

Protocol (version 2, 8 July 2014) for a randomised substudy nested in Hogue’s trial (NCT00981474), with Charles Brown as substudy lead. The file contains only the protocol, not the results.

  • Background: blood pressure targets are currently set empirically. In the elderly, hypertension, diabetes and vascular disease may shift the lower limit of autoregulation, and autoregulation is dynamic, influenced among other things by rewarming from hypothermia, inhaled agents (dose-dependently) and anaemia.
  • Patients: 55 years or older, surgery on cardiopulmonary bypass (coronary bypass, valve or ascending aorta), high risk of neurological complications, and with a TCD window.
  • Measurement: TCD over both middle cerebral arteries and NIRS on the forehead. MAP, flow velocity and rScO₂ are averaged in 10-second blocks. A moving correlation between MAP and flow velocity over 300 seconds (30 points) gives the mean velocity index (Mx), and the same with NIRS gives the cerebral oximetry index (COx). Values are sorted into 5 mmHg MAP bins. When autoregulation is intact, the correlation is near zero or negative; when lost, it approaches 1.
  • Intervention: MAP on bypass is kept above the patient’s own lower limit based on Mx. If MAP falls below the limit, phenylephrine 100 µg is given and isoflurane reduced (to a minimum of 0.5%), with vasopressin if needed. The control group is managed with standard MAP targets.
  • Endpoint: postoperative delirium, from 2014 defined by a consensus committee.
  • Caveats: this is a protocol, not results. Funded by the NIH.
Protocol, NCT00981474 (substudy), Johns Hopkins 2014

What is the blood pressure limit? The evidence is divergent

  • Chapter 11 in Lobo mentions that expert consensus recommends MAP above 60–70 mmHg. Long cumulative time with low pressure, a relative fall of 40% from baseline and MAP below 55 mmHg are linked to cardiac and brain injury, including delirium, and to cognitive impairment and dementia within one year.
  • A meta-analysis found no association between permitted MAP below 60 and mortality, and several studies found no association between hypotension and postoperative neurocognitive impairment.
  • Georgii defines baseline as the lowest measured MAP before anaesthesia. Xu uses an average of measurements before surgery. The definitions are not the same, so the studies cannot be compared directly.
  • “Triple low” (low pressure, low EEG index and low MAC) may be a marker of vulnerable patients rather than a cause. A randomised trial with alerts for such events did not affect 90-day mortality, but few alerts were acted on.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 11

Monitoring perfusion

  • rSO₂: the normal range is wide (55–80%). A fall of 15–20% from baseline, or values below 50%, is regarded as significant. Sensitivity 60–100% and specificity 94–98% for cerebral ischaemia.
  • Carotid surgery: a fall of 20% after clamping is linked to impaired consciousness with a high negative predictive value (about 2.6% develop neurological deterioration with smaller falls). The positive predictive value is low, and many use rSO₂ more to guide haemodynamics than to decide on shunting.
  • Preoperative rSO₂ of 60% or lower is linked to delirium in older patients after cardiac surgery, and below 50% to higher 30-day mortality.
  • Autoregulation: invasively, the pressure reactivity index (PRx) and optimal CPP (CPPopt) are used. With NIRS, the indices TOx and COx can be used as surrogates, with moderate to good correlation but lower precision. TCD requires an awake baseline.
  • The book refers to a randomised trial of 255 patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy in which multimodal guidance (EEG spectrogram, NIRS, TCD and haemodynamics) gave less delirium.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 1, 7 and 9

Positioning changes brain perfusion

  • Head height changes perfusion pressure. The head higher than the heart lowers cerebral perfusion pressure, and anaesthesia blunts compensation. In the “beach chair” position 80% had cerebral desaturation, even though arm pressure was the same as in the lateral position.See
  • In Trendelenburg, cardiac output matters. Cardiac output best predicted blood flow in the internal carotid artery. The largest fall came at induction (about 30%), not at tilt.See
  • End-tidal CO₂ becomes less reliable. Steep head-down position and pneumoperitoneum increase the gradient between arterial and end-tidal CO₂ and reduce compliance. Trendelenburg is contraindicated with raised intracranial pressure.See
  • The EEG index can fall without a change in dose. Lower cardiac output can give a higher propofol concentration than the pump predicts, and hypercapnia gives less alpha and beta. Look at cardiac output, blood pressure, CO₂ and the raw EEG before reducing the dose (interpretation based on the sources).See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Head height and the pressure at the brain

The blood pressure in the arm is not necessarily the pressure in the brain. When the head is at a different height from the heart, the hydrostatic pressure must be taken into account.Source: Breyer and Roth 2025

  • The height difference matters. The head higher than the heart lowers cerebral perfusion pressure and can cause systemic hypotension. With invasive blood pressure measurement, the transducer should be zeroed at the level of the circle of Willis (the ring of arteries at the base of the brain), in practice at ear level by the tragus or external auditory meatus, and any pressure gradient should be documented. Anaesthesia blunts the baroreceptor reflex and sympathetic vasoconstriction. The changes with positioning are therefore larger.Source: Breyer and Roth 2025
  • In the “beach chair”, arm pressure can mislead you. 80.3% had cerebral desaturation in the “beach chair” position, versus 0% in the lateral position, even though arm pressure was the same in both groups. A mean arm pressure of 80 mmHg with a 38 cm height difference to the forehead corresponds to about 52 mmHg at the brain. Caveats: the surgeon chose the position, the study was not randomised, and no cognitive testing was done.Source: Murphy 2010 (cohort study, 124 patients undergoing shoulder arthroscopy)
  • Several mechanisms may contribute. Possible causes are reduced cardiac output, deliberate or permitted hypotension, lost compensation under anaesthesia, head height not being included in blood pressure management, narrowing of the vertebral artery with rotation, and air embolism. Hyperextension, hyperflexion and marked rotation of the neck are also implicated in cervical cord injury.Source: Breyer and Roth 2025
  • The chapter recommends measuring blood pressure with the level of the brain in mind. It also recommends avoiding hypotension and bradycardia and treating them promptly, avoiding extreme head positions and keeping a distance between chin and chest.Source: Breyer and Roth 2025

The studies in detail:

Breyer and Roth 2025 Murphy 2010

Trendelenburg: blood flow follows cardiac output

Cerebral blood flow was maintained in steep Trendelenburg. Two studies of robot-assisted prostatectomy measured perfusion pressure in different ways and got different numbers, but the same main picture.Sources: Kalmar 2010, Nordum 2024

  • CPP was unchanged or fell, but blood flow did not fall further. At 40° (zero point at the external auditory meatus) both MAP and CVP rose, and CPP was unchanged (71 vs 70 mmHg). ICP was not measured. At 30°, CPP fell to 61–62 mmHg after one hour, but blood flow in the internal carotid artery did not fall further. According to the authors, this suggests that autoregulation was at least partly working.Sources: Kalmar 2010 (40°), Nordum 2024 (30°)
  • Induction gave the largest fall. Blood flow in the internal carotid artery fell about 30% after induction (483 to 344 ml/min). Tilt and pneumoperitoneum gave no further fall.Source: Nordum 2024
  • Cardiac output appeared to matter more than MAP. Cardiac output best predicted blood flow: 1 l/min/m² more gave 92 ml/min more. PaCO₂ had a small positive effect. MAP had a small negative effect within the classical autoregulatory range. The authors therefore consider monitoring cardiac output more important than MAP in this position.Source: Nordum 2024
  • Caveats. Both are small observational studies without a control group. Patients varied widely (CPP 49–99 mmHg during tilt), and 78% received vasopressor. None showed signs of cognitive dysfunction at 10 or 180 days. Neither study measured the EEG.Sources: Kalmar 2010, Nordum 2024

The studies in detail:

Kalmar 2010 Nordum 2024

Steep head-down position and pneumoperitoneum: CO₂, lungs and the EEG index

Steep head-down tilt and CO₂ in the abdomen affect ventilation. This affects both how well end-tidal CO₂ reflects arterial CO₂ and what the index shows.

  • End-tidal CO₂ reflects arterial CO₂ less well. In all three studies the gradient between arterial and end-tidal CO₂ increased and compliance fell. The sources disagree on how much this matters. In one, the gradient increased from 1.06 to as much as 1.46 kPa, and the authors advise caution with end-tidal CO₂. In the other, the increase was smaller in healthy women (2.3 to 3.9 mmHg), and end-tidal CO₂ was judged still usable. The gradient is still larger in older patients, obese patients and with low cardiac output.Sources: Kalmar 2010, Pisitsak 2019
  • The lungs become stiffer. Plateau pressure rose from 14 to 26 cmH₂O, and compliance fell from 50 to 23 ml/cmH₂O. Plateau pressure predicted the CO₂ gradient. Oxygenation was still reduced at the end, probably due to atelectasis.Sources: Kalmar 2010, Pisitsak 2019
  • Pressure in the head and eyes rises. Trendelenburg increases intracranial and intraocular pressure and is contraindicated with raised intracranial pressure. Optic nerve sheath diameter increased from 5.8 to 6.4 mm during tilt.Sources: Breyer and Roth 2025, Nordum 2024
  • The EEG index can change without a dose change. The lower the cardiac index, the higher the measured propofol compared with the pump prediction. In the knee–chest position BIS fell when cardiac output fell. Hypercapnia gave less alpha and beta and a lower SEF. A fall in the index during pneumoperitoneum should therefore prompt a look at cardiac output, blood pressure, CO₂ and the raw EEG before the dose is reduced (interpretation based on the sources, see the pneumoperitoneum card).Sources: Ogawa 2020, Chalo 2019, Kalkman 1991

The studies in detail:

Kalmar 2010 Pisitsak 2019 Nordum 2024 Breyer and Roth 2025 Ogawa 2020 Chalo 2019 Kalkman 1991

Pneumoperitoneum, cardiac output and ventilation: can the EEG index fall without a change in dose?

A common explanation is that abdominal pressure compresses the liver, that propofol is then broken down more slowly, and that concentration and depth increase. The sources support parts of this, but no study shows the whole chain in patients.

  • Abdominal pressure can reduce liver blood flow, but the findings vary. In pigs, hepatic artery and portal vein flow fell clearly at 20 mmHg. Other animal studies found no change below 30 mmHg, or even increased liver clearance. In patients, 12 mmHg gave poorer liver perfusion than an individualised lower pressure.Sources: Diebel 1992, Gudmundsson 2001, Hoekstra 2013, Olmedilla Arnal 2023
  • Propofol clearance follows hepatic blood flow. This has been shown in intensive care patients.Source: Peeters 2008
  • During pneumoperitoneum, measured propofol was on average as predicted. In robot-assisted prostatectomy with CO₂ and head-down position, measured propofol was not higher than the TCI pump predicted (median error −1.5%). But the lower the cardiac index, the higher the measured concentration compared with the prediction.Source: Ogawa 2020
  • Measured propofol was higher than the models predicted. The measured concentration was a median 27–111% above the models (Eleveld 27%, Marsh 53%, Schnider 111%). The authors attribute this to the models being based on few severely obese patients and too short sampling, not to pneumoperitoneum. Pneumoperitoneum was not analysed. Some early samples were drawn during the bolus itself and may be artefactually high.Source: Braathen 2024, Oslo (69 patients, BMI 21.6–67.3, laparoscopic cholecystectomy or bariatric surgery; propofol 2 mg/kg, then 6 mg/kg/h for 30 minutes, then sevoflurane; 474 arterial samples)
  • Lower cardiac output appears to give higher propofol concentrations. This is the best documented mechanism of those mentioned here (interpretation based on the sources). In animal studies, arterial propofol rose and clearance fell when cardiac output fell, and the BIS effect appeared at a much lower concentration. In patients in the knee–chest position, cardiac output fell from 5.6 to 3.9 L/min, measured propofol was about 74% higher than predicted, and BIS fell from 46.5 to 37.7.Sources: Upton 1999 (sheep), Johnson 2003 (pigs in haemorrhagic shock), Chalo 2019
  • In long procedures in steep head-down position, the EEG can change for reasons other than the drug. BIS and SEF were stable for hours with sevoflurane, while total EEG power fell, probably because of facial oedema. Case reports describe BIS falling to near 0 after several hours, also under desflurane. The authors suggest brain oedema or raised intracranial pressure as the cause, not drug concentration.Sources: Rubio-Baines 2026, Hoshi 2022
  • End-tidal agent concentration usually overestimates the arterial concentration during maintenance. The difference is about 15–30%. It is due to ventilation–perfusion mismatch in the lungs (alveolar dead space and shunt), not diffusion. For sevoflurane, arterial concentration was 2.09% versus 3.01% end-tidal during maintenance, but equal at emergence. During wash-out the relationship reverses: arterial concentration is then higher than end-tidal. How the patient is ventilated also affects the difference.Sources: Peyton 2020 and 2022, Lin 2015, Frei 1991, Enekvist 2010
  • High CO₂ can lower the index. Hypercapnia (PaCO₂ about 50 mmHg) gave less alpha and beta and a lower SEF, which reversed at normal CO₂. At very high PaCO₂ a marked fall in the index has been described, and end-tidal CO₂ may then underestimate the arterial value.Sources: Kalkman 1991, Ann 2017
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): In laparoscopy with a volatile agent, the brain probably receives somewhat less than the end-tidal concentration suggests, especially with atelectasis and shunt. With TIVA, propofol concentration can be higher than the pump shows when cardiac output falls. The index may therefore change without any change in dose. A fall in the index during pneumoperitoneum should prompt a look at cardiac output, blood pressure, CO₂ and the raw EEG before the dose is reduced.
Ogawa 2020 Braathen 2024 Chalo 2019 Upton 1999 Peyton 2020 Kalkman 1991 Rubio-Baines 2026
EEG is not covered in Breyer and Roth 2025. The EEG section above is based on Lobo and Lamperti and the studies. The evidence for EEG in raised ICP is sparse (see the card on ICP). Mean frequency falls when CPP is below 60 mmHg (Foreman and Claassen). Kalmar measured neither ICP nor EEG.
The studies in detail: Breyer and Roth 2025 on perfusion pressure and sitting position, Kalmar, Nordum and Pisitsak (5 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Positioning (Breyer and Roth 2025)

Perfusion pressure and head height

  • When the head lies at a different height from the heart, you must account for the hydrostatic pressure in the arteries and veins of the brain when estimating cerebral perfusion pressure. The chapter recommends documenting any pressure gradient.
  • Head above the heart lowers cerebral perfusion pressure and can produce systemic hypotension. With invasive blood pressure measurement the transducer should be zeroed at the level of the circle of Willis.
  • Trendelenburg increases intracranial and intraocular pressure, and the position is contraindicated in raised intracranial pressure.
  • General anaesthesia blunts the normal compensatory mechanisms (baroreceptor reflex, sympathetic vasoconstriction). Haemodynamic changes with positioning are therefore more pronounced.
Breyer and Roth 2025

Steep Trendelenburg and pneumoperitoneum (Kalmar 2010)

  • Design: observational study of 31 patients (age 62, range 49–76) undergoing robot-assisted prostatectomy in 40° Trendelenburg with CO₂ pneumoperitoneum at 10 mmHg. Mean time in the position was 159 minutes. Anaesthesia with propofol, sufentanil and sevoflurane (1 MAC).
  • Measurement of CPP: the pressure transducers were zeroed at the external auditory meatus, so CPP could be determined independently of position. CPP was calculated as MAP minus CVP, on the assumption that CVP is at least as high as ICP in this position. ICP was not measured.
  • Results: MAP rose from 79 to 95 mmHg and CVP from 8 to 26 mmHg, and CPP was unchanged (71 versus 70 mmHg in table 1). CPP stayed well above the lower limit of autoregulation. After return to the supine position MAP and CVP fell by the same amount, and CPP was briefly down at 61 mmHg before normalising within 3 minutes.
  • Cerebral oxygenation: SctO₂ (NIRS, second generation) rose from 70 to 73% (p < 0.001) and remained above 55% throughout, which the authors use as the limit below which ischaemia is very unlikely. The authors assume that higher CPP and higher PE′CO₂ increased blood flow and lowered oxygen extraction.
  • CO₂: PE′CO₂ rose from 4.12 to 4.79 kPa, and the gradient between arterial and end-tidal CO₂ increased from 1.06 to as much as 1.46 kPa. The authors recommend using PE′CO₂ with caution in this situation, because it underestimates PaCO₂ most at high values.
  • Lungs: plateau pressure rose from 14 to 26 cmH₂O, and compliance fell from 50 to 23 ml/cmH₂O. Compliance was still lower than baseline after return to the supine position.
  • The authors refer to earlier work describing intracranial hypertension with this combination, and lower SctO₂ in older patients and in patients with raised ICP. These groups were not the focus here.
  • Limitations: small observational study, no control group, no ICP or EEG measurement, and only patients who tolerated the procedure. The findings cannot be transferred to patients with raised ICP.
Kalmar et al. Br J Anaesth 2010;104:433–9

What determines cerebral blood flow in Trendelenburg? Cardiac output, not MAP (Nordum 2024)

Prospective observational study from Ahus (Front Anesthesiol 2024;3:1395973): 44 men (mean 67 years) for robot-assisted prostatectomy in 30° Trendelenburg, propofol/remifentanil with BIS 40–60, deep neuromuscular blockade, PEEP 8 and tidal volume 6 ml/kg. 37 had intraoperative measurements at six time points: blood flow in the internal carotid artery (ICA) by ultrasound, cardiac output, CVP via the external jugular vein, optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) as a surrogate for ICP, and PaCO₂. Cognitive testing (CANTAB) before, and 10 and 180 days after.

  • Induction is the largest fall: ICA flow fell about 30% after induction (483 to 344 ml/min) and CPP from 98 to 73 mmHg. Tilt and pneumoperitoneum produced no further fall in ICA flow, even though CPP fell further to 61–62 mmHg after one hour and ONSD increased from 5.8 to 6.4 mm. After return to the supine position ICA flow rose to 407 ml/min.
  • Predictors: cardiac output was the strongest predictor of ICA flow (1 l/min/m² more gave 92 ml/min more), PaCO₂ had a small positive effect (1 kPa gave 49 ml/min), while MAP had a small negative effect (10 mmHg more gave 29 ml/min less) within the classical autoregulatory range. The authors consider monitoring of cardiac output more important than the traditional focus on MAP in this position.
  • Wide spread: during tilt CVP varied from 10 to 28 mmHg and CPP from 49 to 99 mmHg between patients. Vasopressor was used in 78% during tilt.
  • Cognition: no sign of postoperative cognitive dysfunction at 10 or 180 days; small improvements on several tests are consistent with a learning effect. None of the intraoperative measures predicted cognitive outcomes.
  • Versus Kalmar 2010: Kalmar found unchanged CPP at 40° with the zero point at the auditory meatus; Nordum found falling CPP at 30°, but preserved ICA flow, which argues for at least partly functioning autoregulation. Both found an increased CO₂ gradient and a fall in compliance.
  • Caveats: observational study without control group or power calculation, unilateral ICA measurement (the ICA supplies about 80% of cerebral blood flow), non-blinded ultrasound analysis, vasopressor at discretion, non-Scandinavian speakers excluded, and considerable dropout at 180 days (25 of 37). Publicly funded, no conflicts of interest.
Nordum et al. Front Anesthesiol 2024;3:1395973

How reliable is end-tidal CO₂ in Trendelenburg? (Pisitsak 2019)

20 healthy women (mean 42 years) for laparoscopic gynaecological surgery in 30° Trendelenburg with pneumoperitoneum 13 mmHg, thiopental/sevoflurane/nitrous oxide, PEEP 5 (J Med Assoc Thai 2019;102:122–128).

  • The gradient increases, but only a little: PaCO₂–PETCO₂ rose from 2.3 to 3.9 mmHg after 45 minutes of pneumoperitoneum (p = 0.02) and returned to 2.85 after desufflation. The correlation between ETCO₂ and PaCO₂ was maintained (r about 0.5). Static compliance fell from 32 to 22 ml/cmH₂O. Minute ventilation had to be increased about 14% to keep ETCO₂ at 28–35 mmHg.
  • Predictor: plateau pressure during pneumoperitoneum predicted the gradient (R² 0.40). Oxygenation (PaO₂/FiO₂) fell from 516 to 415 and was still reduced (398) at the end, probably atelectasis.
  • Conclusion: ETCO₂ remains usable with pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg in healthy patients, but the gradient is larger in older patients, obese patients and with low cardiac output. The authors recommend higher PEEP and recruitment. Small sample, only healthy women.
Pisitsak et al. J Med Assoc Thai 2019;102:122–128

Sitting and “beach chair”

  • Hypotension is common. Mean arterial pressure, systolic pressure and cardiac index fall in the sitting position, and the chapter recommends gradual positioning with fluid and vasopressor ready.
  • Possible mechanisms of cerebral ischaemia: reduced cardiac output, deliberate or permitted hypotension, lost compensation under general anaesthesia, failure to account for head height in blood pressure management, dynamic narrowing or occlusion of the vertebral artery on rotation, and air embolism.
  • Cerebral oximetry: in an observational study of 124 patients undergoing shoulder arthroscopy, 80% in the “beach chair” position had cerebral desaturation, versus none in the lateral position. The chapter says there is no gold standard for threshold values, and that trends should be interpreted with stable ventilation and position. Murphy 2010: prospective cohort study with 61 patients in the “beach chair” position and 63 in the right or left lateral position, where the surgeon chose the position (not randomised). All received standardised anaesthesia with sevoflurane, BIS 40–60 and blood pressure within 20% of baseline. Cerebral desaturation (CDE) was defined as a fall of at least 20% from baseline or SctO₂ below 55% for 15 seconds, measured with FORE-SIGHT and treated according to a fixed protocol (increased blood pressure, increased EtCO₂ or increased FiO₂). 80.3% (49 of 61) in the “beach chair” position had CDE versus 0% in the lateral position, with a median of 4 episodes per patient (0–38). SctO₂ fell from about 80% to about 70% within 9 minutes and stayed between 66 and 70%, even though brachial blood pressure did not differ between the groups. Eight patients had 12 episodes below 55%, all in the “beach chair” position. After the first treatment SctO₂ rose in 61%. The authors calculate that a brachial mean pressure of 80 mmHg with a 38 cm height difference to the forehead corresponds to about 52 mmHg at the brain, which may have been too low for some. No obvious neurological deficits were seen, but no cognitive testing was done. Among patients without an interscalene block, nausea was 50.0% versus 6.7% and vomiting 27.3% versus 3.3% in those with CDE, but the CDE group consisted only of “beach chair” patients (none in the lateral position), so position and CDE cannot be separated. The probes were supplied at cost by CAS Medical Systems, and the first author has received honoraria from CASMED.
  • Recommendation in the chapter: measure blood pressure with the level of the brain in mind, avoid and treat hypotension and bradycardia promptly, and avoid extreme head positions.
  • The neck: hyperextension, hyperflexion and forceful rotation are implicated in cervical cord injury. The chapter mentions quadriplegia and spinal infarction. It is recommended to examine range of motion preoperatively and to keep a gap between chin and chest (classically two finger breadths).
Breyer and Roth 2025 (Murphy 2010, Hindman 2011)

Ischaemia shows in the EEG before cells are damaged

  • Synapses fail first, and this is reversible: In mild to moderate ischaemia (15–35 ml/100 g/min) alpha and beta fall, then delta increases, while neurons survive. Below about 10 ml/100 g/min the rhythms disappear permanently. (see “Ischaemia in the EEG, step by step”)
  • The EEG responds within seconds: During carotid clamping, changes appear within about 20 seconds, whereas diffusion-weighted MRI shows changes only after about 30 minutes. The mean frequency falls when CPP is below 60 mmHg, also in sedated patients. (see “Ischaemia in the EEG, step by step”)
  • Loss of fast activity is the first sign: In carotid surgery, preserved cortical rhythms are regarded as a reliable sign of adequate blood flow, and asymmetry measures such as the BSI can quantify the difference between the hemispheres. (see “Carotid surgery and asymmetry: when one hemisphere gets too little”)
  • The EEG has prognostic value, with caveats: A continuous EEG at 12 hours indicated good outcome after cardiac arrest, and an isoelectric EEG or burst suppression with identical bursts at 24 hours indicated poor outcome. In cerebral infarction the predictive value is low to moderate. (see “EEG and prognosis after cerebral infarction, SAH and cardiac arrest”)
  • Much can mimic ischaemia, so check the raw EEG: Sedatives, opioids, ICP changes and sleep confound interpretation, and processed algorithms do not detect suppression until it reaches about 40%. (see “What can mimic ischaemia, and the vulnerable brain”)
  • The vulnerable brain tolerates less: The risk of burst suppression rises with age and impaired neurological status. The evidence for EEG in raised ICP is very sparse. (see “What can mimic ischaemia, and the vulnerable brain”)

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Ischaemia in the EEG, step by step

Synaptic signalling uses a lot of energy, and it fails first when blood flow falls. That is why ischaemia shows in the EEG before cells are permanently damaged.Source: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016

As blood flow falls (ml/100 g/min)
