Tap a step to read briefly about it.
Sources: Foreman and Claassen 2012; van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016
  • Fast activity disappears first, and this can reverse. In mild to moderate ischaemia (15–35 ml/100 g/min) the synapses fail, but the neurons survive. The EEG shows less alpha and beta, then more delta. Even an isoelectric EEG may then be reversible. Below 10 ml/100 g/min the rhythms disappear permanently.Source: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016
  • The sources give the same order, with slightly different numbers. Fast frequencies disappear at about 25–35 ml/100 g/min, slow frequencies increase at about 17–18, and at 10–12 and below the EEG becomes silent and the damage irreversible.Source: Foreman and Claassen 2012
  • The EEG changes within seconds, not minutes. In circulatory arrest the EEG becomes isoelectric within 10–40 seconds. During carotid clamping, reversible changes appear within about 20 seconds. Diffusion-weighted MRI shows changes only after about 30 minutes.Sources: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016; Foreman and Claassen 2012
  • In focal ischaemia the EEG follows blood flow. In focal ischaemia, relative delta percentage correlates most robustly with blood flow and metabolism.Source: Foreman and Claassen 2012

The studies in detail:

van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 Foreman and Claassen 2012

Carotid surgery and asymmetry: when one hemisphere gets too little

In carotid surgery, the EEG under anaesthesia is best studied as a perfusion monitor. The key is the difference between the hemispheres.

  • Loss of fast activity at clamping suggests too little blood flow. More slow activity often follows. The EEG does not see deep structures, but preserved cortical rhythms are regarded as a reliable sign of adequate blood flow, also at depth.Source: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016
  • When to shunt is debated. Moderate EEG changes did not cause stroke, whereas major changes caused stroke in 2 of 22 (57 patients). The stroke rate was 1.4% with routine shunting, 1.6% with EEG-guided shunting, 2% without shunting and 4.8% with shunting guided by transcranial Doppler.Sources: Blume 1986; AbuRahma 2011
  • Which measure works varied with the anaesthetic. Spectral edge frequency captured ischaemia on isoflurane. Relative delta percentage was accurate on propofol.Source: Foreman and Claassen 2012
  • Asymmetry can be quantified. The brain symmetry index (BSI) measures the difference between the hemispheres from 0 to 1, and a change of 0.05 is regarded as significant. The pdBSI variant tracked NIHSS and infarct volume and distinguished infarction from TIA and controls. The study was small, done in awake patients, and required manual artefact removal by an expert.Sources: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016; Sheorajpanday 2009

The studies in detail:

van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 Blume 1986 AbuRahma 2011 Foreman and Claassen 2012 Sheorajpanday 2009

EEG and prognosis after cerebral infarction, SAH and cardiac arrest

Outside the operating theatre, the EEG is used to follow and predict the course after brain injury. Its value varies widely between conditions.

  • In cerebral infarction the EEG predicts only low to moderately well. Even so, outcome at one year was predicted correctly in 85% with the EEG, versus 60% with clinical criteria. In one study, delta power fell 100 minutes before clinical improvement after thrombolysis.Sources: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016; Foreman and Claassen 2012
  • In subarachnoid haemorrhage the EEG may warn of delayed cerebral ischaemia, but the evidence is weak. This concerns changes in the alpha/delta ratio. All the studies are small, and the authors themselves call for prospective validation.Source: Foreman and Claassen 2012
  • After cardiac arrest, the EEG at 12 and 24 hours says a lot about outcome. A continuous EEG at 12 hours, normal or diffusely slowed, predicted good outcome (specificity 91%). An isoelectric, low-amplitude EEG or burst suppression with identical bursts at 24 hours predicted poor outcome (specificity 100%, sensitivity 42%). Mild hypothermia barely affects the EEG, and usual propofol doses usually keep the EEG continuous. After anoxic injury, bursts are identical with abrupt transitions. With sedation they are heterogeneous.Source: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016
  • In dying patients the index may rise just before death. Processed EEG does not distinguish non-specific activation, seizures and EMG from organised activity. The findings concern dying patients, not prognosis in survivors.Source: Mashour 2024

The studies in detail:

van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 Foreman and Claassen 2012 Mashour 2024

What can mimic ischaemia, and the vulnerable brain

An EEG that looks ischaemic is not always ischaemia. Some brains show the patterns more easily than others, and more faintly.

  • Much can mimic ischaemia, so the raw EEG remains the gold standard. Seizures, changed intracranial pressure, systemic illness, sedatives, opioids and antipsychotics can confound interpretation. Normal slow-wave sleep can resemble ischaemia. Automatic artefact removal can mix ischaemic delta with slow activity from eye movements and drowsiness.Sources: Foreman and Claassen 2012; Sheorajpanday 2009
  • The algorithms lag behind. Processed BSR algorithms do not detect suppression until it reaches about 40%. Look at the raw EEG.Source: Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • The vulnerable brain develops burst suppression more easily. The risk rises with age and impaired neurological status, and in older patients the pattern is harder to detect. In septic encephalopathy, EEG slowing is the earliest finding. A metabolic theory, in which falling ATP causes burst suppression, fits with low perfusion producing the pattern, but is unproven.Source: Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • Raised ICP is poorly documented. A systematic review found only 4 studies that met the criteria. That the index may mistake raised ICP for deeper anaesthesia is a reasonable assumption, not a demonstrated finding (see the card on raised intracranial pressure).Source: Lenstra 2026

The studies in detail:

Foreman and Claassen 2012 Sheorajpanday 2009 Lobo and Lamperti 2025 Lenstra 2026

EEG and raised intracranial pressure: sparse evidence

  • Raised ICP probably affects the EEG through perfusion: Increased ICP lowers CPP and thereby CBF, and the cortex gets less oxygen and energy. The EEG changes are thus assumed to arise via CPP, CBF and metabolism (and possibly herniation), not from ICP itself. Neurogenic mechanisms may then dominate over vasomotor, chemical and metabolic ones in the regulation of CBF.Source: Lenstra 2026
  • The evidence is very sparse: Of 873 hits, only 4 studies met the criteria (adults with moderate to severe traumatic brain injury and ICP measured via ventricular drain or parenchymal probe). Three concerned post-traumatic seizures, one the direction between EEG and ICP. Larger studies are needed. The review does not say that a validated pattern is lacking, but that personalised EEG-ICP thresholds must be developed. Case reports, series, children and invasive EEG were excluded.Source: Lenstra 2026 (systematic review)
  • Small series suggest the EEG can warn of deterioration: Cyclic patterns, varying degrees of slowing and attenuated fast activity often preceded clinical deterioration in intracranial hypertension. In presumed plateau waves, generalised rhythmic delta activity and loss of fast activity appeared about 30 minutes before clinical change (seven non-traumatic neurocritical patients, retrospective). In two patients with herniation, increased low-frequency power and asymmetry in the spectrogram appeared roughly an hour before clinical deterioration. These fall outside the review's criteria.Sources: Sheikh 2022 (J Clin Neurophysiol); Alsallom 2022
  • In an animal study, EEG power tracked ICP: The median cross-correlation between total EEG power and ICP was 0.7, and 0.55 for CPP. A model with only three variables had accuracy 0.70, sensitivity 0.53 and specificity 0.79. The direction of the correlation is not stated.Source: Pose (pilot study)
  • No source tests indices and the spectrogram with raised ICP under general anaesthesia: ICP changes, sedatives and sleep can confound EEG interpretation. Intracranial hypertension is one of the causes of reduced cerebral oxygen delivery, and such changes can resemble deeper sedation on frontal EEG, but Guay 2025 shows no data from patients with raised ICP. That processed indices may confuse them with deeper anaesthesia is therefore a reasonable assumption, not a demonstrated finding for ICP.Sources: Foreman and Claassen 2012; Guay 2025
Lenstra 2026
The studies in detail: van Putten and Hofmeijer, Foreman and Claassen, Sheorajpanday, Mashour 2024 and Lobo and Lamperti (9 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

What ischaemia does to the EEG (van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016)

  • Energy: the brain accounts for about 20% of the body's energy requirement. In the cortex about 40% of ATP goes to the resting membrane potential and action potentials, and about 35% to synaptic transmission. The rhythms in the EEG arise from summed postsynaptic current in the pyramidal cells, and action potentials contribute little.
  • Normal blood flow is about 750 ml/min, 15–20% of cardiac output, or 50–54 ml/100 g/min.
  • Mild to moderate ischaemia (15–35 ml/100 g/min): it is primarily synaptic transmission that fails. The neurons retain their membrane potential, and CT and MRI are normal. The EEG shows less alpha and beta, then more delta, depending on severity and duration. In severe cases the EEG can become isoelectric, and even an isoelectric EEG can be due to isolated synaptic failure and be reversible.
  • Below 10 ml/100 g/min: the membrane potential shifts towards the Donnan potential (about −15 to −20 mV), and cytotoxic oedema and cell death follow. The EEG rhythms then disappear permanently. Lack of energy for more than 5–8 minutes produces such changes.
  • How fast: a few minutes without blood flow produce synaptic failure with full recovery when perfusion returns. In circulatory arrest the EEG becomes isoelectric within 10–40 seconds. In figure 1 (syncope), slower rhythms appear after a few seconds and clear slowing around 20 seconds after the arrest.
  • Inhibitory neurons are probably more vulnerable than excitatory ones. This may explain increased synchronisation and generalised periodic discharges in severe hypoxic injury.
van Putten and Hofmeijer. J Clin Neurophysiol 2016;33:203–210

EEG in carotid surgery

  • During test clamping of the internal carotid artery, reduced fast activity (often followed by more slow activity) reflects reduced blood flow. In figure 3, loss of fast activity alone corresponds to a CBF in the ipsilateral hemisphere of about 25–35 ml/100 g/min, and loss of fast activity plus more delta to about 15. These figures are taken from Foreman and Claassen and were not measured in the study.
  • Which changes require a shunt is debated. In a study of 57 patients (Blume 1986), moderate changes (8–13 Hz retained, but an amplitude fall of 50% or more and increased delta above 1 Hz) did not lead to postoperative stroke. Major changes (8–13 Hz reduced to minimal or absent, and a doubling of delta) led to stroke in 2 of 22. Most neurophysiologists nevertheless recommend a shunt for any change, and the authors consider that a fall in alpha/beta amplitude of about 10% can probably be accepted.
  • Perioperative stroke rate in a review (AbuRahma 2011): 1.4% with routine shunting, 1.6% with selective shunting guided by EEG and 2% without shunting. With shunting guided by transcranial Doppler it was 4.8% versus 1.6% with EEG. In the authors' own hospitals a shunt was used in about 3–5%.
  • EEG is not sensitive to deep structures, but preserved cortical rhythms are regarded as a reliable indicator of adequate blood flow deep down as well. This is because reduced flow usually produces a corresponding fraction in cortex and deep structures, and because the cortex has the greatest energy requirement.
  • Quantitative: the brain symmetry index (BSI) measures spectral asymmetry between the hemispheres on a scale from 0 to 1, with normal values of 0.05–0.08. A change of 0.05 is regarded as significant and agrees well with visual assessment. Temporal BSI captures global changes over time.
van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 (Blume 1986, AbuRahma 2011)

EEG in acute cerebral infarction

  • The predictive value of EEG for outcome after cerebral infarction is low to moderate. In a study of 110 patients, pdBSI and the (delta + theta)/(alpha + beta) ratio correlated with mRS at 6 months with a Spearman rho of about 0.46–0.47.
  • Continuous quantitative EEG with BSI correlated well with NIHSS in hemispheric infarction and was used to follow the effect of thrombolysis.
  • Spreading depolarisation occurs in acute infarction and may contribute to growth of the injury, but is difficult to measure through an intact skull. So far it has only been demonstrated reliably with electrocorticography.
van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016

EEG after cardiac arrest

  • About half of comatose patients after cardiac arrest have a poor outcome. SSEP and pupillary and corneal reflexes at 72 hours capture only about 20% of those who do not recover.
  • Continuous, normal or diffusely slowed EEG at 12 hours predicted good outcome (CPC 1–2) with specificity 91%, sensitivity 55%, PPV 84% and NPV 70%. Isoelectric, low-voltage (below 20 μV) or burst suppression with identical bursts at 24 hours predicted poor outcome (CPC 3–5) with specificity 100%, sensitivity 42%, PPV 100% and NPV 55%. The figures are based on two prospective cohorts with a total of 377 patients, all treated with mild therapeutic hypothermia and sedated.
  • Evolution towards continuous physiological EEG within 12 hours gives a very good prognosis. The patient's further prognosis then depends on injury to other organs, and the patients with favourable EEG and poor outcome died of failure of other organs, particularly the heart. Deep coma in the first hours does not rule out full recovery.
  • The authors call it a persistent misconception that EEG cannot be used during hypothermia or sedation. Mild hypothermia to 32 °C barely affects the EEG. At usual propofol doses the EEG remains continuous with anteriorisation of alpha, and isoelectricity usually does not occur.
  • Sedation-induced versus pathological burst suppression: in a relatively healthy brain the bursts are heterogeneous, and they come and go gradually. In postanoxic injury the bursts are identical, the intervals between them are flat, and the transitions between suppression and burst are abrupt. The latter has a poor prognosis.
  • The cerebral recovery index (CRI) combines five quantitative features (mean amplitude, alpha/delta ratio, entropy, coherence and continuity) into one number between 0 and 1. In the patient with good outcome CRI was about 0.7 at 24 hours, and in the patient with poor outcome about 0.3. In the first hours the EEG was almost identical in both.
  • The authors point out that recent guidelines do not include early EEG for prognostication, and expect EEG to be included in future guidelines. Interpretation of reactivity is not simple, and inter-rater agreement is only moderate.
van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016

Consciousness and the dying brain (Mashour 2024)

Narrative review (Anesthesiology 2024;140:1221–1231; Mashour, Lee, Pal and Li) on near-death experiences and EEG around cardiac arrest and death.

  • Incidence: 10–20 % of survivors of in-hospital cardiac arrest report near-death experiences. In AWARE II, 21.4 % of 28 interviewed patients had a “transcendent recalled experience of death”.
  • The EEG indices just before death: in seven critically ill patients without brain injury, BIS and SedLine values rose to levels consistent with consciousness just before death, after withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment. In a follow-up, 13 of 28 (46 %) had such a surge, while none of seven brain-dead patients did. Other series have not found this.
  • Why the indices cannot be read as consciousness: processed EEG cannot distinguish non-specific activation (for example glutamate release as hypoxic neurones die) from organised activity, cannot distinguish wakefulness from seizures, has only frontal electrodes, and EMG is hard to exclude completely.
  • Animal studies: in rats, a brief surge of gamma and theta with increased coupling between cortical regions occurred within 30 seconds of cardiac arrest. During asphyxia, release of many neurotransmitters increased; serotonin rose more than 20-fold within 2 minutes.
  • Humans: in 2 of 4 dying comatose patients, beta and gamma increased after the ventilator was disconnected. Both had a history of seizures, so seizure activity cannot be excluded. In a study of 8 patients, EEG ceased a median 78 seconds before circulatory arrest. None of the findings is linked to an actual experience.
  • During CPR: in AWARE II, SedLine gave interpretable EEG in 53 of 85 during ongoing CPR, and near-normal activity was seen up to 35–60 minutes into CPR. Detailed analysis has not been published.
  • Isoelectric is not always final: in animal models the isoelectric phase can be reversed by rapid reoxygenation, and the authors do not exclude that experiences may arise while the brain recovers.
  • Relevance and caveats: anaesthesia staff take part in CPR, organ donation and withdrawal of treatment. The authors reject non-neurobiological explanations. Funded by NIH, no competing interests. Note that the findings concern dying patients, not prognosis in survivors.
Mashour, Lee, Pal and Li. Anesthesiology 2024;140:1221–1231

Quantitative EEG, CBF and CPP (Foreman and Claassen 2012)

  • Thresholds: when CBF falls to about 25–35 ml/100 g/min, the EEG first loses fast frequencies. At about 17–18 slow frequencies increase gradually, and the authors call this a critical ischaemic threshold at which neurons begin to lose transmembrane gradients. At 10–12 ml/100 g/min and below the EEG becomes silent, and the cell injury is irreversible.
  • How fast: during carotid clamping the changes occur within about 20 seconds and are reversible. Infarction may only appear after hours at this flow level. Quantitative EEG (qEEG) captures changes in blood flow and metabolism within 28–104 seconds. Diffusion-weighted MRI detects changes at CBF 35–40 after about 30 minutes, whereas EEG detects them within seconds.
  • Metabolism: more slow activity (delta and theta) and less fast activity (alpha and beta) follow reduced cerebral oxygen metabolism (CMRO₂).
  • Which measure works: in carotid surgery, spectral edge frequency (SEF) captured ischaemic changes in patients on isoflurane, whereas relative delta percentage (delta/total power) was accurate in patients on propofol. Overall, relative delta percentage gives the most robust correlation with CBF and metabolism in focal ischaemia.
  • Confounding factors: seizures and periodic discharges, changes in intracranial pressure (for example acute hydrocephalus), systemic disease, sedatives, opioids and antipsychotics. Normal slow-wave sleep can resemble ischaemic changes. Raw EEG remains the gold standard, and any qEEG algorithm should be checkable against the raw EEG by someone who knows EEG.
  • The spectrogram (compressed spectral array) gives, according to the authors, the highest ratio of pixels to data and is easy to read, compared with raw EEG.
  • The review does not discuss the operating room beyond carotid surgery. Most of the review concerns intensive care patients. The suggestion of use after high-risk vascular and cardiac surgery, in refractory hypotension and in sepsis is the authors' own, and not documented in studies.
  • What does this mean for frontal EEG? Four frontal channels see only the frontal lobe, so ischaemia elsewhere can go unnoticed. The pattern is probably still the same frontally: fast activity disappears first, then delta increases. A difference between the right and left side can be a warning, but this has only been shown in case reports. If ischaemia is suspected, clinical assessment and full EEG are needed.Sources: Taccone 2026, Guay 2025, Nycz 2022
Foreman and Claassen. Crit Care 2012;16:216

EEG in cerebral infarction and subarachnoid haemorrhage

  • Infarction: in the early subacute phase the EEG correlates well with CBF while oxygen extraction increases (“misery perfusion”). Later it correlates more with CMRO₂ (“luxury perfusion”). Loss of reactivity and absent sleep-wake cycling suggest a poor prognosis. Absence of delta or presence of faster frequencies within 24 hours belongs to good outcome. Regional attenuation of fast frequencies without delta (RAWOD) suggests severe early CBF loss (mean 8.6 ml/100 g/min), and in one series mortality was up to 67%.
  • One year after infarction, functional outcome was predicted correctly in 60% of cases with clinical criteria. With EEG this increased to 85%.
  • After thrombolysis, delta power fell 100 minutes before clinical improvement in one study.
  • Delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) after SAH: occurs in 20–40%. Daily transcranial Doppler is about 60–70% sensitive. In the table of studies: in 34 comatose patients, a change of 10% in the alpha/delta ratio over 6 minutes gave sensitivity 100% and specificity 76%, and a change of 50% over one minute gave 89% and 84%. In 12 patients, sensitivity for predicting neurological deterioration increased from 40% with clinical assessment alone to 67% with qEEG (specificity 73%). In one study, relative alpha variability fell in all 19 with vasospasm, on average 2.9 days before vasospasm was confirmed, but also in 7 without vasospasm, mainly because of infarction or increased ICP.
  • All the studies are small, and the authors themselves point out that the findings must be validated prospectively and in randomised trials.
Foreman and Claassen 2012

Asymmetry and reproducibility in ischaemia (Sheorajpanday 2009)

  • Design: exploratory, methodological study in 41 patients: 21 with cerebral infarction (median NIHSS 11, mean DWI volume 79 ml), 10 with TIA and 10 controls aged 55 years or more with subjective memory complaints and normal MRI. One EEG per patient, awake with eyes closed for at least 10 minutes, 19 electrodes with impedance below 5 kΩ. 128 seconds free of artefacts were analysed after visual artefact removal. The study was not done under anaesthesia.
  • pdBSI: a variant of the brain symmetry index that compares the power spectrum between homologous channel pairs (8 pairs, 1–25 Hz), instead of the average for the whole hemisphere.
  • Reproducibility: minimum Cronbach's alpha was 0.95–0.99 for standard spectral measures and 0.96–0.99 for pdBSI, both within the same recording and between and within raters. The authors say that visual artefact removal by a skilled person is a critical first step that cannot be replaced by automatic artefact removal. Automation can confuse ischaemic delta with slow activity from eye movements and drowsiness.
  • Clinical correlation: pdBSI correlated with NIHSS (rho 0.64–0.70) and with DWI volume (rho 0.79–0.84). Standard measures such as relative alpha and the delta/alpha ratio correlated moderately with NIHSS, but not significantly with DWI volume after adjustment for multiple testing.
  • Group difference: pdBSI distinguished infarction from TIA and controls. The standard measures did not after adjustment. Neither pdBSI nor the standard measures could distinguish TIA from controls.
  • Broad frequency bands: pdBSI over 1–25 Hz was better than narrower bands, and 1–3 Hz alone was not significant. The authors interpret this as the whole frequency range being affected in acute ischaemia.
  • Relative measures: the authors used relative power, because absolute power is affected by skull thickness. The skull is on average about 80 times less conductive than brain and scalp, and a 10% thinner skull can produce a change of 800% in amplitude. The figures are taken from Thatcher 2003 as cited by the authors, and were not measured in the study.
  • Caveats: small study, one recording per patient, and no ambition of diagnostic value for individual patients. Asymmetry measures are not specific for ischaemia, and pdBSI will not detect equal injury on both sides of a channel pair.
Sheorajpanday et al. Clin Neurophysiol 2009;120:845–855

EEG in pathology, age and the vulnerable brain

  • Septic encephalopathy: EEG slowing is the earliest finding and can be seen even with a normal neurological examination. The chapter also mentions increased theta, dominant delta, triphasic waves, periodic epileptiform discharges and suppression.
  • Burst suppression: the risk increases with age and with impaired neurological status. In older patients the bursts and suppression phases are less distinct, and the pattern is difficult to detect.
  • High-dose ketamine does not usually produce burst suppression itself, but can influence the threshold (in rats under isoflurane, a low dose of ketamine increased burst suppression). Pain and nociceptive input can lower the threshold.
  • Processed BSR algorithms do not pick up suppression until it is around 40%. The chapter therefore recommends assessing the raw EEG.
  • Two theories explain burst suppression: cortical hyperexcitability, and a metabolic theory in which falling ATP opens ATP-gated potassium channels. The metabolic theory fits with findings that low perfusion can produce burst suppression, but it is not proven.
  • ENGAGES did not change the incidence of delirium, but found lower 30-day mortality in the EEG group. The book calls this an observation that should be investigated further.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 1, 5 and 11

The physiology behind perfusion and the EEG

  • The EEG reflects the brain’s energy use: About 60% of the brain’s energy goes to the signalling the EEG measures, and most anaesthetic drugs suppress only this part. Once the EEG is flat, more drug does not lower energy use further and gives no further protection. (see “The EEG reflects the brain’s energy use”)
  • The Lassen curve is regarded as outdated: The autoregulatory plateau is narrower than assumed, and the lower limit in healthy people ranged from 57 to 91 mmHg. Without an autoregulation monitor, 70 mmHg is a reasonable limit in most people. (see “Autoregulation: narrower and more individual than the Lassen curve”)
  • Autoregulation can be impaired: Hypercapnia impairs it. Propofol preserves it, whereas volatile agents impair it dose-dependently. Lobo and Lamperti say that sevoflurane during hypercapnia impairs or abolishes it, whereas Patel et al. say that sevoflurane may impair it less than the others. The reserve is reduced with CNS injury, an incomplete circle of Willis and hypertension. (see “Autoregulation: narrower and more individual than the Lassen curve”)
  • Patel et al. suggest optimising volume before vasopressor, and account for head height: Low cardiac output probably adds to low MAP in hypotension, and bolus phenylephrine can lower cardiac output. With the head raised, MAP at the heart must be about 85 mmHg to keep CPP at 60–65 mmHg. (see “What governs blood flow: CO₂, cardiac output, vasopressors and head height”)
  • Physiological control appears to matter more than deeper anaesthesia: EEG signs of ischaemia appear from about 20 ml/100 g/min, and inducing burst suppression to protect the brain is not supported in anaesthetised patients. (see “Thresholds and neuroprotection: physiology before depth”)

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

The EEG reflects the brain’s energy use

The brain uses energy for two things: signalling between nerve cells, which is the electrical activity the EEG measures (about 60%), and “housekeeping” that keeps the cells alive. This is why the EEG and energy use track each other under anaesthesia.Source: Patel et al. 2025

  • Most anaesthetic drugs suppress only the signalling. Barbiturates, isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane, propofol and etomidate lower oxygen consumption as the EEG becomes quieter. Once the EEG is flat, signalling is already switched off. More drug then does not lower energy use further. Ketamine and nitrous oxide do not follow this pattern.Source: Patel et al. 2025
  • Cold lowers energy use even after the EEG is flat. For every degree the temperature falls, energy use falls by 6–7%. Cold also lowers “housekeeping”. Anaesthetic drugs do not.Source: Patel et al. 2025
  • The drugs affect blood flow differently. Propofol lowered regional blood flow by 53–79% at surgical depth, and autoregulation and CO₂ response were preserved even during burst suppression. Ketamine is the only intravenous agent that increases both energy use and blood flow. Volatile agents lower energy use but are also direct vasodilators: at 0.5 MAC blood flow falls, at 1 MAC it is unchanged, and above 1 MAC it rises.Source: Patel et al. 2025
  • Burst suppression is not the same with all drugs. At full suppression oxygen consumption is about the same. Barbiturates lower it evenly throughout the brain, whereas isoflurane and sevoflurane lower it most in the neocortex. The choice of drug can also affect whether SSEP monitoring works (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Patel et al. 2025

The studies in detail:

Patel et al. 2025

Autoregulation: narrower and more individual than the Lassen curve

The classical picture is that blood flow is held constant at MAP between about 60 and 160 mmHg. This picture, the old Lassen curve, is now regarded as outdated (“outmoded”).Sources: Lobo and Lamperti 2025; Patel et al. 2025

  • The plateau is narrower than assumed. It is short and slopes slightly. With rapid pressure changes it can be as short as 10 mmHg or absent altogether. With slow changes it is at least ±20 mmHg. Autoregulation is best described as a family of curves, not one.Source: Patel et al. 2025
  • The lower limit varies widely, but 70 mmHg is a reasonable limit. In awake, healthy people the mean lower limit was 57–91 mmHg, with enormous variation. The authors' assessment is that in most people the limit is not below 70 mmHg. Without an autoregulation monitor, 70 mmHg is therefore a reasonable limit.Source: Patel et al. 2025 (seven studies)
  • Brief hypotension is usually tolerated; a sustained fall is not. The brain can increase oxygen extraction. Blood flow can therefore fall by 50–60% before compensation fails. In awake people, symptoms of ischaemia appear only when blood flow has fallen by 35–40%.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti 2025; Patel et al. 2025
  • Autoregulation can be impaired. Hypercapnia impairs it. According to Lobo and Lamperti, propofol preserves it during hypercapnia, whereas sevoflurane at a comparable PaCO₂ impairs or abolishes it. Patel et al. write that propofol preserves it, also during burst suppression, and that volatile agents impair it dose-dependently, but that sevoflurane may impair it less than the others. The sources are therefore not entirely in agreement about sevoflurane. The reserve is reduced with CNS injury, an incomplete circle of Willis (35–40% of the population) and hypertension. According to Patel et al., autoregulation is nevertheless preserved in hypertensive patients, and treatment to normal pressure does not lower blood flow.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti 2025; Patel et al. 2025

The studies in detail:

Patel et al. 2025 Lobo and Lamperti 2025

What governs blood flow: CO₂, cardiac output, vasopressors and head height

Blood pressure is only one of several factors that determine how much blood the brain receives. CO₂, oxygen, cardiac output, choice of vasopressor and head height all play a part.

  • CO₂ changes blood flow a lot; oxygen only when it is low. Blood flow changes by 1–2 ml/100 g/min per mmHg PaCO₂ between 25 and 70 mmHg, but hypotension impairs the CO₂ response. Hypocapnia widens the autoregulatory range, hypercapnia narrows it. PaO₂ has little effect between 60 and 300 mmHg, but below 60 blood flow rises rapidly.Source: Patel et al. 2025
  • Patel et al. suggest optimising volume first. Low cardiac output probably adds to low MAP in hypotension. Whether cardiac output affects blood flow independently of MAP and PaCO₂ is uncertain: one estimate is that a 30% fall in cardiac output gives about a 10% fall in blood flow, but a meta-analysis does not confirm an independent association.Sources: Patel et al. 2025; Meng
  • A vasopressor alone can lower cardiac output. Phenylephrine and noradrenaline do not change global blood flow when autoregulation is intact. Bolus phenylephrine can lower cardiac output further and slightly lowered the NIRS value in several studies. Ephedrine did not. Outcome studies are lacking.Sources: Patel et al. 2025; Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • With the head raised, a higher MAP is needed at the heart. Pressure at the brain falls by about 2 mmHg per 2.5 cm the head is above the heart. To keep CPP at 60–65 mmHg with the head raised, MAP at the heart must be about 85 mmHg. Intracranial pressure is also affected by positioning, by head rotation that compresses the jugular veins, and by PEEP that impedes venous drainage.Sources: Patel et al. 2025; Lobo and Lamperti 2025

The studies in detail:

Patel et al. 2025 Meng Lobo and Lamperti 2025

Thresholds and neuroprotection: physiology before depth

The blood flow thresholds explain when the EEG changes. Deeper anaesthesia is not a shortcut to brain protection.

  • The EEG signs of ischaemia appear from about 20 ml/100 g/min in Patel et al., whereas Foreman and Claassen report that fast activity disappears already at about 25–35. Normal blood flow is about 50 ml/100 g/min. Symptoms appear in awake subjects at about 30, EEG signs of ischaemia from about 20, and the cortical EEG becomes isoelectric at about 15. The SSEP amplitude also changes at about 15. Between 10 and 20 the dysfunction is reversible if blood flow is restored. The data are mainly from animal studies and vary with drug and species.Sources: Patel et al. 2025; Lobo and Lamperti 2025 (SSEP)
  • A suppressed EEG is not always perfusion or depth. At a blood glucose around 2.2 mmol/L the EEG shows slowing: it shifts from alpha and beta towards delta and theta. Below about 1.1 mmol/L it becomes flat.Source: Patel et al. 2025
  • Burst suppression has not been shown to protect in patients. Anaesthetic drugs protect in animal models, but only in mild ischaemia and not lastingly. In patients, neither drugs given to EEG suppression nor general anaesthesia (versus local anaesthesia in carotid surgery) improved outcome. Physiological control of CPP, oxygenation, normocapnia, temperature, glucose and seizures matters more.Sources: Patel et al. 2025; IHAST; GALA
  • Seizures increase energy demand, and the EEG may be the only sign. Seizure activity can increase energy use by up to 400%. In a paralysed patient the EEG is the only way to detect it. Sevoflurane at high concentrations can cause seizures at induction in children.Source: Patel et al. 2025

Figure: where on the CBF scale EEG and the cells fail

Patel et al. 2025 · van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 · Foreman and Claassen 2012
The studies in detail: Lobo and Lamperti and Patel et al. 2025 on normal values, autoregulation, CO₂ and cardiac output, anaesthetic drugs, epileptogenic drugs, thresholds and SSEP (8 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Perfusion, CPP and autoregulation

  • Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is MAP minus intracranial pressure (ICP). Blood flow (CBF) is CPP divided by cerebrovascular resistance.
  • ICP is affected by volume inside the skull (tumour, oedema, haemorrhage, increased CSF volume), by positioning (for example Trendelenburg), by rotation of the head that compresses the jugular veins, and by high intrathoracic pressure and PEEP that impede venous drainage.
  • With intact autoregulation, MAP between approximately 60 and 160 mmHg does not affect CBF, which is kept at around 50 ml/100 g/min. When autoregulation fails, blood flow follows pressure passively.
  • CBF can fall by 50–60% before compensation fails, because the brain then increases oxygen extraction.
  • Cerebrovascular resistance is affected by vasopressors and vasodilators, by PaCO₂, and can be shifted by chronic hypertension. Treating low blood pressure with a vasopressor alone can reduce cardiac output.
  • Hypercapnia impairs autoregulation, and the anaesthetic agents play a part: propofol preserves it during hypercapnia, whereas sevoflurane at a corresponding PaCO₂ impairs or abolishes it.
  • The brain is about 2% of body weight, but receives 12–15% of cardiac output and uses up to 20% of the oxygen. Approximately 75–80% of oxygen consumption goes to restoring the membrane potential.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 1, 2 and 7

Patel et al. 2025: cerebral physiology and the anaesthetic drugs (Patel, Drummond and Lemkuil)

Normal values, energy use and why EEG and CMR go together

  • Normal values (Miller's box 10.1): the brain is only about 2% of body weight but receives 12–15% of cardiac output. The values below are for adults. “Per 100 g” means per 100 grams of brain tissue.
    MeasureWhat it isNormal
    CBF, whole brainCerebral blood flow45–55 ml/100 g/min
    CBF, cortexGrey matter uses most energy and receives most blood75–80 ml/100 g/min
    CBF, below the cortexLess active tissue receives less blood8–20 ml/100 g/min
    CMRO₂Cerebral oxygen consumption3–3.5 ml O₂/100 g/min
    rSO₂Regional oxygen saturation in brain tissue, measured with NIRS on the forehead55–80%
    SjVO₂Oxygen saturation of venous blood leaving the brain (jugular bulb)60–70%
    ICPPressure inside the skull, supine8–12 mmHg
  • The brain uses energy for two things: about 60% goes to signalling between neurons, that is, the electrical activity the EEG measures. The rest goes to keeping the cells alive and maintained (“housekeeping”). Anaesthetic drugs such as barbiturates, isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane, propofol and etomidate dampen only the signalling. The quieter the EEG becomes, the less oxygen the brain uses. When the EEG is flat, signalling is already switched off, and more drug does not lower energy use further (fig. 10.2). Ketamine and nitrous oxide do not follow this pattern.
  • Cooling acts on both parts: for every degree the body temperature falls, the brain's energy use falls by 6–7%. The EEG becomes flat at about 18–20 °C, and at 18 °C oxygen consumption is below 10% of normal. Because cold also lowers “housekeeping”, cooling reduces energy use further even after the EEG is flat. Anaesthetic drugs do not.
  • Burst suppression is not the same with all drugs: when the EEG is completely suppressed, cerebral oxygen consumption is about the same whichever drug is used, but it is distributed differently. Barbiturates lower blood flow and energy use evenly throughout the brain, while isoflurane and sevoflurane lower it most in the outer cortex (neocortex). The burst-suppression pattern just before the EEG becomes completely flat also varies from drug to drug.
  • Relevance for neuromonitoring: SSEPs (somatosensory evoked potentials) are the cortex's response to stimulation of a nerve in an arm or leg, and are used to monitor the spinal cord and brain during surgery. With thiopental, SSEPs can still be recorded at doses far beyond those giving a flat EEG, but with isoflurane in burst suppression (about 1.5 MAC) they are hard to elicit. The choice of agent can therefore affect whether neuromonitoring works (interpretation based on the sources).
  • What it means for EEG interpretation: a very low index or a flat EEG means the drug has already lowered the brain's energy use as much as it can. More dose gives no more protection of the brain. That is the background for the cards on overdose and burst suppression in the Spectrogram and Agents tabs.
Patel et al. 2025, box 10.1 and fig. 10.2

Autoregulation: the Lassen curve is outdated, the lower limit is around 70 mmHg in most people

  • The classical picture (CBF constant at 50 ml/100 g/min from MAP 50 to 150) was built on a heterogeneous sample with single measurements, and the chapter calls it “outmoded”. Newer analyses give a narrower plateau with a gentle upslope, so pressure-passive CBF applies over a wider MAP range than assumed. With rapid pressure changes (dynamic autoregulation) the plateau may be as short as 10 mmHg or absent; with slow changes over about 10 minutes (static) the plateau is at least ±20 mmHg.
  • Lower limit (LLA): across seven studies in awake, healthy subjects the mean LLA ranged from 57 to 91 mmHg, with enormous inter-subject variability. The authors (Drummond) hold that the LLA in the majority is not below 70 mmHg, which with normal ICP (5–10) gives a CPP of 60–65 mmHg, and that 70 mmHg is a prudent threshold without an autoregulation monitor. Upper limit: about 90 mmHg on cardiopulmonary bypass, probably above 140 in hypertensives. Autoregulation is best described as a family of curves (fig. 10.5), not one.
  • Reserve: symptoms of ischaemia appear only when CBF has fallen 35–40% in awake subjects. This cerebrovascular reserve means that brief hypotension below the LLA is usually tolerated; sustained falls are not. Reserve is reduced with CNS injury (autoregulation impaired for about 2 weeks, restored after 1–3 months), raised local tissue pressure (ICP, retractors, cervical stenosis), an incomplete circle of Willis (35–40% of the population) and hypertension.
  • Hypertension: both dynamic and static autoregulation are preserved in hypertensives, and treatment to normal pressure does not reduce CBF. The intraoperative question is hypotension: the authors limit the MAP fall to no more than 20% below baseline measured at head level in the sitting position, in the section on chronic hypertension they give 30–35%, and state that a 25% fall brings both normo- and hypertensive patients to the LLA. See the discrepancy list.
  • Hydrostatic gradient: 2 mmHg per inch (2.5 cm) the head is above the heart; 12 inches give about 24 mmHg. To keep CPP at 60–65 with the head elevated, MAP at heart level must be about 85. The siphon model (closed loop) is rejected: gravity does affect CPP. See the card on perfusion pressure and head height.
  • Practical MAP target: in patients without acute ischaemia and with normal or well-controlled pressure the chapter regards an intraoperative MAP of about 75 mmHg as adequate, and table 10.2 lists subspecialty targets in brain injury (for example SBP above 100–110 in traumatic brain injury depending on age, MAP above 65 after cardiac arrest).
Patel et al. 2025, fig. 10.3–10.5, table 10.2

CO₂, O₂, cardiac output and vasopressors

  • PaCO₂: CBF changes 1–2 ml/100 g/min per mmHg within 25–70 mmHg; the response is attenuated below 25 and above 75–80. Moderate hypotension (MAP fall under 33%) attenuates the CO₂ response markedly, severe hypotension (about 66%) abolishes it. Hypocapnia widens the autoregulatory range, hypercapnia narrows it. The effect of a changed PaCO₂ wanes over 6–8 hours as CSF pH normalises; abrupt normalisation after prolonged hyperventilation gives CSF acidosis and increased CBF/ICP.
  • PaO₂: little effect between 60 and 300 mmHg; below 60 CBF rises rapidly, linearly with falling saturation. Haemodilution gives a smaller CBF rise than hypoxaemia for the same fall in O₂ content. 1 atm oxygen lowers CBF by about 18%.
  • Cardiac output: Meng estimates that a 30% fall in CO gives about a 10% fall in CBF independent of MAP and PaCO₂; a newer study found that a 10% fall in MAP and a 20% fall in CO gave the same fall (about 5%) in MCA velocity. A meta-analysis nevertheless does not confirm an independent relationship, because CO cannot be changed without changing MAP and PaCO₂. The chapter still concludes that low CO probably adds to low MAP in hypotension, that volume should be optimised first, and that bolus phenylephrine may lower CO further. See the Nordum 2024 card (Trendelenburg) and the clinical example with alpha and cardiac output.
  • Vasopressors: α₁-agonists (phenylephrine, noradrenaline) do not change global CBF in humans when autoregulation is intact; they act via MAP. Bolus phenylephrine slightly lowered NIRS-measured SCO₂ in several studies, ephedrine did not, probably because ephedrine maintains CO; extracranial contamination of NIRS exceeds this difference. Koch found that ephedrine, not phenylephrine, increased local CBF, tissue oxygenation and microcirculation in brain-tumour patients. Outcome studies are lacking. Dexmedetomidine lowers CBF 25–30% via CMR; dopamine up to 100 µg/kg/min does not cause cerebral vasoconstriction; dobutamine increased CBF and CMR by 20 and 30%.
Patel et al. 2025, fig. 10.8–10.10, table 10.3

What the anaesthetic drugs do to CBF and CMR

  • Intravenous agents preserve flow–metabolism coupling, autoregulation and CO₂ responsiveness. Propofol lowered regional CBF 53–79% and whole-brain glucose metabolism 48–58% at surgical depth in volunteers; autoregulation and CO₂ response are preserved even at burst suppression. Etomidate 0.2 mg/kg: CBF −34%, CMR −45%. Midazolam 0.15 mg/kg: CBF −30 to −34% (−12% globally with PET). Opioids: small reductions in the unstimulated brain; sedative remifentanil can increase CBF regionally; a bolus with a MAP fall can raise ICP through autoregulatory vasodilation. Flumazenil can give an overshoot in CBF/ICP in patients with poor intracranial compliance.
  • Ketamine is the only intravenous agent that increases CMR and CBF: subanaesthetic doses (0.2–0.3 mg/kg) increased global CMR by about 25%, most in frontal and anterior cingulate cortex; S-ketamine increases CMR, R-ketamine lowers it. CBF rose 14% (subanaesthetic) and 36% (anaesthetic) without a change in CMRO₂ in one study; CBV +50%. Propofol, benzodiazepines and isoflurane blunt or abolish the ICP rise, and systematic reviews find no ICP rise in head injury. See the ketamine cards in the Agents tab for the EEG pattern.
  • Volatile agents: lower CMR dose-dependently but are also direct vasodilators. Net: at 0.5 MAC CBF falls, at 1 MAC it is unchanged, above 1 MAC it rises (“luxury perfusion”), and autoregulation to rising pressure is impaired. Vasodilating potency: halothane ≫ enflurane > desflurane ≈ isoflurane > sevoflurane. At 1 MAC sevoflurane and desflurane lowered CBF by 38 and 22% and CMR by 39 and 35% (Kety–Schmidt, cortical measurement); PET shows about 50% for both. Maximal CMR reduction is reached at EEG suppression, at 1.5–2 MAC. Sevoflurane lowers regional CBF but not CBV; propofol lowers both. If CMR is already suppressed (for example by propofol), the vasodilation is unmasked: adding a volatile agent then clearly increases CBF.
  • Entropy and sevoflurane: in a dose-escalation study in humans the largest reduction in entropy was at 1 MAC sevoflurane, with smaller reductions at higher concentrations. This fits with CMRO₂ falling sharply with the onset of the anaesthetic EEG pattern and more slowly thereafter.
  • Nitrous oxide increases CBF, CMR and ICP, most alone or with a volatile agent (0.75 MAC isoflurane + 65% N₂O gave 43% higher CBF than 1.5 MAC isoflurane); with intravenous agents the effect is blunted. CBV is little affected.
  • Lidocaine: 5 mg/kg over 30 min + 45 µg/kg/min lowered CBF 24% and CMR 20% in awake volunteers; membrane stabilisation is thought to lower the energy needed for membrane integrity. A 1.5 mg/kg bolus was as effective as thiopental 3 mg/kg against the ICP rise at pin placement, with less MAP fall. After a 2 mg/kg bolus peak concentrations are 6.6–8.5 µg/mL, below the seizure threshold (above 5–10 µg/mL in awake subjects); according to the chapter, lidocaine seizures have not been reported in anaesthetised patients. See the card on multimodal anaesthesia in the Agents tab.
  • Neuromuscular blockers have no direct cerebrovascular effect beyond histamine release; succinylcholine can raise ICP by about 5 mmHg as an arousal phenomenon under light anaesthesia, blocked by deep anaesthesia or defasciculation.
Patel et al. 2025, fig. 10.12–10.19

Epileptogenic drugs according to Patel et al. 2025

  • Sevoflurane: seizures at induction with high concentrations in children, also without a known predisposition. In two healthy volunteers burst suppression at 2 MAC was accompanied by epileptiform discharges with a clear CBF increase (coupling preserved). In patients with temporal lobe epilepsy 1.5 MAC produced widespread paroxysmal activity that was not confined to the focus and did not help localisation. Tonic–clonic movements at emergence have been reported in healthy patients. No sequelae documented; caution in epilepsy. See the card on epileptiform activity and images 19–20 in the Spectrogram tab.
  • Etomidate often causes myoclonus without epileptiform EEG, but can trigger generalised epileptic activity in epileptics; 0.1 mg/kg is used to activate a quiescent focus intraoperatively. Methohexital activates foci. Ketamine can trigger seizures in predisposed patients, with subcortical activity not always seen in surface EEG, but is also used for refractory status (effective in 56%). Propofol is not confirmed as proconvulsant and shortens ECT seizures; high-amplitude beta is described. Opioids: high-dose fentanyl produced electrical seizure activity in 8 of 9 patients with partial complex seizures during temporal lobe surgery; alfentanil 50 µg/kg augmented spikes in temporal lobe epilepsy. Isoflurane gives spikes and myoclonus but is not regarded as epileptogenic and is used for refractory status. Enflurane is epileptogenic, potentiated by hypocapnia.
  • Why it belongs in an EEG app: seizure activity can raise CMR by up to 400%, and in a paralysed patient the EEG is the only way to detect it.
Patel et al. 2025, section Epileptogenesis

CBF thresholds (fig. 10.20), hypoglycaemia and neuroprotection

  • Thresholds: normal CBF about 50 ml/100 g/min. Symptoms of hypoperfusion in awake subjects only at about 30. EEG evidence of ischaemia from about 20. Isoelectric cortical EEG at about 15. Penumbra 10–20: reversible dysfunction, but cell death if flow is not restored. Signs of irreversible membrane failure (extracellular potassium, lost direct cortical response) only at about 6–10 (the legend says 6–12). The data are from the cortex of barbiturate-anaesthetised baboons and awake monkeys, and the levels vary with drug and species; in humans under halothane and N₂O the threshold for the first EEG change matched the animal data. The thresholds are drawn into the figure “Where on the CBF scale EEG and the cells fail” alongside van Putten and Foreman and Claassen.
  • Completeness: with complete global ischaemia (cardiac arrest) energy supply fails within minutes; with incomplete (focal) ischaemia residual flow keeps ATP production going longer, which is why focal ischaemia is apparently better tolerated.
  • Hypoglycaemia in the EEG: with a gradual fall to about 40 mg/dL (about 2.2 mmol/L) the EEG shifts from alpha and beta towards delta and theta; below 20 mg/dL (about 1.1 mmol/L) the EEG becomes flat. Persistence at that level gives seizures and hippocampal injury. Hyperthermia above 42 °C gives an abrupt fall in oxygen consumption (protein denaturation).
  • Neuroprotection: barbiturates, propofol, ketamine, volatile agents and xenon protect in animal models, but only with mild ischaemia and not durably. In humans: in IHAST thiopental, etomidate or propofol to EEG suppression gave no better outcome; in GALA general anaesthesia gave no advantage over local anaesthesia for carotid surgery. Conclusion: inducing burst suppression for brain protection is not supported in anaesthetised patients, and physiological control (CPP, oxygenation, normocapnia, temperature, glucose, seizures) matters more. Etomidate can worsen tissue hypoxia during temporary vessel occlusion. Hypothermia 32–36 °C after cardiac arrest: TTM and TTM2 showed no benefit of lower targets; guidelines keep 32–36 °C and strict avoidance of hyperthermia.
  • Deferring elective surgery after stroke: the risk of death within 30 days was highest in the first 3 months and only stabilised after 9 months; the chapter recommends deferring elective surgery for 9 months, with an exception for early carotid surgery in small infarcts.
Patel et al. 2025, fig. 10.20–10.24

SSEP, ICP and falling blood flow (Lobo and Lamperti ch. 6)

  • The text states that SSEP amplitude changes at a CBF fall to about 15 ml/100 g/min and disappears below 18.
  • Increased ICP changes the SSEP classically: amplitude decreases and latency is prolonged. With herniation, subcortical responses may disappear first.
  • The book does not directly describe how the EEG changes with raised ICP. CBF thresholds for EEG are given in the van Putten and Hofmeijer card and in the figure “Where on the CBF scale EEG and the cells fail”.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 6
Burst suppression

Burst suppression is not needed for unconsciousness, amnesia or immobility during general anaesthesia or sedation, and when it appears unintentionally it is a signal to look for the cause. A common cause during anaesthesia is more anaesthetic or sedative than the patient needs, especially in older patients. Also check blood pressure, oxygenation, haemoglobin and temperature. Here you will find why the pattern arises, when it is wanted as treatment, what it means for outcome, and why the suppression ratio should always be checked against the raw EEG.

Burst suppression: the pattern

What burst suppression is, plainly

The EEG alternates between short bursts of activity and periods in which it is almost flat. The outbursts are the "bursts", the almost flat periods the "suppression". The figure above shows the pattern. That is all the term means.

It helps to know that this is not a gradual pattern. The raw EEG does not simply fall in amplitude as the anaesthetic deepens. At a certain point the brain instead begins switching off and on, and that alternation between off and on is what you see.

How it is defined. The ACNS terminology, which is what the neurophysiologists use, defines it as follows:

  • Suppression is all activity below 10 µV.
  • Attenuation lies between that and normal: at least 10 µV, but less than half the background amplitude.
  • A burst lasts at least 0.5 seconds and has at least four phases. Within burst suppression a burst may last up to 30 seconds.
  • Burst suppression is a pattern in which suppression alternates with higher-voltage activity, and in which 50 to 99% of the record consists of suppression. If it is attenuation rather than suppression, it is called burst-attenuation.
  • The suppression percentage is reported from 1 to 99%. Below 1% counts as continuous EEG, and above 99% counts as suppressed and no longer as burst suppression. Two-second bursts alternating with eight seconds of suppression gives 80% suppression, for example.

But be aware that the threshold is not one threshold. The ACNS says below 10 µV. The chapter on brain monitoring under anaesthesia gives suppression periods below 5 µV. A large clinical study required below ±10 µV for at least 2 seconds in all four channels at once. In newborns, almost no activity below 2 µV between bursts above 25 µV is used. And isoelectric EEG, complete silence, counts as 2 µV or lower.

This means that "burst suppression" is not one number, but a pattern that different communities and different monitors quantify somewhat differently. When a monitor reports a suppression ratio, what you get is that algorithm's definition, not a universal one.

Sources: Hirsch et al. 2021 (the ACNS terminology); Sleigh et al. 2025. See the cards below for why the pattern arises, when it is wanted as treatment, and what it means for outcome.

Hirsch et al. J Clin Neurophysiol 2021;38:1–29

Key points

  • Burst suppression is not needed for general anaesthesia or sedation. Propofol produced burst suppression at about 4.9 µg/ml on average (Pilge 2014), while loss of response occurred at about 2.0 µg/ml with slow induction (Sepúlveda 2026). Unintended burst suppression is a signal to look for the cause, not a sign of adequate anaesthetic depth (interpretation based on the sources).See
  • The pattern reflects the energy balance of the cortex. Too much drug and too little energy (hypothermia, ischaemia) can, on the Ching model, end in the same mechanism: falling ATP opens ATP-gated potassium channels (a hypothesis). The suppression ratio rises gradually until the EEG becomes isoelectric.See
  • Older patients get it most easily, but in them it is hardest to see. The risk rises with age and impaired neurological status. In older patients the bursts are weaker and the suppression shallower and shorter.See
  • Confirm on the raw EEG and look for the cause. Confirm the pattern on the raw EEG and assess symmetry. Gruenbaum suggests reducing the dose if suppression is symmetrical and the dose is high. If it persists at a low dose, he suggests looking for hypotension, hypoxaemia, anaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and hypocapnia.Source: Gruenbaum 2026. See
  • The suppression ratio is an estimate that can be wrong in both directions. EMG can give a falsely low SR. Poor electrode contact, artefacts and low bursts in older patients can give a falsely high SR. Use the number as a warning to check against the raw EEG, not as the answer.See
  • The sources in this app give no single documented target for therapeutic depth. Expert practice describes pauses of about 10 seconds, but no target has been tested against outcome. The content of the bursts distinguished successful from failed weaning in one study (Johnson 2016, 19 patients); pause length did not. The target should be agreed with a neurologist or neurointensivist for each patient (interpretation based on the sources).See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

When is burst suppression wanted, and when is it not needed?

A synthesis of the cards in this tab. Sources are given under each point.

  • It can be a deliberate treatment. Burst suppression is induced in refractory status epilepticus, raised intracranial pressure and aneurysm surgery with temporary clipping, to lower metabolism and ICP. It should be individualised and time-limited, with concurrent attention to perfusion, oxygenation and temperature. In status epilepticus it is part of third-line treatment (Intensive care tab).Source: Gruenbaum 2026
  • Whether it protects the brain is uncertain. The rationale is that oxygen consumption and blood flow fall together. But this coupling weakens with age, vascular disease and anaesthesia. In aneurysm surgery the evidence is mixed, and animal studies suggest that protection does not require burst suppression. After cardiac arrest, a protective down-regulated state is a hypothesis.Sources: Gruenbaum 2026, Jegarl 2026, Forgacs 2020
  • It is not needed for general anaesthesia. Propofol produces burst suppression at about 4.9 µg/ml, whereas movement to incision is prevented only at about 15–16 µg/ml. Unconsciousness occurs at much lower concentrations (Components tab). According to Pilge and co-authors, a «silent second» is too deep for clinical anaesthesia. Excessive cortical silencing does not appear to give additional protection against awareness, and may carry a cognitive cost.Sources: Pilge 2014, Gruenbaum 2026
  • It is not needed during ICU sedation. Burst suppression was associated with higher mortality (HR 2.04), and more time in burst suppression was associated with higher odds of delirium (OR 4.16, observational studies). Nobody had burst suppression as a goal. Burst suppression appears mostly to be a marker of how ill the patient is, but titrating to the lowest necessary dose may have a modest effect.Sources: Watson 2008, Andresen 2014, Hogan 2020
  • If it appears unintentionally, look for the cause. Check blood pressure, oxygenation, haemoglobin, glucose and temperature before increasing or accepting the dose. In one study (104 patients over 60 years) BSR fell to 0 in 55 % of episodes (24 of 44) simply by raising MAP to the patient's baseline. The study does not show causation.Sources: Gruenbaum 2026, Georgii 2022
  • If it is the goal, it must be verified. A flat EEG is not the same as the intended burst suppression (the herniation case under Clinical examples). Unilateral suppression may mean focal ischaemia or a technical fault.Sources: Gruenbaum 2026, the ECMO case in the Intensive care tab
  • Interpretation based on the sources: burst suppression can have a place as a deliberate, time-limited treatment. It is not needed for unconsciousness, amnesia or immobility during anaesthesia or sedation. Unintended burst suppression is a signal to look for the cause, not a sign of adequate anaesthetic depth.

What it is and why it occurs

What burst suppression is: a sign of cortical energy balance

Burst suppression is alternating periods of almost absent activity and high-amplitude bursts. According to Lobo and Lamperti it is not seen in natural sleep. The sources explain the pattern slightly differently, but meet in one common mechanism.Source: Lobo and Lamperti 2025

  • Falling ATP is the common point. Two mechanisms have been proposed: cortical hyperexcitability (extracellular calcium and a refractory period after the burst) and a metabolic theory. In the metabolic theory, falling ATP opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels and the neurones hyperpolarise. A computational model builds on this theory. The model has only 14–20 cells, and the KATP channel is a hypothesis. It explains but does not prove, and other channels and extracellular calcium may act together.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti 2025, Ching 2012, Gruenbaum 2026
  • The pattern can mean too much agent or too little energy. Anaesthetic agents reduce firing and thereby CMRO₂ secondarily. Hypothermia and ischaemia reduce metabolism directly. One process is down-regulation (excessive dose, hypothermia), the other is metabolic failure from insufficient substrate or oxygen (hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, ischaemia). Both are thought to end in the same mechanism.Sources: Ching 2012, Gruenbaum 2026
  • According to the model it is a continuum, not a separate state. The suppression ratio rises gradually with deeper inactivation, until the EEG is completely isoelectric. In the model, 50 % of normal ATP production gave a suppression ratio of about 0.5, and 30 % gave about 0.75. With severe hypoperfusion or anoxic injury the EEG can become isoelectric.Sources: Ching 2012, Gruenbaum 2026
  • The bursts appear to repeat the pattern from just before suppression started. Under propofol this is often alpha and slow-delta. If the EEG had already become mostly slow-delta, that is what the bursts contain. Deeper anaesthesia as a rule mainly gives longer suppression periods and fewer bursts. True bursts have organised spectral content, whereas artefacts give broadband spikes.Sources: Ching 2012, Gruenbaum 2026
  • Ketamine is the exception. Ketamine does not usually produce classic burst suppression, even at high doses, but affects the threshold. Ketamine increases CMRO₂. In a rat study (n = 20), a subanaesthetic dose of ketamine during isoflurane increased burst suppression (BSR from about 37 to 84 %), yet recovery was 44 % faster once isoflurane was stopped. The authors call this paradoxical emergence and propose NMDA blockade during anaesthesia and increased cholinergic activity afterwards as possible mechanisms. It has not been studied in patients.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti 2025, Ching 2012, Hambrecht-Wiedbusch 2017

The studies in detail:

Lobo and Lamperti 2025 Ching 2012 Gruenbaum 2026

Who gets it, and what to do when it appears?

Burst suppression is common, age increases the risk, and its meaning depends on the patient. The sources agree on this, and there is a practical approach.Sources: Gruenbaum 2026, Lobo and Lamperti 2025

  • It is common, and most common in older patients. Gruenbaum 2026 cites a retrospective study of more than 38,000 adults in which nearly half had burst suppression. Likelihood and duration increased with age. The risk also rises with impaired neurological status. In older patients the pattern is less distinct: weaker bursts and shallower, shorter suppression. The most vulnerable are thus those in whom it is hardest to detect.Sources: Gruenbaum 2026, Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • According to Gruenbaum, reserve matters more than minutes. According to Gruenbaum, young, healthy people tolerate burst suppression without measurable consequences. In vulnerable patients, recurrent or persistent burst suppression more often reflects exhausted reserve. Meta-analyses have found an association with about 1.5 times higher risk of postoperative delirium. ENGAGES was inconclusive, but has been criticised for the lack of standardised analgesia and for not taking age and cognitive frailty into account.Sources: Gruenbaum 2026, Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • Pain and opioids shift the threshold. Opioids do not produce burst suppression directly, but can unmask or accentuate it together with propofol or volatile agents. Pain and nociception can lower the threshold. Nociception can produce beta or delta arousal that is misread as too-light hypnosis. Giving more hypnotic may then increase the risk.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti 2025, Gruenbaum 2026
  • Look at the raw EEG, not just the index. The indices are affected only when suppression dominates the analysis window. Acceptable index values can therefore coexist with clear discontinuity. Gruenbaum 2026 reports that automated detection missed burst suppression in about 14 % of cases.Source: Gruenbaum 2026
  • Four steps. (1) Confirm on the raw EEG. (2) Assess symmetry: unilateral suppression may mean focal ischaemia or a technical fault, so keep the dose unchanged and assess perfusion. (3) With symmetric suppression and a high dose: the authors suggest reducing by 0.1–0.2 MAC or propofol by 10–20 %. (4) If it persists at a low dose: look for hypotension, hypoxaemia, anaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and hypocapnia. Caveat: the source is a narrative review without a systematic search, focused on surgery.Source: Gruenbaum 2026

The studies in detail:

Gruenbaum 2026 Lobo and Lamperti 2025

Measurement: the suppression ratio is an estimate

How deep should therapeutic burst suppression be? Pauses, bursts and SR

When burst suppression is used as treatment, the sources describe pauses of about 10 seconds and as little epileptiform activity in the bursts as possible. None of the targets has been tested against outcome, and the evidence is weak.

  • SR below 5 % (Rasulo) does not concern therapeutic depth. The statement “If burst suppression is used, the suppression ratio should be kept at < 5%” (strong consensus in a Delphi panel) sits under the question of whether burst suppression should be avoided. Read in context, it means that SR during sedation should be kept below 5 %, in practice without burst suppression. The figure is not justified. The article notes that burst suppression is still part of many treatment algorithms for refractory status epilepticus, but gives no depth for it.Source: Rasulo 2023
  • Pauses of about 10 seconds are expert opinion, with weak evidence. Experts consider an interburst interval of about 10 seconds for 24 hours reasonable in refractory status epilepticus. In retrospective data burst suppression was achieved in only about 40–60 % of patients. One quantitative study of 17 patients found no association between suppression ratio and outcome.Source: review 2022 (doi 10.1007/s10309-022-00539-z)
  • The target was rarely reached in this study. In 35 patients with refractory status epilepticus, the target was a burst suppression probability of 0.8 ± 0.15. Patients were within the target for a median of only 8 % of treatment time, and below it 84 % of the time. The same weight-adjusted dose gave different suppression in different patients, and some drifted without any change in infusion.Source: An 2018 (Massachusetts General Hospital)
  • The content of the bursts matters more than the pauses. In 19 patients (37 weaning attempts) the amount of epileptiform activity in the bursts was the only feature that separated successful from failed weaning (p = 0.008). Interburst interval, suppression ratio and burst length did not. A maximum burst amplitude below 125 µV had a sensitivity of 84.6 % and specificity of 61.1 % for successful weaning.Source: Johnson 2016
  • SR below 5 % is far below the definition of burst suppression. ACNS 2021 defines burst suppression as suppression in 50–99 % of the record. A scoping review divides it into incomplete (20–49 %) and complete (50–99 %) burst suppression. This fits with the Rasulo statement being about avoiding burst suppression.Sources: ACNS 2021, Fisch 2026
  • SR 40–60 % as a treatment target has no known source. The author of the app has heard it but does not remember the source. It has not been found in peer-reviewed literature, and the 2026 scoping review gives no SR treatment target.Source: Fisch 2026
  • There is no evidence that burst suppression improves outcome. The scoping review concludes that the evidence does not support burst suppression over seizure cessation as the target for most patients.Source: Fisch 2026
  • The guideline accepts seizure cessation on the EEG as a target. The dose is titrated to cessation of electrographic seizures or burst suppression (very low evidence, strong recommendation). A period of 24–48 hours of electrographic control is then recommended before slow withdrawal (very low evidence, weak recommendation). Burst suppression is therefore not required by this guideline.Source: NCS guideline, Brophy 2012
  • Older studies on depth and outcome:
    • Deep suppression was associated with fewer breakthrough seizures, but more hypotension. Titration to background suppression (burst suppression or an isoelectric EEG) gave breakthrough seizures in 4 versus 53 % with titration to seizure suppression, and hypotension in 76 versus 29 %. The goal did not affect withdrawal seizures, early treatment failure or change of agent. Mortality was 48 % and was not associated with agent or goal. Large caveats: nearly all with background suppression received pentobarbital, and all on midazolam were titrated to seizure suppression, so agent and goal cannot be separated. Only 27 % on pentobarbital had continuous EEG, versus 78 % on midazolam or propofol. The authors write that this “may very likely explain” the fewer breakthrough seizures, because seizures without clinical signs are easily missed without continuous EEG.Source: Claassen 2002 (systematic review of case series 1970–2001, 28 studies, 193 patients)
    • A flat EEG was more often associated with lasting seizure control than burst suppression, in a small study. Lasting seizure control after tapering in 17 of 20 with a flat EEG versus 6 of 12 with burst suppression as the deepest level. Isolated epileptiform discharges during the infusion did not correlate with outcome. Recurrent electrographic status after tapering predicted relapse.Source: Krishnamurthy and Drislane 1999 (35 patients on pentobarbital)
    • Outcome was the same with and without burst suppression. Burst suppression was reached in 20 of 33 monitored episodes (61 %). The authors consider the cause of the status to be the main determinant of outcome.Source: Rossetti 2005 (49 episodes of refractory status epilepticus in Boston)
  • What has been shown, and what has not? (interpretation based on the sources): The data are small, old and retrospective. In one review of case series, deep suppression was associated with fewer breakthrough seizures, but also with more hypotension. Agent and target cannot be separated there, and the authors consider that the difference in seizures is “very likely” explained by patients with deep suppression less often having continuous EEG. The target did not affect withdrawal seizures in that review, whereas another small study found fewer relapses with flat EEG than with burst suppression. Lower mortality or better outcome has not been shown. In one study of 19 patients, the content of the bursts separated successful from failed weaning, whereas the length of the pauses did not. The sources report no controlled or randomised studies comparing burst suppression with seizure cessation.Sources: Claassen 2002, Krishnamurthy 1999, Rossetti 2005, Johnson 2016, Fisch 2026, Shorvon and Ferlisi 2011
  • 24–48 hours and repeated cycles rest on usual practice, not studies. The Shorvon and Ferlisi review is among the most cited references in Norwegian guidelines and procedures. Shorvon and Ferlisi state that there are no controlled or randomised studies, so treatment has to be based on case reports and opinion.
    • Depth: “It is usual” to keep anaesthesia at burst suppression, because this usually stops all electrographic seizure activity. Whether it is needed in all cases is unclear, and what little evidence there is conflicts. As a compromise against hypotension, it is common to aim for burst suppression first and lighten anaesthesia in prolonged episodes.
    • Duration: “It is usual practice” to try to reverse anaesthesia every 24–48 hours and re-establish it if seizures recur. After a few weeks, each cycle is often extended to 5 days. How long anaesthesia should continue has not been studied.
    • Monitoring and weaning: EEG at least once a day, and slow weaning over days. No interburst interval, bursts per minute, BIS or SR is given.
    Interpretation based on the sources: the 24–48-hour and 5-day cycles in the Sørlandet procedure correspond to what Shorvon and Ferlisi describe as usual practice, not a result from studies.Source: Shorvon and Ferlisi 2011 (Brain), citing Krishnamurthy 1999 and Rossetti 2005
  • The origin of the target is unclear. The pattern was described in 1936 and named burst suppression in 1949. It later became a treatment target in refractory status epilepticus, but the evidence for putting the brain into burst suppression is “inconclusive”. The origin of a specific number of seconds for the pauses has not been found in the sources.Source: Hawkes 2024
  • Norwegian review: burst suppression is a practical goal. General anaesthesia should be started as soon as possible, most often with propofol. Full burst suppression is “hardly strictly necessary”, but “burst suppression for 12 to 24 hours can be a practical goal”. The right depth of anaesthesia based on the EEG is “not fully clarified”, and the EEG is the most important monitoring tool. The need for continued propofol should be reassessed after two to three days because of the risk of propofol infusion syndrome.Source: Heuser 2024 (Journal of the Norwegian Medical Association, status epilepticus in adults)
  • “Practical” because continuous EEG is often unavailable. Duration and depth are controversial. “Common practice” is burst suppression for 24–48 hours, but the rationale is “limited”. Whether burst suppression is necessary can be discussed, but all epileptic activity must be suppressed for a period. Most hospitals do not have continuous EEG around the clock, so burst suppression can be a practical way of ensuring that anaesthesia is deep enough. Propofol should be restricted to 48 hours and tapered over 24 hours. BIS, SR and bursts per minute are not mentioned.Source: Heuser 2022 (book chapter by the neurologists behind the Norwegian review)
  • The national guideline gives no EEG target. Anaesthesia is step 3, with propofol for up to 48 hours or midazolam. A barbiturate is considered for persistent convulsive status. Neither burst suppression, seizure cessation, SR nor BIS is given as a target.Source: NevroNEL, Norwegian status epilepticus network (updated 2026)
  • Example of a local procedure (Sørlandet Hospital, ICU Arendal, 2026): an openly published ICU procedure shows how one hospital has translated the sources.
    • Target: it is uncertain whether the target should be seizure cessation or burst suppression, and seizure cessation is “probably sufficient”. Burst suppression with 10-second pauses, “i.e. 3–5 bursts per min”, is called a common target. The procedure nevertheless states that no association has been shown between pause length and effect.
    • Monitor: the procedure also gives an index number and an SR as a target, without a reference. Indices are algorithms with many sources of error and should not be used as targets; burst suppression should be assessed in the raw EEG. Continuous EEG is recommended, but availability is uncertain.
    • Duration and weaning: anaesthesia for 24 (–48) hours, then slow weaning over 24 hours, for example propofol by 20 % every 3 hours. If seizures recur, a new round of 24–48 hours is given the first time, then 5–7 days.
  • What do the studies of BIS and burst suppression show?
    • BIS and SR closely tracked the number of bursts. In 12 adults on pentobarbital for raised intracranial pressure (11 after head injury, none with seizures), the dose was titrated by the raw EEG to 3–5 bursts per minute. BIS and SR tracked the number of bursts (r = 0.90 and −0.89). The authors suggested an index and SR target, but it has not been tested against outcome in the sources used in this app. Caveats: vasopressors were given on 81% of days, and BIS was lower on days with vasopressors. Bursts per minute ignore burst length: three bursts of 5 seconds are deeper suppression than three of 15 seconds. The study received an equipment grant from the manufacturer of BIS.Source: Riker 2003
    • BIS tracked burst suppression, but did not separate epileptic bursts from ordinary ones. In 10 patients with refractory status epilepticus (propofol titrated to burst suppression for at least 12 hours, guided by full EEG), BIS separated burst suppression from other EEG in this small study. The threshold used has not been tested against outcome in the sources used in this app. There is no consensus on the number of bursts per minute, but the target is “usually” 3–5, citing studies of barbiturates for raised intracranial pressure (Riker 2003, Cottenceau 2008). Neuromuscular blockade was given only at induction in three patients, signal quality was good, and all received noradrenaline. Limitations, according to the authors themselves:
      • BIS could not distinguish epileptic bursts from ordinary ones: with spikes in the bursts, the same number of bursts gave quite different numbers than during ordinary burst suppression.
      • In two patients, full EEG showed regional epileptic discharges that BIS did not capture, because it only measures frontally.
      • If BIS rises suddenly, it may be lighter anaesthesia or new seizures, and only EEG can tell. Muscle activity, rigidity and movement can cause artefacts.
      The conclusion is that continuous EEG is the primary method. The authors consider BIS usable when continuous EEG is not available, but this rests on 10 patients.Source: Musialowicz 2010 (Kuopio)
    • The monitor's numbers tracked the EEG well. In 4 patients, BIS, SR and bursts from the monitor correlated strongly with bursts on the EEG.Source: Arbour 2015 (4 patients, 1,972 measurements over 33 hours)
    • Overall, these are small observational studies. A frontal monitor cannot rule out non-convulsive status, and the raw EEG from BIS missed periodic discharges in about 75 % of cases in one study.Source: Gimson and Smith 2021
