  • What the numbers mean (interpretation based on the sources): An index number does not show how deep burst suppression is or should be. None of the studies tested a BIS or SR target against outcome. The numbers also do not quite fit together: 10-second pauses give 4–5 bursts per minute, whereas 3 bursts per minute give pauses of almost 20 seconds. The target of 3–5 bursts per minute itself comes from barbiturates for raised intracranial pressure after head injury, not status epilepticus. BIS and SR are also algorithms: EMG from the forehead and noise above the amplitude threshold can give a falsely low SR and a falsely high BIS, and poor contact can give a falsely high SR. Depth must therefore be assessed in the raw EEG, not by a number.Sources: Musialowicz 2010, Riker 2003, Sørlandet Hospital 2026. See
  • The arithmetic (interpretation based on the sources): SR is the proportion of time spent in suppression. Pauses of 10 seconds with bursts of 1–3 seconds give an SR of about 75–90 %. An SR of 40–60 % means bursts and pauses last about equally long. An SR below 5 % means an almost continuous EEG, in other words no burst suppression, as Rasulo recommends during ordinary sedation.
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): the sources give no single documented target. Follow the raw EEG and the content of the bursts (epileptiform activity), not just SR. SR from a frontal monitor is an estimate that can be wrong in both directions (see the card below). The target should be agreed with a neurologist or neurointensivist for each patient.
Rasulo 2023, An 2018, Johnson 2016, Fisch 2026, Heuser 2024, Brophy 2012, Claassen 2002, Krishnamurthy 1999, Rossetti 2005, Hawkes 2024, Shorvon and Ferlisi 2011, Heuser 2022, NevroNEL 2026, Sørlandet Hospital 2026, Riker 2003, Musialowicz 2010, Arbour 2015, Gimson and Smith 2021, review 2022 (doi 10.1007/s10309-022-00539-z)

Suppression ratio and ‘suppression time’: an algorithm that can be wrong in both directions

Many studies and much teaching emphasise minutes in suppression. The number comes from the monitor's algorithm, not from someone reading the raw EEG.

  • The number is the proportion of time below an amplitude threshold. The monitor calculates what proportion of a time window (BIS: the last 63 seconds) lies below the threshold and calls it suppression. It looks for low amplitude, not for bursts (Kratzer 2020). «Minutes in suppression» in studies is this proportion multiplied by time.Sources: Andresen 2014, Kratzer 2020
  • SR can be falsely low. Noise above the threshold prevents the algorithm from seeing suppression, and EMG is a known source. In image 2 of the image quiz (shared case) SR was 0 and BIS 64 while the EEG was almost flat. After a neuromuscular blocker, with no change in dose, SR rose to 82 and BIS fell to 8. In older patients low bursts can fall below the threshold. Gruenbaum 2026 reports that automated detection missed burst suppression in about 14 % of cases.Sources: Kratzer 2020, Gruenbaum 2026
  • SR can be falsely high. Poor electrode contact or high impedance can produce a low-amplitude signal that resembles suppression. Electrocautery, suction and movement can produce large transients followed by signal dropout that resemble bursts and pauses. On visual reading, low-amplitude but continuous EEG in older patients can be misread as suppression if the scale is not adjusted. In older patients low bursts can fall below the threshold and be counted as suppression, so that SR becomes falsely high (Kratzer 2020, not tested directly on the monitors).Source: Gruenbaum 2026
  • Small changes cause large swings. SR is highly sensitive to the amplitude threshold and to noise. Small changes in amplitude or artefacts can cause large fluctuations in low-amplitude EEG.Source: Gruenbaum 2026
  • Measurement error may explain conflicting research findings. In a study of 41 patients, visually determined suppression duration was associated with delirium (p = 0.039), whereas duration from the monitor's SR was not (p = 0.275). Such measurement limitations may, according to Jegarl, partly explain why strong associations in observational studies have not translated into benefit in randomised EEG-guided trials. The data are also coarse in several studies: values read from screenshots every 5 minutes and interpolated, or BIS recorded for only 10–20 minutes per day.Sources: Jegarl 2026, Gruenbaum 2026, Fritz 2016, Watson 2008
  • A separate suppression time number does not make documentation more precise. Many ask for a suppression time (ST) number for documentation. Some monitors give a separate suppression time, others only SR as a percentage of time, and the manufacturer does not always describe the time window and calculation. Interpretation based on the sources: an ST number rests on the same amplitude threshold as SR and inherits the same sources of error, so it is no more precise than the raw-EEG assessment behind it.
  • In practice: read SR together with the raw EEG at the right scale, the EMG bar, signal quality and the spectrogram. The first step is to confirm the pattern on the raw EEG before anything else.Source: Gruenbaum 2026
  • Interpretation based on the sources: ‘suppression time’ in studies and on the monitor is an algorithmic estimate that can be too low (noise, EMG) or too high (poor contact, artefacts, low bursts in older patients, low-amplitude continuous EEG). The number should be used as a warning to be checked, not as ground truth.
The studies in detail: mechanisms and age, the Ching model, four steps (3 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Burst suppression: mechanisms, age and delirium (Lobo and Lamperti, ch. 5)

  • What it is: alternating periods of almost absent activity and high-amplitude bursts. According to the authors, not seen in natural sleep. The bursts are thought to reflect brief periods of thalamic disinhibition.
  • Two proposed mechanisms: cortical hyperexcitability (extracellular calcium and a refractory period after the burst) and a metabolic theory in which falling ATP opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels.
  • Who gets it most easily: the risk increases with age and with impaired neurological status. In older patients the pattern is less distinct: weaker bursts and shallower, shorter suppression, which makes it harder to detect in the most vulnerable (fig. 5.2).
  • Thresholds: high-dose ketamine does not usually produce burst suppression, but affects the threshold; opioids do not produce it directly, but pain and nociception can lower the threshold.
  • Delirium: several groups have found an association, but ENGAGES was inconclusive and has been criticised for the lack of standardised analgesia and for not taking age and cognitive frailty into account. See ENGAGES in the Components tab.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 5

Why burst suppression? A neurophysiological-metabolic model (Ching 2012)

Computational model from MGH, MIT and Boston University (PNAS 2012;109:3095–3100; Ching, Purdon, Vijayan, Kopell and Brown). It attempts to explain why anaesthesia, hypothermia, hypoxic-ischaemic coma and early infantile encephalopathy (Ohtahara) produce the same EEG pattern.

  • The idea: the common denominator is reduced cerebral metabolism. In the model (10 pyramidal neurons and 4 interneurons, Hodgkin-Huxley type), neuronal firing is coupled to ATP production via ATP-gated potassium channels (KATP). When ATP production is reduced, ATP is depleted during a burst, the KATP channels open, the cells hyperpolarise and fall silent; ATP slowly builds up again, and the next burst can start. 50% of normal ATP production gave a suppression ratio of about 0.5, 30% gave about 0.75; bursts and pauses lasted 4–10 seconds.
  • A continuum: burst suppression is not a separate state, but a gradually increasing suppression ratio with deeper inactivation, ending in a completely isoelectric EEG. The authors show an example of rewarming after cooling to 18 °C in which the suppression ratio gradually falls until the EEG is continuous again.
  • The bursts carry the old pattern: during propofol-induced burst suppression the alpha rhythm lives on inside each burst; the spectrogram looks “as if it has been multiplied by a sequence of zeros and ones”. The model predicts that the spectral content of a burst should be the same as just before burst suppression started, regardless of agent. It also predicts a slow frequency drift within each burst (about 11 to 8 Hz) and that fast activity is limited by metabolism, not by GABA inhibition; these two have not been confirmed experimentally.
  • Why it is relevant to perfusion: anaesthetic agents reduce firing and thereby CMRO₂ secondarily, whereas hypothermia and ischaemia reduce metabolism directly without changing the synapses. Both are thought to end in the same KATP mechanism. This is the basis for suppression being able to mean either too much agent or too little energy (Guay 2025, Georgii 2022). Ketamine, which increases CMRO₂, does not produce classic burst suppression at clinical doses.
  • The authors' interpretation: each burst is “an attempt to restore basal cortical dynamics”, and suppression is an energy-saving protection. In severe ischaemia even complete isoelectricity cannot preserve ATP, and injury follows. They suggest that the character of the bursts could be used to detect ischaemia during surgery and to distinguish burst suppression from seizures, and that the difference between a low suppression ratio and full isoelectricity should be clarified before “burst suppression” is used as a target in neuroprotection.
  • Limitations: a model with 14–20 cells, without spatial extent, and the KATP channel is a hypothesis; other channels and extracellular calcium (Kroeger and Amzica 2007) may act together. The model explains, but does not prove. No conflicts of interest declared.
Ching et al. PNAS 2012;109:3095–3100

Burst suppression during anaesthesia: a four-step clinical approach (Gruenbaum 2026)

Narrative review (Br J Anaesth 2026;136:1843–1854; Gruenbaum, Safavynia and Bilotta). The authors describe burst suppression as a context-dependent marker of cortical energy balance, neither a therapeutic target nor a pure dose phenomenon.

  • Two processes: down-regulation by anaesthetics (excessive dose, hypothermia) and metabolic failure from insufficient substrate or oxygen (hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, ischaemia). When ATP falls, ATP-gated potassium channels open and neurones hyperpolarise. Astrocytes supply lactate to neurones, and this works less well with age and vascular disease. Low ATP can also weaken the blood–brain barrier and admit inflammatory mediators; the injury markers S100B and GFAP are linked to delirium. With severe hypoperfusion or anoxic injury the EEG can become isoelectric.
  • Who tolerates it: burst suppression may be tolerated in young, healthy people without measurable consequences, whereas recurrent or persistent burst suppression in vulnerable patients more often reflects exhausted reserve. The authors argue that its meaning depends more on the brain's metabolic reserve than on its duration.
  • Raw EEG over the index: The indices are affected by suppression only when it dominates the analysis window, so acceptable index values can coexist with clear discontinuity. Gruenbaum 2026 reports that automated detection underestimated duration compared with visual scoring and missed burst suppression in about 14 % of cases. On the spectrogram, burst suppression produces a «checkerboard» pattern with dark horizontal stripes. Electrocautery and poor electrode contact can mimic burst suppression: true bursts have organised spectral content, whereas artefacts give broadband spikes.
  • Numbers: Gruenbaum 2026 cites a retrospective study of more than 38,000 adults in which nearly half had burst suppression, and both likelihood and duration increased with age. Sevoflurane produces burst suppression at about 2.9 % (above 1 MAC), propofol at about 4.9 µg/ml, whereas more than 15 µg/ml is needed to prevent movement. Meta-analyses show about 1.5 times higher risk of postoperative delirium.
  • Four steps: (1) confirm on the raw EEG: electrode contact and impedance, artefacts, and the lowest scale that shows the trace without clipping. (2) Assess symmetry: unilateral suppression may mean focal ischaemia or a technical fault; keep the dose unchanged and assess perfusion. (3) With symmetric suppression and a high dose: the authors suggest reducing by 0.1–0.2 MAC or propofol by 10–20 %. (4) If it persists at a low dose: look for hypotension, hypoxaemia, anaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and hypocapnia.
  • Pain and opioids: nociception can produce beta or delta arousal that is misread as too-light hypnosis, and more hypnotic then increases the risk of burst suppression. Opioids can unmask or accentuate burst suppression together with propofol or volatile agents.
  • Caveats: narrative review without a systematic search, focused on surgery rather than cardiac arrest or intensive care. No conflicts of interest. The authors state that a language model from OpenAI was used for editing. Safavynia is a co-author both here and of Jegarl 2026.
Gruenbaum, Safavynia and Bilotta. Br J Anaesth 2026;136:1843–1854

Key points

  • According to Pilge and co-authors, a ‘silent second’ is too deep for clinical anaesthesia. EEG suppression occurred at about 2.9 vol % sevoflurane, 1.5 vol % isoflurane and 4.85 µg/ml propofol. For the gases, that is above MAC. The endpoint cannot be used for ketamine, which usually does not produce burst suppression.See
  • Bursts become weaker with age. In older patients the first burst had lower amplitude (13.1 versus 20.3 µV in the young) and was more irregular. Normalised alpha was unchanged. This suggests that it is the amplitude, not the architecture, that disappears.See
  • Automated detection may become less accurate in older patients. The indices look for EEG below an amplitude threshold, not for bursts. Low bursts in older patients can therefore themselves fall below the threshold and be counted as suppression. Kratzer and co-authors write that the threshold must be adjusted for age so as not to increase the amount of recorded suppression, but did not test the monitors directly.See
  • After burst suppression, the same concentration gave a deeper effect in one small study. After a brief period of suppression, the measured index was consistently below the model-predicted value at the same calculated effect-site concentration. The difference lasted for the rest of the operation, but there was no control group, so time alone cannot be excluded.See
  • Models do not replace continuous EEG. The authors consider that the anaesthetised brain behaves as a non-linear system, and recommend continuous EEG monitoring, especially in vulnerable patients. The study had no control group.See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Dose and age

Burst suppression lies far above what is needed

A “silent second” means EEG suppression for at least 1 second. The dose needed for it shows how deep burst suppression is compared with ordinary anaesthesia.Source: Pilge 2014

  • For the gases, suppression only comes above MAC. Sevoflurane produced suppression at about 2.93 vol%, over 1.4 times MAC. Isoflurane produced suppression at 1.51 vol%, over 1.3 times MAC.Source: Pilge 2014
  • For propofol, suppression comes below the dose that prevents movement. Propofol produced suppression at 4.85 µg/ml (the article states “mg/ml”, probably micrograms/ml). That is under a third of the concentration that prevents movement at incision (15.2 µg/ml). Movement mostly reflects the spinal cord, whereas a “silent second” is meant to measure the effect on the brain.Sources: Pilge 2014; Smith 1994 (movement at incision)
  • Loss of response occurred much earlier. With slow induction, patients lost response at a calculated effect-site concentration of 2.0 µg/ml on average. That is a large gap from loss of response to burst suppression for propofol (interpretation based on the sources). According to Pilge and co-authors, a “silent second” is too deep for clinical anaesthesia.Sources: Sepúlveda 2026; Pilge 2014
  • The agents are not alike. Ketamine was not tested in the study and usually does not produce burst suppression, so the measure cannot be used for ketamine.Source: Pilge 2014
  • The figures rest on small samples. The studies had 55 patients divided into three groups and 23 healthy patients under 60 years. The confidence intervals may be too wide, particularly for propofol.Sources: Pilge 2014; Sepúlveda 2026

The studies in detail:

Pilge 2014 Smith 1994 Sepúlveda 2026

Older patients: weaker bursts that the monitor can miss

This concerns the first burst after burst suppression appeared during propofol induction (102 of 408 patients). The finding ties in with other age-related changes in the EEG and with how monitors measure suppression.Source: Kratzer 2020

  • The amplitude appears to disappear, not the architecture. In older patients the burst was lower (maximum amplitude 13.1 µV versus 20.3 µV in the young) and more irregular (higher permutation entropy). Absolute alpha power fell linearly with age, while normalised alpha was unchanged.Source: Kratzer 2020
  • The bursts appear to be low because the EEG is already low-amplitude before suppression. The same age-related change is seen during maintenance without burst suppression. The spectral content of the burst is also predicted to mirror the EEG just before suppression started. The bursts in older patients are thus low because the EEG in older patients is low-amplitude even before suppression (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Purdon 2015; Kreuzer 2020; Ching 2012
  • The monitor looks for silence, not for bursts. The indices detect burst suppression by looking for EEG below an amplitude threshold for a certain time. Low, flat bursts can themselves fall below the threshold and be counted as suppression. The article did not test the monitors directly. The authors argue that burst information should be used as a plausibility check, but age-adjusted.Source: Kratzer 2020
  • Caveats. Retrospective analysis of frontal EEG, only propofol-induced bursts and no adjustment for comorbidity. The midazolam subgroup among the older patients was small.Source: Kratzer 2020

The studies in detail:

Kratzer 2020 Purdon 2015 Kreuzer 2020 Ching 2012

The dose alone does not predict the effect

A TCI pump displays a calculated effect-site concentration. The question is whether the same calculated concentration gives the same EEG effect before and after a brief period of suppression.Source: Sepúlveda 2026

  • Same concentration, deeper effect. In 23 healthy patients propofol was increased until BIS showed a 1% suppression ratio. The effect-site concentration was then set back to the level at loss of response. Before the perturbation, observed and predicted BIS were the same. Afterwards, observed BIS lay consistently below predicted BIS (largest bias −17.5), with lower alpha power and stronger delta–alpha coupling (Kmod 0.21 versus 0.16). The difference persisted for the rest of the operation.Source: Sepúlveda 2026
  • The models are built on other conditions. Slow induction gave loss of response at about 2.0 µg/ml, versus an EC50 of about 3 µg/ml in the Eleveld model for the same age. The explanation may be that the models were built on bolus and rapid-infusion data without equilibrium between plasma and effect site.Source: Sepúlveda 2026
  • The authors hold that the brain behaves non-linearly. On their reading, the same dose does not give the same effect, and the effect does not return to the starting point. Linear PK/PD models therefore cannot predict the effect after a disturbance, whether experimental or clinical, such as haemorrhage or an altered infusion rate. The authors recommend continuous EEG monitoring, especially in vulnerable patients.Source: Sepúlveda 2026
  • Caveats. There was no control group without perturbation, so time alone cannot be excluded. “The same concentration” is defined by the model being tested, and there were no plasma measurements. Nociception could explain the lower alpha, but the stronger delta–alpha coupling argues against it.Source: Sepúlveda 2026
  • Taken together: read the EEG directly, not just the dose figure (interpretation based on the sources). The threshold for suppression lies high on average, the bursts look different with age, and the same calculated concentration can give a different effect in the same patient over time.Sources: Pilge 2014; Kratzer 2020; Sepúlveda 2026

The studies in detail:

Sepúlveda 2026 Pilge 2014 Kratzer 2020
The studies in detail: Pilge 2014, Kratzer 2020, Sepúlveda 2026 (3 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Burst suppression MAC and CP50 (Pilge 2014)

  • What it is: a study proposing the “silent second” (EEG suppression for at least 1 second) as a measure of the anaesthetic agent's effect on the brain, instead of movement at incision (MAC, which mostly reflects the spinal cord).
  • Design: 55 unpremedicated ASA I–II patients for elective surgery were randomised to sevoflurane (16), isoflurane (21) or propofol (18). The concentration was held constant for 15 minutes and EEG analysed in the 16th minute, and the next patient received a 10% lower concentration if suppression occurred and 10% higher if not (Dixon's “up-and-down” method, six independent crossover pairs per group). The values were calculated with logistic regression.
  • Result: sevoflurane 2.93 vol% (95% CI 2.80–3.15), isoflurane 1.51 vol% (1.45–1.60) and propofol 4.85 (CI 4.25–5.40; the article states “mg/ml”, probably micrograms/ml). That is over 1.4 times MAC for sevoflurane (2.05 vol%), over 1.3 times MAC for isoflurane (1.15 vol%) and under a third of the propofol concentration that prevents movement at incision (15.2 µg/ml, from Smith 1994).
  • Reservations: the starting concentrations were above the population value, and the authors write that the confidence intervals may therefore be too wide, particularly for propofol. The sample is small. Burst suppression usually does not occur with ketamine, so the measure cannot be used for ketamine. The pattern also differs between agents, and the authors write that a “silent second” is too deep for clinical anaesthesia.
  • What the article does not say: it does not state that fentanyl reduces the propofol concentration by about 80%. That figure comes from Smith 1994 via Miller's.
  • Conflicts of interest: none declared. Funded by departmental funds.
Pilge et al. Br J Anaesth 2014;112:1067–1074

The bursts become weaker and more irregular with age (Kratzer 2020)

Retrospective analysis from TU Munich and Columbia (Front Syst Neurosci 2020;14:599962) of the first burst after burst suppression appeared during propofol induction. The data are from Hesse 2019 (Atlanta), recorded with SedLine (Legacy) and analysed by an independent university group.

  • Method: 102 of 408 patients had a distinct first burst after a “silent second” (at least 1 s below 10 µV). Only the first 1.5 seconds of the burst were analysed, so that differing duration and dose would not affect the result. Median age 56 years; 16 patients under 45 years (YOUNG) and a group over 65 years (OLD). Fentanyl equivalents did not differ with age.
  • Findings: older patients had lower absolute power in 1–15 Hz and relatively more power above 15 Hz within the burst. Absolute alpha power fell linearly with age (AUC 0.86 for young versus old), while normalised alpha did not change: this suggests that it is the amplitude, not the architecture, that disappears. Maximum amplitude was 20.3 µV in the young versus 13.1 µV in the older patients (AUC 0.84), steepest slope 1.22 versus 0.86 µV/ms, and permutation entropy was higher in the older patients (more irregular signal). Subanalysis of the 83 who received midazolam premedication gave the same result.
  • Why it matters for the monitor: The indices detect burst suppression by looking for suppression, that is EEG below an amplitude threshold for a certain time, not by recognising the bursts. When the bursts in older patients are lower and flatter, they can themselves fall below the threshold and be counted as suppression. The authors argue that burst information should be used as a plausibility check, but then age-adjusted. This is the mechanism behind Image 6 and 13 in the image quiz: in older patients both normal EEG and bursts can look “weak”.
  • Connection in the app: the same age-related change that Purdon 2015 (BJA) and Kreuzer 2020 described for maintenance without burst suppression, and which Ching 2012 predicts: the spectral content of the burst mirrors the EEG just before the suppression started. Obert 2024 (Older patients and delirium sub-tab) shows that slow induction can avoid burst suppression in older patients in the first place.
  • Limitations: frontal EEG, only propofol-induced bursts, no adjustment for comorbidity, and the midazolam subgroup among the older patients was small. Funded by the James S. McDonnell Foundation (García); no conflicts of interest declared.
Kratzer et al. Front Syst Neurosci 2020;14:599962

After burst suppression the brain is not the same: non-linear pharmacodynamics (Sepúlveda 2026)

Prospective, non-randomised dose–response study from Osorno (Anesth Analg 2026;143:261–270, NCT06417645): 23 healthy patients under 60 years received slow induction (10 mg/kg/h) to loss of response, then Eleveld TCI, remifentanil 4.5 ng/ml and rocuronium. After intubation, propofol was increased to 15 mg/kg/h until BIS showed a 1% suppression ratio (“perturbation”), and the effect-site concentration was then set back to the level at loss of response. Observed BIS was compared with BIS predicted by the Eleveld model (TIVA Trainer), and the EEG spectrum and delta–alpha phase-amplitude coupling were analysed.

  • Before the perturbation: observed and predicted BIS were the same (no significant difference).
  • After the perturbation: with the same calculated effect-site concentration as before, observed BIS lay consistently below predicted BIS (largest bias −17.5 in the phase after the perturbation), and the difference persisted for the rest of the operation. Alpha power (absolute and relative) was lower than before, and the delta–alpha modulation (Kmod) was stronger (0.21 versus 0.16, p = 0.01), which the authors interpret as deeper thalamocortical synchronisation. Same concentration, deeper effect.
  • Slow induction gives a lower Ce at loss of response: on average 2.0 µg/ml, versus an EC50 of about 3 µg/ml in the Eleveld model for the same age. The authors believe the models were built on bolus and rapid-infusion data without plasma–effect equilibrium (“front-end” kinetics), and that ke0 is a mathematical device to collapse the hysteresis loop.
  • Interpretation: the brain under anaesthesia behaves as a non-linear system (the same dose does not give the same effect, no return to the starting point). Linear PK/PD models therefore cannot predict the effect after a disturbance, whether experimental (brief burst suppression) or clinical (haemorrhage shrinking V1, altered infusion rate). The conclusion is continuous EEG monitoring, especially in vulnerable patients. The authors discuss nociception as an alternative explanation for the lower alpha (surgery was under way after the perturbation), but consider that the stronger delta–alpha coupling argues against it.
  • Caveats: no control group without perturbation, so time alone cannot be excluded; circularity because “the same concentration” is defined by the model being tested; no plasma measurements; only healthy subjects under 60; the BIS prediction from Eleveld is itself debated (Coetzee 2024). The numbers in the abstract and the results section do not agree (see discrepancies). No conflicts of interest, public funding (ANID).
Sepúlveda, Barra, Baloian, Gutiérrez. Anesth Analg 2026;143:261–270

Key points

  • Burst suppression is associated with delirium and death in observational studies. More minutes of suppression during surgery were associated with a higher incidence of delirium. Burst suppression during ICU sedation was associated with higher mortality at 6 months (HR 2.04).See
  • More time in burst suppression during coma was associated with more delirium. About one hour versus one minute in burst suppression was associated with four times higher odds of delirium after coma. The delirium was also less likely to resolve.See
  • Burst suppression appears mostly to be a marker of vulnerability. In the causal analysis, severity of illness drove both burst suppression and mortality. Burst suppression mediated only about 10 % of the effect of critical illness on death. Titrating to the lowest necessary dose may nevertheless have a modest effect.See
  • EEG guidance has not consistently reduced delirium in the large randomised trials. ENGAGES and ENGAGES-Canada gave less burst suppression, but no difference in delirium.See
  • Measurement and definitions diverge. Definitions vary, and the suppression ratio underestimates suppression compared with visual interpretation. According to Jegarl, the suppression phase looks the same whatever the cause. Incidence and duration alone therefore cannot distinguish oversedation from ischaemia, hypothermia or hypoglycaemia.See
  • Blood pressure should be checked before the dose is reduced. In patients over 60, BSR fell to 0 in 55 % of episodes (24 of 44) simply by raising MAP to baseline. Burst suppression can also be limited by avoiding hypothermia and ensuring oxygenation.See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Burst suppression and outcomes

The association with delirium and death in observational studies

Three observational studies from the operating theatre and the ICU find that burst suppression is associated with worse outcomes. They are widely cited, but can only show association, not cause.Sources: Fritz 2016; Watson 2008; Andresen 2014

  • During surgery: more suppression, more delirium. In 727 adults, 86 % undergoing cardiac surgery, more minutes of suppression were associated with a higher incidence of delirium, also after adjustment (OR 1.22 per log unit of minutes of suppression). Suppression time predicted delirium better than time with BIS below 20, but both were weak predictors on their own.Source: Fritz 2016
  • In the ICU: burst suppression is associated with death and delirium. 39 % of 125 ventilated patients had burst suppression, although nobody had it as a goal. 59 % of them died within 6 months versus 33 % without (adjusted HR 2.04). In comatose patients who later woke, about one hour versus one minute in burst suppression was associated with four times higher odds of delirium (OR 4.16), and the delirium took longer to resolve.Sources: Watson 2008; Andresen 2014
  • The dose explains only part of it. During surgery, higher end-tidal concentration and lower opioid dose were associated with more suppression, but it is unclear which was cause and which was effect. In the ICU the lorazepam dose in the last 24 hours was higher before burst suppression, but none of the agents differed when the dose was adjusted for weight.Sources: Fritz 2016; Watson 2008
  • The studies are small and the measurements short. One study was a post hoc analysis with only 10–20 minutes of EEG per day, one had 69 patients, and in one nearly everyone had some suppression (548 of 619), so the comparison group was small. The authors of the two ICU studies themselves caution against firm conclusions.Sources: Watson 2008; Andresen 2014; Fritz 2016
  • After cardiac surgery too, those who developed delirium had more burst suppression. The patients were 60 years or older and received isoflurane (about 0.7 MAC) and sufentanil. Of 81, 26 (32 %) developed delirium, most often quiet (hypoactive) delirium. They had a median of 107 minutes of burst suppression during surgery, against 44 minutes in the others. Burst suppression was read from the monitor, not assessed in the raw EEG. The authors themselves write that it is not known whether burst suppression causes delirium or is only associated with it. Two of the authors have received lecture fees from the monitor manufacturer.Source: Soehle 2015 (observational study)

The studies in detail:

Fritz 2016 Watson 2008 Andresen 2014 Soehle 2015

Cause or marker?

There are two possibilities. Either excessively deep anaesthesia is the cause, or suppression occurs more easily in patients with subclinical brain pathology, so that anaesthesia acts as a “neural stress test”. Later studies point mostly towards the latter, but not entirely.Source: Fritz 2016

  • Severity of illness drives both. In 471 ICU patients, severe versus mild illness was associated with 39 % more burst suppression burden and 35 % higher mortality. Burst suppression mediated only 10 % of the effect of critical illness on death. A high versus low cumulative propofol dose gave only 6 % more burst suppression. Unintended burst suppression is therefore primarily an effect of critical illness and a marker of vulnerability.Source: Hogan 2020
  • A small contribution nevertheless exists. 100 % versus 0 % burst suppression burden gave 12 % higher mortality. Individual titration to the lowest necessary dose may have a modest effect. The difference in effect size from the earlier ICU study may be due to different methods and populations.Sources: Hogan 2020; Watson 2008
  • The randomised trials: less burst suppression, but mostly no less delirium. ENGAGES (n = 1232) and ENGAGES-Canada (n = 1140) gave less burst suppression in the EEG group, but no difference in delirium. In ENGAGES-Canada (aged 60 and over, cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, four hospitals) MAC fell from 0.80 to 0.66 and suppression time from 11.7 to 4.0 minutes, while delirium was 18.15 versus 18.10 %. Three different EEG monitors were used. The authors themselves suggest that the difference from CODA and Balanced may be because the control groups there received deeper anaesthesia. They also state that a 17.5 % reduction in volatile dose may have been too small, and that an effect smaller than the 8 percentage points the trial was powered for cannot be ruled out: detecting it would require 2700 to 11,000 patients. The delirium substudy of Balanced (515 patients, 78 % Asian, BIS 50 versus 35) gave 19 versus 28 % delirium (17 versus 29 % per protocol), with a dose separation of 0.21 MAC (0.59 versus 0.79) versus 0.11 in ENGAGES, and differing anaesthetic sensitivity between centres. A blood pressure intervention study also reduced burst suppression without any difference in delirium in the recovery room. Of 27 healthy volunteers given 3 hours of isoflurane at 1.3 MAC, 93 % had burst suppression and none developed delirium.Sources: Jegarl 2026; Georgii 2022; Evered 2021; Deschamps 2024
  • CODA: an effect, but the control group received much more anaesthetic. In CODA (n = 921, aged 60 and over, major noncardiac surgery) EEG guidance gave 15.6 versus 24.1 % delirium (secondary outcome) and 10.2 versus 14.7 % cognitive dysfunction at 3 months (primary outcome). The control group received routine care with the monitor hidden and got considerably more: 0.93 versus 0.57 MAC equivalents of volatile agent and 3.3 versus 2.7 µg/ml propofol (estimated effect-site concentration). In ENGAGES the difference was only 0.80 versus 0.69 MAC. Guidance in CODA was by an index number, which is an unreliable algorithm. What separates CODA from ENGAGES is therefore greater dose separation (interpretation based on the figures).Sources: Chan 2013; Wildes 2019
  • A Norwegian randomised trial found less propofol use and faster emergence with EEG guidance (conference abstract, full publication not yet available). 100 adults scheduled for anterior cervical discectomy and fusion were randomised to dosing guided by raw EEG, spectrogram and index, or to standard monitoring. With EEG, patients woke up faster (median 330 versus 468 seconds, p = 0.002, primary outcome) and received less propofol (median 4.94 versus 6.28 mg/kg/h, p < 0.001). Cognitive testing 3 and 24 hours after awakening (CANTAB) was better in the EEG group, but the abstract does not report the figures. The abstract does not mention delirium. The first author is a co-author of this app.Source: Aasheim 2026 (abstract)
  • In the Safe Brain Initiative, EEG is one of 18 measures. The bundle aims to prevent delirium and includes, among other things, screening for delirium, pain and anxiety, shorter fasting, reduced anticholinergic load, orientation, circadian rhythm, nociception monitoring, temperature control and EEG monitoring (item 13). The whole list is in . In four hospitals in Denmark and Turkey (18,697 patients), delirium in the recovery room fell the longer the bundle was in use (adjusted OR 0.96 per month). In one hospital in Switzerland, delirium in the recovery room fell from 22.45 to 18.11 % between the first and last six months. Neither study can isolate what EEG or a lower dose contributes on its own: there was no control group or randomisation, EEG use was not reported, and delirium was only screened in the recovery room. Both studies have financial ties to a monitor manufacturer, which funded the Swiss study.Sources: Meco 2024; Saunders 2026
  • Low index number: marker or cause? As early as 2012, Sanders and co-authors noted that it is unclear whether a low index number mediates or merely marks later mortality. The findings may be explained by reduced perfusion of the brain and other organs, which also lowers the index number, and the patients with low numbers and earlier death may have received lower doses. The authors therefore argued that disconnection from the environment, rather than deeper anaesthesia, is a more important goal, since the patient then does not experience surgery.Source: Sanders 2012
  • Little alpha and absent slowing may be markers of vulnerability. In an observational study (237 patients aged 65 and over, 41 developed delirium) those who developed delirium had lower spectral edge frequency before surgery (13.1 versus 17.4 Hz, only 18 measured in the delirium group) and weaker alpha after induction (−7.37 versus −5 dB). In those without delirium the EEG slowed at loss of consciousness, while it barely changed in those who developed delirium. The index number did not separate the groups, and burst suppression duration did not differ significantly (32 versus 17 minutes, p = 0.227). The study cannot show cause: doses were not controlled, the delirium group had longer anaesthesia (330 versus 192 minutes), and few developed delirium. One of the authors holds a patent licensed to a monitor manufacturer.Source: Koch 2021
  • Context decides (interpretation based on the sources). Burst suppression in healthy people need not cause delirium. In ill and vulnerable patients it mostly says something about the patient’s reserve. The causal analysis was nevertheless retrospective, with selection towards patients with brain injury, and the associations outside the randomised trials are observational.Sources: Hogan 2020; Jegarl 2026

The studies in detail:

Fritz 2016 Hogan 2020 Watson 2008 Jegarl 2026 Georgii 2022 Deschamps 2024 Chan 2013 Koch 2021 Aasheim 2026 Meco 2024 Saunders 2026 Sanders 2012

Measurement and definition explain some of the discrepancy

Why do the observational studies find an association that the randomised trials do not confirm? Part of the answer lies in what was actually measured.Source: Jegarl 2026

  • Burst suppression is defined differently. ACNS 2021 requires burst suppression to make up 50–99 % of the record and distinguishes suppression (below 10 µV) from attenuation. The anaesthesia literature uses the term more loosely and measures with 1–4 frontal channels. Some studies counted any BSR above 0 as burst suppression.Sources: Jegarl 2026; Watson 2008
  • The monitor may underestimate. The proprietary suppression ratio may underestimate burst suppression compared with visual interpretation. In one study (41 patients), visually determined suppression duration was associated with delirium (p = 0.039), whereas SR-based duration was not (p = 0.275). The same caveat about processed BSR applies in the blood pressure study.Sources: Jegarl 2026; Georgii 2022
  • Time in burst suppression is often crudely measured. Duration has been calculated as the mean suppression ratio multiplied by time in coma, read from screenshots every 5 minutes and interpolated (141 patients), or only recorded for 10–20 minutes per day as yes/no without duration.Sources: Andresen 2014; Fritz 2016; Watson 2008
  • The pattern looks the same whatever the cause. The suppression phase looks the same in oversedation, ischaemia, hypothermia and hypoglycaemia, so incidence and duration alone cannot distinguish them. The content of the bursts (intraburst spectrum, preburst activity, spatial distribution) may be more informative.Source: Jegarl 2026

The studies in detail:

Jegarl 2026 Georgii 2022 Andresen 2014 Fritz 2016 Watson 2008

What can be done: more than turning down the dose

If burst suppression can mean either too much agent or too little energy, the dose is only one of several levers.

  • Blood pressure can be checked first. In patients over 60, MAP at the start of the episodes was lower than baseline. When MAP was raised to the patient’s baseline, BSR fell to 0 in 55 % of cases (24 of 44) without other measures. The intervention group had shorter suppression (5.9 versus 10.1 minutes). The effect came at induction; during maintenance the difference was not significant. The study does not prove causation, and the sample is small.Source: Georgii 2022
  • Temperature and oxygen matter too. Burst suppression can be limited not only with the dose, but by raising blood pressure, avoiding hypothermia and ensuring oxygenation. CMRO2 falls by about 6 % per °C, and the EEG often becomes isoelectric at 18–20 °C (only 60 % were at 18 °C in one study of hypothermic circulatory arrest, Jegarl 2026).Source: Jegarl 2026
  • The lowest necessary dose. In ENGAGES and ENGAGES-Canada, lower MAC gave less burst suppression. Avoiding overdosing probably has little effect on mortality, but individual titration to the lowest necessary dose may have a modest effect.Sources: Jegarl 2026; Hogan 2020
  • When it is intended. In aneurysm surgery with temporary clipping, the evidence for barbiturate-induced burst suppression is mixed. Animal studies suggest that protection does not require burst suppression.Source: Jegarl 2026

The studies in detail:

Georgii 2022 Jegarl 2026 Hogan 2020
The studies in detail: delirium, mortality, causal analysis, context and blood pressure (6 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

EEG suppression during surgery and subsequent delirium (Fritz 2016)

Observational study from Washington University (Anesth Analg 2016;122:234–242), a sub-study of the SATISFY-SOS registry. This is the study most often cited for the association between burst suppression during anaesthesia and delirium.

  • Patients: 727 adults (mean 62 years, 63% men) for general anaesthesia with planned intensive care stay, 86% cardiac surgery. Induction with propofol, maintenance with a volatile agent. Suppression ratio from one BIS channel (Fp1–F7), recorded once a minute, summed to minutes with suppression. In 141 patients the values were read from screenshots every 5 minutes and interpolated. Delirium was assessed with CAM-ICU twice daily on days 1–5 in 619 patients.
  • Findings: median suppression 4.5 minutes (IQR 0.7–17.4). 162 (26%) developed delirium, 73% of them hypoactive. More minutes in suppression gave a higher incidence of delirium across quartiles (p < 0.0001), and the association held after adjustment for age, ASA, comorbidity, type of surgery, opioid, ketamine, transfusion and end-tidal concentration: OR 1.22 per log unit of minutes of suppression (99% CI 1.06–1.40). Suppression time predicted delirium better than time with BIS below 20 (c-statistic 0.62 versus 0.57), but both are weak predictors on their own.
  • What was associated with suppression: higher end-tidal concentration (OR 1.5 per 0.5 MAC) and lower opioid dose (OR 0.5 per 1 morphine equivalent/kg). The authors cannot say whether less opioid led to more suppression, or whether deeply anaesthetised patients without signs of nociception simply received less opioid.
  • Interpretation, the authors' two possibilities: either too deep anaesthesia as the cause, or that suppression arises more readily in patients with subclinical brain pathology, so that anaesthesia acts as a “neural stress test”. The study cannot separate the two; see Hogan 2020 and Jegarl 2026 below.
  • Limitations: observational study without causal inference, delirium measured as part of routine care (low sensitivity), no preoperative Barthel measurement, only planned intensive care patients, and mostly cardiac surgery. Almost all (548 of 619) had some suppression, so the comparison group without suppression was small (71). No conflicts of interest reported. The follow-up ENGAGES (Wildes 2019) from the same group found that EEG-guided anaesthesia reduced suppression time without reducing delirium.
Fritz et al. Anesth Analg 2016;122:234–242

Burst suppression during sedation and mortality (Watson 2008)

Post hoc analysis of a prospective cohort (Crit Care Med 2008;36:3171–3177) from the medical ICU at Vanderbilt: 125 adult ventilated patients without known neurological disease, APACHE II 27, 98% received sedation (lorazepam, midazolam, diazepam, propofol, fentanyl, morphine), titrated to the Ramsay scale. BIS (A1050, 2-channel frontal) was recorded for 10–20 minutes daily together with RASS and CAM-ICU. Burst suppression was defined as BSR above 0.

  • How common: burst suppression in 49 of 125 (39%), and in almost half of the comatose patients (46 of 93). 54% of the episodes occurred in the first 72 hours. None had burst suppression as a goal in the chart.
  • Mortality: 59% (29 of 49) died within 6 months versus 33% (25 of 76) without burst suppression. Adjusted for age, comorbidity, dementia, APACHE II, SOFA, coma and delirium: HR 2.04 (95% CI 1.12–3.70, p = 0.02). ICU mortality 37% versus 18% and hospital mortality 49% versus 24% were not significant individually. Length of stay on the ward after the ICU was longer (HR 1.84).
  • Drugs: the lorazepam dose in the preceding 24 hours was higher before burst suppression (27.8 versus 7.5 mg/day, p = 0.004). Propofol, morphine and fentanyl did not differ, and none of the agents differed when the dose was adjusted for weight. The groups were similar at inclusion.
  • The authors' main point: once the patient is unresponsive, no sedation scale can capture that the sedation is becoming deeper. Burst suppression is an EEG sign of deep sedation that can be read without EEG expertise, and which is probably less affected by encephalopathy than the index value itself. They propose that pEEG should be evaluated alongside sedation and delirium scales.
  • Sources of error they describe: EMG can give a falsely high index in intensive care patients, while hepatic and renal encephalopathy give slower, higher-amplitude EEG that resembles sedation and can give a falsely low index.
  • Caveats: post hoc, hypothesis-generating, 125 patients, only 10–20 minutes of EEG daily (burst suppression probably underestimated), yes/no classification without duration, and the sensor was applied just before recording, which may have stimulated the patient. Aspect provided monitors and partial salary for a research nurse; Ely and Watson report honoraria or support from Aspect, Hospira, Pfizer and Lilly. The authors themselves warn against firm conclusions.
Watson et al. Crit Care Med 2008;36:3171–3177

Time in burst suppression during coma and subsequent delirium (Andresen 2014)

Prospective observational cohort nested in BRAIN-ICU (Crit Care Med 2014;42:2244–2251), Vanderbilt, medical, surgical and cardiovascular intensive care. 124 ventilated patients had continuous BIS for up to 7 days; 69 were comatose (RASS −3 or deeper) and later awoke, and were included in the analysis. RASS twice daily, CAM-ICU twice daily when not comatose. Staff were blinded to burst suppression with a cover over the monitor. None received neuromuscular blocking agents.

  • Main finding: 42 of 69 (61%) developed delirium after coma. Most had burst suppression, but briefly: median 6.4 minutes (IQR 1–58). Adjusted for time with BIS below 40 and a component of APACHE II and cumulative doses of benzodiazepine, opioid and propofol during coma, more time in burst suppression gave higher odds of delirium (OR 4.16, 95% CI 1.27–13.62, p = 0.02) and later resolution of delirium (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.53–0.98, p = 0.04).
  • In practice: about 1 hour of burst suppression (75th percentile) versus 1 minute (25th percentile) gave four times higher odds of delirium and a 22% lower probability of it resolving during follow-up.
  • How time was calculated: BIS recorded the suppression ratio every minute (proportion of the last 63 seconds that was isoelectric); the mean was multiplied by time in coma. Minutes with low signal quality were excluded.
  • The authors' interpretation: sedation scales “lose their usefulness” when the patient is comatose, and pEEG can reveal the deepest sedation. The findings support lighter sedation strategies, but the authors themselves say that no firm conclusions can be drawn until larger studies have been done.
  • Caveats: small sample (69), monitoring did not always start at the onset of coma, maximum 7 days, eight patients would have dropped out with RASS −4 as the coma threshold, and no adjustment for hypoxia, hypotension, sleep or diagnosis. Watson reports research support from Aspect; several authors fees from Hospira and Orion.
Andresen et al. Crit Care Med 2014;42:2244–2251

Is burst suppression cause or marker? Causal analysis (Hogan 2020)

Retrospective observational study from Massachusetts General Hospital (Neurocrit Care 2020;33:565–574): 471 ventilated patients from seven intensive care units (2014–2017) with continuous EEG for at least 18 hours, after excluding anoxic encephalopathy after cardiac arrest and intentional burst suppression (raised ICP, status epilepticus, neuromuscular blockers). Median age 61 years, 27% died in hospital, half had unintentional burst suppression, and 63% had structural brain injury. The authors applied prediction models and causal inference (counterfactual “randomised” comparison, mediation, E-values) to the observational data.

  • Severity of illness drives both: going from mild to severe illness (10th versus 90th percentile) gave 39% (95% CI 8–66) more burst suppression burden and 35% (29–41) higher mortality.
  • Burst suppression contributes, but little: 100% versus 0% burst suppression burden gave 12% (7–17) higher mortality, and burst suppression mediated 10% (2–21) of the effect of critical illness on death.
  • Propofol matters less than assumed: high cumulative dose (1316 mg/kg) versus low (284 mg/kg) gave only 6% (0.8–12) more burst suppression, and propofol had no direct effect on mortality; the whole effect went via burst suppression.
  • The authors' interpretation: unintentional burst suppression is “primarily an effect of critical illness, not iatrogenic propofol use”, either because the illness itself produces the pattern (as in sepsis) or because it alters the brain's sensitivity so that ordinary doses produce burst suppression. Burst suppression thus becomes a marker of vulnerability. Avoiding overdosing will probably have little effect on mortality, but individual titration to the lowest necessary dose may still have a modest effect.
  • Versus Watson 2008: the authors consider that the difference in effect size may be due to differing methods and differing populations, and that intensive care versus operating theatre may be an effect modifier.
  • Caveats: selection (continuous EEG is obtained when brain dysfunction is suspected, hence 63% brain injury), coarse burden calculation in 8–12-hour windows, arbitrary distinction between mild and severe illness, in-hospital mortality only, cumulative dose without time course, binary clinical variables, no adjustment for unit, and seizure burden as an explicitly stated possible confounder. No conflicts of interest reported. Code is openly available.
Hogan et al. Neurocrit Care 2020;33:565–574

Burst suppression: good, bad or indifferent? Context decides (Jegarl 2026)

Narrative review from Weill Cornell (Anesth Analg 2026;142:1169–1179) that attempts to explain why observational studies find an association between burst suppression and postoperative delirium, while the large randomised trials do not.

  • The definitions diverge: ACNS 2021 distinguishes attenuation (≥ 10 µV, but below 50% of background) from suppression (below 10 µV), requires that “burst-suppression” makes up 50–99% of the recording, and that a burst lasts ≥ 0.5 s with ≥ 4 phases. The anaesthesia literature uses the term more loosely, calls suppression “isoelectric”, and measures with 1–4 frontal channels and a proprietary suppression ratio that underestimates burst suppression compared with visual interpretation. In one study (41 patients), visually determined suppression duration was associated with delirium (p = 0.039), but SR-based duration was not (p = 0.275).
  • The Ching model: a neurophysiological-metabolic model in which falling ATP opens ATP-gated potassium channels, hyperpolarises the neurons and produces burst suppression at about a 50% fall in ATP production, with suppression duration proportional to the ATP deficit. The model unifies deep anaesthesia, hypoxia/ischaemia, hypoglycaemia (below 50 mg/dl), the postictal state and hypothermia (CMRO2 falls about 6% per °C, isoelectric at 18–20 °C). Ketamine, dexmedetomidine and xenon do not produce burst suppression.
  • The trials: ENGAGES (n = 1232) and ENGAGES-Canada (n = 1140) gave lower MAC (0.69 versus 0.8 and 0.66 versus 0.8) and less burst suppression (7 versus 13 and 4 versus 12 minutes) in the EEG group, but no difference in delirium (26.0 versus 23.0% and 18.2 versus 18.1%) (Wildes 2019; Deschamps 2024). The delirium substudy of Balanced (515 patients, 78 % Asian, BIS 50 versus 35) gave 19 versus 28 % delirium (17 versus 29 % per protocol), with a dose separation of 0.21 MAC (0.59 versus 0.79) versus 0.11 in ENGAGES. Those who developed delirium had longer suppression (7 versus 2 minutes) (Evered 2021). Differing anaesthetic sensitivity between centres may also matter. 27 healthy volunteers with 3 hours of isoflurane at 1.3 MAC: 93% developed burst suppression, none developed delirium.
  • When burst suppression is used deliberately: in aneurysm surgery with temporary clipping the evidence for barbiturate-induced burst suppression is mixed, and animal studies suggest that protection does not require burst suppression. In hypothermic circulatory arrest, temperature below 12.5 °C and cooling for more than 50 minutes were the only reliable predictors of isoelectric EEG (only 60% were isoelectric at 18 °C), and each degree above the temperature at which the EEG became continuous again gave RR 1.56 for neurological injury.
  • Protective down-regulated state: the painted turtle survives months of anoxia with burst suppression-like EEG and 80 times higher GABA. The authors (via Schiff and Brown) propose a corresponding “protective down-regulated state” in humans after cardiac arrest and severe covid-19, where prolonged unconsciousness without structural injury may be protective. In 795 intubated covid patients, time to recovery of consciousness increased from 9 to 22 days with the degree of hypoxaemia.
  • Conclusion: the suppression phase looks the same regardless of cause, so incidence and duration alone cannot distinguish oversedation from ischaemia, hypothermia or hypoglycaemia. The burst content (intraburst spectrum, preburst activity, spatial distribution) may be more informative. In any case, burst suppression can be limited not only by the dose, but by raising the blood pressure, avoiding hypothermia and ensuring oxygenation.
  • Caveats: narrative review without a systematic search. Goldstein is a co-inventor on patents for alkylphenols against neuropathic pain.
Jegarl et al. Anesth Analg 2026;142:1169–1179

Does burst suppression mean the same under sevoflurane and propofol? (Markus 2026, Koch 2023)

This is one of the more surprising findings in the literature, and it cuts across the way burst suppression is usually talked about. Two studies from the same group in Berlin point the same way: the same amount of burst suppression does not appear to mean the same thing under the two agents.

  • Markus et al. 2026 followed 265 patients over 70 prospectively with frontal EEG, maintained with propofol (139) or sevoflurane (126). Burst suppression was annotated manually using ACNS terminology with a 5 µV threshold. Delirium was assessed with NU-DESC and CAM-ICU to the fifth postoperative day.
  • Propofol produced the most burst suppression, sevoflurane the least. Median duration was 20.6 seconds with propofol against 0 seconds with sevoflurane (p = 0.012).
  • But delirium was commonest with sevoflurane: 44% against 30% (p = 0.017). In the adjusted analysis sevoflurane gave OR 3.27 (95% CI 1.73 to 6.24), and having had any burst suppression at all gave OR 2.99 (1.61 to 5.58).
  • And the effect of burst suppression was entirely different in the two groups. Under sevoflurane burst suppression gave OR 5.98 (2.41 to 14.85). Under propofol it gave OR 1.71 (0.71 to 4.13), that is no significant association. The interaction term between agent and burst suppression was significant (OR 3.80, 1.11 to 13.01, p = 0.033). Compared with propofol without burst suppression, sevoflurane with burst suppression had OR 9.30, but the confidence interval runs from 1.64 to 52.76, so it is very imprecise.
  • The larger study says the same about propofol, but not about sevoflurane. Koch et al. 2023, a secondary analysis of SuDoCo with 1058 patients over 60, found that propofol produced the longest burst suppression time, about 32.5 minutes, and yet the lowest delirium incidence (12.9%). Sevoflurane against propofol was not significant (OR 1.32, 0.77 to 2.26). It was desflurane that stood out, with 25.4% delirium and OR 1.77 (1.05 to 2.97), independent of how long burst suppression lasted.
  • What the authors themselves think it means. The Markus group argues that burst suppression is probably a marker of the patient's vulnerability rather than a cause in itself. That propofol produces the most of it and the least delirium fits poorly with the suppression itself being the harmful thing.
  • Caveats, and they are large. Both studies are single-centre, and in neither was the agent randomised: the anaesthetist chose, so the patients in the groups are not alike. The Markus study found no dose-response within either group, and the continuous measures of burst suppression were not associated with delirium at all. The confidence intervals for the interaction are very wide. This is therefore an interesting observation, not a settled difference between the agents.

Whether burst suppression is cause or marker is dealt with separately in .

Markus et al. 2026 Koch et al. 2023

Burst suppression and blood pressure (Georgii 2022)

  • Design: randomised trial at a single clinic. Patients ≥60 years, at least 60 minutes of surgery under general anaesthesia, without neuropsychiatric disease. 104 were analysed, and 68 had a burst suppression ratio (BSR) above 0 (control 32, intervention 36).
  • Intervention: when BSR was above 0, MAP was first raised to the patient's baseline (lowest measured MAP before anaesthesia, mainly with catecholamines). If BSR was still positive, the anaesthetic concentration was reduced. The control group received standard anaesthesia with the EEG concealed.
  • Result: cumulative BSR was 433 versus 1385 (p = 0.002), duration 5.9 versus 10.1 minutes (p = 0.002) and maximum BSR 35 versus 50 (p = 0.027). The effect occurred at induction. During maintenance the difference was not significant.
  • MAP at the start of the BSR episodes was significantly lower than baseline in both groups. When MAP was raised to baseline (44 cases), BSR was reduced, and in 55% (24 of 44) it went to 0 without other measures. During maintenance this happened in 7 of 11.
  • Delirium: no one developed postoperative delirium on days 1–3. 28% developed delirium in the recovery room, with no difference between the groups.
  • The authors' caveats: the study does not prove a causal relationship between hypotension, hypoperfusion and burst suppression. Processed BSR may underestimate suppression, and 57% had a maximum state entropy of 80 or more. The sample is small.
Georgii et al. Front Syst Neurosci 2022;16:786816

Key points

  • Burst suppression after cardiac arrest should not on its own be read as a sign of poor prognosis. Three patients with short time to ROSC and little cortical injury woke after 17–37 days and became functionally independent. All had prominent burst suppression with theta in the bursts.Source: Forgacs 2020 (see “Burst suppression with theta in the bursts after cardiac arrest: a recovery marker? (Forgacs 2020)”)
  • The content of the bursts may separate good from poor outcome. With a good outcome there was a persistent theta peak in the bursts, and the peak frequency rose over time. With a poor outcome the spectrum was flat, the theta only transient or the frequency falling. This requires full EEG and spectral analysis.Source: Forgacs 2020 (see “Burst suppression with theta in the bursts after cardiac arrest: a recovery marker? (Forgacs 2020)”)
  • One patient woke after 5 weeks of burst suppression. A 71-year-old with a short time to ROSC had burst suppression even after sedation had stopped, and met the criteria for a poor prognosis. The family declined withdrawal of treatment. He woke after about 5 weeks and returned to an active life.Source: Becker 2017 (see “Case report: 5 weeks of burst suppression after cardiac arrest, and the patient woke up (Becker 2017)”)
  • The shape of the bursts matters. Identical bursts that persist without improvement within 24 hours are, according to van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016, linked to a poor outcome. Burst suppression in which the bursts vary and come and go gradually is distinguished from this.Source: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 (see “Clinical example: young patient with prolonged burst suppression after cardiac arrest who woke with good brain function (shared case)”)
  • Prognosis should rest on several criteria over time. The shared case, a young patient with short anoxia time who woke with good brain function, fits the profile in Forgacs 2020. Withdrawal of treatment after cardiac arrest usually happens within 5–7 days. The literature may therefore be coloured by self-fulfilling prophecy. (interpretation based on the sources)Sources: shared case and Forgacs 2020 (see “Clinical example: young patient with prolonged burst suppression after cardiac arrest who woke with good brain function (shared case)”, “Burst suppression with theta in the bursts after cardiac arrest: a recovery marker? (Forgacs 2020)”)
  • The brain can show fast activity just before it stops. Two of four comatose patients had a brief increase in gamma activity when ventilator support was withdrawn. The study is small and says nothing about experience.Source: Xu 2023 (see “What happens in the brain when the circulation stops? (Xu 2023)”)

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

After cardiac arrest

Burst suppression with theta in the bursts after cardiac arrest: a recovery marker? (Forgacs 2020)

Three patients who awoke from coma 17–37 days after cardiac arrest and became functionally independent. In addition, a prospective cohort of 53 cardiac arrest patients, of whom 17 had burst suppression on the acute EEG.Source: Forgacs, Devinsky and Schiff. Ann Neurol 2020;87:618–632

  • The three woke late, long after the drugs had worn off. They had a short time to ROSC (10–20 minutes), therapeutic hypothermia to 33 °C and minimal cortical injury on CT or MRI. Two had preserved SSEP. Eye opening came 23–26 days and command following 37–67 days after all sedation had been stopped, far beyond the half-lives of the drugs. All had prominent burst suppression with a theta peak (about 4–7 Hz) in the bursts.
  • In the cohort, everyone with a good outcome had a persistent theta peak in the bursts. Of the 17 with burst suppression, 3 had a good outcome (CPC 2) and 14 a poor one (13 died). In the three with a good outcome, the peak frequency rose over time. In the 14 with a poor outcome, the spectra were flat or without lasting features (7), had only transient theta or falling frequency (5), or a shallow peak around 4 Hz (2).
  • Prolonged burst suppression may mean the neurons are alive but have impaired metabolism. This is the authors' hypothesis. They propose maintaining nutrition and fluids during the observation period and considering a time-limited trial of amantadine. Withdrawal of treatment after cardiac arrest usually occurs within 5–7 days, so the literature may be marked by self-fulfilling prophecy.
  • Caveats: three case reports and a small cohort, and no causal test. Analysis of burst content requires full EEG and spectral analysis. No conflicts of interest, NIH-funded.
Forgacs, Devinsky and Schiff. Ann Neurol 2020;87:618–632

What happens in the brain when the circulation stops? (Xu 2023)

“Surge of neurophysiological coupling and connectivity of gamma oscillations in the dying human brain”.Source: Xu, Mihaylova, Li et al. and Borjigin. PNAS 2023, doi 10.1073/pnas.2216268120

  • Two of four dying patients had a brief increase in gamma activity. There were four comatose patients whose ventilator support was withdrawn. In two of them gamma activity briefly increased, and the heart rate rose.
  • The brain can display organised, fast activity just before it stops functioning. This is why the finding is interesting.
  • Caveats: four patients, and only two showed the finding. The study says nothing about what the patients may have experienced.
Xu et al. PNAS 2023

Case report: 5 weeks of burst suppression after cardiac arrest, and the patient woke up (Becker 2017)

One patient, described in full text. The authors are from the same group as Forgacs 2020.Source: Becker, Schiff, Devinsky and colleagues. Epilepsy Behav Case Rep 2017;7:1–5

  • The patient: 71 years old, with coronary artery disease, bypass surgery, hypertension, diabetes and atrial fibrillation. Found pulseless at the bottom of a pool, shockable rhythm, pulse back within 10 minutes. CT showed minimal loss of grey–white differentiation. Treated with hypothermia.
  • Burst suppression continued without sedation. During rewarming he developed status epilepticus, followed by generalised periodic discharges. Burst suppression was induced with propofol on day 5, with pauses of up to 30 seconds and 1-second bursts of sharp theta and delta. Propofol and lorazepam had been weaned off by day 13, but burst suppression continued. Burst suppression and a discontinuous EEG alternated for about 5 weeks in total.
  • He met the criteria for a poor prognosis. GCS 3, absent brainstem reflexes, no corneal reflex 19 days after the arrest and no motor response after 7 days. The neurologists suggested withdrawing treatment, but the family declined.
  • Even so, he woke and returned to an active life. Spontaneous eye opening on day 37, following commands on day 50 and discharged to rehabilitation on day 79. He has mild lasting difficulties with attention, executive function, naming and short-term memory, but speaks in public and travels. The EEG was reactive early in the course.
  • Burst suppression may perhaps protect neurons. The authors' hypothesis is that burst suppression continuing without sedation may protect neurons close to cell death, and that hypothermia may extend this effect. Prognostic criteria from before hypothermia may therefore be less valid.
  • Caveats: one patient. Case reports with a good outcome are more readily published than the many with a poor outcome.
  • Interpretation based on the sources: the patient was not young, but had a short time to ROSC and little injury on CT, like the patients in Forgacs 2020. The bursts contained theta and were not described as identical.
Becker et al. Epilepsy Behav Case Rep 2017

Clinical example: young patient with prolonged burst suppression after cardiac arrest who woke up with good brain function (shared case)

Shared with the author of this app. Young patient with a short anoxic time after cardiac arrest. The EEG showed prolonged burst suppression without other criteria for a poor prognosis. The patient survived with good brain function.

  • The term “burst suppression” is not enough on its own – the shape of the bursts matters. Identical bursts that persist without improvement within 24 hours are, according to van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016, linked to a poor outcome. Burst suppression in which the bursts vary and come and go gradually is distinguished from this.Source: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 (Perfusion tab)
  • In this study everyone with identical bursts died without waking. Bursts were regarded as identical when the first 500 milliseconds were alike. Among comatose patients after cardiac arrest, 20 had identical bursts between 12 and 36 hours after the arrest, and all 20 died (specificity 100 %, sensitivity 40 %), but not every death was necessarily caused by the brain injury (see the caveats below). Of the 28 with burst suppression without identical bursts, 18 (64 %) had a good outcome.Source: Hofmeijer 2014
  • Identical bursts look different from bursts caused by propofol. With identical bursts the pauses were flat and the transitions abrupt. With propofol the bursts vary and come and go gradually. The pattern was not seen in any of 183 patients with anaesthesia-induced burst suppression. But most with identical bursts were receiving low-dose propofol at the same time, and some had no sedation at all.Source: Hofmeijer 2014
  • The study has caveats. A single centre, some died of causes other than the brain injury, and reactivity and brainstem reflexes were not recorded. The EEG was not used in treatment decisions.Source: Hofmeijer 2014
  • Those who woke late shared a profile. In Forgacs 2020 (above), the three who woke late and became independent had a short time to ROSC (10–20 minutes), little cortical injury on imaging and prominent burst suppression with theta in the bursts. One hypothesis is that the brain is then in a «protective down-regulated state».Sources: Forgacs 2020, Jegarl 2026
  • According to Gruenbaum, young, healthy people may tolerate burst suppression. Its meaning depends on the brain's metabolic reserve.Source: Gruenbaum 2026
  • Interpretation based on the sources: the case fits the profile in Forgacs 2020: young patient, short anoxic time and no other signs of severe injury. Whether the bursts contained theta is not known. The case illustrates that burst suppression alone should not be read as a poor prognosis, and that prognostication should rest on several criteria over time.
  • Caveats: a single case. Sedation, timing of the EEG and burst morphology are not described here.
Shared case

Key points

  • Unexpected suppression can be caused by haemorrhage. In a shared case, burst suppression disappeared after transfusion and the EEG became continuous again (a temporal association in one case, not a proven cause). Reduced oxygen delivery to the brain can produce the same pattern as deep anaesthesia.Source: shared case (see “Clinical example: burst suppression during haemorrhage that resolves after transfusion (shared case)”)
  • The cause should be looked for before the dose is simply reduced. Haemorrhage and anaemia, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia and hypnotic overdose can produce the same pattern. The EEG does not prove hypoperfusion, but unexpected suppression should prompt a search.Source: shared case (see “Clinical example: burst suppression during haemorrhage that resolves after transfusion (shared case)”)
  • A flat EEG is not the same as the intended burst suppression. In a neurosurgical patient where burst suppression was the goal, the EEG was completely flat when connected. The cause was herniation. An unexpectedly flat EEG should not be taken to mean the target has been reached.Source: shared case (see “Clinical example: burst suppression wanted, but the EEG was flat because of herniation (shared case)”)
  • Connect the EEG early to obtain a baseline. EEG from arrival, preferably before deep sedation, makes it possible to see when the pattern changes. Before titrating towards burst suppression, one should know that the brain can produce bursts. The expert panel recommends that processed EEG be started as early as possible in patients who need deep sedation. (interpretation based on the sources)Sources: shared case, Rasulo 2023 (see “Clinical example: burst suppression wanted, but the EEG was flat because of herniation (shared case)”)

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

Clinical examples

Clinical example: burst suppression during bleeding that resolves after transfusion (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed. It is described from two screenshots of a frontal EEG monitor taken about 20 minutes apart. The screenshots are not reproduced here.

  • During the bleeding, the EEG moved towards suppression. PSI was first around 35–40 and then fell to 10. The suppression ratio (SR) was 44%, EMG 0% and artefacts 0%, and the spectral edge frequency (SEF) was not calculated. In the spectrogram, power lay mostly below about 10–12 Hz without a clear alpha band, followed by increasingly frequent suppression periods in both hemispheres. The raw EEG was almost flat and low-amplitude. Electrode impedances were acceptable.
  • After transfusion, the EEG became continuous again. The suppression periods became shorter and disappeared. PSI was 44, SR 0% and SEF 15.8 Hz on the left and 16.4 Hz on the right. The raw EEG showed high-amplitude slow waves with faster activity superimposed, and the spectrogram showed power from slow-delta up to about 15 Hz.
  • Too little oxygen to the brain can look like deep anaesthesia on the EEG. During the bleeding, power shifted to lower frequencies, then came power loss and then burst suppression. Reduced cerebral oxygen delivery (CDO₂) can produce this pattern, and anaemic patients tolerate falls in blood flow less well.Source: Guay 2025
  • Bleeding hits oxygen delivery in two ways. CDO₂ depends on blood flow, haemoglobin and saturation. Bleeding can lower both blood pressure and haemoglobin, and transfusion can improve both. In Georgii 2022, BSR fell to 0 in 24 of 44 episodes when MAP was raised to the patient’s baseline.Sources: Guay 2025, Georgii 2022
  • The screenshots do not show what mattered most. We do not know blood pressure, haemoglobin, temperature, the patient’s age or whether anaesthetic doses were changed. It therefore cannot be determined whether blood pressure, haemoglobin or both mattered most, or whether other factors contributed. Hypothermia, hypoglycaemia and hypnotic overdose can produce the same pattern.Sources: Patel et al. 2025, Guay 2025
  • Caveats: a single case without measurement of CBF, NIRS or Doppler. The point is not that the EEG «proves» hypoperfusion, but that unexpected suppression should prompt a search for the cause, including bleeding and anaemia, before the dose is simply reduced.
Own clinical example; Guay 2025, Georgii 2022, Patel et al. 2025

Clinical example: burst suppression was the goal, but the EEG was flat because of herniation (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed, and it is described from verbal information.

  • The course: a neurosurgical patient was transferred from another hospital, with no complications expected. The goal was burst suppression. When the EEG was connected, it was completely flat, and this turned out to be due to herniation.
  • Without a baseline, a flat EEG is hard to interpret. When the EEG is connected only after the patient is deeply sedated, there is nothing to compare with. A flat EEG may then be due to the drugs, but also to a brain that has stopped functioning.
  • Patterns persisting without sedation should be investigated as primary neurological disease. Electrocerebral inactivity is defined as 2 µV or lower. The suppression in burst suppression is below 10 µV.Source: Guay 2025
  • The spectrogram can give early warning of herniation. In two patients with herniation, increased low-frequency power and asymmetry in the spectrogram appeared roughly an hour before clinical deterioration.Source: Alsallom 2022
  • Start processed EEG early in deep sedation. It is recommended to start as early as possible and monitor continuously in patients who need deep sedation. Rasulo 2023 recommends that burst suppression only be used to control raised intracranial pressure, although refractory status epilepticus is an exception in practice (see the Intensive care tab). Whether earlier EEG would have changed the course for this patient, one case cannot say.Source: Rasulo 2023
  • What it may mean in practice (interpretation based on the sources): EEG from arrival, preferably before deep sedation, gives a baseline and makes it possible to see when the pattern changes. If burst suppression is the goal, you should know that the brain can produce bursts before titrating towards it. An unexpectedly flat EEG should not be read as the goal having been reached.
  • Caveats: one case without screenshots. The diagnosis, drugs and time course are not known. Frontal EEG sees only part of the cortex.
Shared clinical example Guay 2025, Rasulo 2023, Alsallom 2022

Image quiz: spectrogram and raw EEG

Twenty-one drawn images based on clinical examples and source descriptions (Purdon 2015, Akeju 2014, García 2021, Hight 2020, Cornelissen 2015/2018). Spectrogram: time along x (about 15 minutes), frequency 0–40 Hz along y, red = high power. None of the images are patient recordings. The images show no index numbers: indices are algorithms with many sources of error, and it is the raw EEG and spectrogram that should be interpreted.

What the studies show

  • Sevoflurane, burst suppression and delirium: Markus et al. 2026 found that sevoflurane produced substantially more delirium than propofol (44 versus 30%, adjusted OR 3.27), and that burst suppression was associated with delirium only under sevoflurane. Koch et al. 2023, from the same group and with four times as many patients, found no significant difference between sevoflurane and propofol (OR 1.32, 0.77 to 2.26) and pointed instead to desflurane. Both are single-centre and without randomisation of the agent.
